As someone who could never get into the original Deus Ex/Thief series for their lack of guidance, I find myself surprised how Deus Ex: HR and Director's Cut got me into the "immersive sim" genre. I am also shocked how a "photorealistic" modern game can stay true to the genre.
Unlike the original--which was marred by terrible gunplay and RPG mechanics, but redeemed by its chaotic, player-driven shenanigans like the Postal series--Human Revolution is a great game to play. You don't need to play the game twice (or have a guide) to play it correctly.
Is it the best in the series? Perhaps, but it's the first I can easily recommend in spite of its missing qualities of the original. The real beauty of HR is not whether or not it's a true "Deus Ex" game; it's the fact that immersive sims can still be made with all the fluidity of the player's consequences and all the accessibility of modern games.
I am fortunate to have bought HR before it was taken down from Steam, and I have played both games to completion recently with 18 hours in the original and 16 hours for the DC (w/ commentary).
Here are the many changes I have found:
- Performance is slightly WORSE on DC than the original. The new textures (and omission of the filter) caused me to lower the quality slightly as well as suffer many missing texture issues. (Textures with flat colors like neon-green shoes.) For comparison, I never suffered any graphical issues in the original.
- You seem to have more ammo in DC. I always played non-lethal as I saved up for bosses, but I noticed my inventory was often packed with 150 to 200 ammo for three guns. This could be because they added in more weapons to the game. (And yet I had fewer gas-grenades.)
-Boss fights are significantly better for hacker-playstyles with stealth being an option.
-Contextual dev commentary on the map that can be interrupted in-game or it may prevent you to progress.
-You can no longer get the Missing Link for the original if you own it. (Adds maybe 3 - 4 hours of padding.)
-Energy cells recharge to two cells below "Give me Deus Ex" difficulty.
The DC offers a significant change in quality, sometimes for the worse, but I think if you want the "defintiive" experience you will want DC. The commentary is exceptionally helpful for added details to explain the subtler parts of the narrative.
The core idea behind not only immersive sims but of Deus Ex goes back to the Latin phrase, "Deus Ex Machina." The player is the driving force that brings about change in guiding the protagonist; s/he makes choices for how to resolve obstacles with violence or avoiding it.
HR mostly abides by that philosophy save for the forced boss-fights and choices where you choose between two options (or neither). The latter aspect can be excused for dramatic tension but the former goes against Deus Ex. Even if you used non-lethal means it will be a fatal blow. Aside from that issue, which is addressed in the DC, the consequences found in older Deus Ex games are here.
Ironically, although this modern take is more realistic with its gameplay, graphics and storytelling, the gameplay feels more "gamey" than the original. You won't be making ladders from trip-mines like the original, but there are changes made that I don't think was for the better.
For starters, the XP system. It is too rewarding for non-lethal, hacker playstyles and if you want to make the game more entertaining than a standard FPS it's also better to play with discretion. Stealth is optimal for all playstyles, and the third-person cover system makes it satisfying while being simplified from peaking around corners. Perhaps if non-lethal ammo was more scarce I would be fine with how non-lethal builds are rewarded but you will hoard ammo if you ration it carefully.
Second, which ties into the first, there always seems to be an optimal solution. "Social Boss fights", air-vents and other deviations always seem structured to give you the best reward if you follow a specific path. If the XP system wasn't an huge influence for getting augmentations, I could ignore it rather than feeling like I made a mistake. It's a greater problem if you want the replay value of the original where it had items and skill-points based on exploration.
Lastly, which is also a criticism of the story, the game is too linear of a progression. The HUBs are nice distractions to offer more non-linear options for every playthrough, but my favorite parts of the game are the missions you do outside of the HUB. If the progression was designed for choosing  various missions in whatever order the player desires like in Shadowrun Dragonfall, then we would have a greater value for replaybility. It would be demanding to pull off but it's something that would have made HR vastly superior to the original.
These blemishes on an otherwise flawless recreation of a forgotten style of game doesn't make HR terrible. They are sources for improvement now that there is a foundation to make games in a similar vein, and where the series can improve from here.
When it comes to the story I am of two minds about HR.
On the one hand, the plot itself feels too straightforward for a conspiracy story. Clues for the next objective can be made spontaneously and without player involvement, which is somewhat the fault of designing a game with a linear mission progression. (Perhaps if it was an open-ended route of missions you could uncover different clues or facts that lead to the same conclusion. It could still be bottlenecked to the truth but the process would be more rewarding.) For what the game offers, there is still the mystique of uncovering the truth but it's without the player's involvement.
It would also help the plot if the "villains" were not confused with the bosses because they are also pawns, and depending on who you wish to side with it will influence who you consider to be the villain(s). The way antagonists in this game are handled is rather commendable.
What I was surprised about the most was how the theme of transhumanism is handled. It is treated so carefully it actually becomes a part of the gameplay that won't click until you finish the game. Neuropozyne addiction, industrialism on augmentations for working classes, economic influences on augmentation and many other aspects offer a thoughtful discussion about the matter without being preachy. The resistance against augmentation wasn't as ignorant as I first thought it was.
In fact, when it comes to the game's subtext about "humanity", I didn't catch how it tied into the core gameplay itself until I chose my ending with Hugh Darrow.
"How many times, in the call of duty, did I almost fall in the trap of making shortcuts using the abilities or resources at my hand? I resisted because I valued human lives [...] [U ]sing technology to become something more than we are risks losing our ability to love, to aspire and to make moral choices. The very things that make us human; it also risks giving some men the power to make men how they choose to regard human dignity."
These words make more sense of the player's role if you change "to love, to aspire" to "to empathize, to think through obstacles." Unlike the original where the player is a deus ex machina, the player of HR is the hominum ex machina for Jenson. To what end you think is best for humanity, of how you handle fighting other men and of how humanity should progress are questions the game lets you ponder for yourself and to make your own conclusions.
I've always wondered if a game could tell a story solely by player's actions with open environments. Fallout New Vegas proved it could be done in mass; HR proved it could be done with thematic purpose enclosed.

The dev team thought of everything.
Other reviews can praise this game's stealth, combat, upgrades, art, characters, and story, I just want to show my appreciation for the sheer amount of player choice in this game. Sometimes I was flabbergasted after a mission, going back through the level and realizing just how impressive its design was in terms of making sure that you can get through it ANY way you want to. Pacifict? Check. Terminator? Check. Hacker? Scavenger? Little-of-everything? All of the above. I loved it.
And more than just the amount of choice was the implementation. I've said in other reviews that what I want in a game is one where the challenge comes from fighting the bad guys, not from fighting the controls. 99% of everything I tried in this game was a fair challenge. No shoddy, sloppy work. I push the button; thing happens the way it's supposed to. And there were plenty of times when I had a nutty idea and thought, 'Can I do that?' Yes I could. Punch civilians in the head! Throw turrets into the sea! Make modern art with piles of unconscious enemies! Steal EVERYTHING!
My only real complaint was with the implanted DLC. While I did grow to enjoy it by the end, (especially Quinn), at times it felt uneccesary and shoehorned in, and there were parts when the writing was bizarrely sexist. Oh well. Once I got off the boat it was back to the main game and everything was fine again.
Overall, DXHR is going in my favorites list. I look forward to New Game+. The D-Row Ballers won't know what hit 'em.
P.S. Major congrats to Adam Jensen's voice actor. The Neo-esque gravelly growl could have easily been monotone and emotionless, but he managed to put a ton of subtle personality into the performance. Often through taking the lines as read, and knowing exactly which words to punch emphasis into. Kudos!

8BitMMO, created by Robby Zinchak aka RobbyZ is a old school styled Free Roam Rpg. 8BitMMO is a game that takes inspiration from many games such as Minecraft, Legend of Zelda, and even Mario. In 8BitMMO you start off waking up in a man's house who is completely aware that he is in a video game by breaking the 4th wall. He sends you off to complete quests in order to just get you out of his house, he references that he has done this multiple times and that strangers waking up in his house has become a common problem for him. This snarky dialogue made me enjoy my first 10 minutes of the game, as it reminded me of dialogue coming from games like Saints Row. I love it when games make fun of the fact that it is a game. Unfortunately after the tutorial this dialogue seemed to cease and enjoyment of my gameplay experience began to decrease more and more. The combat in 8BitMMO is simple enough to play with one hand, with occasionaly reaching for your mouse. Only having the WASD keys for movement and the space bar for attacking made hunting quests and fighting off enemies a bore after the tutorial. There is also another element that makes 8BitMMO a little more entertaining; the ability to build. You are able to build a houses and environments like a top down Minecraft or Terraria. The building can become tedious with blocks stacking not the way you want them to and having a lack of tools to do anything truly spectacular. Although I didnt enjoy this feature, I did see many interesting and cool user created homes and even areas that put the building and combat to good use. The music is probably what I enjoyed most from 8BitMMO, it had beats that went along with the art direction and it had the convenient feature to skip the current song as if i was using Pandora radio. The game does have a leveling system like most other MMO's that encourage you to rank up in order to get certain items or get to certain areas. I have to completely honest and say that I didnt have a great time with 8BitMMO. It is free on Steam and does offer microtransactions, BUT doesnt flash them around begging for money. The game might be fun with a few friends looking to make your own quests and adventures but playing alone is just plain boring.
Overall:
8BitMMO has a lot of great ideas that just dont work out yet. After sometime and update the game can be great. The music fits in with the world perfectly and the combat is a little bland. In my opinion I would like to see RobbyZ create either more content for this game or make more games with the same amount of snark and wit that the tutorial of this game had. I loved the original dialogue and was set to play a game that knew how to make fun of its self but instead, I got a bland and lifeless world that could and should be improved dramatically. And could be alot of fun if your bored with nothing new to play or if you find a group to play with.(Roleplaying could be fun in this game)
Verdict:
7.0
Worth a try.(hey its free!)

It's really a tricky one this, there are both positives and negatives, but the latter isn't related to the game which as always, is a must buy if you don't own it in any other form. If that's all you need to know, don't read on, buy it and i'll focus the rest of the review on what could have been.
A turn based strategy offering, Colonization is a timeless classic that has immense replay value and an excellent soundtrack to boot. If a turn based strategy game is your thing, you cannot be disappointed, it's impossible.
However, if you did already own it in another form, whether DOS, Amiga or other, what reasons are there to buy here, other than to have it in your library? I cannot honestly see any other reason.
The files and structure are identical to those that have been freely available (rightly or wrongly, it's always a point of debate) as 'Abandonware' for many years now. To run those files, you would have needed DOSBox which has handily been included as part of this package. That may in fact be a positive, Colonization in your Steam library, with one click access to DOSBox and no need to mount a path or create a config file. Some mention of DOSBox on the store page would have been helpful though, given other reviews now appearing about the release.
But it could have been so much more, more than what is offered which is essentially old files bundled together by someone that has bought the rights and is selling them at a price, albeit very reasonable. It's just a case of doing very little work and putting it for release on Steam.
What about achievements? Imagine 'Achievement Unlocked: Armed Natives & Subsequently Beheaded'. What about visually improving the look of the game itself? Of course, there is a certain romance about playing an older game and the way it looked all of those years ago but it can work, look at Leisure Suit Larry & Secret Of Monkey Island, there is a place for a visually enhanced version of an older title. Such a missed opportunity in my opinion, Colonization: Special Edition* could have been something to take an even bigger pride of place in the collection.
*And no, 'Civilization IV: Colonization' isn't it......

For those who saw this and thought they could re-buy a classic marvel, adjusted to work on modern PCs and even Linux: no. They could have at least mentioned it on the store page.

This is the classic game you all remember, unchanged in any way as far as I can tell.  For those new to Colonization, you'll find this to be a solid Sid Meier strategy game that deviates from the strict formula of the Civilization series.  If retro games aren't your thing, this game was also remade using the Civ 4 engine.
The gameplay focuses on building up an economic empire in the New World, with your primary source of income coming from shipping valuable goods back to Europe to sell.  Your eventual goal is to create a self-sufficient nation and declare independence from from your parent country back in Europe.  Along the way, you'll have to compete with other European powers settling the New World, as well as increasingly troublesome (but wealthy!) natives.
Starting off, the game is quite forgiving.  The other European powers are generally more focused on building their own empires than on wiping you out, but can and
cause you trouble later.  Similarly, the Native Americans all start off friendly toward you and even give you free stuff, but their attitude will gradually sour toward you, even if you just leave them alone.  This will sound cold and heartless, but in the end, genocide is the best solution, as they
harass you without end otherwise.  The huge amounts of treasure you'll get from looting Indian villages is just a bonus.
As I said above, the gameplay deviates quite a bit from the standard Civ fomula.  There are a lot more resources, for one thing: 16 material goods, as well as a few immaterial resources, like liberty bells (increases rebel sentiment, which gives bonuses to production, and attracts Founding Fathers) and crosses (attracts immigrants).  Of the material goods, most are meant solely for selling, but the rest are vital for running your colonies.  I'll explain this a bit more indepth further down.
Another difference between this and Civ is that Population = Units.  Aside from ships, wagons, and artillery, all your units are colonists that can be given different equipment to create different units.  Each colonist can be trained in one profession, giving them a bonus to performing that job (usually, increasing resource yields).  When asigning a colonist to work a tile around your colony, they can only gather one resource at a time, but you won't usually need more than one of any type of gatherer except for farmers.  You can also asign colonists to work the buildings inside your colony.  For example, the weaver's house converts cotton into cloth.
Colonists are also your units.  Give them tools to turn them into a Pioneer so they can build roads, clear forests, and plow fields.  Give them horses to turn them into a Scout, which moves faster, sees farther, can interact with native villages, and gets better results from lost cities.  Give them muskets to turn them into Soldiers, your most basic and most common military unit, or equip a Soldier with horses to make them a stronger and faster Dragoon.  Also of note is that
; there's no "settler" type unit like in Civ.
As far as ships go, most of them are used for hauling loot and trading.  Of special mention, though, is the Privateer.  A Privateer's ownership is invisible except to the player that owns it.  This means that Privateers can attack other players even when you are at peace with them, but at the same time your Privateers are also fair game to any Frigates in the area.  Hurray for piracy!
Another difference from Civ is that there is no research or tech tree.  The closest analogue would be the Founding Fathers, which confer various bonuses, including things like unlocking buildings, and are earned with liberty bells.  Since liberty bells also increase the desire for independence among your colonists (which will eventually net you bonuses to resource production), you'll want lots of them anyway.
If you want a strong and self-suficient colony, there are a few things you absolutely need:
OCEAN ACCESS:  Since a large part of the game revolves around trade, you absolutely need a way to load a ship up with goods.  Landlocked colonies aren't impossible, as you can use wagons to transport goods to a colony with a port, but I'd reccomend beginners stick with seaside colonies at first.
FOOD:  Your colonists need to eat.  Shipping food to a perpetually starving colony is no fun and better avoided altogether.  Fortunately, food is pretty easy to get as long as you're not settling in the arctic.  Food can also be converted into horses, which is important for a strong military.  You need at least 2 horses in a colony and then they'll breed automatically.
LUMBER:  Lumber is converted into hammers by a carpenter.  This is how you build buildings in your colonies.  You can buy buildings with gold, but that quickly gets expensive.  You can also ship lumber in from another colony, but this can be a pain.  Just make sure to keep one forest tile next to your colony, as you shouldn't need more than one lumberjack.
ORE:  Ore is converted into tools, which are used by Pioneers for terraforming.  20 tools are consumed for every terraforming job.  Also, all but the most basic buildings will also require tools to build.  As such, you'll need to have a steady supply of tools.  And once you're done terraforming and building buildings, tools can be turned into muskets.
Aside from the above, everything else is optional.  You don't need sugar, or furs, or cotton, or tobacco.  These will help you make some cash, but they're largely interchangeable with one another.
Some last tips:  Remember, the natives are not your friends!  Or, at least, they won't be for very long.  Whatever you do, DO NOT give them horses or muskets.  You can make a
of quick cash by trading with the natives early on, but they'll quickly wise up that you're scamming them.  You can prevent tax hikes by reenacting the Boston Tea Party, which will increase rebel sentiment in that colony, but also makes you unable to trade that resource in Europe anymore.  Lastly, make sure you're ready for a war of apocalyptic proportions before declaring independence.  I'm not kidding.
This game was perhaps my favorite growing up, and while it's aged a bit (really missing edge-scrolling and right-click-to-move), it's still a very solid game, and I'd heartily reccomend it to anyone interested in the genre.

This game has one of the most akward layouts from tech trees to system management that I have ever played with and I have played with a lot of them.
For example one of the most important things to have a chance to survive at all is increase fleet size. The techs for it are scattered all over the place. Meanwhile your so zoomed in that it becomes a pain to just glance over nearby techs you might want to be able to see so you end up wandering around in the zoomed in mode. Some might not care but to me its just tedious and annoying. They need to get rid of the useless and crappy story descricptive nonsense for each tech and make the actually techs easier to read. Then you get to the system management ... you only have 1 building queve for the entire solor system whether you have 1 planet or 6. You can only make one thing per solor system. I got this game with the DLC while they were on sale for $7. I thought it looked like a fairly entertaining, outer space turn-based strategy, and honestly wasn't expecting much after looking through the negative reviews. Then, I spent an hour just reading the applied science and military branches of the tech tree in game. And I don't normally care about such detail in a game.
Don't listen to the bad reviews. If you like space stuff, strategy and/or turn-based games, or Civilization-style games, you will enjoy Endless Space tremendously. It is a beautiful, surprisingly humorous, addictive, and intense masterpiece. The graphics are very playable even on the lowest settings, but look phenomenal if you can run them at their highest. The universe is interesting and pulls you in. The game is deep, and manages to be very balanced while also keeping every race unique as far as their strengths and weaknesses.
The attacking side in battle always starts with a better firing position, forcing the defenderer to take sustained fire for a little while before being able to shoot back at maximum efficacy. That was one thing I didn't like. In fact, the combat system seems bad at first. I wish that players had more direct control over their ships. The combat is nevertheless quite fun once you get used to it, because it has the oppossing sides choose cards to play at each phase, and there is basically a time limit. It has that inexplicable joy that card games like Pokemon have. Due to the factions being well-blanced, the slightest difference can decide the outcome of a battle. As in real life, it is only "safe" to attack when you have a clear advantage.
Overall, an amazing game for its genre and worth the price even if you don't get it on sale, in my opinion.

Deus Ex:Human Revolution isn't a terrible game.  It has a lot of terrible things about it like the level design, the story, the antagonists, an absolutely terrible DLC, etc.  Side quests, the aesthetic, some interesting world building, and more casual gameplay really save this game though.
The story is a prime example of a good concept gone wrong.
INCOMING SPOILERS:
The Illuminati plot for this game is actually pretty interesting.  They control the augmented population via Neuropozyne manufacturing and distribution.  Neuropozyne is a drug that stops the natural bodies of augmented people from rejecting their augmentations.  Without the drug, they experience extreme pain and potential death.  Their control over augmented people becomes threatened when David Sarif develops a way to potentially stop augmentation rejection using his Adam Jensen's (Protagonist, head of security at Sarif Industries) DNA (He was genetically experimented on as an infant by White Helix who is a subsidary of Versalife owned by Bob Page).  So they attack the labs, nearly kill Jensen, and kidnap the scientists to force them to develop a new biochip that will give the Illuminati direct control over augmentations.  Adam Jensen uncovers all of this after being extensively augmented by his boss.
Sounds pretty great doesn't it?  I think so too.  As I mentioned earlier though, it's executed horribly.
"Okay Zeke I saved your life at the factory, you're going to help me out right?"
"AYO ESSAY I PAY MY DEBTS THIS IS WHAT YOU GET."
"Zeke this is just a bunch of random codes for keypads that I could easily hack the next mission.  Aren't you going to open up some interesting side plot that will further uncover the conspiracy?  I didn't spare your life because I liked you, give me something interesting."
"YO MY DEBT IS PAID ESSAY HOMBRE SENOR GET OUT OF HERE AUG."
"Jensen sneak into gang territory and disable this device."
"Wait there's a helipad right next to the device I need to disable, why can't you drop me off there?"
"Jensen you dense ♥♥♥♥ we need to progress the plot at a natural pace, stop using your brain."
"Jensen I am boss number 1, I will stop you"
"I have defeated you boss number 1, tell me your secrets because I know nothing and the plot cannot progress without you spoon feeding me information."
"Oh no Jensen you have defeated me, I will now tell you the location of our base of operations despite being on deaths door so the plot can progress."
"Darrow why did you modify the chip to make every augmented person go crazy?"
"I AM THE SUPREME MORAL AUTHORITY, THE ONLY WAY I CAN PROVE MY POINT AND REVEAL THE ILLUMINATI TO THE WORLD IS BY CAUSING THE DEATHS OF MILLIONS OF INNOCENTS."
"You couldn't just make everyone raise their right hand, block out their eyesight, make them feel a jolt of pain, or something less extreme than killing millions?
"SUPREME MORAL AUTHORITY!"
This is just a few pieces of♥♥♥♥♥♥in the turd pie, but I think you get the point.  The execution of the plot is just bad and only gets worse as you go on.
Now I'm going to shorten all my complaints/praises into one small paragraph because the story only thing worth caring about in this game:
Level design is very linear and boring.  Nothing really interesting to discover in Hubs or Levels.  Bosses are terrible.  Because these things are terrible, gameplay being casualized is a good thing.  Let's me blast through levels real fast.  World building is surprisingly good despite the horrible main story writing.  Side quests are mostly interesting.  Art design is very good, yet strays very far from the original Deus Ex.  World seems more technologically advanced than Deus Ex's because of how clean and lovely everything looks.  The DLC takes the worst parts of the game (linear levels, storytelling, bosses) and crams it all into a short 2-3 hour DLC.  Adam Jensen is stripped of all his augmentations for the beginning of the DLC and you need to upgrade EVERYTHING again.  Makes the DLC not only boring, but sometimes very SLOW to go through.

Considering this game was made by one guy with a little help on creating maps, a composer for the soundtrack, and play-testers, the fact that it's a great game is saying something.
The story is an uncomplicated, yet intriguing little tale. You are tried for a crime (you pick) that you are either guilty or not guilty of committing. (This determines your alignment and sets up some starting plot points in the game.) You are then dumped on an island penal colony full of criminals and monsters, but as you visit Lukatt's many locales you begin to uncover a deeper mystery as you seek to escape its shores and back to civilization.
To accomplish this goal you recruit other felons to your side, but it turns out there are some who join your band that have also been railroaded by corrupt officials. Each unique character has their own backstory that you learn if you level him/her up and talk to them once in awhile. Fair warning though: anyone offended by extensive homoerotic banter and lots of exposed pixel flesh (mostly male but female too) might be put off by this game. If you're bothered by that I suggest playing your main as a female.
I didn't understand the combat system at first and why I was getting beaten so badly, but it turns out that dishing out multiple hits in a turn is not a skill but a core combat mechanic (called "risk") modified by stats, group alignment dynamics, and chance. It lends a certain level of unpredictability to a fight, but managing it is how you survive. That keeps you on your toes during a fight as it can be easy to keep attacking, fumble a move, and leave an opening in your defense because you didn't opt for the safe action (that ends your turn) and blew your risk stack.
Replay value is good. There's too many locations to explore in one play-through. It's also possible to miss unique NPCs (and thus miss their backstory as well as any achievements that involve them), either by never finding them or by recruiting a NPC that blocks the inclusion of another NPC in your band. Also, any character template you create in the game menu can show up in your game as a random, recruitable NPC -- which is kind of cool if you want to take time making a bunch more than the ones the game start with.
The game pokes a bit of gleeful fun with common tropes of the male-catered fantasy setting. For instance, the ever popular high-stat chainmail bikini is replaced by a leather chest harness that is only slightly less protective than full plate armor. There are also similar bits of highly protective male undergarments to discover.
Could the game be better? Sure. You could suggest any number of things that would be nice improvements, but as a one-person job it does what it sets out to do very well. Overall the game keeps a tight focus on exploration and combat with a little on the side for puzzle-solving and campsite management and making or recovering more powerful weapons.
Well worth the full price to support an indie dev who crafted this little gem with obvious love for the genre.

There's some good things and bad things about this game, but the good outweighs the bad. I bought this completely on a whim.
Some of the things that I enjoy:
The character statistics matrix is an interesting change from standard character stats.
Naked orcs. That alone makes the purchase worthwhile.
Risk Mechanic. This is really the core feature of the combat system and it works well. You can take one or (usually) two actions safely per combat turn, but more than that and you run the risk of leaving yourself wide open.
Game content. I've put in about 15 hours so far and I've just scratched the surface of available areas.
Game lore. There's not a whole ton of it, what what I have found so far is pretty interesting. I'm going to be stealing some of the concepts for tabletop games - they're really that good.
You can start out as a convicted bugger! There's other crimes of course, but I found that amusing.
It's personal taste, but I generally don't enjoy pixelated graphics. These work well enough though, and things are generally identifiable.
There's a few annoying issues, though:
The isometric view works, kind of. I find it difficult to understand where walls are sometimes because visually it's just difficult.
Path finding doesn't always work well. Sometimes creatures will get stuck in corners. I think it's a function of the area that is searched when looking for a valid path to a destination - if that were increased it might help.
Certain aspects of the game are not explained very well. In particular, it took me several hours to really understand what a combat "turn" really meant and how Risk factored into it. I'm still trying to figure out how to best increase my strongold's capabilities. I have no idea what many item abilities do. Some simple mouse-over information, or an in-game glossary, would be extremely helpful. There's game tips shown on loading screens, but the loading screens are gone so quickly I never have time to read them!
Aside from the Risk mechanic, combat isn't particularly engaging. Throw a tank up front, backed up by a ranged guy or two, and an additional melee combat guy. Rinse, repeat, hope you outlast the baddies. There's also no zones of control - you can block a doorway, but your characters will happily allow an enemy to say, "'scuse me, I'm on my way to stab your mages" as they slip by.
Overall, 15 hours in, I'm still enjoying the game. It was obviously crafted with love, a lot of thought went into the world, and from what I understand, it's a one-orc effort on the development side. It has its blemishes but the overall experience is will worth the time.
Recommended for people who enjoy turn-based combat RPGs with some lore that matters, and a touch of party and town management thrown in.

So, having completed the game, an update!
First the bad, because I'd like to end on a good note:
The simplistic combat model does get tedious, and is rarely challenging. Many of the later areas in the game don't seem to serve any purpose other than filling out the map. In theory, you can get some special dialogue in a few places if you have the right person in your party, but I never really saw any hints as to who should go where, so you're left to guess.
Character interaction in your party is also lacking. You can level up and talk to people and eventually get them to tell you a little bit about themselves, and that's cool, and you get this token item, but they don't seem to do anything (or I missed it somehow).
The story line is also thin. The game started out with some very promising bits of lore dropped here and there, and I was very excited for more, but it just didn't really appear - not in the amount and depth that I expected, much less wanted.
Some of the "puzzles" in the game will lead you straight to the guide, or drinking (I recommend drinking AND the guide), as there's often no real hints at all as to what you're supposed to do, or they're "cleverly hidden."
Party building also seems to have little real value. You're required to have a certain number of people in your group at one point, but there's no real incentive to have them in your party unless you need to level them up for better camp capacity.
After a while, the game starts to feel more like a chore.
And perhaps the greatest crime of them all: You never get a chance to face your accusers. I was thrown in prison - and I didn't even do it! - where is my justice?! )o:
Overall, a bit of a letdown. There's so much potential here, and the game was obviously crafted with love, so I can't give it a negative rating.
There IS some cool stuff here, and there is a touch of the unexpected, and the early game in particular gives a wonderful sense of exploration and a list of questions that need to be answered. Some of the areas, especially a few of the smaller ones, have some great ways of telling a story without overloading you with exposition.
I hope the developer makes another game. There's a great vision, it just needs some help with the execution. There's a fantastic world to explore, but we need to be able to experience it.

If you take one thing from this review, let it be this: the configurable nature of the Steam Controller all but guarantees you will find a way to use it that you will be comfortable with. I bought one controller at launch with the Rocket League bundle and liked it so much I got another so I could indoctrinate my friends on the wonder that is the Steam Controller.
The grips on the handles alone make this a more versatile controller than any you've used before. No longer do you have to play "claw" if you want to run or jump while you maneuver the camera-- this makes it a superior choice for Dark Souls or Rocket League, both of which I have used this controller with, to great success. The right touchpad/pseudo analog stick has excellent haptic feedback and adequately simulates both a joystick and a mouse. I've found the "mouse-like joystick" configuration works great for third-person games, as the camera swings around fluidly exactly where I want it. It took a bit of practice, but now it's so much better than the old way of waiting for the camera to creak around with a normal right analog stick. With acceleration, it only takes a moment to adjust the camera so you can put your thumb back on the face buttons-- great for hectic fights in Dark Souls.
Whenever you play a game with the Steam Controller, the overlay is automatically in Big Picture mode, meaning that when you press the center Steam button it brings up a controller-friendly overlay that doesn't require you to switch to the mouse to navigate. Typing with the Steam controller is about as fast as it gets with a controller, as the twin touchpads let you type out messages like two halves of a keyboard. It also lets you configure controls right from the overlay, meaning you don't have to exit the game and you're not totally screwed if the game itself doesn't allow custom controller button bindings.
If you ever plan on using this controller for games that involve driving, you'll be happy to hear this-- the triggers are dual-stage and very responsive. I haven't used a controller with such satisfying shoulder buttons since the GameCube. Additionally, with the handle grips I can drift and adjust the camera simultaneously, giving me an edge and keeping me out of trouble on the track.
One of my personal favorite things about the controller is the fact that the d-pad is also another touchpad, so in theory you have three analog sticks. You can configure the touchpad to do something different when it's touched than when it's pressed, leading to some very interesting possibilities. I haven't encountered a game where I quite needed that many buttons for actions, but it's something to consider. The touch d-pad comes at the cost at not being ideal for 2D fighting games, but Dragon Ball Xenoverse plays just fine with it. I should mention that this controller is adequately sized even for giant hands like mine, so even a frantic game like Xenoverse doesn't have my hands cramping as bad as they would on a smaller controller.
All in all, if you're not loyal to a particular build of controller, if you're looking to step up your game or you're looking for something new, the Steam Controller has got you covered. The firmware updates keep adding more and more features, so this is an investment that will grow in value over time. Here's a handy tip: if you start a non-Steam game using the Steam client, you'll be able to use the Steam Controller in that game (although I believe in most games it's recognized as an Xbox controller).

Presented in surprisingly effective understated retro art and inspired from classic adventure games but nevertheless completely unique and incomparable to any prior title. Minimal interactions are not about solving puzzles or managing inventory. Players mostly decide in which order they want to let events unfold.
The first free episode is in many ways not representative of the rest of the game as subsequent chapters play substantially differently. They are considerably longer and more complex but they all retain the same vibe and common connections. They also offer more readily apparent branching potential.
All four episodes are brilliantly unique, touching, and foster a wide range of emotions. The 2nd chapter is probably the most imaginative of the lot and resonated deeply with me. The 3rd episode in particular resurfaced some heartfelt anger during the final confrontation, something the others didn't, though it also felt less intuitive and perhaps too academic. The final chapter gracefully ties all others together and opens up to grander events taking place in the same time period.
The Connections room is a very interesting concept. This special room you may optionally visit in between episodes clearly shows the existence of alternate paths but gives no indication as to what they might be or how to achieve them.
Be prepared for lots of reading. You can't rush this game, but it is also not very long.

I'm going to start off by saying this is not a review. This Is a suggestion that you try to find a demo or some way to play the game before you buy it. I have not played this game nearly enough to review it, This could be a really good game, There are certainly solid design ideas and game mechanics but... I'm really doubting that I'll be able to get into it.
Allow me to explain. In a game like civ 5, my experience has been that while there is strategic depth to be had, its not forced on you. I was able to pick up the concepts of civ 5 fairly quick, and I didn't have the feeling that I needed to understand everything to play the game. This game was precisely the opposite.
I was so completely overwhelmed in the tutorial by the sheer number of screens, boxes, information tabs, icons, phases, etc, that I quit the game out of frustration because I felt like I was retaining almost none of the information dumped upon me. Add to that the fact that almost every tab background was the same semi-transparent grey box making them all look fairly similar and the unnessary complication of the  renaming of game concepts like money and resources to things like "dust" and "FIDS", and it's pretty clear to me that there were plenty of things that could have been made so much simpler without any real loss in depth.
To fans of the game, Please don't misunderstand me. I'm sure its a terrific game. I wanted to enjoy it as much as anyone else, but I have neither an extraordinary amount of patience nor a fantastic memory, and I feel like one of those things is required to enjoy this game.

One of the best games of this decade; modern video game developers need to take notes.
Everything in this game is well constructed, and put together perfectly, to give you a hugely immersive experience.
You are effectively getting 2 different games in 1:
-If you choose an action oriented style of play, you will have tremendous amounts of fun.
-And if you play an explorative, quiet and stealthy gameplay style [which I HUGELY recommend you do], you will find yourself sinking in an amazingly written, shockingly realistic story, where you discover dark secrets, lies, deception and most importantly THE BEST set of characters in video game history.
Every major character in this game is beautifully complex and highly logical; every single one of them is on the extreme end of the specter, yet if you logically analyse the thought process of each one of them from his point of view, you will logically reach the same conclusion as him and start understanding why each one choose to act the way they did.
Story: 9/10
Character arch & development: 10/10
World and environment: 10/10
Music: 11/10
Graphics: 8/10
Gameplay mechanics [weapons,abilities,hacking,etc.]: 9/10
Extremely recommended

As a MASSIVE mechwarrior series fan with way more hours in this game than I should have on a separate non-steam linked account, I can only begrudgingly recommend this game.
Do you have a serrious adiction to mech combat? Massive fan of BattleTech? Did you play countless hours of the old Mechwarrior games? You'll probably love this and spend way too much time and money on it, knock yourself out!
If you are new, be forewarned, the grind is real. If you want to get a decent collection of mechs expect to spend real money, And if you are new expect to die horribly; a lot. You only get one life per game, so the learning process is going to be a bit painful as you spend a lot of time in the lobbies between matches, and then get utterly smashed for overheating, being out of position, missing your shots, targeting the wrong components ect. The new training is nice, but once you start fighting real people you'll probably get wrecked your first 20 or so games. If you aren't a fast learner, you should probably avoid this game. Also, another con is that you won't be able to customize many mechs. You have to own mechs to customize them and they are very expensive. You dont get many mech bays to start, and you need to buy three variants of the same type of mech and grind with them to unlock the piolet traits that make a huge difference in the mechs combat effectiveness. To buy more mech bays so you can own more mechs requires premium currency as well. So if you do grind enough to buy more than a few mechs you will need to spend money. I recommend that you spend a lot of time testing the trial mechs extensively. Get a good feel for what you want to play. The trial mechs are now always champion variants as far as I can tell, and this is great because they are often the best builds possible for the given mech type. Although, “Best” is relative to the meta at the time, and understanding how to play any given mech is not exactly self-explanatory for a beginner. Still, give them a spin, figure out what you like, and start grinding. If you like the idea of slowly building up to the perfect set of mechs optimized to your taste then you might just get to see where this game really shines.
Once your past noobdom, or if your a veteran of the series, the combat is as rewarding as it is challenging. If you are looking for (What IGN called) "A thinking person's shooter" This game is for you. Manage heat, ammo, armor, target lock, weapon groups, and target key components where enemies' main weapons are, memorize mech layouts to engage and strip them faster... On its base level, if you are a fan of huge mechs trading blows in team centric combat, this is your game.
7/10 They should have just launched a real $60 title, but this is way better than nothing for another 10 years.

...at the sale price and given my relatively specific usage, situation, and desires explained below:
I should note that I don't play many FPS, and when I do, they are via keyboard and mouse. This controller was not required to perform under such conditions that could have otherwise factored in this review.
I didn't own an XBox controller at the time of purchase, so the decision for me was between playing certain role playing, fighting, and snowboard games with a keyboard or with a more precise joystick on a controller, rather than a choice between a new controller versus an old one I own and already know how to use. Because of this, when choosing to buy the Steam controller it was against buying another controller for a console I didn't own as well as a potential adapter on top of that.
After using the device to a moderate degree on a variety of game types, I was relatively disheartened with this piece of equipment and its trackpad learning curve and applicability--I also imagine this was a source of frustration for many of the negative reviews that I've read for this product. Well, this was true until I (recently) found an article on how (and all the possibilities there are) to configure your controls (the right pad being the priority)
. Now it's my
controller I've ever used. Knowing that I can configure the controller to behave as I want it to specifically for each game that I care enough for that made me even happier that I didn't bother buying an XBox or offbrand controller. The only thing to add to that sentiment is that most games defaulted to or near my desired configuration as one would hope, which is a huge time-saver--I honestly think this controller has a lot more to offer than some of the negative reviews näively give it credit for.
It's not a bad piece of hardware. Don't expect to play FPSes with this thouugh.

The Steam Controller is a beautiful example of the truism "If it ain't broke, don't fix it." It's a gorgeous-looking controller, and feels extremely well-made and durable. In theory it's a brilliant, hyper-customizable design, but in practice it takes hours of fiddling to configure it properly, which needs to be done for -every- game. I loaded up an old standby -- Borderlands 2 -- to learn the basics. I went from "Oh cool! Look at all this customization!" to "I've been trying to make this work for two hours now and the controls -still- suck." within about 4 hours of getting it. Incidentally, I spent roughly ten minutes of that time actually PLAYING anything with it. The rest was fiddling with the configuration, trying (and failing) to find a comfortable, effective way to play.
Even if you find a way that kinda works, the overall layout of the thing is an unintuitive mess. The track pads just aren't as efficient or easy as analog joysticks; in all the time I spent rejiggering it, I NEVER found a sensitivity level that worked. If I could coherently aim, the pad wouldn't keep up with my thumb, which meant lots of recentering it (and readjusting since you have zero tactile feedback of the angle of the virtual stick), or aiming so wildly sensitive that I might as well have just been knee-walking drunk. Further, replacing a standard analogue d-pad with a thumbstick means that even games that -don't- require a joystick are awkward to control. The face buttons are so far in and down that they're uncomfortable to use; you have to either awkwardly hover over them with your thumb and occasionally reach up to use the track pad, or vice versa. Either way severely slows reaction time in FPS games. The bottom two buttons, as well as the click functions on both track pads, are practically useless. because they require EXTREMELY firm presses. Don't get me wrong; I'm always impressed by the sound of a good hard click from a button, but the firmness utterly wrecks precision. Trying to hold a cursor or camera steady while clicking is damn-near impossible.
Um... You can customize the little beepy tune it plays when it turns on and off, though. So that's nice, I guess?
I give it 1.5 out of 5 Steam Logos.

I really wanted to love the Steam Controller for being such an innovative product only for the PC, but after almost a year of struggling with its compatibility issues and bugs I just gave up and settled for a classic Xbox 360 wireless controller that simply works.
Too many games just don't work (well) with the Steam Controller and as always Valve doesn't move a finger when it comes to actively improving the situation, but rather fully relies on community efforts, meaning the creation of specific game profiles and so on. I imagine smaller developers don't receive any help at all in making their games (fully) compatible and the result is my pretty dismal experience with it.
Then there are those constant "connection issues" despite a distance of 2 meters to the receiver *and* despite the fact that the controller actually works fine while showing this message, just until I hit that "okay" button after which the controller (at least partially) ceases to function in 50% of all cases. If I ignore the message, I can continue playing forever, but unfortunately it's really annoying and it obscures part of the screen. Upon clicking the "dismiss" button I have to restart the controller and therefore also the game I was just playing. Never once did a firmware update solve these problems and at times it just became impossible to play even simple side scrollers like Inside due to the high frequency of the bug occurrences.
It's really sad to see a company like Valve, that makes bazillions of dollars, creating hardware that's so underdeveloped and then abandoned like the also pretty buggy Steam Link or the nowadays entirely forgotten Steam machines.

tl;dr: This is not a game for everyone. If you're here for a deep and enriching story or great tactical gameplay... Keep looking. This is not the game for you. If you're unsure, there's a really lengthy demo, go play it.
The story is basic at best and though it is simple enough to follow, the overarching plot is really not the point of the game. Rather, much like the name implies, the point of the game is forming "bonds" with the "bast.ards" that you find scattered around the island (AKA, your party members). This is quickly undermined by the game actively encouraging (although not forcing) you to constantly switch party members. Since you're forced to have at least twenty of them to finish the game, it's pretty much impossible to fully care about more than a handful, let alone the entire set. More often than not, you'll grab a few of them to be your manpower slaves and then only touch them maybe a dozen hours later to level them up again so you get some more manpower. A task which is mercifully super fast and simple due to the game's levelling system.
The gameplay is "good enough", and even that is something I say with a some reservation. Enemy AI is dumb and predictable - the moment you put a strong enough tank between you and the enemies, the battle is already won. Unless on the odd case where the enemy gets six crits in a row and you're forced to adapt. But that happened once within 40+ hours of gameplay so I'd wager that's far from the norm. The risk system is cute and seems deep at first, but once you get the hang of it, it becomes just as boring a system as the rest of the combat. Labour/Weaver/Thwart challenges are also, frankly, stupid. I'm still trying to figure out a pattern to beat them other than "hope you don't click on the wrong tile" except on the few times that the wrong tile is actually the correct one.
So what *is* good about the game? The fact that the game has a really bad case of the ga.ys for one. In an industry where the concept is almost always either avoided entirely or put in a negative light (with only a handful of exceptions, most of them being implied rather than explicitly stated) it's refreshing to see a game that is not ashamed of what it is without being gratuitous about it - yes, the game has nudity, but it's far from the main focus of it. The amount of times the nudity really is a """key factor""" (massive quotation marks there) can be counted on one hand, and all of them are both optional and obvious. Despite that, the entire game has a lot of gay undertones, which can be easily ignored or embraced for all their worth. It does end up leading to some hilarious things too, such as a piece of armor called the "Mystic Thong" - a literal thong that increases your magic resistance.
The character creator is definitely another. There are a *ton* of possibilities for your character. Something like thirty different body types, divided between male human, female human and male orc, probably over 50 different clothing choices, whose colors you can change and you can even choose what piece of clothing is above another. Also the fact that any character that you create gets automatically added to a saved roster, and can turn up as one of the random roster characters in your future playthroughs.
One thing this game does *really* well is emphasize the fact that the island isn't just a game location - it feels like a real place. There are many areas whose gameplay purpose are basically just "be a bridge between other areas" or just straight-up have no items or combat inside. Yet they are still fairly fleshed out. Some of them being old homes destroyed by the elements with only small traces of who used to live there, others being actual monuments to the story's legendary hero. If nothing else, Lukatt feels a lot more like a real place than most areas in other games.
The game is also definitely going to scratch a completionist's itch - there are a LOT of areas for you to explore, a lot of sidequests to be done, a lot of hidden stuff to find. If you're looking for a game with lots of content and replayability - even if the core gameplay is a little on the weak side - then this game's got you covered.
Overall, I came into this game expecting horrible and I found something that, on a purely technical level is just "meh". On a more subjective and personal level, I found something that I could actually enjoy playing through. Despite the rather negative tone of this review, do keep in mind that I *do* recommend it, so long as you keep in mind that this is *not* a game for everyone.

It takes some getting used to but I really enjoy the game. There's lot of plot that the player will get from investing in pre-made story characters but one is free to create their own party members that they will randomly meet in the world. Alignment, skills, character utility, they're all intertwined and your hunger for high quality pixel graphics will be satiated. There is a "Risk" system involved in which you gamble to press your characters being able to act more within the same turn. The more you do, the higher chance you fumble and spend the rest of the round being an exposed target, you and enemies do this so it's a nice layer of strategy.
Characters and creatures will exhibit partial to full frontal nudity involving all manners of gender. If this bugs you well, that could be a problem but I think it's fine. The desperation of the island you're on, things aren't meant to be conventional or covered up. This is the reason for the adult rating. Also character sexuality is not conventional and that only piqued my interest regardless of what I like to eat. The writing I really enjoy and it was motivating to use pre made characters where normally I don't in my tactical rpgs.
I love the music. This is too personal a taste to guarantee you will.
You can also, in time, recruit monsters/enemies as well. Most of them anyway and you get to decide how they develop on level ups. Humanoid characters don't have any strength or weaknesses, monsters will have weaknesses....some just strenghts, so it's always good to consider recruiting them. Speaking of which the monsters are fairly well thought out and composed, all the way from demure to beyond the pale. This really satiated my hunger for an immersive but fantastic experience.
My only qualms are so small that I humbly accept any flames. The fonts are sometimes small in game. Plot based scenes they're fine. Also I dont' like only being able to hover over one area of a map and then I must move to a different location to reset it to view another part of the overworld map, like checking out stronghold information. After completing a map or leaving it I would rather a quick list of my shop and what it sold instead of listing item by item, but this could be a game mechanic rolling each item to see if it sold. If these issues were enough to get me to actually not really enjoy this game then I'd have slapped myself long ago.
My advice if you play this: Keep in mind melee fighter type characters NEED defense too. Don't just put points in attack, you will get one shotted. If you have someone that uses distance weapons like bows or something, fine but otherwise DEFENSE! You will be frustrated otherwise. Most other builds are fairly straightforward. Also read signs in the tutorial dungeon.
My final piece of advice: Who cares about my review?! If you want a tactical rpg with a few edges just download the demo, I promise if you like that, you'll like ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ Bonds.

You start off being tried for a crime, found guilty regardless of your plea, branded, and being sentenced to a prison on the island of Lukatt. You then get rescued by different people depending on your crime and your guilt. The character customisation is great, and you can run into these characters while playing a different character, which is a nice touch.
The game plays similar to Tactics Ogre, or Final Fantasy Tactics, turn based movement on a square grid, but there are interesting differences. The combat is very simple, you can either move, attack, standby, or defend, but the risk mechanic makes for rewarding gameplay, it lets you take multiple actions per turn, but the more you take, the higher chance of you fumbling and losing the rest of your turn, and getting a debuff to defence until your next turn. The game also differentiates itself with the recruitment/ransom system, which lets you recruit the enemies you are fighting if they happen to hesitate in combat.
Almost every creature you come across is recruitable, as long as you, or someone in your party, is able to talk to them. They can then be used to help claim strongholds across the map, with bigger strongholds needing more manpower, but also able to house more allies. Some creatures are better than others and some of them come with rare skills or traits, they can also be levelled up in any direction you see fit which means you can always venture out with a diverse and capable party.
I was exploring some old mine, and I unearthed a bunch of mummies and a pharoah, I was fighting them, only the pharoah was left, and all of a sudden he hesitated in combat, and I was lucky enough to successfully recruit him. He started off as a pretty dour fellow, but over time he came to think I could remove whatever curse was keeping him in a state of undeath from the island, and became one of my favourite characters, and he went from just some random enemy I recruited to one of my regular party members, which i think is really neat.
There are also other people you can find on different part of the island and recruit, these are unique characters with interesting stories and how much you bond with them can change things later on in the game, as well as decide what happens to them at the end of the game. The game doesnt have a deep story for the player but is more centred around the island and your companions.

First review here.
I mostly don't bother posting my own opinions, but these devs deserve some praise for what they tried and what they achieved.
Lion's Song is a simple point & click. There is no big puzzles to be had. The focus is the story and it's good that way, because this game thrives on great characters and their development.
Add to that a charming soundtrack and really lovely art. (which I admit, might not be everyones cup of tea, but bear with me!)
The setting of Vienna, which is reoccurring throughout all episodes, lends itself well to the art style as well as the theme.
The characters over all are easy to associate with, but still quite refreshingly represented.
Being realistic for it's setting but still giving you a sense of hope and wonder.
I think the story over all clocks in at 6 hours but since there is still little tid-bits and several different options to pick you will find yourself going back through parts of the story quite a lot. The menu set up really helps with that. Saving choices and giving you a quick way to jump back in.
I won't go too deeply into the story or spoil anything since it is such a short game. The experience is what you pay for.
I personally felt the last episode wrapped everything up very nicely and left a good bitter-sweet aftertaste, that I doubt I will forget anytime soon.
I encourage you to look past the 'oh so old' pixel graphic aspect, and the 'oh so overused' episodic set up and really give this one a try!!
If you are on the fence why not go just with the first episode, it's free so you can't go wrong!

This game is amazing.  Everything is well made, the game modes are fun, and there is a lot of stuff to do. For one, it's just great in terms of gun assembly/disassembly. You can take apart a weapon to the very core, every little spring, pin, and bolt can be removed and replaced. You can also simulate operations, i.e., firing, reloading, unloading, etc. Moreover, you can do it in slow-motion, or simply pause and scroll through the footage and frames manually to get an in-depth view. There's also different view types such as X-RAY, which shows the weapon's insides while assembled, and there's plastic mode, which shows the weapon in a sort of toy-like fashion using color coding, making it easier to distinguish major parts. You can also toggle having part names displayed.
The texture quality is more than decent; it's not like a realism mod, but you can see every little groove and angle that would be present in the real weapon very clearly. For example, I know nothing about guns, just like them in general, got this, then figured out thoroughly, simply through slow-motion footage, exactly how an AK-47 fires with every little detail.
Beyond having various vehicles to assemble and disassemble on top of guns, you can take apart and reassemble skeletons of various animals, obviously including humans. Whether you prefer biology or engineering, this is a game/program for all academic enthusiasts and hobbyist's alike.
The
is not free to play. The
is. You don't get even a tenth of the full game content without puchasing at least an $8 pack. However, considering you can still take apart a few weapons and run operation demos for free, it's definitely worth the download for anyone who likes taking things apart. It's especially worth the download if you want to educate yourself on guns and their anatomy and functions. I'm already much more fluent in the nature of firearms from the small time I've played. However, you can buy new guns using experience points you earn through various activities in the game, but they often cost  a lot of experience points which aren't easy to earn through actual gameplay; but, what you can do is simply log in to the game on a daily basis, and by doing so the game rewards you experience points. Each day you get more EXP, and on the 7th consecutive log-in, you receive 7,000 EXP (whereas earning EXP from gun activities only ever yields a couple hundred). A nice gun, e.g., the M14, costs about 30,000 EXP, so it is quite possible to get new guns frequently enough to keep you interested in the game.
I'm waiting a while to see if any packs will be on sale, like the 4 cars pack is as I'm typing this, and if I can't find anything soon I'll probably purchase the lifetime access. It's overpriced, but not by much, and I'm willing to spend a bit extra for this kind of content.

You might see this game has very few reviews despite the release date and think "There must be something wrong with this game." And you'd be right, there is something wrong; NOT ENOUGH PEOPLE KNOW ABOUT IT!
First off, yes, this is a RPG Maker-based game. BUT!!! It's one of the few good ones!
Between 10 and 20hrs depending on your pace and your interest for completion, this game involves a group of adventuring friends in the form of cute-looking sprites, a balanced group, spells you can teach any of your mage-wielding characters and skills that depend on what weapon your warrior has equipped.
A simple, straight-forward and yet entertaining story easy to follow with a journal to check if you forget where you're at. It also involves backtracking after acquiring certain items so you can open areas you couldn't the first time you visited a dungeon. But the world in this game is somewhat small, so easy to revisit everything over and over once cleared if you can't remember where was that ONE place! The monsters don't respawn once killed in dungeons, and the ones on the map quickly become too weak and easily avoidable or escapable from.
A bunch of sidequests, easy to spot with "?" over NPCs heads, but the one downside is there is no list of sidequests in your menu, so either take notes, or only pick them one at a time so you don't forget where you're supposed to go. But that's a minor inconvenience because any new area reachable by obtaining a sidequest becomes marked on the world map (meaning when you're outside, you can see an arrow over a cave or a forest entrance. You don't have a map key item)
The community for this game is surprisingly small but the developers are ready to answer any questions you might have.
TL;DR
For the price, this game is very much worth it. I have unfortunately seen worse for more than this.

If you have any interest in playing a cyberpunk FPS with very open-ended level design, a reasonably good story, and some light RPG mechanics, you should definitely play this game.
In most respects, it's a worthy successor to the original arguably-best-game-ever deus ex, and in gunplay and graphics, it even excels the king.
If you played the original Deus Ex - the only area where I feel the game has a major shortcoming compared to its predecessor is that it has a lot less relevance to real world politics. The original Deus Ex challenged you to think about your worldview by having various characters with different, and at times opposing, points of view present you will real-world, historical evidence that favors their point of view. This game, not at all. The characters are actually very well-written and, superb by video game standards even, but the political and philosophical dimension of the original is missing.
Human Revolution tried to supplant that dimension of politics and philosophy with a very forced and badly-handled debate about whether people should be allowed to own augmentations. There are a lot of ways the debate could have been good - here is what I think the characters COULD have debated and had it be sort of politically relevant - 1) most jarringly, is it acceptable that a few companies control the supply of drugs that prevent your body from rejecting augs 2) do augmentations create an upper and lower caste in society 3) can augmentations be used by the government to infringe on freedoms (or, depending on your POV, maybe fight terrorism, and that's good), 4) Are augs actually SAFE yet (this is brand new tech.
But no, what we get is "Mechanical arms are the next stage of human evolution" (♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t) vs. "God didn't intend no robot arms" (♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t). Maybe Squeenix didn't want us to think about politics because it would get us thinking about their business practices, I don't know.
Aside from that one gripe, it's a fantastic game in terms of level design, gameplay, pc port quality, story, character development, and very solid in terms of mechanics, and I don't give games an easy time.

Technically, this is free to play. Yeah, well, technically. In reality, if you want  to compete you'll be plunking down cash for one of the two in-game currencies you can only buy with cash. Works like this: To max out your pilot's abilities on a chassis, you need to level-up four different variants of that chassis, so you need to buy four different variants of that chassis. To compete in something other than skirmish play (random pubbies) you need to have leveled up four different chassis. So four variants times four chassies equals sixteen different variants.
Problem: you only start out with space for four chassis. So if you want to avoid paying cash for more you'll be selling chassies for underwear-streaking losses to fit the next one. While you could *technically* do this, it's a giant waste of your resources, which means it's a giant waste of your time.
And the very best variants of every chassis are only available if you pay IRL money. So, yeah, enjoy losing to whales who can drop $600 on in-game purchases.

I only died to traps that I didn't see coming or by doing impatient things like using my squishy characters to blindly go around corners. There was never a time where I had to spend a few minutes devising a strategy to beat enemies, which was a let down because I like a challenging game. Okay, Here's the thing.
This game is awesome in almost every way.
The risk mechanic makes the combat interesting, the character creation makes the replayability an actual thing. The lore is tastefully distributed, giving little details actual sense, among other things. But if you don't want it, you can simply ignore it and go on without it. (Many things are hidden in the details, so if you ignore them, you may have a hard time)
But really, what makes me love this game so much, is the core characters.
These twenty-something characters have their own stories, perks, and personalities. The interactions between them, (if you manage to find them) gives them a greater depth. And their comments have been anywhere from hilarious to tragic.
An extra point for this game, is that it has given most characters skimpy clothing (and in the case of your character and enemies, potentially no clothing at all) And it applies to both genders.
Do you want a group of naked ladies fighting with you? You totally can!
Do you want a group of naked fellas fighting with you? They're right there!
None of the above? You can recruit Huge animals or monsters or slimes!
You like none of those? You can fully visually mod all of your party (including your character) to look however you want with a 80x64 PNG file for each. You only need their names!
The only flaw that I can think of is that there is only one romanceable character. Adding romance stories for a few more characters would have been amazing! But with only one developer, it is understandable.
The only possible reasons for you to not like this game are:
If you are allergic to pixel-art
If you can't play tactical games
If you are too prude to deal with pixelated nudity and occasional dirty jokes (in which case most mature games are off the table)
Or if you have an extreme case of homophobia (I have read comments of guys who apparently can't deal with the game because there are a lot of shirtless men for their delicate eyes).
Really, You should at least give this game a try with the Demo the Developer offers at his website. It is really worth it

Longer version:
Just as with the Life is Strange, it was a good move to make the first episode for free. They dropped the hook and cought my attention. Even though the story in the first episode wasn't so great for me, it had nice atmosphere, unique visuals and very interesting compositions (which sadly weren't  used in the next episodes :( )
Lion's Song isn't for everyone. It's a slow-paced point-and-click game with lots of conversations. There are people claiming that it has different endings, but so far I've played it just once so I can't confirm whether they are that different or just slight differences in the conversations.
Very nice and unique visuals. Animation was minimalistic but still quite good. Only thing I thought was overused was the fade-in/fade-out effect. They used it instead of cuts between the scenes and sometimes even just between the action even though it was completely unnecessery and they just could animate the action in few frames. So after some time it started to be little bit annoying.
Beautiful music and good sound design. I really can't complain in this field.
Story....I don't know. I had mixed feelings about it. First episode was quite simple with just few 'wow' moments, so I wasn't very amazed but still enough to be curious about the next episodes, which were more complex (but with poorer visuals) and each episode was better than the previous one. At least for me. So the last episode was like the icing on the cake. Maybe that's good because it had some graduation which climaxed in the interesting plot twist.
Overall: I definitely recommend to try this game's first episode. If you like it at least a little bit, then I think you will like the whole game because it gets better. If you don't like it, it would be a gamble to buy the whole game, so try to reconsider if  you are willing to pay 10€ for a game you might not like.

World of Guns is a game about disassembling guns, as simple as that. Practically, this product has one of the clearest headers in the whole market.
Basically, there are many (priced) products theming disassembling things. Most famous on Steam are the Surgeon Simulator 2013 and the Car Mechanic Simulator 2014/15. Both of those hardly giving you any real knowledge, just some queery "fun moments" mostly.
World of Guns is very different. Generally, it's not much of a game. It's not about fun. Of course, if only you're not the one seeing fun when you don't lose any screws while disassembling something. Most likely, it feels as a big manual on "how to operate with guns". And that is a good thing. You can find many books, pictures, videos on "how to keep the gun", but you don't get it unless you'll try it by yourself, even if in 3d model (yeah, like those in ikea shops).
It has its flaws, sure. If you want a manual to specific weapon from list, you have to pay for it - or to get it by achieving "points". You can collect those points for practicing with already unlocked stuff and answering some quiz to unlock next weapon closer to one you want... Over and over, until you'll get them all. And yeah, if it sounds grindy to you, that's because it is.
Also, while you not only be playing with screws there - there will be some ranges to shoot, some paints to make your dream gun if you like them coloured... that's not all you can hope for from a weapons "Hustler" game. For example, if you were wandering not only how those irons disassemble and blazing, but how to oil them... alas, there are no such useful info.
So! People doesn't like to see a price in F2P game for quick access to something that could be opened later for free. People don't like "grinding". And even if they are alright with F2P gaming basics, the game itself is not like a wet dream for a gun ate-ups, as there are not so much content, as one can imagine... and new additions comes not so fast.
Still, it is quite a good project. Even if it's just 3d models and not real iron, it's much, Much better than nothing. I can only hope it could be improved to become something greater. Like the "Jane's" magazines in the XX century.
There will be no usual mark 'cause it's not a game you'll play to enjoy. It's education... of some kind.

The pixel art is nice and the controls are good but perhaps not perfect.  The addition of separate buttons for high and low jumps makes getting the rhythm a bit tricky.  Additionally, when using a controller, crouch is assigned to the left thumb stick which also controls movement.  This can result in some cheap deaths when your character crouches unintentionally.
