I'll confess to not having the patience for these types of platformers but the game itself is solid.  A bit pricey at full asking but a reasonable value at 50% or more off - with the prior caveats of course.

I bought a Steam controller on launch. I was very excited, invested some time into trying out the different features and trying different configurations on different games. Even though I could see the potential, it just didn't click for me. I thought at the time I had wasted $60...
Fast forward to when Steam decided to expand the Steam controller configuration software to support Playstation controllers... Wow. Like Christmas as a kid times a million. Best gift EVER.
(For people who use Xbox controllers on Steam, let me try to explain my pain. Imagine that about 50% of the time you buy a new game, you fire it up and realize it won't support your controller. So you get a 3rd party key mapping software and get used to creating new maps almost every time you get a new game. But it gets worse. If you're using a psx controller, about 20% of the time, it registers your controller incorrectly, messing up the axises and making it hard or impossible sometimes to use the keymapper. It's completely infuriating that so many PC games don't even bother to support traditional ("generic") pc controllers, while so many have controller support for one and only one console controller.)
Now I have integrated Playstation controller support in all of my games, Steam games and external games! Not only that, we get to leverage the incrediby powerful Steam controller customization software. They even covered extra features like changing the LED colors. It's everything I ever wanted. It fixed the only complaint I ever had in Steam, which wasn't even Steam's fault but due to lazy or cheap game studios. In one fell swoop, Steam resolved every controller issue I had with every single game I own. I would gladly and happily have paid $60 for this alone. That's less than $1 per broken game for integrated support of my favorite controller.
TL;DR
My Steam controller may sit in the corner gathering dust but it's a purchase I will never regret, not if it helped drive the development for the Steam controller configuration software in any way.
Thank you, Steam. Thank you. <3 <3 <3

This is a fantastic game for a mature audience.  I cannot recommend it enough.  The skill system is well-conceived and easy to understand, but open to a wide variation of characters.  The game is made up of vignettes - many of which are terrific - which allow you to play for 15 minutes or forever.  The world is populated with fleshed-out companions, generic recruits, and, awesomely, conscripted monsters.  You can claim various maps for strongholds, allowing you to hire various help.
If there is a weakness, it is the lack of a strong plot.  The player is given enormous leeway to wander the game, but the trade-off is a less structured plot.  Again, there are vignettes and nice moments with companions, but nothing sustained over the length of the game.
When I look at the other reviews, I don't see criticisms as much as I see a wish list.  That is encouraging.  You don't ask for the impossible.  You only ask for what you think can be done.   And I think Big Fingers can do a lot.
What is on my wish list?  Only two things, really.  First, a stronger plot.  There's never going to be another Planescape: Torment.  I recognize that it would actually be really hard to impose a plot within the structure of the game, but it would be nice.  Second, a more complex stronghold system.  It is really neat to claim half or more of the maps for your stronghold.  But I would prefer to have less available stronghold maps but more complicated strongholds.  I would love to restore Ruins of a Royal Court or the Ebony Tower!  Maybe run Hotel Zisa or the Brimstone Lodge.  I think Big Fingers could do better than NWN2's Crossroad Keep.
But take it as a great compliment that I am pointing Big Finger at some of the best games of all time.

If you like Mobile Suit Gundam, Macross, Pacific Rim, or even played any of the BattleTech games (tabletop from the 80's or video games in the franchise) you'll want to give this one a go. It fills in that niche giant robot slot you've been craving.
The game appears like your poorly-interactive-MMORPG at first glance (it took me a couple days to figure out just WTF is going on in the Mechlab), but once you get the hang of the wealth of information presented, it becomes much more intuitive. Every piece on the screen, in-game or in-menu, serves a purpose and tells you something. It just takes a bit to get used to it.
The piloting segment of the game is very fun but is a challenge to do well. Many aspects are occuring at once, and it's up to you to manage them all effectively (ex. heat management, ammo, presenting armor, etc.). If you are a tanker (World of Tanks, War Thunder, Armored Warfare, etc.) you can apply your knowledge directly to this game and do pretty well. If you aren't, the learning curve is about the same. The idea is to play smarter, not harder. Coordinate with your team and you'll likely take home the big money.
My biggest credit to this game after playing more Pay2Win games is the free-to-play model. The game is very much playable for free; in fact, the game will help you grind for your first 'Mech, and even so, supplies you with "rental" Trial 'Mechs throughout the game. There also isn't a progression tree, so you choose what you want to play, grind it out, and get the one you want. Beyond that, the Mechlab will allow you to customize the components on your 'Mech to suit basically any playstyle (look up B33f's Direstar build: it's a riot!). All of this is free, you don't have to pay a dime to them. The cosmetics of your mech will be what they grab cash out of you on, but that is entirely optional.
After seeing so many dull, indless games come up, it's good to see a game that requires a good mind. I would definitely recommend this game.

I cannot as of the writing of this review comment on if Invisible War is a worthy sequel to the original Deus Ex, as I have not played it yet. What I can say is that Human Revolution certainly is. HR is a prequel to the original game and manages to modernize the Deus Ex franchise while maintaining the things that made Deus Ex Deus Ex. Multiple paths in levels, a story that changes depending on your choices, and different augmentations and weapons that change your playstyle. The setting in HR is a world divided (not Mankind Divided) between allowing human controlled evolution or not. It is very engaging and something that I have not seen in other science fiction storys. The game does not favor one side or another in the debate, letting the player come to their own conclusions on the subject as they play a cybernetic Batman. I've just finished it and I'm left feeling it was decent, but nothing that special. I've always wanted to try the series and now that I have I'm not blown away by it, but I will pick up Mankind Divided once it's heavily discounted in the hope that some small improvements will bump my overall score up a notch.
I'll start by saying the story itself was great, it was engaging and interesting throughout and the voice acting was really on point as well which helped sell it, the story was what kept me playing until the end. It's just a shame the lip syncing often fell out of sync during cutscenes.
The gameplay just didn't match quality of the story for me, though, the AI was often quite brain-dead and just clunky, with obvious hard leashes which made tougher encounters easier as you could just run out the door, regain health and go in again. Swapping through weapons and items was clunky and slow, I would have happily spent an augment point on upgrading the speed I could switch weapons but I didn't see one (please tell me I didn't miss it), the cover system was quite awkward and often I'd try to lean out to shoot and the game just wouldn't let me for no apparent reason. One of my biggest complaints has to be the inventory though, I maxed it out but was still constantly full and unable to loot items, if items stacked, or stacked in higher quantities it would have eliminated this major annoyance. I get that they don't want you to carry around everything at once, but I felt it was overly restrictive to the point it hurt the gameplay.
Technically the game fell somewhat as well, I mentioned earlier the lip sync issues, there was also a weird bug where the combat rifle had slight delay on its audio after pulling the trigger, apparently it's a common issue with Asus cards which I happen to have. I also suffered with a lot of stuttering, especially outside in open cities and once again the Steam forums are filled with complaints regarding this issue, which apparently was fixed in the non DC version, but not the DC which is bizarre to me. I will say I GREATLY reduced this by forcing the new Fast Sync technology using Nvidia Inspector, it eliminated almost all of the stuttering and removed all tearing all while having VSync off so the mouse didn't feel heavy, Fast Sync is incredible and I highly suggest you guys try it in place of VSync as you get all the benefits without the negatives.
Overall it was a fantastic story let down by the core gameplay and mechanics which felt clunky and often became frustrating. I will say I'm not a massive fan of stealth games so I was probably playing it "wrong", often picking my silenced pistol over simply hiding and dodging enemies which often made the game harder (and it was surprisingly hard even on normal, you die so fast) but that didn't negatively impact my enjoyment of the game, other than some fairly large progress losses because the autosave system is quite stingy, I used F5 a lot more towards the end.
6/10
Nvidia users: Force the new Fast Sync technology, it makes the game much smoother. Download Nvidia Inspector and force the VSync bits to "0x18888888". You need the latest version of Nvidia Inspector and the latest Nvidia drivers for this to work. Fast Sync gives you all the benefits of VSync without the negatives like input delay and mouse heaviness, it's really great and made the game much more enjoyable for me.

I bought this game and played it to Hell and back(literally) before it made it to Steam, so don't let my hours played fool you.
Overall this is a really great game, and I'd recommend it to anyone as long as they can handle pixellated nudity and having to read. If either of those things are unappealing to you, then B*stard Bonds probably isn't your style.
On the flipside, if reading and pixellated nudity are your favorite things, then B*stard Bonds is probably also your favorite thing.
In my opinion, the greatest features this game has to offer are the character creator, the story, the music, and the characters. The combat system is also pretty cool, and the skill system is a lot of fun as well.
The combat is quick, simple and fun. It can start to get a bit repetitive towards the later half of the game, but since it's so quick it never really gets annoying unless Mohrgs are involved. The risk system is really cool. I had a build with Greave that meant that any time he took damage, his risk reduced to 0, and it was awesome.
Skills are tied in with the combat system. All the cool stuff you can do in combat comes from either skills, or unique equipment. Utility skills are also really cool. Unlike most games where they're horribly useless, utility is probably stronger than offense or defense. It doesn't help a whole ton with killing stuff, but it helps an awful lot with everything else.
The music is great. It's fun, atmospheric, and has a couple of really catchy tracks. I bought the soundtrack and I do not regret it in the slightest.
The character creator is pretty awesome. I've never seen any other game which gives you as much freedom over your character's appearance. My only gripes are a lack of variety in hairstyles and a lack of weapons, but since the game supports custom sprites that's not too much of an issue.
Another neat feature of the character creator is that any character you make has the potential to show up as a recruitable character in another save file.
The story is not like most games. Usually, "story" refers to the train tracks the game follows from start to finish. In B*stard Bonds, you're given a little bit of story as an introduction, and then after that you have to hunt the story down yourself, and it's not always easy to find. There are no train tracks. If you want to make it off the island, then you'd better be paying attention to every map you pass through, especially on the eastern half of the island. Clues can be cryptic and vague, and if something seems impossible or unfair, there's a good chance you missed some vital detail a while back.
This is the kind of game where even seeing the final boss at all is an accomplishment, let alone beating him.
The characters provide a good chunk of the story, and I can guarantee you that the way you feel about your party will have a significant impact later on. Aside from being able to use the character creator to make whoever you want, you can also recruit ALMOST any enemy you run into. While I did not try to recruit Frico, I get the feeling he probably would have said no.
In addition to recruited enemies and player made characters, there is also a group of unique companions scattered throughout the game. These guys have a bit more story and personality to them, and they interact with the world a lot more. They show up in the epilogue as well, and they don't all get happy endings if you neglect them(I'm sorry Kirilo! T-T). I would highly recommend that you keep a camp slot open at all times, recruit any unique characters you come across, and take the time to get to know them.

A great game that's obviously not for everybody (and it shouldn't be!)
The amount of content and breadth of the game is amazing for being done by mainly one person; there's easily over 40 hours if you explore around looking for everything. The writing's good, the character recruitment system is great, and there are enough hidden interactions to make it replayable on top of that.

A Simple game but with a lot of complexity and customisation to it. The game is aimed towards people looking for a Turn Based RPG experience but yet are looking for something alittle bit more grown up and not scared to go into some dark topics. The type of game you can play for 20 minutes at a time or play for many hours long into the night. Highly recommended to people who like to Role Play during a game but focuses more on your actions over what you say. Over 30 hours in total including non steam play through time, still have not completed the game but so far I would say it was worth my money and I paid full price for the game.
Pros
A Mature Turn based RPG Game for mature people with a dark story line of redemption.
Character creation changes what events and people you meet in the game making multiple play through's different each time depending on what you choose.
Mixed up gameplay focusing on Dungeon crawling, base management and world exploring with intractable NPCs.
Hire as many companions as you find and level them up to suite your needs from Attack, Magic and Labour to help build your bases for more companions and to make them better in battles.
Huge world containing hundreds of locations to explore and to claim as your own.
Hundreds of Creatures to fight along your travels with randomized sprites to make combat interesting and not feel the same every time.
LGQBT friendly game but with no unnecessary sex scenes and all LGQBT can be avoided depending on options during character creation.
A simple 16bit art style which is created for just this game (No reused RPG Marker assets, do not go into this thinking its another RPG Maker game, this uses a completely different engine)
Dungeons can be a simple or difficult affair depending on how well you plan before entering a dungeon, making companions abilities and equipment very important to plan out carefully, perfect for people who like tactical games.
Cons
The AI can be problematic in dungeons with companions getting stuck on walls and objects.
UI can be difficult to understand at first with some important features slightly hidden (The “Save” is on the world map screen)
Alot of micromanagement is required for the party and what things do in dungeons like how certain enemies can only be damaged by certain kinds of attacks and abilities, this is difficult to remember what does what with hundreds of different kinds of creatures to fight.
Difficulty seems alittle all over the place with sometimes I can go from dungeon to dungeon without having to XP grind and then having to go back and XP grind due to a huge difficulty spike in a dungeon.
Dialogue options is limited but yet the main focus of the game is your personal story rather then others.

I usually like difficult games, but I'm not a huge fan of this one.  The premis is good, the controls are decent enough, the graphics/sound is tolerable (but comes with the territory of being a nostalgic 8-bit style).  I think I don't like it because I'm not a fan of "gotcha" deaths.  Meaning certain death from something that you couldn't have anticipated.  This game has a bunch of those and they get pretty rage-inducing.  I much prefer a game that challenges your skills and relies on upping the difficulty and variety of what you face versus booby-trapping parts of a level that mean (almost) guaranteed death if you haven't died to it yet on that level, thus making you start over.  If they were all small like Super Meat Boy levels, I wouldn't mind as much, but some take at least a little bit of time so it feels like a waste.
In short, if you like old school platformers and don't mind dying a bunch of cheap deaths, you may like this.  Otherwise, move along.

I had World of Tanks before and saw World of Tanks Blitz on Steam, so thought I'd give it a try. World of Tanks was giving me lag issues, and Blitz lighter package might of reduced this or it's just designed better. I once did have another old issue return on me, where the program just closes itself right before a game starts. Overall, Blitz seems to be far more stable and lagless than World of Tanks original.
For Blitz, I enjoyed the game and it felt a bit more balanced compared to the original. The price system still doesn't seem thought out well and the tier system is also bad. In some games, you may find yourself about useless if lacking the right equipment. Everything else feels improved, although I liked the original more in some ways, but it's not important to go into that in full detail. If I had to chose something I would change first, it would be to remove distance invisibility and remove names/outlines. The driving mechanics doesn't feel realistic either, sudden top speed and sudden stopping, plus the ram damage.
The only reason I'm not recommending the game is the bot issue. Half the players or more are obvious bots. This can be seen by their unintelligible behavior or simply not moving the entire game unless shot at. It quickly reduces the game’s quality when half your team is on the other side of the field in a ditch looking around in circles. In one case, there was a player that scored 7/7 kills during the round. I click their profile to see 100% victories, so I’m not sure if he was just good and made a new profile or if it was a bot. In the original World of Tanks, bots were easy to report, but I didn’t see a report system for Blitz. This would explain why there are so many useless tanks just sitting around or making poor decisions.
If bots were removed, I'd recommend it. But after playing for a few days, I'm already tired of having so many useless players laying around.

A great game, even by today's standards. The environmental design is amazing, and while the really ugly characters distract a little, the whole world feels very immersive (also thanks to the incredible soundtrack). The story is convincing and an actual protagonist with characters keeps you interested. The game does not pretend to give you the illusion of choice regarding plot (thank you!), but as written in a million other reviews the actual objectives can be completed in multiple ways.
Not that many ways tho. There is mainly the shooty way which involves somewhat shoddy cover, random headshots and fun inventory management with lots of upgrades for your weapons. Alternatively, you can sneak around and since there are only a few weapons you need this way, you spend it all on skill upgrades and end up not just sneaking but also hacking, jumping and carrying around garbage containers.
The sneaking is fun tho, even if it does not hold up to newer games like Metal Gear V.
All in all, the game has it's own distinct character and is worth a try. Get the Director's Cut version, it has some minor changes, good DLC and redone boss battles (which had to be done the shooty way before, even if you were sneaky). I have to say though, not giving you the upgraded version if you own the original is a bad move, especially since other companies handle it better. So wait for a sale. :)

Definitely one of my favorite games out there. It is simple and challenging at the same time; has good background, and endless hours of gameplay to try new empires and tactics. If you like civilization type games, you need to try this one.

The short of it: This game is really good, BUT ONLY WITH THE EXPANSION! DO NOT BUY AND PLAY THIS GAME NAKED!
Unlike a lot of 4X games, Endless Space is more about building your empire than about developing your colonies or really fighting wars. Not that you won't fight wars, the AI is usually vicious enough to wait and plot and it will build up an overwhelming force based on your existing military might before waging war on you. And it WILL do that. Every single chance it can, unless it can't, it will do that. Never think it won't, since it has no reason not to.
We'll get more into that later, but right now let's focus on the empire-building. Building up the empire is the primary focus of this game. Oftentimes if you look at too little at a time, you'll tunnel vision yourself into a corner when you should be keeping yourself as distant as possible. A prime example of this is expressed in happiness. The morale of a system and its subsequent production bonuses are NOT more important than the overall happiness of your empire. After all, a 15% production bonus across 4 stars is better than a 30% bonus in just one. If, when settling a new system, you have a planet with lots of production, or a planet with a high amount of happiness-boosting, you pick the one that makes your empire happy, or you lose the game.
Now then, let's talk about war. War is problematic in this game because A) it's inevitable, and B) it's boring. The game takes a very hands-off approach to combat and in the vanilla game technology is both everything and a linear arms race. The guy with the most ship tonnage and the best weapons will always win. You can employ tactics cards, but these will only have a minimal impact on the outcome. This leads to a very boring experience, and can force you into certain types of tech progression and thus certain modes of gameplay. To deviate from established doctrine is to lose in the vanilla game.
DO NOT PLAY THE VANILLA GAME. Instead, do yourself a favor and get the Disharmony expansion. The Disharmony expansion does away with about 75% of the weapon-tech in favor of just four generations of guns. Each is a sizable improvement over the last generation, and keeping up the with the AI is definitely important, but with tactics, ship design, aimpoint selections, and formation management you can steal victory from the jaws of supposedly assured defeat.
Endless Space encourages you to use your distant veiw not to mess with the minutae of your own empire, but rather to mess with the other guys. Through trade, trade routes, blockades, invasions, explorations, treaties, and wars you are charged to take away the choices of the enemy for as long as possible while you improve your own choices. How you do this is entirely up to you, and Endless Space: Disharmony actually allows you quite a bit of wiggle room on how you do it.

In addition it wasn't very clear how the players choices affected the outcome of the game. As a player I want to feel as if my choices ended up having some impact on the story, but instead it felt like the same conclusion would have been reached no matter what dialogue I had chosen throughout the story.

I'd also liked to have seen more complicated puzzles and player choices that affect the game more dramatically than whether someone recieves a phone call or not. Do not use this software. Even if it didn't cause major damage to my computer, it gave me a justified feeling of insecurity.
Most of the times, the software did work, but the recent session that I had with this program was frustrating and had me question "why?". Here is some of my experience:
- I run the software once per week to check for driver updates, and there have been times that the program suddenly tells me that one or two drivers are outdated, out of the blue, and puts me drivers dated from the previous year (2016). If the driver was OK, no rollback was made and the program suddenly recommends me a driver from previous year (remember: previous week it didn't say anything, and at the next week it suddenly recommends a driver that is older than a week ago), then something is not right in the software.
- At the time of redacting this review, my Nvidia Geforce driver is not up to date, and the program didn't list the driver in the list of updates needed. I know that people will call me dumb and tell me to use Nvidia GeForce Experience or to go to Nvidia website to download the driver (and I use Experience to update the graphic driver). My point is that the Nvidia driver is A DRIVER, and should be treated as such.
- The progress bar didn't move after the 1% for a very long while even with my antivirus software deactivated before starting the updates/installations. I checked the Performance tab on Windows Task Manager and the CPU wasn't being used at all, like if the process of installation wasn't delivered to the CPU.
- When I tell the program to stop/cancel, it doesn't react after the confirmation. I have to close the window and restore it from the taskbar so it could realize that I told it to stop. And then it may suddenly say "installation complete, you'll need to restart".
If the program is doing a doubtly good work (remember, it should list EVERY outdated drivers, including graphic cards), how I am suppose to trust in this software?
Download the drivers directly from the companies websites (including Nvidia, Ati and even the motherboard's company), or use programs that are more trustful than this one.
And now I'm going to update my Nvidia Geforce. Thanks for reading.

A brilliant game. Incredibly simple, yet diverse. The rules and mechanics aren't difficult, once you get the hang of them. Having the ability to create characters to add to your roster, and custom sprites on top of that, is just icing on the cake. If the wonderful character creation doesn't fit your needs, then you can draw up your own sprites or search around online. Check out the artwork section of the community hub for a few of my custom sprites to use.

As an adult gamer, I love games that have adult content and I don't just mean games with sexual encounters but games that tackle mature themes about sexuality, society, survival and comradery. Most game either just add sexual encounters or subplots to their otherwise non-sexual story in an attempt to be more “mature” or focus on just being a dating sim game with not much in terms of gameplay. ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ Bonds finds a happy medium in being a fast-paced tactical RPG with having mature themes as once would expect being on a penal colony. The gameplay and exploration is addictive; I've been playing well over 50 hours (I bought the game a month before its Greenlight released on Steam) and I have not been able to stop playing.
The things I love about this game include the large number of unique bandmates, each with their own interesting backgrounds and the ability to have other player made characters appear in your playthrough and join your group. There’s also base-like component about the game that makes use of your stats outside of combat and I’m always a sucker for crafting systems that allow you to make good use of duplicate items that you would otherwise just sell for gold. I also love going through every new map and learning more about the history of Lukatt and the society of this world through context and objects on the maps. The music is amazing and sets the right mood for the situations.
Some issues I can see people having with this game is that the combat can seem repetitive but it gets better as strong enemies appear, new weapons are found and characters learn new skills. Other people may be put off by the lack of animation but given that the game supports fully customizing character sprites with player's original art, it would be difficult account for every possible player creation. The only real annoyances I've had with the game is party members not always being able pathfind, which doesn't happen often, and the lack of bandmates having more dialogue at the stronghold when talking to them while trying to earn their trust. Their dialogue does change once you've earn their trust but then it doesn't change from that. There were some annoyances caused by bugs but those were promptly fixed before the Steam release.
If you’re into turn-based tactical RPG’s set in a fantasy world of orcs and magic and are not shy about adult themes and pixel nudity, I highly recommend this game.

At first glance, B*stard Bonds seems like a normal turn-based RPG. The usual run-of-the-mill story of saving something or killing something else with all the normal RPG items like leveling, inventory management and micromanagement of your bases (eventually). However, there's something unspoken about the game that seems to draw you in. Not at first, no, at first you'll start off roughly, die a couple of times, begin to resent magic (which is a disturbing tread in RPGs nowadays), you may even wanna rage quit because "Oh my god, I just got murdered by a group of nutcases running around naked and howling at the moon!!! ARGH!!!". But then... You get over the 'Tutorial hump' (the early moments in an RPG when things go slow and are as fun as grinding your face against gravel). Then you start to kill things faster, cleaning up maps. You find a new fort, finally get to sell those coins you picked up 4 hours ago because you thought they'd fetch a good price (along with all the other junk you horded to sell).
It's here, at this point, that you begin to enjoy yourself. Your crew somehow click better, monsters don't hit as hard, attack land more, you praise your allies even if they're not the same alignment as you cos, hey, he pulled off several reckless attack chain and never fumbled, he deserves praise. You find NPCs you made, unlock story segments about characters you actually start to get attached to. When someone's down in battle, you can't help but feel your attacks have a little bit more malice against the SOB who took down your buddy. Simply put, the second you start to feel power in this game, you get sucked in. You're not power, you can die at any moment and you'll get served time and time again if you don't manage your allies right, but you can't help but enjoy the moment.
It's not the best game, it'll drive you insane for the first few hours, but it's seriously good when things go right. Indepth customization of sprites, a hefty selection of strangers and freaks to partner with, a ton of battling and that ever going question of... When the bloody hell can I take that fort as my base? It isn't an easy game, it simply gets easier as you adjust to your situation and team. It's unrelenting, yet you love it.
Don't believe the propaganda saying this is just smut. This is an RPG at its core, a little old with a little new, and doesn't pretty itself up like other games to please those screaming "Think about the children!". It is what it is, realist not smutty. Rough, but yielding.
And that's something to be respected.

This, right here, is a hidden gem of a game.
It's been a long time since I've played a game with so many original ideas, such a diverse selection of characters and so well-thought-out deep lore.
+ The character creator is beyond original, allowing for thousands of different looks. And if that's not enough, you can make your own pixel-art and use it as your avatar. I know everyone here has already pointed this out, but it'd be a crime not to. Also, if you've created a template character in the main menu, you'll have the chance to run into them in the game and recruit them!
+ Instead of the usual RPG classes, here you have a brand, AKA a crime you've been accused of. Different crimes (and whether you're guilty or not) make for different stats, as well as different companions. And, on that note, skill trees? Ha! Here you have a skill matrix, where any point you allocate increases not only that skill, but all the skills in the same row and column. Also, as there are no "classes", there are no restrictions either. You want to make your newly-recruited sasquatch a mage? Or a tiny goblin an indestructible tank? Go wild!
+ Thanks to the two previous points, replayability is through the roof. Different character with different companions can find completely different secrets and details in the same location, so no two playthroughs will be the exact same.
+ The world map is huge, and you're mostly free to go wherever you want. Some places are full of enemies, some are peaceful zones. A lot of them have bits of lore, and some have unique dialogues with your companions (if you bring them along, that is).
+ The turn-based combat system is not overcomplicated, but has a unique risk system, allowing you to pray to RNGesus for extra turns.
+ (spoilers just in case)
The only things I was not a huge fan of are as follows:
- The music is not very varied. It's great, don't get me wrong, but it wouldn't hurt to add some more themes. Especially battle themes.
- Sometimes you'll have to grind some manpower in order to recruit more people (= powerlevel the companions with high utility stat). It's not excruciatingly long, but can be a bit frustrating. Also it undermines the stronghold feature a bit - you need manpower not only for recruiting, but also for hiring services. Being unable to hire a blacksmith because you just moved to a bigger stronghold is not fun.
Overall, I can't recommend this game enough. I will definitely look forward to the author's next projects... And hope for the sequel, of course. =D

If you enjoy old school open world (C-)RPGs, this is for you. Truly innovative gameplay which to explain right would take more than a mere paragraph. While you actively only choose one out of 9 skills, the 4 skills in the same row and column gain a smaller, but not insignificant boost. This allows you to choose your strengths, but not give up variety. Depending on your preference, of course.
Combat is pretty innovative - or rather old school - in that positioning matters a lot. Combat isn't easy, but also not hard. If you can't beat a fight, you can just come back later once you've got better equip or better skills.
You are also able to set up and manage strongholds which offer some useful and fun features. This strategic level, however, is not near as deep as the combat. It suits the game very well, but it doesn't turn into a genre mix. It stays a combat focused RPG.
Speaking of which, as far as I've played plot seems to be rather sparse. The game's universe is very intriguing though and you learn about it bit by bit. It defies a lot of standards and cliches, without becoming too alien.
Great game. Do buy if you enjoy challenging, open RPGs.
Edit: After 20-30 more hours I have to add a caveat: As a completionist that likes to try out stuff, the core battle gameplay becomes rather lowbrow for a majority of the time, turning it into somewhat of a grind.

Some background:  I'm a backer of this game, huge fan of Battletech and long time mechwarrior fan.  This game could have been so much more than it is and to make matters worse, the devs have largely lost the trust of the community.  So much so that very very few people were willing to fund their followup game(known as transverse).
But lets get to the positives:
-The art design of the mechs is pretty nice.  Alex Iglesias nails the concept art.
-Its the only mechwarrior you're going to get that isn't ancient in game industry terms.
-Lots of mechs and variants to choose from and even more to customize.
-Good controls for the most part despite the defaults being goofy.  Check the options menu.
-Community Warfare features are starting to turn into a fairly appealing mode.
-The clan equipment sound design is top notch.  I wish the IS stuff sounded as nice.
And then the negatives:
-The weapon balance is awful and so many little jury rigged fixes have been placed on the system to "fix" the problem.  PGI's gameplay design team is horrid at math and has been since beta.
-The game is growing more and more poorly optimized and it stutters on systems that used to run it silky smooth with nothing to show for it.  NVidia cards can have serious problems despite the made for nvidia intro vid advert.
-The player base has largely been chased off by false promises and bad ideas so there aren't a lot of people playing the community warfare.
-The game is buggy enough to be frustrating.
-The community mildly toxic but not the worst.
-Clan tech is implemented as though its 1:1 with IS tech and you'll be matched against it as such.
-All these assets and no mechwarrior single player campaign...
-The mechs are horridly out of proportion.  This makes the speed of the mechs feel extra sluggish since you're closer to 20 meters up rather than 12.  Additionally, some mechs are punished a lot more by their size.  The Centurion, for example, is heavy/assault sized despite being half the weight of the Atlas.  Mechs should be in the 8-12 meter range not 6-20 meters.  That range is insane.  Update:  The recent rescale did nothing to fix this although it did bring mechs in the same weight class more in line with each other.
Hopefully you enjoy the game.  I grow quickly frustrated with the choices the design team makes.  Give the game a shot though, it is free to start playing after all.

Despite all the advancements in gaming today, the indie development world still manages to turn out some fairly simple games for those looking for a breather from the big name franchises of today. This is the case with
, an Action/Puzzle style title from independent publisher and developer named Yokcos. According to the official blog, it's a game that was "crafted in forty eight hours" through
, as well as
to create the audio. The venture has received a fair deal of praise from users and the media alike for being an example of "minimalism" in a complicated world, but does
have anything to offer gamers today, or is it actually something far more pointless?
is, by all accounts, a truly minimalistic experience. The core concept is simple: Avoid the incoming obstacles. You are presented a limited grid and are allowed to move frequently on it, as well as move off the edge to appear on the opposite side. There's also two different ways to play. The main allure is "Infinity", which is essentially a survival mode that pits you on a three-by-three field against various obstacles such as the bullets and random lines that can block your path to safety. There's also various short levels you can tackle, forcing you to stay alive until a rich block outline appears, which you need to let make contact with you in order to finish the stage. There is a total of thirty of those short stages.
Pretty much everything about this game screams the early days of Intellivision and Atari 2600 titles, just with a crisp presentation and a limited .MIDI soundtrack that sounds like a Punk song turned eight-bit against simple effects. The other dramatic alteration is more of a cosmetic one that lies within the Options menu, which manipulates the colors on screen. You have your traditional black and white/white and black appearance, but there's also a "changing hues", "rainbow", both of which are about the same thing, and finally "seizure", complete with a justified warning due to the intense strobe light effect it creates.
But, all this said, is it fun? Well, it all depends. Are you looking for something relatively simple but with a growing difficulty curve? If so, then
is something you'll get a kick out of. The main killing point is that this release costs two dollars US at this point. While it does offer a good amount of replay value thanks to "Infinity" mode, the game itself does get incredibly repetitive pretty quick. Plus, knowing it was developed in forty-eight hours does make you feel as though you're being a bit overcharged. If you're tired of long, convoluted stories with complex controls and just want something simple you can pick up and play,
is worth grabbing, though worth waiting for a sale on if you can't justify paying the full price given the aforementioned blog post description dismissing an extensive development regime.
Not worth two bucks. I give props to the people that put this together in 24 hours or whatever at Ludum Dare, but I have buyers remorse.

I would only honestly recommend this game on a sale if you aren't super interested, but if you are a huge fan of the retro platformer style as well as difficult games, it may be worth the full price.
Be prepared to die. A lot. No matter how good you are at these types of games because there are MANY cheap mostly unavoidable deaths unless you know they are coming. Trial and error is key here, unless you watch a guide. The game is also highly centered around 'cycles' where if you miss just 1 jump or snag yourself on 1 block, everything you remember about the level will be different when you reach it, and will likely kill you. If that doesn't turn you away too much it is for sure worth playing. It's very well made and comes with 60+ levels as well as some side-mission style content. Several unlockable characters with unique abilities exist as well as alternate costumes for certain characters. For a platformer it really offers a lot.
One thing I think the game has a problem with is one-off mechanics. A certain level will have a very difficult mechanic that you've not learned or been introduced to somewhere else and then it will be gone forever following that. It would have been better if each zone had revolved around a certain theme of level with one or a few mechanics being focused completely on for each zone.
As far as completion time, I 100%'d the game with all achievements at my 16.2 hours played. 8-9 of those were spent beating the main campaign, and nearly all the rest were spent on an annoying grind achievement. If you chose not to look up videos for the collectable locations, as well as some of the harder levels, it may take much longer to finish. Especially because the collectibles are annoyingly just hidden in breakable blocks or behind walk-through walls. I wish they had made the collectibles an extra challenge in the level like an inconvenient or difficult route rather than hiding them in ridiculous places.
I would say you definitely get a good amount of content especially for a platformer, and would definitely recommend playing it.

Superb, difficult precision platformer with a fully-realized NES aesthetic -- just far more content than would reasonably be crammed into a NES cartridge, including a ton of different characters with animated cutscenes.
If you've played any number of these super-difficult platformers you know there is a spectrum of fairness. At one end of the spectrum, the difficulty in games like Super Meat Boy is entirely up front: you can see every buzzsaw and spike before you even start to move. At the other, you have I Wanna Be The Guy, where apples don't just fall down from trees and kill you, sometimes they fall upwards because f*** you. They always intend that you die a lot; 1001 Spikes pretends that you have a limited supply of lives (... only 1000).
It's somewhere in the middle of the spectrum. Many levels in the first half of the game work as a logical progression of hazards, each slightly more difficult than the last, ranging from hard to seemingly impossible. A common pattern, however, is for the second of two similar-looking segments to hide this difficlty in some way (e.g., a safe spot the first time around now features a hidden deathtrap); this is inevitably discovered through trial and error. A related pattern is for a challenging segment to be immediately followed by a safe-looking death zone. High on finally getting past the hard bit, you relax your guard, and... "YOU ARE DEAD."
You can imagine the level designer(s), sitting there with trollface on, gleefully imagining players' screams of frustration.
Level designs really are superb, however, and the progression works both as training and as puzzle. My favourite levels are those where you can, and sometimes must, think outside the box, because what looks like the difficult path forward is actually a red herring. You work it out and you can't help but groan. Again, trollface.
The mian downside is that difficulty is uneven (e.g. I died 145 times before clearing level 4-4, more than twice as many times as any other level prior to world 9), which can be immensely frustrating. Levels can be skipped, which just prevents you getting the true ending, but it's worth suffering through them since avoiding the crucible might mean missing out on learning a necessary trick.

Mechwarrior online is a Free to play shooter where you pilot mechs from the battletech universe against other players, this game has a few features i really like and i felt the need to voice my own oppionons about this game, so let's begin.
#1 this game is free with in-game premium content. Now i know what you're thinking "OMG P2W BLEEEEEEH" i promise you it's nothing like the "World Of" games. The mechs you can access with only premium money are no more or less powerful than any other mech in the game. The only diffrence is a 30% boost to your chasis EXP and C-bills gained from gameplay, and of course a unique paintjob. You CAN buy only a limited amount of mechs before you start needing to buy mechbays, but even these go on sale and are usually only about $2.50 a pop usually. But once again, this game is free.
#2 This game is easy to learn and hard to master. When you boot up the game you get a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ of information thrown at you unless you play the tutorial, which is about 15 minutes long and explains everything you need to know about the basics of gameplay. BUT there are many high-level tactics such as twisting and jump-jet fluttering you'll need to learn about before you get to tier 1 or 2 play.
#3 This isn't call of duty! This game is a bit slower paced and about tactics and position. Teamwork will make or break you almost 100% of the time, don't expect to get many kills early on, it takes about 25 games before you start getting one or two kills.
#4 Trail mechs. My god do i love the devs for this. Every week or so the free mechs switch, and you never have to buy them, thinking about buying a timberwolf but you're not sure you want to spend 15,000,000 c-bills? play the trail version a few times and see if the mech suits your playstyle.
#5 This game is beutiful, the sound effects, maps, visuals, and mech designs are stunning and you really feel as if you're piloting a 30+ ton war machine. Plus the faction warfare map is awsome to zoom in on and look at all the diffrent planets. The battletech universe is incredibly lore-heavy and the game reflects that.
alltogether i give this game 9/10. the gameplay is amazing, as are the sound effects, but without a group of friends you won't have a whole lot of fun with the grinding.
now a few tips for new players:
your first 25 games you will get a "account injection: cadet bonus" this will give you a bunch of c-bills, you'' feel rich and want to buy a mech but take it from me: wait until you know what you're getting into! Outfittting a chassis takes A LOT of in-game cash and can eat your money up if you spend recklessly.
find yourself a mic and a player who knows a thing or two about this game, listen to what they have to say and you'll start crushing in public games!
Dont feel discouraged if you die without getting kills, damage is where new players need to focus, support your team and stay with the group. You can't take on 2 or 3 enemies by yourself!

I played for more than two years, played over 8,000 matches in that time, and participated in every worthwhile comp league before the comp scene died completely following the steam release. MWO was good for quite a while, with a fairly balanced meta and an active comp scene. A week prior to the steam release, they broke all of that, leaving the game in the worst state it's ever been in; this hasn't changed at all in the intervening months.
The devs are horribly incompetent, barely able to implement even the simplest of features in half a year of dev time. The latest mode added, which is a sloppy KotH mode that has all the polish of a 24 hour game jam, took them a year to put together. The latest new in-game mechanics took them half a year of work, and were discarded a week later because they were terrible and the community playtesters unanimously hated them.
There's a backlog of promised features a mile long that are all but forgotten in favor of bumbling balance changes, half baked ideas that get even less engineering work devoted to them, a slow trickle of poorly designed maps, and an endless parade of $100+ mech packs scraping the bottom of the barrel of canon mechs.
Add on to that a terrible community that's shrinking faster than at any point over the game's lifetime, and it's readily apparent that MWO is dead and gone, it just doesn't know it yet.

The Steam Controller is a completely different way of controlling your PC. It is not meant to replace conventional controllers. Rather, it's an entirely new type of input: two touch-pads for your thumbs.
Pros:
- Works well for basic tasks like browsing
- Controls feel responsive
- Good analog stick and buttons
- Typing is intuitive
- Fully customizable input mapping via Steam
Cons:
- Thumb strain is a big problem
- No second analog stick
- Inconsistent results per game
In conclusion, this controller is impressive at first, but the novelty wears off. Thumb strain is no good.

This game caught my eye with the fact it might play like masters of orion. This star based conquest game has alot of details to manage which after a few hours appears be a good of options. The interface is a little hard to get used to just alot of symbols and small buttons. The reseach system is pretty normal being a tree based items. The Ship editor is litte over simple but still useful. The AI is to be expected with turning their backs on you randomly. Interesting enough tho there is a system that determines their status with you based on actions and score. The multi player is a little slow but is nice in the fact every one takes turns at the same time. There is a player icon for all players that aren't done yet. The planet upgrades can get pretty interesting and change the game quite a bit. The heroes can get pretty powerful even staying on a system getting XP. I do feel the game can get a sluggish while trying to get better upgrades to defeat enemy fleets. Which can get annoying since they use a tactic where you can only attack once but if they split their ships up into a ton of mini ones so your planet is always under siege. All in all this game is really well built and has good game play.

Don't waste your money! I don't know why but for some reason, a decent amount of people seem to like the Endless Brand.  I bought both Endless games because of the reviews BUT, like Endless Legend, Endless Space is boring, clunky and just plain uniteresting. If you buy this game, do not expect an epic space battle like the ending of Mass Effect 3. In fact do not expect some sort of control over war affairs that you would expect in a 4X game. While it did provide the 4 "x's", it doesn't offer a complex gameplay that players wanted and expected in a 4X game.
Playing this game is like playing a facebook game. It felts like a point and click game. There is no such thing as a micromanagement. What they have is not enough. For example, you can't micromanage your Spaceships apart from making a fleet or "pimping them up". You can't even group up fleets to better defend yourself from a strong enemy. The battle scene is quite sad! You are literally watching a 60 second clip where the ship move to one direction while the other is right behind them.  There is not a lot of options you can choose from during a battle except for selecting "Battle Cards" which if you play the game for quite some time, it gets pretty boring and repititive.
The ship design is unimaginative piece of crap. Also, upgrading a ship changes the stats but not the appearance which can really break focus on the game. You may think that since you can pimp your ship that the apperance would look different but that is not the case. The battle animation is lack luster. Like I said, you don't even have any control of the movement of the fleet or try a daring strategy. The planets and systems are quite boring. There is no lore to them and you don't even feel any sort of feeling of belonging towards your empire.
If you are looking for a decent sim space/4x game, check out Sins of the Solar Empire.

Bully is one of the best game I've ever played, the nostalgia, the atmosphere, the soundtrack, the story, I could go on and on about why Bully is a masterpiece of a game more than worthy of a sequel.
Sadly, the PC version of the game is in a bad, broken stage. But if you want to play the game as badly as I did it won't be too much of a problem. The game crashes every 1-2 hours, so you have to constantly save the game after each mission or class (chances are you will have to re-do some of them due to the game crashing anyways) which does of course take away some of the immersion as you will always have that thought in the back of your head. So my advice is just that you regulary save and re-start the game as much as possible.
But looking beyond the crashes and other problems this version of the game suffers you will discover a truly amazing, one of a kind game, that I would even go as far to call a timeless classic.
The soundtrack is spot on, there's a small but interesting open world for you to explore on skateboard, bike, mopped and a few other vehicles/transportations.
You have a handful of "weapons" at your disposal such as marbles, a slingshot, fire-crackers and much more.
Bully is one of the games I'd say you have to try before you die, and since you can get it for really cheap during the sales there is no reason why you shouldn't pick it up and try it (as long as you can make peace with the crashing problems).

Well, it's like everyone says: It's GTA at a highschool. The gameplay and mission are great fun, the storyline and characters are funny, even if the dialogue is a bit clunky at times, and the world is interesting and immersive. What I particularly like is that the story follows exactly one schoolyear, so that at the start of the game it's fall, a few chapters later it's Halloween and winter etc. It really gives a sense of progress, like you're not just playing a game set on Groundhog Day.
The story does repeat itself a fair bit. Every chapter plays out basically the same: You meet a faction, you do some missions with them, then something happens that makes the faction hate you, you beat their leader to♥♥♥♥♥♥ and then they love you again. This very thing happens like 4 times in the game, and by the end you can see every betrayal coming from a mile away.
There's a lot of cool weapons and vehicles to unlock and use, like a spudcannon, cherry bombs and the slingshot. You can take classes in which you complete a little fun minigame to unlock weapons or clothing, or you can look for collectibles. I don't recommend trying to get all the collectibles though, because there are way too many of them and the rewards are disappointing.
Overall, I think this is a good game. Even though the story is a bit repetitive and the dialogue is a bit clunky, The gameplay is amazing, and it's a lot of fun. And in the end, that's the important part.

Alright I am going to break this into pros and cons. Honestly it is very hard for my to give a strict recommendation on this game as it truly falls into "If you like the pros more than the cons" deal. Alright first a little bit of background, I started with Mechwarrior 2 and have played nearly every game out there for the franchise so I was excited about this when I first downloaded it. However, over time I don't think it has lived up to my expectations for a variety of reasons, which will be listed in cons. I will continue to play the game (I really like the Battletech universe even if they are desecrating its dead carcass) but I won't ever sink money into the game. Alright into the pros and cons phase:
Pros:
A lot of the mechs you may know from games past are scheduled to be added in (at some point?) or are already in the game.
It's a mid scale (up to 12 v 12) mech game that does pretty decent.
It has nostalgia factor for a lot of people.
Some of the matchups can be quite enjoyable.
Cons: (aka why I won't spend money on the game)
The developers actively hate one side of the factions (the Clans), don't want them to exist and kneecap them at every available opportunity. The clan technology is suppose to be superior at this stage in the timeline. Instead IS mechs routinely have better options through their quirk system (which clan needs then to add huge weight, multiple slot options like super advanced targeting computers to catch up), are routinely buffed for output and exceed what clan can do (and are supposedly the weaker faction until much later in the timeline).
They continuosly abuse the idea of cannon within the established storyline, unless for some reason it lines up with the above point to continue curb stomping the Clans.
They don't even bother to try to line it up with any other game or the Table Top experience.
They can't make matches that make sense (lets make objective based gameplay where you get absolutely nothing from completing objectives, and force you to have issues completing events because you need the match score which comes primarily through mech damage). (See the faction warfare where invasions require you to destroy orbital cannons or scout intelligence, and neither gives you any score boosts even though that is your objective.)
They consistently hand out even more and more bonuses to the side that is already ahead in terms of strengths, but nothing to see here folks, move along. Meanwhile Clan tech receives nothing or actually gets nerfed further. I theorize this is because they would like everyone to stop playing clan, but there are too many die hard clansmen and clanswomen for that.
So like I said I will play this game for now (at least until the Battletech game comes out) but I won't spend money on it because they like to steam roll weaknesses into the faction I want to play. The developers "don't like them". I am sorry but if you want the license to an iconic universe that has two very distinct sides and you want to make money, your likes and dislikes don't matter.

I was an original founder back in Closed Beta.  I bought in because I loved the original PvE games and was looking forward to how this panned out.  I didn't end up playing long back then because the Meta-gaming was just terrible.  Stacked builds like Dual Guass Cats, and 170Kph Jenners that you could just not hit because of hitbox and shocking bad latency issues.  It was like old school shooters where you had to lead/guess half a second ahead of where your target COULD be.  Also it was very easy to lose funds in anything but a poorly equipped mech.  The fancy geared ones you just could not afford to run.  8 man teams coming into PuGs and just squashing Newbs wasn't good for keeping players interested either.
April 2016.  I decided to revisit, and it's changed.  You now can run whatever you can afford to build as most of the cost is in the initial purchase, and Repair/Rearm costs seems significantly lowered.  Possibly removed entirely.
Hit detection seems a lot better now even on 300ms ping to NA server.  There is an Oceanic server which is great for me.  The Metagaming BS has been trashed.  There doesn't seem to be any 'cheese' builds anymore.  However the more expensive Clan mechs still seem way better than any equivalent Inner Sphere design, and there is some serious inconsistency between model size/stature and actual tonnage.  Now there is Faction based warfare and rewards, and altough I haven't tried it yet  it does look interesting.

If you are a fan of space 4x games, then this is definitely worth a try.  Endless Space has replaced MOO2 as my favorite 4x game.  Yes, MOO2 was still my favorite (after all these years) until now.
The economy in this game is balanced very well.  It can take some practice until you learn some of the nuances of the FIDS system.  You can't just build the same exploitation on each planet.  Well you could, but each planet type is better suited to a different production type.  You will also have to decide between colonizing a terran world with an anomoly or a desert one with an artifact.  Which one will yield better FIDS?  Which one will allow you to progress faster than the rest of the galaxy?
The ship designs are not customizable in looks and style, only the modules you want on them.  This is not a complaint, as every game I've played where I could customize the look I did...for a few minutes.  Then I got bored with it and wanted to get back into the action.  You can, however, customize the attributes of the race that you choose to play as.  This is similar to other 4x games like MOO2 where you can set up your race to match your playing style to enhance your strengths and mitigate your weaknesses.  Better at research and expanding defensively?  Better at mass-producing fleets and colonizing aggressively?  Somewhere in the middle?  You can play that way.
The graphics are decent.  You do not get close-up views of the planets per se, but you can get up close with the ships in battle.  The music is great, and I find myself humming it to myself sometimes at work.
The gameplay is easy to get into and before you know it you will log 100 hours.  And then more.  And then more...

When we except a synthetic art such as movie or game, we use two kinds of human sense which is vision and hearing. If the vision is limited, sound brings something more and in opposit situation, vision do so. That's what proper direction is but how about in this game? Nope. Both of senses for this game got so lazy, it makes this game boring and juvenile. I can't even count how many ways of directions are limited! Fixed camera angle, repeating few face expressions, Scripted cheap-same sound effects... instead of good direction, what only we have from this game is neverstop-wordy words which fills the screen over and over. I feel like 1001 Spikes is the Lawful Evil counterpart to I Wanna Be The Guy's Chaotic Evil. Both are hard as nails and obsessed with killing you with surprise death traps, but IWBTG will do literally ANYTHING to score a cheap kill, while 1001 Spikes follows a more strict code. Everything works exactly like it's supposed to work, instead of the rules suddenly changing halfway through.
I feel like, when people try to make hard games, it's way too easy to resort to just being unfair instead of the more difficult to achieve "tough but fair" level, and I feel like 1001 Spikes reaches that level much better than a lot of it's contemporaries in the platform hell genre. You're obviously going to be dying a lot, but rarely as I was playing the game did I feel like it wasn't my fault. It didn't take long for me to able to spot certain traps at a glance and even for the ones that I couldn't I still often got a feeling that there was something waiting for me just up ahead. And it definitely helps that it treats death like Super Meat Boy does, spitting you out at the beginning of the level as quickly as possible to minimize frustration.
It's not perfect of course. A couple of the final levels ended up veering into ridiculous territory. Especially one section near the end of the game where you have to low jump over a bed of switch-toggled spikes with a deceptively large hitbox and on top of an ice block without accidentally pushing the ice block; an act that requires nothing less than pixel-perfect jumping and comes near the end of the level, meaning you're going to be redoing most of the level immeasurable times just for that one section. The final boss also veers into outright unfair territory. Aside from those moments, though, I found the game to be rather well-balanced in it's difficulty.

♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ Bonds is an indie, turn-based, tactics game where you control a party of up to four characters, exploring, fighting, and looting your way through many hours of content. You can have much larger armies of people to draw upon, recruiting more characters as the game progresses (including character you can make in the excellent character creator).
The combat system is fairly simple, but allows for a great deal of strategizing, and makes for some deep and difficult fights. It boils down to either taking a safe action, or a reckless action. If you use a safe action, your turn ends for the combat round, but you succeed at the action. If you use a reckless action, you can get another turn on the combat round, but you have a chance of fumbling, and exposing yourself to more damage. Every time you take a reckless action, your "risk" rating goes up, and the more risk you have, the greater a chance to fumble. Get enough risk however, and you get a combat advantage. It's a simple but excellent risk/reward system that sees both sides of a conflict pushing their risk to squeeze in as many combat actions per round as possible, while trying not to fumble.
The game feels like a mix of Japanese, tactical RPGs (Final Fantast Tactics) combined with 90s, Western CRPGs such as Baldur's Gate or even older PC RPGs, and a dash of rogue-likes. And I mean this in all the best ways as far as the game mechanics are concerned.
It doesn't have a deep story, so if you're looking for story driven games, you might want to skip this one. That said, it does have a lot of opportunity for emergent stories and story that happens mostly in your head with it's large world and wide range of characters. What story and writing the game does have is solid, if nothing mind-blowing. I haven't finished it yet though, so who knows where it might go.
The art style is definitely old-school, with a pixel graphic style. If you don't mind that sort of thing, it's very well done and looks great. There isn't any animation, with characters being essentially fixed images on the screen, but it is a one person developed game, and the great character creation system makes up for the lack of character animation imo. If graphics are a big deal for you though, this might not be for you.
The music is also solid and really sets the mood. Not much more to say about it, it's just very good. Again, a bit of a retro quality to it, but if that doesn't bother you, you'll enjoy it.
It's rated "mature" for what is essentially pixel-nudity, with plenty of naked men and women in the game content. Not much more beyond that though, with only one romance sub-plot in the game. Oh, there is also swearing. Just stating for people who want to avoid that sort of thing.
Overall, this game came out of nowhere for me, but really hit the mark. I've been really enjoying it, and would recommend it to anyone who likes this sort of thing.

I love this game. It's a truly amazing experience, especially given that it was made in 2011 (and still holds up very well!).
Graphics-wise, the game does show its age, but it doesn't take away from the experience in the slightest. Of course, certain textures won't have as much detail as we have become accustomed to, certain animations will appear slightly inhuman or other such events may appear, as they would with any older game. However, the artistic style of the visuals completely makes up for this, and I can still find myself easily immersed into the world of Deus Ex.
The level design and stealth mechanics make the game incredible to play, especially for a stealth enthusiast. Huge maps, with tiny details make the entire experience a nonstop adventure, with the constant search for the best path to infiltrate a given zone. The NPCs are also balanced, I didn't experience any seemingly omniscient demigods automatically knowing my exact position, and there weren't any deafblind ones either. Everything made sense.
Now, to one of my favorite parts, the story. I prefer not to say much, as it is something best discovered on your own, but it is AMAZING. I had no idea what to expect, and despite that my expectations were blown out of the water. Nothing is rushed, everything makes sense (Along with unexpected twists), nothing is overlooked and everything is thought out perfectly. I could not recommend it enough, especially for those who love a good story or who are looking to play Mankind Divided.
Finally, the music. Sends chills down my spine.
I strongly recommend this game.

Call to Power 2 is the second and final Civilization competitor (clone) made by a very different Activision than the one that merged with Blizzard. In fact this very game almost bankrupted Activision, and it shows. The development of game was released content unfinished, it is very buggy for its time, support was quickly dropped, and the development team was dissolved. However, some developers on their own time helped the Apolyton community try to understand and modify the promising game. A long time after, and yet a long time ago, a much healthier Activision released the source code, but as it was stripped of all comments, perhaps the full potential of the game has never been realized. Nonetheless it allowed a very extensive overhaul of the game, the benefits of which can be found in the Apolyton Edition, which maintains the game content as released, but few mods. But since the source code was released so late, and then so much time was required to put it to use, many more high quality mods never saw the benefit of these finishing touches.
Gameplay is actually very different from the Civilization games. Compared, Call to Power 2 is far more streamlined with constant and smooth progression through the ages. The tech tree and in-game guide called the "Great Library" is where this game really shines. It is much more mature and realist than Civilization games.

I'm an owner of the original call to power, when it still had civilization on its name before the rights were taken. That game was probably one of the most fun I've had as a child, and was my introduction to strategy based games along with age of empires 2, and I have no doubt I'd spent more than hundreds of hours on each.
I never got around to playing its sequel and had eventually forgotten about it until I foundthe activision's classics sale , in thoughts of buying for the nostalgia, as I've heard the games were just about the same, which ultimately I did.
I don't remember the game being this terrible.
It runs like utter crap, as oposed to the original. It is slow and choppy, does not work at a suitable framerate, the HUD is somewhat similar to the prior game, and had I not have some prior knowledge of how it worked, I would've deemed it just as intuitive as the gameplay.
The game also presents some issues. The one I found most upsetting was how I couldn't ALT+TAB away from the game or it would crash.
As for the graphics, maybe you should take it with a grain of salt considering it's an old game, but ultimately I feel the need to express that it looks horrendous on an 1080p resolution as this wasn't so much the case on the original. Besides, when it came to options within the game, I would have expected some improvement towards graphic settings, but the most you can manage is turn off certain effects in the game and change your resolution which is very disappointing.
Honestly, I'd stay away from it. Perhaps there is some mod that can make it run smoother, but I shouldn't have to be searching for that to have a fully functional game. If you're still interested however, I'd advise you to go look for a copy of the original. Fair warning however that it might not run depending on how updated your OS is at the moment.

I tried to get into this game but I couldn't.  As others have mentioned, space combat has some major flaws (features?) which make it all but unplayable for me.
1.) Rock-paper-scissors type of combat resolution.  I never enjoyed automated combat in GalCiv and didn't enjoy this in Endless Space either.
2.) Fleet logistics - As someone mentioned, a numerically superior fleet can lose to a smaller one simply due to the "tech tree" fleet size one can field.
3.) Player styles are limited.  You can't hyper-expand even with all the logistics ready; the game paradigm simply punishes you as its not in the developer's vision.
4.) Diplomacy behaves oddly.  You could be the best of friends one turn but accidentally send a ship into their borders and war is declared.
That said, the graphics were still very nice and ship designs were a treat (if somewhat visually lacking in the customization department).
Edit: I decided to give Disharmony a try after reading the feedback on my review and gave the game another run.  It seems much improved over the time I orginally bought it.  Combat is still a bit of a chore but no longer the confusing gameplay I had originally concieved.  It still requires more luck than actual tactics in my opinion but with the expansion is a lot easier once I understood how logistics worked.  This brings my decision to actually recommend the game but just barely.  In general, I would still prefer games of the type like MOO2, SOTS, or even Sins of a Solar Empire but I can see (and enjoy) the appeal of Endless Space.

The puzzles in this level were very "gotcha," traps that attack you with little to no warning, requiring twitchy game play and memorization of all the levels after dying multiple times. The story was badly written (to the point of satire/parody). After the 15 minutes were up, I watched the ending on youtube and the writing never got any better.

Spikes should not be completely invisible to the player until they step on them. Overall the game is really frustrating for all the wrong reasons. I love games that are really hard, like Super Meat Boy, but this levels are designed to be progressively more unfair rather than more genuinely difficult. Once I know how to beat a level I can beat it in about 5 tries. A game that would normally take about 50 tries and 30 minutes to complete is artificially lengthened by these cheap traps in literally every level to the point where some levels take upwards of 100 deaths the first time you play them.
