The  store page may not make the best first impression, but it turns out that it is actually a pretty decent game, with a somewhat unique* combat system.

Each turn, you can have your unit “act” which will move, attack, cast a spell, whatever. Doing so ends the unit’s turn. Or, you can take a “reckless action” which will let you attack/et cetera and then place you at the back of the initiative order allowing you to take another action in the same turn. Each reckless action carries an increasing chance of a fumble, which immediately ends your turn. This “press your luck” mechanic adds a fair amount of depth to the combat system.
Outside of combat, you march your people around the island killing monsters, and other assorted jerks, building strongholds, and recruiting more miscreants for your company. Inventory and abilities are pretty streamlined and may rub some people the wrong way. The quick game play, and risk mechanic keeps the game from feeling too shallow.
Overall, pretty entertaining. Each encounter/map plays in around 20 minutes or less, so this is
an ideal short break sort of game.
*Vagrant Story also used a risk mechanic, though a bit differently.

At first glance and upon a relatively short amount of fiddling, this looks promising. I'm feeling optimistic about it, over all! I mostly wanted to be sure it's not a "definite refund" title before letting it sit too long.
The character customization is decently robust, although limited to orc/human. The skill and ability management is rather interesting using a 3x3 grid setup, where anything in the same row/column contributes accordingly. The game is definitely taking a shot at a mature audience, which in my opinion is good!
Some of the chatter text is a bit too often, or at least not varied enough to be that frequent. Furthermore, the initial controls and such are not at all intuitive, leaving you fumbling around a bit when you begin the game. It definitely has a lot of the jive and feel, at first glance, of FFTactics and such, though seems to lack the deep class/job/skill progression of those games, as far as I can tell at this point.
Graphically it's overall.. decent to good. Biggest draw back is some of the animation is done via very tacky squash-stretch, which just looks like junk with pixel art, unfortunately. :( The pixel art is solid, although the resolution chosen is a bit off - the pixels feel a bit too big and some aspects are a bit too nondescript because of this, but overall it's not bad and has surely been done far, far worse, for hat that counts.
Edit: So I finally came back to this after a while and really dug in. Overall I still leave it as a definite "Yes!" but it comes with a few caveats.
The biggest is combat mechanics, characters, skills, etc. There just isn't enough here. Every character has a physical attack and maybe magical attack, each of which can be modified slightly by weapons (affecting mostly reach and damage, plus a potential added debuff effect) or other items (such as those that change the "element" of your magic) but that's it. No really choices to make, so much so that all combat is handled via right-click, because you never have more than one option based on where you are. For me, this is a crippling flaw for a turn-based tactical style game.
Coupled with the fact that the AI is, frankly, pretty dumb.. well.. the combat quickly turned into a one-dimensional slog that ended up Not Very Fun (tm). I'd throw my more tank-y character up front and defend, then queue up everyone behind them with magic/reach. The AI would never fight any other character, and I'd win. Funny enough, though, it was all but necessary - enemies can hit staggeringly hard at times, and there's not much you can do to mitigate it besides positioning.. and some characters, such as Ratlings, have dramatically reduced health as a racial trait, making them incredibly too-squishy for a game like this!
But with that said.. it's still pretty solid. Given the development team and the nature of the game, I still think it warrants a play for those who are curious about it and its genre. It lacks a lot of depth that, in my opinion, gives games like this the 'Fun' when it comes to their combat, but otherwise.. there's a few nitpicks but none too major. It'd be nice of the 'Labor' thing was a bit better explained, as far as how to generate it, for example.
I really like the way they handle skill choices though with the 3x3 grid and spillover points, that's pretty neat! I just wish it all did a bit more and there were some choices to be made in combat besides position, bottleneck, kill. It's really the only shortcoming that really takes me out of the game, because I enjoy most every other aspect.
Alot of charm and interesting plot/story progression. Loving it so far can't wait to see whats next.

In as few words as possible, this game's a stellar example of what tactical RPG's should strive for. I adore this game and if you're a fan of the genre then I'm pretty confident you will, too.
The most important feature in any game, I believe, is the gameplay. ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ Bonds does a magnificent job of keeping the game just complex enough not to frustrate you but also give you plenty of options to micromanage your party.
You start off with a series of questions that, depending on your answers, determines your first party member and nudges you in the direction you want your class to be. However, there's no concrete classes in this game. You're able to mix and match your characters however you want when they level up. With every character in your party, you're able to level them up, equip them with a weapon, armor and accessory, and upgrade their inventory. After a while you're also given the chance to start up a stronghold. Depending on how much labor you accumulate, you're able to afford bigger and better (and super cool looking) strongholds that'll allow you more party members and passive NPC's such as merchants, healers, appraisers etc. There's also a chance you can recruit enemies if their health is low enough and you have the right skill.
As for the battle system, it's fairly simple in that when you left click you move and if you right click you do an action. Depending on where your cursor is you'll end up attacking an enemy, defending or healing an ally. Personally I'd like a bit more control over my actions and some more options than right clicking an enemy to auto-attack but it really doesn't bother me that much. Even though it sacrifices a bit of the complexity I personally enjoy from a tactical RPG, the system seems to work out pretty well regardless. Depending on the accessory or weapon you have equipped, it can change up how you attack so at least there's that. It still feels good and it's fun as all hell.
As far as the design goes: it's gorgeous in how grotesque it is. When I first saw this game I assumed it was just going to be some slapstick edge-fest but the theme actually suits it perfectly. The island you were left on is filled with magnificent looking monsters and loaded with interesting areas, many of which have their own story. As dead and dreadful as this game feels, it couldn't be any more alive.
So give this game a shot. It was made by one developer and you can tell they are passionate about this genre. They earned every bit of my money with this title.

It's faithful to the original Doom's run and gun style, but it has some really weird problems. It would get 10/10 for gameplay if it had a proper save system.
Inventory:
Right at the beginning of the game, it says F1 and F2 are used to switch inventory items, and LCtrl is to use items. There is also an upgrade tree for inventory items. I'm currently 8 hours into the game and I have never found an inventory item. I'm still hoping I eventually find one.
Saving:
There's no way to manually save the game. This is a huge  problem because the auto saves are based on plot points rather than locations or a timer. Dying can easily set the player back by 20 or 30 minutes. All of the found secrets are lost, all of the enemies need to be killed again, all of the items need to be picked up again. Although the game has a lot of secrets and areas to explore, the game severely punishes players for exploring. You might die because Doom Guy didn't grab onto a ledge you expected him to grab, and now you're back to where you were 30 minutes ago. This forces an ultra conservative play style that clashes with the run and gun theme of the game.
Data Corruption:
The game crashed when I was about 2 hours into playing, and my save file was corrupted. Since there is no manual saving, and the auto save only keeps 1 save state, this means a single crash can wipe out all of your save data. All of your secrets are gone, all of your little doom guy trophies are gone, all of your upgrades are gone.A few people on the internet have complained about losing save data when they're deep into the game, and those people are justifiably angry as hell. This also means you shouldn't play Doom if your computer has any stability problems or if your neighborhood has power problems. If you get a blue screen or a power failure while playing Doom, there's a good chance all of your data will be corrupted. It's just bad game design to not allow manual saving.

All of my experience on this game is with at least one other person I know, I note this to ensure a review that's fair by playing the game the way I imagine it was meant to be experienced.
To cut it short for those who don't want to read; the game is mainly ruined by its community. I waited all these hours before making this review just to make sure I didn't make a mistake.
I originally started playing this game due to wanting a game other than Counter-strike to play with my colleagues at work. This turned out to be a very good choice due to how well it runs on my work computer. It is an i3 with Intel HD4000, quite low specs compared to the majority of PCs today.
I'll start with praising how well optimized this game appears to be; I get about 45 fps solid on lowest settings, and it looks great. I have experienced it on my home computer, and the graphics are of course, even more impressive; but that's not where I choose to play this game.
The game has a cool concept; build your own gun and fight in teams in various game modes. When you first play it, you'll get a very TF2-style vibe from it. It's fast paced and cartoony.
The first problem arises in the perspective of third person. This isn't a heavy criticism, because the developers are trying something a bit different here; setting third person in a fast paced environment. In games like this, I like to be able to look around a lot, checking my back, and it gets a bit annoying with the camera behind you. This is just my personal criticism, so I'm sure some people like it this way.
There is something incredibly off-feeling about the aiming in the game, someone I know also noted this. I'm experienced in playing shooters, and I cannot at all get the hang of this, after 70 hours. There is some weird depth-perception issue for me, where I will often shoot the ground in front of myself, instead of an enemy further back. I can't put my finger on this, but I'm going to note it in the review (and yes, I have increased the FOV).
Next, the servers and client issues. There is a lot of client-side control in this game, it seems. You will often die, but still manage to kill someone after it's stated you are dead; simply due to lag. You might not see yourself die for a few seconds, giving you chance to shoot at people before it updates. With the gamemode 'Jackhammer', the hammer carriers will very often kill each other at the same time. Some might say it adds more fun into the game, but I find it mildly fustrating and in general it just looks buggy.
Now, the main gripe. The community. To put it simply, the community is not what you expect. It's not friendly like TF2, nor is it as awful as counter-strike. It's worse. You will get a lot of arguing in the chat between players, and constantly spammed with 'ez', regardless of the state of the game. But that's not really it.
It's the amount of cheaters that infest this game. The game developers, as far as I can tell, haven't put a lot of effort into countering cheaters. There is a report function, but I have no idea if that actually works, of course. Some cheaters are more obvious that others, but due to the way the community is, you'll often bump into these people the next day, and the next day, and so fourth, as I've experienced. Now, these players do get banned, eventually; but the fact it goes on for so long is pretty terrible.
One factor I've also noticed regarding gameplay is the unbalance of the weapons. I say unbalance, because I have been unsuccessful in reaching the damage other players have with very similar guns. I've had people with standard-looking pulse guns that kill you in three hits, without reduction in firing speed. Now, this could be part of the cheating fiasco, simply aimbots shooting the head for extra damage, but it's not really possible to tell.
I hesitated for a long time for atleast 30 hours of gameplay, deciding on whether to recommend this game or not. It's a cool game, but in the end, the community just makes it not worth it. I also don't really like the boasting-emotes the developers put out there, just adds to the doucheyness experienced.

I bought this gamepad when it first came out, for ~$60.  I had high hopes of finding a gamepad that could do well with all my non-FPS games.  Sadly, this is not the case.
I've tried this controller with a few platformers, a couple racing games, some third-person shooters, and a couple flight sims, and found that it never had a fully-functioning pre-made configuration, forcing me to emulate the already-crappy keyboard/mouse controlls as Steam Controller buttons.  The track pads are either way too sensitive/"twitchy" or not nearly sensitive enough, making them all but useless.  The D-Pad presure points work OK, but don't have enough tactile feedback to work well with platformers.  Getting trigger half-pulls to register properly is a pain in the rear, and simply won't work on some games.  To get a working setup often takes hours, and I'm just not that dedicated to using a Steam Controller.  If there were an option to have it "just pretend to be an XBox controller", that would be a vast improvement over how this controller currently performs; but really, it needs to have 2 joysticks to compare.  The trackpads just aren't that great.
I hear it's good for FPS games, relative to other gamepads, but I have yet to see someone play an FPS as skillfully with a gamepad as can be done with a keyboard and mouse.  That control schema just doesn't do it for me.  I've heard it's good for Portal and other Valve games, but I've already played those to death, and probably won't seriously get back into that type of gameplay until Half-Life 3 comes out (ahem...).
I'm back to using an old XBox 360 gamepad for all my non-FPS games.  I hope Valve makes another attempt that actually works well with most games, but for now, the only honest review I can give is a negative one.

So, good game.  Definitely worth a download to try it out.

So let's get one thing clear, is it perfect? No, not exactly. Along side a few glitches that are rather annoying, but not game-breaking, combat seems a tad generic. I've found myself many a times taking cover, lining up an easy shot, and quickly popping headshots left and right without taking damage. Making things unnaturally easy.
But other than that, if you enjoy a good variety of various combat styles, I'd highly reccomend this game, as it not only allows you to go full on guns blazing, killing everyone (including civilians with little to no consequence..), you also have the ability to become a ghost, avoiding combat all together (except for bosses of course), and you can do everything in between as well.
My first playthrough was a mix of stealth and assault, where I'd kill those who stood in my way, and those who could be completely avoided, I did so. I definitely feel that this game has a lot of choice, not only in your choice on combat, but heavy moral choices as well.
When it comes to the moral choices of the game, it can be a little generic (for today's standards) being the simple "So and so did this, but for what he precieves to be a good reason; should I choose option 'A' where it allows him to get off scott free, or option 'b' where I tunr him in, etc. etc. (this was a hypothetical situation, while there may be somthing similar to it in game, the one I've stated was falsified to bring forth a point).
Also, staying on the subject of morality, it doesn't seem that the moral choices you make at arbitrary times, like one point where you're forced to choose between one of two (techiqally 3) choices (no spoilers, but those who have played it, should know what I'm talking about.) I thought this choice would be optimal for the overall ending I get, but instead it seemed to not make a difference at all.
When it comes to the glitches though, it's not so much bad things, but mostly just graphical twitches when in dialog with another character. Like one moment they'll be looking at me, then they do a nice T-pose and look the other way. Other than that, I haven't experienced any severe glitches.
Overall I'd have to rate this game a solid 8.5/10, simply because of the seemingly arbitrary moral choices that overall don't mean anything. I will definitely be playing this game more over time.
Definitely worth a buy.

Deus Ex: Human Revolution is a first-person/rpg style story-heavy game set in a world where cybernetic enhancements, also known as augmentations, are taking over and quickly redefining  what it means to be human.  These augmentations serve to improve and build upon the human condition by providing its hosts with superior physical and mental characteristics that surpass what an unenhanced body is capable of.  For some people, augmentations can be used in defense of the greater good such as ridding the streets of dangerous criminals.
Not everyone believes augmentations should be so widely accepted though. As you will find progressing through the story, there are those who seek the abolishment of augmentations due to the threats they pose against ordinary folk - those threats being an establishment of dominance, control and overall superiority.  The evolution of the human species is brought into question and whether it is okay to interfere with its progress by introducing unnatural enhancements into the fold. Corporate greed plays a major role in the midst of this revolution as well - groups with a lot of money seek to use augmentations for their own malicious purposes.
Deus Ex: Human Revolution has a deeper and significantly more profound narrative than most games you will ever play.  Throughout the game you will be forced to make some questionable choices that raise philosophical and ethical concerns relative to real life.  The gameplay is an amalgamation of stealth similar to Splinter Cell where you must take down opponents without being seen or avoiding them altogther, and guns-blazing action just like a traditional first person shooter except you have unique augmentations and abilities at your disposal.
In closing I should mention that from my own experience the game is not without its STRICTLY technical hiccups.  A good bit into the game the hotkey tab where all your equipment/food/drinks are no longer appeared on the screen - it completely vanished and not only that the hotkeys themselves stopped working.  I had to manually go into my inventory to equip weapons, use items, etc.  Additionally, the hotkey tab would occasionally randomly decide to appear in the middle of the screen on the far left while I was playing.  Other issues I had included the reticle of all my weapons disappearing entirely.  I arrived at a point in the game where I could no longer properly aim with my weapons, making long range combat so frustrating I gave up on doing it.  I should also note that there is a setting to turn the reticle off but I did NOT tamper with this whatsoever.  The last but rarest issue I came across was the inability to use cover. It happened a few times so it was not a huge hindrance.
Despite some of the technical mishap I encountered, that apparently nobody else I have talked to has, the game is a masterpiece. The handful of inconveniences, at the end of the day are negligible all because of the satisfying experience it had to offer.

FIX for random crashes every 10 min:
Open the registry editor:  "Run" (Win+R), then type "regedit"
Find this path in the registry:
HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Contro l\Session Manager\Memory Management
Double click on "PagedPoolSize". Hexadecimal is listed first. Change the "Value Data" to one of these below:
Note: You only need to enter EITHER Hexadecimal or Decimal.
Code:
Megabytes___Hexadecimal__Decimal
192Mb______0c000000____201326592
256Mb______10000000 ____268435456
384Mb ______18000000____402653184  (use this for Bully: Hexadecimal or Decimal)
Default______0___________0 (Remember to restore the value after finishing the game)
Also:
+ Run game as "Administrator" and with compatibility mode: Windows XP (Service Pack 3)
+ Turn off FRAPS (If it's on)

Played this game for over 50 hours off the steam, I don't regret a single minute spent with it. If you love 4X strategy games, this game has everything in spades.
Empire menagement is enjoyable, there's also an option to automate your empire growth if it becomes too tedious to manage yourself (I found the system to be very smart, and prioritize the upgrades well).
The ambience is fenomenal, it all feels like you are trully in space. Visually the game looks very nice, and the design of the cares and the whole overworld feels unique and alien, which is a trademark of all Amplitude games. Thanks to that, the game feels very fresh and different from the competition, while still remaining familliar gameplay wise.
The combat is where the game is the most different. I have heard a lot of different opinions about it, all of them very split between hating it and loving it. Personaly, I find it very thematic and fitting for a 4x game, while also very enjoyable to watch the spectacle of your ship armada blasting the oposition to pieces (or the other way around...).
You do not have direct control over the combat flow, you can only select the ship formation and change the targetting of your fleet over the three combat phases (long range, medium range, melee). Although you do not control the fight, there are two deciding factors in the combat that you directly control. One of them is giving a special order each combat phase that changes the performance of your entire fleet, you can order your fleet to do various things depending on your commander experience and perks. There's a varriety of orders, ranging from ordering a full out assault and neglecting the power to the defensive systems, disrupting enemy missle attack, to ordering full power to deflectors or an offensive retreat. The trick to the system is predicting what the other opponent is going to choose, because the orders counter and are countered by some other ones. For example, if your enemy chooses to enchance his deflectors next phase, but you order to direct all power to offensive systems and disable defences, you will overpower his deflectors and do major damage to his fleet. That system allows to win (or lose) fights that would normally be impossible, or do way more damage than anticipated with very little ships. It also emphasizes levbeling up your fleet commanders, beacuse the more experienced commanders can use more orders that are also more powerful, and utilize fleet's ships to a better degree.
The second important factor in the combat is ship design. The ships can do three different type of weapon damage, and use three different types of weapon defences to counter them. Every weapon can also be calibrated to be more effective in different phases of the battle (for example a long range plasma weapon will have very good accuracy and hit enemies during long range phase, but when they get into melee they won't be as effective as melee plasma weapons that have lesser accuracy but much better rate of fire). Designing a fleet with ships that directly counter what enemy has is a very good and effetive way at overpowering it, but they will do the same to you if you don't switch it around. Sticking to one ship design will get you killed very easily, and building ships that are good all-around will make them much less effective at fighting specialized fleets. There's a lot of tactics to explore, you can design ships that serve only as damage sponges and place them at the head of your fleet and try to absord fire, while your glass cannon back line blows the enemy up, but that tactics can be countered if your enemy chooses to spread his fire, and so on. The combat is way more about preparation and planning, rather than execution during the engagement itself. That gives it a very unique feeling, and makes you feel like a tactical mastermind if your careful scheeming works perfectly.

What Endless Space did right
Smooth 4X gameplay
Endless Space plays great with smooth 4X gameplay. it plays a lot like a Civilization game, with the player having to manage your government, your tech, your military, and foreign relations.
Strategic Combat
In Endless Space instead of directly controlling battles you choose your battle strategies. like EMPs, Missile Barriers, and the such. choosing the right battle strategy can help you win against even a larger fleet.
Epic Thematic Battles
once you've chosen your battle strategy the only thing to left to do is sit back and watch the fireworks. getting to see your epic fleet destroy (or be destroyed) is just great.
Lots of factions
Endless Space features 12 factions with their own lore, game art, and space ship design. to add to that you can also create your own faction with their own traits.
Custom fleets
in Endless Space you can choose what weapons and systems your ships have, this means you can make ship designs for certain purposes like planet invasion or fleet carrier.
Heroes

The Lion's Song is a beautiful Point & Click Visual Novel with no real Puzzles.
The game mainly takes place in Austria in the city of Vienna some time before the First World War, overall the game goes for a realistic vibe with creative artistic touches--and in so doing break with the stale humdrum of the average adventure game, were the genre has been stuck since its silly inception--albeit, it for instance portrays Freud as being more inane than he was.
We mainly follow a female violinist, a male portrait painter, a female University mathematician and  humans related to these three as well as a journalist. We get to choose the main casts life choices, be they small or more significant as we're taken through a beautifully structured narrative, which is rather warm and profound in its simplicity and humane relevance.

This is, without question, one of the most beautiful games I've ever played. Mipumi provides three seemingly disparate stories in the first three episodes, with a finale that ties them together in a very emotionally satisfying (but bittersweet) way. The choices you make along the way do influence the course of the storyline, but not always in ways that you might expect. The art and soundtrack are also quite excellent. Play this game, and play it again and again.

Undoubtedly one of the greatest point and click adventure games ever conceived.
The Lion's Song takes interactive storytelling and interactive art work to a new level, and is indeed a level I've never before experienced (and I've played hundreds of point and click adventure games in my time).
There was a definite standout point within chapter 2 where I instinctively knew what I wanted my responses to be at a particular point within the game, but I was nevertheless still unprepared for the emotional response I would subsequently encounter. I can't really describe it. All I can say is that I was so absorbed within that particular scene that I didn't much care for the other possible responses I could have chosen, for I was motivated purely by my passion to exert my own feelings; the responses to which seemed to just flow perfectly.
I will end my review here and finalise it as and when the last chapter is released next week, but this is a masterpiece!

The Lion's Song is a retro-styled point-and-click adventure with a focus on choices and story, and the first episode tells an inspiring tale accompanied by beautiful music. There is no inventory management of any kind, just the story and the player’s decisions, and this simplicity greatly amplifies the emotional experience as a whole. The way the writing and the melody subtly change depending on the inspirations players choose in their composition is also a nice touch. Replaying the episode multiple times for the achievements dispels much of this magic, however.

An amazing RPG, it's a lot of fun to make different characters because there are so many looks to choose from, and there's also so many different skill combinations (it pays to play around with the crime+guilt thing in the beginning, trust me). ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ Bonds brought back so many memories of spending days/weeks playing the Exile games on my junky Mac back in the 90's. Hits the buttons that has me searching every nook and cranny for possible secrets and items as well as picking up and keeping every seemingly useless item in case it can be used later.
I bought the game prior to it coming to Steam and most of my 20+hrs was spent trying to get a bigger and better Stronghold and improving the services I could get(and I was still on the first section of the island). Speaking of the Stronghold, unlike other games where you can get alot of party members that ultimately get sidelined when you pick your favorites, the people you recruit can still passively contribute.
The character creation has a good amount of choices and its very nice to see that the actual crime your accused of can also effect your character. Another thing to note is that if you create multiple character templates theres a chance you'll run into them in-game. And for the more creative people out there, in the game folder, theres the standard Read Me file but it contains instruction on creating custom sprites for an even more unique look; heck I think I recall watching a stream where the dev used Garr's sprite from Breath of Fire 3 and had him runnin around in-game busting up monsters and such.
The combat can take a lil time to get used to it but once you get it down its smooth sailing from there. The combat paths you choose for characters to take can make or break you so be careful, thankfully though it isn't permanent if you find your current build isn't doing quite like you expected. There's a reset function in one of the early maps you can use for a fee that will take you back to square 1, literally, so you can experiment  with what does and doesnt work(be wary though, the reset function can have a sublte consequence  to those who aren't your main character, won't say what >:) ).
Other things I liked: that exploring and finding bits of lore here and there rewards you with answers to questions like why so many/only male orcs at the character creation. The campfire scenes and hidden map events, the realisticly expected things like a ♥♥♥♥♥house(and the choices offered) or the strong treating the weak like crap, your action/inaction having consquences etc etc.
There's alot more I could say but I think its pretty clear that I found it worth the money and recommend the game. If you do pick it up I do hope you enjoy yourself!

This game was a total surprise for me. I've never heard about it, didn't think it would be much fun, and the price seemed too high. I almost went passed it, but then heard that the game had a demo you can get it on their website and it's pretty lengthy. After playing it for a couple of hours - I was sold!
The combat is quite challenging and you have to think about stuff like "Do I run from the map now or do I try and get a higher EXP multiplier? Do I try and recruit the enemy or just finish it off? Do I use one of my super valuable healing items or do I just defend, hope for the best, and then eat some food after the battle?".
I've played it all day and I think I only made a dent in the campaign, they weren't about it being long and handcrafted. Hell even the lore and the writing are deep and well crafted, something I really didn't expect.
If you like turn based RPGs in short, if you like turn based RPGs, beautiful pixel art (and including orc pixel ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s), morally grey areas (your character can be a "Violent Buggerer") and nice retro tunes - then you should totally check it out.
The only "con" so far is the lack of character animations, which is a bit disappointing, but I guess animating all of the movement would have cost a ton, so I can see why they've done it.
If the devs are reading this, my main suggestion would be adding the demo to Steam, it would really help people make a decision.

I'd already beaten this game once, and was about to beat it again, before it came out on Steam, and I re-purchased it just to support it a little more. Great dev, love the game, and glad to see it doing well! So, on to the review:
Pros:
1. The dudes. Let's not beat around the bush: If you're into bara fellas duking it out with half-naked monster guys, hop into this game ASAP and don't look back. Don't even bother reading the rest of this review; just buy the game and thank me later.
2. The music. Atmospheric, finely-crafted, always sets the tone well, and very fitting aesthetically.
3. The character creation. Separate from the presence of burly blokes, the breadth of options available for your main character (as well as any NPCs you inevitably want to craft) is really quite nice. Lots of body types, fashion options, and color choices, along with the unique "What is your crime?" and "Are you guilty?" options.
4. The writing. Engaging, humorous when appropriate, with touches of melancholy and surprising horror here and there. Occasionally sentimental when an NPC decides to settle down by the fire to chat with you. I was also pleasantly surprised by the story, much more unique and thought-provoking than one would expect from a "prison island" premise.
5. LGBT+ friendly and body-positive. Should be obvious, but may as well say it outright.
Cons:
1. Relatively shallow combat. Although the stat allocation system is neat and there is technically a variety of combat options, it's fairly easy to figure out a simple strategy or two and just proceed with few changes. The risk system is engaging and interesting, a solid idea, but it surrounds a combat system that is otherwise quite basic. For me, this is fine, but be wary when you see the "tactical" in "tactical RPG".
2. Animation-light. The sprites almost never actually change except for minor warping, with movement achieved through "hopping" on grids. While the digital paintings are lovely when you get them, most of the game has rather simplistic visuals overall, with animations being the most obviously lacking feature.
I liked this game enough to buy it twice. That should say something. Regardless, I hope this review is helpful.

I don't think a lot of these reviews do the steam controller justice. IMO this is the best gamepad on the market.
Ergonomics
Even though the shape isn't what we are used to when we think of controllers, it fits very comfortably in the hand. I am easily able to use all the buttons and without any discomfort. The layout takes a bit of time to get used to, with the face buttons in a different place than normal, but overall no problems here at all.
Construction
Feels pretty light, but still very solid. It has a nice feeling in the hand. No problems here.
Back Grips
This is what sold me on the controller. There are no other gamepads anywhere near this price point that have buttons on the back. This is absolutely key for any games that use the right stick (touch pad in this case) for looking around, since you can access them while keeping your thumb on the pad, and games that sometimes need X & B or Y & A simultaneously. I've occasionally resorted to using a very uncomfortable 'claw' grip on the controller in the past to get around this limitation, so this was a huge selling point for me and it did not disappoint.
Dual stage triggers
I was really surprise by how well the dual stage triggers work. They feel a lot like a gamecube controller, with an analog portion and then a solid click at the end. Both of these sections can be mapped to independent actions, which effectively adds 2 more back buttons. I find that now that I am used to it I never activate the second stage accidentally when using the analog portion
Hair triggers
The triggers can be configured to use haptic feedback to simulate a trigger stop in the analog stage of the trigger. This is great for anything where you want to perform an action repeatedly and quickly (like shooting a semi-automatic for example). Its not the same as a real trigger stop would be, but I honestly think its pretty close. A very good feature.
Track Pads
The focal point of the whole controller is the dual touch pads. They work excellent. For games where you control the camera its about as good as with a second stick, but in games with aiming or mouse movement it is phenomenal compared to the usual dual sticks. Its still not as good as a real mouse, and you aren't going to be playing CS:GO on it but I don't have any trouble playing slower paced game that use mouse input or single player fps games.
They are also pretty good for casual browsing on the internet/computer. The virtual keyboard valve has created for them is good compared to going through letters individually, but still a grind compared to a real keyboard. Its more like typing on a smart phone, but a little slower.
Cons
My main con is that there is no real rumble support. Valve seems to be working on simulating rumble using the haptic engines, but so far its not great.
Overall
I don't know of any other gamepad that can offer functionality competitive with this controller, so I absolutely think it is the best controller on the market for PC gamers.

I've always wanted to write a proper review for this game but I still can't be arsed to write a lengthy, detailed writeup over a video game; everything I'd want to say has already been said again and again anyways. So I'll just get down to the important stuff.
This game has its pros and cons but the important thing to remember is that it -IS- free and if you play semi-regularly the grind doesn't really feel too hard. Everything performance-wise you can get with real money you can get with in-game money except for Hero mechs, which aren't even remotely P2W but do have unique playstyles and loadouts compared to their standard variants. Also, some of them look sexy as hell. (Most of the pay model in this game is cosmetic btw)
There are a LOT of mechs you can pick from and decent variety between the individual models. You can customize the loadout and there's a fair bit of playstyle flexibility for MOST of the mechs. However, this game suffers from a terrible state of "forced" meta due to the way rebalancing is handled (or not handled), making things considered non-meta really hard to be competitive in. Still, if -you- like it and you can put in the performance, go for it and do you. All my clan mechs are ballistic-based and I love the unexpected facetime and carries I get against people expecting pulse vomit or streams or other meta Clan stuff.
This game hates AMD FX processors!!! Full stop. It's a known and somewhat long-term issue and, while not incapacitating, can be really frustrating because it causes small, infrequent hiccups/bottlenecking during gameplay. For everyone else, this game has the optimization of a flint axe! Bear that in mind if you crank up the graphics settings. However, the mechs on higher settings look amazing, as do the particles and shaders. The LODs are terribad but I guess that's the price you pay for super-sexy giant stompy robots with full first-person cockpit views.
Another big con for this game is that the developer doesn't always make the best or brightest decisions in regards to balance passes and content updates. But!!! Things have been way better in that department in the past few months/past year, and we actually got the new CW when they said they would put it out, so that's refreshing.
TLDR: Should you play this game? Yes. It's free. It's fun. There's no P2W. At least give it a shot before you decide you hate it.

There's a review of this game by StrictlyHappenstance (near the top of the Most Helpful Reviews), which seems an unecessarily existential review for a 'free to play'. But I have to say, I concure.
Here's the pitch.
The 'game' on the surface, allows the player to run an expanding number of several 'types' of businesses, each 'type' costing expenetially more to buy, but being expenentially more profitable, whillst taking expenentially more time for it's profit's to come to fruition.
The good thing about the game is also why it provokes such exestential thoughts (for me and StrictlyHappenstance anyway), namely that it's essentially just a calculator working on layers of multiplications simultansously which is all (so long as the player adds no more calculations) completely predictable. Thus allowing the program, having been shut down and reopened a minute, hour or day later, to 'calculate' the progress of the players finances, in the interim...as though it hadn't been shut down.
All this reminds me that the same thing is going on in any game, it's all just calculations...rendered into, simulations of actions, of men killing each other, or of animals walking around a zoo, or whatever.
But it can go further if you let it. If these mere calculations can produce such immersive and 'realistic' experiences in a game, what of our own lives? Matrix anyone?
or it's just a fairly fun and easy to play capitalism simulation game to dip into every so often.

I will be reviewing the graphics, music, controls, story, cinematic, content, game play, and giving you my honest opinion of the game.

[Graphics] One thousand one spikes is a throwback to 8-bit platformers that uses a 2D minimalist pixel art style, with a parallax background that adds both atmosphere and depth to the world. It has a retro style that feels nostalgic, bringing me back to the NES days. However, 1001 Spikes choice of colors are limited. Using shades of black and gray through most of the game. Graphics 8/10

[Music] Though this game uses 1980s styled chip sounds, it still manages to please the ears, with the pacing of the music increasing as you progress through a level. The Music does however get repetitive after rerunning the level over and over again. Music  7/10.

[Story] In 1001 you play as Aban Hawkins, son of Jim Hawkins, who is lost in the frozen tundra of Antarctica. Aban and his sister Tina was left with a map to the forgotten ruins of South America. Together they explore the temple and try to retrieve their father's legacy. And that's about it, you get past the tutorial and a short cutscene later and you are in the game. I will have to say this was a disappointment. Using the mice at the beginning to help you along could've further the story in some way. Instead, the story stops there leaving you to complete challenging levels with no more than their father's legacy to fulfill. Story 4/10.

[Cinematics] 1001 Spikes brings you into the forgotten ruins of South America with no cut scenes till the tutorial is over. The cut scene look like the beginning animation from Pokemon. There is no voice acting, only text. The text animates in using a typewriter style that yet again reminds me of Pokemon. There are even references like “pocket monsters and Poko-mum” in the text itself. 1001s cutscenes match the art style of the game and add some fun to this sad story with its subtle references to other games. Cinematics 7/10.

[Content] While you spend your time gritting your teeth in frustration, there are gold skulls hidden in each level that unlock bonuses, like new character to play as and more lives. There is more to 1001 Spikes that is incredible difficult levels. They can all be played in co-op mode with a multiple friends. This makes for incredibly fun and frustrating times. You can choose to skip levels that may seem to hard at the time but you will have to beat them to unlock the last temple and to enter the second half of the game.  Content 8/10

[Controls] The controls of 1001 are simple to use and unlike games from its time, controls beautifully. 1001 has a unique jumping mechanic which allows you to low jump and high jump, mapped to separate buttons. Movement is tight and accurate, making your character easy to handle. Controls 9/10.

[Gameplay] 1001’s levels are designed to be challenging, but not unbeatable. You enter the game with 1001 lives, but don't take that for granted. You will need all of them your first time through. You will need patience and persistence to beat each level. You will spend a significant amount of your time dying and repeating till you have all the traps memorized. Every level is designed to frustrate you but also teach you along the way. Gameplay 8/10.

1001 has a lot to offer in terms of level design and gameplay making up for its underwhelming story. The repetition can become a bit much, as you’re forced to run the same sections for extended periods of time until you perfect a jump or shot. This game is not for the casual player for the difficulty and time required to complete the game. If this sounds like your kind of game, I would definitely pick this game up on whatever you play on.

All in all 1001 Spikes Receives a 7/10

1001 Spikes is a game with two different jump buttons.
This is significant because when designing a game, generally you want to condense the controls as much as possible. Long have we been freed from the terrors of old PC gaming where every key on the keyboard provided some obscure function that required having an overlay or info card so you knew what to do if you wanted to 'q'uaff a potion or 'w'ear some armor. Which was different than 'Q'uitting the game or 'W'ielding a weapon!
But just like most forms of art, knowing when to break the rules is just as important as knowing the rules in the first place.
1001 Spikes is a masacore platformer where you're provided with a variety of levels that challenge you to clear them and expect you to die many times to do so. This is the type of game where it can throw surprise spikes from a wall or have the floor drop out from under you and after trial and error, you emerge victorious and ready for the next challenge. In that respect it's actually one of the easier masacore platformers that I've played. Certainly there's a lot of challenge here, and I'd recommened it to people of all skills levels interested in these types of games, but there's a lot more of just memorizing how to do a room rather than performing challenging maneuvers.
Which brings me back to the two jump buttons. In 1001 Spikes, you can do a small jump or a big jump and while many games just check for how long you hold down a single jump button or test the pressure used, this game smartly splits them up into two different buttons altogether. I say 'smartly' because a lot of the game is designed around using the correct height jump and knowing which to use in each situation and splitting them up removes any execution barrier and any ambiguity in what the character is going to do. And this sort of design smarts shows throughout the game. Every part of the design feels so well thought out that it's a joy to experience and play through.
There's a variety of different play modes and tons of characters to unlock who can have unique abilties that change the way you play, too. So what it comes down to is that there's a lot of content in here and it's all fun.

My expectations going in: persistence platformer, retro, loads of deaths, I'll grind through it in a few hours and be done.
My impressions playing: 'Wow, this is actually well-designed. Doesn't feel cheap, but is challenging. Wait, there are arcade modes? More story levels? You can play as Commander Video?!'
1001 Spikes has a boatload of content, far more than I'd anticipated. On top of the regular 30 story missions, you have another 20+ after you beat the main game...and the characters that you unlock aren't just reskins. They all play differently, and even have their own cutscenes for the story missions. There are, potentially, hundreds of levels to play if you enjoy going through with slightly varied mechanics. It's a good thing this game doesn't have leaderboards, otherwise I'd be enslaved for months.
It's a persistence platformer, with all the swells and pitfalls that entails. You will die - a lot - and there's very little that you can do about it when you first run a level, unless you're preternaturally gifted and/or untrustworthy of any flat surface. Yet, it never feels outright unfair; every time you die, it's invariably due to your own errors rather than the game cheesing you, and you learn from every death. It's a fine line to tread, making a game like this. Too difficult, and people get turned off by cheap deaths; too easy, and the target demographic isn't getting the sense of trial and accomplishment that they're looking for. 1001 Spikes manages that particular high-wire act quite well, with the obligatory transition from simpler beginning stages to monstrous latter levels not being too stark. There's no I Wanna Be The Guy-esque horrors lurking within.
The game has quite a quirky undertone to it conveyed via cutscenes, and the different costumes and characters certainly add to the fun. Although it's relatively barebones in terms of assets, the levels are designed very well and you can tell that plenty of love went into the game. Hats off to Nicalis for another game that's fun both in tone and gameplay. For example, the artifacts in the game give you tons of lives (which you'll need), but if you replay their levels and try to collect them again for farming purposes? Nope - it disintegrates, and it'll be a 1-down for you. It's those little details that help foster goodwill towards a game and dev team.
The characters and costumes, as mentioned before, all play quite differently. Commander Video is floaty, some have a double jump, some can cling to ledges - even Aban's costume changes make him toss Hadokens around, or be able to tank a hit without dying. Controls are simple, but tight enough and I experienced very few BS deaths due to hit detection or glitches, which is a major plus in the genre. The OST is good too, albeit somewhat repetitive after you perish for the umpteenth time due to uprooting spikes of doom.
1001 Spikes - not perfect, but a fine example of a game that packs a lot into a framework, doesn't overreach, and makes sure everything is designed and plays smoothly. If you have a hint of masochism about you and don't mind dying repeatedly while you inch incrementally forwards, this is a game you'll want to look at.

If you like very hard platformers that require almost pixel-perfect jumps, this is the game for you.
If you like games with bonus levels, unlockable characters, and actual replayability, this game is for you.
If you like pixel graphics, great (and different) controls, this game is for you.
Otherwise, this game is NOT for you.  Simple as that.
That being said, this is easily one of my favorite platformers ever.  Too-3, easily.  If you're a fan of games like Super Meat Boy, you'll love this game.

Great gamepad if you are willing to tinker.
This controller replaced my wireless x360 controller and is used for most if not all of the games (action/adventure/sports/solo shooters). Comparably they are in looks and input very much the same with the exception of the dual stage triggers, grip buttons and the touchpads, for which the latter in my mind is the love/hate it part of the controller. As all games designed for controllers are designed for a dual stick solution, this controller will probably never fully be what the developer intended. On the other hand, the touch pads don't really detract that much and personally in most games I actually prefer them (especially when set-up correctly for mouse input).
In terms of customizability there is no comparison, Steam controller wins and with new updates only gets better. E.g. with the steam chord update, basically pressing buttons while holding the steam button in center, now allows me to quickly change volume or to alt-tab out of a game, switch some youtube/spotify music and jump back without touching the keyboard/mouse. There is a lot to customize and I probably haven't touched all of it yet, definitely recommended to investigate beforehand (and afterhand) what is to be gained here.
Pros compared to x360 controller
-Durability, steam controller still looks spotless while the 360 sticks usually degrade quickly
-Battery life, I somehow only replaced my batteries after 1-2 months of owning the controller
-Fully customizable
-Can be used both for gaming as well as other stuff on the PC
-Input can be more accurate than other gamepads though for me never reaches accuracy of a physical mouse
Considerations
-Can take some time to get used to the touchpads
-Somehow FIFA never felt right with the touchpad (though this is the only game for me of all tried)
-Some batteries can be difficult to get out, as the compartments don't allow for much room
-Several buttons (e.g. touchpad) are loud
-Not all games magically work nice with gamepad+mouse hybrid settings
-Controller works (best) through Big Picture overlay, external games therefore need to be added to Steam and therefore Steam is required to use the controller at all.
Don't let the list of mostly minor cons detracts from the fact it's a great controller, I would definitely buy it again. Note that this is however not plug-and-play like other hardware out there, it does make up a lot due to this reason but may also not be for everyone.

This controller is a great companion to the Steam Link, but not a replacement for a traditional controller for some games. When you're in the living room, this controller will shine with games designed for mouse and keyboard play. Civ 5 is perfectly playable with the steam controller as are many other mouse and keyboard games. However, I've felt uncomfortable using the controller with FPS games. This is where keeping your USB 360 controller will be useful, the two analog sticks just seem to feel more natural than the touch pad for rotating the camera. (At least so far)
My final note is on hooking up your controller to the Steam Link. I recommend using the USB cable to connect your controller to your PC first. This will allow the controller to be associated with your Steam Account AND it will update the firmware reliably. Then head out and sync it to the Link without using the dongle.
I had a situation where the update didn't fully apply to the controller, making it unable to connect to anything wirelessly. I  did the USB connection to the PC to fix it, but I did get frustrated for a little while. Steam should really recommend wired updates for the controller.
Overall I give it an 8/10, it works well but it feels a little light and has too many quirks for being a $50 controller. Pick it up on sale and you won't be disappointed.

This game is vaguely reminiscent of Final Fantasy Tactics, but with simpler graphics and combat system (not a bad thing). The characters are fairly static with little to no animation (perhaps my only gripe), and move on the isometric map like chess pieces.
The unique stat allocation for character building is refreshing change from most RPGs I've played, in that you have a 3 by 3 array with every point you put in on square it also boosts the same skills in that row and column (Strength being row 1, Guile on Row 2,  down to Magic being on row 3, with the columns being direct attack on the left, defense in the middle, and utility on the right).
The overall story (and side quest stories) and characters are engaging, with large doses of environmental storytelling throughout the numerous levels. There enough secrets to keep things interesting, as I had easily sunk over 60 hours into a pre-steam release of the game.
If you enjoy dark atmospheres, with tinges of Lovecraft and horror, and tactical style RPGs with mature themes (there's never any graphical sex, at least that I've seen, but there are times where it's heavily inferred and mentioned), then this title is well worth the $20.

A hesitant recommendation. It will suit some people and not others so it's going to be very hit and miss. I refunded it for the reason that it DIDN'T suit me but it's still good enough to deserve a thumbs up. The levels are well crafted and the base building element adds to the game as does the absorbing storytelling and the variety of character types you can make. Also, despite seeming cliche, the WAY the "you're a criminal banished to an island of criminals" works is actually done in an original way and, indeed, the whole story progression is satisfying. The problem is that the combat is fairly one dimensional and not that 'tactical' for a turn based game. You basically have two attack types and they are ranged or melee. I suppose the tactical part comes more into play when you consider resistances and when to heal but this doesn't alter the fact that it's just hit, hit, heal. You could categorise it as a TBS lite but it's also borderline hack 'n' slash. Some will find that the superbly done other elements will be enough to make you ignore the one big fault but for me it was the deciding factor. This said, I should point out that the 40+ hours indicated play time is likely to be very much an underestimation for those who are sufficiently drawn in and I'm sure you could easilly double that 40.

Easily the best FMV game I've ever played. You play as Doctor Dekker's replacement and try to solve the mystery of his violent murder. Oh, and the mystery it is.
Every time you start a game, the killer is chosen randomly and that's something I really like, despite the fact, that this game is not really replayable - the answers don't differentiate enough to make second gameplay interesting and, which is slightly more disappointing
The story is fascinating and unsettling at the same time, but acting is what make this game so good. All actors did fantastic job (with Jaya being my favorite) and they brought to life memorable, believable and deep characters, that you really want to know more about.
The only issues I have with this game are related to gameplay mechanics. The ability to type your own question is something that I really looked forward to, but sadly, it just doesn't work properly. It's difficult to find right combination of words, sometimes I typed question and got "sorry, don't know!", just to then discover that it was in the "suggested questions" category, with just another word added or removed. Also, sometimes the answer you get doesn't seem to be related to the question. There were times I was honestly confused by what I was hearing, since I couldn't link to anything. "Suggested questions" are great help here, but you can't find all the answers that way. Luckily, you can use "hint" mechanic, to help you find out what you've missed.
To sum it up, "The Infectious Madness of Doctor Dekker" is a great, although most likely one-time experience, well worth the price. I can recommend it to anyone who enjoys games with great story and doesn't mind limited game mechanics.

I love FMV games and this was my favorite one this year. It's a surreal murder mystery that plays out like a mash up of Contradiction: Spot The Liar and Her Story. You're finding key words by asking questions and sussing out who's telling the truth, who's lying, and who's just plain crazy. The acting is cheezy in the best way and the actors go all out with their bizzare characters. The text parsing can be hit and miss, but a generous hint system will keep you from getting stuck. Multiple endings are possible and the killer is randomized each playthrough but there probably isn't much replayability unless you're obsessed with seeing every variation or getting every achievement. Overall the dozen or so hours I got out of this one were very enjoyable.

First review. I don't tend towards the hyperbolic, so I think all this is fair.
Great
-F2P done right. Fans of Planetside 2 will enjoy this model. You could grind for ages and still have the best equipment eventually. I ended up paying about $180 and it was all well spent. No regrets. Recommend budgeting at least $80.
-Matchmaking. Going up in tiers really helps weed out poor players and griefers. Lunatics will always be present, but you can mute or block them.
-Clans. You don't really have to join one. You can find a group of folks and they will always be happy to associate with you. They may be a clan or just other individuals (your friends list).
-Mech combat. Well balanced (aside from typical forum bemoaning) that is ultimately gratifying. Go fast, go slow; go long range, go 120m brawler. Whatever you want.
-Mechs. Customizable, skinable, and relatively true to lore. You can roleplay yourself as a hardcore pilot or just play casually. Fun fun.
Good
-Developers keep on developing. They are slow, promises tend to be 2-8 months after delivery date. It'll arrive eventually though.
-Content continues to be released, along with rough timelines published each month. New pre-orders are always in the hopper. Enjoyable to watch the options grow.
-Faction content/loyalty. I enjoy repping my faction but the differentiations are pretty slight in general play.
Poor
-The engine has some pretty crappy object hit detection. Not ballistic - think mechs running into each other (weird clipping) and terrain issues. It can't really be fixed without upgrading the software engine...which is probably never.
-UI. A bit arduous to do relatively simple inventory management and accounting.

I will start this off by saying I've done at least 4 100% runs, and have hundreds of hours in Bully on both PS2 and Xbox 360 over the last 10 years. I adore this game and consider it as the second best Rockstar game ever made just behind Red Dead Redmption.

With the crashes, they easily remedied with changing the compatability mode and running the .exe as an administrator, but it certainly doesn't get rid of crashes altogether, it still crashes after 2-3 hours for me. This can prove to be an annoyance since there's no autosave system, you can only save at safehouses or the main school building.
With changing 30 fps to 60 fps, it bugs out the game a bit, some are minor (bugging dialogue, missing stuff in cutscenes, other noises disrupting cutscenes etc), but some are major and bug out the game like rendering some mission incompletable without performing some heinous action. I'd recommend sticking to 30 fps personally.
Outside of these problems, this game is charming inside and out, is funny from beginning to end, and is honestly just barrels of fun.

Absolutely love my Steam Controller. Picked it up the other day and haven't been able to put it down. Don't listen to those bashing on the awkward/uncomfortable shape, it actually fits quite comfortably in your hands. As someone who's never used a controller regularly until this point, I got used to the trackpads relatively quickly. The haptic feedback is a cool addition, and the paddles on the back are unexpected favorites.
On the other hand, as much as I like the controller and want everyone to like it, it does have its downsides. The ABXY buttons are awkawardly placed and sometimes I press the wrong buttons. The controller tends to act up if the receiver USB isn't within direct eyeshot of the player, so I find myself using the extention micro USB each time I play. Creating custom configurations for the controller is a bit confusing at first, but given some time I got the hang of it. My biggest issue is it's connectivity with my Mac, as sometimes it's tempramental in working with certain games and transitioning to them from Big Picture mode which I would assume is a problem that PC users aren't having.
Given its few quirks, I adore the Steam Controller and look forward to trying it out with a wider variety of games. Rocket League, Portal 2 and Left 4 Dead 2 are some of the more controller-friendly games I've played so far. I'd recommend it for sure if it's on sale and you want to try something different from your keyboard-mouse setup or simply want to play from your couch for a change.

After using this for over a  year, I can say that the Steam Controller is by far my favorite controller.  There is a small period when you first start using it where it feels weird, but once you get past that, the Steam Controller is the ideal PC gaming tool.
Pros
- Lots of functionality
- Very easy initial install
- Great battery life
- Light and ergonomic
- Just so many buttons and functions (Didn't know of the third set of "shoulder" buttons on the inside of the grip for months)
- No wires at all
- Works very will with Steam Link device
Cons
- Uses 2x AA batteries, not rechargable
- Not user friendly when trying to work with games outside of Steam
- Can be easy to mix up controllers' wireless USB plug if using more than 1 controller (I labeled mine)
- The right Analoge Stick/Mouse Pad is frustrating at times, and can require a lot of tweeking to make it work as desired in each game
Neutral Points
- The price point is a bit higher than most XBox360 controllers
- Controlls can require varying degrees of tweeking from game to game
- You can customize the Turn On and Turn Off tones, but can only use certain presets
Overall
It's a great controller, and very easy to use with most Steam Games right off the bat (save for some Analoge Stick tweeks).   If you don't use your controller outside of Steam too often, it is well worth you time.
As a side note, the controller works exceptionally well with the Steam Link, and save some router communication errors which load up the Keyboard Presets to your controller on reboot, the two pair together wonderfully.

1001 Spikes is punishing, difficult and downright unfair at times. And that's what makes it great. Right from the start of the game you are told to "Always be on your guard", which is then followed with an arrow being shot into your face.
If you're not vigilant at all times, you will die. If you don't react fast enough to traps appearing or terrain falling, you will die. If you're unable to remember the path of the level, you will die. 1001 Spikes is a challenging game, so as the recent reviews show, it's not for everyone. But if you enjoyed Super Meat Boy or other similar games, you'll like this too.
The environments are detailed even with the pixel graphics, the soundtrack is excellent and the platforming is perfect. There are two seperate jump buttons to make sure you always nail the height you need to, and the movement isn't floaty or slippery at all.
Every level has its own Golden Skull to collect, an optional extra objective. Upon pickup it grants you an extra life, so as long as you get to the Skull each time you can try endlessly without fear of running down your lives. These unlock a multitude of extra characters, each with their own abilities and music, and a few other game modes, which again completely change how the game plays. The amount of variety is great.
If you find the prospect of dying near the end of a level just because you didn't notice a different wall tile you may want to pass. But if you want a challenge and don't mind repeating levels several dozen times (or the entire game, if you lose all your lives!), give 1001 spikes a go.

Also it does sometimes remove some questions after asking, which I find little bit annoying as sometimes you might want to listen them again, so you need to reload the game. Aside from that the GUI and mechanics are better than on the last two Tex games. Pixel hunting is much easier this time because textures are much more clear.
When compared to other FMV-games the acting is decent, sometimes there is a little bit overacting but mostly they do fine work especially Chris Jones starring as Tex Murphy. Frank Schimming and the guy who is playing Gideons CEO all are doing very good job, so it feels like watching a good movie and If I remember correctly many of the actors have been also acting in some A-grade movies.
The puzzles are logic and need some out-of-the-box thinking, gladly there aren't any illogical game stopper like the Pandora Directive's last puzzle, but they aren't too easy so it takes some time to figure them out. The game has build-in hint system so you won't get stuck easily, but I strongly recommend to avoid using it as solving the puzzles by yourself is part of the Tex experience.
The story, which is mix of filmnoire and cyberpunk, is compelling and keeps you excited to the very ending to see where the story goes next. The ending clearly tells that they planned to make 6th Tex Murphy right after release of the Overseer, unfortunally Access ran into some financial problems and got bought by Microsoft and got canceled, but thanks to the kickstarter we finally got the Tesla Effect, the sequel to the Overseer.
There seems to have some problems to get the game working. I have tried this with Windows 7 and 10 and got it work on both. You need to install ffdshow to get the cutscenes to work and install MIDI emulator to get music to work. Just follow the guide:
Even after these fixes on the Windows 10 the game might crash on some puzzles, I didn't find any fix for that other then transferring the saves to my Windows 7 machine where the game seems to be more stable and didn't crash on anything.
So aside the technical problems on modern systems the game is excellent FMV game which I can recommend to anyone who likes filmnoire and detective stories.

Alright, I've had my Steam Controller for a while now. I'll first say, I would NEVER buy this or any controller at full price. The fact that controllers are getting more expensive than AAA games is absurd to me. I also don't use it wirelessly, I play right next to my computer and only use a controller for third-person action games and ♥♥♥♥♥♥ ports. Anyways, let's get this♥♥♥♥♥♥started. Drop to the bottom to get a TL;DR list of pros/cons.
First of all, I've read a lot of reviews saying the controller feels cheap. While I wouldn't say it feels sturdy, it certainly doesn't feel cheap to me. It just feels very light. It's even lighter than my 360 controller that it replaced (one of the buttons was messed up). The only thing that comes off as being particularly cheap to me is that the trigger and bumper buttons aren't labeled on the controller at all. The real problem, for me at least, is the lightness translates to the rumble. Maybe it's just my controller (which I got from Amazon with other things included in the package), but this controller has probably the most anemic rumble I've ever felt. I grew up during the N64 era when rumble was a feature you had to pay extra to get on an already bulky♥♥♥♥♥controller, and when it rumbled, your entire ♥♥♥♥ing house felt it. That's the way I like my rumble. My 360 controller's rumble will make enough noise that you can hear it on the other side of the house if I set it on my desktop tower. The Steam Controller, on the other hand, is only about half as powerful, even at the highest setting. It's not a dealbreaker or anything, but you can't set the default rumble strength (rumble is still in beta, even after nearly a year, and they only recently added the option to have it on by default for all games). This means you have to go through each game you use the controller with to set up the rumble if you want to feel it at all. Mine also makes a lot of noise when it rumbles, like it's a 30 year old car on its last legs. Maybe mine is just defective, but we'll never know for sure.
Another big nono is the controller has ♥♥♥♥ing DRM. You have to link it to your Steam account. If you want to use the controller on a game, you have to run the game through Steam. This is a very bizarre design choice and it doesn't really benefit anyone. It's just less inconvenient for people that already play all their games through Steam anyways. I'm guessing this is because Valve refuses to make any actual Xinput drivers, so Steam is basically emulating all the controls for you. You also can't set default settings for games, so if you don't like the mouse-like trackpad, you have to mess with settings for each game. Let me try to explain it. Basically, when the right trackpad is used like a mouse, you have to start your finger in the middle and swipe, say, right to turn right. Let's say you're playing Skyrim. Imagine swiping over and over and over and yeah, it gets real irritating really quick. Joystick settings basically make it so you hold your finger on a part of the trackpad and it'll just keep moving in that direction (as if you were holding a joystick down). I suppose it's not as accurate as mouse-like settings, but it's thousands of times more convenient, in my opinion.
Other than those things, I LOVE the controller. It's pretty clear that Valve DID do extensive research into controller design to come up with something that's comfortable and requires very little time to adjust. I was surprised at how fast I got used to the button/joystick placement when, at first, my thumbs just kept bumping into each other. The only particularly bad choice seems to be the Start button being too close to the right trackpad. Fairly often, my finger will hit the trackpad and make the camera spin in a third-person action game when I go to hit it. It may have been a better idea to move the Start and Back buttons somewhere else or make the controller slightly bigger. I have pretty average size hands and fingers, maybe even a bit on the small side, so I imagine this being much worse for people with ham hands. That said, it doesn't happen every time, and it could just be an adjustment issue on my end.
Another welcome addition are dual-stage triggers and grip buttons. For those that don't know (and you should easily know just by reading the controller's description), dual-stage triggers basically means that the triggers are pressure sensitive AND there's a button underneath that can be pressed. For example, you can set up a game so that putting pressure on LT will scope and pressing the LT button will fire while scoped. The two buttons on the underside of the grips aren't too sensitive and work fine (hey! if you have problems with that Start button, you could always assign it to the right grip!), but are usually used for Mode Shifting.
Now, this is where things get really good. The customization options for the controller are far better than anything you've ever seen. Sure, you can use the controller for console ports that play better with a controller, but you can also use Mode Shifting to effectively double the number of buttons you're using to play, say, Guild Wars 2. Basically, when you press a button assigned to Mode Shift, it will make your buttons use a second set of assigned hotkeys. Let's say you have numbers 1 and 2 assigned to the B button. Pressing B will be like pressing 1. If you press or hold the Mode Shift button and press B, it'll be like pressing 2. You can do this for pretty much every button on the controller, letting you do what should normally be impossible - play PC-designed games with a controller. I wouldn't recommend it, but it's VERY welcome. As a quick sidenote, the customization is very good. Even if you're playing a gamepad-focused game, you can customize things like making a grip button emulate pressing two buttons at once (for those weird ♥♥♥♥ing games that want you to press A + Y to throw).
This is probably going to sound insane, and it probably is, but the feature that really put the controller over the top for me and constantly makes me think, "Goddamn am I glad I picked this up over another 360 knockoff!" is the gyro controls. Yes, gyro controls. This has to sound incredibly bizarre, but I found using gyro in tandem with joystick right trackpad controls made shooting in Metal Gear Solid V very precise and VERY fun. This is reflected in the community configurations, where you'll find that the top configurations will typically have one config that uses some form of gyro control. Some of you may remember the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ motion controls of Wii games, but trust me when I say, in the words of Todd Howard (or as some of you may know him, "that man who ruined my childhood by making Skyrim and Fallout way too easy to play"), it just works and you can thank the incredible levels of customization for that.
PROS:
+More buttons than your average controller thanks to grip buttons and dual-stage triggers
+An unprecedented amount of customization, more than Joy2Key could ever do for you
+There are community configurations, even for games that aren't available on Steam
+Don't be put off by the unorthodox design, it actually feels pretty good after a very short adjustment period
+GYRO CONTROLS ARE GREAT! This alone overcame every single negative for me!
CONS:
-Start button being too close to the right trackpad can cause problems
-Rumble is absolutely terrible, and still in beta after nearly a year
-No drivers (SEE KELLZAP'S COMMENT), so all games MUST be started through Steam to use the controller
-Extreme levels of customization could put some people off, ESPECIALLY if some of the default settings don't feel right
-Default templates cannot be customized, you have to change it game by game
-DRM for a controller
-Don't buy it unless it's on sale
-Valve spent time and money developing this instead of Half-Life 3
Don't be put off by the long list of cons, it's just a bunch of small things that don't add up to all the good/great things!
