Bought one over a year ago when these first came out, and have been using it since for many kinds of games. It took a lot of time to get used to the Steam Controller. It's just so unique and different. I gotta say I'm glad I took that time, because I now think this is the best controller I've ever used.
The design is nice, and very ergonomic in hand. Once I learnt to hold it with my index fingers on the shoulders, and middle fingers on the triggers, it feels great. It's not for everybody though, and might not be the best if you have very small hands.
You will have to tinker with the settings, and practically configure it for every game independently, and there are a LOT of stuff to configure. You can, in theory, use Steam Controller for basically every game. Ofcourse it's not great for every game, but still usable.  Community setting profiles help greatly, and most of the time I choose one, and only change a couple of small things, and it doesn't take more than a minute.
All in all, I'm glad I bought one. My XBone controller has been gathering dust ever since.

The controller is nice to hold (at least on my hands), the build quality is mostly okay (a bit lightweight, but acceptable) and the trackpads feel good to use (useful when in desktop mode or binded with a mouse for any games). The inclusion of gyro control and two grip buttons are eally helpful for extra inputs of certain games. Having a fully customize layout with an ability to share and download the custom settings for each game is definitely a good thing.
There a few things that I don't like about the controller. The first thing is the triggers; they are too short to press and have less resistance, which make it a slight less accurate for the analog control reading, especially when using acceleration/brake control on racing games. The face buttons are too small for my right thumb and often, I accidentally press B instead of A. Also, they are awkwardly positioned at the bottom, near the right trackpads, which also makes my right thumb accidentally touches the pad that triggerred the unwanted inputs. The buttons (shoulders, triggers, and pads) when pressed are very loud, which I wish they are a bit quiet. Lastly, no rechargable battery is a bummer to me.
If there is a second revision of the controller planned on the way, I would love to see and try it, if it can pretty much follow or imitate the DS4 controller layout, with trackpads and grip buttons still intact. For this controller, I say I just slightly recommend it for a try, only if you are curious enough to use it and can handle the controller shape, layout or you want to have some challenges to use it on certain games. Otherwise, there is no need to use this controller, especially if you have DS4 or Xbox One controller that can be used on PC as well, with more compatibility and supports.

The story mode is very good and the graphics and cinematics that go with it are incredibly well done.
However, as for replay value and online experience the game is incredibly lacking.
Aside from numerous connectivity issues there are a lot of bad parts about the online system.
For instance, players can simply disconnect from an online match with very little repercussions. Expect about half your games to be incomplete due to either the opposing player having a bad internet connection or simply because he/she refuses to accept defeat and ragequits or the servers malfunctioning.
Matches are extremely frustrating as connectivity issues result in the message "transmitting" appearing constantly over your screen which pauses the match, input delay, etc.
I was very disappointed after having read that there are "over 100 different playable characters" I was not expecting 7 versions of Sasuke to count as 7 characters. If you would actually count all the actually different characters you would have a count of around 50-70, therefore I think the character amount was falsely advertised as well. It could very well be over 100 "different" playable characters and it is disappointing that some characters from the Naruto-series were not included at all.
It is very common for maximum-rank players online to simply reset their levels in order to play with lower levels which in turn makes it harder for people to actually competitively rank up online. This "smurfing" is incredibly common and also makes it harder for new players to actually get immersed into the game.
You cannot mute your or others' microphones in-game which is extremely frustrating for people who do not wish to talk or do not wish to hear their opponents. This is even more frustrating when they are playing loud music, cursing all the time, ... A workaround is to simply mute your microphone from Steam settings yet it is quite impractical having to keep muting it this way.
Aside from this there are a lot of small bugs which can completely turn the tide in an online battle such as:
- Character targeting messing up moments after the opponent has leader switched
- Combos not connecting properly when you leader-switch to continue a combo
- Characters that can continue combos even when they're dashed at or even guardbroken
This and many more small bugs can flip a battle around in your opponent's favour.
There is also an immense lack of options for online matches, a few of these are:
- Spectating option for tournaments (seriously, why do other contestants have to simply watch a blank screen while others are fighting?)
- 8-player endless mode
- More stages, perhaps from previous games of the series (you can simply retake characters from the previous games and parade it as "over 100 playable characters!" but you cannot give the players the extra stages?)
- Better music, the current music feels very bland and even non-existent
The graphics, cinematics and story mode are really well done but the replay value is all in the online experience which is very terrible, lazily made making it very rare to actually have a match with someone online which is enjoyable. I would not recommend this game for any hardcore PvP-oriented players out there. However for any die-hard Naruto fan this game is right up your alley, be it with it's many flaws.
I will continue to play this game only for the very few matches I have to be in luck with to enjoy. This as well as separate duels with friends, just to avoid the online matchmaking as much as possible.
EDIT SINCE ROAD TO BORUTO LAUNCH:
This poor excuse for a DLC is simply apalling and for me was the final slap in the face.
Not only did it simply increase the instability of the game as crashes are much more frequent now, it also offers very little in terms of content.
The spectator option for tournaments and endless was a very welcome addition, yet this option quite frequently leads to instable matches, usually ending in the game crashing.
Barely any new characters or new characters the community openly asked for, this shows that the players' voices are not ones they are interested in listening to.
Having deinstalled the game because of this I feel very disappointed, being able to only look back at Naruto: Ultimate Ninja Storm 4 as lost potential.

ARGHHHHHHHHHHHH. This started out with such promise. A nice film noir detective point&click - and with a cool twist to boot. If that's your thing as well, AND IF YOU'RE TRYING TO AVOID THE PSEUDOPSYCHOLOGICAL 2 BIT HORROR GENRE that's haunting the point&click games recently like the plague, stay away from chapter 3, at least until the developers decide to remake it with an storyline and vibe that's consistant with the first two chapters.

Bear With Me came out as a series of three episodes, and so I've held off on a review until I'd completed the final episode, and it proved to be well worth the wait. The atmosphere of the game is very heavy noir, within the context of a child's imagination. With the mechanics being a point and click adventure with some standard crafting, I'd rather compare it to a lot of the Daedalic Entertainment games (like the Deponia series), except the humour isn't as absurd and is a bit more referential, and the puzzles aren't frustratingly obscure (in other words, even the puzzles that took a while made sense when they clicked).
Basically all text in the game has V.O. work, and there's some points where the voice acting could have been done better and the lines are read in a bit stilted of a fashion, but I think part of why that bothers me is that I think it's done well enough that the occasional bad read stands out and breaks immersion a little, rather than if I ever got used to the bad reads.
The strength of the game is, by far, the writing. That goes for both the micro level, the dialogue, the flavor text on scenery, etc, but also for the macro level of the overall plot. The biggest strength for that is how fleshed out the characters are, especially the main characters, the 10-year-old Amber and her gruff partner, Ted E. Bear. After the gaps between episodes, it was their characters that brought me back to play the 2nd and 3rd installments. And the final episode shows them particularly well, and the game ends on a very powerful note.
From a cost-benefit standpoint, I got a bit over 9 hours of play out of this, and probably having picked up some of this on sale, this was probably about $10-12 investment all told, and I totally think I got my money's worth. If you're interested in a game that's got some comedy, somewhat spoofs the film noir style, and shows some real heart while using a point-and-click framework, this is a definite must-play, in my opinion.

Ignoring the usual traits of Dogenzaka Lab's budget VNs (annoying music you turn off on first launch, low res backgrounds which this one mercifully doesn't suffer from, being glorified softcore smut), the main problem Amazing Shinsengumi suffers from is brevity.
The writing feels first-pass, like they put in all the beats but forgot to go back to flesh it out. The speed in which you go from house burnt down, living with the shinsengumi, sleeping with one of them, being separated by some sort of conflict, then reunited will make your head spin. The bullet points are all there, you understand how they work and that you should care but you're given no time to develop these feelings.
You'll see some reviewers complain about being assaulted with choices, one after another. The truth is, there aren't any more choices per chapter in this VN than other Dogenzaka Lab VNs. It only seems like a barrage due to how fast chapters breeze by.
How fast the chapters go by also ties in with other reviewers complaining about how uncomfortably nonconsensual the sexual encounters seem. The encounters themselves aren't really any different than, say, My Secret Pets or Men of Yoshiwara, but they stick out in this because the men are basically strangers to you and arguably continue being so even at the conclusion of the route. Without any context or connection to the men, it becomes incredibly difficult to handwave whatever abuse they pile onto the protagonist.
If you dislike Dogenzaka Lab VNs, this one won't change your mind. If you liked some of their other VNs, you're still probably going to dislike this one.

The MC is the cheesy little airhead that most of readers of these kind of visual novels are used to. Each phase of the game is different forcing you to change the way you play. Overall, war has a strategic facet that Civilization: Beyond Earth lacks.
Downsides: The pirates are annoying and overpowered (You can turn them off). It is nearly impossible to achieve a diplomatic victory, making winning through diplomacy not an option. FMV games are on the rarer side at the moement. I remember enjoying 'Her Story' and its use of discover new FMV to create a narrative. The Infectious Madness of Dr Dekker follows along in the same way whilst spinning its own story,
You are the successor to Dr Dekker, a psychiatrist tending to multiple patients on the weirder side, bordering on insanity. Your predecessor was murdered. Find out about your patients and solve the case. If you don't want supernatural elements in game, this isn't for you.
Where Dekker shines is its ability to create a strong narrative with a number of moments that give you the goosebumps. Each of the people you interview has a well written, well acted story that you can explore along with various side characters. Gameplay involves typing questions/words into a free text box and reacting to responses. The game is more responsive than many older adventure titles where free text was used, and there is a hint system so you'll never get stuck with how to phrase a question/sentence if you want to use it to advance the story.
Personally I had a lot of fun exploring these characters and their backstories. If its a story driven game you're after and enjoy implied horror give it a go at its low price point.
Recommended for people playing alone or alongside a friend/ significant other

This is another FMV in a long list of FMV games I've played and enjoyed (Tex Murphy, Late Shift, Contradiction:  Spot the Liar), and much more. I love the genre.
And Doctor Dekker delivered.
The storyline is a simple one:  you take over Doctor Dekker's insane collection of patients after Doctor Dekker is murdered. You're simultaneously treating them and finding the killer at the same time...and the killer is one of your patients.
I'll have to replay through this again sometime to see if I can unlock every response (and get a new murderer, as the murderer is randomized with each playthrough), but this game is well-worth the $8.99 Steam is charging for it. The UI is easy to use, the stories are engaging, the actors are excellent, and you can have some fun with your stream (if you're a streamer) by asking off the cuff questions.
In short, this game is a mind-trip I'm glad I took.

Doom is game that conjures memories for many of us.  While most seem to remember it fondly, I was one that never thought it was anything special.  I truly despised missing secrets and having to start a stage over.  Also, the degree in which secrets were hidden that all but required a guide or friend who learned from a friend who lied about finding it on his own; no one believes you.
The good news is that Doom 2016 is a fun game if played on Nightmare.  The combat is challenging but fair.  The "challenges" per weapon/level/rune force you to variety your playstyle which is both healthy and amusing.   The secrets were well implemented and findable with the proper suit upgrade with the majority being simply slightly hidden path.

The much awaited sequel to 1000 Spikes this masocore platformer delivers a steady flow of brutal levels filled with multiple paths and hidden traps to challenge even the best of players.
The game's difficulty is both the game's greatest strength and weakness, relying heavily on 'gotcha' traps that will get a cheap kill on players learning the level, but the satisfaction from clearing a level makes up for most of the pain.

If you like retro-style hardcore platformers that make you want to pull your hair out, then 1001 Spikes is for you. Seriously this game feels like it wants to screw with you at every moment. This game is the definition of a trial and error game; whereas you have to study each individual part of the level in order to beat it. Everything in this game is designed to be cheap, unfair and unforgiving. But don't worry, the game is completely aware of its brutal difficulty and it almost seems proud of it. This game is incredibly frustrating and will infuriate you just trying to complete the main story.
Now with that rant out of the way...
1001 Spikes is a 2D style action platformer. A very, VERY hard platformer. It’s also a sequel/remake of the game “Aban Hawkins and the 1000 Spikes.” Each world has its own theme and obstacles to overcome. These include falling blocks, bottomless pits, poisonous scorpions, and most of all, spikes. Lots and lots of spikes. So on top of being incredibly difficult, because this game loves to harken back to the days of old school retro video games, there are also lives in this game. How many? 1001. Now that is admittedly funny and you can more lives throughout the course of the main campaign, but in today's day and age lives are an archaic design choice the artificially extends the game's length. However even with the 1001 lives, you will die a lot in this game. First off, all it takes to kill you in this game is one hit. Whether that's getting crushed by a collapsing ceiling, getting stabbed by randomly appearing spikes, or getting shot by a dart, you will die. This game pulls no punches and will surprise you at every chance it gets.
But with all that said, 1001 Spikes is a very well designed game. The graphics look very retro and look good for the game it's trying to be. The music is good and fits the stages very well. The sound effects are fitting and satisfying. There are also plenty of other game modes to keep you busy and frustrated once you finish the main story. The only thing that might be hard to adjust to is the fact that there are two jump buttons. A short jump button and a high jump button. You will need to get used to using both of them because there will be times in which you have to utilize both in order to beat some levels. So don't think you cheese your way through the game by abusing the high jump. The game will punish you for it.
But anyways, if you want a hardcore, unfair, brutally difficult retro-style platform game, 1001 Spikes will satisfy your retro hunger. Just be prepared to die.

1001 Spikes is challenging, that's true, the problem is that the game's challenge pretty much entirely comes from how unfair it is. You'll find yourself dying less because you mistimed jumps and more because a random floating block fell on you or a spike trap came up from a block you were standing on, despite that block being identical to the completely normal block you were standing on seconds ago. Trial and error isn't very fun.

This game is a hidden gem. This was a very unique and interesting concept, and it worked beautifully. The game's story is great, being mislead by one of your fellow classmates, used for his "ultimate plan" and gaining rveenge upon him. There's allot of drama that also goes on in between the story, allot of tasks for you to complete, providing hours of gameplay. And there's also small jobs you can take on for some quick cash (which isn't really enscessary since the tasks give you money, but neat nontheless.) All of the tasks are unique in some way, have their own small story for you to sort out, this game goes deep with certain tasks and knowing Rockstar, not afraid to go into great detail sometimes. So, you play a boy by the name of Jimmy Hopkins, who goes to a High School, Bullsworth whilst his mother and fiancé go on a honeymoon for a year, so he has to stay there. Now, going into gameplay mechanics, you can easily tell that this is a console port, as the controls can be stiff with mouse and keyboard sometimes, like how slow the camera moves in ceratin events and how the default key binds are questionable (which can be modified,) and when on a bike, barely touching the mouse makes the camera go crazy lol. But the gameplay is definately fun, and this game is heavily based off of one of GTA's engine's, you can just tell from the mechanics, so if you like how GTA plays, you'll like this game's mechanics. Being a game made years ago, the A.I can be a bit glitchy sometimes, with NPC's rarely getting stuck, and some weird shenanigans which can break immersion. The faction system is pretty cool, and gives you a constant threat in the game, as well as many other threats throughout the game, depending on the choices you make. There is a fully explorable town, which is really big, and you start off in Bullsworth to explore. You can make some ladyfriends throughout the game, which can provide you with a small health boost with a kiss, :P (obviously you need to complete tasks beforehand.) There's also quite a variety of weapons to use as well, which you'll get throughout the game, as well as customizable clothing (depending on choice can cause clipping issues on cutscenes,) speaking of which the cutscenes are also not prerendered! And run on the game's engine, whihc is again awesome. The combat works well, and I don't have any problems with it, it can be a bit simplistic, but it's nice. There's also allot of minigames (aka the classes) in the game, some are interesting, others can be "press button at right time to win." Now as for issues, the first major problem is the crashing, got about 9 crashes throughout the game, and from research is unfortunately the game being unstable on Windows 10, and Rockstar not really bothering to fix it, which is a shame. There is an offical patch, which doesn't even work, just gives an error code, luckily there's an extracted version available online, which increased the runtime of the game from crshing under an hour, to allot longer, hour and a half approximately, but I just saved after every task to help prevent progression loss. Also, some of the models' legs starting spazzing out during cutscenes, and there was the occassional glitchy texture throughout the city, but nothing major. Also, encountered an interesting bug where the shcool bus driver would sometimes be invisible and change model, which is just comical. Overall I really enjoyed this game, and it is a gem, however I would wish Rockstar would take the time to fix it up for Win10 useres, having a game that crashes constantly without patching on Steam is not a good idea for reputation. Overall, loved the game, would recommend it.

Mech warrior online is a thinking mans shooter based on the Battle Tech system.
You have to select what parts of your mech are armored the most.
You have to select what type of weapons to install on your hard points.
You have to setup good cooling, or you will not enjoy this game, anything above value 1.1.
For new users I would recommend nothing below value 1.3 cooling.
You have to decide which mech is right for you.
A light mech with the best speed, low armor, superior maneuverability, most often jump jets. Little room for cooling.
A medium mech with balanced armor, slightly more fire power, good speed, and lesser to great maneuverability. Some times has jump jets, has a good balance for adding heat sinks and pretty much any equipment you may need.
A heavy mech, the back bone of mech warrior arsenal, great armor, slower movement, and low to lesser maneuverability. Fewer heavy mechs have jump jets. You will have to decide what is more important. A higher alpha stike with higher heat spikes, or better sustained fire with very balanced heat.
An assault mech can have the most fire power, the highest armor, slowest speed, and poor to very poor maneuverability. Very rare to use jump jets in an assault. Heating a cooling on these mechs is completly custom and up to the user.
Roles
Light mechs often are the tie breaker of any match. If you take out the enemy light lance early on you have almost full control over the battlefield during the course of any match. Lights are the bane of assault mechs. Light mechs are the scouts and the ace in pocket for advanced users.
Medium mech are great for support. They can take a few more hits than the lights and are well balanced to fullfil almost any role long range or short, scouting, sniping, anti missle. You name it there is a meduim mech that can do it, they just make poor battle tanks.
Heavy mechs are the real bread & butter of battle tech. Not always slowed down by a massive amount of armor and the can carry enough fire power to topple almost any mech in seconds 1v1. Heavy mechs also are some of the hottest mechs in the game, so beware of cooling issues.
The assault mech is more than a tank. If built right, an assault mech can wipe out an entire lance quickly, but their slower speed and poor maneuverability make them prime targets for enemy light mechs and lrms. Do not chase the squirrels in an assault mech it will always end badly for you. If you have a squirrel climbing up your leg, call out to your team for assistance, or you better pray a lucky snap shot can take dispatch them quickly, otherwise your SOL.
Very immportant words,, STAY WITH YOUR TEAM or die alone.
Any first time player should stick with Inner Sphere medium or light mechs for the best playable experiance, they dont cost much but the equipment to add to them can cost a bit more than the mech alone.
Plus the Inner Sphere light's have the most customization and max speed of all current mechs.
Then work your way into a medium, heavy, or better, or even Clan mechs. The bigger the mech the slower it is and the bigger target you are for the other team. Light and fast is what I enjoy the most.
I can not recommend Clan mechs for new players. The clan mech are sometimes gimped on tonnage for custom equipment because you can not change your engine on the common omni varients, and the heat build up is sky high. They do have better range and more custom hard points, but the heat build up is crazy, not easy to balance max fire power with max cooling. The max cooling is never enough for a Clan mech. The Origin ii c mechs trade omni pods (custom hardpoints) for the ability to change engines. They actually work quite well and can be cooled very well.
Hope this post was helpful, and do remember to torso twist.

I struggled over whether or not to recommend this one. Ultimately, I'm choosing not to, but please feel free to read my review to see if my concerns about it will bother you. The story has its good points too, so there may be many people who are happy to overlook what I didn't like.
---
My first impression of the game was that it was "otome by boardroom" because the prologue is flat terrible and the characters felt like cardboard cutouts. Considering the mess of many of the routes, I still sort of feel that way.
I ended up playing the most upsetting route first, which negatively impacted my enjoyment of the rest of the game. It did end on what (for me) was the "best route", and that softened my feelings towards the game. Ultimately, my feelings are very mixed.
There is at least one character (Heisuke) who outright treats the heroine as a sex toy. He sexually assaults the heroine multiple times. His route was actually rather horrific to me and as the first route I played in the game, I almost dropped the game entirely. I'll talk about him a bit more in the "Love Interests" section of my review.
I'm not sure whether this game is rated R-18 or closer to X. It depends on the route. Some routes are very 'fade to black' with gentle language. There are other routes where the language was rather vulgar and distasteful. I write erotica for a living, so I'm not prudish, but the poor translation made the sex scenes very hit or miss.
Otherwise, I'll give my general warning of, "This game is created originally for Japanese audiences/sensibilities and set in a historical period. Please be forewarned that you might be taken aback by some situations."
It feels like not much care went into the translation. There are the usual offenses from this publisher such as missing punctuation, typos, confused words (your/you're; etc), smashed sentences (missing the end of one and the beginning of the next) - something some people don't care about much or are willing to overlook. There are also frequently giving people the wrong names, once a characters name hadn't even been translated from the Japanese, and there were frequent missing words (sentences like "Have eaten today?"). The translation appears to have been done fairly literally, leading to awkwardly worded scenes or scenes that lose their feel because they're written in short, declaritive sentences, like a child's What I Did On My Summer Vacation essay. It also makes the sex scenes extremely awkward and sometimes very vulgar. Honestly, of this publisher's games, this is the one whose translation/editing I am least impressed with.
About half of the character designs felt strong and the other half felt rather boring. A couple of the CGs were pretty good, but most were just fairly generic "affectionate heads" - that is to say, the couple in question tucking their faces close and looking sweet on each other. The art wasn't awful, but there were few moments where I thought, "Oo - a CG!"
Bland as bland can be. Sometimes she had sparks of personality - but in those cases she was extremely selfish and/or stupid. She also seemed to have no backstory other than, "My family died in a fire. Also, my father was a fireman." What was she doing to support herself before the Shinsengumi came into her life? Apparently nothing, but how is that possible?
To entertain myself, I decided she was probably secretly an arsonist. Honestly, it fit. In every route there were at least two fires - often more. In most of these routes, many of the fires were fairly mysterious and seemed to start for no apparent reason... unless you realize that a lot of what happens in the game is honestly classic arsonist moves. She always happens to be on the scene, happy to help, throwing herself bravely into the fire; etc. Yes, yes - I know how common and how terrifying fires were in the period, but play the game with the idea she's an arsonist in mind and see if she's suddenly not actually somewhat interesting than if you accept the idea she just is this paper-cut-out heroine.
For the most part, most of the routes were okay. I really enjoyed Sanosuke's route - his was the only route where his character stayed consistent. The other men were all over the place - it was like someone kept forgetting which route they were writing. It felt as if the scripts were probably handled by multiple writers except for Sanosuke's. He was "himself" in other routes and in his own. I really enjoyed Soji in everyone else's routes, but when I got onto his route, he was only "that" briefly before going off the rails. Every route started out promising and, except for Sano's, got sloppy in the middle. Most of them ended strongly, at least.
The route I hated - hated! - was Heisuke's. It was honestly horrifying. I'm going to spoiler in the rest of this, so skip the rest of this section if you don't want to be spoiled. It started out cute, with him being all "genki-desu" and friendly and childishly charming, as you'd expect from his type. Then you were immediately his favorite toy and all the adults around him were sort of, "Well, I mean, please forgive him... Not like we can stop him." Probably because he's absolutely DANGEROUSLY INSANE. He's Id incarnate. All he thinks about is his immediate desire. He sexually assaults the heroine multiple times in public - even drags her directly into dangerous situations so he can get off on it. He literally does not care that it upsets her. He doesn't care about even so much as also helping a little girl escape a fire when he comes to rescue the heroine. The heroine has to basically beg him to take the girl along. The endings for his route show him at least trying to understand the heroine wanting him to think of others, but it's pretty clear that even in the best ending that he doesn't really get the idea that other people are real.
I mean... what can I say about it? There wasn't really a story. The Shinsengumi help put out a fire and immediately start hitting on this poor girl. They weirdly introduce themselves/each other, ignoring the fire in order to hit on her. Their leader turns to the girl and says, "Pick one of my captains and live with him - you don't have a home now, right? It'll be fine!" The most threadbare reasoning to get a random girl to live in close quarters with them. She picks someone and is almost always immediately in love with him - and don't worry, he almost always immediately was in love with her from the prologue. Why? No reason I can tell. Possibly because she was cute and helped them fight the fire? But with maybe 20 words exchanged between them and he's jealous of her attention and she's lonely without him. It's positively insulting. Certainly, it's unfulfilling to have no build-up to romance. Often, there's not even build-up to the sex scenes. Oh, right - sometimes there will be events that happen that parallel historical events, but they're given no real weight. Sometimes it happens as pure info dump that has a character spouting something that sounds like it came out of a history book. I guess it's just to remind everyone that they're the Shinsengumi, not firefighters. Because that's like 90% of what some of the routes are actually about when it wasn't about trying to sex up the girl who is constantly saying, "No!" I usually say, "Story doesn't much matter to me - I prefer characters." but I think I'd honestly have preferred if it were a game about Shinsengumi-era firefighters to this.
Bleh. Sano's route is lovely and a couple of the others had their nice moments hidden in the rough, but unless you read my review and thought, "Oh, but, that doesn't sound bad, actually?", I wouldn't recommend getting the game.

The story in the introduction was okay. While I liked the opening for the game (at the beginning of the prologue), the prologue itself wasn't particularly thrilling or exciting. The route plots varied... somewhat. They were mostly focused on relationships. I liked that to some extent, but I felt the situations were cliché and I could guess what was going to happen. The clichéness I could handle, but if I play a game, it should be interesting. If I can all the time guess what happens next, it's not exciting anymore. (Gosh, I sound like Heisuke...) So no particularly adventurous plots and if there were moments like that, they were gone in an instant.
I liked the art. The characters were all attractive, the backgrounds didn't stood out to me (which can be good or bad, depending on you)... So I won't really complain about that.
As for the characters. Gosh, some of them made me SO ANGRY. This is a game so I shouldn't take them too seriously but I was mostly really annoyed by how forceful some of them were and didn't take NO for an answer. The MC didn't resist enough in my opinion, so I don't know whether she truly disliked it or not. BUT. They were a couple of sweethearts that made me squeal in their routes. It's a MUST in my otome games, at least.
I did notice some typos. Words that didn't belong together, some odd phrasing... But it wasn't enough to put me off. Except, in some riskier scenes, I felt like facepalming. And laughing.
So. This game has good and bad things. I don't regret buying the game but I think you shouldn't expect too much. I suggest buying it on sale, if you don't mind some cliché romances and hilarious (or not) misunderstandings.

As a preface I only played the first episode, but I'm not really interested in buying and playing the other two. The world was interesting and it's a great idea to have an immaginary toy world be a genre-aware noir story. That said, the main character, Amber, didn't really seem to fit? Other than the side note of her liking art, she only seemed to fill the purpose of being a snark-generator. There wasn't much about her room or comments to indicate that she would have a detective, true-crime toy world. Until she outright stated her age, I had pegged her for being 12-14 based on her voice, choice of reading material, and socio-political comments.
A few times I thought I would get to play a puzzle mini-game, but just didn't, most notably with developing the photo. With the book on the shelf, it seemed I should have had to read some instructions from there and execute a sequence right to progress. Additionally, some of the pathing was jarring. Amber glid through a desk to reach a target, rubbed her face into a wall to sidle to a target, stepped into a wall before coming back to open a door, and walked very very far away from the attic door before swiping up with the hook no where near the door or ceiling to open the ladder leading up.
The game is cute, and has humor, when the timing lands. The voice acting is pretty good, especially Mr. Bear's. But the lack of polish on the movement, lack of real puzzle solving,  and the low emotional investment in the protagonist leads me disinclined to play the rest of the story.

World of Guns: Gun Disassembly is a good game, so long as you don't invest real cash into it. The game starts you off with a rather annoying tutorial, which you can't skip at all, focusing on exploring the game's various features and how to disassemble/reassemble the starting firearm, the AK-47. The modeling and texturing of the AK-47 is very intricate and appealing, however this level of polish is only present for the first two 'starter' weapons, the second being the M1911 handgun, -also very detailed and highly polished. Every other weapon that I have unlocked using the in-game currency-based unlock system are awfull, low-polygon, muddily textured guns that come no where near the standard set by the starter weapons mentioned earlier. If you were to invest real money in this game to bypass the game's very grindy nature, you'd sorely regret it because the awful weapon models heavily reduce your enjoyment of exploring the intricate designs of the weapons provided.
However, if you can look past the blantantly lazy design of the models unlocked later in the game, you'll get a lot of enjoyment out of disassembling/reassembling a very wide array of both modern day and historical firearms.
So, in conclusion, for the low price of nothing, World of Guns: Gun Disassembly is well worth trying out, if you're interested in firearms. I do not, however, recommend that you spend real money on the game's firearm models, unless you just want to support the developers.

This game was very ambitious, and the story was really engaging and interesting.  No character was overly dull.
POSITIVES:
+Pretty decent FMV acting, with the exception of your receptionist.
+Engaging story
+Ambitious design (an interesting take is always good, even if the execution isn't stellar)
+Adjustable hint cooldown timer
+Subtly Lovecraftian with a slow buildup
NEGATIVES:
-While the game certainly tries hard and has a ton of FMV responses, the questions to ask are often unintuitive.  More than once I asked what should've been the most logical follow-up question and it was a dud.
-You'll be relying on hints a lot, even to complete the game.
-The story is really ambigious regarding everything except the main plot; they introduce a TON of side stories that go nowhere.  It's okay to maintain a good mystery, but a lot of them were so interesting it's a shame to have them go underdeveloped.
Overall, a really interesting project; just don't expect to achievement hunt.  Either way, highly recommended.

There is so much to do in this game, and so many options to explore. As you play, you get to know your patients, asking them questions that may vary from professional and casual to extremely personal and inappropriate. You can play as a good doctor, trying to help them with the reasons they come to see you, or a bad doctor, encouraging them to do things that made them come to you in the first place, as both you and your patients fall deeper and deeper into the rabbit hole. The use of Full Motion Video in games is a lot like Marmite; you either love it or hate it.
If you hate it, then move along, this is not the game you’re looking for, however if like me, you’re a fan of FMV’s then you should stick around for this review because The Infectious Madness of Doctor Dekker is a feast of full motion video goodness.
The premise behind TIMODD (I can’t keep typing the whole title, I swear the names of games are getting longer) is that you are a psychiatrist called in to replace the recently murdered Doctor Dekker.
In addition to filling the dead doctors’ shoes by treating his colourful array of patients you’ll also need to investigate his murder, one of those oddball patients almost certainly did away with Dekker.
The game starts with a short montage video and a rather abrupt conversation with Jaya, the dead doctors (and now your) assistant. You’ll then find yourself sitting in the big chair, ready for the first of the previously mentioned “odd balls” to take their place on the couch in front of you.
The core of this game is all about the conversations you’ll have with these patients, and they really are an eclectic bunch.
What you say to them, how you treat them and what you find out about Dekkers murder are all up to you.  The more you ask, the more you’ll learn and you’ll want to uncover as much as you can because these are some of the most interestingly bizarre characters I’ve ever met.
Each patient has their own distinct personality with their own unique problems, the depths to which their problems extend are slowly revealed throughout your sessions (and maybe the occasional dream sequence).
I’m not going to talk about the patients’ individual conditions, I recommend going into TIMODD as spoiler free as you can to get the most enjoyment out of it, but you can expect some dark twists and turns as you uncover the extent of their madness...
... or maybe it’s the truth?
The dialogue is so well written and the interlinking story so well thought out that no matter how bizarre the events patients describe to you become (and they get pretty weird), they always seem just on the fringe of being plausible. It’s a tricky thing to pull off and it’s done here with style.
Of course the best writing in the world will fall flat with a bad delivery, but TIMODD pulls another ace out of its sleeve here with the quality of the actors involved.
Every performance strikes the perfect balance between realistic portrayal and the over the top hamminess we all expect from titles like this and whilst every actor involved did a good job there were a couple of standouts.
Millin Thomas does amazing work in bringing the character Bryce to life, balancing the more sinister aspects of the character against a kind of hopeful naivety and of course Aislinn De’ath for her hauntingly seductive role as Marianna which was as disturbing as it was endearing.
So we know that TIMODD tells an interestingly dark tale through a cast of believably bonkers characters but what about the game part of the game?
It’s time to explore the interactive part of this movie and that is done through a dauntingly empty text box sitting at the top of the screen.
That’s right, this game takes the free form text approach to interaction, you type what you want to say and the patient sitting in front of you will reply, revealing a little more about themselves, their condition, relationships and their feelings towards Dekker.
So keeping in mind that they’re all crazy, one of them is probably a murderer and you’re supposed to be the sane one...
It’s time to start typing...
... and that’s where you’ll come across the most frustrating part of what is otherwise a hugely entertaining experience, the text parsing interface.
Now remember that text parsing isn’t new thing; it’s been around for ages, if you’ve ever played a game using this type of interface you’ll already be aware of its limitations.
There is no denying that the ability to type what you want to say directly into a game can create a really immersive experience, type “Hello” and get a “Hi” back, type a question and get a coherent answer, it all adds to the experience.
At least that’s the theory and it can be an amazing way to interact with a game.... when it works; the problem is that as a gaming interface it doesn’t work well consistently.
The reality is that you can’t just type what you want and expect the program to understand you.
The software will look for key words or phrases in your text to help it identify which reply it thinks will be appropriate.
You need to learn how to talk to this type of interface to get the most out of it, and even when you have gotten used to the invisible phrasing the system expects, you will still find yourself bombarded with endless “I’m sorry I didn’t understand that” responses as you struggle to make yourself understood.
What should and could be an immersive interface can quickly become a huge frustration as you type countless variations of the same sentence desperately trying to make the software understand.
The impatience this causes will inevitably lead you to abandon the full articulate sentences you input at the start of the game for a kind of keyword short hand hoping to hit on a combination that will prompt a response and move the story forward.
You’re also going to need to take your time typing these key words, spell something wrong and the software isn’t going to understand that either.
It was a brave decision for D’avekki Studios Ltd to go with this form of interaction for thier psychiatric sleuth’em’up.
So does the problematic interface sap all of the enjoyment out of the game?
Thankfully no, it’s an obstacle that can’t be ignored but there is a hint system to ease your typing troubles.
If (When) you get stuck and can’t bear to watch another of the several “ask me something else” video clips, all you need to do is type the word “hint” and the game will suggest a question you should ask which will push the narrative forward (you are going to use this hint system a lot, I guarantee it!).
There are also additional clues to help guide you as you play.
You have the option to watch replays of the patients responses, the important ones will be marked indicating that you should press the patient further on something they’ve said.
You also have the option to turn on subtitles which highlight any key words in italics, using these words in your questioning will likely uncover new secrets.
This extra help means that the text parsing interface is by no means a game breaker, but there is no denying that it is cumbersome and definitely a detriment to the experience as a whole...
...but the experience as a whole is still a positive one.
The fascinating characters and the tale they tell it worth the price of admission alone, the interactive elements are just a bonus.
If you enjoyed “Her Story” or “Contradiction: Spot the Liar” then you’re almost certainly going to enjoy TIMODD.
Yes the interface is clunky but persevere and you’ll uncover an amazing, intertwining and subtly dark tale revolving around control, the supernatural and of course, madness.
At the start of this review I asked if you were an FMV fan and if you’re still here with me now I’m guessing you are.
So as an FMV fan (and assuming you can see past the text interface) you’d be crazy not to pick up a copy of the Infectious Madness of Doctor Dekker.

What is often overlooked in DOOM, because most game "journalists" have lost any ability to play a game like that, is the multiplayer.

- the loadout system make you ready at all times. It's also friendlier for beginners. The weapons are all perfectly balanced and from time to time someone will surprise you in the way he uses a weapon you never thought was so effective
- the game is very easy to get into. No complicated rules, but it's rich enough that you'll still find new techniques to master even after several days
- the network code is top notch
- the maps are plenty and varied (hint: explore them in practice mode and notice all the little details)
- there are various match modes
- the graphics and the sounds are perfect
If you miss the old Quake or Unreal Tournament style multiplayer games, this is the one you need. It's also not just a pale copy but really bring in new improvements. There's nothing like it (and forget Quake Champions, it doesn't compare).

Utterly charming visual novel (not an adventure!) about bright young minds in turn-of-the-century Vienna. Each episode covers a different character, Ep. 1 a composer secretly in love with her mentor, Ep. 2 a portrait painter struggling to capture all facets of his subjects, Ep. 3 a mathematician who needs to disguise herself as a man to be taken seriously. Each character is shown to perceive a hidden reality, be it sounds, images or ideas where they draw their inspiration from. Along the way you encounter famous Viennese such as Sigmund Freud and Gustav Klimt. It's really beautiful, artistic, grown-up stuff - just be prepared that there is almost zero interactivity, only four or five different choices you can take per episode.

Yes, this game's difficulty is not for everyone. Yes, this game will troll you several times. And yes, you'll die a lot — sometimes just a couple of steps away from clearing a level! If you can't stand any of that, then I'll get this out of the way for you right now: just give this one a miss, but at least strongly consider buying it. Otherwise, go right ahead and grab this game! It's pretty cheap and yet provides a fair amount of bang for your buck.
The presentation is amazing, the 8-bit-style art looks great (both in-game and during cutscenes), and most notably the controls are tight, precise, and work like a dream. You have a button for each a low and a high jump (one and two tiles high, respectively), and you also have a shoot button to take out the occasional critter, stop projectiles that are coming at you, break blocks to unveil secret collectibles, and change the trajectory of spinning blade traps. Mastering these controls is key to survive the increasingly deadly gauntlets you'll come across along the way.
Throughout the game, you'll be able to unlock guest characters from other indie games. Each character has their own gameplay gimmicks such as higher jump height, hovering, or rapid-fire shooting. There are also a few unlockable extra game modes but I personally didn't find them that interesting.
If you're a fan of NES-styled, tough as nails titles, I can't recommend this one enough. The levels are tough but they never feel like they're impossible, although a few of them may have an RNG factor which could lead to some unfair, perhaps even unavoidable deaths. I will admit that I quit the game a few times because of stuff like that, but there was something about it that kept me coming back. It's fun, addicting, challenging, and very satisfying once you get the hang of it.
(P.S.: The adorable Curly Brace from "Cave Story" is one of the guest characters in this game!)

1001 Spikes is a game that seems like it should be frustrating, which makes it all the more impressive that it generally isn't. Between the well-cultivated atmosphere and the responsive, reliable controls, a death doesn't feel like you've been cheated, even when spikes suddenly skewer you from the platform you thought was safe - rather, it feels like you and the ruins are each constantly plotting to outwit the other.
That's not to say that it's not difficult, just that the difficulty, speaking as someone who is just past the halfway point, seems fair. In general, even the most nefarious traps give just enough warning that in theory you could avoid them all the first time  you saw them - though, well, that's not too likely. While the game makes a point of being 'hardcore' with your life counter steadily ticking down from 1001 and autosave keeping you honest, it's more forgiving than it looks there as well - the relics you collect at the end of areas give you bonus lives and it's fairly reasonable to stay 'on pace'. There's also a nice variety of levels and challenges to face - some where you'll be carefully planning out each move, and some where you'll be madly dashing through corridors.
In all, 1001 Spikes feels as though it turned out exactly as intended - simply put, it's a well-crafted game, and one worth experiencing.
Totally worth the purchase IMO. Old-School memory skills required, eye pleasing pixel-art to consume, and Souls-Like courage recommened.

Tribes: Ascend is an excellent reincarnation of the old Tribes franchise. With a "high lethality" design players are constantly rewarded with kills and dying is merely an inconvenience. The game is incredibly fast and fun, with excellent tense moments that require solid teamwork to succeed. The game is a few years old now, but is still my go-to game for a 30 minute match of exciting fun.
HiRez made some poor decisions with weapon releases and monitization design which prematurely killed the game balance, and subsequently, the community. With their MOBA Smite leading the way in successful competitive gaming, Tribes: Ascend is left with naught but few HiRez-hosted servers, a small selection of maps, and no developer attention for over a year.
Now you are lucky to find a half-filled server of players, but I find the smaller games to be much more rewarding. Despite it's waning lifecycle, the die-hard fans still play every day, and the game is just as much fun as it was at launch.
I highly recommend playing Tribes: Ascend for it's fast-paced, exciting gameplay. But don't be too discouraged when you come across minor issues; unless HiRez changes their plans, they're here to stay.

I wasn't sure how much I'd enjoy this game going in.  Any time I hear the words "troll" and "platformer" in the same sentence, I get worried.
Turns out I needn't have worried.  Yes, the game is full of hidden spike traps.  Falling boulders.  Pits.  You name it, there's a way to die.  But it also turns out that giving the player 1001 lives to start, and more upon retreiving each relic at the end of each set of stages, makes things more palatable; even more so considering a good run through most stages takes under a minute.
There's a lot of memorization there, so in a lot of ways, it's a speed-runner's dream game.  It takes a lot of attempts, but you'll start breezing through early traps to get to the trouble spots over and over, and eventually, you'll get the perfect run down.  You'll bask in the exultation of victory when you get through that doorway at the end of each stage.  In many ways, it's a very, very compressed version of the sorts of deaths something like Battletoads threw at you; deaths you won't see coming, but in stages that are far shorter, with a much more generous helping of lives.  In other words, tweaks that would have made a wildly creative game like Battletoads nearly perfect.
It also certainly helps that the game controls wonderfully.  Controls are tight and responsive, with a unique dual-jump setup.  Not a double-jump, but two different ones: a single-block jump, and a higher double-height one.  You'll use both to make it to the end, and you might think the double-height one would be the way to go, but the single-block jump will keep you from impaling yourself in quite a few spaces, or bopping your head on a ceiling and plummeting to your doom.  It's quite efficient, and perhaps more precise than using a hold-the-button system for higher jumps.
It's actually a very nice-looking game, too.  It's very pixelated, but the art design is very cohesive and strong in this one.  It's clearly a step above the usual 8-bit indie look.  Matt Kap, who also was responsible for Castle in the Darkness, headed up the graphical design.  The soundtrack is pretty limited, but you'll get pumped when that "key obtained" music starts playing.  RushJet1 did a lot of the work here, and hearing him put his NES music skills to use is a joy.
If you've got any sort of patience for games like Electronic Super Joy or Super Meat Boy, you will likely enjoy this one as well.  I actually prefer it to either of those games, because I like the theme and the controls more than either of those games, but they're different variants on the same theme: short-but-brutal platforming.  Two thumbs up.

I'll start by saying I only played this game for the first time just over a week ago, so this isn't a review based on nostalgia or anything. I also don't care about graphics. A good story, well developed characters and fun gameplay are what's important, and Bully has all of those. Now, onto the review... So you play as Jimmy Hopkins, a 15 year old who's been expelled from so many schools his parents have tired of him and sent him to stay at Bullworth Academy. From the offset, the other students seek to make Jimmy's life miserable. After the initial few missions where you're introduced to the games various mechanics and features, the game begins proper. As a student, you can attend classes, like Biology, English and Music. All these classes play out differently. For example, Music and Chemistry require you to press a button at the correct time, while English has you making as many words from a given set of letters as you can. All the lessons are done very well and (except the Dodgeball lesson in Gym and every Geography class) I enjoyed them. After you complete each class, you earn clothing, upgrades, perks and improvments for Jimmy. If only real life school rewarded you for attending each lesson... Anyway, I won't delve too much into the story aspect of the game. But, I will say there are some exciting twists in store. Another thing: this game's music is AMAZING. Seriously, I've not been able to get the music that plays when you fight the 'Greasers' out of my head for days! Ah yes, I should mention the gangs, or cliques as they're known. They all have distinct appearances, attitudes, hang out in different areas and have different music associated with them too. There's the bullies, nerds, preps, greasers (my favourite), jocks and townies (also known as 'dropouts', since they dropped out of the school). The different groups are handled really well and really give the game a unique feel. Honestly, anyone expecting this to be a 'child version of GTA', prepare to be blown away. I had high expectations for this game, seeing as it's held in high regard and is pretty unique in it's concept. Happy to say, I was blown away and Bully has quickly become one of the greatest games I've ever had the pleasure to play. It has a really well designed open world, handles seasonal holidays wonderfully (I LOVED the Christmas missions) and the combat is so much fun. 10/10 for sure.

But he soon realizes that the whole school is full of mean bullies who need to learn a lesson.
Going to classes isn't obligatory to finish the game. Some are quite interesting though and you can earn cloths and improve your stats if you pass them which can help you down the road. Also, you can get punished for not going to classes. So be ready to stand your ground or don't get caught.
+ you can go to classes again. yay!
+ interesting mission variety
+ you can ride bicycles to get faster from A to B
+ you can earn a skateboard and a slingshot which are very useful
+ makes fun and is motivating to play further
+ lasts around 12-15 hours for doing only the main story. but if you want to reach 100%, it will need much more hours.
+ Rockstar has guts to show crazy stuff
+ you can customize your appearance in the early game
- bad console port. this game runs with only 30 FPS. You could use the 60 FPS fix, but you would have to change back to the vanilla version of the game for certain missions.
- the music is horrible. luckily, it can be turned off completely
- some controls are awkward to use
- fighting is easy. Often times, you can just spam the punch button to overwhelm most enemies.
- it's not always clear what you have to do
- story is more linear than it needed to be. i wanted to join a social circle group, but the streamlined story made it impossible.
- game feels a bit dated. where is bully 2?

I've used the Steam Controller for about a year now, coming from a DS4 and Wii U Pro gamepad. It had a rocky start software-wise, but with the more recent updates (radial menus, activators) it has finally come into its own. I use it to play Overwatch, TF2 and the occasional Civ V game from across the room and it has worked flawlessly once you customise your setup.
The touchpads take some getting used to. I'm not convinced that the left touchpad works well for movement, despite a lot of community configs trying to push for it. Instead it makes a perfect pad for touch menus to keep all your hotkeys on. The haptics are impressive, though I wish more games specifically supported the SC haptics instead of generic rumble.
The other main draw, the gyro, works amazingly well with first person games. It has become second nature to try to move the controller around Splatoon-style trying to aim, and feels a lot less accurate without it (though the trackpads alone can work fine if you really hate it).
If you're willing to set up your config for each game to your liking, the Steam Controller is a fantastic device. The only thing I'd improve is take the Wii U Pro's d-pad and stick it somewhere near the left pad - platformers can get finicky and I still can't get used to analogue controls for them after all these years.

When I ordered the controller I questioned if it would be worth it. I've now had the controller for a little over a month and I don't regret it. There are some downsides to it, for example, some games like Trine do not work well with the mouse-like joystick and games without controller support can be difficult to make a configuration for but overall I think it is a worthwhile purchase.

This is hands down my favourite gaming controller. To compare, I've used all major console controllers starting with the NES all the way to the PS4/XBOX360. My second favourite controller has to be the XBOX360 controller, but the Steam controller beats it by miles for many reasons in my opinion. Here are just a few highlights that have stood out for me:
- Battery life is really good; I'm only on my second set of AAs and I've had the thing for over a year, gaming at LEAST 3 days a week for over an hour.
- The haptic pads are a functional compromise between a joystick and a mouse with many advantages of both, and coupled with the accelerometer, they are amazingly accurate (touch pads for fast motion + accelerometer for fine motor control)
- Customizability is miles ahead of anything else I've ever used. You can adjust the joystick to compensate for the angle of your thumbs, how cool is that?!
- Steam overlay typing mode is the best controller based keyboard input I've seen. Really intuitive and fast.
- Works in Linux.
Notable disadvantages:
- The trackpads did begin to hurt my thumbs after a couple of hours of gaming (but seriously, this should be a sign you have spent enough time gaming for the day), however, coupling the accelerometer with them does make a big difference here and I haven't had this happen again since.
- It only works through the Steam overlay, which is a huge bummer. I'd love to be able to use it without Steam except to configure it.
- The developers missed an opportunity to put a convenient storage location for the controller dongle inside or on the battery door. There is an accessory battery door that does provide this, but it should be the standard.
- The LG/RG buttons are a little loud and feel flimsy. I would prefer something a little smoother with adjustable haptic feedback like many of the other components.
I love it. I recognize it's not for everyone, but I am really glad I took the chance on it.

I just came off a replay of Hakuouki, and was desperate for more interaction with the Shinsegumi. This game caught my eye initially because not only was it on sale, but the art was beautiful and even though I knew it wasn't at all connected with Hakuouki, I decided to give it a shot. Before I get into the review proper, a little note: I did my best not to compare this game with Hakuouki, since the two plots are pretty much night and day, and that's fine. The Shinsegumi are a popular subject for media material, so Hakuouki definitely didn't 'do it first' or anything.
That being said, let's start with the negative and end on the positive.
Negative:
- The available guys all seemed to be in-love with the heroine from the moment they met her. This isn't exactly new for otome games of this nature, but most of them offer some sort of buildup. This one never did, and it was jarring.
- The heroine, likewise, seemed in-love with them right off the bat. I tried to rationalize it was her being swept up in the events of that night since they did just rescue her, but again it was weird.
- I wasn't expecting a deep, complicated plot when I bought this. But I also wasn't really expecting to finish every route, extra stuff included, in a couple of hours. A short game wouldn't bother me, if the plot was at least decent and the plot for this game just fell flat. It was the same thing, time after time, and each route only offers minor changes (in my opinion, at least).
- The soundtrack has some issues, which I've seen mentioned in other reviews. While not awful, the looping isn't done well and it's a little choppy, the way it shifts between tracks. This wasn't a huge issue, since I just turned the BGM off and listened to my own music, but still.
- No Hijikata route. I guess there was a trade off? We could romance Shinpachi here, but not Hijikata.
Okay, look, no bullet points for this complaint: I'll be honest and say forceful guys are not exactly a turn on for me when it comes to romantic plots. I don't mind if the guys are a little rough around the edges, but when it starts to become physical then it crosses a line I'm not comfortable with. I mention this because in this game, nearly all of the guys are extremely forceful in their attraction to the heroine. Given the period the game is set in, I am used to the guys being 'protective' of the heroine and holding her back, expecting her to listen to their orders. If that had been the case, I'd have overlooked it. That was, sadly, not the case.
I can't even remember the amount of times the situation turned sexual and the heroine spent most of it trying to tell the guy to stop. Most of them continually said it was 'her fault for being so cute' and that 'it seems like your body likes it' and I just, I was disgusted. Maybe it was translation? I'm not entirely sure and at this point, I don't really care. The only two options who didn't do this to such an awful point were Nagakura Shinpachi and Harada Sanosuke; the former was actually rather sweet and I'm glad I did his last, meanwhile the latter wasn't perfect but it was better than some of the others.
Souji and Hajime both had varying instances of these bad scenes; it was disappointing because outside of those scenes, Hajime's route wasn't awful. Souji's route left almost no impact on me either way, which is disappointing as he'd been my first pick.
Heisuke's route, however, made all of the others look tame. Now let me start off by saying that it was Heisuke's route that caused me to break my rule of not comparing this game to Hakuouki; in Hakuouki, Heisuke took me by surprise as being one of my top three routes, so seeing the way he acted here was...hard to swallow. His overall personality would have been fine, I'm not really into guys that act like bratty kids but, whatever. No, it was the way he treated the heroine. He was constantly groping her and basically violating any and all personal space boundaries.
That scene during the fire where he sexually assaults her? I had to walk away for a moment. It gets worse from there, and what's worse is even after spending so much time telling him no, in the end the heroine is in-love with him and accepts his actions. She does this in all of the routes, but not until Heisuke's did it just drive home how
this game was at handling relationships. Again, I know that given the time period, women did not experience some of the freedoms we do now, and so when I play games set in these kind of settings I try to remember that. Does that mean I support plots that use sexual assault for the sake of drama and shock? Hell no. It also means I don't agree with notions of 'violence = love' which is an awful trope and shouldn't even be a thing.
It was just a huge slap in the face when after repeatedly telling him to stop, the heroine found herself liking his actions. She even tells him at one point 'no means no' and he then tries to guilt her into complaining about how she always tells him no. Ugh, if there was ever a moment I wished we could get refunds on games from Steam...
The positive aspects are pretty much what I stated earlier: the artwork was very lovely and the game was on sale. If I had to come up with another, I guess Shinpachi's route was pretty nice? I got the sense that he and the heroine did have some sort of connection, and even the scene where he had to strip her was given context, plus he clearly wasn't happy doing it. His route is the only one I can safely say I didn't mind playing.
Overall, this game was a huge disappointment and while I'd gone into not expecting much, I left with such a bad taste in my mouth. Every person is entitled to their own opinion, but I'd give this game a pass if you're considering it.

A compelling pulp story with horrible gameplay.
It's hard to describe how awful this text parser is. Often, to ask questions, you have to retype the question with "yes" or "no" in the front. Also, the game teaches you to just... retype sentences, without changing the subjects, even if it makes no sense. For example: "yes what do you think doctor".
I would just set hints on immediately. I'm not because I'm stubborn, but it's made the game a complete ♥♥♥♥ing chore. As far as I can tell, the game was designed around this hint system--and that's extremely goddamn lazy. It defeats the point of making a text parser game. I've stumbled onto answers there are NO earthly way of getting without hints except through mad guesses--that are plot critical.
This game doesn't have that many creative responses baked in, anyway. It doesn't feel investigative like Her Story since the responses seem to be heavily gated and the keyword pool is anemic--and when you sequence break, it makes no sense and it's really hard to retrace your steps.
So, this is a horrible GAME, it's a very cool MOVIE THAT PLAYS. There are infinitely less obtuse retro text adventures, IF games, and other indie text parser games.
I've never played a game that made me so frustrated... when I typed in the right answer.
I hope there's a sequel. Devs, if you're reading this: don't design a text parser game like this. Either redesign how you write questions or have conversation nodes. Every element of interaction in this game is joyless, immersion breaking (since I can't ask actual questions), and dull.

A very different from the usual FMV adventure game, with a welcome mechanic of a text parser where you can freely type questions and answers.
The acting is very good, the characters and the themes are interesting (albeit a few times a bit disturbing too) and the story packs quite a few surprises.
The text parser does have a few issues. (As it is currently) Sometimes the game will expect specific wording for a question or answer. For example (not an actual question from the game) "How did John die?" and "How did your son die?" could refer to the same thing, but the game would accept only one of the two. A few other times a keyword in your text will trigger a response that is not what you intended to ask and in fact is further into the logical development of your dialogue with that person.
But there are other times that the text parser works surprisingly well, and the developers seem to be actively patching the game, so this could get even more improved down the line.
Also, there is a hint system that will help you get unstuck at any point.
Overall, I do recommend the game. I've spent quite a few hours with it, loved most of its characters, and was very impressed by the production values and quality.

This is a very good entry in the sci fi 4X field - you have the standard strategic choices to make of how fast to expand, whether to push economic, technology, military or colonization efforts, choose where to explore and settle, when to go to war, and within the technology trees you have largely the same dilemmas of which areas to develop.
For me this is were Endless Space excels - there are no easy answers most of the time, for example when choosing the next technology to work on there always seems to be a number of that you really want, but rarely anything that stands out as much better than the rest, and there isn't much in the way of filler either (only really military technologies that don't fit your play style/game situation, diplomacy related techs in some situations/game setups, and the later happiness techs if you are playing on the easier levels).
As in most of these sorts of games getting a tech lead is key, but in doing so you still have to cover the bases and have enough military to deter or hold up the enemy if they attack, and enough production to churn out an actual defense force quickly before your enemies are at the gates, plus to research fast you need to expand your empire to some good locations, and expanding means you need to start dealing with the rising unhappiness of your growing population, which then distracts your technology aims towards happiness related techs, and diverts your tax money into panem et circenses.
The ship design system works fine, and gives a lot of flexibility to try out lots of alternatives - you basically have a doubled rock-paper-scissors system of short range quick firing cannons, medium range lasers, and long range but slow missiles, and three matching types of defenses you can put on each ship to reduce or avoid the damage from each type. Plus the customary massive range of other things (repair systems, weapons boosters, troops, anti-population/infrastructure weapons, scouting modules, etc). You can try to specialize (with "wall" ships protecting "glass cannons" at the back of the fleet, specialist support ships that carrry power modules that increase the rest of the fleets weapon damage, and many other options), or just lots of similar ships maybe not as strong due to being jack of all trades, but meaning damaged fleets can just merge together without missing a key element, etc. And that is even before considering what your scouting of enemy fleets tells you about what weapons systems and defenses they are using and whether you want to adapt your fleets to take advantage of that (and risk being weak against a third party attack, or the next wave of his fleets that have a completely different weapons systems/defense preferences).
The battle system is pretty much "auto calc" only, although you can watch (and they look fairly cool the first few times through), and you make a few strategic choices (and if you watch you can adapt to the enemies tactics or changing situation slightly). Personally I think it works fine here - it keeps the strategic part of the game flowing, especially in the late game when there are lots more fleets around and turns would otherwise take an eternity while at war (as many half won games of MOO2/MOO3/Ascendancy/etc. got eventually abandoned due to being too close to autocalc everything, but too slow to actually feel like taking the time to grind out the last remnants of the enemy).

I really enjoyed this game.
some of the pros of it are the available tanks and upgrades you can get for them, the detail of it and the customization is perfect! the maps are pretty good too. (though i wish there were more) You can play as all the factions involved in WW2: U.S., Britain, Germany, U.S.S.R, Japan, and France. I am still hoping for Italy to come in even though there are already chinese tanks you can play as.
Some of the cons that i have found:
-I think its really stupid that you can stick your gun into an enemy or vica versa and do damage to them. or the fact you can move your gun and turret through buildings but not your chasis? why not if your going to ignor logic, why not go all the way.
-I think there should be an option in the matchmaker to only play on teams that are only 1 faction instead of the usual mix, i like the other way but i think it would be more fun to see how factions do against eachother.
-the whole spotting system, i think it should all be "line of sight". the spotting system destroys my experience during gameplay and gives hugely unfair advantages in tricky situations that require you to be able to see an enemy. for example: instead of you noticing an enemy as it is moving from around a corner to shoot you, with the spotting system you have to wait a few seconds before the game ALLOWS you to see them, and by then he has gotten of his shot and has retreated back. this is extremely frustrating and im surprised everybody who plays the game is okay with it.
-the XP system is broken. the game has an XP multiplier for when you win your first battle of the day, and it has never worked for me. also the amount of XP you earn per battle never goes above around 1000 for a victory even as you advance into the higher tiers, which makes grinding out for tanks an extreme bore, and i love grinding for stuff its just it takes forever to advance through the factions in this game.
-I have noticed something peculiar that is kind of hard to explain. lets say i have just won a battle i got 3 kills and mildly damaged. i recieve about 10k credits. now lets say the next battle i also win, however in this battle i get heavily damaged and almost die and get no kills.even though i have won AND i survived i would probably get -10k credits. now lets say the next battle we lose however i survive the battle, i would probably recieve 2k credits, even though we lost. what i want to point out is that there is no clear set rules for how much XP and credits you earn and why. there is also no bonuses for whether or not you win the battle, how many teammates survive, how many enemies YOU kill. or whether or not it is a "flawless victory" (no allies were killed) this gives the players no real incentive to win when i think there obviously should be.
-one final thing i want to point out is the new crate system. i want to start out by saying that i appreciate it, i just want to add something. I wish we could get the opportunity to win back old premium tanks like the Fury or the Cromwell B or the Mk.1 Heavy tank (which was taken out of the game completely for some reason). i think it would not be uncalled for and give us the opportunity to still play with tanks that cannot even be aquired with money now that they have left the game and only those who had the money when they came out can purchase them. I think that  would be popular with the players, and really cool if you added that content back into the game.
All in all i love this game, however the cons kind of destroy my experience playing it and i cannot with 100% confidence recommend this game
