OK, so you are probably reading the reviews for this game, wondering if you should download it or not. Well, I'm here to tell you that you should.
Now some people think that if they want to play Blitz, they'll play it on their mobile devices and if they want to play it on their PC... well they won't, they'll just go get the regular PC version, right? I agree, that's even what I would do. But what if you have a laptop, or a PC not powerful enough to run the desktop version of World of Tanks, and you find that the mobile version is hard to play due to the controls? Well, that was my situation. I tried playing the PC version of WoT but my laptop would not run it very well, and I knew the hours of grinding would be painful if they would be spent running the game at 15 fps constantly. So I downloaded this, and I kid you not when I say it fixed all my problems. It's World of Tanks Blitz (which I didn't mention I LOVED) with PC controls (I hated the mobile controls!). But enough with that; let's get to the contents!
WoT Blitz is easier. No doubt about it, and I know some people don't like it easy. But it's easy compared to the desktop World of Tanks. It still requires skill and strategy (somewhat) if you want to be successful. Just not as much as it's popular big brother. What mainly makes it easier is the grind. You don't need silver to buy the modules, and the experience is gained easier (I believe). The 7v7 matches go by quick and the small maps make sure there is action throughout the entire battle. There are also many events that take place that allow you to score some goodies, like boosters, credits, gold and premium tanks! Like the Lost Division event going on right now. These events always keep me playing because I'm working for something, I have the chance to win tanks and other valuable prizes (although the chances in this current Lost Division event are very small!). They also like to get creative with their tanks, for example; the Helsing HO or the Tankenstein. The tournaments are also exciting as they can reward you and your team.
So, the conclusion. With all the content in this game and the keyboard/mouse controls (if you don't like mobile controls), there's nothing else I can say but get it and enjoy it! As long as you don't depend on insanely great graphics to have fun with a game, you'll love this version of World of Tanks as you would any other.

The game itself is alright, but you don't get enough of an experience in this first episode to make a full review of the game or to build a decent opinion about it. The story is somewhat predictable and the riddles/puzzles are also very simple. The dialogue is however very well written and comes with great humor.
Ted is definitely the star of the show, it makes the most fun to play with him and to mess with people.
Even though it looks like a dark, jumpscare filled game on first sight, it does not have much of a horrific aspect to it at all, making it playable for the younger audience.
Do however keep in mind, that plushies were harmed in the making of this game!
+ The pretty artistic graphics are clearly outstanding
+ Nicely written dialogue that goes from cute to badass
+ Ted being the badass, Amber being the doll
+ Premise is basically Amber's house and playground, which is a good concept
+ Great noire crime detective story of the old days
+ Good humor even for adults
+ Exploration is rewarded with developer jokes and eastereggs.
+ Lots of 4th wall breaking
+ Lovely voice acting
~ Dialogue choices don't matter. You one way or another get what you want, making it linear.
~ Riddles and puzzles are too easy, but that's a personal opinion.
~ The game is somewhat predictable.
- Episode 1 (this one) is way too short to start with. The other 2 episodes don't add up much. It does make it good for achievement hunting, but I wish it was longer...
- No info that you are required to buy the other episodes as DLC to complete the game on the store page. (Similar point & click adventure games, like from Telltale, did this better).
Personal rating: 8/10
I think they could have made more out of it, especially considering how many extras they've put into special dialogues for clicking on certain objects. There should also be a clear info in the product description that DLCs are required to be purchased to acquire the full game.
Overall riddles could have been harder too, but maybe they've aimed for a younger audience with this game.
However, it is a good point & click adventure and in fact, if you'd like to get into this genre, I sure think it's a great game to start with!

Instant classic:
Story: A very realistic portrayal of how human greed and lust for power would look in a not-so-distant world where cybernetic enhancements are real: limbs dealing; shady organizations pulling the strings from the shadows, conspiring to control how people treat their bodies, their morality; racism towards others with or without augmentations, towards the ones that are not like you. A masterpiece of storytelling in which every decision that you make matters, in which every little action has its consequences. If you love thought provoking sci-fi, like Philip K.♥♥♥♥♥♥s, you'll love it.
Gameplay: First/Third person stealth mixed with heavy RPG elements (meaning you gain XP and upgrade your augmentations), with controls based on Rainbow Six: Vegas; but make no mistake, being caught usually means an instant death. You'll have to use your head and augmented body to make a plan to avoid confrontation (although you can simply augment yourself to be a tank, that's possible too). One of my favorite moments are the "conversation bosses"; those are purely word battles with terribly bad or good consequences that depend on your ability to anticipate the personality and weaknesses of the "boss". It feels like a Telltale game, really.
Music: One of the best soundtracks I've ever heard. If you like Vangelis' classic-electronic music, as seen in Blade Runner, you'll absolutely love this (in fact, I secretly love this more than Blade Runner's, but ssshhhhh). Michael McCann is a master composer.
Graphics/art: THIS. The way colors and clothes merge to talk about how the world feels on the inside -- a new renaissance that is losing momentum -- instead of simply looking realistical has a very deep impact in how the story is told. This is how visual art should work in a game or a movie. It's absolutely brilliant. Even if the tech of the game will eventually get old (spoiler-y: it's already old), the composition and colors will always hold up; that's how you make a classic.
Overall, a worthy successor to the original. Damn, I believe I have to play it for the fourth time. I never asked for this!

This game is a lot of fun, but newer players should be aware that the difficulty settings in this game are kind of broken.
That site breaks down the bonuses and penalties that human and AI players receive and as you can see, even on the easiest setting the AI gets help while the player doens't. There is no difficulty where there is an even match between the human and computer players in this game. Even on normal the player is getting slammed by penalties to approval while the computer players get not only ludicrous bonuses to approval, but also substantial bonuses to everything else. I would expect something like that on a higher difficulty setting, but not on normal.
While there are ways to mitigate the negative approval from expansion, the fact that approval is the only real way your expansion is limited is much bigger problem. In Master of Orion 2, for example, building a colony ship during the early game is an expensive undertaking; in Endless Space it is almost trivially easy. Making it harder to build a colony ship early on would have eliminated the need for the something as silly as expansion disapproval, at least to the extent it was implemented.
Giving players an actual easy setting would also lower the learning curve for those newer to 4x games. Also having an actual normal difficulty, in which neither side has any penalties of bonuses, would have made a lot more sense.
Ok, that is the bad news, and as bad news goes it really isn't all THAT bad. It can be annoying, but in the end I don't mind so much that the game makes me work for my victory. If you are someone who enjoys challenging 4x games, and like me has dumped a few thousand hours in to Master of Orion 2 and Galactic Civilizations, then you really do need this game. Not only is it beautiful, it runs very well and combines a lot of very good ideas into a game that is as enjoyable as it is challenging (for me anyway).

Endless space.  Well it definitely seems endless until some random AI or player appears out of the blue with tech that would take you 80 turns to catch up to. Like another reviewer wrote it is an excersize in walking down the middle of the road, straying too far one direction or another leads to punishment.
So lets break it down
Pro's
-Graphically better than average
-Very long scenarios (if thats your thing)
-Tons of tech paths
-Customizable balanced races
-Potentially huge universe
Cons
- While tons of options exist, viable strategies are severly limited
- Tech extremes (either you dominate vs enemy tech or you get completely destroyed)
- Zero forgiveness / ability to react to enemy tech - by the time you know its way to late
- Extremely long build up for a rapid end game desicion win or lose
Many games will end up 300 turns in with you dominating by teching one or two directions just to have the game end in the next 20 turns when you come against another that has teched to your weakness, it is merciless and gives no method of comeback.
Even if you continue to dominate non stop the game takes for ever. It becomes an effort in picking every weed from the proverbial garden chasind down every last fleet and spending turn after turn invading planets with you puny limited fleet.
Fleet size limiters basically strangle you throughout the game and create a near singular military tactic.  Attack every system all at the same time.  There is no ability to focus because your fleet size is obscenely limited and each fleet fights solo 1v1 then the next, and the next etc.
So much is not explained in this game, it lacks detailed tools to let you know exactly how things/tech will effect your empire making it difficult to plan without using a wiki or having only a vague idea of how something will effect your empire.
I really wanted this to be the next big 4x but sadly I have to not reccomend it as there are definitely better ones out there.

SOmewhat of a missed opportunity. I played many 8-bit platform games back in the day, and this game has the potential to recreate some of the best. The gameplay is simple, and easy to get the hang of. The look, feel, and sound are all top notch and recreate the 8-bit environemnt very believeably.
Sadly, the game falls into the trap that most 8bit platformers avoided like the plague. Because traps are hidden, it is not possible to plan a route through any given level, or to use skill to beat the game. One learns the route through a level by dying, repeatedly. One has to then remember all the correct moves, and execute them at the correct time. Beating a level owes a lot less to skill than to being able to remember exactly when to do what and where the traps are.
I gave it an hour, but put it down when I died for the 10th? 20th? time on a level after having got through all the traps I had spent ten minutes learning about, only to fall prey to yet another hidden trap. The level requires a series of jumps over blocks which melt under you, so timing is vital. But add to that the gun which shoots JUST as you are about to land on a vital brick and.. yeah. Sorry, but I got bored repeating the exact timing of jumps to get to that part of the level. I just don;t have the heart to do it another 10 times just so I can learn - little by little - the timing of the jumps needed to beat that last gun. The bullets travel too fast and there is no visible warning that the gun will fire: so it comes down to "just knowing" the exact, split-second timing of the jumps which are needed.
That's not fun. Which is a shame. Because, as I said: this game could have been very awesome indeed.

OK, so you are probably reading the reviews for this game, wondering if you should download it or not. Well, I'm here to tell you that you should.
Now some people think that if they want to play Blitz, they'll play it on their mobile devices and if they want to play it on their PC... well they won't, they'll just go get the regular PC version, right? I agree, that's even what I would do. But what if you have a laptop, or a PC not powerful enough to run the desktop version of World of Tanks, and you find that the mobile version is hard to play due to the controls? Well, that was my situation. I tried playing the PC version of WoT but my laptop would not run it very well, and I knew the hours of grinding would be painful if they would be spent running the game at 15 fps constantly. So I downloaded this, and I kid you not when I say it fixed all my problems. It's World of Tanks Blitz (which I didn't mention I LOVED) with PC controls (I hated the mobile controls!). But enough with that; let's get to the contents!
WoT Blitz is easier. No doubt about it, and I know some people don't like it easy. But it's easy compared to the desktop World of Tanks. It still requires skill and strategy (somewhat) if you want to be successful. Just not as much as it's popular big brother. What mainly makes it easier is the grind. You don't need silver to buy the modules, and the experience is gained easier (I believe). The 7v7 matches go by quick and the small maps make sure there is action throughout the entire battle. There are also many events that take place that allow you to score some goodies, like boosters, credits, gold and premium tanks! Like the Lost Division event going on right now. These events always keep me playing because I'm working for something, I have the chance to win tanks and other valuable prizes (although the chances in this current Lost Division event are very small!). They also like to get creative with their tanks, for example; the Helsing HO or the Tankenstein. The tournaments are also exciting as they can reward you and your team.
So, the conclusion. With all the content in this game and the keyboard/mouse controls (if you don't like mobile controls), there's nothing else I can say but get it and enjoy it! As long as you don't depend on insanely great graphics to have fun with a game, you'll love this version of World of Tanks as you would any other.

The mobile version of World of Tanks ported to PC( note different queues between mobile and PC). Now if one is not able to play the PC version or is looking for a quick side game. The Blitz version will suffice.
Taking into the key mechanics of the WOT and more or less simplfying them in a compact version. Hence why for mobile users. 7v7 quick matches are seen that can be strategically challenging or a complete zerg rush and of course the return of the grindy tech trees for nations. Nevertheless PC users can still find some fun if the criteria above are evident.

Been playing on and off since beta and I highly recommend this game if you want a different kind of FPS experience. The gameplay is slower and more tactical than about any other FPS on the market, not only in the way you have to focus on team play but also how you have to fight. With the ability to destroy parts of the enemy mech you have to make choices in the heat of the battle, do you go for the kill by destroying the center torso or do you first destroy their ability to fight efficiently by destroying their weapons (arms and/or side torso)? The game gives you a lot of different possibilities on how you want to fight, just keep in mind, this game will punish you hard of you try to do the "Rambo".
The game has its problems, game balance is a big one that has plagued the community for a long time. With 3 big weapon kinds (laser, ballistics, missiles) and with different weight classes and kinds of each of those makes getting everything equally  viable, very hard. And since the two factions both have their own variants of almost all the weapons with range, dmg etc differing between them, I imagine that its hell to make it all balanced. PGI do try and each patch has new tweaks to make it better. (Some times they do fail big time! ;)
Graphics and sound are really good, all crankt up the game looks amazing, sadly turning the settings down gives you an edge since you will have better visibility due to less particles in the air, less effects from weapons etc.
Seen some people saying that there is pay2win in MWO, but there isn't, there is no weapons, armour, "gold ammo" etc you can buy for real money. You can buy colours, skins, cockpit items, premium time (extra XP and cash rewards) and mechs. The newest mechs are only available for cash for a time after release, they will then come available for in-game currency. And since "new" mech doesn't equal "best" mech I fail to see the problem with that. F2P games need to make money and this is probably the best way they can do that with the player count they have. There is no content locked behind levels or any such nonsense (looking at you WoT, Warframe etc ). You can buy any mech in the game if you can afford them, want the first mech you buy to be a 100ton murder machine? No problem, with the in game currency you will make from completing the tutorial and your 25 first matches will reward you with extra cash (Cadet bonus, I believe that still in effect?) you will have lots of cash to spend on your first mech, I would recommend that you don't buy the most expensive one you can find, read the forums for great tips on what to go for depending on what weigh class you want to play.
Try it and don't give up just because to die without killing any one your first match! Believe it took me 5 matches before I got my first kill and man was it rewarding after all the fail in previous matches! ;)
I also recommend checking out the forums, MWO has a great community and will help new players with tips and tricks for getting started. Many will also drop in game with you and help you, great community of guys and gals!

A thorough delight of a game. Normally I tend to read game spoilers before I buy a title, out of habit and for a sense of control. This time, I decided to take the plunge and go on blindly, mostly because the title felt like a reference to one of my favourite horror characters, psychologist-of-dubious-morals Dr. Decker in Clive Barker's Cabal / Nightbreed.
I don't think the similarity ends at their name, nor do I think it was unintentional. There are a lot of genre references in the game that made me smile - the art gallery named Providence, the cat named Church, and so on. It's great fun to play a game that makes you realize the creators love the genre as much as you do.
The script is solid and the text recognition works intuitively enough (if not without a niggling technicality or two). I was impressed with how immersive and captivating the story was, the minimalist style in which it's told is impressive. Speaking as an actor, I can only applaud the work of everyone involved in front of the camera. Everyone nailed their characters and made each enthralling.
I'm currently on my second playthrough, and am planning more.
I'm not sure whether the randomization of the murderer was that good an idea, given that the questions you can ask the subjects remain the same, but I suppose it adds to replay value for some. (I'd replay it regardless.)
10/10 for me, a complete winner. I wouldn't change a thing. Will be following the creators to see what they cook up next!

IMDD (as I'll call it here) is an enduringly solid, lovingly crafted (no pun intented) game of dialogue, cosmic mystery and investigation. You may look at the FMV features, recall that somewhat infamous lineage, and write it off. Don't. Give this a chance, especially if you're a fan of slow-burn supernatural horror.
The game is structured not unlike the old HBO series "In Treatment" in some ways. You are a therapist seeing a core cast of five people, all patients of your predecessor, who was recently murdered. Ostensibly you are there as an investigator vetting suspects into the murder. But it soon becomes clear that something has invaded the lives of these people. Something sinister...
Gameplay consists of asking free text questions to any of the five (plus a few minor players showing up on different days) and slowly unraveling their secrets. Sometimes this is easy, but if it gets too difficult you can always summon hints that will point you toward new lines of questioning, and replay any unlocked dialogue (with or without in-line hints).
It's really impressive what they got out of their clearly limited budget. The HD video is crisp, well-lit and well edited, effects are used sparingly and in clever ways. Actor performances are never less than good although I will say nobody truly knocks it out of the park, either.
So basically, if you like Lovecraft, you like mysteries, and you came out of Her Story thinking "they should make more games like this", IMDD is well worth trying out.

FMV – the beast that should not be. It’s such an unlikely underdog, such an inexplicable contender for revival, such a shambling, clumsy mess. To those of us who played and somehow enjoyed the first FMV games of yesteryear, the very idea of bringing them back should seem almost scandalously ill-conceived. It’s that incongruity between the impossibility and reality of new FMV games that makes them such an irresistible treat. But more than this, what distinguishes Dekker (like Her Story before it) is the fact that it takes the stilted, on-again, off-again interactivity of navigating FMV sequences and grafts it onto a heavily constrained search engine. Given that I grew up in an Internet-deprived place and time, and so that FMV for me belongs to a decidedly pre-Google era, searching for keywords in these more recent offerings lends them yet another intriguing note of juxtaposition, between the dated and the modern.
I’m glad I picked up Dr Oetker. It strikes an entrancing balance between promise and the problematic, as all the while its rough course is somewhat softened by the warmth of its underlying humour. Without wishing to seem crass, it also bears remarking that Dekker doesn’t cost a lot, so it really doesn’t represent much of a risk if you’re considering dipping into this peculiar FMV/text movement (again). It certainly makes for an excellent alternative to a B-movie night, either with friends or on your own.

As someone who really enjoyed Her Story, seeing an ambitious game like this in the same genre was an instant buy. This is a kind of game i care about, so i'll try to go into some detail on what i liked and didn't like about it.
You are a psychiatrist. Doctor Dekker was the former psychiatrist and he died and now you're replacing him. This means you are now responsible for all his patients. The goal of the game is trying to help your patients with their crazy problems while you find what exactly happened to Doctor Dekker and who murdered him. The game is divided in acts and in each act you get to ask questions to your patients. To ask questions to your patients you just write the questions or keywords about the topic you want them to talk about.
New games on the same style of Her Story and Contradiction are always welcome for me, and this one is no exception. Even though i think this game doesn't live to the full potential of what fmv mystery solving games can achieve, it was a good effort and brought different elements to the table and that's why it gets my recommendation.
Let's just say that all Doctor Dekker patients are crazy to say the least :) But they are crazy for very different reasons and listening to their problems and hearing their stories was very enjoyable. The stories are all very different and interesting.
The murderer of Doctor Dekker is randomized at the beginning of each playthrough. This means that two different people playing the game will likely have two different murderers of Doctor Dekker and so the process of solving the case will be slightly different for those two players, with different events a happening in each playthrough. This also means that you can play the game more than once with a different murderer of Dekker in each one. This adds some replayability to the game and creates interest in seeing other people's playthroughs to see the different events that happen in each one. Even though some events change, most of the questions and answers you get from the patients are still the same in each playthrough, so don't expect a massive difference, but it's there and i see it as a good thing.
If you feel stuck you can always ask for a hint and the game will tell you something relevant you should ask next. The hints you get are good, i never felt like a hint was confusing, quite the opposite, the few times i asked for hints they were always helpull. Depending on the kind of player you are you will use this system a lot or avoid it completely and use only when necessary. Either way, i see it as a plus, since being stuck is never fun and with the hint system you'll rarely find yourself in that situation.
The acting is incredibly good. Most of the cast is made of professional actors/actresses and that shows.
The game is constantly getting updates. Since the release of the game a couple updates were released. Most od those updates aim to improve keyword searches to make sure you always get an appropriate video response to your input. Other are quality of life improvments that really help a lot.
Oh boy, this girl... <3
My main problem with this game is that it doesn't encourage you to think that much. In each act the process of progressing trough the story and asking questions is linear. Basically you say hello to them, they answer something, you take note of some important words they said, you input those words as questions, you get answers which contain more words, you input those new words, rinse and repeat. There are some questions you should ask that don't follow this pattern but they are not hard to figure out on your own. The main mental exercise of the game is probably at the end, where you have to accuse someone of being the murderer of Dekker, based on all you heard and the information you have, but even that i tought was relatively easy too.
It's not game breaking or anything like that, but a few searches can get unexpected results. Sometimes you make a question about something and get an answer unrelated to what you asked, most likely because you entered a keyword in your question which triggers multiple answers, even though the nature of the questions was different. The most extreme case of this happened to me when a patient asked me to do something, i answered with "no", but the system gave me the response as if i said "yes". There was also some questions i asked but because i wasn't using the exact keywords the game wanted, i got no answer, even though the question should have an answer. With this said, these issues related to searches are something the developers are always keeping a look at and trying to improve. Since the launch, the game received already some updates who fixed some of these problems related to keyword searches, and i expect them to keep doing these updates.

I avoid these episodic games, but they just released the 3rd/final episode so I played it. [And check what you are purchasing: You'll want to buy all three episodes. It's not a story and two sequels, it's just one story]. I'll guess the game is about 6-8 hours long, but a lot depends on how fast you are in the point and click puzzle solving, it could be finished much quicker.
It's an adorable film noir point and click adventure. A 10 year old girl and her foul mouthed, hard drinking (but still rated T for Teen) stuffed bear have a mystery to solve. You'll interrogate her other stuffed animals, explore her house, in a neat combination of the real world and her imagination. The art is styled and fun. The humor is great, the voice acting is spot on (seriously - well done on that. In a game with this much dialogue
The first two episodes are some of the best examples of how a point and click should be, solving many of the problems in the genre. Walking between rooms looking for something? Double click and you'll teleport. Really stuck? Ask the bear, and he'll give you hint that doesn't feel "cheaty." (Go into a different room and you'll get a different hint). If the mouse hovers over it, it's either an important item, or a joke. If you're stuck, you only have the ability to do a handful of things at a time, so recheck the rooms, recheck your inventory.
But the third episode? WOW the difficulty spike. Suddenly, there are some that are just obtuse, or you can figure out, but they are a pain. I was so invested in the story, I just Googled, and I don't feel bad about it. (Actually, check the forums on Steam, "Bear With Me" did not Google well, but the Steam forums were helpful).
But even with the extra pain in the third episode (and I guess the last part is supposed to be harder?), this game was well worth my time and money, and thanks to the devs who made it.

All in all, this game is funny and also moving, and well worth your money. If you're not sure, the whole first episode is available on demo, and it does a good job of showing the game, both mechanics and hints at the upcoming lore. Give this one a go!

A flame that burns twice as bright, burns half as long.
Tribes Ascend unofficially died within a year of its release, in large thanks to a very toxic community, but also thanks to a very dodgy developer. Some would say it was doomed from the start with the unrewarding unlock system, and its very liberal use of micro-transactions, but what really killed the game was the "we didn't break through to a big enough market in the first year, so let's make something else" attitude from the studio.
Tribes Ascend was pushed aside, all future support and updates were suspended, with only the barest of support of some multiplayer-servers remaining to squeeze out any additional funds; And instead Hi-Rez focused all of their resources on the continued development and support of Smite - a MOBA game.
Personally, Tribes Ascend was the best shooter experience I'd ever had; It was fun, it was exciting, and it was difficult - But pulling off a flag grab and then securing a capture was among the most rewarding things I'd ever done in a competitive video game. I played quite a few hours of Tribes Ascend, starting in late 2011 to somewhere in the middle of 2013 (though most of it done outside of Steam because of client issues), and I shelled out quite a few bucks too - not because I had to, but because I wanted the developers to know this was a game worth the money.
But that didn't matter, and in the end Tribes Ascend simply went too fast for the devs.
[VGTW]
Hi-Rez has revived Tribes Ascend, and are planning on making big, big changes to the game, most of them set to change the way the game is played. Whether this turns out to be a success, or another failed project on Hi-Rez part remains to be seen. But knowing that the community on r/tribes has been given a very large voice in all of this, I remain skeptical.

The game was much better about ten years ago, with a super big community full of fun people and modders. Now, the community is very small and quiet. Currently, there is always at least one server with enough people in it to reasonably call it a "server". If you play it long enough, you will start to see the same names popping up. There is an internet forum that has plenty of people on it that you can ask for help or just chat with. I don't take part in it, but I know that lots of people love it. I'd recommend buying it if you have a friend to keep you company the whole way through.
The game, if you are interested in building, is basically everything you've ever dreamed of doing with LEGO. You can make anything you want, and make it interactive in any way you want. The "Events" in this game are very easy to learn, and very possible to master. I've seen some incredibly beautiful builds in this game. (Take a look at my screenshots, just ignore the ones of me ♥♥♥♥ing around).
There are enough things to keep the game interesting. Here are some examples:
A frequent blockhead named Ana. "She" is actually a bot that joins people's servers and takes pictures of everyone. I've heard a rumour that she's a part of the CIA. If you dig a little, you can find a database on the internet of all the pictures she's taken, sorted by usernames. At the time of writing, she's taken three pictures of me. If you dig a little more, you will find an ARG behind her. Spooky.
At some point, I joined a nearly empty server (three people) and decided to explore around. At the center of the map was this ginormous ♥♥♥♥-off castle with tons of detail. It's one of the most beautiful things I've ever seen in a video game. I took like thirty screenshots of the thing (Check my profile) since every angle could totally be some pretentious painting. At some point, I found out that you could crawl through some air ducts. After crawling for a minute, I stumbled upon the guy who created the castle just sitting there AFK. The entire thing felt like a dream.
Another recurring blockhead I've found is some guy whose name starts with A (I'm great with names, aren't I?). I'm pretty sure he doesn't speak any languages, as all he communicates with is gestures. He once made a menu for the restaurant he was making; and when I went up to read it, I noticed he only used numbers and symbols with no obvious patterns. Think "3488 2222 43~3 !!!!!!!". A weird quirk of his is that he likes to build his projects approximately one block away from other peoples'.
Lastly, I was exploring a map with a friend, when we come across this tiny easily-missed hole in the wall. Once we went inside, it turned out to be an incredibly elaborate super-hard cooperative platformer/puzzle game. It took me and my friend like two hours to finish, and we felt super accomplished. While we were doing it, the guy who made it teleported in to watch us do stuff. We were so bad that at some point I locked myself in a cage, and the guy just went "my god, this hurts". The lesson we learned? We really hate ladders.

Not many developers can pride themselves in making a modern sequel to an all-time classic and not screwing it up completely. Even less can put out a game that lives up to the huge hype that surrounded it, and boy, what hype it was (remember the fetus teaser? concept art in The Nameless Mod?).
Eidos Montreal nailed it perfectly, surely not without some shortcomings that usually come with console ports (simplified UI, resource limitations) and time constraints (rushed ending, outsourced bosses). Its strongest point is how it feels like a genuine love letter to the best game ever created, they knew exactly which elements were the most important to implement into the new game and how to do it with a modern touch (the good kind), hell, they even got the (bad) voice acting right in some places! To the point that the locations are almost beat by beat based on archetypes of the ones from the original game, which some could see as a detriment, I didn't mind it that much, because there was enough new "cyber-renaissance flavor" to mask it. Unfortunately there were also some places cut, like India or Upper Hengsha.
What has buggered me the most about the story though, is that it didn't match the level of worldbuilding the first one had, focus was shifted hard onto transhumanism, often felt like everything was revolving around it most of the time, forgetting about the usual people stuff and foreign affairs, the in-game books didn't flesh out these topics as good as the books (and even some conversations with NPCs) did in the original. More locations would have probably remedied that, but they were cut. What a shame.
Of course it didn't lack ideas of its own, like the brilliant "social boss fights", the hacking minigame or amazing interior design of the offices, labs and various other places, as well as the atmosphere of city hubs, accompanied by a great ambient soundtrack. I also quite enjoyed the focus on media in one of the chapters, a nice little springboard from the constant augmentation debate, there just wasn't enough conspiracy stuff for my taste. I loved the Alex Jones-like radio DJ.
As for the Director's Cut edition: I didn't mind the♥♥♥♥♥♥filter that much, wish there was an option to toggle it, in fact I think it masked the blurry textures pretty well. Combat boss fights are actually fun now, with new tools to deal with them on-site. The Missing Link DLC is quite lengthy with interesting level design, where each conversation and the action you take has an impact on later stages of the DLC, really cool stuff that they could experiment with, without worrying about time constraints, and on top of that it has a good sidestory behind it that ties into the main story.
The "making of" video is pretty cool, but the main feature that makes Director's Cut worth buying is the commentary that
checking out once you play through the game once or twice, it's really interesting and very funny. You can't not notice how passionate they were about it, the commentary discusses a lot of content that was cut, as well as design choices, inspirations behind the concept art and a lot of other very subtle stuff that you probably missed the first time around, and some you'd probably never thought of. One thing I didn't get is why did they remove the photos of devs from the ending credits, those really made the "passion project" vibe that much more authentic.
Now, Deus Ex "predicted" 9/11 right? While replaying Human Revolution in 2016, I got a funny feeling about the anti-"fascist police state" riot group, funded by global elites and supported by the mainstream media pushing an agenda.

Once you find the genres you love, you absolutely can not get enough of them. Looking through pre existing games to see which ones you will most likely like and seeing if more are going to be released. Craving more and more as you become more aware of what makes a good game and a bad game in that specific genre. FMV games are one of those genres I adore but also look into them as it can frequently not work out.
In The Infectious Madness of Doctor Dekker, you come in right after the events of a dramatic event. A psychiatrist by the name of Doctor Dekker was violently murdered in his office by one of his patients. But who? No one knows except the one that did the act. This is where you come in, not as some cop asking them questions but taking Dekker’s spot as a psychiatrist for the same patients he had. The same patients that hides the mysterious killer.
The way they decided to do this game is very interesting. You have six patients, one of which is your assistant going for grief counseling, to talk to. Their names being Nathan, Marianna, Elin, Claire, Bryce, and Jaya. But you don’t get overwhelmed or anything. It’s used as just talking to them by themselves as you are the Doctor here. Not so much as an interview thing but a one and one appointment. This makes it extremely easy to get caught up with them and being interested in their lives and condition. They are all so different that they leave an impression on you early on just by the way they talk. There are also optional patients you can talk to that does make an impression with their short stay. Showing you that Doctor Dekker had more patients that was probably also affected but they do not have enough significance to be part of the investigation.
They almost seem to suck you in with how their questions are answered and how open ended they are, especially when you are meant to ask questions about their responses. They are also separate entities from each other, not really meeting another patient unless they see them in the waiting room. But they are connected by the one and only Doctor Dekker. You sympathize with them and feel for them. Making you want to get them to feel better because you get so involved and may have seen them in yourself. It is also interesting hearing their different opinions on Doctor Dekker, as you will never know him personally. This will also give yourself a character in the game, you enter in your own opinions that the patients remember and they all will have different opinions about you. Even going as far as applying that you are sitting down like you probably are right as you are playing the game.
It is very important with FMV games to have good acting and the atmosphere to coincide with what is going on. And it is not disappointing in these sections. The acting is great as they do keep up with their character consistently. With the atmosphere goes with the mystery and how a Cthulhu monster is somewhat real and influencing this world.
Your interactions consists of asking questions to your patients and hearing them out. Using a text bar so you can input those questions so that certain patient can see if it lines up with what they will say. This mostly focuses on certain keywords it will look for, whether it only be one or a combination of two or more. Some even not available unless a certain question has been asked or information has been. You also get two logs, one of all the questions you asked and the other with the questions that you got responses for. So if you want or need to watch a response again you easily can.
As you continue talking, the color by the patient’s name will turn orange to signal that you can continue on or be curious about their life and ask more questions. With green being the indicator of nothing left for you to get out of them in this session. If you have no idea of what to ask, a hint system has been incorporated. No hidden strings, if you need help just ask the game.
However, learning about your patients does have strings attached. You and your patients have Insanity Points. These are based on your interactions and decreases or increases at different levels. One of the common increases for you is bringing every patient to a green status and for patients it is to encourage their use of their powers. How many insanity points you and the patients will have by the end will determine how you guys will end up.
I would also want to bring up another game that somewhat uses the same interface and amount of characters but failed.
uses a similar interface where keywords brings up newspapers or cds that correspond with what is said in them. Along with this the amount of characters is overwhelming as they all call for attention when only one needs it. But with The Infectious Madness of Doctor Dekker, it solves this by putting attention on all the characters with the excuse of your job description. The intimacy of asking them yourself and them being in front of you right at that moment helps you remember them and their story easily, with their simple connection to Doctor Dekker making them significant as a cast. They both have problems with the interface but at least Infectious Madness does show that the response has been achieved already and shows which one it is rather than bringing it up again and not showing what you are missing.
The only bad thing is that it is janky the interface is at some points. Sometimes it will think you asked a different question than you actually did and reveal information you do not know about. Having you scramble to find what they are talking about and figuring out the keyword needed to unlock the response you were originally going for. Luckily this usually happens once or twice but it is annoying when it happens. Some questions also lead to just the same information you get from another question you asked. This can be a problem as it seems like nothing needs to be done with that since hey Marianna told you that the club she goes to sells Vodka shots, why would I need to ask about the club to get the same information except that they do great black lighting.
+ Easily pulls you in
+ Acting and atmosphere
+ The killer is different with each playthrough
- Interface can be annoying as you try to find the right question to ask
The Infectious Madness of Doctor Dekker is a memorable FMV game as it provides us a murder mystery for us to solve as we talk to our patients. Bringing it Even with the user interface being an obstacle to continue, the want of finding out more about your patients brings enough motivation to keep playing. If the developers decide to make more games, I can not wait for what else they have up their sleeve.

1001 Spikes has the misfortune of coming at a time when we feel like we've had enough of its ilk. We've played Indiana Jones-themed platformers (La Mulana and Spelunky), short-level-many-lives platformers (Super Meat Boy, I Wanna Be The Guy), and technologically accurate retro homages (Shovel Knight). It's unfortunate because 1001 Spikes is all these things, but it's also something more.
It tosses out the fiddly analog jumping of Super Meat Boy in favor of digital two-button jumping. You know where your jumps are going to take you, even if you play blindfolded. The challenge is picking the right place and time to jump. There are no leaps of faith. The limited pallet of hazards allows you to grow muscle memory. Far from being an exercise in trial and error, 1001 Spikes is a game you can get good at. My second playthrough took 10% as long as my first.
Instead of the single-screen levels of Super Meat Boy, you have levels that you can't finish while holding your breath. There are parts where you really have to think hard about how you can pass an obstacle. There are shortcuts. If Super Meat Boy is a triceps dip, 1001 Spikes is a push-up.
If you've played IWTBTG, you'll know that that game can kill you in ways that are funny. 1001 Spikes has jokes too, but they are funnier.
1001 Spikes has a story, and a damn good one. It's told in Ninja Gaiden style cutscenes which are long but don't overstay their welcome. It's about a love-hate relationship. The protagonist goes on an adventure to prove something to himself -- when you play this game it will be to prove something to yourself. 1001 Spikes is a Japanese indie game, and when it comes to story it seems like Japanese indie developers can do something that Americans can't. They can set their games in worlds that seem real. They can be sentimental without being sappy.

It might have languished a bit over time, but Endless Space is a good turn-based 4X game.
Progressing through the stages of gameplay are seamless, the art is good, and planetary management is one of the best, if missing some depth it has breadth to make up for it. Micro can be a problem.
Combat--the card-based system--is as much a curse as it is a blessing. Being unable to take direct control can sometimes make battles that should be a hard fought affair seem...trivial, after sinking so many hours into the game.
Counter to that, it makes the chore of fighting stacks and STACKS of fleets by end-game easier. But, it instills a sense of units being easily thrown away.
There's generally some things noticeably off or missing, but apart from that, it is still a good title to put at the top of the list. If the card-based combat isn't your thing, best avoid ES.
I do still recommend Endless Space for people looking for a 4x game that doesn't delve into depths of gameplay in any particular area.

I recommend this game, with some caviats.
The gameplay is generally pretty solid, the visuals are beautiful, and the audio is very satisfying. 'Mech customization is very thorough, and combat is supremely fun. It requires a lot of teamwork, and is slower-paced than a typical shooter.
However, waiting for Community Warfare matches can be very frustrating. This area of the game seems particularly poorly designed. I frequently wait 10-30 minutes on a match, which for the most part renders this mode unplayable for me and a lot of other players.
Because the game is entirely dependent on teamwork, whether you win or lose a match doesn't have as much to do with individual skill, and so when you wind up on a team full of noobs or uncooperative players, it's a landslide loss. That's usually how matches go. When your team works together and communicates, win or lose, it's incredibly fun, but the overwhelming majority of my matches involve silent, uncooperative, and/or seemingly bewildered players, which unfortunately has a dramatic effect on the quality and trajectory of the resulting gameplay.
The ranking system isn't particularly fair. I'm a good player but remain stuck in the bottom-ranked "tier" 5 because my teams lose most of the time. You can have a great match, sticking with your team, doing lots of damage, pulling off great tactics, and your rank will still go down if your team loses. It can be frustrating when you are stuck playing with new and low-skill players because your success is overwhelmingly dependent on the team effort. I understand that wins and losses should play into your ranking but they need to adjust the formula to account more for match performance.
Combat is far too focused on the use of Long Range Missiles (LRM's), the "noob tubes" of the game. Not only do they do quite a bit of damage, but they lock onto you and can hit you behind obstacles (except for tall buildings or geographical features). There is also a consumable item called a UAV that allows the enemy team to spot you without having line of sight, making the use of these LRM's even easier (granted, UAV's can be shot down but they don't show on your minimap). What this means is that the overwhelming majority of matches play exactly the same, regardless of game type (Assault, Domination, Skirmish, etc.)--you hide behind obstacles while people with LRM's slug it out, and this involves a lot of waiting because LRM's have double the range of smaller energy weapons. It's just a shame for the most boring and easy-to-use weapon to be so dominant in almost every single match, more so on some levels than others of course.
The game has been out for several years and the updates pretty much focus on release of new mechs, so I doubt any of these issues will be resolved, and may or may not even be regarded as issues by the developer or the broader community, depending on who you ask.

A flame that burns twice as bright, burns half as long.
Tribes Ascend unofficially died within a year of its release, in large thanks to a very toxic community, but also thanks to a very dodgy developer. Some would say it was doomed from the start with the unrewarding unlock system, and its very liberal use of micro-transactions, but what really killed the game was the "we didn't break through to a big enough market in the first year, so let's make something else" attitude from the studio.
Tribes Ascend was pushed aside, all future support and updates were suspended, with only the barest of support of some multiplayer-servers remaining to squeeze out any additional funds; And instead Hi-Rez focused all of their resources on the continued development and support of Smite - a MOBA game.
Personally, Tribes Ascend was the best shooter experience I'd ever had; It was fun, it was exciting, and it was difficult - But pulling off a flag grab and then securing a capture was among the most rewarding things I'd ever done in a competitive video game. I played quite a few hours of Tribes Ascend, starting in late 2011 to somewhere in the middle of 2013 (though most of it done outside of Steam because of client issues), and I shelled out quite a few bucks too - not because I had to, but because I wanted the developers to know this was a game worth the money.
But that didn't matter, and in the end Tribes Ascend simply went too fast for the devs.

But knowing that the community on r/tribes has been given a very large voice in all of this, I remain skeptical.

As a musician and avid psychology researcher, I loved what I've seen of this game thusfar for a number of reasons. Aside from showing how the mind of a composer and performer operates, it reflects some of the modern difficulties of pursuing admiration and success, particularly to the point that you stop listening to your inner voice. It gives a great example of how failing to accept and confront the more difficult aspects of life can manifest into a bigger problem and the ways we may go into denial after refusing to acknowledge it.

Maybe you've heard the tales, of how Hi-Rez has abondoned their golden child. Whilst yes this is true, fear not! The gaming community has more than enough leverage to bring them back to this game and these are the reasons why. Don't worry there's a TL;DR at the bottom
Tribes Ascend is as unique as it gets when it comes to FPS. In Tribes the maps are so huge and its ski feature allows you to go so fast and at times you can sometimes feel adrenaline pumping through your veins. Add in the weapons which are mostly splash related and the only way to survive is to be moving. Stand still and you will die- not only does this make it the fastest pace shooter, it also means there will be no campers (except snipers, duh). The tactics, strategies and innovative ideas that spring up as to how to defeat the other side gives the game a lot of depth and lot of shazbots. To list all the features, I'd be writing a PhD, so to make my life easier, there's this:
Just because the game appears dead doesn't mean it's not good already. Sure things will seem a little empty but if enough people read this and enough people get into it, I guarantee we can change things.
All the classes blend together to create a synergy close to perfection and they individually cover so vast an angle that every class is needed and you will always see every class at work in a game. You won't see an entire team of Juggernauts because they'd be easily beaten by a nimble Pathfinder. Every class has it's pros and it's cons, and when put in a team form one mechanised unit that will steamroll the enemy. But you can also be flexible in that you won't have to stick to one class the entire time, you can switch it up. Sneaking in isn't working? Why not go in spinfusor toting and blow everything up? You don't have to invest too much into any one class and personally I find some of the starting weapons are amazing once you warm up to them. Spend hours trying them out. And if you like it, tell your friends to sign up, get the world united to bring this back, eh?
And of course, there's the one quintessential aspect of the game I haven't explored a lot. The fact that it's free! This is a lifesaver for anyone-stingy or not and oh boy am I glad it's free. For such an amazing game, so unique and so complex I was dumbfounded at first when I found out it was free. There are those who say it's pay to win but don't take any of that nonsense. NONE of the weapons are "better" than the starting ones, they're all different and suit different people or different scenarios. For the one class you may prefer blowing people to kingdom come with the satisfaction of seeing the killing blow, having your enemies blasted out of existence with you a mile away or gunning them down while chasing them and see them try to escape. With the multitude of weapons and items available, Tribes offers you the chance to try them ALL out in the practice mode so you can set your sight on a new weapon and grind and shoot your way to the top with a goal in mind. And when you've gotten every weapon you possibly want, or every item there is available, you don't stop or run out of steam *badumtsi* because you're always trying to be the best and the adrenaline rush, the satisfaction of a Blue Plate, a headshot, a melee or anything is reward enough.
TL;DR Not a moment in the game will you be bored and hours will fly by so quickly. So if you've played this before, but have felt defeated by Hi-Rez, get back on your feet or if you're completely new, go headfirst in and have a little faith. Login and start. Get your friends to jump in too. The more people we get, the more of the gaming community there are, the great ther chance of getting Hi-Rez's attention and bring this thing back. So spread the word, bring people into it, tell the gaming community and the world- even tell that random stranger on the road to. This game didn't deserve to end so quickly, so let's give it another shot.

Great GAME for learning a lot of the smaller parts of these weapons, interesting design and different gameplay types.
First starting with a field strip, then full disassembly, and reassembly.
Then moving onto the operating of the weapon, from unloading a single round, to a full magazine, to firing (which they are going back and animating gas pressures for blowback weapons - only a couple available right now)
Finally moving onto some time-based game modes, including a hardcore mode which allows you to remove different pieces at the same time as long as they don't have any other dependencies being acted on or not removed.
Fun and interesting for those interested in the inner workings, or who have no access to weapons because of country laws, or other such reasons.
There are some items which require money to unlock, but on the whole, the others are easily enough unlocked, especially if you play the memory game ( weapon recognition ) as well as play all the games for each weapon.
Conclusion: Enjoyable for the right person.

If you can 3D model or program you don't need Blockland, it needs you!
If you want to design and host minigames, you don't need Blockland, it needs you!
Heck, if you just want to populate a server and hang out, it still might need you!
If you're not willing to be creative and create things, you might not like this game as it is now. It's a lot about creating minigames, as well as playing them. Almost all minigames need a map, you'll have to build one or find one to use. Anything creative, you'll have to find out how to implement. There's a rudimentary cause-and-effect event system which can do basic logic and counting on its own. With an addon, you can create and manipulate variables for bricks and players for more complicated logic. If you wish, there are basic AI bots that can be controlled via events and made to do tasks, such as moving, looking around, and shooting. Depending on how they're set up, they can ignore outside stimuli or be set to react to players entering a radius or their field of vision, or to always seek out and attack players. Thus, you can create PvE gamemodes, where hordes of zombies or enemy soldiers attack and players must defend themselves.
If you're not willing to create things, however, there's usually something running; Prison Escape, a game more like an actual prison than Jailbreak, plenty of basic TDMs, capture-point maps, and CTF minigames, and racing games. There are also murder-mystery games (some better than others, try Despair Syndrome if you can), games where you build to survive natural disasters, and games where you build fortresses and fight.
However, while there's usually SOMETHING running, not everything is always up. There are plenty of opportunities to host servers.
If any of this seems daunting, don't worry. Setting up a minigame is as simple as pressing "Minigames" and "Create", then punching a few mostly self-explanatory settings if you'd like and hitting "Create" again. Events are simple and generally do what they say on the tin. "onActivate, self, door, toggle" toggles the door brick when you activate it by clicking on it. "onPlayerTouch, player, addHealth, 1" heals the player while they stand on the brick. There's a large number of addons to add to the eventing system and add new items, and if you'll bother to learn TorqueScript, you can add to it relatively easily.
Maybe you've heard of the toxic community. Just don't reply to anyone in the NC, the TP, or autism(tm) clans if you go on the forums, and if you don't, you'll have no issue. The toxic people rarely are seen ingame outside their private servers and typically are focused on playing the game.
The more people buy the game and stick around in the community, the better; if enough people show up, not enough people will know "the rules" and new unspoken rules will come about, theoretically better ones.
It's a good buy. I have to say it, it's a good buy.
BUT WAIT! Don't buy it here! Whatever you do, do NOT buy it on Steam! Steam's DRM makes it impossible to host an authenticated, dedicated server and an authenticated client on two machines! It's the same price on Amazon and Blockland.US, and you can redeem it on Steam! The end result is still the game on Steam, but also a key that can be used to host a dedicated server without authenticating through Steam!
Hosting a non-dedicated server (one run through the same process as the client, meaning if you quit the server shuts down) is possible, as is running two processes to run a dedicated server and a client on the same computer (Steam only cares if you run it on two machines.)
I must be honest here. This game is dying. It's been shown that a third-party master server can be used for authentication, meaning if the official support is shut down, you'll likely be able to authenticate your client and host LAN games, or even perhaps with a small community of people who really want to hang on. The developer has shown no interest in shutting down the master server nor the forums, and he even makes security patches when needed.
However, we're losing players. When I first started playing, there were probably about 100 servers up at any given time. Now there's about 50, a year or two later. Help us host more servers with more players. It is not a support issue. The game works fine and all necessary services are running. We simply need players.

Review taken from my original post at
Bear With Me: Episode 1 - PC
Exordium games is a Croatian video games studio founded in 2014, their website shows that they have released six video games in the space of three years and all seem to be of varying genres. I must admit that I haven’t had the fortune to play their other titles (although some definitely caught my eye) and so this is my first experience with the developer.
Within the first few moments of being given Bear With Me to review, I knew I’d be in safe hands when the launch trailer music reminded me of soundtrack to the mighty 7th Guest. Also, being a sucker for point and click adventure games with a self-aware Noir feel (Tex Murphy, Grim Fandango, Gemini Rue etc.) my hopes were instantly raised and after playing the game for some time I can safely say that those hopes were met and indeed, surpassed.
The main story of the game is that you play Amber Ashworth, a young girl who lives with her (strangely absent) family in a house just outside the borders of Paper City who discovers that her brother Flint is missing and a mysterious ‘Red Man’ is starting fires throughout the city. In order to find Flint she enlists the help of her erstwhile companion and burned-out private snoop Ted E Bear (literally her toy teddy bear). Paper City itself is based on 1940’s era New York and populated by anthropomorphic versions of Amber’s toys. It is place of constant night and rain although the tone of the game is lightened by both Amber’s chipper demeanour and the snappy dialogue between the characters, which are fully-voiced and very well presented.
The dialogue in the game is one of the first things that struck me, as all of the characters in the game are quite verbose and clearly have a history with each other which we learn of through well-constructed conversations which reveal personalities and foibles without seeming too intrusive and forced. It is a pleasure to interact with the various classic stereotypes in the game, Ted E. Bear being a classic Chandler-esque burned out Private Eye and Amber’s other toys representing thugs, maternal figures and dopey but lovable bodyguards, among others.
Not once did I find myself wanting to skip the dialogue because it felt too long-winded (One of the characters in the game ends EVERY sentence with word ‘see’, which tickled me), this is a real strong point of a game such as this where conversations play such an intrinsic part in the story, especially the constant banter / bickering between Amber and Ted.
The title screen instantly sets the tone of Bear With Me, the main menu being an American style cinema circa 1940 being beaten by heavy rain (at night-time, naturally). The ‘New Game’ button is in fact a retro ticket stub making the point that the adventure that you are about to embark on is a narrative-driven piece.
The vast majority of Bear With Me is monochrome with only the occasional splash of red. This reminded me initially of Frank Miller’s Sin City however that is where the similarity ends as the tone of the game is entirely different. Amidst the smoky jazz music and Noir cliche's are various pop culture references, an amusing clash against the faux-serious retro backdrop.
The general tongue in cheek, self-aware tone of the game is sometimes punctuated by darker moments, such as flashes of strange red writing on the walls and Ted E. Bear’s dismissiveness whenever Amber’s parents are mentioned. There’s a real sense of something larger and possibly sinister happening in the real world, causing Amber to envelope herself so deeply in her toy-filled fantasy, something I assume will be addressed in future episodes.
The cut scenes in the game are shown from the point of view of Ted, through a series of comic book style panels he gives us his thoughts on the investigation so far, his gruff speech peppered with Private Eye slang were some of the highlights for me, it’s enjoyable to listen to his over the top rehashing of recent events and pessimistic outlook on his seemingly inevitable fate during this ‘one last case’.
The puzzles in the game should pose no issue for someone who has played this style of adventure before, the entire game is controlled with the left mouse button, which when clicked on an object in the game world will give you one or two options, to look at something and possibly the ability to pick it up or interact with it. This simplicity works in the games’ favour as it allows the player to focus on the narrative and atmosphere of Bear With Me and not get stuck on illogical puzzles which would hamper the unfolding of the story. There was one moment which resulted in a few minutes of pixel-hunting but other than this the game moved at a very steady pace, allowing me to complete the first episode in just under two hours.
Summary:
Bear With Me is currently price at £3.99 on Steam which I think is a good price for the quality on offer here. Rarely have I played an Indie game with this much polish and attention to detail. The characters casually mentioning Paper City throughout this episode gave me a real yearning to visit it for myself to see what it had to offer and how the story would unfold, making me dedicated to trying solving the mystery of what happened to Amber’s brother and who this mysterious ‘Red Man’ is. If you are a fan of point and click adventures rich on atmosphere I would heartily suggest that you pick up Bear With Me.
Right, it’s onto Episode 2, I’ll see you all in Paper City, see.

Sometimes, you're an almost well-balanced member of society. A graduate student, working on a thesis, who also cares deeply about the current state of society, who pets fluffy animals and cries at movies, and apologizes to doors for closing them too harshly.
And sometimes, you just really want to dig your thumb into the eyesocket of a demon and pull on their jaw until their entire head rips apart in a splash of tearing flesh and dripping blood.
DOOM is the game for those times.
This is one of the most fun games I've ever had the pleasure to play. Even at low graphics settings, it's polished and looks good, whether the action is in a sterile space-corporation environment or in a blood-soaked hellscape. The soundtrack is nothing but bangers, the sound effects are all very well put together, and the experience is amplified with headphones.
The mechanics themselves incite you to let loose, and to leave aside the safety of a sniper position--the kind of thing you tend to go for as a noob--in favor of the playstyle the game shines at: constant movement around the map, and delivering unrelenting death on anything that stands in your way.
I cannot overstate just how fun this game makes it to go up to a big pile of demon, plant two solid rounds of shotgun square into their face, and then proceed to punch said face off of the demon.
And still, you don't need to concern yourself with thoughts like "am I doing the right thing?" or "is it truly justifiable for me to just keep killing everything I encounter with such violence?". The bad guys in this game are the literal forces of Hell  and un-checked capitalism, and I think most of us can agree that both of those deserve all the shots to the face they can get.
Rest assured in knowing that there's a time and a place for careful observation, for considering the points of view and needs of your fellow human beings, for thinking about your place in the universe and what really it means to be a fragile sentient being in this complex reality.
And then there's a time and a place for DOOM.

1001 Spikes is a difficult platformer made by Nicalis (Cave Story+, The Binding of Isaac). Father of the protagonist is missing - only thing there's left by him is a map and a letter to seek Ukampa ruins in South America. Challenge accepted.
Controls are made pretty tight, you won't have any problems regarding movement or jumping, which are required for hard platformers anyway. Jumping isn't depending on the intensity of your button pushing and is always same height, because you actually have two buttons to jump - you can do a small (1 block up) or a big (2 blocks up) jump. But that isn't something bad, you'll get used to it quickly.
Level design is nice, all levels are made with emphasis on speedrunning, so they are not long - expect usually about 1 minute per level from start to finish. That doesn't mean you'd need only one minute to beat every level, you'll be dying a lot. There are many traps and passages that just asks for you to die so you know what to avoid next time.
The game also requires some basic multitasking skills, as there are passages where you have to check spikes around you, and throw daggers at shooting traps meanwhile - you'll have to count the time of trap reset to throw at the right time. Do you still thing that 1001 lives for 1001 Spikes is enough for you?
Controls, game menu and overall presentation of the game is polished and worth the price. That includes sweet pixelart graphics and great 8bit soundtrack that won't get old (well, it did, but you'll still like it).
This game is a great buy for those who want a 2D platforming challenge. It's not easy, it requires proper training for every level, and is rewarding enough in the end, with the feel of success.

This game is incredibly difficult, but that's what makes it so tremendously rewarding. The controls are very tight, giving you a lot of precision to work with.
Some people say the game feels too trial-and-error for them, which is sort of true, but that's part of the reason that I love the game. There are a lot of patterns that you'll start to learn that will help you to avoid obstacles, but sometimes you jump onto a platform that look safe and suddenly you're full of spikes. Sometimes you'll say "that block DEFINITELY has spikes in it;" you land on it, there aren't any spikes, but you're expecting them so you freak out and jump off in a panic only to fly face-first into a dart.
Sometimes this lack of "red blocks = spikes, yellow statues = darts" means that you'll die to traps that you couldn't possibly predict; I can see how that could become frustrating quickly, but with 1,001 lives to burn through, I never thought "wow this is 100% ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t," it was just something to catalogue into "sneaky traps on this level." And honestly, I love that tense feeling of "what could be in this next area that's going to kill me?" It's not so random that you can't outwit some of the traps, but it isn't so formulaic that you can learn "this means this so do this" to breeze through levels.
I think this game could have VERY easily gone in an entirely different direction if it wasn't for the level design and the soundtrack. All of the levels are built in a way that makes it possible to speedrun through them if you're willing to spend the time learning the traps and perfecting the technique. I've had hours of fun just playing one level with a friend, passing the controller back and forth while we try to perfectly time a jump, then a knife throw, then do a crazy high-jump wibble-wobble to fall underneath a dart with surgical precision. That was fun because the levels aren't overly long, some of the trips are hidden but not completely unknown (spikes flash for a second before they pop out, darts only come out of statue mouths, etc.). There are no invisible blocks that you're going to bump into. There are some tiles that fall out from under you or ceiling blocks that will fall onto your head, but these will usually (I can't say "always" with 100% certainty) be marked or have some sort of audible warning; you can escape them if your reflexes are fast enough. However, my reflexes are not usually fast enough and I have to learn some of these things by getting killed by them.
The soundtrack is well-made and a real pleasure to listen to if you're into chip-tune music. It definitely has that 8-bit NES-era feel to it, but it's all layered and orchestrated in a way that makes it so much more complex than "bleepity bloop background noises." You typically won't get new background music until you progress to the next area of the map, which means you'll probably be hearing the same music for a long time. That might not be your bag, but I can say that personally I never got tired of the soundtrack, even when I spent 400 lives on the same level. I do still get a weird sense of anxiety whenever I hear the music from the fire maps, though...
Overall, this game is really a blast to experience, especially since you can unlock new characters by finding the secret golden skulls on each map. The unlockable characters will only be able to grab coins from the main levels, but they all have their own little differing mechanics that makes them fun to play the extra modes with.
If you're planning on playing this game solo, go in knowing that there's going to be a lot of repetition while you try to learn the levels. It's still a lot of fun, but I would recommend having a friend to share in the good-natured cornucopia of death that you're about to experience.
In short, buy this game because it's great.
