A friend of mine recommended this game and before commiting to it I read a bunch of reviews on this site.  There were several "Do Not Recommend" reviews which complained of a grindy nature, lack of infantry/vehicle targets and a power imbalance due to skills unlockable through regular play which noobs have no access to.  So I was pretty skeptical but DLed anyway to give my friend the benefit of the doubt.
Gee, I'm glad I got this game.  Despite there being a fair amount of truth to the negative reviews this game is great fun regardless.
I would like to address those issues from negative reviews mentioned above:
The game is grindy?  Well, if you call playing a lot of games driving around in giant stompy robots shooting lasers in the faces of other giant stompy robots a grind, I guess it is.  The whole point of the game is to drive around in giant stompy robots and blow♥♥♥♥♥♥up.  Not to level up those skills.  First: Blow♥♥♥♥♥♥up, second: gets skills.  Blow♥♥♥♥♥♥up, it's so much FUN!  When you unload on someone with a bunch of lasers or short range missles and their arm falls off or you cripple their leg, or your first solo kill!  Revel in it.
No other targets besides giant stompy robots shooting lasers and massive autocannons around the place?  Well, if I was infantry and there were giant stompy robots blowing♥♥♥♥♥♥up all around me, I wouldn't want to be poking my head out.  And if I was driving a tank around said robots, I'd think it prudent to drive away as fast as posible.  There should be NO other targets both from fluff and gameplay perspectives (though there are infantry and vehicles in the original game and fluff, once the Mechs arrive, the little guys don't really matter anymore).
IMO, anything other than Mechs as opponents would be a pointless distraction.  Any infantry or light vehicles would have to be AI as they would die in droves, no one would want to play them.  The players are there for the giant stompy robots afterall.  That these have been left out of the game serves to keep the gameplay focused on the PvP, robot vs robot theme of the game.
There is an imbalance between newer and experienced players?  And this doesn't happen in any other game?  When you start out in any new game you'll likely to get your♥♥♥♥♥♥handed to you a few times.  The learning curve might be a bit steeper in this game as it doesn't play like a typical FPS, thank Google for variety!  Persevere, click on "Spectate" when you get killed, watch how other people are playing, learn and get better.  Games are over pretty short and there are no significant repercussions for dieing in a dozen games, except that you might get a bit better each time.
Yes, there are skills that can be unlocked on Mechs which give them small bonuses.  I don't think these are especially unbalancing towards a new player in a trial Mech.  Though it might be if the game was one on one.  It's not, you have 11 other allies backing you up.  In fact, a much more significant factor in whether you survive a game is how well your team co-ordinates together.  And it's also likely that the other team will have as many noobs or vets as your team does.  It balances out.
If there is anything i would gripe about it is the cost of purchasable packs.  Especially the Steam bundles.  I'm not sure how they have decided on their pricing for these packs but it would be great if they were about 50% cheaper.  But would they sell 50% more packs?  Saying that i've still bought two 3 Mech* bundles.  These are the lowest tier on the purchasable packs and are pretty good value at $20US.  Even better value if you preorder and get early adopter rewards.  There are also periodic sales on various things in the store.  So if you are patient you can make savings.
(*  Three Mechs of the same chassis are required to fully unlock all tiers of skills available and these bundles come with a months premium time which gives extra XP to help you along.  Each chassis also has distinct quirks and weapon hardpoints so you don't have three identical Mechs.  You get decent variety)
The game also rewards noobs quite generously with bonus in game currency for the first 25 matchs.  After this time you could get virtually any Mech you wanted that is available for cBills.  Buying bundles is not necessary.
So, in summary:  Yes you grind, if you call game after game of robot battles a grind.  If you don't want to battle giant robots you came to the wrwong game.
There are no other targets to shoot at or drive around.  If you want tanks there is a game for that.
There are skills.  Your teammates will have a greater influence on the battle than the skills will.  See who plays well in your games and Friend them, then ask to group and learn from them.
Bundles can be expensive but there is some good value in there too.
Your biggest hurdle will be getting past the CoD playstyle and learning to play within the limitations of what sort of mech you are driving.  There is a lot more to this game than running around the map blasting people.
Oh yeah, you wont respawn either.

Endless Space is a fantastic addition to the 4X genre, if only because it is so unlike most 4X games. It is not a Civ/GalCiv/Pandora-style game. It is not a grand strategy game. It is not a SoSE/StarDrive/StarRuler-style game.
ES has all of the traits of a 4X game; it just does them somewhat differently. The game *feels* more abstract--probably due to its interesting art style, which feels minimalistic until you zoom in on a planet or combat scene, or zoom out on the galaxy--but it's got all of the micromanagement that 4X players love. It has a complex, multi-pathed research system, divided into four categories: military, science/tech, socioeconomy, and colonization/terraforming. Trading is not something that comes standard: you've got to do research to enable trade, build structures to make it profitable. Giant list of structures: check. Terraforming to maximize particular resources: check. Luxuries and production resources: check.
The game has a particularly interesting unit creation system, though again, not in the typical sense, but it's closest to Pandora: you've got a limited amount of hull types, which you can then customize for a particular role. Given the incremental changes in certain weapon systems--like GalCiv, it's got the three "mass drivers/kinetics, beam, missile" weapon selection with associated defensive systems--and the selection of other ship modules (e.g. engine buffs, weapon buffs, invasion modules, colony modules, fighter/bomber hangars), you really can make a large variety of ships.
However: the combat system is given additional dimension by the 5-round combat turn, the card system, and the hero system. Each combat comprises 5 rounds: prep, long range, medium range, short/"melee" range, and resolution. Each of the "range" rounds comprises three sub-rounds, during which weapons may be fired. Each weapon system can be customized to be a particular "range": long, medium, or short. During each range round, weapons of that range have the highest chance to hit (90%), while weapons not of that range have reduced chance to hit. But long range weapon systems are more expensive and take up more room on your ship. Do you outfit a ship with long weapons and hope to kill your opponent in the first round of combat? Or load up with defenses and cheaper, smaller short range weapons, aiming to survive until the last rounds of combat? In vanilla ES, each weapon system has a specific range (e.g. missiles were the long weapons), but now you can customize those ranges--if your opponent favors shields and point defenses, and you've got a hero who has a long-range hero ability, load up on long range kinetics.
The card system allows you to assign a particular type of action to your fleet during each combat range round. There are five types of action cards: offense, defense, engineering, sabotage, and tactics. Each card directly counters
another type of action card; your goal is to choose action cards that benefit you, whilst trying to guess what classification of action card your opponent will choose--if one player's card counters the other, not only are the countered card's effects voided, but the counterer gains an additional bonus. (Don't worry: the countered fleet still gets to fire their weapons.) Example: I want to survive until the medium range round, and my opponent has long-range
missiles, during the long round I choose ECM (Sabotage): -25% missile damage (Counters Offense -15%). If my opponent tries to play an Offense card, not only is it countered, but now I take 40% less missile damage that round.
Bonus: Sometimes both players' cards can be countered!
The hero system is not necessarily new to 4X games, though seeing it in a sci-fi setting was new to me when I first started playing ES a couple years ago. Each hero has a pair of classes of five: Administrator, Corporate, Admiral, Pilot, Adventurer. Each class allows a hero to select from various abilities upon level up, the first two classes particularly suited to system-management, the next pair for fleet combat, the last as a catch-all category. It's otherwise pretty straight-forward: hire heroes when you're able, level them up, use them to make an otherwise untenable system stable, or to counter an otherwise much larger fleet.
Because each star system can only be accessed using travel lanes (e.g. SoSE), ES might initially seem somewhat linear, but eventually you gain access to warp drive, and the limits are gone! The one hard limit you have: you can't touch down onto planets. System invasion is another abstractualization: even "system invasion modules" only give you a chance to instantly take over a system. Given this lack of functionality, however, it doesn't necessarily feel like the game misses out on ground combat, any moreso than we miss it in GalCiv--the two systems are, truly, just about the same mechanistically.
If you're a fan of 4X games, you already own ES. If you're looking for some way into the genre, ES does a pretty good job of not making things too cumbersome. I wholeheartedly support this game!

TL;DR:  Endless Space is a turn-based strategy game that offers little in terms of visual stimulation and even less of audial stimulation.  It is, however, a very in-depth strategy game with a lot of different paths you can choose.
Rest of the review:
Endless Space is turn-based.  You make decisions in a style similar to a board game.  You build fleets and colonize planets and do a variety of other tasks all while worrying about how many turns each task will require.  It can be very time-consuming to play this game properly, but due to the turn-based nature, you can quit playing at any time and pick right back up where you were at a later time.
Not much of the game is ever explained.  You have to learn how to navigate the menu choices and how to move fleets.  You will undoubtably find yourself confused at least once while playing this game, because the controls are less than intuitive when navigating menu screens and there are some odd fleet behaviors.  You also are not given a proper explanation of the UI and must settle for a numbered manual-style tutorial that explains where basic elements of each screen are located.
Overall, this 4X strategy game is a lot of fun, but I am left with unsatisfied civilization-building needs.  I felt a lot like a number-crunching math wiz rather than a grand builder.  I hope the developer spends more time focused on building options in future games.  That said, the game offers a lot of interesting possibilities and is very in-depth when it comes to the research tree.

Don't listen to people who say this is just a gimmick. This is to mouse and keyboard games what the GameCube controller is to Smash Bros - a must have. The mouse pads can be mapped like a trackball, so flicks of the thumb can determine how far and how fast to look in a certain direction (huge for FPS). Of course you can also map the pad as a regular 1:1 mouse input. Being able to remap any button on the fly is a huge plus, especially since you can save those mappings to the controller itself, go to a friend's house, and have that mapping instantly ready with no need to mess around with controls at the friend's house. Battery life is good too, although annoyingly they weren't built with rechargables in mind, which are slightly thicker than regular AAs, so getting the batteries out is always annoying as they get stuck.
I use these things for every single PC game I play, even those outside of Steam like Overwatch, WoW, and HotS (Just map your controls to the "Desktop" setting and it will work perfectly.) I think if there are any two genres they would be bad with, it's RTSes or MOBAs (wouldn't know too well- I'm a scrub at both), although I did feel like they worked well with HotS, so make of that what you will.
When you first get this, you won't fully appreciate everything that you can do with them. Start by utilizing the most popular control-sets in a game's community, and then when you start to think "Man, I really wish I could do ___ with this controller", start experimenting. If you ever find yourself thinking that the controller is too limited for your specific need, you're probably wrong. You need to be willing to experiment, which may be a legit reason for you to not buy them, but eventually if you're patient you'll reach a point where it becomes immediately obvious how you want to map each game to the controller. There is so much you can do with this that it would be information overload to explain every single option up front. The firmware and Big Picture integreation is constantly being updated, which is good, although if I'm being honest, that piece is still occasionally a little buggy. Getting better, though in the early days it was pretty terrible.
Make no mistake, there will be a learning curve. Anyone who expects to break it out on Day 1 and start kicking♥♥♥♥♥in an FPS is sorely confused. You have been using a mouse for most (if not all) of your life. You will have to learn to use this controller which is a different skillset than using a mouse. BUT I'm telling you, it is so worth it to be able to kick back on your couch or comfy chair, sprawl out in any position you feel like, and not be chained to your bulky mouse and keyboard. Start with games which are not time sensitive (Civ 5 and Civ 6 are the perfect games for these things), then move on to lighter time sensitive games like Terraria or indie games with low stakes. After enough time with them you will be able to use them on competetive games too. I use the Steam Controller for Overwatch, and I'm better with it than I am with mouse and keyboard. The key is to not coddle yourself and go back to mouse and keyboard when feeling discouraged. You will suck at first. If that's not acceptable to you, do not buy these. Again, remember, this is a new skillset for which you have no muscle memory. Once you start using them, jump out of that birds nest and start flying until you feel used to them. I promise, it is worth it.

The Infectious Madness of Doctor Dekker is a really fun and entertaining tale of insanity in the Lovecraftian sense.
The player is a psychologist who has to step up to fill in for the mysterious Doctor Dekker, who has recently died under equally mysterious circumstances. The job is to interview the patients and try to get to the bottom of their problems, and what problems they have! One insists that they are reliving the same day over and over again (until some great tragedy comes along and breaks the chain). Another mysteriously blacks out and wakes up naked on the beach. A third chap claims to be able to live through an extra hour each day, a "midnight hour" which only he is aware of. All of it sounds far fetched but they might not all actually be crazy...
The game is played much like 2015's indie darling Her Story. The player watches the patients' answers in FMV form, then tries to pick out key words to further ask about. For the most part this works quite well, but there will be situations where you'll absolutely be stuck. The game will insist there is something crucial you have to ask about in a given statement, but you can't figure it out. Luckily the answers are available to be replayed as many times as needed, and the game has a generous hint system as well, so you'll get moving eventually.
Doctor Dekker has a lot in common with Contradiction. The game has a similar B-movie style, but in a good way. The actors and actresses are obviously having a lot of fun with their characters and the material, which translates to an entertaining experience.
I personally enjoyed the game a great deal. It's not for everyone, but fans of murder mysteries, the occult or just different gaming experiences will find a lot of fun here!

I'm really not sure whether to recommend this game or not. When it's good, it's really good. The plot is interestingly twisty and the problems described, supernatural bits aside, are all pretty believable. The mentally ill are more or less presented sympathetically. When the parser cooperates you feel like a real therapist, helping people with their problems (or making them worse, if you wanna play that way.) The characters are complex and engaging, the acting is good. If you're a fan of character driven stuff or H.P. Lovecraft, you might like this game.
The big word there is 'if.' This game suffers from the same problems as the Ace Attourney series, in that there is a One True Sequence that the developers expect you to follow and if you deviate from that, you cannot progress. Compounding this is the fact that the parser can be painfully obtuse, you might have the right way to progress but you didn't get ye therapy in the proper way, so it didn't recognize what you meant. I understand the desire to have it be a more conversational style, but it backfires a lot. Thankfully there's no penalty for using hints. Also so many of the female characters in this are weirdly flirtatious with you for no reason. Your gender is never mentioned but it does rather assume you're playing as a male character, which is kind of irritating. If my character is pre-defined then just tell me. It's also incredibly unrealistic that you don't have access to whatever records or patient files Dekker compiled on these people beforehand, since the conceit is that these are his patients you are inheriting it makes no sense to start with a blank slate.
Despite all these problems it has kept me engaged enough to keep plugging away at it, so I would tentatively recommend this.

I've spent hours upon hours building everything from boats to castles to spaceships, and playing games with other people online, most likely making Blockland my second-most-played game of all time. This was a long, long time before the game appeared on Steam, however, so you'll just have to take my word for it. I have yet to find another sandbox building game that gives you the level of freedom that Blockland does, with an endless supply of user-created add-ons in the form of blocks, game-modes, and more. LEGO sets were one of my favorite toys as a child, so being able to not only have endless bricks to build with but also the ability to explore my creations up-close as a small minifigure and interact with them was a dream come true.
While some people will use their imagination to bring physical form to whatever they can think up, my forte was always recreating things from other media. Not the most creative thing in the world, but it was the most enjoyable for me. At various points I worked on reconstructing playable versions of Team Fortress 2's ctf_2fort, Pokemon's Kanto region, and the entirety of Portal, as well as a large-scale model of Halo's Rocket Launcher. My only regret is that I'm not very good at finishing what I've started, as the Rocket Launcher was the only thing that ever reached total completion.
Most people tend to complain about the userbase, but it's only as bad as any other place composed mostly of people in grade-school who haven't been a part of an online community before. Certain problematic users will insist this game is bad, but only because they've been punished for misbehaving time after time after time. Overall, it just takes time to adjust.

1001 Spikes is a game about dying. A lot. It is a game where you will fight your way through a level for half an hour, finally dodging every single spike, arrow, pit, and scorpion, only to get killed by a surprise trap at the end door. But it feels pretty great once you've done that.
Really, it's a good game. The levels are not challenging in the way that the game is cheating you, but are instead challenging by clever and well-placed obstacles that will make you feel like you can beat the level in just one more try.
Otherwise, the music, by chiptune musician Rushjet1, is amazing, and the graphics are great as well, utilizing pixels to make nostalgic levels and great cutscenes.
So if you're a game masochist, a manic completionist, or a hardcore retro gamer, this is the game for you.
This game advertises itself as having a lot of spikes. So unlike most games, I can't fault it too much for not having any goblets. It does have a lot of spikes.

I'm having a lot of fun with this game.
The graphics and music draw a ton of inspiration from NES games, as does the incredibly hard and often trial-and-error style of gameplay. While the game is very challenging, and often unfair, it still feels incredibly rewarding because you get a little bit further with each attempt. It's twitchy platforming action with a lot of projectiles, and some cruel traps thrown in. That's probably not for everyone, but I like it.
The graphics are beautiful, and I'm very excited to see each new area. It looks and feels like a NES game with some subtle modern touches that wouldn't be possible on a real NES. For example, background vines animate when you walk past them. There's tons of references to classic games like Mario or Ghosts n Goblins, and the cutscenes even have intentional spelling errors!
There's tons of content and different game modes too. I've still not seen everything, 11 hours in. And then there's replay value on top of that.
However, a lot of what makes 1001 Spikes great also hurts it. The difficulty does ramp up pretty damn high. At first I was playing this game together with my girlfriend, and that was awesome - the levels are well designed for multiple players. But eventually I had to dump her because we were progressing too slowly together. It's hard to concentrate with a group of people when playing such a difficult game.
So I guess if I had to complain about something, I'd say more could have been done to make this game more accessible. Maybe an easy mode? Or maybe the whole game should have just been easier in general. I love it as it is, but I would have liked to play the whole thing with friends.

Endless Space was mentioned in many reviews and articles that it was basically Civilization in space. Many of those same articles also said what I am about to say: It is, but it isn't.
It does play a lot like Civilization except that instead of cities you control various star systems. Each Star System will have multiple planets (some have only 1 but it seems to be rare). Improvements upgrade the whole system (like Buildings do for cities in Civ). But each planet can have different resources, planet type, anomalies and wonders which add to the specialization of each system.
It took me a while in Civilization to get used to early game expansion, but this game forces you into it. That isn't a bad thing, but it takes some getting used to.
The Tech tree also differs from Civ, in that there are 4 main paths that can be followed but you aren't stuck on a certain branch at a time so you can go from one to the other.
Endless Space also has Heroes. Heroes can be recruited to add to either a System you control or a fleet you control. They offer benefits to either based on their class type (Each hero has 2 classes out of 5 possible). As heroes level up you can choose new abilities for them that either offer increased stats for the system/fleet they are in or new abilities for when their fleet is in battle.
There is a lot in Endless Space and is a fun game that takes some getting used to (I am still trying to figure out a few things without looking at strategies). While, in my opinion, it isn't "better" than Civilization it does bring a lot to the table in regards to strategy and customization. (Did I mention you can build custom ships based on the technology you have researched and even make your own "species"?)

24 hours after buying this game I had spent 14 hours playing it. It's an excellent 4X game with a suprising amount of depth. I am very tempted to pick up Endless Legend as well but I'm afraid I might forget to eat.

I think I picked this game up on sale for £5-6 a while back.  On the face of it, It's a turn based strategy game and has a number of interesting game mechanics hidden within it.
The tech tree is extensive and the brain power required to decide what order you will need things in is interesting.  Picking your colonies, even nice planets, and then wondering why moral hit rock bottom is a fairly big part of the game.
Quickly you learn how to do better - expand, drop the tax to 35% or less to maintain moral for a bit, scout the area and hope for free hive ships and then make your fleets as big as possible.
Would I recommend it... full price? (£20+)  Heck no.  On sale? (sub-£5)  Yes.  Especially if you like turn based strategy or want a game to play while you watch TV.

I work full time, and play a lot of mechwarrior, so I don't have time for a big review, but here's the gist of it:
Come in with no expectations, and be very happy. It's pretty much like getting to play multiplayer mechwarrior of old. The effects are cool, the graphics are okay, the gameplay is slightly different but still about shooting lasers, autocannons, and missiles at enemies and blowing off their limbs.
However, I have never seen such visceral hate for the developer as I have in this game. Everyone who plays routinely poops all over PGI (the developers). I understand the REASON people are mad. The mechanics are so solid in this game, that it's just BEGGING for some cool stuff. Cooperative missions, single player campaign, more multiplayer modes, really cool base sieges and destructable buildings. Those would all be really, really great. And yes, the developer talks about how those are going to be in the game, and yes, they are not in the game yet. Should that equal anger and a vicious attitude to the development staff? I guess that's up to you to decide.
As for me... I still play for a few hours every day, so I can't complain. It's a good game, and it's a mechwarrior game. See you on the battlefield.

Still terrible after all these years, no surprises here!
Maps are a joke, always have, always will.  They are either small and wide open, or large and wide open, and are generally all very flat and poorly segmented, if at all.  Little to no thought was put into their design, and they allow for nearly zero movement options.  There is no flow to a match because of this, and many matches are just simply mexican standoffs, or head-on charges, as there is literally no way for anyone to actually move without being seen or covered between map segments, making it almost impossible to properly flank or apply any strategy mobility wise.  This is probably the single biggest failing concerning MWO's gameplay and overall design.  24 Players on these maps is simply absurd, and downright boring, they could really use another playlist or 2 with tweaked maps and lower player counts, but that would require work with some more robust servers, and PGI will never pay for more then the bare minimum to support this game.
As far as loadouts go, there is literally only a single usable "strategy" available, and that is "which weapons provide the best DPS", and tends to favor specific ranges, and it all depends on what the dev team deems to be the best at any given time.  This is frustrating, as mobility, positioning, and flexibility, don't mean squat in the face of nowhere to run (bad, over-crowded, open maps) and superior DPS (especially using Coolshot items).  Gameplay is severely limited, and features downright stupid design for this so called "thinking person's shooter".
Still contains awful "pay2win" elements, such as the dreaded Coolshot, which is an expendable item that basically acts like coolant flush from the older mechwarrior games, except it is a one-time-use-only item, and will cost you either your earned C-Bills, or real life money.  because, you know, this is a "thinking person's shooter", you need "skill" to win.
Everything cost SOMETHING, and I mean EVERYTHING.  They literally have a price tag on everything in the game, and have so many "meta currencies" that it's downright absurd now.  Basically, every little thing you can think of to do or change in the mech lab will cost you either a bunch of your time, or money, and it's all split between 2 separate currency pools.  Jesus.  Christ.
PAINT cost money, as in, you can't use your earned C-Bills, and they charge for it by the individual COLOR.  This is old news, but still hilariously bad.  The new skill point system literally cost you money, in order to allow you to spend MORE money, in order to "upgrade" mechs with marginal improvements to things like acceleration and heat dissipation.  It's not as bad as the old system in some ways, but now forces you to use far more C-Bills to bring a mech "up to speed" in order for it to be more viable, and in the end, it is still on the same level of "LOLWTFBBQ!!?!?!" that is never addressed or cleaned up in their incredibly messy and downright parasitic f2p model.
They still lock new releases behind pay walls, then nerf them.
They still charge way too much, for far too little.
They still refuse to fix any of the games actual core issues, or legitimately better their horrible f2p/p2w model.
There are still ways to abuse the quickplay matchmaking, and when population starts to thin out later in the day, you will suddenly find yourself getting 2 shot by medium lasers from over 1000m away.  I wonder what that could ever possibly be now.  Not cheating, no, never, MWO is just TOO PERFECT for that!
PGI is downright awful about banning known cheaters and grifers, as in, they never do it, despite having a report system.  Most griefers can be seen still playing years later, even after tons of reports, from just about everybody they play with.
Mechwarrior Online is still just a shameless, money grabbing F2P.
Nothing has changed with this game, and it never will.
And don't even get me started on the absolute sham that is "Faction Play".  Know of several other losers, I mean buddies, willing to both pay out of pocket, and grind until the end of time, just for the pleasure of stomping people who have no idea what is going on, and are also horribly underpowered?  Do the words "point-and-click to win" make you feel aroused?  Congrats, you'll ADORE Faction Play.

I'm not just referring to the 4-bit desaturated backgrounds. I whole heartedly put the Lion's Song up there with games like Kentucky Route Zero and Dear Esther which push the artistic and intellectual boundaries in games.
Some will think I'm smoking an expensive vegan platter for thinking this game is amazing, but I have an appreciation for original, poetic writing which conveys complex emotion, experience and atmosphere in just a few words.
It's close to a visual novel. Single mouse button interface, no verbs, inventory management or direct character control. Linear. Only an occasional lightweight adventure game puzzle earns it that title.
None of the cheap gimmicks of most casual adventures like repetitive puzzles or hidden object BS to pad out the game. It's completely focused on the atmosphere and characters.

Overall the difficulty here is a lot easier than in the original Deus Ex, and is less hard core as an rpg. RPG-wise this game is actually very casual with simple perksystem. I myself don't really mind that since I'm all about the immersion, which this game handled really well in my opinion.
Character design is something that probably gets mixed opinions. I have to admit that I didn't like it too much, characters looked a bit foolish and Jensens lens augments looked like what they call "pirikiikarit" here in Finland.
I'll give it an 8/10. I played this mostly sneaking, and I have to admit that I have played better games than this one in that sense with a theme and design closer to what I enjoy more.  Play-time was generous 19 hours for me, which I think is very satisfactory amount. I have understood that this is also very replayable experience, so it's most definitely worth the full price anyway. I myself am not planning to return to this for a while at least since I have hundreds of other games in my library not completed yet.
We'll see how the new Deus Ex will hold up against this one.

The Infectious Maddness of Doctor Dekker, for what it is, is a deeply compelling experience with just the right amount of camp.  The experience is, interesting and surprisingly complex:
Take on the role of a Psychiatrist who's predecessor was murdered by presumably, one of his previous patients.  Meanwhile, as the game progresses, the player either becomes enthralled in the believable madness of each of their patients, attempts to cure them, or discovers the murderer, or all three.  Despite the simplicity of the game, it was found to be enthralling on many occasions.  The Infectious Maddness of Doctor Dekker is wonderfully shot with a minimalist UI, with believable actors and surprisingly believable surreal moments, provided they allow themselves to fall into the mystery of the game itself.
On the down side... the game's primary mechanic is fidgetty at best.  In order to interact with the patients, the player must ask questions of their patients related to a previous question or statement that the patient had asked or made.  The part that gets fidgetty about all of this is that, occasionally, you have to be incredibly specific with your responses.  For example, if a patient says "I have a photo and a rocking chair, which one should I  destroy?"  If you try to ask about either of these things, the word "Photo" or "Rocking chair" will trigger a response you may not have actually wanted.  Other times key words in their statements can trigger entire monologues and reveal mountains of info.  Other times, you might be asked  a yes or no question such as "Do you like to dance?" And you might assume that you can answer simply "Yes," But you'd be wrong.  You need to answer "Yes I like to dance," otherwise the game itself becomes confused.  All in all these are the primary complaints of the game, and with all things considered, they are minor infractions in comparison to the game as a whole.  They do not take away from the experience, nor do they frustrate the player for long, as the answers that you seek are just a "Hint" away most of the time.
if you are looking for a game experience that you can share with someone who might not 100% be into gaming, and has a compelling storyline?  Give this game a shot.

Although the concept of making a program that allows you to build tracks and export them to dedicated sims sounds really cool, this is NOT a very good execution of it.
- The program provides a feature that allows you to export the track into rF2 or Assetto Corsa format. There is actually NO way to directly export the track into either rF2 or Assetto Corsa, unlike its predecessor, Bob's Track Builder. It only exports it into an .fbx file with the image files used in the project. Unless you have advanced knowledge in Blender, 3DS Max, etc., then consider making anything good out of this program
. Even if you do know how to do this, this is very time-wasting and I don't think you would want to do that.
- Due to the vaguely-placed user manual, you would be stumped for a while when you use the program for the first time. If you go into the actual program's installation files, you would find the instruction manual in the form of an .html file. Why is this not linked directly to the library? No clue, and this is time-wasting to find.
- The customer support really takes the cake for how bad it is. Although it never happened much to me, I have heard from others that the only person who knows more about this program than anyone else is Brendon (he's the creator of it, duh), and he has actually banned people from his forums for having issues with this program and... pretty much giving it the rating it deserves. You would be lucky to get any sort of response at all from Brendon, because he rarely responds to any feedback or issues (somewhat understandable since he actually has a family of his own, but why not hire moderators?); he rarely even updates the program anymore and has not yet added any support for the games the program claimed it could export to.
This program is simply Brendon pulling the middle finger to those who wanted to build tracks for games quickly and easily. I do not recommend buying this, especially with the outrageous price tag for the minimal amount of content it has. I recommend Bob's Track Builder much more; it's a stellar program that is far better than RTB, and also cheaper.

World of Tanks Blitz was originally a simplified version of the PC game World of Tanks, for the mobile market. As such, it had simplified controls, simplified models, simplified textures, simplified UI and simplified everything else. This was fine, and in time the game has gotten a small community of it's own. But porting the mobile, severely dumbed down version back to PC, has not made it a true alternative to the original.
I'll make it simple for you.
If you play Blitz on mobile devices a lot, and only occasionally want to play a game on the PC, do go ahead and try this. It will let you play the same game, so you keep your progression and everything else between your mobile devices and the PC.
If on the other hand you don't play mobile games much if at all, and just want a game to play exclusively on the PC, please forget about this. Then you should go download the full, original World of Tanks for PC from their webpage. It's just as free, much better, more content, bigger community and more fun.
Oh, and if anyone thinks they can use this game to sit on a PC with keyboard and mouse, and stomp on players running it from mobile devices. Sorry, but there are separate matchmaking queues. Even Wargaming was not going to allow that kind of rampant sealclubbing.

I understand what this game is going for, I understand that it is supposed to be nightmarishly difficult, but in the end it just goes too far. Placing multiple dart-spitting statues along a moving platform section is fine, but the speed they come out at and the split-second they are telegraphed for is just that little bit too fast for you to react to them naturally, and they are in every level. Giving the player a difficult drop where they have to hit a switch on the way down is fine; immediately shooting them a half second after landing, at the very end of the level no less, is just irritating.
Meat Boy worked because it had a great sense of flow, and even when things went wrong you could pull it back by feeling the ebb and flow of the situation. This game is almost pure memory, and does it in a way designed to kill you in the most pointlessly spiteful ways possible.
The visuals and music are great, the controls are excellent and I want to love it so very much. But it just batters you relentlessly and vindictively until you've lost all will to go on - not from being bested by a challenge, but from not even being able to care anymore if you beat it.
I guess if it's going for pocket change then give it a look maybe, but not at full price.

1001 Spikes is a very smart, enjoyable, and extremely difficult platformer game. You take on the role of a treasure hunter who must navigate through temple areas to retrieve a key to proceed to the next level, optionally finding a hidden skull.
The primary mechanics in the game involve 2 styles of jumps - one short and one high, but both are at a constant height. The other ability the player has is to throw a knife.
The level design in this game is very well done. It is very much in the Megaman or classic game style of teaching you by showing you. You learn by playing and observing your environment - nowhere does the game ruin the pace by insulting your intelligence and forcing you through a scripted tutorial.
That said, this game is very difficult. I would recommend this to people who enjoy a challenge. This is the sort of challenge where the game is really testing your skills, not difficulty for difficulty's sake.

(Review is for the first two episodes)
Bear With Me, a traditional point-and-click adventure game, stands out for its terrific, inventive world. Blending a noir-like atmosphere and dialogue with the interactions between a child and her anthropomorphic friends (who may or may not be part of her vivid imagination, an element I really liked) leads to some rich slices of a world.
The game doesn't quite take full advantage of that in its first episode, keeping the focus narrowed to the child's house, but once the game has its legs under it in the second episode, the game starts to explore the much more intriguing Paper City, as well as introducing some teasers for what's to come.
The humor can be hit and miss, but I largely like it. Even the referential humor is mostly cute and inoffensive, which isn't something I'd normally say about jokes like that.
The machanics are solid - you pick stuff up, you combine said stuff with other stuff, and you progress a bit in the story. This is typical adventure fare, but it recognizes the strengths of the genre and doesn't try to stray from them, creating a smart, simple UI and keeping the focus squarely where it needs to be - the characters and the setting. I do wish the hint system - disguised as conversations you have with your teddy bear detective pal - wasn't quite so obtuse at times. Giving vague, unhelpful comments about where the characters need to eventually head to doesn't help me figure out that I've somehow missed a very tiny grate in an environment.
Overall, Bear With Me is a phenomenal start to an adventure series, one I look forward to finishing once the future episodes are released. It should be checked out by any fans of the genre.

This game introduced a lot of amazing new concepts, and truly is a revolution in 4X games; By all accounts, this game is absolutely incredible except for one excrutiatingly painful deficiency that, alas, destroys the entire gaming experience: The combat system is defective by design.
In Endless Space, you have three types of weapons (and respective defenses) that can each be employed at any of three ranges (each weapon excels at one range and sufffers penalities at the other two). Ordinarily, this would make for a very diverse combat experience, except for the fact that combat is only controlled at the strategic level and not the tactical level. In other words: You can can only give extremely high-level orders to your forces, but cannot control them on a per-unit level. As such, it is easy to win virtually every battle by only making long-range glass cannons in which you obliterate the enemy in the first volley. While the AI does adapt its ship designs often, they never do so to the extent necessary to counter such a threat; specifically, they insist on some degree of balance and therefore will never opt for perfect defense or mutually assured destruction as would be necessary to successfully oppose such a force.
Unfortunately, the deficiencies of the combat system carry over to multiplayer as well, so it's not an AI-only issue.
If a new expansion comes out to address these issues, I will update my review accordingly; in the meantime, I would avoid this game in favor of other games.
Personally, Fallen Enchantress: Legendary Heroes is my favorite 4X game in terms of mechanics and gameplay experience, though the lack of multiplayer is a bummer and the AI at higher difficulty levels could use some improvement without resorting to ludacris degrees of cheating. Age of Wonders III is also a great game with decent AI and multiplayer that in many ways is more advanced than FE:LH, but at the expense of missing some bread-and-butter features that no 4X game should do without.
It is worth mentioning that the game Endless Legend is the fantasy, on-the-ground counterpart to Endless Space. The mechanics are almost identical, and the combat system improved greatly with the addition of tactical combat. Unfortunately, Endless Legend also has its deficiencies (including the combat system), so I cannot recommend it to anyone other than perhaps newcomers to 4X and novice strategists.

Deus Ex: Human Revolution really surprised me.  I expected Human Revolution (HR) to be another filthy cash-grab by a game studio eager to slap on a successful face to an otherwise forgettable game, and to some extent that is true of HR... But what I didn't expect was that the developers would put so much effort into replicating the feel of the original Deus Ex.
(TL;DR: very average game in terms of gameplay, but it has beautiful art & scenery.  The plot is predictable at times, but ultimately, at the end of the day, Human Revolution is an AMAZING homage to the original and faithfully brings the FEELING of the original Deus Ex into modern gaming.  I HIGHLY recommend for anyone who enjoyed the original Deus Ex or for anyone who thinks Deus Ex sounds cool but missed the boat on the original.  For people who don't like sci-fi themes, it'd probably be a game you'd play once and forget about.)
It's been a while since I played through the game, but my first impression of the game was that it was very generic.  Another game using the same engine as Batman: Arkham Asylum/City/Knight games, with a couple neat but predictable features like hacking, persuation mini-games, and character upgrades.  These are fun, but they're nothing that hasn't been done before and HR doesn't add any spectacular twists or anything.
The art and story are where this game really shines, and why I feel this game is a worthy tribute to the original.  From the beginning the art is fantastic, the little tutorial/prologue has you go through a science facility to see all the futuristic stuff going on & to foreshadow what's going to happen.
The story starts off very boring and cliche: (former) love-interest is kidnap! What do??  You go around exploring the city, getting a feel for things, checking out the scenery and character designs, fighting bad dudes... nothing seems particularly interesting, but all the while they're dropping hints about secret government etc. etc.  If you're genre savvy you know exactly whats coming and think you're totally prepared.
Then you take the WRONG F**KING ELEVATOR and everything falls into place: The technology, the art, the story, you really SEE  all these elements in motion in a living world and it feels like being thrown through a glass wall.  Suddenly it's not just a game, it's a real world, one of our possible futures.  As I rode the elevator down and saw everything that was going on I kept thinking, "let me off this ride, I'm not ready for this yet!"
From that point on I really felt like I was playing the game and invested in the story, rather than playing just to play. I sort of coasted on that investment until the end of the game.  The developers tried to get some cool battles and boss fights going, but I felt nothing quite reached the point of memorable until the end of the game.  For me, what really sealed the recommendation of this game is the ending.  I don't want to spoil it, but you have to make a choice that affects the entire world similar to how you did in the original Deus Ex.  It would be easy to claim that the developers were simply copy-catting the original, but that's flat-out wrong.  Imo the decision at the end is much more than a simple copy-cat because it ties everything from HR together.  All the plot lines, all the little notes you find, everything that happens, it all comes together and all of your options make sense from the perspective of the character.  It doesn't feel forced, it doesn't feel like it's thrown on, it feels like it's the logical conclusion to everything that happened up until that point.
The game doesn't have quite the depth and complexity as the original, but it captures the best feelings of the original and puts it into a fresh story with modern graphics and modern gameplay.  To anyone who enjoyed the original Deus Ex, to anyone who just thinks Deus Ex is cool, this is a MUST OWN.  To everyone else, I'd recommend giving it a try if you have the spare cash and time, you might get a kick out of it.  If you don't like sci-fi, if you hate conspiracies, I'd pass on HR, as the gameplay isn't strong enough to carry the game or make it stick out from the dozens of other shooters.

Deus Ex Human Revolution is  the second (errr third) game in the series and is a prequel to the Deus Ex franchise in which the core concepts both mechanically and thematically remain intact and in many cases are improved upon. Deus Ex has always been about expansive levels with multiple solution sets and that remains true for this game. It is very refreshing to have a modern AAA game which stays true to player agency when that is becoming a dwindling quality in most AAA output. Eidos Montreal not only kept faithful to the core mechanics and themes of the original game but greatly improved many of its interactive systems such as its stealth, combat, hacking and even dialogue interactions. In addition to being faithful, they have also made their own mark with this entry in terms of style and visual aesthetics, to make the game more than a cover band entry but something which is distinctly their game as well. The game is somewhat a reboot despite being set before the original (a preboot?) since it takes great liberties with the setting and technological advancements of the time period supposedly long before the original game that it doesn't really feel like it belongs to the same game world as the original Deus Ex. Despite that the game is seamlessly interwoven with the lore of the Deus Ex universe, and even though it is a prequel the content seems written to be most enjoyed for one who has played the original game first, which is something you should do anyway if you haven't already.
Despite the many successes of this game there are some critical design flaws, some due to poor decisions and the rest because of either time or budget restraints. At this point in time long after its original release and with its sequel right around the corner, some of these flaws are likely redundant to bring up since they have already been much documented by other reviews and fans and because Eidos montreal themselves has indicated that the flaws of HR are exactly what they are going to address with Mankind Divided and more so its possible the developer has already learned from their mistakes.
There are some problems I personally had with the game. For example the game does a really bad job of making a decent first impression upon starting up. After a prerendered cutscene, you start off in a room full of interesting easter eggs except your supposed love interest nags you incessantly for deciding to explore. Afterwards you stand on a conveyor belt of a pseudo-cutscene you can't skip followed by more prerendered cutscenes and a forced tutorial. After FINALLY starting the game for real, your boss nags you to hurry out of the hub zone you've just been introduced to and to possibly miss out on circumstantial character interactions which can't be found upon returning. If you decide to ignore your boss and explore at your own pace the game punishes you terribly for it. After this though the game never pulls this funny business again and plays like a real Deus Ex game from that point onward. This seems nitpicky but is important because everything about those first 15 minutes is completely unrepresentative of the rest of the game, and what more is antithetical to the Deus Ex experience as well. Those first 15 minutes were so bad for me that I almost gave up on what is in actuality a very good game. I have to wonder if that entire segment was requested by some executive who thinks that every modern AAA game needs an exciting, relentless and """cinematic""" beginning.
The range of agency isn't quite as vast as the original, likely because the original game didn't use nearly as many detailed and resource taxing visuals which limit how expansive the levels can be. Also that the upgrade tree is imbalanced in that the combat upgrades are underwhelming, especially on the highest difficulty where the damage resistance and typhoon explosives are pretty inconsequential. The game makes a pretty big deal out of the human landmine that is the typhoon augment, in theory a localized explosion of 8 meters sounds useful, except for the fact that in a world where people fight with guns, this is something you will rarely find the need for. Even if you try to setup uses for it by running into a group and activating it, you'll be left standing there like a doofus after it's over as enemies elsewhere plug you full of holes. Even the demonstration of the weapon in the beginning seemed bizarre as it showed a dozen test dummies standing around a single typhoon as a practice application. The only uses that would seem to fulfill are terrorist attacks or blowing up everyone after being taken captive. Either way, seems like a one trick pony.
The inconsequential combat upgrades don't matter too much since the combat is sufficiently effective from the very beginning. Cover based shooting is static but reliably effective, and there aren't really any improvements to obtain except better weapons and upgrades. The game also has a bias in what methods you use to advance. Even though you can proceed however you want, it grants hefty point bonuses for advancing unseen and for using nonlethal methods to take out enemies. This in itself isn't a problem, but it means that the entire game, with its more fleshed out infiltration rpg abilities and its overt encouragements to be stealthy, means that stealth becomes the "proper" way to play the game, which is an influence the original game completely avoided. Luckily, the stealth of HR is quite great, possibly one of the highlights of the entire genre, and also shows the AI at its strongest. Which of course makes the forced boss fights even more baffling but that has already been commented on before.
What really stands out to me the most about this game is that DXHR is a game that comes from a dev team that really seems to care about the source material (unlike a certain other dev team of a series whose main character name rhymes with Shante, they sure seemed invested in letting the fans know how much they hated the source material), and more importantly care about providing an engaging experience for their players, corporate middle man meddling aside. This is a development team that isn't another developer farm of segmented lackies pumping out the current model of focus test approved formula, but one that might actually want to make a game they can be proud of, which is surprising coming from a dev team published under Square Enix, but also evident in the making of segment included in this game. All that said, I highly recommend you play both the original Deus Ex and this prequel, as they are both worth the time and money for any person interested in the unique genre fusion of stealth, action, rpg and adventure which comprises the Deus Ex franchise.

Another interesting game. The idea of skiing and jetting is very good, and is quite usable. It makes the gameplay more fluid, and requires prediction and anticipation. The maps are pretty, with the rolling hills and mountains. However, there are some major issues. First off, the vehicles are terrible. FMV games have made quite the comeback in the last few years, and The Infectious Madness of Doctor Dekker adds to the growing library of great titles in the genre.  Of course, it's not a perfect game (what game is?), but the quality of the writing, acting and production all place this murder mystery amid the cream of the FMV crop here on Steam.
Doctor Dekker has been violently murdered by one of his patients.  As his replacement at the psychiatric clinic,  you are now tasked with investigating his death while helping his patients navigate their various maladies.  Toss in a little Cthulhu mythos, and you have a recipe for madness that's altogether delightful to behold.
Gameplay consists of free typing questions and key words to engage each patient in therapeutic conversation.  While the wording required to trigger responses can sometimes be finicky, once you have a handle one the game's logic, figuring out which phrases to focus on becomes second nature.  In the times that you find yourself completely stuck, typing in "hint" will give you suggestions on what to ask next, thus you should never be scratching your head for too long.  Hints are unlimited, so I suggest using them liberally unless you're working towards specific achievements, in which case you'll want to wait until a second or third playthrough to target them.  And there's plenty of room for replayability as the killer changes with each new game.
My one and only complaint with the system is that sometimes your question will trigger a response that doesn't line up at all with what you asked.  This doesn't happen often, but can be a bit confusing when you're trying to follow a train of thought and end up derailed by a completely unrelated answer.  Still, it's only a mild annoyance compared to the entertainment the characters and story provide.
As an FMV title, it all ultimately comes down to the acting, which is excellent and the highlight of the entire game.  Not only does each actor totally sell their respective madness to the player, but you'll find that even the most wicked of patients will grow on you as you delve into their stories and more intimate thoughts.  Toss in a cameo by John Guilor of
fame, and you've got quite the awesome cast.
The Infectious Madness of Doctor Dekker may not be for everyone, but if you're an ardent FMV junkie, do not miss out on this gem.  For those wanting to dabble their toes in the genre, or are just intrigued enough to take a look, it's definitely worth your while IF you take your time to savor the experience.

Ive been playing MWO for a few months now.
I do like this game a fair bit, and find it fun to play however there are some problems Im sure EVERYONE would like to see fixed or changed at very least.
First and foremost is COST, buying mechs, MC, and "decals" such as paint colours and cockpit items is FAR TOO EXPENSIVE. Yes the vast majority of mechs are purchasable with some grinding, and there is a huge in-game-currency bonus for shiny new players; however many mechs one may want cost cold hard cash and are TOO EXPENSIVE.
Experienced players have a huge advantage as there IS a learning curve, and on top of that the bonuses for "working in" mechs and buying "modules", which is really cool and gives motivation for grinding. Some new players may feel intimidated.
PLEASE PLAY THE TUTORIAL. PRESS "R" to target (to share targeting data and help with teamplay).
A Great game, please give it a chance.

The good:
>Lots of customization of mechs AFTER you buy one (there are lots of guides available on which mechs to buy for what playstyle once you've familiarized yourself with the game.) Want bigass cannons? Go for it. Like EZ aim mode lasers? Pew pew.
>Graphical update in March made this game look amazing. Every mech has 2k textures and the game set to ultra high looks awesome on systems that can run it.
>BIG MECH. Knock over ALL OF THE TREES. RaaaaAAAAAAA.
>Smart play and tactics get rewarded. Idiots that rush in alone die, even if they bought a "pay to win" mech.
>There is no pay2win model here. Most purchases are cosmetic; extra mech bays can be earned thorugh faction warfare (please save this for when you've played lots) and most mechs you see only for sale for real money are later available for in-game currency.
>Your first 25 matches have a HUGE bonus to in game currency earnings. Save it for when you're ready to buy; the 17 million total plus whatever you earn playing will be enough to buy an assault mech.
>Hot damn, the animations are great.
>PGI is somewhat connected to their playerbase and actively tries to improve their game.
>Free to play; if you don't enjoy it, all it costs is time. If you love it and never spend a cent, WOO. Free game!
>Active and helpful community. If you have questions, there's always someone or somewhere you can go to get them answered.
>Supprt is generally helpful and almost always polite yet concise. Even though they have a small team, they are a damn good team at that.
>It FEELS like you're driving a 20 to 100 ton machine of doom. Even the smallet of these things dwarf some of the buildings in this game. The scale is AWESOME.
>Every cockpit of every mech is different. It's awesome.
The bad:
>Limited maps in both quick play and faction warfare. You will learn them all fairly quickly.
>If you want to own ALL of the mechs, you will have to pay for them in the long run. For some people, that's fine. Just be aware of what you're buying first. Do research on mechs before you buy. DO RESEARCH. You will hate yourself if you get something you do not enjoy playing.
>Despite the few years this game has been out, not a lot has come out aside from a couple maps here, a UI update there. PGI has a small team; expect the game to evolve somewhat slowly.
>Not every mech is a good one. There are balance issues like in any other online game with player versus player, but it sucks to buy a crap mech. But yes, research. You can avoid this with KNOWLEDGE.
>No single player mode. There is work being done for a PvE campaign, but I don't expect it to be done any time soon.
>Meta play gets to be a bit.. well.. obvious. Just be ready for the occasional tryhard with a 100% optimal build that can three shot you with alpha strikes. Of course, you can always shoot them back.
>In game currency earnings gets really slow after those first 25 matches. Sorry. It'll be grindy to get that second or third mech you want.
>Premium time in-game is used even if you are not actively playing. If you have 3 days of premium, it will be gone in 3 days. Regardless of if you play or not.
>Faction play needs work. I'll not say more. It's fun and all, but it needs work.
>Third person mode sucks. If you despise first person, well.. good luck?

After owning Race Track builder for about 6 months now, I thought it was time to write a review.  This product has really developed in the last month or so, making it very usable and a powerful tool.
I am a complete noob when it comes to modelling, and track creation, but even I am able to make a track using Google Earth terrain of my local hills.  If you are thinking of buying this, be prepared to do some research. There is a lot to learn, (which is great), and studying the program first saves time when creating tracks.  You could be trying to tweak something for 2 or 3 hours and then find out the tools you are using in the program has an easier way to do it.
There are a lot of Youtube tutorials and information on forums.  A great video to help you get started is
.  You can then move onto the official channel from Brendon to help you learn all of the tools
Overall it's a great program that is being actively developed, with a great community contributing to mods etc.

For a first time track builder like me, you can't beat this product.  The first time I installed it I had some difficulties using it.  But it's like any other software, you have to take the time to learn it.  There isn't a lot of information out there, but with a bit of digging I was able to find enough to start creating some great tracks.  Still have a lot to learn, but I have enough knowledge now to create topos from google maps, transfer BTB xpacks into RTB, and work with the tools of the program.  If you are like me and don't feel like learning how to use blender, or any relevant 3D software, then RTB is the best dummy track builder for you.  I'm great at Sketchup, but it's kind of useless for xpacks, as you still have to import it in to other 3D software.
It's still early days, but every BTB user will be using RTB soon enough.  I read complaints about lack of support and I myself uninstalled the program first time I got it, mostly because I was just too lazy to do any research on my own.  You have to remember that this product was created by a one man team.  I don't know the guy, but he's created something that I was looking for, as I'm starting to get bored with all the tracks in RBR, Dirt Rally, and Assetto.
Create an API address and watch tutorials on how to convert BTB xpacks into RTB.  Then google BTB xpacks for free ones created by the community on various forums.  There are so many packs that include, crowds, buildings, vehicles, vegetation, and so on, that I won't really need to create my own for a long time.
If the developer is reading this, I would only urge you to make two more tutorials.  One for converting BTB xpacks to RTB (this info is hard to find), and how to create an xpack from scratch by going through the entire process from start to finish, including bits about blender or another free 3D software.  There are some tutorials, but are either incomplete, don't fully apply, or are badly made.  Even if you make the BTB xpacks to RTB conversion tutorial, I guaranty you that everyone will love the product!  Best of luck!

I had high hopes for Endless Space, since the space-based 4X genre is my favorite. The game ended up leaving me a bit disappointed. It's good, I guess, but really feels limited. It marries a well-executed strategic empire management game to a paper-thin tactical space combat engine. To be honest, the space combat seems like an idea that just didn't succeed, so the developers threw in the visuals because they'd already done the work. If this was the space combat they envisioned from the start, I really wonder why they bothered. The "manual" combat mode leaves you basically as an observer with almost no control over the battle once it's begun (other than ordering a retreat that, due to the mechanics of the game, would almost certainly come too late to be useful).  The combat mechanics are disappointing as well. While you get to design your ships (a must for any game in this genre, IMO) the design choices are really only reflected in the power ratings for your ships, So, all your research basically just increases the numbers a ship has, but not its play style or tactics. The tactics themselves are basically a set of rock-scissors-paper decisions (beam-projectile-missile and long-medium-short range). They only play into the game pre-battle, when you pick tactics. So, the tactical combat basically just ends up being empires throwind ever-larger stacks of ships against each other to compare numbers and have one side win.
The strategic game is better, but except for the setting (a universe in which a powerful elder race came before you and left ruined wonders) it's basically like every other space game. The developers seemed to want to create variety through many different playable races, but they all basically play the same, so it doesn't work.
All in all, it scratched my sci-fi 4X itch for a while, though not particularly satisfyingly. I'd give it a 6 or 7 on a 1-10 scale. It treads the same path as Master of Orion, though not quite as well. For my money, if you want a space-based 4X game, the gold standard is the indie series "Space Empires". SE is not a perfect game by any stretch of the imagination, but it's the best combination of a strong strategic game with a functional tactical one.

This game was a huge disappointment for me. A Deus Ex game should have delivered a great story with nefarious conspiracies, and game objectives that could be completed in multiple ways. In this game the story makes absolutely no sense, the biggest "conspiracy" is that television lies, you barely discover anything about the organizations and the people behind the events, the whole augmentation debate is discussed on kindergarten-level, and the ending is mind-meltingly stupid. I could write an entire book about how badly written this game is. It's true that multiple playstyles are supported, but there is an optimal one that is heavily favored by the game rules: stay undetected, use only nonlethal melee takedowns (yes, this game is not a shooter), and hack everything. If you follow the optimal style, all weapons, ammo, and weapon mods are useless (take the laser rifle to the last boss though), all health-restoring items are useless, and there is no difference between the difficulty levels either, because every enemy goes down with a single button press. The only difficulty is finding the correct order of taking down the guards without alerting the remaining ones, but thanks to the rtarded patrol routes it's usually quite easy. I could list the flaws in the game mechanics for pages, but it's tl;dr anyway. The boss fights are often criticized for being out-of-place, but the real issue is that the boss characters have no part in the story other than appearing as an obstacle at a certain point. Overall, this game is not completely awful, for example, the dialog challenges are interesting, the hacking minigame is nice, the visual design is impressive, and I liked some of the side-quests. My biggest grief is that for lots of people this is The Deus Ex Game, while in reality both its predecessors were vastly superior in almost every way. Oh, and why does the DC version occupy twice the disk space as the original release?
Edit: I watched the developer commentaries on youtube, and it's mind-numbing how incompetent and clueless they are (except for the sound designer guy).
Edit 2: I watched some steam broadcasts, and it turns out most people play this game like CoD. Disappointing.

I'll keep this pretty brief because others here have already described Deus Ex: Human Revolution a lot better than I can....
This is the best game I've played last year. it's perfect (no game is 'perfect') but because it represents the ceiling in modern gaming -- this is what other video games should aspire to be in 2011. Human Revolution allows and encourages player experimentation and freedom. There is no 'right' way to play it, be it good, evil, stealthy, talky, actiony, or any combination thereof. The level design is freeform and there is always more than one route to your objectives. The dialogue writing is solid, and the plot is compelling. The augmentation system is fantastic, and if you choose intelligently you can make Adam Jensen whatever kind of superhuman you want him to be. Minor quibbles include some spotty voice acting and stiff animations, but neither detracts from the fact that this a strong game of the year contender. I recommend this to just about anyone who likes video games. There's something in it for everybody.

There is a lot to be said about MWO, and most of it is good. The graphics are nice. The customization of the mechs is nice. The handling of the mechs is great. It all feels "right."
There are plenty of memorable and epic moments to be found even though the missions are typically fairly short. The maps are nice and varied, allowing for the different classes of mechs to have environments where they fair very well in one game and very poorly in another. This adds challenge and forces adaptation of play style.
Updates are still occurring, including new mapes and, recently, a new play mode.
The system by which mechs and skills can be upgraded is reasonable and does not always require actual money for the transactions. I have played over 100 hours without spending a dollar, though soon I plan to make some purchases - there are things worth buying, after all, you just don't HAVE to buy them. This is definitely not a pay to win game.
Generally, if you like mechs and PvP on-line games, its pretty good. I spend some time with it almost every day.
Now for my only gripe:
The only thing wrong with this game is the number of trolls playing it.
Sure, die first and then spend the entire rest of the round typing about how everyone else and their mech loadout sucks.
Sure, pilot a light mech and then refuse to acquire targets so that the slower but more powerful long range mechs can use your scouting to rain hell down on your enemies.
And let us not forget the necessity of having a mute button so that we don't have to listen to the constant nagging of the 5 different "commanders" in every company.
This game is designed to be a team event - consistantly winning any of its various mission types requires team work and an understanding not only of your own mech's/ lance's capabilities and strengths, but also an understanding of and cooperation with the strengths and capabilites of the other lances you are fighting with. Never the less, almost every single mission ends up being a free for all skirmish followed by idiotic critiques by people who have too much time to type while everyone else is fighting.
This is why I don't usually play on-line games. And more than likely, it is what will drive me away from this one.

1001 spike and is a classic 2D action platformer where you play as Aban Hawkins, basically indiana jones minus the whip, who sets out on an adventure to Ukampa to find not only his father but the treasure of the temple in order to prove he is better than him. The 1001 in the title is actually refering to the number of lives you start with. (Though it could mean the spikes because there is a damn lot of them).
You have 1001 lives to best your way through all '30' levels of the Ukampa tomb but don't let that discourage you or make you think that's all the lives you have. At the end of each section, you'll find an artifact which gives you a large chunk of lives. Along with those, there is a skull collectible in each level (including the room that's just a straight walk to the artifact) which I highly recommend collecting. Not only does it grant you a life every time you pick it up (It has to be recollected every time you die) but it also lets you unlock new, fun characters.
These unlockable characters really encourage replaying the game to see how much better you can do with them, the different ways they can clear the levels with their unique abilities (These characters are also characters from different games which helps to encourage unlocking them just to see who they are. See Super Meat Boy if you wonder what I mean by 'From different games') Lastly these characters also have a different collectible to the skull. In this case, a coin that gives you money from 100 to 1000 and beyond as you get to the later levels which allow you to buy even more lives.
For the price you're buying, you're definitely getting your money's worth. Not only is there the main game 1001 spikes but there is also side stories that unlock which take Aban to new dangerous adventures and *Bit of a spoiler* After beating the 'boss', a whole new set of levels open up.
It's definitely worth the buy.

Mostly fun, recommended for fans of challenging platformers, not for impatient people.
Pros:
-Tight, precise controls
-Good amount of levels, extra content
-Simple mechanics - quick to learn
Cons:
-Worst complaint is some levels being too long with crazy difficult stuff at the end that requires a ton of trial and error. I've beaten every level in the game exactly once, but I feel like I've beaten the first 80% of most levels like 30 times each, to the point where there is zero challenge and fun for that section because every jump becomes memorized up to the point where I'm having trouble. As someone who also beat every level in Super Meat Boy, I think SMB handles level length much better.
-Many (perhaps most?) deaths are from trial and error. A major flaw of 1001 Spikes here is that there's no way to safely play a level the first time even if you're patient and alert like other platformers allow. Rushing through will kill you somewhere for sure, but equally often playing it safe after every jump will kill you because you're often standing on a spike trap or falling rock. Keeping one or the other type of death consistent throughout an entire level would be better design IMO.

DON'T USE FULLSCREEN!
This is not a review of gameplay but a warning.  If you use full screen, there is a game breaking bug that can crop up that will not allow you to start the game up after quiting.  The only fix I know of is to delete the common file (and possibly save data) from your Documents/My Games/1001 Spikes/Saves file.

If you enjoy platformers and the high diffulty is what you see as a challenge, not discouragement, this is the right game for you. I call it 'a mild version of I Wanna Be The Guy'. Just like in legendary IWBTG, 1001 Spikes levels are designed to ♥♥♥♥ you over, but beating them is certainly possible, if you are smart, swift and patient. Because like in every hard platformer, patience is what you will need the most, to learn how to deal with different kinds of traps: arrows flying from level walls, falling rocks, lava, moving platforms, disappearing floor and of course, countless spikes. The game will provide you with few hours of entertainment for the main campaign only - and few other gamemodes plus local multiplayer are what you can play right after.
To me, it is my third favorite platformer, right after Super Meat Boy and Electronic Super Joy.

This game is not a brutally difficult platformer in the vein of Super Meat Boy or a challenging platformer in the vein of Braid or a casual platformer in the vein of New Super Mario Bros. Wii. This is a trial-and-error platformer in the vein of Limbo, but without the visual aesthetic to go with it. This game has the precision platforming of Super Meat Boy, but it's coupled with cheap, un-telegraphed deaths that force you to play the same level several times, not only to time the jumps and attacks but to learn the environment. It's an artifical difficulty, not a fair one. If you're looking for another experience like Super Meat Boy or a challenging platformer, you are looking in the wrong place.
