Impression after 1 day of fiddling with it:
Good:
+ Touch pads are versatile, can support even up to 9 buttons each (can do 12 but I haven't tested) comfortably.
+ Dual-action triggers work as advertised, and are minutely customizable.
+ Grip button is insanely ergonomic and easy to press.
+ Software is ground-breaking, even though UI could be easier-to-use for people who are doing the configs using their mouse/keyboard.
Functional:
> Left stick works like a left stick. Small size makes it slightly easier than other controllers, but might be preference.
Bad:
- Shoulder buttons are stiff and slightly hard to reach up to. I say "slightly" but slightly is a big thing if you want to use them regularly. I now allocate them to my least-used functions.
- ABXY buttons are too small and as a result are difficult to press.
- If you have smaller hands, the X button requires a reach. This is exacerbated by the bulbous hand holds. Would have preferred PS3 handholds (swept back) instead of bulbing forward.
Overall:
Don't have a daughter but if I did I would imagine the handholds would make the controller slightly too large for her.
However, this controller is a true innovation, and is the way forward for such devices.

First let me say that I recommend the Steam Controller but it is not easy to do so. Simply put, the Steam Controller is not for every one and is dependent on the games you play. The controller shines when it's used for mouse and keyboard specific games. I have been able to play Total War, Cities Skylines, point and click adventure games, and Grim Dawn from my couch with no issues. Being able to customize each and every button press makes the controller amazing to use. It is my preferred way to play Elite Dangerous as the touch pad is great for the thrusters, and I use the built in gyroscope to look around the cockpit at the same time. Something I haven't seen mentioned is that the controller can be used as a mouse when Big Picture is minimized. So, if I need to go to the internet from the couch, I no longer have to get up to get the mouse.
Where the controller suffers, in my opinion, is when it comes to console game ports to the PC. I tried playing Sleeping Dogs DE, Hitman, and a number of third person games on the controller.  While the controller works as intended and can be adjusted for additional camera control, and in many ways is superior to a 360 or XBONE controller; it just isn't the same. I never got totally used to aiming with the touch pad as it was always too sensitive or not sensitive enough. You can create your own custom controller config in the settings and have it be just as you like it. Or, even find configs from other people. But this takes time, patience, and willingness to get used to a new controller.
Even after I created my own custom config with the camera controls just the way I like it, I would still chose to play Hitman with the 360 controller I have sitting literally right next to my Steam Controller.  It works, but I don't think it will ever fully replace a dual stick console controller especially if you already own a few.
So your mileage my vary with the SC and it depends on where you play and what games you play. It's is perfect for me to play Keyboard and mouse specific games from the couch, but I don't think it will fully replace your 360 or XBONE controller

After more than a year on my wishlist, I finally picked up a Steam controller.  I got mine half off because I bought it from a coworker who had a spare.  He didn’t use this one, so it’s a brand new controller.  I’m going to break down what I like and what I don’t like about this controller in a good, bad, ugly type of list.
The Good:
-The shape and design of the controller are nice, it fits nicely in my hands and is comfortable.
-The analog stick, trackpads and buttons are all nice and responsive.  The stick is nice and tight and works great.  The pads work, but with some issues that will be described on down the list.
-Works as a mouse, even without Steam launched (Linux.)  This is handy for couch usage.
-Works on Steam in or out of Big Picture mode, which is good, but with a minor issue (below.)
-Works in non Steam games, but with a caveat (listed below.)
-Absolutely no lag in the wireless.
-Button configurations are simple even without the game loaded.  You can even configure buttons for each game in a vault style game collection, such as the Atari Vault.
The Bad:
-Wired mode doesn’t work (Linux.)  It tries to work, but the controller stops responding after about 15-30 seconds.  I don’t know if this is just a Linux issue, but it is an issue.  I tried both the cable supplied and a micro USB cable I already had that I know works.  I tried in the same USB port where it works flawlessly in wireless mode.
-Rumble doens’t work (Linux.)
-Works a heck of a lot better in side scrolling 2D games than 3D games (see next.)
-Trackpads DO NOT replace a second analog stick.  This is especially evident in first person shooters.  With an analog stick for looking, you can move it an any direction and your look will move in that direction indefintely, unless you’re at the vertical limit.  However, moving the stick and holding it left or right will make you spin around in a circle.  Looking with the trackpads is limited to the edge of the pad.  When your thumb gets to the edge of the pad, you stop turning in that direction.  This is a massive issue if you’re trying to spin around and kill an enemy that is behind you.  Perhaps playing with the look sensitivity will make you spin around faster, but it’s still a problem.  This renders FPS games hard to play.  In front of your computer, this may not be an issue as most people will probably play with mouse and keyboard, but this is a deal killer for couch gaming.  A $20 wired XBOX 360 knockoff controller would be more useful than this thing for FPS games.
-Twin Stick Shooters don’t work well either, as you don’t have twin sticks.
-Can only be turned off in Big Picture mode.  (may be a Linux only issue, but it’s an issue)  I hate Big Picture mode and try to avoid using it.
The Ugly:
-Only works on non Steam games if you add them to Steam.  I have a lot of games from other stores and from my Linux respositories that I like, I don’t want to have to run Steam to use a controller with them.  Other controllers work with them just fine without Steam.
-The shoulder buttons are very clicky, as in they have an audible click sound that is louder than my mouse.  This absolutely sucks in games.
-The layout is a bit wonky with the buttons where you’d normally have a right thumbstick.  Controller buttons are where they are on most controllers for a reason, it’s more of an ergonomic thing.  Also, the buttons are smaller and closer together than they are on XBOX and Playstation controllers.
At the end of the day, I like this controller well enough to recommend it, but please take into account the issues I listed above.  If you want to couch play games that don’t require a quick look around to kill things on all sides of you, the trackpads are OK.  But, they’re not for FPS games or other games that require a quick look.  I also woulnd’t want to play games that require driving or flying using the twin stick method.  It works fine as a mouse, which is handy on a couch, but kind of useless on a computer with a desk setup.  I’m glad I didn’t pay full price for this controller, as it can’t totally replace the wired XBOX 360 controller that I’ve had for close to a decade.  So, do yourself a favor and wait for this piece of hardware to go on sale, as it’s been doing more and more lately.

There once was a lad who played this game. He wandered around and built a house. Then he discovered that he could become a potato. So, he lept at the opportunity. The lad enjoyed being a potato and hopped around happily. Until one day the lad met a man with an eyepatch and fancy suit. He said to the man "Hi there I have mixed feelings about you. You are wearing an eyepatch. That makes me distrust you, but you are also wearing a fancy suit. Despite that the fact that I cannot figure out why it is so fancy, it makes me trust you."
"Well my lad no reason to fear me for I am a mayor. Follow me to my city and I will grant you citizenship and a free plot of land."
The lad happily followed the man to his city until they arrived there.
"Here is my city lad. Go in and make yourself at home."
"But sir it is a cave."
"Oh my silly boy. It is an underground city. See?"
He said as he walked into the cave. The boy saw this as proof enough and went on in.
"No boy you must pay a small fee to pass this door."
"I thought you said it was free of charge."
"Oh yes but this a toll for all people. No exceptions."
The man waited as the boy deposited the fee. Then the man walked through the door and the boy followed. Except the boy felt the floor move and as he looked he felt himself falling. He did not understand what was going on.
"Thank you for the gold my dear potato, but I must bid you farewell."
The boy fell for about three more seconds until hitting a spike pit and subsequently dying.
(Moral of the story never trust a man with an eyepatch no matter how fancy a suit he wears.)

I've never been a fan of point and click games, I actually avoided them for the most part. I was more then surprised when I found myself enjoying this game.
Gameplay - The Good
- To start us off I'll say the game perfectly on it's highest resolution settings. No frame drops or issues of any sort.
- Hilarious/Funny interactions between the two main characters and others that you meet later.
- Supporting characters are funny and interesting. Actual thought was put into there point of existance.
- There are easter eggs to other shows and movies that make for a lot of laugh out loud moments(for me atleast).
- Great story that could have been generic but was expanded upon as you find more clues about your brother.
- Voice acting was great
- Everything you clicked on was explained by Ambers voice actor. In funny ways for the most part.
- Love that the game is being played out as a 10 year olds imagination. How the stuffed animals are considered real people.
- Puzzles were easy and rewarding. For almost every puzzle, you'll have to combine items to further yourself through the game.
- Short loading screens between rooms.

This is a short, boring game.
The trailer looked great. The gameplay trailer looked fun! Sadly Bear With Me turned out to be a boring pixel hunter. To make matters worse it’s really, really, short. Painfully short considering it’s price. $4.99 of point and click fun should feel like an experience, not a paid half demo.
A half demo really?
Yep, Bear With Me feels like the first half of a Kickstarter Demo for a game that could be. I get the feeling that this was supposed to be a free intro chapter and maybe devs decided at the last minute to charge for it. Long story short, nothing of interest happens in this first episode.
Nothing.
You meet some of the main characters, hear some plot, find some hidden objects and make it to the attic and then BAM its over and you watching the credits in disbelief.  How this game is getting so many good reviews on Steam is totally beyond me. I found myself stuck for a long while trying to open something with no clear direction at all. When I finally gave up and tried every random thing in my inventory to open it, a small nail did the job. It was such a stupid answer the game called itself out for lazy writing.
Really?
While the voice acting was alright, I found myself getting more and more annoyed at hearing the same lines over and over again. Especially Milly’s annoyance with me for not knowing what to do next. This leads to a huge problem with Bear With Me, no story/progress journal. If you take a break from this game and forget it’s forgettable tale and come back to it you are kinda screwed if you were in the middle of looking for something. You have no way to keep track of what your objectives are and what you accomplished. I cannot believe this is missing.
Sigh.
I want to love Bear With Me. Heck, I’d be OK with liking it and having honest hope for it. But the truth is Bear With Me feels like a short wasted opportunity. That said this is just the first chapter. Granted it’s a pitifully small chapter, but maybe, just maybe, it might get better from here. Then comes two important questions:
Is this game worth your time and five dollars?
I hate to sound like a jerk, but no. I was annoyed through most of it thanks to the unclear gathering puzzles and lack of objective tracking system. The promise of a good, engrossing introduction to this world story kept me on the hook, but ultimately let me down. That being said, I cannot recommend this game to you. I played through it twice while making different choices hoping for a better experience, but I didn’t get one.
Will I buy the next episode?
Kinda doubtful. Maybe, just maybe if I am lucky enough to be flush with money I might. But really for what I got out of this initial experience it doesn’t seem worth it. Also since most of the Steam reviews for this game are totally glowing, I get the feeling that it will end up as more of the disappointing same.
I hate writing bad reviews for games I wanna love, but what you just read is it. I’ll follow this game on Steam and hope for updates that make me hopeful for the sequel. Lets see what happens.

The game suffers from both porting issues and age, but otherwise is a good entry in the Rockstar sandbox series.
Though I was a huge fan of GTA3 and Vice CIty, I never played Bully when it came out.  I picked it up a few years ago during a Steam Sale and finally got around to playing it.
First up - technically, the game has not aged well.  Trying to play it at 1080 resulted in an immediate crash.  The highest I could run it was 1440.  Even then,
There wasn't anything I could do to repeat the issues...I'd play a mission, it would crash, and when I'd go back and do the exact same things it would be fine.  Secondary to this is mapping controls.  The game allows some basic remapping, but it will handle conflicts by automatically reassigning other controls to other keys.  I ran into a particularly irritating issue where I tried to remap Mouse 4 to jump, but the act of slightly moving the mouse as I positioned my hand on it made it so jump got reassigned to moving the mouse backwards.  This happened with several other keys, and because it was reassigning other keys as I would remap an unrelated one, it took far too long to get something playable (but far from optimal).  At one point, Select got remapped to moving the mouse to the right...that was fun.
Another big annoyance is that you can't skip time.  In Vice City or GTA3, when you saved it automatically advanced time a few hours.  In Bully, the only way to advance time is by sleeping, but you can only do that after 7pm and you wake up at 8am the next day.  Many missions are time restricted such as during school, after school, or late at night.  Classes take place at 2 set times per day, but if you don't have class you'll just need to find something else to do to pass the time.  After I passed all my classes, I'd spend a lot of minutes during the days just standing in one of my rooms waiting for a certain time so I could go do a mission.
Story-wise, the game is not as immersive as something like Vice City, and having such a small map really shows off how repetitive they were with level design elements, street chatter, and so on.  Briefly, the story is that you're on as many schools as your mom has had husbands, and as she prepares for yet another honeymoon, you're being shipped off to boarding school.  Various cliques can be found - bullies, jocks, nerds, and greasers are immediately present.  As you progress the game, you'll also have to deal with Townies who resent the stuck-up kids who go to the private school down the road.  Your character's goal is to rise to the top of the school hierarchy by taming each clique starting with the bullies.
While all of this is going on, you're also expected to attend classes, stay out of trouble from the watchful eyes of the prefects, and maybe even kiss a girl/boy or two (which regains your health up to double depending on good you are at it).  The classes are mini-games, such as multiple choice math tests, pin the flag on the map geography, and press the right button rhythm games.  Progressing through the classes will unlock abilities and other extras.   Passing Shop classes, for example, will unlock better bikes while passing Geography will improve your map to show the locations of certain collectibles.  There are also a set of errands and tasks that you'll be asked to do by random students and adults.  They can be fetch quests, escort missions, or random tasks like throw a firecracker in the toilet.
All in all, this was fun, but to complete it today you have to really want to.  The game just hasn't aged well.  I finished the game in about 25 hours with a 72% completion percentage.  My hours show higher because I accidentally left the game paused for a full day.  Getting 100% is pretty straightforward, however, the game is just too buggy to try.

Obligatory header to the review: I focus on four primary areas whenever I review a game: gameplay, story, graphics, and sound/audio/general things that go into your earholes. Gameplay and Story get a rating scale from 1 to 10, and the AV stuff gets a rating from 1 to 5. My philosophy on this is that there are some instances in which a game may not necessarily have that much in the way of gameplay (take Amnesia for example), but the story/atmosphere/whatever it may be is reason enough to pick it up. Also, take the cumulative score with a grain of salt; it's just a numerical feeling about the game as a whole. That's part of why I do these subscores. Also, keep in mind that I'm not going off of school grade based rankings. A 5/10 denotes what I feel to be an average game. Likewise, 7/10 is a game that I think is pretty cool, and something that gets a 2/10 is near-abomination level. Pinning scores to an even further obfuscated rating scale is kinda senseless, but for the sake of my backloggery, I'll repeat again that 1.0-2.7 is a one-star game, 3.0-4.7 is a two-star game, 5.0-6.7, 7.0-8.7, and 9.0-10 are three, four, and five stars, respectively.
Gameplay: 1001 Spikes is about as simple as it gets from a gameplay perspective. There are levels. You must jump through them and not die. One of the things that I'm glad they did from a control perspective is have two different buttons for different jump heights. Variable jump heights from holding the jump button always proved to be one of the biggest issues back when I was dumb and played SMW romhacks. Lives are infinite in some perspective, since you're given 1,001 of them to beat the game with (you also get more lives from the x-6 stages). I never came close to losing all my lives, since the lowest I ever dropped was to ~830, but I do know that you can get more lives from the shop.
Levels in this game are a mix of very well-thought out and well executed platforming challenges and spikes that sometimes come out of the ground because they feel like it. Or blocks dropping on your head because they feel like it. Or arrow traps... okay, you get the point. Needless to say, not everything in this game is the most fair. In fact, there's more than a few moments in the game that you'll be thinking you've started playing an I Wanna Be the [Noun] game. I talked to a friend/game designer about this, and his general attitude toward it was that the levels are short enough so that it's not a big deal.
I don't really feel the same way. As a video game player, I get much more enjoyment out of struggling with and beating an excellently crafted stage than I do where blocks/spikes just show up and kill you. Ultimately, I never felt like I was getting better and better at the game. Instead, I just felt like I was memorizing trap locations. This is further enunciated by the fact that when I went back and got the Key of Serpentis, I died as many times on that level the second time through as I did the first. This may just be my personal preference, but I really do wanna feel like I've surmounted an obstacle when I'm playing a hard game.
Another thing that I found kinda annoying at times were the hitboxes. I know, I know; "nub's complaining about hitboxes." I don't think Aban's hitbox is all that bad, but there are a few instances in which I feel like hitboxes kinda screwed me over. The biggest issue with hitboxes I had was in 4-3 aka Dangerous Exit aka The Worst Level In the Game; specifically with the jumping totems. There were many times where I was certainly not underneath the totem, but the game sure thought so. Another issue I had with hitboxes were the arrows from the arrow traps, where I can be standing two blocks away from the launcher, be throwing knives and still be killed.
Even despite the sometimes downright unfair level design and sometimes very questionable hitboxes, I still had a great bit of fun with the game. While I don't have an easy opportunity right now to bring friends over to enjoy the Tower of Nanaar (which looks crazy fun for multiple people), I will definitely check that out in the future. 7/10.
Story: story plz
Actually, it'd be wrong of me not to talk about the story for this game. The core story of the game is Aban Hawkins, an archaeologist, and his journey to punch his dad in the head. Hard. Yeah, it's not Shakespeare, but what do you expect? A thing that I did  like, though, was that all of the unlockable characters get their own unique intro to the game once you beat the first world with them. While I only saw Commander Video's intro, I'm sure everyone else's cutscenes are equally as good. 7/10.
Graphics: I can tell that the goal of this game was to make it look as much like an NES/Famicom game as much as possible. That's not just because it's an 8-bit styling; anyone can do that. Rather, this game really does capture that indescribable feel of an NES game. In fact, I wouldn't be surprised if someone with considerable Assembly experience couldn't "port" this game to an NES cart. Regarding the technical aspects, it runs windowed by default at 720p, but it fullscreens to your native resolution without any issues. My biggest problem with the graphical side of things (and this ties into gameplay as well) is that there isn't a cohesive pattern of signaling for hazards. Blocks that look exactly the same can be two different traps entirely. I really feel like a lot of my issues with the game could've been fixed if they had just used some universal signaling throughout the game. Even though this is gameplay related, it's still worth talking about in the graphics section. 3/5.
Sound: Well, the sounds are blips and the music is chippy. You don't need high-end equipment to make this stuff. The music is pretty good, and every world in "the first half" of the game has their own unique song, which is usually pretty good. I just wish "the second half" (yes, I'm being ambiguous) had world-specific music. It got REAL tiresome hearing the same song for 32 levels. Other than that, the music is enjoyable. I don't think I'd grab the OST, since I heard bloody enough of it during the game, but you may enjoy it more. 3/5.
Overall scores are 7/7/3/3; cumulative score of 6.7/10. Unfortuately, a lot of the high points I had with this game were neutralized by the low points. I still did have fun, though; it's just after coming from a game like Volgarr, the sometimes (seemingly intentional) questionable level design left a bit of a sour taste in my mouth.
1001 Spikes is the first time you work out after a lifetime of laziness

It's one of those games. You know the sort. Spikes pop up out of the ground and then spike shooters nail you when you jump over them and then you have to ride a moving platform that slides just enough that you can't counter the spike shooters with your own projectiles and then there's a big long segment of precise jumps where you have to jump JUST as the moving platforms disappear. But the level is really short so you just keep doing it over and over and over and over again until you get it all just right and then you're rewarded with another harder and yet still tedious level to attempt over and over and over and over until you beat it and shrug or are overcome by ennui and find something more rewarding to do with your time.
It's a competent if unimpressive example of the genre, the sort that looks like an NES game but plays like absolutely none of them. Ditching Meat Boy's awful sliding physics, Aban has a two button jump that sounds weird but is just marvelous in execution, the high jump especially is noteworthy. While it does clear two blocks of height, it has all the natural arc of a graceful plumber soaring through the air rather than the sprongy up and down of some dismal C64 era protagonist. Mega Man wishes he handled this well. The music and graphics do the job without irritating (Unless you like 30 second loops, I recommend you avoid trying to pay extra for the soundtrack. Sample it first, at least.).
Anyone who suggests that it transcends the genre is full of poppycock and balderdash. It's bog standard from top to bottom. You could do worse if you must have more, but I know you, reader; you're only here because you probably already have Meat Boy and likely six others in the genre. Have you truly beaten Meat Boy? Cleared every good Castlevania and Mega Man? Perhaps La Mulana if that's your thing. I'm fairly certain you have not beaten that one. If you like the repetition, I tend to find going for the 1cc in the shmups on Steam to be generally more rewarding... I mean, really, there's nothing here you have not seen before.
But if it sounds like I am full of it and this is still exactly what you want in a game, then, by all means. It is definitely competent in execution by any standard, nailing the design and feel and there's a a decent bit of variety and a gradual difficulty curve. If you played Spelunky or Rogue Legacy before this, you'll have a whole new appreciation for REAL levels, DESIGNED levels (And then quickly a new hatred for them.) when you take Aban for a swing.
But I must still attempt to warn you off into more satisfying endeavors.
EDIT: By the way, that o in endeavors at the end? It was a spike trap. Sorry. You'll have to read the review again and take care to avoid that next time.
EDIT Part Deux: I must return to mention this when I think of Aban's adventure. It's not entirely unexpected in the genre but the game does offer quite a few paths to facilitate speedrunning (Which, really, as a hobby is really a close cousin to  this ghastly genre.). Some of them are goofy secret paths to bypass a few traps here and there (Oh what a game where the reward for clever play is to play less of the game. Seems an apt enough reward.) but a few do turn out to be clever synergies in the game's various timing mechanics where, with rhythm toned to the beat, you can zoom through a segment you might have paused and considered carefully before. Discovering those tended to be far more rewarding to me than actually completing the levels I found them in.
Do you know how hard it is to make such a challenging game not only frustration-free but also highly-addictive? I assume it's hard. I laugh every time I die.

As someone who LOVED MechWarrior 3 and 4 and played the hell out of these games, I first was not confident, that a F2P-MP-game might be the right for me. I was afraid of P2W, OP mechs not properly balanced by the devs and all that stuff.
After a friend convienced me to give it a try, I got addicted. This is the "shooter" I was looking for. Not that focused on reflexes and fast pace movement like CS:GO or similar FPS, but more tactical approach with steady aim and a deep thought in positioning to maximize your damage outpot while staying alive.
And the theorycrafting, oh good, I've never thought that you could talk 3 hours about the best loadout for a certain chassis of a mech. But you can. And I friggin' love exactly this kind of depth this game delivers.
Patches are rolled out on a monthly basis. The devs, well, TRY at least to be as much community driven as they can, the playerbase, although you find your foul apple every now and then, is mostly calm and mannered, which is absolutely rare for a F2P-title.
But, you have to be that honest, there IS a small, but really really small, Pay-2-Win-factor in this game. There are some mechs that you can only buy with real money that have a specialised loadout and weaponry that may seem OP in certain situations. But a mech is still only as good as the pilot and when you suck at piloting, the best mech falls in a few seconds because he doesn't know how to torso twist or how positioning functions.
As a BattleTech-fanboi, I rate this game a solid 9/10. The one point missing is for maps like Viridian Bog. ♥♥♥♥ Viridian Bog. Oh, and ♥♥♥♥ LRM-Boats on Polar Highlands, too. That♥♥♥♥♥♥s awfull.

Survive in Space is a space shooter that blends Defender's left and right controls with Asteroid's single screen presence. I like Survive in Space, but its still tough to recommend, because the entire game is a grind. The 50 levels that the game boasts are all the same. Each level consists of three waves of enemies, each enemy gives experience that you use to buy upgrades. Even with upgrades, I never feel like I'm making little progress, because each level feels the same.
Like all shooters, you have your basic machine gun, but to make things interesting, there is a fat laser that lasts a few seconds and homing missiles. There seems to be a color coated mechanic where when you're red, the four orbs get tucked close to your ship while when you're red they're far away. Once your a super weapon get used, you need to wait for them to recharge. Since enemies spawn left and right on a single screen, the game has mercy on you and lets you face left or right ala Defender. Because you push a button, that means you can fly right while facing left and vice versa.
You have a versatile set of controls and the game does a good job of explaining them. You can use mouse, keyboard or a controller, but some of the menus seem to need a mouse.
The enemies feel like a good variety and they feel different than other games of the same caliber. The problem is that you see them all on each level, making each level feel the same. To the game's credit, every new level includes a new enemy, but they're always hard to spot when mixed in with the same foes that you've seen for hours. Your foes come at you from all different angles, so you need to stay in front of them and destroy them before they can come at you from awkward positions.
To break up the monotony of what it is, there are boss fights every 10 or so levels. Each boss has several bullet patterns as you fight them one-on-one. These feel like a good diversion among a sea of the same. Its odd that I can enjoy a classic arcade game to no end, but when I feel like I'm locked into a 50 level campaign, it begins to feel like a chore. Perhaps if I took it lighter and not as a goal and just played the game over the span of years I'd feel better about it.
The upgrades come in tiers. You first make a few minor upgrades to each weapon and then make a few major upgrades before the next tier unlocks. The upgrades include shorter recharge, more experience, more damage, vampire health from enemies, the chance to kill an enemy with one shot or do critical damage. Everything makes the game a fraction easier, but its never enough to notice a difference. One of the double-edged swords is the upgrade to split beams. In theory that sounds great, but in practice you shoot in a V which means you need to maneuver around differently when enemies are coming toward you.
On the plus side, you can upgrade your vessel too to do more damage, have better shields, more armor and so on. Since this is a game about killing things, I recommend just pour everything into attack power. The quicker your foes die, the safer you are.
Some of your own attacks are questionable. The strong straight laser feels powerful, but the homing missiles are slow and detonate if you destroy the vessel they were aiming at. So by the time they get to their target, its dead, making the missiles almost useless. Good thing there is an achievement for using them. One thing that the game has going for it are the easy achievements that a low percentage of people have.
Perhaps the most aggravating part of Survive in Space are the cheap deaths that come in two forms. The first are the invisible ships that decloak. You can see them and they move in a slow, straight path, but when it gets chaotic they can decloak in on you. The other cheap death is something similar where a vessel will make a portal. The portal starts small so you can see it... unless you sit and shoot, then the portal opens wide and throws out a vessel. These two cheap deaths are the only time I ever die.
To the game's credit, you can make your own challenge for each level. Its more then difficulty, there are three check boxes for more enemies, fortresses that fly by and shoot at you and asteroids. Yes asteroids fly at you, which makes me feel the Asteroids vibe even more. I have gotten to the point where I am unstoppable so I add asteroids and fortresses. You get extra experience for the extra challenge. More enemies seems to spawn a little too much to handle and when this is a grind, you need to play it safe.
I have avoided perhaps the worst thing about the game and that is the art. In the game, the art is fine, but there are several cut scenes with art that just feels out of place. I am sure someone worked hard on the art, but it cheapens the look of the game. In the end, I'm just there for the arcade experience, so I skip the cut scenes.
Another downside to the game is with your ability to chose between red and blue on the fly means you shoot the same color of bullets. However, enemies fire their own color coated bullets, so if you're red and red bullets are being fired at you, then they just blend in with your own. Now that I've said it, you do have plenty of health and shields to compensate.
If you need a reason to stay in the game longer, there are other vessels to play. That might keep your interest, but after the sheer investment of time into one vessel, its best to just stick with what you know.
In the end, I'm still on the fence if I can recommend it. Its enjoyable, but a chore. Its fun, but there's just too much of not enough. There are other similar games out there, that feel better to play or have more charm or a better look. Survive in Space is still a fun time waster, but I'd like more diversity when I'm playing the same level over and over again with a new hat. For the right price its well worth the risk to see if you enjoy it.

Bear With Me is a new episodic, point-and-click adventure game developed by Exordium Games. It follows the story of 10-year old Amber Ashfield, as she attempts to find her missing brother Flint who has seemingly disappeared. Or has he been kidnapped? It's not completely ceratin, but with a case this complicated, she must enlist the help of the veteran, supposedly retired private detective Ted E. Bear (her...um...teddy bear).
The first episode proved a highly promising start to this new series. Filled with self-aware humour and plentiful fourth wall breaking, it has a very humourous and not-at-all serious tone to the narrative. Somtimes self-aware comedy can be over-bearing and obnoxious, but the writers use it sparingly - it only surfaces in relevant situations. The film-noir style was also a very fitting touch, reminisant of The Maltese Falcon or Chinatown, with the flawed (often drunkard) private detective near retirement, pulled back into work for one last case that proves the trickiest yet. Oh, and Amber's the femme fatale. Maybe in a future episode they could get in a Blade Runner reference? Gameplay is the usual point-and-click style; moving around the environment, picking up clues and objects which can be crafted to produce tools to progress through the area. It's nothing particulalry innovative, but the writing is so sharp, and the black-and-white 2-D environments so atmospheric, that it didn't really bother me. The original music was excellent as well in solidifying that film-noir aura.
Overall, the first episode was very fun, and the series as a whole offers a lot of promise. For the price, I'd say it's more than worth a look-in. I am definitely awaiting the future episodes to see how the mystery develops!

The basic idea of the game is that you disassemble the guns and assemble them step by step. When you have enough XP, you can unlock the next gun.
PROS:
-Very skill based. You need to memorise what parts to move.
-Leaderboards. Very competitive. You will think that you have the best times. Although some people clearly cheat, Noble Empire, get your♥♥♥♥♥♥together.
-Very engaging mechanics. It's very satisfying to see all those animations.
-Really easy to understand how to play.
-If you are the plenty of time kinda player AND a gun enthusiast, this is the game for you.
-As you get better at the game, you unlock achievements faster and faster, thus getting more XP and more guns.
CONS:
-Slow start in terms of XP. The game requires you to be good quite early.
-Poor variety of music.
-Inconsistent order of disassembly/assembly. You would think you can take that part out. Unfortunately, the game requires you to follow a specific order.
-Inconsistent duration of the animations. Ruined many "speedruns".
-Very small parts are hard to spot or don't come with the bigger parts.
-Hidden guns are much more expensive unless they show up in the unlock tree.
-Not recommended for casual players who just want to play and relax and not have to bother with the XP. But that's the life of free to play.
When I started playing this game, I only had one weapon available which is the AK-47. Honestly I think they should introduce simpler weapons first, and maybe sort the weapons by type: handgun, assault rifle, smg... Oh well.
I was immediately compelled by the mechanics of the game, the animations, the sounds, and the neat organisation of the parts in the 3D environment. I wanted to play more, I wanted to get better at the game. It's very easy to learn how to play.
Then it told me that it has some modes of playing, Field Strip, Disassembling, Operation Assembling, Game, Super Game and Hardcore. Each mode is more difficult than the previous except for paint and operation. The hardcore mode requires you to know exactly what to do.
Operation mode is quite fun. You can attach different stuff like suppressors, laser sight, bayonettas, etc. You can slow down the time and see how the weapon works when fired. It doesn't require you to disassemble the gun or anything.
After I got good at the gun, I got enough XP points and unlocked my second gun. The pacing of the game in terms of unlocking is really well done, because you can get a weapon, and you can complete a lot of achievements for each weapon. I still haven't finished some weapons and I already have 2 guns in reserve to play. You could get a lot of XP really quickly if you dedicate your time to it. If you don't well, well then I don't recommend the game for people like you. You can also login to the game daily and amass more XP.
I actually managed to get the complete set for 2 weapons. Very satisfying, would do it again.
Yes, you can't choose any weapon you want to disassemble, without paying time or money. Yes, if the gun isn't showing up in the main screen, it's a lot more expensive on the store.
But, all in all, still would recommend the game. Just because it's free to play.

EDIT 1 ( MAIN PART OF THE REVIEW BELOW ):

Since people actually somehow managed to find this review, I decided to put at least a little bit of an actual review in here. Not a detailed one because I haven't played the game for a long time, but my personal information about the game.
(SIDENOTE: If you want a review that follows a linear flow of explaining information, this isn't the one. I mainly jump around from topic to topic, mostly because this came from the top of my head.)
( Sorry random OCD guy.)
Tribes:Ascend is a great game, but sadly, a lot of players are missing from the game because developers have moved onto SMITE and they abandoned this game a while ago.
They have made some changes to the game though, that has varied since the release of Tribes:Ascend. One thing they did was cut back on the amount of grinding required, which was really nice for F2P players. The game certainly isn't pay-to-win, but it is deterring to see that a playstyle you want isn't available for you. Most of the default stuff are mostly usable, but I do have to point out that the other weapons are just more fun to use. ( And sometimes more effective. )
The gameplay features high-speed combat, which will be very rewarding to those who value skill.
Coordinated roles and classes give the game a nice feel for it's objective based gameplay, and offers multiple different playstyles. Supportive roles, defensive roles, and offensive roles are ALL viable, and they all help you win the game. There's also a in-game voice communication system that slightly helps with immersion ( if you're into that sort of thing. )
There's also a few game modes ( many of which are probably dead. ).
My personal favorite is Capture the Flag, because it requires a variety of roles by the team.
Maybe you want to be the guy who grabs the flag at high speed.
Maybe you want to be the guy who sits on the flag and laughs at the guy who just died because he rammed into you at high speed.
Or maybe, you want to be like a sneaky ninja and blow stuff up. ( People included. )
The amount of skill required in this game is more than any normal FPS. You can't just aim down the sights of your gun and kill a guy in 1 second. You need to actually try to kill him, because 95% of the weapon in this game are not hitscan, which means you WILL have to shoot ahead of a moving target and if you want your projectile to even land CLOSE to him.
Experienced players will 'blue plate' someone. ( Blue plate is when you hit a poor guy directly with a spinfusor. )
Newer players may find it easier to use rapid-firing weapons until they're ready to try out the Spinfusor.
New players will also learn the term 'Shazbot!' ( Which will not be explained here. )
There is progression in this game, but they unlock different playstyles and weapons, rather than directly upgrading your weapons. ( Not counting some of the other things you can upgrade, but let's forget about those for now. )
You don't unlock a grip for your gun to reduce 15% penalty to accuracy, you don't get a scope and whatever, you'll actually want to unlock other classes and weapons. One of the classes has access to a fractal grenade ( the disco grenade ) and another class has invisibility. I'm not going to list every single class, but you get the point.
Weapons play a large part of Tribes as well as the classes. While a technician can put down a turret, some guy on a hill can make it rain explosives on him and clear the objective for a friendly to move in.
Sadly, you won't be able to unlock TotalBiscuit's voice unless you pay real money.
Yes. His voice is in the game.
You can also buy skins and stuff so you look different. Not like you'd show it off to anyone anyways.
You can also get credits or whatever to buy resupply points and call in orbital strikes.
Credits are only for the duration of the match, so feel free to call in the thunder.
As for performance, I've always had a problem on low-end PCs, so this isn't really the game you want to be playing on a low budget, but you shouldn't really have any performance problems if you have a medium to high end rig. There's a few performance.ini's on the internet somewhere if you really wanna play this on a potato. Trust me, I tried, and I at least went fast enough to kill something.
If you've read the original portion of the review, I joke about how no one plays this ( because no one does ) but that doesn't mean I don't want anyone to play it.
If you have slogged through this thing that steam calls a review, give Tribes a try. If you like it, tell your friends. Maybe it'll actually have some people playing it. ( Yeah right. )

A clever, creative, and (mostly) successful spin on the 4x genre, Endless Space does a few things differently than we've come to expect.
The thing to understand about this game before getting into it is that it's very macro-oriented. This means that they can afford to streamline and abstract away things, especially in the economy and combat spheres.
The thing is, a lot of people play 4x games for those gritty details. It worked for me, it might not for you. There are only four resources in the game, and the combat is pre-determined and largely static. It's still fun to play, but it's misleading.
Visual design and UI design are excellent. The game is rarely confusing and always looks good, which is uncommon for 4x.
The soundtrack fits the tone of the game perfectly.
The setting and lore are really detailed, but not enough of that makes it through to the game. Factions and setting are very original, though. A lot of background details never really made in, which is a shame. If you like lore hunting, check out the forums.
Though I will say the lore that is in the game is excellent. ES probably has the most interesting tech tree since Alpha Centauri.
AI is generally clever, if a bit static and lifeless. Again, this applies to a lot of the game.
A great game to spend hours and hours on. Endless Legend is better though.

This game is so beautiful it was probably made by Horatio.
Not just fancy graphics, but it's... simply beautiful the first moment you open the main menu. In fact, I was just expecting a Master of Orion sequel-ish with good looking graphics, but the menu screen, the art, the minimalist but beautiful and ergonomic UI and font, the way every screen transitions so smoothly and most of all the music, overwhelmed me with its beauty, and I was like, "wait a minute, this is too beautiful, not what I was expecting at all".
The gameplay can kind of grind on you a bit, the diplomacy screens could be more personal like in Endless Legend and the level of ship customization leaves much to be desired. I have nothing against the simple combat mechanics, because I enjoy it as a cinematic experience. However, it gets repetitive to look at anyhow, which is a shame, maybe if they could have more customizable (as in, colors and attachments whatnot) ships, and more detailed weaponry (the bullets just directly come out of the ships). The rest of the gameplay is pretty solid, and you could even make your own races if you so desire.
However, the biggest flaw of this game is its almost-complete lack of personality, which is a massive shame because they've already made a rather expansive backstory regarding the United Empire and (especially) the Endless, but didn't really implement any of that in-game, as Endless Legend did with its quest system.
All in all, if you want a game this beautiful, I would probably recommend Endless Legend more than this, but it's a go if you're looking for an Orion-like 4X

If you've played
, then this game is going to feel very familiar. When I started playing
, I didn't realize that both games were by the same developer, nor that they were released a few months apart from one another. I can definitely say one thing though, this game is a huge improvement over its predecessor.
The basic goal of the game is to survive several waves of alien attacks. A variety of ships, all with their own patterns and weapons, will assault the player from both sides of the screen. Your survival depends on balancing the ship's offensive and defensive capabilities. Playing defensively involves the use of rotating shields, which protects against enemy fire, and possibly collisions. However, you'll soon discover that the ship is underpowered against the constantly encroaching adversaries.
So that's when you have to trigger... the Edge. This is the aggressive mode, which causes the shields to expand outward, your HP to drop by about 40%, and your damage to substantially increase. In this mode, you definitely have to rely on your dodging skills to survive, but at least you'll have less trouble destroying foes. Alongside these modes, the player has access to a main cannon, as well as two secondary weapons. Both the laser and homing bullets operate on cool-down timers, so it helps to save them for truly necessary situations.
As with
you can level-up your ship. Aside from increasing its offensive and defensive capabilities, you can also unlock new abilities for the ship, and add new functionality to its weapons. Above all else, I recommend grabbing the upgrades that increase the range of your attacks. By the end of the game, you'll have a huge spread-shot, a laser that covers both sides of the screen, and a large mass of homing bullets.
The level of challenge is thoroughly customizable. Aside from difficulty settings that increase the enemy's attack and defense, there are also modifiers. The enemy waves can be bolstered with more troops, and assisted by Death Stars. Also, if you didn't get enough from the last game, you can also toggle the option to be assaulted by asteroids. Boosting the difficulty and adding modifiers will increase the experience rewards, so it's a fair trade-off. However, don't be surprised if you can't survive with everything turned on... at least before you upgrade your ship.
As far as complaints go, I have some nitpicks. A number of achievements are tied to the difficulty level, but let's say that you complete all of the stages on "medium". Normally this means that you'd also get the achievement for doing the same on "easy". Unfortunately, it doesn't work like that. Every stage has to be beaten on their respective difficulty in order to obtain all of the achievements. This can make large stretches of the game really dull. Naturally, this is all entirely irrelevant if you don't care about achievements. Still, this minor issue does tie into the larger problem with this game. Even with all of the modifiers and the difficulty maxed out, the game becomes a little too easy.
For the next game, I think that it's important for the controls to be refined even further. While the player-ship controls decently with the analog stick, it isn't nearly as accurate with a d-pad, which is really odd. Without improving the controls, I don't think the challenge of these games can be taken to the next level. It would be interesting to see this style of game-design, but with bullet-speeds and patterns typical of the arcade shootemup. You know, something like
.
In conclusion, if you were a fan of
, then you're guaranteed to love
. By all accounts, this is a superior sequel. If you weren't a fan of the previous game, there still might be something for you here. Still, I'm a little surprised that the devs can hammer these games out so quickly.

is a 2D space shooter, based around Sasaki, who lives in a galaxy that has been taken over by an evil people known as "The Chronicles." Sasaki discovers the truth about The Chronicles and the history of his people, and must fight to earn redemption.
In game, the graphics are great, and all the art compliments each other perfectly, making this game a feast for the eyes. Outside of the gameplay, however, the graphics seem to be lacking.
The main menu's art is quite nice, with an animated picture of Sasaki on a seemingly deserted planet. The graphical design of the actual menu part, however, leaves much to be desired. While when the player hovers over an option, the menu fits with the aesthetic of the game, when the player is not hovering over the menu options, they are just gray boxes with a font closely akin to Arial. This font is used throughout the game, and it really draws away from the rest of the game's aesthetic.
The art style in the cutscenes is extremely unpolished compared with the rest of the game, even to the point of looking unfinished at times. The voice acting in these cutscenes is very much a mixed bag. The narrator and the "servant of darkness" are both voiced extremely well, but the main character, Sasaki, is not. The voice actor sounds like he is reading a story to a kindergarten class, and manages to do it with no emotion. Any emotion given to Sasaki's character through the voice acting seems very forced.
The music, while it sounds great, does not really fit in with the atmosphere of the game at points. The player can also add their own music, as long as it is in .wav or .ogg format.
The user interface is generally very easy to use. The only major problem with it is that to access the upgrade and ship select screen, the player has to leave the level select screen to go to the main menu, where they must select the "Upgrades" option. A casual player who has never played this game before might totally miss it, as it is not mentioned in any tutorial, and try and get through some of the harder levels without any upgrades, or without realizing there were other ships in the game.
The controls are quite comfortable and make sense. On a keyboard, the game uses the MOBA system for attacks, using Q, W, E, and R for attacks, while on a controller it uses the regular buttons.
The game follows Sasaki as he fights The Chronicles. He has the truth about The Chronicles revealed to him by an ancient writing of some sort, and is then seduced by a "servant of darkness," who is also seeking vengeance against The Chronicles.
The script is poorly written, with Sasaki's emotions or thoughts only ever being revealed through him saying directly what they are. It does not flow well, with the characters often speaking in short or fragmented sentences, and going out of the way to make sure that the audience does not have to infer anything.
The game tries to be a sort of bullet hell space shooter, but fails in that it is too slow paced. This becomes apparent at the very beginning, when the first enemy to spawn takes eight hits with the base weapon to kill. This does not change as the player levels up - at level one, that enemy takes eight hits, at level five it takes the same.
Ther is a large variety of ships for the player to chose from, each having its own advantages and disadvantages. The only problem with this is that there is no indication of this capability from the level select screen or the main menu. To change ships, the player has to go to the main menu and select "Upgrades," then go to the "Shipyard" tab.
The player is given three weapons - the basic weapon, a laser, and homing missiles. The basic weapon is able to be fired every tenth of a second or so, and the other weapons take a few seconds to recharge, which can be upgraded to be less. The basic weapon is a machine gun which does about two damage to an enemy. The laser is a solid laser beam which does more, and the homing missiles are, well, homing missiles. They do a ridiculous amount of damage, but take a while to recharge.
The player is also given a "super mode" upon pressing R, that makes the players attacks more powerful, but moves the ship's shields farther away, rendering it more vulnerable to attack.
The player's ship can only shoot in two directions: left and right. This, coupled with the fact that the ship moves quite slowly, makes defeating enemies a chore sometimes. The player's ship also cant move to the very top or very bottom of the screen, rendering enemies in certain positions unreachable.
After completing the 50 levels with the game, the player can continue leveling up indefinitely, playing through those 50 levels again and again, eventually becoming ridiculously overpowered.
, while promising, is plagued with a myriad of problems, chief among those being the slow pace and a lack of general polish.

DISCLAIMER: I received this product for no cost for the purpose of reviewing. However, this does not affect my views and opinions of the game.
The team at Just1337 must really love space and space themed games, as this is there 4th space game on Steam. Survive in Space is a 2D Space Shooter. The story is kind of interesting so I won't spoil it, but throughout the stages of of this game, you pilot a space fighter. You can choose between 5 initially, though I'm not sure if more unlock as you continue to play. Each ship has a set passive abilities that are different from the other ships, and you can choose a ship to cater to your playing style. You can also switch what ship you want to use before each stage. You have a basic attack and 2 other skills you can use in combat, and after each stage your character receives experience as well the ship that you are using. When your ship levels up you can assign more passive abilities to it, and the same applies to your character.
The combat itself puts you in a space battlefield for each stage. You are tasked with taking down all enemy ships as they appear on your screen with your various abilities to complete the stage. You can manage the difficulty of each battle from the classic presets of "Easy, Medium & Hard" as well as choose to add more asteroids (which pose as flying obstacles) as well increasing the amount of enemies you have to defeat. Of course the more difficult you make it for yourself, the more experience your will accumulate. The game can be a bit bullet hell-y at times, and there are boss battles at certain stages.
--------
The art style might be subjective. It's a 2D western animeish design for the characters, which isn't something I tend to enjoy but I could see how a lot of people would appreciate it. The back drop for the battles is decent, though I feel it does get a bit repetitive after awhile, although I haven't played all the stages to know if it's different later on. The animations are also decent, and the combat effects as well as the menus are designed pretty nicely. There shouldn't be any problems running the title on any graphics card or CPU as it is not a demanding title.
--------
Everyone has different tastes in music, but I feel like anyone who can enjoy EDM music; this title has a nice soundtrack for you. I personally enjoy the music in this game, it reminds me a lot of their other title Neon Space, which I believe some of the music is also from. I noticed in the music interface that they have various types of EDM styles like: Drumbass, Dubstep, Electronic and House music, and as someone who enjoys this type of music, I would rate it pretty highly. There is also options to skip to the next track as well as shuffle and repeat features. The in-game and combat sound effects are also decent and surprisingly didn't feel repetitive. There is also some voice acting within the game which is also very subjective.
--------
For a title like this, the mechanics are pretty solid. You have your basic attack, and your 2 other skills. You more around with either a controller, your arrow keys, or your mouse, and shoot down enemies on your screen while avoiding their fire. Unlike some shooters, you also have the option of flipping your ship and shooting in the opposite direction. I do find it a tad frustrating not being able to shoot up and down at times, though I feel the controls might be too messy if something like that was implemented. You can switch between two different modes while playing, attack mode and defense mode, which both offer benefits and disadvantages. The enemy variety is pretty good, there's quite a few different looking enemy ships with different abilities. You can upgrade your ship as well as your character with experience at the end of each battle as well as toggle the difficulty level.
--------
I think Survive in Space is a good title for beginners who want to get into 2D shooters. It's not as intense as some bullet hells but it can give you some rush and satisfaction when you're able to take down all the enemies. The art style isn't  something I personally enjoy but I do like the soundtrack and how you can upgrade your ships as well as your character. The story seems interesting but also kind of cliché, but I see it hooking a lot of people. In my experience with playing the game, I preferred to stay in attack mode rather than defense mode. It's a bit riskier when you take a hit because you take more damage in addition to having your health points already lowered, but you deal a lot more damage, and it's easier to take out enemies.
Thanks to the Devs for giving me the opportunity to review the game, as well as anyone who took this review into consideration, I hope it helped.

AdVenture Capitalist is a clicker/idle game which is in some ways an improvement over the rest of the genre - it has a decent interface (though strangely, lacks such things as money per second), and you never are incentivized to click after the start of the game - the game is really designed around hiring "managers" to run your "investments" for you, making it into more of a pure idle game.
As with all idle games, the real "strategy" of the game is figuring out the optimal upgrade path/optimal time to reset your progress and start over again with more ability to earn money.
Like most of these games, AdVenture Capitalist eventually runs the player into a brick wall a ways into the experience, beyond which it becomes increasingly tedious to progress. The first of these walls is early, before you get your first angels; the second comes a while afterwards, when you should be going expontential, but the math of the game forces you to restart many, many times without much of a sense of progress.
This really saps a lot of the joy out of the game; knowing that you're going to have to grind away at this for a long time, doing the same thing, really eliminates a lot of the interest. Its clean interface doesn't really resolve some of the deeper issues, and while it doesn't waste your mouse or fingers on clicking, it does, ultimately, waste the player's time without any real sense of payoff.

Technology is a double-edged sword. While it provides us with many benefits, in a way it also causes mankind to become divided. Deus Ex: Human Revolution is a game which questions mature themes such at this, and delivers an amazing story complemented by satisfying and fun gameplay, providing players with choices that determine the how the game plays out, giving us control over the game world that other game rarely provide. Let me go into detail below.
As hinted a while ago, Deus Ex: Human Revolution is set in the future, 2027 to be exact. In this age, technology has advanced to the stage where humans can implement technology into their own bodies, to change and supposedly "improve" one's capabilities. These are called augmentations, and usually replace parts of our body. The discovery and invention of augmentations by celebrated scientist Hugh Darrow has caused much conflict among mankind: some think that augmentations are very useful for humans, as augmentations such as retinal augs and neural augmentations can make life very convenient for us; others, however, think that augmentations take away our humanity, and binding of flesh and metal is against our very own human nature. In the game, you play as Adam Jensen, an ex-Swat with a troubled past, who gets hired by Sarif Industries, one of the leading developers of augmentations, as a security guard. However, a mysterious group of augmented mercenaries attack Sarif Industries headquarters, killing many scientists and badly injuring Jensen. Against his will, Jensen is subjected to extensive augmentation to rebuild his body, giving him new and powerful abilities, but causing him a certain extent of mental scarring. Back on his feet with the new augmentations, he is tasked with investigating the attack and finding the people behind it, eventually uncovering a conspiracy that is not only against Sarif Industries, but the whole world. The game has a very strong premise, and it takes many twists and turns which I cannot divulge here, as it would ruin the experience. The best way to experience the story is if you have almost no clue about the plot, since the surprises had a much bigger impact on me that way. The story is able to surprise the player many times, and it is able to explore themes such as whether progress is truly for the greater good. Characters and dialogue are all very well-done and thought-out, and the game contains many memorable characters that each have motives that are neither black or white.
A big part of this game is choice: you have a choice on many aspects of the game, which all influence the outcomes of situations and the ending of the game, as well as the attitude NPCs in the game will have towards you. Your playstyle is one of the major choices you have to make; the game supports both loud and stealthy playstyles, and you can also incorporate a bit of both, like I did for most playthroughs. The stealth in this game is pretty basic, and you cannot lure enemies with noise or anything like a lot of stealth game; as long as you stay out of enemies’ line of sight, and stay away from cameras and sentry guns, you can remain undetected. For a loud playstyle, the game becomes pretty much Call of Duty and every other first person action shooter ever. The game, however, seems to encourage stealthy approaches more, as seen from NPC reactions and overall outcomes, as well as giving more XP for stealthy approaches. Despite this slight bias, I think that the game is very open and allows the player a lot of freedom. Through a few playthroughs of different scenarios, I found that many missions can have lots of different approaches, and countless different outcomes depending on how you play.
And that brings me to the skill tree in this game, known in-game as augmentations. XP is earned by doing actions such as discovering secret areas, performing takedowns, killing enemies, completing quests and being able to persuade someone in a conversation. Once you have enough XP, you are rewarded with Praxis points (which are basically just skill points), which you can use to buy augmentations. These skills are all generally useful and fun to use, but many are evidently meant to be used in certain playstyles. For example, the hacking skills are best used in stealth playthroughs, since by hacking, you can deactivate cameras and sentry guns, and also gain access codes or even gain entry to alternate paths. Alternatively, armor strengthening skills are more ideal for loud playthroughs, as they allow you to hold on longer in firefights. Since you have limited points, you must choose wisely, and forces players to use critical thinking and tactics during gameplay. I like this type of style, since you won't be blindly blundering into an area and firing at everything, but instead thinking about approaches and planning strategies. Because it is impossible to just enter a room and kill everything. Like I said, the game seems to support stealth more, as enemies can have a ton of health and even at medium difficulty, Jensen may only be able to survive a couple of shots. The game forces you to think, which is a good point in my opinion. However, while for the most part, the game seems to be stealth-oriented, you are forced into combat in several unnecessary boss fights. Boss fights are really one of the biggest negative points of this game, as they are unavoidable. Sure, the Director's cut allows you to use stealth to an extent during the bosses, but you are ultimately forced into direct combat with these bosses, who are all underdeveloped and just cartoonish, with only Namir seeming to have some sort of backstory.
Choices also extend to dialogue choices. In the game, you will interact with several NPCs, who will have information you need or are in a situation you must defuse. Such examples include an NPCs holding a hostage, an NPC threatening to commit suicide and so on. In these situations, your choices will affect the fates to the NPCs, and requires quick thinking and intuition to succeed. Augmentations can also be used to ease this process. Overall, it is a great mechanic in the game and it is interesting to see the various incomes of different attitudes towards them.
The game, while having beautiful architecture and some downright stunning backdrops, as well as atmospheric lighting, the game's graphics are hardly its strong point. Water effects and many character models look dated, and seem as though they walked straight out of a decade-old game. Adam Jensen and a few important NPC character models look amazing at certain angles, but it seems the developers focused on the quality of story and gameplay more. Luckily, the graphics don't detract much from the overall experience, and the game is optimized well enough, maintaining 100 fps or above on my rig.
The Director's Cut Edition includes the DLC, the Missing Link, which is a mandatory part of the game, and feels like a standalone section of its own, detailing a little adventure that Adam has while stowing away on a boat towards the final section. The story is alright, with several plots twists, but it ultimately suffers from a cliched villain and an overall feeling of unnecessity. Backtracking several areas, as well as mostly being forced into stealth, is among the reasons this DLC is overshadowed by the main game. Also, all of your skills and weapons are removed, which takes a lot from the enjoyment. However, it is not as bad as many people say, and is a cool little mission of its own that takes one to two hours to complete, adding a new stunning environment for Jensen to explore, although without the memorable characters of the main game.
Deus Ex: Human Revolution may not be a genre-defining game, but it takes all the great things from modern-day RPGs, combined with a great story, to deliver an amazing and engrossing game, and you owe it to yourself to try it out.

Played this game on release back on 2011, and I must say first things first, it has visually aged quite poorly for the most part, unfortunately, especially when i remember being absolutely blown away first time playing it. The director's cut version of this game provides the extended DLC called the Missing Link that was I believe to be a separate game (typical transaction bs from publishers). REMINDER: THE DLC PLAYS IN CONJUNCTION WITH THE MAIN STORY, IT IS UNMISSABLE, so don't worry about somehow skipping it.
Human Revolution is a game about politics, philosophical questions on what makes us human, and throwing vending machines at people. It is also set in the Year 2027, which from playing the game, it seems they probably shoulda pushed the years quite a bit further into the future, because we are FAR from reaching this point in technological evolution.
The game's story, characters, and development throughout is refreshing, and the atmosphere put down on the table is one of a futuristic Renaissance-esque type, floral patterns and colouring indicating a style they were going for. Quite different from the original Deus Ex's straight up cyberpunk atmosphere. The change, while making it more mono coloured, is a very unique one, giving it a very distinct feeling.
The soundtrack also deserves a special mention because it truly encapsulates the feeling of Deus Ex on a whole, providing an epic score of emotional but revolutionary sounding music, blending a mixture of the old and new.
The gameplay itself is one of great variation, and like many stealth games on the market, like Dishonored and MGS, the game provides whatever playstyle you want to go for, whether it is guns blazing, stealth approach making little noise, strongman which can jump 3 metres in the air (no I didn't make that up). The best part of this is, unlike other games, where the options are available but are gimmicky, and provide no real advantage over just doing the same thing over and over, is that EVERY playstyle is important. playing non lethal and stealth will punish you in some aspects, along with rewarding in others, so preferring to one playstyle will make it more difficult on the player in certain areas, and vice versa.
It really feels like the developers wanted to balance out the augmentions (essentially your character's skill trees) to make it feel like you werent some overpowered player, unlike certain games like Dishonored, where you become some one man army. Careful preparation and strategy is rewarded in the long run, and can also affect the game's AMAZING variation in speech in dialogue based on decisions and choices, along with your own playstyles. characters in game will react differently to your different playstyles, while one person may like your upfront "kill all" playstyle, another character may take interest in your "stealthy infiltration" playstyle. The game makes replayability a joy, just like the first game in the series.
I didn't wish to discuss the story, because while it is incredibly good and engaging overall, it is best that the player unravels it himself, and like I said, you carve your own path based on decisions, so most people's storylines will vary.
Overall, a game of incredible depth and enjoyment, a close call to its ancestor in the series, and shows what developers can do when they are creative.
Here's hoping to a successful and wonderful sequel, Deus Ex: Mankind Divided.

Deus Ex: Human Revolution is a Tactical First Person Shooter developed by Nixxes Software BV and published by Eidos Montreal. You play as Adam Jensen, a no-nonsense security manager at Sarif Industries where one of the top researchers in this biomedical company has just begun providing a major breakthrough in mechanical evolution. From this, events transpire, turning you into an apathetic stone-cold killing machine with a conscience.

It includes all the nifty add-ons from launch date such as the Silenced Sniper Rifle, the Explosives, and the Missing Link DLC (or so I'm lead to believe). You also receive a neat 45 minute developer commentary at the beginning, as well as some optimizations to make the game feel smoother.

DISCLAIMER: This review is mostly a first impression after an hour or so of playing and looking at some footage of later sections online to see if much changes, but it seems that my opinion of the start of the game would hold true for the rest of the game.
1001 Spikes is another addition in the trend of "The harder the game is the better it is!" that has captivated many players over the past couple of years. And I won't tell you that the game is hard, any other user review or critic can tell you and probably has told you that. If you just want a hard game then 1001 Spikes is totally for you and you should already know that. This user review however is for those out there who want to know the answer to the question "What is 1001 Spikes, other than hard?"
And the answer is almost nothing. Its a nostalgic hard game and seemingly nothing more. It seems to have no goal but kill you endlessly with surprise deathtraps that seem inspired by some strange and horrid idea that I Wanna Be The Guy should be viewed with anything but irony. The majority of my deaths playing this game so far have felt cheap and put there merely to make me replay the same content over and over. The game doesn't feel like a spicy challenge, but more of an unwanted chore.
Even within its niche 1001 Spikes doesn't seem that good. Super Meat Boy had better controls, felt generally fair and had a stronger art direction. La Mulana which has quite similar elements although is part of a different subgenre of nostalgic hard platformers offers a great sense of exploration and mystery. 1001 Spikes offers a lot of spikes and warningless deathes.
So to those out there who want more than just a hard game. Move on, 1001 Spikes seems to having nothing to offer you.

After buying this game on a whim after noticing it was developed by the cave story guys, I found myself fully enganged to the point of finishing the entire campaign (while collecting all the golden skulls), and unlocking nearly every character all in one sitting. I had NO IDEA I would get hooked so fast on such an impulse purchase.
At first glance, this game seems like a simple platformer with retro graphics and unrelenting difficulty. But under the surface, there is SO much more to this game.
While the game is hard, and by hard, I mean INFURIATINGLY hard, it isn't hard because of broken controls, bad mechanics, or unfair elements. It is hard, because it puts YOUR skills and YOUR reflexes to the test. The controls are extremely tight, leaving every single mistake jump, or accidental shot up to you to make. Did you just land on a spike trap and die? It was your fault. Did you just throw your knife in the wrong direction to block an arrow trap that you almost didn't notice until it shot at you? Sucks to be you.
Every level is designed with traps, spikes, enemies, and lava for you to die from, and if you don't pay attention, you will miss something important. Observation is the key to survival. If you find a spot to take a breather, (which in the later levels is VERY rare I might add) you better use it to look around and plan your next move. It almost becomes a strategy-puzzle-platformer on certain levels due to the sheer depth of the mechanics.
But even in the most hellish pit the game has to offer, (I'm looking at you 4 - 5) it never feels unfair, or like the odds are against you. You can do this, and you KNOW you can do this. and after you fail, you only get that much stronger. And there is no comparison to the satisfaction you get from finally beating that one level that gave you SO much hell. The relief from the adrenaline alone is worth it.
In a nutshell, get this game. Just do it. Learn a thing or two about completing a game with true skill, and not because the developer gave you this pretty little path with rainbows to follow, and checkpoints around every corner, making sure that every failure feels as if it didn't even matter.
