There is probably some joke or pun to be made about the 1001 spikes but I'm coming up empty. So I'll just say that it looks like the spike maker counted up the order wrong and ...
Ok I have nothing. Luckily Nicalis have something quite special in this platformer from the affectionately named "♥♥♥♥ing troll♥♥♥♥♥game" genre.
The gameplay is simple enough (with one oddity, which I will get to). You enter a level, you avoid traps and make some jumps while also shooting knives at the occasional enemy. You find the key and perhaps the hidden mask object and make your way to the exit. You then repeat this process through longer and more difficult stages until you run out of things to do. Along the way expect plenty of water, fire, snakes, scorpions, crushing blocks, spikes and even more spikey spikes. There isn't anything particularly original here if you have played similar games in the past (stretching a long way back) but what is here has been proven to work.
The controls are a little strange in that you have two jump buttons, one "high" and one "low". This saves you having to judge how hard to press a button (high enough to clear a spike, but low enough to avoid the fire above?) but it can get a bit fiddly at times. Personally I always found myself using the high jump unless a situation specifically seemed to call for it. In these cases, such as jumping on a block without triggering an arrow trap it was handy, but I'm still not sold on the concept. Still, everything works and you can aim your jumps properly and it doesn't feel floaty. If anything, jumping and shooting fails a bit more often than it should, when trying to line up a small object like an arrow (when you are standing shots line up perfectly). This isn't a big deal though, so in this regard the controls get a solid pass.
To complement the tight controls, the level design is all important in a game like this and 1001 Spikes doesn't let you down. The levels all seem lengthy but not "too long" and there is a good variety in the challenges. For example, one level will have you carefully negotiating spiked passages, waiting for just the right moment to advance forward. The next level will require you to make a series of fast paced jumps as everything falls down around you. Levels feel unique, despite reusing a lot of assets and the effort required to pass them should make them memorable long after.
That is, if you don't give up on it. The magic of "♥♥♥♥ing troll♥♥♥♥♥game" is in how much they troll you and how much of it you can take. Think you have finished the level? Well you forgot about that block, right at the end which will drop on your head without warning. This will kill you, forcing you to restart the level (no checkpoints here!) in an increasingly infuriating manner. So where does it sit on the troll meter? Above Super Meat Boy, some obstacles you just can't avoid. But it is also well below something like I want to Be The Boshy. Most traps give you a split second of warning, such as the tips of spikes showing before they impale you. Because of this, most deaths (but not all) feel like they are a result of you not paying close enough attention. The game does a good job of training you too. Chance are if you find a good place to rest while you evaluate the next section of a level? There are spikes on that block.
So you'll die, but you'll learn and progress always feels achievable (or you can skip levels, so it isn't a big drama). Note that you do technically have a life limit (x1000) but 1ups are easily farmable by redoing short stages and finding the bonus pick up. So 1001 Spikes is tough but just fair enough (think 1-5 deaths on an easy stage, 20-30 on a hard one), which will hopefully not put off too many people.
Having said that, one of the most difficult challenges the game offers is getting through the story parts without hitting "skip". They are long, stretching on forever and the text forwards far too slowly. I kind of enjoy the ironic tone to the writing, but little of importance is said and there doesn't seem to be any need for a story at all. Rest assured you can safely skip it and get back to the spikes.
To round out the package, the game offers other arcade style modes which can be played in 4 player local coop (sorry online fans). These include challenges such as climbing a high tower and competitive modes like holding an urn the longest, which remind me strongly of old NES or even C64 titles and other treats like an extra difficult tribute to a past game. Rest assured too that the coins you collect in those modes are not completely going to waste.
Now I'm not a big coop gamer (people who are will love playing through the main game with a friend), so these extras are not necessarily for me, but they do make an easy purchase decision even easier. Further the game provides a wide variety of unlockable characters, each with their own abilities (longer jumps, double jumps etc). This lets you tackles the levels again with different approaches and helps alleviate any concerns about the number of available levels (although there are enough anyway, without spoiling anything, probably a lot more than you think!).
In terms of presentation, 1001 is more functional than impressive, but everything does the job. The music is suitably excellent and the sound effects inoffensive. If anything the menu systems and cutscenes could use an extra coat of polish, but as mentioned before they are best skipped anyway, so perhaps skimping on them was the best approach after all.
I really like 1001 Spikes. I realise it will not be for everybody, given the brutal style. But it is just accessible enough that everybody should give it a go, just in case they get the right level of sadistic fun out of it.
Just keep an eye out for that 1001'th spike. That'll be the one that gets you or ... yeah still nothing.

A really hard platformer, and a homage/love letter to both old platformers and Spleunker. (As well as to the NIS platformer, Prinny, a Disgaea spin-off, due to the large amount of lives.) 1001 Spikes does a really good job at it's name, giving you a spike death for each of your 1001 lives! It has a ton of content, either local co-op or single player, and tons of stuff to unlock for fun, like extra characters.
Each level has a collectable Golden Skull to find, usually hidden, at each threshold they have some extra content for those who dare to get collect them which come in the form of extra modes or characters. When you play as one of the unlockable characters, your level progress is seperate from the main hero and each other unlockable character, and the skulls replaced with coins which you can use to unlock even more stuff with in the shop. Each almost every character plays entirely different, even the cosplay ones for the main hero have entirely different playstyles and plenty of little details to them. (The Belmont cameo cosplay removes your ranged option of a throwing knife, to a shorter distanced whip, in an exchange for damage power, stuff like that.)
It might seem a bit pricey at $15.00 USD, maybe even still at the $10.00 USD discount price, but it's worth it. With all that content, along with the option to try a hand at speedrunning the game with the timer aid, or getting a better time on a certain level, there is a lot to love and your dollar goes a long way.
The bad side: There are a few bugs, some people are having a little trouble launching the game or getting music to play after death in a level and having to restart, but hopefully they will fix it soon. There are slight workarounds for each bug at the moment, and they aren't making the game cripplingly unplayable.
Overall, if you like the idea of the game, and you are up for a tough challenge, it's worth picking up. One of my favorite platformers, for sure!

Before I start the review, let me get this stuff out of the way. I strongly recomend you create an account with
before playing this game. That way you can access the same content you have unlocked in game on Steam and on your mobile device, including your ingame purchases. To set up an account, simply go to
or any of their other "World of _____" games. If you already have a Wargaming account, you can use it here too. This game is much better here on Steam than on iOS or Android. Though it is the same game either way.
Game Overview
World of Tanks Blitz (Blitz) is a simpler version of World of Tanks (WoT), another
creation and I've spent considerably more time in WoT than Blitz; however, I started my WoT expirence with Blitz. Blitz is an MMO where two teams of 7 using tanks and tank destroyers from the early 20th century (read: 1918 - 1960) the "golden age" of armored conflict. Teams are not country specfic, so seeing German and Soviet tanks with American and Japanesse Tanks on seperate teams can and will happen. Your goal is the work with your team mates to either capture the neutral base, or destroy all enemy tanks. There is no respawning, when you're dead, you're dead and can exit the battle to queue for another battle.
The Good:
Blitz is fast passed, battles tend to last five minutes at the most whereas WoT battles can go for 15 minutes.
This is a good game to play if you intend to statr playing WoT on PC or Mac. Many of the tanks in Blitz are in WoT (with the exception of Self-Propelled Howitzers (Artillary)).
Hacks are rare (I've never seen one in my year of play).
Gameplay is easy to learn, but difficult to master.
Core game and most content is free (but those grinds can be tough)
The Bad:
Community can be quite toxic.
Game is grind heavy.
Wargaming loves its in-game purchases (five minutes in game and you'll see what I mean).
Always a lottery when the matchmaker builds teams (Sometimes your team is so good you can't kill anything, other times your team dosen't even know what a tank is let alone how to win the battle).
Overall:
Blitz is a game to not play too seriously. If you do you'll tear your hair out. Just remember the golden WoT / Blitz rule: never count on your team, and play as best you can. Everyone has a terrible game now and again so just accept it and move on.

Deus Ex Human Revolution skillfully delivers a fulfilling and compelling cyberpunk narrative and serves it alongside some seriously engaging mechanics. Giving the player the ability to adopt stealth or work loudly depending on their skill level, Human Revolution is a game you can approach from many different angles, and still reach the same ultimate, satisfying goal at the end of each section. If you're into cyberpunk culture, this game is a must have.

brought the cult-classic original back into mainstream in 2011, but did it’s changes bring a classic back into it’s heyday?
revitalized the long-gone semi-linear first-person action shooter RPG genre that was widely popular in the early 2000s. In its attempt to bring the cult-classic back it’s made a seemingly cohesive blend of old elements (grid-like inventory system, emphasis on stealth) with new mechanics (aiming down ironsights, emphasis on melee takedowns). Coupled with it’s non-linear level design and it’s huge skill tree of augmentations, it allows so many diverse playstyles to enjoy the game as they see fit.
The one thing that sets me back when it comes to the original
is that by today’s standards, it feels like a terrible mash of genres where none of the RPG Mechanics, Shooting, or Stealth was actually good but just “good enough.” With a more solid structure, Human Revolution’s Stealth is significantly enjoyable, it’s shooting is stiff but solid overall, and the RPG mechanics are incredibly sharp and do their job well. Design-wise, it took everything about the original in consideration and did it all again with a much more polished execution. It’s not perfect, but it sure as hell pulls off of the ambition of the original and improved it just enough to make it an incredibly addictive and enthralling set of intricately designed game mechanics.
Unfortunately, this does not carry on in the game’s boss encounters, which play out as a simple shooting gallery with simplistic strategies and no way to non-lethally defeat them. They’re not only boring and easy, but they flat out go against the open-ended approach the rest of the game takes towards encounters. This is further worsened by the game’s last segment, which just felt like a long shooting gallery that felt like they had to throw out their design philosophies to get the game done at the last second.
One of the most striking elements of the
games is the universe itself. Through its political themes, diverse landscapes and strikingly relevant messages,
connects itself as a possible “What if” scenario for our world today. Although it often shoves it’s themes right up your face too often, it does add enough subtlety and nuance to make it a intelligent and entertaining take on the future.
However,
’s writing often ruins this potential with it’s cheesy, often laughably cringey dialogue. Out of all of the major components of the game, the writing itself is the one aspect of the game that seemed as if it didn’t get the touch of intelligence and ingenuity as the rest of the game. However, that definitely doesn’t mean the story isn’t entertaining as hell though. Coupled with a great soundtrack and it’s visually unique art-style,
oozes atmosphere.
Now, you have all of the components of what is basically a really well-crafted experience. However, there’s one major issue I have with the overall package.
The
. The re-release for this game is mind-bogglingly mismanaged, with it’s poor attempt of integrating the game’s DLC “Missing Link” into the main story and running a buggier, less optimized build of the game. The game’s color palette somehow looks terrible in this version as well. While it’s not a huge deal-breaker, if you already own the original on your account, play that instead of this version.
But if that’s not a big deal-breaker, then what are you standing around for? Play this game. You won’t regret it.

1001 Spikes is a hardcore platformer in every sense of the word. It will stop at nothing to impale you on spikes, crush you with a boulder, burn you alive, and then impale you on even more spikes. Some may even call this a rage game by how hard it gets, but stepping up to the challenge and completing each level is really satisfying.
Here's a quick look video that goes over the postives and negatives of this game. But for those of you who just wanna read about it, continue below. (Info about other modes below since this only covers story, which is the meat of the game)
Let me begin my review with what this game is about. You're an adventurer exploring trap-infested dungeons, and the whole reason you're there is because you want to get the treasure to prove to your late father that you're a real man. Yeah, a guy with daddy issues. The reason this is called 1001 spikes is because you get that many lives to complete the game with, but you can get more by collecting artifacts and golden skulls. It's pretty straightforward, but the fun comes with the challenging maps.
In every level, you need to collect a key, then go to the exit. But it's not as simple as that. Hidden spikes will pop up without warning, dart traps will suddenly fire when you go near, and platforms with fall without warning as soon as you step on them. Because of this, you will die many times and have to start over from the beginning. Yet each time you will become a little wiser and learn the patterns until you eventually reach the end. Very much a trial and error system, but a good one that keep things challenging, but not enough to feel too cheap and make me want to quit.
Another good thing is the ability to drag your friends in for some local co-op or minigames. Things can get very hectic and fun as you try to complete levels together or kill each other. Every character plays a bit different too, such as playing Knight Arthur from Ghouls 'n Ghosts and having his armor get knocked off after a hit for a second life. There's even an interesting tower-climbing mode with boss battles if you collect golden skulls to unlock it, so don't forget to grab them as you play the story mode. The last mode you get is basically the same as the story, but the levels are hard right off the bat and you only get 100 lives.
However, this game isn't without some faults.
-There isn't any online multiplayer, nor is there any bots. So if you're all by your lonesome, half of the game's selling point doesn't apply to you. Sure you can play the levels by yourself, but it's kinda boring and the levels lose most of their dynamics since they cater to multiple people.
-Some people may take issue with the pixel graphics and over-saturation of them in today's market. And while I personally don't mind the graphic style, lots of people avoid games simply for this reason alone.
-Even though I do like the difficulty, sometimes I found myself frustrated with some of the trial and error gameplay. Can't tell you how many times I was so close to the end only to be sent back to the beginning from a hidden spike trap.
-Honestly, I think this should be a $10 game. I was halfway through the campaign after only one and a half hours, so with it being so short on its single-player mode, it may turn a few people away. Though admittedly, the later levels are gonna take you much longer to complete since they start getting insane.
To wrap this up, this game is for those who like a challenge. It even caters to those who are perfectionists and want every collectible and the best times. So if you have buds to play with, this is a good buy. But if you only want it for the single player, get it if you've been itching for a game that really pushes you to beat it. And if you're still on the fence, wait for a discount and this will definitely be worth it.

My impression of the game in a nutshell is "OK". Meaning that it is not knocking my socks off but is decent enough representative of its genre to justify probably playing it through once.
Endless Space is rather generic space 4X. Some attempt has been made at storyline or something representing that by trying to make the races somewhat unique and one is free to assemble his own custom race as well by buying abilities for points. The good parts are tech tree and diplomacy system which are somewhat above average. Annoying parts are various artificial limitations - I mean, my empire is allowed to have up to max 10 different ship designs? Only 10? You can't really do a pearl harbor either, as when you cansel peace there is 10 turns cooldown before you are allowed to take any agressive action, etc. On one hand this makes diplomacy meaningful, on the other hand it feels like removing some of the options I should have. The "Hero" system is interesting twist that is not too common for the space 4X genre.
Game is stable and during the first ~120 turns or so there has not been a single glitch so far so in that regard its well polished. GFX is good and the game works out of the box without needing any additional tweaking on non-standard aspect ratios and resolutions. I have played it on 5400x1920 (5x1 portrait eyefinity with 1080p screens) and 4608x2048 (3x1 portrait eyefinity with 2048x1536 screens) without the usual UI scaling issues and such which tend to be common in the games aimed at specific aspect ratios. So the game engine is in that regard very solid.
If you see the game on Steam sale and are looking to spend some time feel free to grab it. It's decent enough for that. If you are looking for something that would keep you going for hundreds of hours it is probably not the game you are looking for. Perhaps give a try to Space Empires series in that case although that is not without its own issues. But on Steam sale - go for it.

I'm going to do a review from a newbie perspective, for anyone looking to buy the game. First off, this game reminds me of Sins of a Solar Empire, but done in a better way IMO. It's a 4x turn based space game with a nice amount of depth to the gameplay, but not in a overly complicated way like some reviews may lead you to believe. It has a nice R&D system/tree with several different branches that looks to me iike it could offer many types of gameplay for any race. There is several races to choose from, each with their own perks etc etc.
------------
The combat, I saw some hate on. Personally, I think it's very intuitive and enjoyable. It is based on a "card system" of sorts, but that doesn't ruin the enjoyment of it to me. You get to watch the fights unfold, and unless I'm mistaken it also looks like you can change tactics mid combat while the fight unfolds before you.
------------
The graphics are quite lovely to look at. My computer isn't the best in the world (mac mini mid 2011, 8gb ram, 320m nvidia geforce 256mb) and the game runs VERY smooth with graphics cranked up towards the high range. Space battles are nice to look at, as is everything else really.
------------
Overall, I recommend the game to anyone who might be interested. I just recently started getting into turn-based and 4x games and this is one of the games I don't regret purchasing so far. I see myself investing a large amount of time into this. I haven't played multiplayer, nor do I even know if anyone else plays it (might have to force some friends to play with me >_>), but I don't think it would be a bad thing at all.  Everything else in the game seems well implemented to me so far. If anything I typed happens to change for me opinion wise in the future as I invest more time into this, I will be sure to edit my post, though I doubt I will have too.

It has a very cohesive style, clearly knows what it’s going for and I’m looking forward to playing more episodes as they show up. In fact, I can
contain myself.

Bear With Me is a story driven episodic noir point and click adventure game. It has been developed and published by Exordium Games and is released today.
The game tells the story of Amber who is awoken in the middle of the night to find that her brother, Flint, has gone missing. In order to find him she relies upon the assistance of Ted E. Bear, a retired detective who is also her beloved teddy bear.
It is made clear at the beginning of the game that Amber’s relationship with her teddy has become strained. They’ve gone through a number of adventures together. As a result, Ted has become grumpy in his elder age. However, their bond is undeniable. This is the type of character and relationship writing that is on display from the start of the game. As a result of this and a continuation of the high level of character writing throughout the game I was suckered in immediately. There is a certain level of charm that is certainly not common place in adventure games anymore.
If the quality of the writing isn’t considered sufficient for a point and click adventure game anymore then the quality extends through to the professional voice over work. The immediate character writing acquired my attention but the voice over work sustains it. I am particularly fond of the voice over work performed for the Ted E. Bear character. The actor was able to perfectly marry the noir theme of the game.
I’ve come to expect surprises from small indie studios. However, to see the quality of the voice over work on a studio’s first ever adventure game – and their second game overall – is one of the most significant yet. I am thoroughly impressed with the majority of the work. The passion and the tone injected into each line is a driving force behind what should be a successful game.
If you are a fan of dark comedy then you’re in for a treat. The game is funny from start to finish with much of the dialogue using cleverly delivered puns and sarcasm. It is in my opinion that the script is a significant reason why the voice over artists are as enthusiastic as what they are.
Yes. Bear With Me comes with trading cards and 27 Steam achievements. Some of the achievements are generally considered to be a little on the aggravating side (for example ensure that you click on every painting and lamp that you come across). Some of them contain references and easter eggs. For example, there is a lamp that humorously mentioned Resident Evil. There is part of an achievement  in the study that deserves to be heard.
For someone who hasn’t spent significant time playing point and click adventure games recently I was impressed. The genre is generally too slow for my liking and I don’t enjoy spending time trying to solve puzzles that don’t always make a lot of sense to me. However, Bear With Me is an entirely different story. The pacing is well done and the humor  and the overall presentation was something that I was very surprised to see.  I honestly haven’t enjoyed a game in the genre as much as this since some of Daedalic’s best works and before that games such as The Secret of Monkey Island. This may be on the next level below that but for an indie studio it is a wonderful achievement.

+ Fantastic relaxing soundtrack filled with Electronic, Trance, House, Trap, and Dubstep that fits very well with the space action theme. You also have full control to switch the songs at any time during the game.
+ Visually the game looks great with very bright colorful neon ships, bullets, and explosions along with some great looking outerspace backgrounds.
+ A unique mechanic where you can turn your ship left or right, so basically you are fighting waves of enemies that appear on both sides of the screen and generally stay in the center.
+ Upgrade / experience system, you can upgrade each of your weapons along a separate skill tree. You have player upgrades to increase your damage, shields, evasion, etc. And finally there are 5 ships to choose from that you can essentially level as you play to gain additional perks .
+ Great difficulty settings  / modifiers, to gain additional experience you can turn up the difficulty OR you can set modifiers to make the game more challenging such as more enemies, asteroids, and "planetary fortresses" which will send a few planets at you during the mission which have rocket launching turrets on them.
+ Challenging bosses which have a variety of unique abilities and movements to really keep things entertaining every 10 levels.
+ A surprising amount of voice acted cutscenes which you don't normally see in games of this genre.
- The story is a bit confusing to fully understand
- The voice acting / dialogue felt a bit forced at times, but as an indie project it's pretty easy to look past that
- Even though there's 5 ships, you only have 4 abilities that you will be using repetitively throughout the 50 missions. It would have been nice if each ship had unique abilities to mix things up a bit.

Deus Ex HR is a great game in which the best path is not always the most obvious. You'll always have multiple ways to get past an obstacle:
Enemy in your way? I mean sure, you could pump them full of lead, but there's other options available. You could take a longer path and go around them entirely, knock them unconscious (either from a distance or close up), sneak past them, distract them and run past, etc.
I would really suggest playing the first two games first - but if you don't want to, at least read through the synopsis for the original and Invisible War. You may have a hard time understanding the background of the game if you don't.
The game has its faults and you will get frustrated, but the leveling system and different ways to complete missions really makes it one of the most replayable recent games .

I do enjoy a good stealth game, and Deus Ex does it well.  The AI is fairly intelligent and thematically appropriate.  The stealth mechanics are good, but the variety of augments are what really sets this game apart from other similar games.  I enjoy the variety of ways to complete each mission.  The "conversation boss battles" are really neat.  The only thing missing from this game is pick-pocketing.
Also, the hacking system is not good on a controller.  Fortunately, hacking is mostly optional because you can find 99% of the access codes by looking around or searching guards.  There's even a consumable device that lets you bypass the hacking minigame.

Every once in a while, something will come along in life that just feels *right*. Those crazy friends you stay up waaaaaay too late at night with; the homemade, 6-hour-smoked BBQ ribs your dad cooks; that band you love, or movie you've seen a hundred times. You can't quite put your finger on it, but something about it just makes you feel fuzzy. Like it's good for you.
I'd never played Deus Ex before Human Revolution. I've heard of the franchise, but always had other games to play. But now, having played HR this spring, picked up the original this summer, and begun waiting for Mankind Divided this fall - this game feels right as rain.
It's not perfect. The graphics are fine, but a little outdated. The bosses can be irritating - I turned down the difficulty, just so I could get past them. There isn't much incentive for run-and-gun combat, though it's certainly not *terrible*.
But make no mistake, Human Revolution is good. The story is complex, well-told and well-developed. The characters are memorable, and easy to get attached to. Some intriguing moral choices are present, and the ending is nothing if not extraordinary. I felt a heaviness entering that final area (which I won't spoil), a feeling that told me this game resonates with me.
And it does. The dichotomy between "natural" humans and augmented "augs" is told beautifully, and at times poignantly.  Sometimes the lines between "good guys" and "bad guys" get murky and blurred, and you have to stop and think about whether your actions are right or wrong. Or even, if it really matters (and I mean that in a good-job-devs way).
The music is sensational. Michael McCann is a great composer, and this game is living proof. The "Icarus" theme (AKA - the song you hear in the HR trailer) is one of my all-time favorite video game compositions, both mesmerizing and haunting. In fact, let me give a shoutout to the game's whole sound-design execution: it's immersive, it's bold and it's beautiful.
Stealth in this game...I'm sure there's a gazillion other reviews about it, so I'll just say it's fantastic. Loads of fun.
And in the end, that's what this game is. Loads of fun. It's a game I wish I'd picked up years ago, wish I had time in my life to play over and over again - I spent roughly 44 hours on my full playthrough.
But though I may not have the days to waste, you do. So pick up Human Revolution today, play it, get hyped for Mankind Divided this August. It's because of HR that MD is one of my most-anticipated games in years. It just feels...right.
When a video game does that, you know it's earned every penny.

So the Steam controller is goddamn amazing. This is, by a wide margin, the best controller I have ever used. The only complaint I have is that it is light. It'd really be perfect if it was closer to the Xbone Elite controller in weight, but this is just personal preference.
There may be people like me out there who have what I call "stupid fingers" and just can't use WASD controls, for whatever reason.  I don't know why, my brain just doesn't get how to work my fingers as gracefully as my thumbs.  As such, I've been unable to play games such as KOTOR, Mass Effect, and Guild Wars 2, as well as other amazing games that don't have normal controller support.  I cannot thank Valve enough for allowing me to finally play these gems.
All the levels of customization are incredible. Between mode shifts, you can effectively map SEVENTY FOUR buttons (II think.  My math may be a tad off), plus mouse control to this thing. Seventy eight if for whatever reason you don't need a mouse. You can change sensitivity on both pads and analog stick individually. You can assign two different buttons to each trigger, one for half presses and one for full.
If your controller comes out of alignment a bit, you can tell it where dead zones lie and it will work around them if small enough.
I still haven't messed around with all the settings, but what I have seen so far is outstanding.
OH! AND YOU CAN CHANGE THE CONFIGURATION ON A GAME BY GAME BASIS! You don't even have to make your own configurations, as there are tons that are available that people have made that you can import. This importing is available from WITHIN EVERY GAME.
I love this thing.

A little troublesome trying to get used to. Tha's the biggest complaint. Something I didn't realize until I switched back to my wired controller is how amazingly ergonomic this controller is. The left and right sides for most controllers when using your index finger, you don't realize how much you are straining your tendons unil you give them a proper break. After using the Steam controller for about a month, then switching back, my index fingers, specifically the first knuckls, were physically hurting. I would highly recommend if you have arthritis in your family, this could save you a lot of trouble later in life (and allow you to keep playing games too!)
Worked great and feels very responsive and comfortable

If you like to play casual games, like Poker Night, Bloons, HuniePop, Civilization, then this controller is for you. If you want to play anything else, you may want to get an XBONE or DS4. This is certainly not a bad controller by any means, but it isn't perfect. I still prefer M+KB for most games, but this is a good option for playing on the TV. I'd hate to say try it for yourself, especially when it's $50+$10 shipping, but it really depends on your preferences. I will say that the controller does work as a standard mouse for your KB, so I've been using that as a way to become more used to the controller.

From what I can tell, Valve essentially developed this so they would have a controller to go with their Steamlink. At some point, instead of developing games like people want them to, they got it into their heads that playing PC games on a TV from a coach was something a huge amount of people have been clamoring for. It isn't, but all the same here we are with a gamepad whose primary function is to provide decent emulation of a keyboard and mouse for playing PC games from a distance.
It fails miserably at this goal. I've tried it in a variety of games of different genres, and at the absolute best it merely achieves 'not too terrible', and rarely even that. It's most abysmal in FPS's, and this is coming from someone who plays quite a few shooters on consoles with gamepads, so I'm not being some kind of KB+M purist. Killing Floor 2 was an actively unpleasant experience with the Steam Controller. CSGO? Forget it. Completely lost cause, and that's not just my opinion, a friend who really likes the Steam Controller and plays a ton of CSGO is of the same view. Hilarious, considering they sell CSGO skins for the thing...
Anyway, what about strategy games? Lots of reviews say it's okay for that, right? Not in my experience. There's simply no substitute for a mouse for such games, and that's the end of it. The touchpads aren't anymore a viable replacement than analog sticks are (and that's why you rarely see RTS on consoles).
Let's talk about those haptic feedback touchpads, one of the chief gimmicks of the Controller. They're touted as the next step, the futuristic replacement for analog sticks. Pure ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. They're♥♥♥♥♥ 'Despise' is the proper word for how I feel about them. But first, what actually are they? They're touchpads, like those ♥♥♥♥♥♥ things on laptops that no one ever uses because they always get a USB mouse instead. The 'haptic' part is that they have tiny motors underneath (that make an obnoxious creaking sound when in use that fortunately can be turned off). That's it. It's a touchpad that slightly vibrates. Is it better than a laptop touchpad? Yeah. Is it good? No. It's crap as a mouse, and worse as a substitute for a second analog stick.
And there are two of these atrocious things, the second is the replacement for a traditional D-pad. What's that? You didn't like the old 360 D-pad? Well how about no physical D-pad at all, ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥? This left pad is actually worse than the right one, and I've seen a fair amount of discussion even among people who like the Steam Controller that it really needs a proper D-pad. It defaults to being the D-pad, but it's just a second touchpad (with a slight indentation in the shape of the traditional plus symbol), and you can remap it to be whatever you want.
Which brings me to the customizability. It has plenty of that. Every button (including the two additional button pad things on the interior underside) can be mapped to anything you want, deadzones and sensitivities can be changed at will, and that's just the start. There's also a (clunky, with no search bar) system to download other peoples configuration profiles. But all the software customization in the world won't help fundamentally bad hardware. The touchpads are♥♥♥♥♥ The face buttons are comically small, and in an odd position. I'm not actually going to say this layout is inherently terrible, I'd be interested to see someone make an Xbox or Playstation controller with this layout and with analog sticks, it might actually be good. But with the Steam Controller, you'll frequently accidentally brush the right touchpad while reaching for the face buttons.
Build quality is fine. It's not up to the standard of a Dualshock 4 or Xbox One gamepad, but it's better than the Dualshock 2 and 3. It has a comfortable heft to it. The construction, where it's reversed compared to every other gamepad and rises up into your hands instead of having downward facing handles, is...okay. It's fine. It doesn't feel terrible, but it's not some revolutionary advancement either. I can take it or leave it.
I should also note, because this may be a dealbreaker for some people, that it doesn't have proper rumble. Currently there's an optional beta feature you can turn on or off in software that provides a kind of improvised rumble with the haptic motors, but it's very weak and frankly pathetic.
Okay, I don't like it at all as a KB+M substitute, what about purely as a gamepad, for games designed for a gamepad? Meh. I actually bought this because my 360 gamepad was getting rather frayed and worn, and hey, Black Friday sales. At the best, which was in DiRT 3, it was equal to the 360 controller. Equal, not better. And this was entirely because I didn't have to use the touchpads to drive. The single analog stick that the Steam Controller comes with is perfectly acceptable. It even has texturing on the side similar to the Xbox One controller. If it had two of these and a proper D-pad, I might like it. But then it wouldn't really be the revolutionary advancement Valve wants it to be, would it? The early prototypes didn't even have this single stick, so sure were they are the superiority of haptic feedback. Hah. While writing this it occurs to me that they probably went with these all digital pads because of the customizability they opened up, rather than any real conviction that haptic feedback is THE FUTURE.
Again, I simply don't like the haptic touchpads, and find them an awful replacement for a proper analog stick. So that right there throws out a huge amount of games, and the second touchpad replacing the D-pad throws out even more. I do a lot of emulation of older game consoles, and was led to believe Valve had basically created the ultimate emulation gamepad. Very possibly, if you like the haptic feedback pads (and plenty of people do, apparently). One interesting feature is that the Steam Controller has dual stage triggers, which means it can properly emulate a GameCube gamepad. That's a genuinely cool feature (shame about the rest of the controller...).
Speaking of emulators, there's a bit of a software-side problem on that front. The Steam Controller doesn't support XInput; everything has to be done through Steam (because closed ecosystems are one of the best things about PC gaming, right?). What this means is you can't simply plug your controller in, go into an emulators settings, and map the buttons as you want. There is a third-party program that can enable XInpuit support, but it's inelegant and works by fooling the computer into thinking the Steam Controller is a 360 gamepad. At that point you might as well just use an actual Xbox controller. The actual process of mapping out keys with the Steam Controller involves binding a function to a keyboard key, and then binding that key to a button on the gamepad. You know, like that janky Joy2Key program, though this is far more refined, but it's the same principle.
Ultimately though, you shouldn't take this (or any) review as gospel. The Steam Controller is something you absolutely have to try yourself before deciding on. Find a friend who already has one and use theirs for a while, or try it out in a store display or something. Decide for yourself if you can tolerate, or even fall in love with, the haptic touchpads.
In the end I obviously don't like it, and hope to hell other developers don't think of adopting haptic feedback as a replacement for analog sticks. I plan to sell the thing to a friend who actually likes it, and replace my battered 360 pad with an Xbox One controller. This is a damn shame, because the Steam Controller was the only one of Valves hardware projects I had any interest in at all.

Now this is a hidden gem of the strategy game universe. Endless space is a 4x game (xplore, xploit, xpand, xterminate) that shines in so many aspects of gameplay (so many good aspect that i had a hard time just trying to figure out where to start).  All I can do now is point out the many good (and not so good, but there are very few of these) points that this game has to offer.
Benefits:
1. The User Interface:
In my opinion, any developer who wishes to make 4x strategy game user interface should take a look at Endless Space. The user interface was so friendly to the player that I'd navigate between micro and macromanagement without even thinking about it. The time I had saved from not having to learn how to properly use the UI were spent enjoying the game for the most point. There were a few issues with fleet management, but they were really minor and mostly simple to learn.
2. Factions
The factions were all really unique and enjoyable. Almost all of the faction (except the harmony) start with unique skills and tech that give them their distint advantages over the other factions, without distrupting the balance of the game. Ship designs for each of the factions were candy for the eyes; you will want to play each faction just so that you can see the ship designs. Finally this game allows you to create your own custom factions (this is one of the best aspects of this game); I've spent countless hours just customizing my own factions and pitting them against each other in the fights for dominion over the galaxy.
3.  Updates
When Endless space got disharmony it got two major changes that completely changed how the game as a whole. The first major change they implemented was the way you outfit your ships with weapons and armor. the second major change was with the resources you aquire and how they affect your empire. With the first change, the way we build our ships completely changed (now you have to design your ships to adapt to specific threats to your empire that will change throughout the game); With the second change, we got a clear cut idea of what the strategic resources did for your empire.
4. Battlephase
This is what truely seperates Endless Space from the other 4x games. instead of the game autoresolving the battle between you and another empire, you conduct the fight in a "Rock, Paper, Scizzors" type fight  in three stages (or one of you either retreats or dies). In these stages you choose a battle option that can perform two seperate actions (one action determines if your battle option can work; the other performs the battle option if your option hasn't been negated). These battle options can easily and quickly tip the scale of a battle, so there is no guarenteed winner of a battle until the battle has reached a conclusion.
there are many more great features to this game, but it's better for you to try them out yourself.
Negative features:
there was only one major issue I had with the game that was the content that was provided outside of the major game changes in the DLC.
While Disharmony brought alot of updates that improved the game, it did not bring much in terms of DLC. The only major content outside of the core updates were really the inclusion of the harmony and drones into the game. The Harmony is a disappointment, as it cannot use dust or anything affiliated with dust, which puts the Harmony at a major disadvantage to the other factions in the game. The drones are okay; they can be outfitted assist in space fights or the invasion of other systems, but they also don't provide any major benefits to gameplay (they are good to look at though).
At the end of the day, I would recommend this game to anyone and everyone who was interested in a good strategy, as this game has so many features that make it feel fresh and new (in terms of both first impressions and replayability). This is not the game to miss so give it a shot if you are curious.

Endless Space is cast in the grand tradition of 4X turn-based strategy games. They’re so-called for their emphasis on four key gameplay elements: explore, expand, exploit, and exterminate. Endless Space is aptly named, because you’re responsible for shepherding a spacefaring civilization into the stars.
Besides expanding the borders of your civilization (with several unique races to choose from), you need to learn how to adapt to new planetary environments, manage relationships with other races, and handle the continued development of your own species. A four-branch tree of very different technologies, each focal point of which helps you direct your race’s development, either into exploration, applied sciences, warfare, or diplomacy and trade.
As your technology improves, so will your adaptability to the environments of different worlds you discover. You’ll also need to assimilate resources to grow. The four basic resources managed in Endless Space are Food, Industry, Dust, and Science (FIDS for short, an acronym you see pop up from time to time), and you can direct your civilization’s management of those resources on a colony-by-colony basis.
Dust is the “currency” of Endless Space, the gold bullion that greases the wheels of commerce, simplifies the development of technology, facilitates trade and commerce with your neighbors, and more. The uses for Dust are a bit of a wildcard, unlocked as you get further and further into the game.
A growing interstellar civilization demands a fleet of vessels to manage exploration, expansion, trade, and defense. Fleet creation and development is an important component of the game. You can customize your vessels with a tremendous amount of detail depending on your needs and the state of your development.
Inevitably the expansion of a civilization’s borders creates friction for its neighbors, and in Endless Space you have control over how that friction occurs. Each of the eight playable races has a base disposition either using diplomacy and trade as your tool or, let loose the dogs of war. Combat in Endless Space is more football coach than player: You issue fleet commands to direct your ships in the two-minute skirmishes that follow. But like the coach of a football game, you can’t control the players on the field directly.
Every time you play, Endless Space produces a new galaxy to explore, so there’s endless replay value here. You can adjust the parameters of the galaxy extensively (though not endlessly) and you can customize the race you want to play. This leads to some daunting moments for the new player, but the reward is constant challenge no matter how many times you play.
Endless Space is lovely to look at and sounds great too thanks to an electronic soundtrack which fits the stark beauty of the outer space visuals. The galaxy is your sandbox, and you will get immersed for hours, days, weeks at a time. If games like Master of Orion or Civilization appeal to you, there’s a lot to love in Endless Space.

Endless Space is a game that  fulfills a role that until recently had been left empty. A space based turn based strategy civ building game. The Civ series in space. While Real time games like Sins of a Solar Empire have always existed the lack of a turn based space game has hurt those who enjoy games like Civ while also enjoying aliens. The game itself has a vareity of options. You can create your own race using traits, hire and upgrade Generals/admirals/governors/spies, you can colonize the planets in a system and upgrade them as you see fit, and  you can even build your own ships and field them against your foes. This level of customization and freedom of choice is furthered by the tech tree in the game. It is a web that allows you to pursue whichever path you need at the time to further your empire's goals. This means that you have a fully customizable empire with fully customizable ships at your disposal. The game works in a turn based system and allows each turn for you ships to move depending on weight to propulsion ratios and for each of the systems under your control to generate reasources. The game runs into issues in a couple of places. The game does not necessarily explain the maps in the slightest expecting the player to have an advanced knowledege of planetary objects and how they react to one another. The game also does not really have a very good battle system instead working on a turnbased rock-paper-scissors system using cards that are given depending on ship tech, admiral level and faction tech. This means that a smaller force can overcome a large one and a much larger force and suffer heavy losses against a small one purely based on the luck of what cards each side picked. Although at a certain point cards cease to matter as a small scout is going to be destroyed in 1-2 shots by a battlecruiser regardless of the cards played. This system is still odd and while new to the genre would probably require some fine-tuning to be able to work in a Turn based game of this magnitude. You nation as  a whole does feel like it matters and your fleets moving about work well however there are no strong stationary defenses and if, due to a bad card, you lose a fleet you will have to pull another one to help secure your worlds as the scant amount of planetary defense available throughout the game will more than likely be unable to defend the planet from the heavily damaged enemy fleet. This is sort of annoying and damages the otherwise great game signifigantly. I would honestly have to give the game a solid 7.5/10

I fell in love with Master of Orion II when it came out first (1996) and since then I look for a worthy successor. Played several 4X games and they had their pros and cons. Endless Space is one of the better 4X games and absolutely worth buying, in my opinion. Wouldn't have played 300+ hours else, heh. I am reviewing it including Disharmony expansion.
Galaxy: Endless Space offers some variety of galaxy shapes and sizes, some favoring defensive players, some favoring offensive ones. Additional finetuning of the galaxy is possible. I miss the opportunity of creating a REALLY huge galaxy, but maximum size with just one opponent works ok as a sandbox mode. During exploring you will find nice bonuses, a few pirates, wormholes (basically dividing the galaxy until you can travel through them) and finally different wonders, so exploring is actually fun.
Background story: You learn about the Endless (usual Elder civilization which went extinct) during playing. The game lacks lore summary articles, but there are traces of this ancient civilization everywhere (galaxy wonders, technologies, factions, leaders), which adds to immersion.
Factions: The games comes with 10 to 12 moderately unique prebuilt factions (depending on whether you get Harmony and Vaulters). Each gets specific traits, innate bonuses, ship bonuses and a few special technologies to encourage certain victory types and hence playstyles. Prebuilt factions are different enough to motivate you to try them all. Additionally, you can create your own faction by modifying a prebuilt one. Meaning you can replace their traits completely, but you have stick with their innate bonuses, ship bonuses and special technologies. It has still a high degree of freedom, I enjoy building my own faction a lot.
AI: Computer opponents (artificial intelligences respective AIs) offer a solid challenge. Especially the 'evil' factions tend to attack you early on, so you cannot simply expand all over the galaxy or rush through the technology trees. Later most AI will attack you when they run out of colonization space - unless they are busy with other opponents. But they also attack each other for same reasons and their reasoning is mostly transparent (+x for long period of peace, -y for common borders etc.). At higher difficulty ratings they are more unfriendly (but not hateful) and get the usual strong production bonuses to offer more of a challenge.
Leader: You can hire a few people for boosts to your empire or your fleets. They make a real difference and usually have a nice background story. It takes some time to learn about their feat trees, but once you became familar with it, your leader can turn a fleet into a nearly unbeatable force. Which you will need to fend off the many enemy ships at higher difficulty ratings... Using leaders to improve your empire helps a lot at the beginning but loses importance as it grows.
Production: Production is done on system level mostly, saving you some time compared to games which do it on planet level. So most buildings affect all colonized planets, ships are produced by the entire system etc.. However, you can specialize your planets (usually: food, industry, research, money), explore their moons and terraform the planets. Terraforming is an interesting feature here because depending on faction and situation you can be better off with unfriendly environment. Since production shouldn't be automated, you will spend a lot of time with tweaking your systems. But that's true for many of these games...
Technology: There are basically four technology trees and they sometimes offer different paths to specific technologies. It honestly needs quite a while to get used to them, but it offers interesting decisions to make. Technology names are often NOT related to their benefits, so at the beginning you will have to check their descriptions often. Other games did that better. Well, on the plus side you have many interesting concepts in the tech description texts - some scifi fans will like them.
Diplomacy: The negotiation with aliens is a solid feature. At the beginning you are at "cold war", meaning you can invade other factions' outposts but not colonies - a bit confusing first. Of course there are war and peace. Peace can be upgraded a bit by two more treaties (open borders, cooperation) and there are alliances. Alliances are usually a short-lived thing with AI empires, but a few traits and technologies reward you for allying. Upgrading from war to cease fire to peace to additional treaties / alliance goes slowly since there is a hardcoded turn amount between them. For instance you have to be at war with your opponent for 10 rounds, then both sides can offer cease fire. At the beginning of the game this makes some sense (why ally instantly with some empire you barely know?), later it becomes kind of a burden. AI empires sometimes ignore the turn amount, speeding up the process. Beside this you can trade dust (basically money), technologies, systems and special resources. At the end of a long war you can even make an AI empire give you all its colonies.
Covert operations: There is no secret service in any empire which is a bit of a letdown. Leaders can steal some dust (money) and technology points from other empires, but that's it.
Ship design: This game gives you rather much freedom how to design your spaceships. The weapon choices are a bit dull: Level 1, 2 and 3 versions of mass drivers, beam weapons and missiles, plus some fighters and bombers. You can defend your ships with thick armor, defense systems or simply taking out the enemy ships fast enough. Finally some special systems make your ships truly unique: Better engines for raids, better scanners to avoid getting surprised, siege for slow invasions, marines for fast invasions (they cost population!), multiple colony pods for quick expansion or multiple layers of armor to accept and shrug off enemy hits.
Battles: Endless Space has a somewhat simplified battle system. You cannot control single ships or squadrons, instead you set the overall strategy by picking a card and probably refine it by formation and general targetting tactics. Leaders add a bit of complexity with their special cards. 'Manual combat' just means you can watch the battle (which looks nice) and change cards every combat phase. Of course this card system means you lose some control (compared with other games), but it also reduces micromanagement and makes the AI more competitive in battles. Some people hate it, some love it, I'd say it's ok.
Bugs: Endless Space crashes ocassionally, let's say every other game. In every case reloading the latest savegame fixed the issue. According to the error messages it's mostly about AI diplomacy - playing with less opponents and in smaller galaxies might help. Given the fun the game provides, I accept the rare crashes though.
If you like complex 4X games, you will (very likely) enjoy Endless Space and its addon Disharmony.

World of Tanks Blitz is a fun free to play game for any person or persons interested in PvP. Particularly when you take the role of a Tank Commander, with your own tank to use in combat.
The aim of the game is simple: choose the tank you desire from 6 different nations and play against enemy teams of 7 with your own randomized team and win in whatever map you've been put in. You can choose from Britain, France, Russia, The United States, Germany and Japan.
Each tank is unique across each nation's tank 'tree'. Although they are divided into similar branches such as Tank Destroyers, Heavy Tanks, Light Tanks (scouts) and Medium Tanks, you don't have to worry about not getting the tank you want because there are so many across all 6 nations. With various shapes and sizes, you are guaranteed to get the tank you desire.
As you progress through the game, you are awarded credits and experience from each battle which you can use to either customize or upgrade your tank by getting better equipment or armaments. If you get enough experience after fighting enough battles, you can buy the next tank in line which follows. There are 10 Tiers of Tanks: Tier 1-10 and each get tougher and harder to get as you progress in tiers.
If you want to play with a friend you can platoon with one and fight alongside them in matchmaking. You don't have to wait long once you've joined the queque in matchmaking because it usually only takes a few seconds before you're off in a 7v7 match.
If you feel you're not ready against other players, you can go to the training room and fight bots.
Now, one of the biggest gripes that many people have with this game is the in-game currency system. Some feel that it's a pay-to-win type of game because you can exchange real money to buy 'gold' which allows you purchase (with said gold) Premium accounts which allow you to get 50% more credits and experience from each battle. You can also use gold to speed up the rate at which you buy equipment (there's a certain time delay), buy tanks, improved tank rounds, credits and camos. Rest assured that while gold does play a role in the game, it doesn't hinder it as directly as some might make you feel.
Every day you are given missions which award you credits, experience and award tokens. If you collect 20 award tokens, you can exchange these for premium certificates that can last 24, 9 or 1 hour in game. Missions always give out award tokens in groups of 4 and you can complete up to 3 each day. Recently they've also added 3 of various sizes which refill every few days containers, which give out a variety of items such as credits, combat boosters (which can increase the amount of xp your vehicle attains in battle), gold or a premium tanks (which when used award more credits then those of the same tier: a Farming tank if you will that you may or may not be able to get in the game's store using gold).
To use gold, you need to use your real money to get it (except if you get it from tournaments and event awards). And the use of gold only speeds up the rate of progression that you will attain. If you grind your way through the game using the game's resources that they give you, you'll learn through experience and build up a wealth of knowledge which will allow you to beat other players who haven't learn't the funner and more thrilling way of playing through experience.
Good luck and have fun. Also remember to type in chat, at the end of each game 'gg wp' (Good Game Well Played) as courtesy.

I would have finished the game in around two hours but I spent around an hour looking for an item in the background that you need to proceed in the game. The game ends just as the story gets going. Bear With Me is a good start but it is just the start to a story.
The only main issue I have with the game is that it isn't particularly challenging. The good news is that you don't have to waste time just guessing what you need to do next. The problem is that the puzzles are so straight forward that there really isn't much puzzle solving in the game.
At this point I would say that Bear With Me is a good start for a larger story. If the game's premise interests you I think you will enjoy the game.

Metal Slug 2 remains a must play for people of all ages. Whether you're introducing a child to the roots of modern gaming, or simply revisiting an old classic for nostalgia purposes, MS2 doesn't fail to deliver. Although short, MS2 offers enough replayability for this not to matter. This is a tough one to review. It most certainly has annoying downsides, but I did enjoy myself. If you're on the fence, play Lines Free by the same developer which is a free demo (same game and mechanic, about half the length but with unique content).
I like the core gameplay. A lot actually. For the roughly 70 minutes of content (including the free DLC), I did enjoy myself and the price is fair for that (especially on sale). I can see myself going back and replaying it in a few months. Windowed mode is supported, though undocumented (Alt+Enter, then drag to resize the window), which is a must for me on puzzle games. The sounds are pretty good. The visual style is nothing to write home about, but decent and randomized so it never gets boring.
On the negative side the game absolutely swamps you with useless and uninsipred achievements. The handling could be improved as quickly drawing lines is a bit finnicky and you cannot break-up completed lines to fix small issues. The game forces you to redraw the whole thing, so it's better to leave everything unfinished at first. On the flipside you can start from both sides, which is rarely useful but really nifty and I haven't seen it before anywhere else. There are also relatively frequent graphical glitches, but they are only minor annoyances and don't impact the gameplay.
If you still haven't made up your mind, just play the free demo version Lines Free. The paid version is literally just more of the same. If the achievements were toned down and if you could break-up completed lines this would be an easy recommendation and since those are only minor annoyances I'll give it a thumbs-up.

Every once in a while, something will come along in life that just feels *right*. Those crazy friends you stay up waaaaaay too late at night with; the homemade, 6-hour-smoked BBQ ribs your dad cooks; that band you love, or movie you've seen a hundred times. You can't quite put your finger on it, but something about it just makes you feel fuzzy. Like it's good for you.
I'd never played Deus Ex before Human Revolution. I've heard of the franchise, but always had other games to play. But now, having played HR this spring, picked up the original this summer, and begun waiting for Mankind Divided this fall - this game feels right as rain.
It's not perfect. The graphics are fine, but a little outdated. The bosses can be irritating - I turned down the difficulty, just so I could get past them. There isn't much incentive for run-and-gun combat, though it's certainly not *terrible*.
But make no mistake, Human Revolution is good. The story is complex, well-told and well-developed. The characters are memorable, and easy to get attached to. Some intriguing moral choices are present, and the ending is nothing if not extraordinary. I felt a heaviness entering that final area (which I won't spoil), a feeling that told me this game resonates with me.
And it does. The dichotomy between "natural" humans and augmented "augs" is told beautifully, and at times poignantly.  Sometimes the lines between "good guys" and "bad guys" get murky and blurred, and you have to stop and think about whether your actions are right or wrong. Or even, if it really matters (and I mean that in a good-job-devs way).
The music is sensational. Michael McCann is a great composer, and this game is living proof. The "Icarus" theme (AKA - the song you hear in the HR trailer) is one of my all-time favorite video game compositions, both mesmerizing and haunting. In fact, let me give a shoutout to the game's whole sound-design execution: it's immersive, it's bold and it's beautiful.
Stealth in this game...I'm sure there's a gazillion other reviews about it, so I'll just say it's fantastic. Loads of fun.
And in the end, that's what this game is. Loads of fun. It's a game I wish I'd picked up years ago, wish I had time in my life to play over and over again - I spent roughly 44 hours on my full playthrough.
But though I may not have the days to waste, you do. So pick up Human Revolution today, play it, get hyped for Mankind Divided this August. It's because of HR that MD is one of my most-anticipated games in years. It just feels...right.
When a video game does that, you know it's earned every penny.

The Numberlink puzzles in this game ultimately boil down to trying to fill all the space on the board rather than trying to connect the nodes, and have numerous possible solutions. I never felt that any level was hard, challenging, or interesting. Most of the puzzles feel very empty, and have only a tiny number of nodes for the board size (for example several puzzles on a 10x10 board have only 8 nodes that need connecting). This leads to puzzles that have dozens if not hundreds of possible solutions, most of which feel extremely trival and obvious. Interestingly the short Wikipedia page on Numberlink puzzles says "It is considered that a problem is well-designed only if it has a unique solution and all the cells in the grid are filled", something that isn't true for any level except maybe the first. The 'intended' solutions to the puzzles quickly become obvious after doing several of the levels and pretty much all consist of unnecessarily long straight lines that needlessly wrap around each other. It feels as if the puzzles are generated based on a valid solution, but most of those base solutions aren't remotely close to how a human would connect the resulting puzzle. This makes intuitive solutions feel unintended with tons of zig-zags in the path just to fill space. An example of the issues mentioned here can be seen in the following level (it was level 25, not one of the intro ones) or by looking at a guide of the game showing level solutions:
The minimalist UI works well for the puzzles, and it probably the best part of the game, but there's just a plethora of other issues that detract from the gameplay (the same issues the free Lines game suffers from). After every level you're returned to the level selection screen rather than moved to the next puzzle, which leads to tons of unneeded loading time. Other than the first couple, the levels don't seem to be ordered according to any pattern, with large puzzles followed by smaller ones, then back again. The UI buttons are abriviated to single letters which obscures their meaning. People shouldn't have to ask in Discussions what the buttons do, the UI should make it clear. When moving the cursor quickly, the game would sometimes not pick up on the motion or briefly display multicolored trianges on the board. This is particularly annoying when the solutions to most levels are very clear from the start. The sound, which I listened to only briefly quickly felt repetitive, but most importantly wasn't relaxing at all, and I found the game much enjoyable when it was entirely muted.
In my mind, the most glaring issue with the game is the pointlessly spammy achievements. The game has nearly 600 achievements with only an hour of gameplay. The first 50 levels award 8 achievements every time you complete a level, which means the unlocks just scroll and scroll nonstop at the beginning of the game. Then levels 51-75 don't award any achievements, and levels 76-100 start giving 8 achievements each again. The achievements don't even relate to the game in any way, most achievements are just random words or phrases. What's the point of achievements if you aren't achieving anything when you get them? It was due to the pointless achievements that I opted to play the game on another account (hence low playtime).
There's just so many things wrong with the execution of these puzzles, I just can't recommend it under any circumstances. If you're willing to look past the issues of the game, still then I don't recommend this game, just play the Lines Free. It is the same exact game except without a pricetag. If you're keen on purchasing a game of this type, I'd recommend Dots Extreme. Same Numberlink concept, significantly improved execution and variety of puzzles.

From what I can tell, Valve essentially developed this so they would have a controller to go with their Steamlink. At some point, instead of developing games like people want them to, they got it into their heads that playing PC games on a TV from a coach was something a huge amount of people have been clamoring for. It isn't, but all the same here we are with a gamepad whose primary function is to provide decent emulation of a keyboard and mouse for playing PC games from a distance.
It fails miserably at this goal. I've tried it in a variety of games of different genres, and at the absolute best it merely achieves 'not too terrible', and rarely even that. It's most abysmal in FPS's, and this is coming from someone who plays quite a few shooters on consoles with gamepads, so I'm not being some kind of KB+M purist. Killing Floor 2 was an actively unpleasant experience with the Steam Controller. CSGO? Forget it. Completely lost cause, and that's not just my opinion, a friend who really likes the Steam Controller and plays a ton of CSGO is of the same view. Hilarious, considering they sell CSGO skins for the thing...
Anyway, what about strategy games? Lots of reviews say it's okay for that, right? Not in my experience. There's simply no substitute for a mouse for such games, and that's the end of it. The touchpads aren't anymore a viable replacement than analog sticks are (and that's why you rarely see RTS on consoles).
Let's talk about those haptic feedback touchpads, one of the chief gimmicks of the Controller. They're touted as the next step, the futuristic replacement for analog sticks. Pure ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. They're♥♥♥♥♥ 'Despise' is the proper word for how I feel about them. But first, what actually are they? They're touchpads, like those ♥♥♥♥♥♥ things on laptops that no one ever uses because they always get a USB mouse instead. The 'haptic' part is that they have tiny motors underneath (that make an obnoxious creaking sound when in use that fortunately can be turned off). That's it. It's a touchpad that slightly vibrates. Is it better than a laptop touchpad? Yeah. Is it good? No. It's crap as a mouse, and worse as a substitute for a second analog stick.
And there are two of these atrocious things, the second is the replacement for a traditional D-pad. What's that? You didn't like the old 360 D-pad? Well how about no physical D-pad at all, ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥? This left pad is actually worse than the right one, and I've seen a fair amount of discussion even among people who like the Steam Controller that it really needs a proper D-pad. It defaults to being the D-pad, but it's just a second touchpad (with a slight indentation in the shape of the traditional plus symbol), and you can remap it to be whatever you want.
Which brings me to the customizability. It has plenty of that. Every button (including the two additional button pad things on the interior underside) can be mapped to anything you want, deadzones and sensitivities can be changed at will, and that's just the start. There's also a (clunky, with no search bar) system to download other peoples configuration profiles. But all the software customization in the world won't help fundamentally bad hardware. The touchpads are♥♥♥♥♥ The face buttons are comically small, and in an odd position. I'm not actually going to say this layout is inherently terrible, I'd be interested to see someone make an Xbox or Playstation controller with this layout and with analog sticks, it might actually be good. But with the Steam Controller, you'll frequently accidentally brush the right touchpad while reaching for the face buttons.
Build quality is fine. It's not up to the standard of a Dualshock 4 or Xbox One gamepad, but it's better than the Dualshock 2 and 3. It has a comfortable heft to it. The construction, where it's reversed compared to every other gamepad and rises up into your hands instead of having downward facing handles, is...okay. It's fine. It doesn't feel terrible, but it's not some revolutionary advancement either. I can take it or leave it.
I should also note, because this may be a dealbreaker for some people, that it doesn't have proper rumble. Currently there's an optional beta feature you can turn on or off in software that provides a kind of improvised rumble with the haptic motors, but it's very weak and frankly pathetic.
Okay, I don't like it at all as a KB+M substitute, what about purely as a gamepad, for games designed for a gamepad? Meh. I actually bought this because my 360 gamepad was getting rather frayed and worn, and hey, Black Friday sales. At the best, which was in DiRT 3, it was equal to the 360 controller. Equal, not better. And this was entirely because I didn't have to use the touchpads to drive. The single analog stick that the Steam Controller comes with is perfectly acceptable. It even has texturing on the side similar to the Xbox One controller. If it had two of these and a proper D-pad, I might like it. But then it wouldn't really be the revolutionary advancement Valve wants it to be, would it? The early prototypes didn't even have this single stick, so sure were they are the superiority of haptic feedback. Hah. While writing this it occurs to me that they probably went with these all digital pads because of the customizability they opened up, rather than any real conviction that haptic feedback is THE FUTURE.
Again, I simply don't like the haptic touchpads, and find them an awful replacement for a proper analog stick. So that right there throws out a huge amount of games, and the second touchpad replacing the D-pad throws out even more. I do a lot of emulation of older game consoles, and was led to believe Valve had basically created the ultimate emulation gamepad. Very possibly, if you like the haptic feedback pads (and plenty of people do, apparently). One interesting feature is that the Steam Controller has dual stage triggers, which means it can properly emulate a GameCube gamepad. That's a genuinely cool feature (shame about the rest of the controller...).
Speaking of emulators, there's a bit of a software-side problem on that front. The Steam Controller doesn't support XInput; everything has to be done through Steam (because closed ecosystems are one of the best things about PC gaming, right?). What this means is you can't simply plug your controller in, go into an emulators settings, and map the buttons as you want. There is a third-party program that can enable XInpuit support, but it's inelegant and works by fooling the computer into thinking the Steam Controller is a 360 gamepad. At that point you might as well just use an actual Xbox controller. The actual process of mapping out keys with the Steam Controller involves binding a function to a keyboard key, and then binding that key to a button on the gamepad. You know, like that janky Joy2Key program, though this is far more refined, but it's the same principle.
Ultimately though, you shouldn't take this (or any) review as gospel. The Steam Controller is something you absolutely have to try yourself before deciding on. Find a friend who already has one and use theirs for a while, or try it out in a store display or something. Decide for yourself if you can tolerate, or even fall in love with, the haptic touchpads.
In the end I obviously don't like it, and hope to hell other developers don't think of adopting haptic feedback as a replacement for analog sticks. I plan to sell the thing to a friend who actually likes it, and replace my battered 360 pad with an Xbox One controller. This is a damn shame, because the Steam Controller was the only one of Valves hardware projects I had any interest in at all.
