I've been using this controller for a few days and I can say it works like a charm, although with some caveats.
It's a great device to play any game with on the couch, if you're willing to get used to the touchpads and do a lot of tinkering.
It does exactly what it says on the box, it enables you to play any game, regardless of it being a keyboard-and-mouse or controller type game.
The community support is superbe, every game has a list with most used, community created layouts that make any game playable with the controller.
That said, you'll tinker with those settings until you got something you can comfortably play the game with and you'll have to reconfigure it for almost every game.
But once you got a configuration that works for you it feels smooth and fun to play with the controller.
At one point I forgot I was using track pads and completely immersed in a game, without having to look down to see what my hands were doing.
The only downside to the controller is when you're using it as hybrid input, with some buttons mapped to controller input and others to keyboard-and-mouse.
Per example, when playing Just Cause 3, I mapped most buttons to controller buttons but I mapped the right track pad to mouse movement for accurate aiming, because using the track pad as a virtual analog stick feels a bit weird to me...
Because of this, the tool tips in JC3 kept swapping from controller inputs to keyboard inputs, because they change based on the last input the game received.
Other than that, after figuring out the controls myself and learning to ignore tool tips, the game played fine using the steam controller.
Funnily, I've found that browsing the internet is actually pretty fun with the controller. Using the right pad as mouse, the left as a scroll wheel and being able to summon a virtual keyboard with the "back" button works alike a charm, and feels a lot more relaxed than having both hands on the desk.
I would certainly recommend this controller if you're looking for a way to play your entire steam catalog from your couch and if you like to tinker with new things. It's a really inventive piece of hardware that allows for a lot of new ways to play your games,

The controller is pretty good. It has enough weight to make it feel solid, without being tiring to hold. It fits comfortably into your hands, so you won't get tired with prolonged use. Be aware, however, that the controller itself does not have a slot to store the much more fragile wireless dongle, and if, like me, you decide to leave it in your usb port when you put it in your backpack, it will shatter into a billion pieces. It would be nice if there were a way for me to buy a new one, and even better if they included a stoage slot with the controller, but, well, c'est la vie. All in all, would still recommend.

This is actually a pretty good game. Endless Space is a Real Time Turn Based Science Fiction Strategy. Yeah, something like that. Basically turns happen simultaneously and next turn begins when everyone clicks "end turn". You have quite a lot of races to choose from, and if you don't like them you can create your own races from the other races' set parameters.
The first thing that hit me is that the lore of the Endless universe is absolutely stunning and well thought out. They have many mainstream sci-fi cliches but also very creative and sometimes funny technology tree. The first time you play this game you would think that it has a storyline due to the immersion and random events etc. The scope of the game, within some couple hundred games, is huge: you evolve from a species habiting one single fluffy terran/jungle/ocean/arid planet in a faraway galaxy into a galactic superpower with the ability to colonize gas giants and tear down space-time. What I really like is that they have actually managed to keep the game interesting even into the late game. For example, your population can be hard to manage, at least in the start (you can't expand too quickly or they will get very unhappy), but they won't get pushy and won't drag you to too many details. One way they have done this is that battles are pretty straight forward and there's really no strategy there, except good scouting and finding out how your adversary is equipped so you can counter him/her in the rock-paper-scissors battle mechanic. Hero is a must in a battle, and heroes can really boost your stuff, also when assigned as planet governors.
On higher difficulties and versus multiple enemies a lot of things are luck based. You can simply end up in a bad spot with a cheating AI with no way out. Also the fact that moving of ships & battles is somewhat weird, it actually happens in real time, and is not turn based is a pretty stupid mechanic especially vs AI. Sometimes you would want to move ships between fleets before combat but you can't because the other player forces you to enter combat. I suppose the point here is to cut waiting times in multi player so that turns can happen simultaneously. I have not played MP so I can't say anything about that, although I would "guess" that the game's balancing probably favors single player.
In single player you can easily beat all opponents on easier difficulties, but the game gives you lots of options for handicapping yourself. Too bad that AI is mostly quite stupid, and like many other games, higher difficulties only give bonuses for AI and handicaps for the player or make the AI cheat but I guess that's the only way to make challenging AI's in strategy games... One real point of discontent is the planet menu, it is really hard to organize when you have a lot of things queued, and there is no "bring to top of queue"-button. This is really frustrating if you want to manage things yourself. You can always automate buildings though, but it's not very feasible if you are playing vs 8 AI's in endless difficulty and need to be pretty precise about things. In the trading system the AI is pretty smart though, and is really difficult to cheat.
Ok, so I wouldn't pay 20€ for this game, but definetely recommend it especially if you get it on sale. If you are looking for the ultimate competitive strategy experience, then I don't think that this game is it. However, it can be quite fun to play. I also have Dungeon of the Endless and recommend that as well.

Let's keep my review simple. I will assume you know what a 4X space game is about and just list how Endless Space fares in my opinion.
What Endless Space does really well:
- Impressive graphics
- Keeps micromanagement surprisingly low
- Balanced tech-tree
- Even with differences in research levels, battles are still not one-sided
- The KI opponents are quite capable diplomats. Where I usually NEVER accept an offer from KI-opponents in other games, the "Endless Space" ones managed to "sell" me deals by offering the right incentives.
What it does okay (meaning it's nothing special):
- Several ways to win
- Different species and the option to create your own
- The KI opponents are quite good although they do get an unfair ingame advantage. I would prefer to be able to choose their difficulty AND the amount of "advantage" they get seperately.
- Diplomatic options have to be researched. While it does make for an interesting game mechanic I would still prefer to have all diplomatic options from the start.
What is missing:
- No espionage, sabotage, inciting rebellions etc.
- There is basically NOTHING besides the respective faction-intro to evoke some atmosphere in the game. Even when you finally win you only get a small picture of your faction and a rather neutral text telling you that you've just achieved economic / military / scientifiy victory.
Summary
All in all I would give it 4 out of 5 stars. It's very good and addictive but putting some atmosphere in there (voice-overs, a few animated messages etc.) would go a long way. Having some espionage and full access to diplomatic functions from the start would also help to make it even better.

I'm conflicted about this title...
The concept is hilarious and the quick, team-based gameplay is loads of fun - but the developer made some unfortunate and frankly sketchy-looking decisions that cast the game in the worst possible light. Appearances are that the dev used the steam early-access program and general user-base to beta-test a title meant for ps4. To hear the CEO tell it, he "lost" most of his PC-side team (unsure if that means an exodus, routine "game's done" layoffs or infighting that lead to terminations) and PC patches CANNOT be done anymore until the PS4 title provides enough income to hire a new team. That may be totally accurate and honest - but no one on steam is going to give a♥♥♥♥♥♥past "there's no content/patches". We tend to go from steam reviews, to Full/halfchan, reddit - anywhere - and we tell everyone who will listen that this game is dead and the developer fleeced us. Even if intentions were different and best efforts were made - they have done and we have every right to be fed-up.  The way this title has shaken out mirrors the entire reason I'm starting to avoid any "indie" title or developer at this point. The steam community has thrown a lot of money, time and word-of-mouth behind "indie devs" who have an interesting  concept, but too much ego - or not enough business experience or talent, etc  to finish their title. Then there's EOR. Great concept. They got micro-transactions nearly perfect. Game itself is an imperial ♥♥♥♥ton (3 metric assloads) of fun. Regardless, it's still a shell of a game - even compared to what the ps4 version includes. Most insultingly, our version DID HAVE the campaign mode at one point. It was taken_away_from_us and we were left with nothing but co-op matches. Given the size of the player base, 50-90% of participants in EVERY match will be bots with aim-bot level AI. All this while their steam videos still advertise the campaign mode on steam.
All that said, there are ways out of the hatestorm for EOR - but very few. Their options are basically these:
A. Do whatever it takes to get PC content rolling again. If they believe in their product as much as they expect us to do,  actions speak loudest.
B. Admit they ♥♥♥♥ed-up, admit they cannot/have no intention to restart PC development for this title...and then OPEN IT UP TO THE MODDING COMMUNITY. We'll take it and make our own content and they can concentrate on PS4. No, they won't be able to monetize it. No, it will no make them rich and important - but it's the right ♥♥♥♥ing thing to do at this point, for the PC end.
Lastly, C. Roll it all up and go away. I hate this option, but they aren't winning any battles at the moment. In fact, every single CEO post we see restarts the brushfire of loathing (tm) online. They need a good-faith gesture to get out in front of this - and it needs to be a big one.
TL:DR: This game is rude, nude and socially hilarious. 10/10 - I love this game and am having a blast - except that I can't recommend it with a clear conscience.  So "not recommended until fixed" given that the dev seems to have ♥♥♥♥ed us and gutted our version in favor of a ps4 release, which gets 100% of the updates, while we get excuses.♥♥♥♥♥♥like this from "indie" devs is dry-humping my last ♥♥♥♥in' nerve... I haven't taken the time to make a top 10 games of all time (for me, personally, of course) list, but if I did, I'm fairly certain this game would go on it. If you liked the original Deus Ex (I thought it was alight), or if you liked Vampire The Masquerade Bloodlines (that would be #1 on my top games list), you would be likely to enjoy this game. It's the same premise: small hub areas populated with NPCs who have a few quests/missions for you. Some of these missions are clearly to complete the game, while others are to get money and experience to improve your character and arsenal. You can save your skill points and spend them at any time, so you can be bold and invest them all as soon as you get them, or you can hold off on spending those points until you see a must-have skill to take care of a situation that's troubling you (i.e. a breakable wall or movable vending machine you need an upgrade to handle.
You get experience points just from finding multiple paths through places, so it's very beneficial to search each nook and cranny, and you'll likely find more experience and ammo by doing so. Inventory space is limited, and if you're a total miser with your items like me, then you'll have to sell some things at shops, or drop the least awesome items you have. You could just pick a spot on the hub map and dump your crap there that you don't need, and come pick it up later. That said, if your character is leaving the entire city to go to a different city (it's pretty obvious when this is happening), that's when you'll want to consolidate your stuff or lose those extra items forever. It's not very stressful, though. I get butthurt over this sort of thing, but it didn't even trouble me all that much on my three playthroughs (I completed non-Director's Cut twice and Director's Cut once...or maybe I did the original more than that? I can't recall. I digress!).
If you sell a lot of items and don't just buy whimsically, you'll have tons of money. Have one gun you want to fully upgrade? You can afford the parts, sure. You might want to wait and see if you get any from searching the various levels, though, because you find a lot of parts for free.  Long story short, don't go nuts with your cash and you'll have plenty. I always had piles more than I needed, while another one of my Steam friends was bankrupt pretty much the whole game.
Sneaking is easier than fighting, and despite me sucking at video games, I whooped this game on the highest difficulty, because if you're sneaky, it's hardly any tougher than the easier difficulties. You're also rewarded with more XP by using stealth non-lethal takedowns. You can beat this game and only kill the bosses, in fact. Heck, there's an achievement for it; same for setting off no alarms (one alarm goes off at the top of a building in a cutscene, but it's scripted and does not count against you ;) ).
The story is pretty decent, though not amazing. Some of the characters are pretty memorable, though hardly as many as in VtM Bloodlines. This Director's Cut doesn't really change anything story-wise, except it inserts the DLC of the original game into this game as a natural part of the narrative. It's a little odd, but it sure beats having to load a separate game file and having to stop late-game for it to make any sense, as was the case before the Director's Cut. Also, everyone's (including mine) biggest gripe about the original release, is that the major enemies/bosses were only capable of being dealt with in combat, which made a hacker/sneaker character worthless and spoiled the multiple path and playstyle gameplay that the title proclaimed to have. In the Diretor's Cut, on the other hand, these bosses have hacking/stealth alternatives in the main game. You won't be doing stealth takedowns, but you can run like hell, hide a little, and activate very deadly tech which you can use to take out these bosses without firing a single shot from your own weapons.
Long story short, this game is great, and if you enjoy cyberpunk settings, first person RPGs with stealth, cybernetic abilities, and skill acquisition where you can hang onto points and spend them as you please, you would likely really enjoy this game.

Endless Space is a great take on classic 4X genre. It does have that "small studio" look and feel to it (high ratio of text to voice over for example), but what content is included and highly polished.
I think the biggest flaw of Endless Space is AI. It's not broken nor badly made - it's just not really convincing. Most players with some experience will notice mechanical actions taken by AI. Basically: when you already know how the game works, you can usually outdo AI every time. I think it's a bit of a trade-off: game is fairly complex (yet superb GUI makes it very clear and readable) and AI is just not really ready for the possible number of approaches to victory.
If you can find some other freaks that like this kind of games to play for several hours with you - great, you're all set. And if you don't - well, I've spent a 100 hours just playing mostly and having fun. Definitely got my money's worth.
Just one more thing: if you have just seen screens or bits of gameplay, you might not be aware: the 3D space battles are mostly eye-candy - you cannot order your ships around, you mostly sit and watch (there is rock-paper-scisors card system in place which is great, but still...). It's nice, but just an addition - most battles you're going to skip (auto-mode), because you know you're either screwed, or enemy is - so manual mode is just a waste of time.
I've pointed the bad things mostly. The good things, things you might like, you can instantly spot by looking at the game or some "let's plays" on YT - so no reason for me to list it out :)

Flawed, but still the best 4X space game since Galactic Civilizations 2.
At first, I didn't like the combat much, but after playing other 4X games, I have a new appreciation for it... It is a double edged sword. The battles are simplistic and often a crapshoot, but inspecting your enemies capabilities and employing the right cards goes a long way to winning a battle, even if most of them are countered. The tactical combat also keeps the pace of the game up and helps you understand what happens if you skip manual combat.
In more complex tactical battles in 4X games (e.g. Fallen Enchantress, AoW3), you never want to use auto-combat because the game will arbitrarily kill off units when you know you would never lose them in manual mode, so you end up going through the tedious process of a turned based tactical engagement in a one-sided fight just to make sure you can keep a veteran unit. Endless Space battles, while not nearly as complex, leave you the option to auto-resolve battles with confidence, which saves a lot of time while doing battles with an overpowering force - which in my experience encompass the majority of battles in 4X games. Icing on the cake; sometimes manual combat in Endless Space is worth it just because you want to actually  *see* your new fleet/commander/ship design make your enemy explode.
Long and short - plenty of reviews cover the simplistic tactical combat, even though it is more complex than Civilization V. If we take the tactical combat out of the equation, Endless Space is a near-perfect 4X game. You can design ships, empire management is meticulous, and there are many ways to win. If we do add in tactical combat, I'd rather be playing Total War, but I'm not always in the mood, nor do I have that kind of time. 3π/10.

MWO is unique in the world of modern games, the F2P model is solid (though I find the prices a little high, you are not forced to buy anything to be competitive).  It's definitely more of a sim than a shooter, heat management and trigger discipline net you more kills than charging in with guns blazing.
A couple things you should know before you drop in:
1. Stay with the team - A solo 'Mech gets scrapped in short order, always.
2. Press 'R' befpre you start shooting at something - Your target lock is shared with all other players on the team, by letting us know what you're shooting, you might get some assistance befor you get scrapped.
3. Trigger Discipline (this is NOT CoD with robots) - As you fire weapons, your 'Mech begins to heat up, keeping an eye on your heat gauge and knowing how much heat your weapons generate per shot is vital to your success.  If you overheat, your 'Mech shuts down until heat levels are within spec again, leaving you an immobile target in the middle of a battlefield.
4. Jump into VoIP!  - MWO is a game that heavily emphasises teamwork, grab a headset and coordinate.  Even if you don't have a strategy, you can call out targets that are too far away to target lock, and you can call for help if you get ambushed.  The difference between winners and losers is coordination.
5. Read up! - MWO has some great guides available to help the new MechWarrior in understanding his place on the battlefield, read some of them (Google is your friend) to get a leg up on the competition.

I bought the Steam Controller in its earliest batch over a year ago and I really wanted to like it. It's okay at most things, but not truly exceptional at any. When playing games that are heavily mouse-reliant, like FPS or strategy, it works, but it always just feels frustrating because it's not nearly as good as a keyboard+mouse. When playing platformer or action games, it never feels as comfortable or responsive as a standard controller. It's also worth noting that over the life of this controller, I've encountered countless software glitches for it, including things like double input, disappearing customization, and crashing Big Picture on Mac (I mostly game on Windows, but I used it a bit with Mac on a vacation once).
I have heard that, with enough customization and learning, this controller gets better to use. However, I have at least a few dozen hours with it and, even trying out lots of customization, I still don't really like it overall. These days I basically just use it as a wireless touchpad for my HTPC and the handicap controller when I have some friends over for local multiplayer games.

I really did try to like this controller. I played with it soley for about a year before finally giving up and going back to my simple logitech controller. Here's my experience with it:
I got used to the trackpads, even thought it was cool. When I went back to dual-sticks, however, I suddenly realized how easy those were, and how much effort I was expending to get good with the trackpad. It really shouldn't be that way.
The controller is big. A little too big, to be honest. Always felt bulky in my hands. Which is funny, because....
The ABXY buttons are too small and too close together. Which is silly, given the large size of the controller. I got used to the placement for the most part, but I would still occasionally press the wrong button. Maybe I have fat thumbs, but I've never had that issue on any other controller I've played with.
The ability to customize this controller really is amazing, though. And there's lots of different scheme's people have come up with for each game that you can try out. My problem though, is that I was always looking for a control scheme that matched a regular controller. The controller never felt "right" for any game I played. First person shooter? Mouse and Keyboard felt infinitely better. 3rd person action game (Assassin's creed, witcher 3, etc) felt close enough to be playable. Top-down RTS never felt right, and I never felt like I could get the precision I needed.
Maybe that's what it boils down to. Precision. I never felt precise with the controller. For games where that unnecessary, the controller was fine. But when precision is needed, I found myself switching to Mouse and Keyboard every time.
I suppose, in the end, its going to come down to whether you like trackpads or not. I got used to them, sort of, but never felt precise with them, which ultimately led me to letting go of the controller and switching back to a normal one. I'd be interested in seeing what a Steam Controller 2.0 might be like, though.

Endless Space is a lovely looking 4X game, but has a number of strategic flaws which, while adding elements to gameplay, don't make sense (and hence, break suspension of disbelief), and don't work in an entertaining manner.
Economy is well abstracted, and there are lots of options for expanding your economic foundations, but there are some factors which are largely out of direct player control -- population happiness is one of them.  Happiness affects everything, as in most 4X games, but unlike other 4X games, you don't seem to be able to invest much into helping your populace be happy (commenters claim this ability is merely hidden along particular tech tree paths, which seems restrictive -- do you have to choose those paths to succeed?).  Wars, in particular, make your people unhappy -- to the extent where an aggressive military playing style is basically out of the question.  The game's design limits the options for the "kind" of player you want to be -- you basically must play by the rigid set of rules the developer has laid down, or you are penalized to the point where you simply cannot beat even the normal AI.
Wars must be routinely tempered with diplomacy, and expansion must be limited during growth periods... or your expansion will fail, no matter how large your military, economy, etc.  Conquering opposing races is almost out of the question, unless it is done over a protracted period.  DIfferent races have different features, in this regard, but the trouble with such a setup is that your playstyle is largely known from the outset, by every other player in the game.  This basically boils down to a rock-paper-scissors "you chose your strategy, now live with it" game that is largely decided before the game starts.
Space combat is visually spectacular, and has some interesting tactical twists, in the form of a rock-paper-scissors tactic system.  Ship design, is fairly involved, even though weapons basically boil down to 3 types, with levels 1 throgh 5.  Ship designs can vary the amount of weaponry and defenses they have, but the game often boils down to something of a "who researched the right techs vs the other guy" fight, yielding a boring, balanced research mechanism as the most effective in basically any game, unless you know your opponent is researching rocks, papers, or scissors in particular.
The most severe issue with space combat, however, is that fleet size is limited by elements of the tech tree.  You can build a fleet of 50 cruisers, but can't put more than 1-2 in a fleet, plus a couple destroyers/corvettes, without researching the right aspects of the tech tree, and even then, the numbers are quite limtied.  Thus, an economically superior empire cannot necessarily win with sheer numbers, as each fleet engagement is limited by the number of possible ships in the fleet -- a small empire, with a fleet of 9-13 ships, with a similarly hard-to-come-by "hero" admiral (also limited to a very small number, unless you increase the number with tech), could conceivably defeat an armada of 50+ ships of the same technology level, based upon these nonsensical fleet-size limitations.  As such, increasing your effective fleet size is nearly the most important aspect of space combat, all by itself.  This enforces military balance between empires of radically different military sizes and capacities, effectively making large-fleet empires which rely primarily upon exploitation a weak approach, compared to empires which favor other 4X techniques. I would argue that the limitation is so restrictive, as to diminish strategic & economic options to the point of boredom.  No zerging, due to small fleet sizes.  No concentrated attacks.  Ship design heavily favors quality over quantity/inexpensive, etc.  Your opponents will be exactly the same as you, unless they're looking to lose through neglect of a balanced approach.
The inclusion of "heroes" in interesting, except that you are limited to a very small number of them.  It is nowhere near as easy to acquire, or utilize a hero in ES, as it is in a game like, for example, Heroes of Might and Magic.  You may have 1-2 heroes that are "Admirals" typically (the rest are typically governors of single star systems), but those heroes may not command any more vessels than are allowed by the fleet size limitation.  Thus, the benefit to a hero in a small empire is much larger than that of a hero in a large one -- and large empires can be easily overwhelmed by a sum of smaller nations, simply due to the number of heroes involved, and the fleet size restrictions.  Even 2 vs 1 can be almost impossible odds under these conditions, and the happiness issues with warfare.
Diplomacy is limited in much the same fashion as combat is -- by options in the tech tree.  A player cannot even offer a peace treaty without researching the idea, first.  Thus, much of the diplomacy of a game is hidden until the mid-way point of a game, and even then its fairly limited.
WIth all these important techniques locked up, via the tech tree at the beginning of each game, the tech tree seems reminiscient of a "tutorial" system, that locks down interesting aspects of the game in literally every game you ever play.  Since many of these options are fundamental to basic gameplay, as expected in most 4X games, your traversal through the tech tree is pretty much forced to visit these nodes each time... or you lose.  The nodes are spread out amongst the branches of the tree, and neglecting any of them seems like a typically fatal flaw... thus balance, balance, balance, at all times.
Endless Space boils down to an exercise in walking down the middle of the road.  Straying too far in any direction is just an expensive diversion, and won't work against the AI, or in any interesting MP game.  No blitzkriegs, surprise attacks, radical technology developments, or diverse battle tactics allowed.

First and foremost, if you are into the Japanese anime style mechs that have faces, lazer swords, and move around like the mutant offspring of a fighter jet and Jackie Chan (shame on you) you should bail right now. This is a tank warfare game where the tanks happen to have legs and are designed with that classic Battletech 80's retro vibe. For those of us that envision mechs as believable (abiet cheesy) machines of war, you've come to the right place. These things move with a sense of weight and momentum that simply isn't conveyed by other vehicular combat games. The torso section of the mech moves independently of the legs (think tank turret), and the arms can in many cases actuate indepently of the torso. All these factors require you to think about motion and positioning in a way most other first person games never touch on. This is also a fiercely team-oriented game, so all you lone wolves out there best stick with CoD.

As a three year vet, I love this game.  There are too many reviews to wade through for me to egotistically believe that a long meandering review will cut through the rest.  So I'll keep this short and sweet.
It's a free to play FPS game where giant stompy robots shoot each other in 12 v 12 matches.  To the new Steam players that are joining us: this is not a simple game.  Your twitch skills from other shooters will definitely help you, and may even give you an edge over the old timers eventually.  But prepare for a steep learning curve.  There is SO MUCH nuance to understanding this game, let alone succeed at it, that no one will be an elite pilot without some serious time logged.  But, if you want a challenge, this game is it.
My advice to you, the new player, is this.
Join the game.  Jump into the tutorial system and get the hang of the basics of movement and shooting.  Play 10 matches or so in quickplay to get a taste of combat.  Save up that starting cash and play trial mechs at first.
THEN: Ask in team chat or General chat if there are any vets that would be willing to help answer your questions and show you around.  You can lone wolf all you want in this game, but there is simply too much to understand if you don't ask questions.  Established units all have teamspeak servers and would love to help you learn the game.  Please take advantage of the existing community.  Most of us are drinking beers, having fun and are ready and willing to share both with anyone that wants to learn.  You don't need to make any commitment to joining units.  The community of vets truly want the game to succeed and grow, and we know that the best way to do that is to tutor new players.
When you know what you're doing, you've built a stable of mechs that fit your playstyle and you drop with a group of pilots that you have grown comfortable with, there is simply no better gaming experience to be had anywhere.

Peiper and the Devil Dogs are a great group of guys that switch between Wolf and Steiner and enjoy roleplaying.  FFI is a growing and emerging comp merc unit that switches between Clan and Inner Sphere and are a blast to hang out with.   6RCT, 5RCT, OCP, LoP and on and on and on all have vets that play every day and would love to help you out.

MWO once had been advertised as "a thinking man's shooter". And this almost feels like an understatement when you have spent enough time in the game.
This is certainly not a game for those who love fast-paced shooter mechanics that allows for a prolongued series of kills via headshots. This is not how this game works. Nor is it particularly well suited for those who want to outshine their teammates.
This game is all about teamwork, about coordinating your own movement with that of eleven other players. There is no way that an individual player can turn the tides of the battle unless he learns to read his team and communicates with them.
Outside of the matches there is a lot to do too. The mechlab is about the ultimate customisation tool in a game. There are very few real limitations besides what type of weapons a specific mech can mount. Other than that the level of customisation is pretty limitless. Don't get me wrong. For the average player there is a way to build things right or wrong. But for really good players there is really non such things. I saw people wreck all sorts of faces in mechs I wouldn't last a minute in and I am not the worst player myself being onboard since closed beta.
The downside of the game is the immense grind that has to be put in the game. I would highly recommand to anyone who starts the game to invest 30$ and get 6000 MC for it which is the real world currancy in the game. That will buy you up to 20 character slots. And you will need these as it takes you 3 variants of a mech to actually completely level it up.
But for those who can endure the grind and are willing to put in effort, skills and a lot of thinking there is hardly a better shooter out there. Escpecially for free.

Sadly, this game is not a good game in the Ultimate Ninja series. It really pales in comparison with others.
The Story mode is now basically a series of battles. There is no free roam involved here, but I can understand why: the story takes place during the Fourth Ninja War, and it would be strange to see Naruto do missions in the middle of the war. However, the transitions between battles are quite rubbish in my opinion. The cutscenes are basically just screenshots from anime or static pictures. For comparison, in Storm 3 you had beautiful fully animated cutscenes. Those static frames made me so bored, that I finished the Story mode half way through and I doubt I will go back to it.
The Adventure mode is basically free roam taking place after the end of Naruto. Sadly, all the locations are copy-paste from previous games and most of them are just one room with no additional sublevels. The world therefore feels very small and not very fleshed out. I think there was one cave in Ultimate Ninja 4 that had more sublevels than the entire map in Storm 4. And now we come to missions, which are probably the most horrendous part of this game: they are all more or less about one thing:
For me, romantic aspect in a shonen series and especially in "Naruto" is completely secondary and I would prefer to immerse myself into the Naruto's ninja world by doing actual missions and quests.
The only positive I have noticed is that the port to PC is pretty good and works very well.
All in all, not recommended. Better grab Storm 3 and play that (I'm currently finishing it).

Metal Slug 2 isn't awful but it's the weakest game in the series by far, and SNK later released an updated version of it called Metal Slug X. I'd say that there's really no reason to buy this old and inferior version of the game. A) Metal Slug X is on Steam, so you can just play as that, as it's the superior version of Metal Slug 2. B) The port job by DotEMU isn't great. Metal Slug 2 definitely had plenty of slowdown when it was an arcade game - it was kind of notorious for it - but this Steam port has even *more* slowdown, and the visuals just look disappointingly blurry. C) This is 7 bucks or almost 8 dollars CAD, which I think is way too much to ask for a sloppy port of an unspectacular game. If you have any other way to play video games other than Steam, you can surely find an SNK collection or Metal Slug anthology that has this game on it along with other entries in the series.
If you *do* decide to get this version, it's got the same Metal Slug gameplay that everybody loves from the original, plus you get to pilot a couple of new vehicles and there are new weapons. This game also has a bit of globe-trotting in it, as you'll go to stages all around the world. The issue of cultural diversity is, of course, handled with all of the sensitivity that you can expect of a 90s arcade action game. It's fun for what it is and it's a good multiplayer diversion for 40 minutes, but the other games in the series are way better. I think this game is less dynamic and exciting than the original Metal Slug and nowhere near as epic as Metal Slug 3. It also has the worst final mission in the series, in my opinion.

It could be educational, and be a useful tutorial if you ever need to go beyond feild stripping your firearm. However it isn't that. It is a acheivment paced game. And for a game like this it is far to time comsuming, and in some ways complicated. For example in order to unlock a gun you may have to take a gun apart, and back together in a certain amount of time without help. Now that's not a bad skill or entirely bad, but for the game iteslf it is a pain, exspecially when its to unlock a gun you want, and you can't because you don't have the time to constantly memorize every part of firearm that you neither own, nor want to take the pain staking waste of time to do.
Honestly if you like that sort of thing be my guest, but it would be better just to look up videos of guns being dissasembled, rather than having to work your way up to unlocking anything you want to do. If it was just a game where you can choose any gun, and take it apart, and have the timed stuff be mini games then that would be great, but sadly it's not that, and it just isn't any fun. Well for me anyways. Because I would rather be shooting my real guns, or guns in video games, than wasting my time jumping through hoops just to look at one on the screen.

World of tanks blitz is a bit of an oddball in the libray of games tat Wargaming has to offer. It started out as a IOS port then that port became a steam port. It is also more in nature of a free to play game than its orignator with skins and decarative tanks a dozen. Its libary of tanks is also not as up to date than the orignal, but world of tanks console still lacks behind blitz ironicly.
But you know whats the reason why to play to game? Its not the fact that both casual and hardcore players can play. It is not the fact either that it is to progres compared to the orignal. It is not even nice simplistic controlls and subtle community.  It is the fact that blitz alot more enjoyable than the orignal world of tanks. Like its name sake, blitz is face paced, incredibly so. It is a completely different experince to that of the other world of tanks games. Matchs end less than a minimal 5 minutes! It does not take its self seriously either, which the orignal suffered from. World of tanks is not a tank simulator, nor is it a game based on the historical nature of tanks. Its about PLAYING tanks, nothing more,..nothing less.

An excellent reboot of a loved classic. It stays true to the Tribes look and feel, and is a blast to play.
I've heard lots of friends and colleagues bash the game for an (apparently) pay-to-win structure. This is simply not the case. Upgrades do take time to earn (but you'll get there if you simply play the game). A good number of the upgrades, in fact, make the game harder to play (from my perspective anyhow). In that way the game is as balanced as it can be; it is an FPS after all, so you need more than just a meta-game proficiency to be any good. Reaction time and motion prediction are skills that do you well here, this ain't no point-and-click adventure (MOBA players stay away; I dont want your filth in or around anything that I love :D )
The visuals in this game are excellent as well. Like I've said before, it stays true to the Tribes look and feel, but pushes the envelope further than it has ever been.

DOOM is one of the most fun FPS games I've played in quite a while. The action is very fast-paced and the gameplay is extremely satisfying. The formula is simple but I didn't find it repetitive and boring. It has enough variety to keep me at the edge of my seat almost all the time. The campaign is very well-designed and directed. You won't regret taking your time exploring an obscure spot because you most likely will find a secret or a collectible. I haven't played the multiplayer aspect yet, so I have nothing to say about that for now.
Another thing worthy of mention is that this game performs really well. I've never had a crash in my entire playthrough, (maybe except for the glitch in the achievements which forced me to replay the entire campaign!) and the game plays buttery smooth all throughout. Probably the only complaint I have for this game is the achievements, where almost half of it comes from the multiplayer aspect which will take you at least 100 hours to get. That doesn't make sense for me. Finally, the standard edition includes all the DLC so you don't have to worry about purchasing anything else.
If you like some fast-paced shooting game then I would highly recommend that you try this game. Now go and crack some demon skulls!

Well, I guess I'll take on the task of being the first reviewer to give a thumbs down to Metal Slug 2, but that's okay; none of the other reviews here mention most of what I'm going to be talking about, nor are they in-depth. So take great consideration when picking up this title. I'm a massive fan of the Metal Slug franchise, and while there's nothing exactly bad about Metal Slug 2 itself, we already have this game on Steam. Us, the fans, have been waiting almost a year for the next installment to be ported to Steam, was it 6? No. How about the amazing 7? Nah. Even 5? Nope. We get shafted with the inferior version of Metal Slug X. This game is already on Steam, just under a different name.
Yes, that's correct, inferior. SNK originally released Metal Slug X to be an updated version of Metal Slug 2, because there were bugs, glitches, and other issues with the arcade chips that were hard to fix. So not only did they fix those issues with X, they improved upon the game itself, and even added more content. There is a difference of 5% between X and 2, and it's mostly negligible. The bosses are the same for the most part, save for the last boss fight which is a good 10-15 minutes SHORTER in Metal Slug 2 than it is in X. Let me also take time to mention that there is no online co-op mode in this game, but there is in X! Even if you do not own X or 2 at this point, you should just go with X since it's longer, better, and has online co-op.
There is absolutely no reason to purchase Metal Slug 2, unless you're a die hard fan with $8 to throw down because you absolutely love the franchise and wish to support it. However, even as one of these die-hards, and having urged and encouraged many people to purchase these titles on Steam so that we can get more in the future, I feel incredibly shafted. Not only over the long wait, but knowing that there's less of a chance of DotEmu and SNK porting the remainder of the series if there isn't enough support to earn back what they at least put into spending to port these titles, only for them to give us something we already have instead of putting their time and resources into something that we don't have.
As for Metal Slug itself? The franchise is one of the greatest run-and-guns of all time. The series has a varying amount of characters, but in Metal Slug 2 and X you get your choice between four. There are six levels in this game, all of which will take you around 40-50 minutes to complete in total. The bosses are big, the levels are greatly detailed, you have a decent variety of weapons that will randomly drop for you such as the heavy machine gun and flamethrower, and the soundtrack is awesome, though not as great as in X. I have gone into more detail in the past about what Metal Slug is in general, and I recommend to take a look at my reviews for Metal Slug and Metal Slug X for that if you are not familiar with the series.
So the bottom line here is to just avoid Metal Slug 2 unless you're crazy about the series, or unless you want to keep supporting DotEmu and SNK's ports of the franchise. It's the same game as X, and if you don't have either just get X instead since it's the updated, longer, better, and has online co-op version of 2. I never thought I'd have something overly negative to say about Metal Slug, but I really cannot believe DotEmu and SNK have released this instead of any of the other 4 remaining titles. As well, I've seen a lot of people complaining about the "slow downs" and "FPS drops", as in the review sections of the other Metal Slug games, these people just have no clue what they're talking about. The game runs at 60 FPS, and the slow downs are intentional; as it was in the Mega Man Legacy Collection. It's how the games played in their original form, and these are true-to-original, great ports.

Deus Ex Human Revolution is a prequel to Deus Ex, which means you don't have to know about the first game, but I would still highly recommend playing the first Deus Ex at some point. Human Revolution was made by a different developer, but you can tell this different developer understood what made Deus Ex such a good game, and made a wonderfully moody and enjoyable game with a story that can keep you hooked and large environments to explore and missions to fulfill at your leisure, and using the methods you prefer. Sometimes you can get what you need simply by talking to someone and saying the right things, or maybe you could sneak around and spend an hour avoiding guards and getting your way behind everybody's back. Or kill everybody, I dunno, it's your game, you decide!
Only a few things are less good than in Deus Ex in my opinion:
- the boss fights can't be circumvented; most of those in Deus Ex could be avoided without too much trouble
- the leveling system is very simple, not very RPG-like unfortunately
- there's no swimming, the game feels more limiting with more closed maps than Deus Ex (but over a larger area)
- takedowns are shown from third perspective and often look completely unrealistic, where you pummel someone to the floor, and another guy like a meter (that's like maybe 3.281 feet) away didn't hear that? That's what happens if you don't put in ear plugs at concerts, kids!
- speaking of takedowns: they use up a whole battery? Maybe a bit much. I want the takedown system from Dishonored, that'd be perfect and slightly more resembling Deus Ex (in that it doesn't take you out of control and first person view)
None of these problems are deal breakers; I am a big fan of the game after all. Many things are imho much better than in Deus Ex:
- hacking mini game is actually fun
- from a gameplay perspective, the cover system allows for smoother game play: less doubt about when someone sees you
- it's much more beautiful; I really like the design
- the voice acting is also much better than in Deus Ex
So in short: there's no reason at all not to play Deus Ex Human Revolution. It offers choice and a lot of options in dealing with situations. You can play Deus Ex first if you haven't, but it's really not necessary. But it IS necessary that you play Deus Ex if you haven't already!

In my opinion, one of the best controllers one can get.
If you´re  like me, and spend a lot of time in desktop enviroment browsing etc. the steam controller is just superior compared to xbox or PS controllers.
I really like the design and layout of the controller, even though it has a steeper learing curve to get used to compared to other controllers. But with the amount of customization available to really tailor everything to you liking, for me is worth the time spent getting used to it.
I think many people are so used to the "standard" layout of controllers that if it doesent feel familiar immediately, it´s  no good. Like the lack of two joysticks is probably the most noticable difference.
But I think Steam has done the right thing and went outside the box, and have given many people exactly what they wanted with this piece of engineering.  Sure, there are always room fo improvement, but that goes for everything.
A few pros / cons:
Pros:
- Customization till the end of day ( even in-game! )
- responsive ( though not suitable for games like CS:GO )
- overall good build quality
- ergonomics
- double trackpads
- Battery-Life
Cons:
- Directional buttons in the pads can be a bit difficult to feel
- maybe a bit to light
- the configuration menu ( could use a bit of clarification on what does what. Maybe put more extensive examples in the description? )
Conclusion:
I higly recommend this product! And if you´re willing to give it a little time, you´ll end up with a far more competent controller than its competitors.

A couple things to note. (mixed review)
*an expensive toy
*an expensive toy that is sized differently from others (xbox, ps..)
*has a lot of problems working along with other Steam controllers. something to do with controller"mousepads" apparently. Games with classis xbox controller config work normally, on other games it takes pairing up a mix variety of controllers.. (easy solution is not to buy a 2nd Steam controller for now..)
*it often happens controller doesnt work "out of the box" on a new game. For the most part its easy and solvable, sometimes it is not. it really shines on games with countless hours on them. custom configs are awesome once one reaches the point of needing them..
*I play some racing games with it, and after getting used to it, its hard to go back to other controllers. the bottom backside two buttons are amazing for gear up/down, steering button feels softer than others (my thumb doesnt hurt)
*"partial support" games, or even normal ones.. it happens a game is unplayable even if we *can* play it, but cant aim fast, move accurately enough etc.. take info with a grain of salt. how do consoles deal with it, not having mouse and keyboard to fall back onto? xD
Long story short
**a bit like a relationship. it comes with the good and the bad. and problems. which ultimately served to raise the quality of my gaming experience. where it applies. exactly like a relationship...
Rating as not recommended since Steam controllers should mostly only be used in singular as is now. One per family max. where it applies.. Minus games where it doesnt work, its a wonderful piece of wonder plastic that develops into a stormy relationship soon enough.
If only there were two.. (facepalm)

The Steam Controller is quite possibly the single best controller ever made. It is easily the most versatile controller I have ever laid my hands on. No longer do you have to worry about games not being compatible with controllers because the Steam Controller is compatible with every Steam Game, you just have to configure it. Even if you don't feel like configuring it more likely than not someone has already made the perfect configuration for you! The Steam Controller also has two back plates which make controls with a controller much quicker and fluid. Never have I been able to switch from browsing youtube/reddit in my bed straight to gaming with the same controller. Also lets not forget how cheap it is. ---------------
As mentioned in my SS2 review, I can't get into the original Deus Ex, the hit detection is seemingly random and sporadic. This made it very difficult to play even though I enjoyed SS2 being an even older game than Deus Ex.
---------------
The main reason I enjoyed this game more than I should have is the theme of the game; human integration with technology and how it will impact society is a very recent topic (only within the past 10 years or so) and it's an idea that I have much interest in. The art direction for a future setting is almost perfect, not overdone like Bladerunner, but seemingly futuristic enough that it seems incredibly real and pragmatic reasoning to the Deus Ex-World development.
---------------
The gameplay for the most part rewards a stealthy approach and even changes the ending, a feature that most people like. Amusing diversion, after coming from Big WoT, which is often aggravating for soooo many reasons (other season World of Tanks players will know what I am talking about). The skills are easily transferable, but there are many nice features of this version.
1: Equipment is priced to the tiers of tanks played rather than being one large lump sum. Makes playing lower tier tanks better without having to shell out large amounts of credits, creating a major disparity between seasoned and newer players.
2: Crews are easier to train up and work across other tanks in the same category.
3: Lower tiers are more playable due to higher HPs and more moderate damage, making for more engaing play, whereas in Big WoT low tiers are just there to get through and forget about, or to go back and terrorize less experienced players, which is a♥♥♥♥♥♥move.
4: I've barely scratched the surface yet, but the general impression I get is that the Cult of the Stat ♥♥♥♥♥ is not as prevalent here (again, experienced WoT players will know), so it's refreshing.
5: NO ARTILLERY. This is probably THE most appealing aspect for Big WoT players.
6: More fluid combat. It's just nice to be able to run and gun without having to feel like you need to be Field Marshall Rommel to figure out what the heck is going on. Mini-Map is still important though (and a little hard to read in this version), so that's nice.
It's pretty funny, I got my first Raisainai's Hero's Medal after only playing four games, which was a real chuckle for me. Again, mini-map is still important. A more... palatable WoT experience, kind of like a light beer.

*Short personal summary of my experience with "The Lion's Song: Episode 1- Silence" as well as a fleshed out review*
Where to begin...
"The Lion's Song: Episode 1" has already intrigued me. With a short but effective narrative and with a beautifully paced arch, it is truly a great experience. Now, this is not a long game (or episode of a game). I managed to complete "Episode 1- Silence" in about fourty minutes. But in those fourty minutes...I felt like I was somewhere else. That I really was the main character (Wilma). That I really struggled alongside her with love, the composition of the piece. Truly magical. Her parents sends her away to Vienna, and it feels like they send me away. And her brother Otto, my brother Otto, is also sent away several years (I presume, don't take my word for it) later on the same train. And this is where the story begins.
Plot: 9,5/10
You play as a young girl named Wilma, an up and coming musician and composer who is currently learning from a man named Arthur in Vienna, Austria. Arthur requests a meeting with you to explain that he wants her to create a new piece; and make it the best she has ever composed. Wilma is stunned. "How am I supposed to write a piece when there is so much distractions around me" she asks. Arthur offers his cabin in the Alps as a refuge from Vienna. He sends her there the next day, and when she arrives, Wilma is filled with determination. She is going to compose her best piece yet.
A relativeley simple, yet elegant story. While some characters don't feel fleshed out enough (Arthur, her mom and dad and her little brother, Otto) the truth is they don't have to be. What is there is enough to keep the story moving forward and keep it intriguing all the way to the end.
Estethics (graphics in basic english): 10/10
I was first surprised by the design choice of making the entire game pixelated and in 2D. But it works so well. I would've probably not liked if this was a 3D game, it feels more like an indie title. So, great choice there by the developers. It suits the game perfectly.
Gameplay: 8/10
"The Lion's Song" is a point-and-click game. Now that surprised me, but in a good way. Point-and-click games have always been hit or miss for me. Either they work perfectly, or they fail miserably. But in this, "The Lion's Song" suceeds. It fits the story so well. Finding inspiration in your surroundings, blocking out distracting noises, choosing to pick up the phone or not. It just works. A problem is that there are very few hints in the game, so you have to find out for yourself how to make the piece. But when you do, it's oh so satsifying.
Final verdict: A strong 9/10
"The Lion's Song: Episode 1- Silence" is a breath of fresh air in a world populated by FPS:s. With a simple yet effective pixelated art style and a beautiful and elegant story, and with gameplay that genuinly suits the story it is trying to tell, "The Lion's Song" caught me offguard. I was not prepared to enjoy the game as much as I did. I can't wait for the next episode to come out, "Episode 2: Anthology" which follows an artist with a destiny...
Try it. It will not dissapoint you.

MWO is, and probably always will be, something of a work in progress. It has it's faults, but can be an amazing game as well.
Pros:
- BattleMech customization: They have struck a fairly good balance between the standard tabletop construction rules and a hardpoint system to prevent rediculous boating and encourage customization. You CAN make pretty much an kind of variant you want, even if it's not always smart (See the Cons)
- Variable gameplay: You can make your play as involved (or not) as you want. Quickplay gives you the ability to jump right into a match, which lasts for a maximum of 15 minutes. More depth can be had in Faction Play (also known as Community Warfare), where group play is strongly encouraged and players fight across various planets in the Inner Sphere. Keep in mind, this mode is scheduled for significant changes in the next few months (CW: Phase 3)
- Community: This can be a negative in any game, but MWO at least has the redeeming feature of a strong population of mature gamers and Battletech veterans to balance out the annoying trolls. You can find groups to match what you're looking for.
- Visuals: It's made by a small dev studio, and some of the graphics can show it at times, but they are rescued by an indredibly talented art department. Mech models in particular are almost universally superbly done.
- It's an F2P that is most assuredly NOT Pay2Win. Real life purchases are for cosmetics and boosters, as well as early access to newly released Mechs. It may take a month or two, but any mech that is initially released for $$$ will always subsequently be released for in-game currency
The Cons:
- Time-sink: Yes, it's a time sink. The grind can be pretty severe at times, as in-game earnings can take quite a while, especially if you are playing as a solo player.
- Release Schedule for mechs: This can be a matter of perspective. While the game is not pay2win, there is a tendency for new mechs to be initially relased (during the real life $$$ period)  with "op" characteristics. Sometimes it's oddly coded hit-boxes, sometimes it's poorly thought out design quirks that give an advantage. The design is then fixed/nerfed just as or shortly before the design becomes available for in-game currency. Taken individually, any of them appear to just be mistakes by the devs, but it is slightly suspicious that the pattern has repeated itself so many times.
- The "pro" or "comp" community: MWO has a small but dedicated group of competetive players. They play in the Faction play, and third-party tournaments. While there are plenty of good people who participate, the overall comp scene can be quite abrasive, and it's members pompous and annoying. It likely stems from being the top dog in a very small community, like being boastful of being elected Class President of your home-school class of 1 person. If you've ever known that team in an adult rec league that take things too far, as if they're pros or something, that's exactly what this is. Most enjoy showing how "leet" they are by clubbing seals over and over. It's possible that revisions to CW and the influx of new blood from Steam will help, but that remains to be seen.
- Teamwork is required, but rarely to be found: Teamwork is huge, people playing as a team have a huge advantage. The game has built-in chat and VoiP, but they are usually just used to troll/abuse. Especially on the weekends, there is an influx of low-skill players who simply do not work with their team at all, and this can be frustrating as it can virtually guarantee losses if you get stuck with that team.
- The "meta": While you can theoretically build any type of mechs you want, certain weapons/combos/variants are just plain better and stronger. If you want to have any success at the higher skill levels, you have to use the meta.
Mechwarrior Online is pretty much everything I could have hoped in terms of mech customization and competitive online multiplayer.

I want to start off my being clear that I'm a returning founder who left the game initially because of problems with balance, meta, and PGI's inability to deliver.
I picked the game back up again about a month ago, figuring i'd get in, check out CW, and lose interest within a day or two.  And to be honest, i still feel like i could lose interest any time now.
For better or worse, this is not a direct port of TT.  To be hoenst TT had some mechanics in it that were just not suited to real time simulation.
PROS
The mech models are really good.  There are some technical issues with some models (hit boxes, scaling), but i think that on the whole, the mech models are in good shape.
We got the Unseen showing up.  While the mech modles are altered, they are still immediately recognizeable.
Most of the weapon and component implementations make sense when ported over from TT
Community is generally less toxic than most others (That said, this is a team-based game and people do ge frustrated when people ignore attempts to organize in match)
The number of mechs now available makes it less likey that during drops (at least in the lower 3 tiers) you will encounter  cookie-cutter meta teams.
CONS
Ballistic weapons aer still just a hair to accurate.  While rounds drop in flight, they don't really seem to deviate in any other way.
Some of the weapon conversions are just badly implemented:  A 5 second cool down on gauss rifles, then charge time before you can fire, which really adds up to a double-lencgth cooldown
Clan implementation was just baddly handled, and it still causes gameplay and balance problems
Gameplay/Mech balance issues can take some time resolve, and are sometimes knee-jerk reactions (Ask a veteran about tackling)
Community Warfare just isn't ready yet.
All in all, despite having some issues, the game does have promise, and is fun most of the time.  There are some changes coming up in the immediate future that address some of the outstanding issue and open up more content for Community Warfare.
So with all of that, for now, yes, I'd reccomend it, because you can get damn near everything out of the game without spending any money, though obviously people who spend the money get access to new chasis sooner.

OK, i have now ''finished'' the current content as of the date of this review.
This game is a light survival/build-a-thon game. There are plans for dangerous creatures (tiger sharks) but the current black tipped reef sharks are harmless. Which is actually realistic as most sharks wont attack you for no reason in real life. For the most part, what you will be doing in this game is spending a lot of your time underwater (whilst you hold your breath), gathering raw materials to build things on a floating platform.
This means, hacking away at things with a knife, axe or simply just picking them off the sea floor. There are not all that many steps involved in building things, however the game is still relatively new. You harvest planks either from picking them up off the sea bed, or by using the axe to hack the wooden decks of sunken ships. Alternatively you can hack the same things with the knife to yield sticks instead of planks.
To build things, you access a ''box'' on your rubber raft and then use the hammer to place the structure pieces once the item is in your inventory.
The current goal of the game is to build a floating house on the surface of the sea, then build the crafting stations to advance in technology.
However, there are no ridiculous leaps in technology. You start out with a flint knife and a flint hammer and at the point i am currently at (the current end of content), i still have a flint knife and flint hammer. A slightly better one, but still the same technology. You dont suddenly and miraculously go from having a wind powered mill to having solar panels and a engine powered speed boat! The same can be said about suddenly having a revolver and the ability to craft bullets! What you start out with, IS the technology you are stuck with.
It is a bit odd to be hacking away at the wooden decks of boats or on sunken metal drums to suddenly yield planks and metal, but i can think of no better way to present the concept of harvesting raw materials.
I have played 10 hours and apart from the short period at the beginning where you are barely surviving, it is quite manageable. If you plan ahead - like most survival games - you can completely nullify the need for food and water. It is still there of course, but by stockpiling food and water, you can make it a non-issue.
One sticking point i should mention is the sheer amount of resources you will need to build everything. Not to the levels of Subnautica mind you (empty an entire zone of a particular resource and still not have enough) but be prepared to spend hours JUST harvesting planks. Not all at once, but it adds up.
So be warned that you will be clearing entire fields of sea weed, hacking up many sunken ships for a long time and picking things off the sea bed for hours.
But having a two storey building with everything at my finger tips, is a great pay off for all the long hours i put in.

One thing I pay attention to is how playable, buggy and how much content has been implemented during a games development. i judge accordingly depending on the specific phase the game is actually in.
I also base my decisions to get involved with a title in EA by reading reviews thoroughly, good and bad. I watch dozens of streams and youtube videos and I follow up by reading the forums. I get as much info as I possibly can before I decide to take that risk on a EA title. If I deem the game worthy of the risk I generally jump in and find that I have made a pretty good decision to get involved. And for the most part, things generally work out.
This doesnt mean Ive hit gold with every title in EA I have pruchased. However, out of the 10 EA titles I own, I only have one that I wish I hadnt bothered with, even if it happens to release (Never again Funcom)! You can say my odds at EA have been pretty good though.
With that said, I dont think Im going to be dissapointed with this title, knowing what type of game it really is and what to expect.
Try not to let the time I have spent in the game get in the way of what I think of the game thus far. Yes, its short, but I have researched this title thoroughly (as with all EA titles) and pretty much knew what I was getting into and what to expect as far as gameplay goes. With that said, lets get into what exactly Bermuda is!
Where does Bermuda fall into the "survival" genre?
I would say you are looking at a very relaxing title that does have a bit of micromanagement in order to survive. There is sleeping, eating, drinking and being able to craft specific things in order to be successful at surviving. building and crafting is another aspect for survival in Bermuda. Getting thirsty? Better craft a specific workbench cause the rations you get in the game at the start doesnt go far! Same goes for food, etc... Harvesting seems simple enough and pleasant to do, however, watch your air meter or face a grave at the bottom of the murky depths! Building structures is a must if you want space for all your benches and future survival gear.... in essence, the game does hold to the basics of a survival title and does a pretty good job of balancing out those needs without a heavy mechanic of micromanaging. The fun factor is there and the tedious micromanagement is less than a lot of other titles that require you to survive!
Dangers in Bermuda...
Little to none atm, however I read that the Devs do plan to add more aggressive sharks in the future with a chance of them attacking you depending on how you interact with them. Devs have said they want as close to relaistic shark behavior as possible. As of right now, the only enemy you have is the elements and the basic survival mechanics of eating, drinking, sleeping and coming up for air once in a while.
Hows the game look?
Decent graphics and the devs have already been remodeling and reskinning a lot of content to give the game that more realistic look. But so far, I think the game is decent in the looks department and does a good job of mimicking water physics as well as underwater structures and aquatic life.... no gripes on the looks, but could be slightly better and from my understanding thats what the devs are currently working on.
How buggy is it? Really!
So far, I have yet to come into any sort of bug that I can think of. I generally look past gltiches and bugs (depending on the severity) and look more towards what types of bugs keep me from progressing in the game! If a bug or glitch causes me not to be able to progress in a game I consider that a serious matter and one the devs should focus attention on. As for small, miniscule bugs that really dont affect how I progress, I dont lose my mind and start complaining in threads about it, I will, however, fill out a report in the forums and let the devs know of whats going on. So far, I have yet to run into anyhting that I could consider "game breaking".
Fun factor?
Yeah, I would say its a bit of fun, atm. Exploring is a big part of this game and though some areas sorta look the same, it is done well enough to hold my attention. Exploring in this game is also vital if you do plan to survive and well worth the journey. The colors are vibrant, the models are well done and animations is actually pretty good. If you can nail down keeping a supply of water, food and making medical supplies (for when you take on damage) youll be able to relax a bit and focus on building and crafting more.
The game isnt too punishing when it comes to eating, drinking and coming to the surface to catch a breath. I wasnt paying attention to my oxygen levels when harvesting and though I ran out of air, I was losing health at a gradual rate instead of a instant death fom not breathing. So the game does a decent job of not punishing you a great deal with survival. But if you dont pay attention to your meters, you may find your self sweating a bit!
Overall, this is a more relaxing title that balances out the survival aspects, not as punishing as some other titles yet challenging enough to keep you busy and moving forward. Hardcore survivalists might find the game a bit too easy for their tastes. Just remember, the game doesnt hold your hand! You will have to do a bit of experimenting to figure out what you need to do in order to survive and I think thats half of the fun of this title!
Recommend?
Yeah, I would recoomend the title atm for a EA alpha developed game. So far, so good and is in far better shape than some games I have played in EA. Content is a little lacking, but theres hours of play here till devs implement more content. From what Ive read, theres more coming in December this year.

Pick it up, give it a go and if the game isnt right for you, then theres always the 2 hr refund.

As a fan of any game that has big, heavy and powerful mechs to pilot I could already recommend at least playing this game for free. It starts you off with four "Trial Mechs" for each weight-class of mech. You have Light, Medium, Heavy and Assault mechs to try out with rather optimized loadouts, but on the whole they'll be suited towards default playstyle rather than individual tastes. The game's intro academy run and tutorial is very nice and simple, it even gives out some free in-game currency (C-Bills), and for the first twenty matches you drop into you get cash injections. By the end of the twenty matches you WILL have enough to buy your own mech to fully customize.
For those who want to drop cash on a starter kit? I'd recommend it, though I also recommend looking at the website for the developer, "MWO Mercs". It has active bundles for specific mechs, iconic mechs, pre-order packs and "al a carte" style purchasing to pick and choose. It is a bit of an advantage over other players earning mechs via hard fighting, though trial mechs also build XP for those buying that variant. All in all, the game is fun. There's many ways to play and be a credit to your team, and this isn't even touching upon Community Warfare which introduces more organized combat that offers rewards such as in-game items for decoration and "real money" Mech-Credits to buy custom colors and such with.
In the end, it isn't Gundam, it plays heavier and slower for most mech pilots. You're in anything from a 20-ton Locust with high-speed capabilities to a 100-ton Atlas that can literally bludgeon through enemy lines to open up holes for the team.
I recommend this game, while it might not be for everyone, it's definitely a "Freemium"/Free to Play title that is worth trying.

TL;DR - It's not perfect, but it's my perfect.
First off, my credentials to write this review: I've been a fan of Battletech and Mech based games and shows in general since I first picked up MechAssault for the Xbox around 12 years ago and shortly thereafter fell in love with the MechCommander games for PC and have been a giant stompy robot lover since.  I've also purchased every top package for MechWarrior Online from Legendary Founders through the latest unseen mechs and have probably sunk about 300+ hours of play time into this title before the steam launch and have been playing since beta.
Ok, on to the review: MechWarrior Online has had it's rough points in the past and it's still not entiely perfect.  The graphics aren't mind blowing.  The in game music basically has to be supplied by you running an old mechwarrior OST in the background.  The camos and paints are overpriced.  The cockpit items are cheesy and borerline immersion breaking.  The UI is inherently flawed.  The gameplay can be repetitive on certain maps.  The default keys and some of the game options are questionable.  Some of the warhorns can be headache inducing.  And the power level difference from a new mech to a "mastered" mech with modules and a custom build is a vast bottomless chasm.
However, it is fun.  The community is fantastic.  The in game chat is professional.  The devs do listen and are trying.  The redone maps are fantastic.  The selection of mechs is excellent.  The weapon and chassis balance is a lot better than it used to be.  The customisation is awesome.  The gameplay is tactical and skill based.  And finally the feeling you get from coring a mech with your last salvo while limping and with only one arm barely hanging on is unparalleled.  I have experienced some of my favourite gaming memories from this title and I don't regret a moment of it.
I have no doubt there are both positive and negative points about this title that I've failed to mention, hell, there's probably things I have never encountered having not played through the "new player" or f2p experience.  But I've had fun with it and if you're a fan of Battletech or of giant stompy robots in general then I'm sure you will too.
One more thing, if you're just getting into the game here are some basic tips:  Fight from the cockpit, unlock your arms, torso twist when you're reloading, use double heat sinks, assign left click = left arm, right click = right arm, side mouse buttons = torso weapons, press R to lock target, remap shift to full zoom, set your FOV to 0.75, concentrate fire, stick with the team and watch your heat.
With that all said, I hope you found this at least a little informative and it helps you out with deciding whether or not this is the game for you.
Good luck, Mechwarriors.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.
