This feels very much like a beta product that could surpass other controller with a few tweaks.
Pros:
The concave shape of the face of the controller makes it feel comfortable in the hand without over extending your thumbs. Feedback from trackpads is hard to describe, yet feel natural to whatever input method you choose. The software customisation by far is the best selling point for this controller. Setup can be done quickly with tweaks on the fly when needed, but you can easily spend and hour tweaking everything to perfection. A bonus is the little speaker inside that you can customise little stings for powering the controller on and off (Victory! ftw). Aiming with mouse input on the trackpad eventally feels more natural than a joystick, and I'd argue that does work well with FPS games contrary to some other opinions. The flappy paddles have an ok click. They  basically add two macro keys on a very unutilized side of a controller which hopefully becomes more common in the future. The gyro function dosen't seem to work too well for drving games on it's own (yet stupid fun), but used in tandum with either joystick or trackpad and you have a buttery smooth response to precision turning.
Cons:
This controller does have a learning curve, even with all the software tweaking. The plastics from the touchpads, buttons, and shell do feel hollow and cheap. Most buttons have a short travel (especially the shoulder button) which while it dosen't get in the way of gaming, dosen't feel as satisfying as they should. Triggers also suffer from a short pull before its maxed out before the secondary click, which also feels a bit mushy. The joystick is functional but could use some improvements. D-pad, isnt. It's a touchpad with a very shallow concave outlineof where a D-pad should be. Pressing too close to the center of the trackpad can send the wrong imput simply by what direction your thumb is pushing towards and not where it's pressing on the pad. It might have been better if it was raised up instead to feel it out, but the single-click of the trackpad still wouldnt fix the feel of the input being a bit off. A major problem is the lack of a keyboard button. either in-game chat or menu; if you have to type something, you have to press the steam key to the overlay, then scroll down to keyboard, then type, then enter, THEN go back to steam overlay and close the keyboard. A dedicated keyboard toggle for a controller that's supposed to bridge the computer-to-couch experience would make the transition a lot smoother, but somehow got overlooked during its design.
Opinion:
The issues with the controller could be address in the next itteration. It's very tweakable, but the controller itself needs more polish. It needs better action on the buttons and triggers. There are better plastics out there for the shell alone. two paddles on each side would be kinda cool in comarison to what the elite xbox controller did. While they can be mapped to buttons, I feel that there should be some function keys loacted on the top of the controller just above the steam key. Most of the quality improvements would make the controller cost more, but if done right would easily be worth the extra $10-$20. Could used more weight, maybe a metal shell/buttons/triggers, just something that feels more solid.
TL;DR
It works, feels cheap, stupid fun, still fun, gl hf.

First off I'd like to say this was my first thing I ever purchaced using Bitcoin.  Anyway I really like the Steam Controller. I've only used for Rocket League so far and it works really well for that. Feels really good in the hands and everything is layed out well.

As someone who doesn't like conventional gamepads for most games (I just don't like the thumbstick camera controls) I absolutely LOVE the Steam Controller. The trackpad + gyro gives you surprising accuracy, and it is also very good for games that usually don't support gamepads, like strategy games or city builders.
It is highly customisable, so in order to get the most out the SC, you have to spend some time to configure the controls to your personal preference. Of course there are lots of good communtiy presets, but most of the times, it's best to make your own.
For example, I often like to map the left joystick to the left trackpad, and use the thumbstick as the D-Pad. This way, I can run by just laying my finger on the top end of the right trackpad, which prevents my thumb going numb after playing RPGs for a longer period of time. And for games with sprinting like Witcher 3, I configured the outer zone of the left trackpad to press the print button in addition to the joystick output, so if I want to sprint, I move my finger closere to the edge of the trackpad.
As you can see, there's a lot of stuff you can configure.
Another great thing about the Steam Controller is how easy it is to operate the PC with it. In desktop mode, it emulates a mouse, and it is surprisingly easy to navigate Windows with it.
So, bottom line is:
If you want two thumbsticks, this controller isn't for you.

I bought this as an early access game, and I have to say, so far I am pretty impressed. The basic premise of the game is that you are lost in a life raft somwhere in the Bermuda Triangle and you need to stay alive. You need to source everything for your survival from the liferaft and the ocean.  Inside the liferaft are a few cans of food/water, some first aid supplies, a bed roll, and a crafting table. You need to take to the water for everything else.
The first couple of days are by far the trickiest, learning how long to stay under water for, how long you can last without water and food, and managing to scavenge enough resources to keep yourself going before running out of the essentials.
There are some positives... and some not so positives about this game so far:
Pros:
Visually appealing
Good crafting system
Reasonable time limit for diving.
Good amount of resources available.
Cons:
Game is quite jittery and laggy on my machine. I'm running an i7 with 16GB ram. Super frustrating. I suspect the generation of the ocean/ surface would have a lot to do with that.
Actually, all of the cons come back to the lagginess of the game on my machine. Fishing is potluck, character shudders when too close to the ocean floor. Jumping is inaccurate.  You get the idea.
One last con... The user controls aren't intuitive.  'F' button to interract, when you'd expect LMB. I've found I kinda need to  'relearn' the controls if I come back to the game after a while. Not really a big deal, but worth mentioning.
Deconstruct command doesn't seem to work yet.
At this point, I'll give the game a tentative recommendation, but only in the hope that the devs improve performance, This game show a lot of promise, and I'm super keen to see how it evolves, but for me at the moment, it's pretty unplayable.

Amazing

Overall this is a nice take on the same old idea of ocean survival. Find food, find mats. The big pros over a few other, or one specific title in this genre:
You can choose your sex. Which is really just aesthetic. But it matters to a lot of gamers.
The crafting is not a simple build two things and you have no reason to worry anymore type.
The simple construction of food and water crafting stations do not mean your set for life. You have to work at providing the mats to them, and the balance is pretty good on needs, to include sleep. Not 100% but not spend all your day eating sim.
The ocean has drift.
The crafting items lead along a small at the moment list, but make some sense. And they all serve a use vs just being a grind factor add-in.
Over all not a bad game. I had no problems with bugs or issues so far, tho' I ve read some do. But again I admit to not a lot of time in it.
I will be pondering this one still.

Stronghold is a classic staple of the Medieval-themed RTS genre. Set in the middle ages in Britain, you play through a surprisingly lengthy campaign of various mission types such as economic development, settlement building & defense of that settlement and straight up castle sieges.
It has a plethora of both unit and building types, which you will need as the combat in this game is balanced well. No mass production of a single unit type to win, as you'll need different unit types (along with the pre-requisite buildings of course) to defeat what the enemy throws at you.
The combat is well thought out and with some depth. With various offensive and defensive units, the ability to build moats and drawbridges, siege equipment, spike pits, engineers pouring boiling oil over the walls... the list goes on for quite some time. It requires some strategy and thought which provides a solid tactical element to the game, as charging a castle defended by crossbowmen will ensure your attacking force is cut down in no time.
Asides from the combat, the castle building elements are among the most enjoyable. There are multiple ways to feed your population from the most basic deer hunter to baker, requiring both farms and grain processing to exist. You can keep them happy via religion, generous quantities of alcohol or decorations. Or, you could keep them oppressed but highly productive due to their fear - the choice is yours.
Graphically the game is quite attractive, but its not going to hide that this game was released a long time ago. The HD upgrade does go towards helping that however. The soundtrack is as great as it ever was, providing atmospheric medieval lute and panpipes when building your castles and settlements and war drums and trumpets when under attack.
Hours of fun are to be had with this, and I would say that even the non-sale price is completely worth it.

I'm writing this review for the sake of any fans of the genre who may wonder if this game holds up against more modern titles, and might hesitate to buy it because of it's age.
The entire Stronghold series somehow passed me by.  I've never played any of them before recently purchasing Stronghold HD, so I have no nostalgic or other sentimental connection to it.
And after playing through the entire main campaign and sinking over 40+ hours into the game, I can say this is a should buy for anyone who enjoys games of this kind.
I love having access to a variety of units in RTS games.
But I hate that, in some of them, there either isn't much reason to use more than one or two troop types, or simply not enough difference between them in practice.
In Stronghold HD, not only is there a healthy roster of classic medieval units - you virtually cannot get through the game and be effective without making use of their unique strengths, weaknesses and abilities.
Macemen are excellent shock troops with a strong attack, and just enough armor that they can take a few arrows before falling.  They're also faster than most other troops, and break into a run when they're near the enemy to close the distance quickly.
Spearmen are basically farmers with pointed sticks who were born only for the purpose of having their guts spilled by the swords of better men.
...But they also have the ability to push ladders off of your castle walls, something no other unit can do.
Crossbowmen are useless in so many games. A more costly and less efficient solution than massed archers.
Not so in Stronghold HD.
Later in the game once the enemy starts to field armored units, you really can't get by without them.
One place where many RTS games can falter is in failing to provide an adequate AI.
And I really found Stronghold HD to stand out in this regard.
No, it isn't a genius. This thing isn't going to become self-aware one day and seek revenge on humanity for creating it and then sticking it in a box just so that we could all play Stronghold HD single player.
But it does a reasonable job for this kind of game.
And your units *generally* behave sensibly and do what you tell them to do, rather than dissolving into utter chaos once the fighting begins.
Castle building is a big part of the game, and castle defense is a lot of fun.
You have a great deal of freedom within the bounds of the terrain in each stage to lay out your castle however you like.  And you discover as you go along that the quality of your design makes a big difference in your chances of survival.
The game gradually introduces new elements as the scenarios progress, and you eventually gain the abilty to create pitch ditches.
Pitch ditches are glorious fields of pitch, invisible to the enemy, that can be set ablaze with a flaming arrow once the bad guys come marching through.
Watching a big mass of attacking troops die in a huge field of fire outside of your castle walls is very satisfying.
This is an older title, and the age is reflected in the graphics relative to more modern games.
But after playing for a while, I find it's more drab and weathered aesthetic charming and I wouldn't change it.
And both the graphics and music do a solid job of creating a thoroughly medieval atmosphere.
The user interface does take a little getting used to when you're first starting.
Elevation matters in the game, so it's often necessary to rotate the screen or press the spacebar to flatten the terrain to get a better look while you're building a wall or etc.
And there's a bit of a learning curve as well, but the game does a great job of teaching you how to play both in the tutorial and as new units and buildings are introduced.
One thing that should be noted is that scenario 15 is arguably a bit messed up.  On hard difficulty or above, it's nearly impossible to get through without methodically exploiting the AI.
But in light of everything right with the game, it's very forgivable.
There's a great deal more that could be said, but it already has been by other people.
If you like games like this, don't let the fact that it's a re-release of an old game put you off.
As someone who has played many other, more modern RTS games, I can say that Stronghold HD's gameplay has stood the test of time well and I highly recommend it.

What kind of idiot turns down a drive a walking tank simulator; for free? Exactly, no one.

This game takes a lot to get into, but it is totally worth it. Mechwarrior is a shooter that doesn't reward reflexes rather than it rewards careful strategy and knowledge. Understanding the game is your key to winning, but unfortunately it can be a bit difficult to get into.
There is lots of things to juggle and pay attention to at one time while you play. Heat, Armor, Ammo, Movement speed, Limb Strength, current torso direction, current leg direction, radar. Its a lot. When you first play it is a bewildering amount of information that confuses you and makes it hard for you to really know what you are doing. But once you get it, it becomes second nature. You find yourself calling out enemy locations while getting missile lockons, targetting air strikes, and keeping your heat/armor carefully managed.
This is the game's strength. When you finally master the game you really feel like you are piloting a 100 ton battlemech. It feels good to fire autocannons and break the leg of an enemy mech and see him limp away in fear. It feels dire when you run as a light mech, dodging enemy fire and attempting to sabatoge the support units of the enemy team.
Sure the game is complex as all get out, but that makes it all the more *real*. Nothing gives you such grim satisfaction as turning off your heat protection and blowing out your engine in order to suicide kill an enemy mech. Feeling the loud slam as Particle cannon tears off your left arm and you retaliate with your remaining right. Never before has any game but the Mechwarrior series made me feel like I'm actually driving something. You feel connected to your Atlas or Timber Wolf as you would your car or truck. They even made it to the point where you can hear your engine malfunctioning if you are on low health, and you can listen to the hissing of your failing heat sinks if they are destroyed.
Make no mistake. This game is in beta. It still has a long way to go before it is perfect. There's also a lot of skill involved, and it isn't the kind of game that you can learn in just a few hours. But once you do, it is great fun and it is also free!
So join me, and maybe I'll see you on the battlefield mechwarrior.

When I first came across the Lion’s Song it was purely at random, but when my gaze fell upon some of the screenshots from the game, I quickly added it onto my wishlist and waited patiently for its release, until today.
The Lion’s Song, produced by the Austrian studio Mi'pu'mi Games and whose moto is “Great games don’t have to be big” (and I couldn’t agree more), is an episodic, point & click series that takes place during the early 20th century. In the first episode of The Lion’s Song we follow Wilma, an up and coming violinist who is under a lot of pressure to finish a piece that she has been struggling to complete. When her professor, Arthur Caban offers to send her to his cabin up in the Alps where she could potentially find inspiration, Wilma accepts and arrives to find herself surrounded by her fears, insecurities and pressure from both her peers and herself.
The Lion’s Song first episode, titled Silence, is a wonderful piece of art about the pressure we allow others to put on us, the pressure we put on ourselves, our fears and how they can be interpreted of visualised, whether through dreams or the world that surrounds us, but it also is about patience and overcoming obstacles, big or small. In the first episode, you will be required to pay attention to Wilma’s pleas and fears, and help her find inspirations in the things that surrounds her and the sounds that will sometimes scare her, or inspire her, in order to complete her piece.
The game allows you to learn various type of things about Wilma or the people in her life, different games will offer different types of information, and through some events, you can shape Wilma’s will, fears, and even the ending of the episode.
Although the music is an important part of the game, a lot of it resides in the in-between, when you are searching inside of the cabin for something to spark Wilma’s attention and inspiration. Rain tapping against the window or a clock ticking, there is a surprising amount of objects for you to interact with, and the sounds, text and sometimes music that accompanies it are absolutely wonderful.
I am extremely excited to see what Mi'pu'mi Games has in store for us, and to meet the other character that will be the protagonists of the next episodes.
10/10 – I was pleasantly surprised to see that episode 1 was being given out for free, as I was more than ready to pay for it, but having experienced it now, I will most certainly be purchasing the season pass and wait for more wonderful storytelling.
“Great games don’t have to be big” Absolutely.

This is the MechWarrior game I've been wanting since my childhood days playing MechWarrior 2. So how to describe it compared to other games? Well, it's not exactly a shooter and it's not exactly a sim. It's somewhere in between. The F2P setup is actually reasonable which is a rare thing to see, especially after my experience with World of Tanks and World of Warships and the obvious money sinks built into those. With MWO throwing money gets you nothing gameplay related that you couldn't get otherwise for free.
Yes you can get cosmetic stuff, yes you can get first access to new mechs for a bit before they're available to earn for in-game currency, and yes you can buy "hero" mechs that give a little boost to XP earned, but little Billy with his daddy's credit card is going to get wrecked because cash won't do anything but save you time in unlocking things.
Other than that, there's events for unlocking free stuff that happen on a very regular basis, and the community is actually full of (mostly) decent folks who just want to have fun blasting the crap out of each other in giant stompy robots.
Mechwarrior Online is a game that takes a bit of grinding to get your gameplay experience wholesome and fun, but then its free. and fun.
Sells the fantasy of walking around in a big stompy robot shooting other big stompy robots really well.

Creative freedom
Few limits
The game held up for many years
It is easy to mod
CONS:

MidBoss is an interesting game, combining grid-based combat akin to Final Fantasy Tactics to a rogue-like Binding of Isaac. Players fight and possess different monsters to gain new abilities and stat increases. Each monster is effectively a new class, unlocking abilities as the form level ups. Gaining new abilities like Scurry or Envenom is a nice bonus to the stat boost that come with the leveling up.
The music is nice, and fits well with the dungeon theme. The graphics are nice, but items can be hard to spot at times. Luckily, the game has a feature that essentially highlights the item location to allow for easy pickup.
Each floor that you progress through adds new enemies, some are just varients of previous foes, but some are suprisingly tough. Enemies slowly increase in difficulty, and murdering everything on a floor is usually necessary to gain levels to make up for the difficulty. Also picking the proper monster to level up as is important. Zombies give constitution bonuses, aka more health, while rats give general bonuses. Focusing your levels is important to a long run. Likewise, picking which stat to level up is important, since you only gain 3 stat points per level to be divided amoungst 4 stats.
I originally played MidBoss when it was in it's early alpha stages at MomoCon a few years back. It caught my attention then, and was a delight to play in the indie showcase. Even surprised one of the devs by carefully kiting an enemy around the exit of the floor, slowly widdling it's health down with poison, while I had only 2 hp myself. Won a free copy of the game, and promptly lost the code once I got home. But it's for the best as paying for the game supports the devs to make more interesting games. I strongly recommend MidBoss, or if you don't want to buy it, I recommend at least watching some gameplay of it.

Footage of the game:
Midboss is a fun idea for a dungeon crawler. You possess different minions and eventually master them as you use them. Their stats and abilities get added to your base character, making you a more formidable fighter. The game scales up pretty well, with you running into tougher enemies as you progresses, keeping up the challenge. I enjoyed the humor and music as well.

Let's just get this out of the way.... I may have rated this game thumbs up as it honestly is one of my all time faves, but the Director's Cut - despite being on paper the best version of the game released - has some *horrendous* bugs that you need to be aware of. Two quests in particular - an early sidequest and THE FINAL MAIN QUEST SECTION - can be rendered unable to complete if you don't do things in a very specific way. I can't really say what these are without spoiling it but rest assured they *are* doable, if you want details checkout the game's Steam forum.
Now that we have that out of the way, I can get to the game.
Did you like the original Deus Ex? Did you like X-Files? Did you like 24? If you answer yest to all three then you will like this, as it's basically a hybrid of the three.  There's plenty of reviews out there for the original version of Deus Ex: Human Revolution so I won't bulk this out, but suffice to say the storyline, gameplay, music, art style and voice acting of this title really are something else. Your main character is a complete badass and gets even more badass as the game goes on, and the level of customisability and user choice is insane. It is very much a worthy successor to Deus Ex.
This specific version incorporates all the DLC that the original version had - in particular, the excellent Missing Link expansion is now integrated into the campaign and barring some wonky equipment and XP mechanics, allows seamless transfer of your character's gear and powers between it and the rest of the game. DLC gear is not placed directly into your inventory but made available in the game world, and very easily so.
Graphically... this game's engine was never that amazing (although weirdly it seems to do lighting extremely well, but not texture quality or animation) but given how the game flips between dark and grimy to cold and clinically clean, you don't actually notice the engine's shortcomings as much as you'd think. What is here has been upped a bit from the original release and looks pretty good, given it's a few years old. It's not Crysis, though.
Boss encounters have been reworked a little, in that you don't have to engage in a pure firefight with them anymore - there's now avenues to hit them with controlled robots or environmental hazards - but they're still very much combat encounters and you can tell that they're modifications rather than re-designs. IMHO they're still best done as a straight-up fight.
Overall, this is an excellent game with some awful bugs and rough around the edges where it shouldn't be - but if the new Deus Ex: Mankind Divided garners your interest, you might find this worth a playthrough to see what Adam Jensen got up to prior to it.

Project Pulsation is a desperate attempt to cash in on the latest iteration of Unreal engine. To be honest as I was playing the game I had a feeling that this would fare better than most of the Unity-based FPS games here. I am referring to those that are nothing more than an asset flip. Plus, you have those that were made with the use of the GameGuru.
In any case, this game is about a project that went awry and you are tasked to find a hidden artifact in the location in question. It is a space station / ship with some robots and monsters. First of all, the main menu looks terribly simple and ugly. It is also very dark. You cannot rebind your keys and graphics options are limited. Even if you change the settings you barely notice anything.
You start off the game on the level called "elevator". It is, in fact, an elevator shaft without an elevator as you just keep falling for minutes without hitting ground. When you do so you realise you must be invincible since you did not get hurt, at all. But monsters can easily kill you later with one shot so you realise you are in danger, after all. You have one weapon only and finding ammo is possible at the beginning but later on I did not find any extra ammunition. In fact, if you get killed and restart from a checkpoint you have the same amount of rounds available i.e. if you die many times you simply reach zero.
The game is dark. VERY DARK! Your flashlight helps but not always. Your weapon has a laser sight but as soon as the enemies are at a distance you realise you cannot hit them. Often when you hit objects such as chairs, computer consoles or machinery parts with your gun these mentioned assets just fly away, sometimes literally out of the screen. The problem is that the textures are usually quite ugly and the game frequently changes your vision - while this is part of the story it is annoying to see things blurry around yourself for several minutes.
The story is barely explained. Sometimes texts are found but beside the English the creator thought the inclusion of the Russian language was a must (ever heard of a subtitles option?). Because of this the text takes up a major part of the screen and the English almost always has a couple of words outside of our view. Then there are sections (such as the asteroid level) where walking is almost impossible due to the FPS drop. This is area-specific so regardless of how many times you relaunch the game the resulting values will be the same. This is the reason why I quit as for 20 minutes I was walking just under 10 FPS.
Sound effects are generic and while there's an acceptable soundtrack you always hear when the track ends and restarts as not much work went into the editing, either. The most annoying part of the game is when you die. For instance, a turret hits you with its laser. You are down on the ground and your vision changes, let's say by 90 degrees. Funny thing is when dead you can still move (more like slide) and if you hit the laser once again it adds another 90 degrees so when the checkpoint system kicks in you see everything upside-down. Only for 5-10 seconds, though, as the game makes a correction.
There are sections where scripted events begin such as a platform starts moving. If you die along the way you are put back near the last save location but the game forgets to reset mentioned event. So, you cannot continue (the platform is already high up somewhere and you cannot recall it), therefore, your best bet is to quit and hit "continue". I could go on and list many other mistakes, glitches and bugs (not to mention the many typos in the English text) but there's no need, to be honest.
Project Pulsation is a bad game. An interesting idea, but executed horribly. Unreal engine 4 or not, the game has ugly textures and effects and it is too dark for you to see and there's nothing, I repeat nothing, that make you want to continue once you're an hour or so in the "story". It's too bad that the developer (VGstudio) has other software with similar negative outcome. If you are desperate to do some trading card grinding then for half a euro this game can be of some value.

In The Lion's Song, you play as a young but talented musical composer, Wilma. She struggles with a big piece, with no help from her professor Arthur, about whom she has confused feelings. Arthur sends her to his cabin in the Alps, where Wilma gradually finds inspiration in the elements all around her and composes her piece around them. While the play style is not innovative, the art style is pleasing to the eye and fitting to the type of game. It is a calming and interesting game overall. I look forward to the next episodes.

I'm pleasantly surprised by the simplicity that is The Lion's Song.  As you can see by my time, as well as other reviewers'', the game is not exceptionally long.  Despite that, the brief hour you spend with the game will be delightful.  The Lion's Song boasts an impressive pixelated artstyle, a thoughtful score, and a nuanced story.
However, the game's enjoyment will be dependent on the player.  If you're not the type to really get invested in a character you may not enjoy the first playthrough that much.  Gameplay wise it's not very intricate, which might also put some people off.  Puzzles are almost non existant, save a few with very simple solutions.  The story can be a bit predictable as well.
That being said, I do recommend the first episode for anyone who thinks they'd be remotely interested in it.  It's free and truly worth taking slowly and reading all the dialogue.  There's a good chance I'll be replaying this game to get achievements and also see if the song at the end changes based on choices.

I remember first hearing about Lion’s Song a few years back on RPS and I played the really early demo of Episode 1. It was neat enough, but I forgot about it until I saw its Steam page on the upcoming game list. Seeing is that the first episode was free I had no excuse not to play it.
Lion’s Song Episode 1 takes place in Vienna during the turn of the 20th century. You play as Wilma, a young woman that aspires to be a great violinist. She has the skills but she has recently fallen into a block. Her teacher, Arthur, (who she secretly has feelings for) sees it as pressure from the bustling city around her and offers Wilma to stay in his isolated cabin in the Alps by herself. Wilma agrees but at the cabin she learns that Arthur has planned a big concert with her in it and she has only a week to finish her new piece. As she begins to fret over this development she receives a phone call from a friendly Bohemian innkeeper named Leos who wanted to try out this newfangled phone he just got installed and is awed that he ended up calling someone hundreds of miles away.
At this point it is up to the player to decide what to do. And that’s Lion’s Song’s gameplay, it’s a very streamlined point and click game where it focuses on how you have Wilma deal with her situation and her relationships with other people. Will you be determined to finish the composition, putting it above all else? Or will you take the time to just talk to Leos? Stuff like that. The game has really good atmosphere, the aesthetic is that of a sepia-toned photograph and it has a real nice soundtrack. It all really adds to the feeling of being alone in woods on a stormy night. The writing is good stuff too, I actually didn’t get to talk a lot to Leos out of my own choice and because of that the game became more of Wilma dealing with some soul searching on her own.
The only real major flaw I can say is that you can’t have multiple save files so I’d have to lose my progress if I wanted to replay and take a different path like spending more time talking to Leos but I don’t want to override my original choices.
Overall Episode 1 is a real solid start and I’ll probably buy the whole season pass.  Also you got no excuse to not try it, it’s free.

Neat little roguelike. The main possession gimmick is implemented pretty well and hitpoints not regenerating naturally help the game a lot. There's also a "Death Card" system where it generates a trading card with death information, map seed, and equipment at death that's super cool and shareable. The main negative is that the UI is a bit rough around the edges, as well has having slightly blurry scaling.
Bonus: it has good humor in it and proper accessibility options.

This is a roguelike that creates a cool combat system around the concept of possessing monsters. It plays more like a "traditional" roguelike with things like turn-based combat, procedurally generated dungeons and permadeath. It does break out of the mold but in a good way, like their "death card" system where you can save all your character's information in a png image, and you can literally drag and drop someone else's death card image into your game and load it into your game, play that same seed, or even import one of their items to start with.
The combat is what this game is about, and the idea is that possessing stuff is not only done as a way to get stronger, but it's also your primary, and often times only, means of healing. Combined with the fact you don't regenerate HP naturally, this means that to survive hairy encounters you have to time your possessions carefully AND choose who you possess carefully.
A pet peeve of mine with roguelikes is that some tend to obfuscate information, forcing you to dig through a wiki to find out what to do with your stats or what decisions to make during combat, but MidBoss is very "up front" with information, letting you make tricky decisions in a informed manner. There's some notable exceptions where the game is deliberately obtuse about certain mechanics, but these exceptions don't seem to affect gameplay significantly or at all, which is very much appreciated.
Game length felt pretty long specially for a first playthrough. which can be pretty scary if you're not used to losing a character 6+ hours in, but I see that as a feature. If you *really* don't want to die you can look up a guide so you know what to expect on later floors but it's not as fun that way IMO.
As of this review I do have to say that backtracking in large levels or going up and down floors repeatedly can get tedious and affect replayability, BUT according to the developer map sizes are being adjusted and there's a fast travel feature coming up soon which would solve that issue.
Even with the aforementioned problem, for my first playthrough there was enough content to go through that I had a lot of fun, I have around 20 hours in this game (not including idling) which is awesome value for what you pay, I definitely recommend it.

Kitsune Games has managed to do what I thought nearly impossible: create a rogue-like that makes me want to come back.
Two things jump out at me as especially intriguing. First is the possession mechanic. It's been done before, but MidBoss manages to make it feel freshby allowing for the use of the abilities of the creatures you possess without requiring you to possess them every single time you want to use them. For example, I made extensive use of the vampire bat's leeching skill in pretty much every form I used.
The second thing that I took notice of — and the far more meaningful thing, in my opinion — is how much thought went into this game about accessability. This naturally includes the color-blind graphics mode, which has never really been more than an afterthought for most games. More surprisingly, though, MidBoss also includes mechanics that help players enjoy the game, even if they aren't a fan of rogue-likes. The presence of Quick Play mode and Death Cards — which act both as a record of your game and as an assist for your next playthrough — demonstrate that MidBoss is actively avoiding the insular elitism that plagues genres like rogue-likes. I can only hope other games and genres follow suit.
I should also note that this game is wonderfully easy on low-end systems. I played it on a 2-year-old budget laptop without any notable slow-downs or stuttering.
My list of cons about this game are few, and mostly revolve around the controls. The game can be slow to accept inputs, and some movements are puzzlingly unavailable: most notably, you can attack diagonally around wall corners, but you can't move that same way.
If these are the worst problems I have with the game, though, I'd say it's a small price to pay. MidBoss is a fun, engaging game with a delightfully snarky sense of humor and a welcoming approach that many of its fellow rogue-likes seem to fear. Whether or not you usually enjoy rogue-likes, I heartily recommend giving MidBoss a shot.
P.S.: The color scheme produced by the CGA retro potion brought me more glee than might be entirely healthy.

MidBoss is a loot driven, permadeath roguelike with a twist. It's satisfying enough although starting at zero again can get tedious. Some of this tedium is relieved by a few other interesting mechanics like death cards and custom games.
Pros:
Combat - The possession system means your available skills and stat build are always in flux, so how you approach each fight changes according to who you are fighting and who you happen to be at the time. This makes combat a fun exercise in strategy.
Loot - There is lots here, tiered randomly generated rarites and uniques. Each playthrough will have you wearing something different and hoping for the next big drop.
Graphics - The graphics are crisp and easy on the eyes. They're not 3d masterpieces, but that's unnecessary in a game like this.
Death Cards - You die in this game a LOT. Fortunately, you can use a card to use a previous run's seed. This allows you to know what loot will drop, what monsters will be where, what the layout will be, etc. You can also use a card once to give your new imp a piece of equipment that your old imp died with. If you had a favourite unique or legendary you can pass it on and get a headstart. While this can only be done once per card, you can save death cards and use multiple cards for a single run, potentially decking your new imp out in some impressive gear.
Custom games - If the standard mode has got you annoyed, you can always make a custom game with the cards stacked in your favor. This doesn't mean you won't die, it just means you can have a bit higher chance at living.
Cons:
Unlockable modes - I like the idea of "retro graphic modes" but they seem to be just overlays. The problems arise when the text becomes unreadable because it. For example, the P&P mode is nice looking, but because it just strips out color the text becomes white blocks with thin black outlines on a white background. In an actual p&p setting the writing would be bold black. Overall I collectively call the retro modes "aaaah my eyes!."
Repetitive - Honestly this is something that all permadeaths inherently suffer from, so it's not much of a con as long as you know what you're getting into. Every death means going through the same motions from the start again and again.
That's about it. It's fun as long as you're into permadeath roguelikes.

DOOM (2016) is a soft reboot (meaning, a new chapter for a new audience, but keeps the continuity and established universe of the previous entries) of the legendary first person shooter series. Now, I never played the original version of DOOM nor its sequels, rereleases, mods and whatnot, because I was young and not a PC player, but I was aware of its popularity and quality. It's literally part of gaming culture and history.
So when Bethesda and id software showed up on stage at E3 2015 with a game they simply called "DOOM", I raised an eyebrow and looked for reactions from my pals who did play the originals, and they were less than impressed. The game fell off my radar until a few days before release when Bethesda released a multiplayer beta that failed to impress people so hard it got one of the worst review scores in Steam's history.
Cue release day and reviews drop, and both the gaming press and public seemed to have done a complete 180 overnight because all of a sudden, DOOM was considered good. Scratch that, people called it a worthy successor, a refreshing shooter experience, and a masterpiece, and by the end of the year it would make it into many top 5 games of the year. I was intrigued, so I bought it during a sale around summer of 2016, around the same time I built myself a powerful new gaming computer, and gave it a shot.
And I wish I could swear openly in these review because holy♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ nothing could have prepared me for the shotgun blast to the face this gem of a first person shooter this game is. DOOM (2016) is now one of my favorite games ever, in no small part thanks to its incredible single player campaign, but also a solid multiplayer, tons of post launch content, a high replayability, a stellar soundtrack and the ability to rip and tear like nothing else.
So here you have it, a breakdown of why DOOM (2016) is a fantastic experience, which you can get for a pretty good price nowadays. Multiplayer still has a decent population, the single player campaign is worth the price of admission alone, the soundtrack rocks your ears off and the gameplay is nothing short of superb. I can't recommend this game enough, and if you're still on the fence, it's time to pull the trigger. Rip and tear, baby !

I've only had for a day or two, but I love this thing. It takes getting used to. That will be a common phrase you will see associated with this product, but it's very much true.
I particularly like this controller because of what it allows you to do. It's basically a blank slate controller that allows you to emulate virtually any control function out there through its advanced (and initially intimidating) configuration settings . You can assign each button to act as virtually any customized input. It allows you to create a profile that emulates a classic controller, with the added functionality of mouse movement using the right haptic pad. Additionally, you configure it to use it's gyro-capability. Pretty fun for flying simulators and driving simulators or just for dumb fun. If you don't want to deal with manual configurations, you can always access the online library of community-created configs for individual games. Just select it from the list in Big Picture mode and load it up.
The haptic input pads on each side works very well in a variety of circumstances, most notably to simulate a computer mouse. It can never fully replace a classic kb and mouse, but it does allow you to play games in your living room you would otherwise never be able to play comfortably from your couch.
In sum, Valve succeeded very well in their intent to create a universal controller that, with enough knowledge and understanding, can be used for anything.
The downsides are primarily the time required to set up the controller yourself (if you prefer not to use a community template, or there isn't one). Additionally, the controller design itself can feel a bit clumsy/big at first, but after some time, it feels comfortable enough. The joystick,  A, X, Y, and B buttons are [placed a bit too far to the middle imo, but that was likely to avoid accidentally touching the haptic inputs.
I disliked this controller for the fact that they could have had joysticks instead of mousepads, the mousepads are infuriatingly hard to look around with

It's functionality and custmizability are probably it's redeeming factors though, considering you can customize the hell out of this and use so many combinations of things, along with it's haptic feedback, gyro aiming/steering ability, and back trigger pads.
The looks of the handles might decieve one into thinking they're unconfortable, but even a guy with small hands like me can feel very comfortable using them for long periods of time. This isn't meant for FPS games or precise-aiming based games, rather it's for casual games like Rocket League or games that do better with controllers than mice and keyboards. The best thing about this is compatibility with games that would otherwise not be usable with regular controllers, due to the fact that this is technically a mouse and keyboard emulator formatted to work as a controller. You can play almost any Indie game with this, though some would be best with a mouse and keyboard.
But the biggest thing for people to look out for when buying, is to understand that you WILL need to get used to it. The best way to describe using the pads is like using a mousepad on a laptop. Again, not an fps based controller, it's just for casual gaming and such from the couch.
Would I reccomend this to anyone? It depends on what you plan on doing with it, but generally yes. Honestly, I would buy this again if I ever needed or wanted another one due to the fact that it's just really convinient to have if you want to casually play on the couch, but it won't replace your mouse and keyboard.

Disclaimer: You have to use the Steam Beta client to get many/most of the major improvements to the software and firmware related to this device. You also, as of this writing, still need to use Big Picture Mode to configure a few things, but you can change the controls without Big Picture which is the most important thing.
Best controller I've used on a PC with more use cases than official console devices. Absurdly long battery life. The set of regular disposable Duracell batteries that came with the controller lasted me a full year of frequent use. The batteries didn't even actually die on me. I had some object messing with the wireless signal and I thought it was the batteries finally giving up. I threw them away and replaced them only to notice the problem was still there. I checked the wireless receiver and moved some objects near my computer around and that was all. Latency is not an issue (unless you have very specific low latency needs) and it has the wired option.
Rumble concerns: The existing haptic feedback in the Steam Controller has been updated and customized considerably over the year. There is an [experimental] toggle to use the rumble signals games send with the haptic feedback of the Steam Controller. For getting the "feel" of the game through rumble this feature does not create the same vibrations that will make your controller scare the crap out of you when you forget you left it on and boot up a game, but the same information a traditional controller rumble sends to your brain through your hands can be felt with the haptic feedback rumble simulation.
I recommend this controller over the other contenders (except maybe the Xbox One Elite but that is crazy expensive), but my only reservation with buying one of these right now is that I feel like Steam Controller Rev. 2 is around the corner. That could be months though and the sales on the current controller have been very generous compared to most controller prices. Some talk about Revision 2 from a few months ago suggested it would be mostly a look and feel type upgrade and not necessarily add new features. What you buy now should be the same as Rev 2 on the inside with the things that matter most for using them.
My criticisms: The shoulder "bumper" buttons, R1 and L1, don't feel good to click and once in a while I can press the button and hear the click but it does not receive the input unless I press it a bit more than just till it clicks. I feel similarly with the grip buttons on the back of the device. It is cleverly designed, but sometimes the back plate that covers the batteries and functions as the grip buttons feels like it isn't snapped in correctly (and I've tried to fiddle with that).
Cosmetically speaking, it does do much in the way of trying to look pleasing to the eyes. Some of the textures that are intended to help grip the device, while they work, do not feel great. There is a bit of "cheapness" to the overall design and materials used here. You get over that fast because what is inside this controller is what really counts. The lettered face buttons, start and select, both trackpads, and even the analog stick seem to places the controller could add some very small touches to give the controller character in the same way Xbox face buttons have a unique translucent look while PS4 has mostly flat but soft to press face buttons. The years and years of iteration after iteration of controller prototypes and release products show in their controllers with many barely noticeable finely shaped contours all over the controllers than help define the feel of holding a Microsoft or a Sony device.
Right now, with Steam Controller Rev. 1, it is the most PC gaming♥♥♥♥♥controller. It is the most powerful and customization but not always easiest to just turn on a game and make stuff work.
There is also a very accurate and customization (and optional) motion control feature that many people swear by for getting those sweet headshots in their shooter of choice, but I find that completely baffling. Maybe I just need a controller teacher for that MLG level stuff.

After a few months of using the Steam Controller, I learned a few things:
1. This controller definitely does break norms, and does a good job of it.
2. Norms are norms for a reason.
While the customizability of these is godly, the design of most controllers is similar because it's a system that works. The Steam Controller attempts to be different, but the changes it makes are far from necessary. The Xbox One and PS4 controllers have much nicer builds, and are more comfortable to use.
The only advantage the Steam Controller has - or should I say HAD - are the customization options built into Big Picture Mode. But now that these options are becoming available to other controllers, there's honestly not much reason to buy a Steam Controller anymore. You're better off shelling out the cash for a different controller.

Let's just get this out of the way.... I may have rated this game thumbs up as it honestly is one of my all time faves, but the Director's Cut - despite being on paper the best version of the game released - has some *horrendous* bugs that you need to be aware of. Two quests in particular - an early sidequest and THE FINAL MAIN QUEST SECTION - can be rendered unable to complete if you don't do things in a very specific way. I can't really say what these are without spoiling it but rest assured they *are* doable, if you want details checkout the game's Steam forum.
Now that we have that out of the way, I can get to the game.
Did you like the original Deus Ex? Did you like X-Files? Did you like 24? If you answer yest to all three then you will like this, as it's basically a hybrid of the three.  There's plenty of reviews out there for the original version of Deus Ex: Human Revolution so I won't bulk this out, but suffice to say the storyline, gameplay, music, art style and voice acting of this title really are something else. Your main character is a complete badass and gets even more badass as the game goes on, and the level of customisability and user choice is insane. It is very much a worthy successor to Deus Ex.
This specific version incorporates all the DLC that the original version had - in particular, the excellent Missing Link expansion is now integrated into the campaign and barring some wonky equipment and XP mechanics, allows seamless transfer of your character's gear and powers between it and the rest of the game. DLC gear is not placed directly into your inventory but made available in the game world, and very easily so.
Graphically... this game's engine was never that amazing (although weirdly it seems to do lighting extremely well, but not texture quality or animation) but given how the game flips between dark and grimy to cold and clinically clean, you don't actually notice the engine's shortcomings as much as you'd think. What is here has been upped a bit from the original release and looks pretty good, given it's a few years old. It's not Crysis, though.
Boss encounters have been reworked a little, in that you don't have to engage in a pure firefight with them anymore - there's now avenues to hit them with controlled robots or environmental hazards - but they're still very much combat encounters and you can tell that they're modifications rather than re-designs. IMHO they're still best done as a straight-up fight.
Overall, this is an excellent game with some awful bugs and rough around the edges where it shouldn't be - but if the new Deus Ex: Mankind Divided garners your interest, you might find this worth a playthrough to see what Adam Jensen got up to prior to it.

This was my first foray into the Deus Ex universe, and man was it a doozy.  I really enjoyed it.  The customization options you can get for your character by way of Praxis augments is fun and challenging.  The methods through which you can accomplish your mission, be they stealth, gunfight, or something in between, also give nice variety.  I also like that there are chances for you to miss entire questlines, even if you're thorough, because if you're going to give the player options and a sandbox, make there be consequences.  The plot is fan-friggen-tastic, and the cutscenes are really awesome, and not so frequent as to make you feel like you're just pressing buttons during a long movie.  The DLC is DEFINITELY worth playing, and man, is it difficult.  There are some plot loose ends that I wish had been wrapped up, and the pathing of the enemy soldiers becomes mechanical and takes away from the realism, but all in all, a solid, great game.

Excellent twist on the traditional rougelike genre.
The game is pretty simple to pick up, but there's a lot of depth. I think the difficulty curve is perfect for me - you don't get roflstomped from your first playthrough, but there's a lot to learn before you are really progressing through to deeper levels.
I NEVER write reviews but I am doing so for this game because I think it's totally worth adding to your library, but it looks like it's slipping under the radar. Don't pass it up!
PROS:
-Unique possession mechanic allows for great flexibility of playstyle each game
-Updates address QoL wishes from player base. Awesome devs!
-Good humor throughout game
-Learning curve is perfect. Not really easy at all, not "go **** yourself it's a rougelike" hard
-Encourages replayability by allowing you to pick an item from a previous playthrough and use it in a future game
-Game design is... really good. Hard to explain, but the game GUI just FEELS well-made.
-Easy to start up, save, and pick up later. Game doesn't seem super story-driven, so forgetting where you are isn't really an issue. This is a big pro to me as I often shuffle between 5-10 games and might not come back to something for a month or two.
CONS:
-Mediocre graphics (I don't care, but some might)
-Sounds are repetitive
-Inventory management is not excellent (but is slated to be improved in the next update)

tl;dr: Has potential, but is THAT kind of roguelike and has absolutely no variance in the early levels.
I really tried to like this game. There is huge promise here.
There are also many annoyances here (such as no having no shortcuts for items - wtf?) and the death card mechanic simply not working (I have many cards, yet always the same two ones show up when a new char is created), etc.
But what really breaks this game is that when you die, it will not be your own fault.
Now, I know this sounds like whining from someone having no clue what he is doing, but let me tell you, I have played them all: ADOM, ToME, Dungeon Crawl: Stone Soup, Caves Of Qud, Dwarf Fortress, Rogue: Legacy, Everspace, etc. And also finished them all (at least those that really have a "finished" state). I do know what I talk about when talking about roguelikes.
In good roguelikes (especially the best, ToME), you will know what you did wrong when you died. You might have been too brave, ill-prepared, used wrong spells, etc. You get punished for mistakes and rewarded for playing well. As it should be.
In bad roguelikes, the game may at any point throw random **** your way that you have no way to be prepared against and that will just kill you, no matter what.
Unfortunately, MidBoss belongs to the second category. It doesn't matter how well you play, how much attention you pay to your stats. You can do everything perfectly (as will be evident by having a generally easy time and some momentum) - and then there will be some enemy that has stats so far above anything you could have achieved so far that he just obliterates you. If you manage to get to floor 5, which has no doubt the craziest difficulty spike I have ever seen in a game, you will know what I mean.
Now, Caves of Qud does that, too, but at least the beginning of the game is varied.
In MidBoss, you will have to live through the first floors again. And again. And again.
And let me tell you, the first floors are ALWAYS the same. Slightly different room layout, yes, but the enemy types are always the same, your loot will always be the same (as the right piece of equipment for you is easily discernable). Everything is the same, always.
There is nothing like in Rogue: Legacy or Everspace that would give you a boost after a while so you could at least skip those early levels and get to the interesting parts. Nope. The death cards are a drop in the ocean, since what really matters is your character level. Plus, they seem to be very buggy - as written above, they don't even work right for me.
You will grind through the early floors, "collecting" the same essential enemies to mastery, leveling up the same stats best for your chosen playstyle... it is a nightmarish version of Groundhog Day with no variance whatsoever.
What a shame. It could be easily resolved by randomizing the abilities of enemies or simply which enemy appears on which floor, but since all of that is fixed, you will be bored out of your mind by the 10th time you have to do it all again - latest.

Midboss is a simple Roguelike with just enough mechanical depth to keep the experienced player interested, while maintaining enough simplicity to keep the new player attached. The familiar trappings are all there; gods, tomes, potions, scrolls, weapons and armor, but the way they are presented is somewhat simpler than tradtional roguelikes such as Dungeon Crawl Stone Soup or Nethack. Potions start off unidentified, but can largely be quaffed with impunity, for their effects are largely unpunishing. Altars exist, but function as a one-off sacrifice mechanic that lets the player experiment to discover each god's preferences.
This simplicity is carried over into the enemies. At first, Midboss's enemy selection could be seen as meagre, but this is largely mitigated by the possession system; Midboss's main point of difference. Any enemy in the game can be possessed, as long as you possess the strength to defeat it. Each "form" you take has its own skills/abilities, and is levelled up independently to other forms. Forms can also be mixed and matched in order to combine the abilities of your fallen foes in interesting ways. The depth of the possession system is what sets the game apart from other roguelikes. Do you take a rat's speed over a Zombie's strength? Do you take a warlock's magical prowess over a minataur's charge? These are the sorts of decisions you have to make constantly in order to survive the game, especially when it starts throwing enemies at you with powerful specialisations.
In conclusion, whether or not you'll enjoy Midboss is largely dependent on the sort of gamer you are. Midboss functions as a perfect entry point for new and semi-experienced roguelike players, but might not have enough depth to keep veterans of traditional roguelikes interested.

Ok. So to start, let me say that I have played longer than listed above, about an hour, but have not touched story mode. Therefore some people may enjoy that aspect of it and I can't make a judgement call on it as i haven't gone near it.
Now, what I can say is that this game suffers from regular crashes, framerate issues or drops, time glitches, and even has had multiple issues with just starting up the game. Furthermore, (and this is just a peeve of mine) the game is locked at 30 frames anyway so you lack the fluidity you get with a lot of other games on pc.
The gameplay (the combat) is frankly subpar. While the game looks pretty and does look like a naruto game and battle, it doesn't FEEL like one and your options are severely limitted. For the most part, you have an up, down, and basic button mashing combo...i mean the SAME button for each combo just tilt up, down, or not at all. Then, there is your standard shuriken/projectile throw and your three basic jitsus. A weak one (y then x on xbox controller) a strong one (y then b on xbox controller) and the ultimate (yy then b on xbox controller). There is also generally one mid air combo and a grab. Excessively basic. Furthermore, the combat feels almost sluggish, without the fast pace I had hoped for in the naruto battles. The jutsus, while asthetically pleasing, don't combo with anything thus leading to battles seemingly existing just to try and hit each other with jutsus. This could be excusable if there were a number of minute aspects to the combat that pulled some tricks  with agility or combo canceling into more outrageous ones or if you even had a few combo based jutsus for each character. However, while there is some inkling of those first two, it ultimately comes to naught. Very little skill is required to "git gud" at the game and the skill cap tops of pretty quickly.
Honestly, it plays like all the other ninja storms. I had hoped they would add some depth to this one but was disapointed. If  you liked the others and just really love the simple combat style, then you'll probably like this one. But if you didn't or have never played before, I recommend against it.

I was an original Elite Founder of this game when the funding campaign launched in 2012...before Steam Greenlight and many other community funded games.  I eagerly backed at the Elite ($60) level and chomped at the bit for ever to get into the game and then I did.  I was elated with how fun the game was in it's early days and was enthralled with the promise of what was to come, so my friends and I waited eagerly for that content...and waited...and waited...eventually got frustrated and stopped playing feeling like we had wasted $60 on broken promises.
That's what things were.  We backed the game with that understanding but PGI's approach was not that same as what you see on Kickstarter or Greenlight today...they did it all independantly.  So in short, we kept up with what they were doing for a while hoping to come back one days and things just seemed like they were going down hill and the game was going to crash and burn.
When we saw it launch on Steam, my initial thought was "Well, one last ditch effort to keep the game alive it seems."  Then one day we were talking about it and decided to pop in one last time to see if things had changed...and were very surprised.  So now I have over 70 hours in the game in less than two weeks and am eating crow.
So, I may not agree with everything that PGI did when they got started but I think they've been trying to find a way to make it work and had to grow some thick skin in the process to keep things afloat.  I'm not defending them by any means but this was an early learning lesson in crowd funding a game.  Lots of things they promised came very late or are still not in the game today.  That's OK, I'd rather them get it right but they had issues communicating this to their backers.
In short, mistakes were made and some people are still mad about it.  I'm happy now and hope to see more of the content come to fruition.
Would I recommend this game?  Yes, so long as you know what it is and isn't.  There are plenty of reviews that details this info, but in short:
-  This is not run'n'gun, you do you die, fight alone, die alone
-  Teamwork is essential for victory as is communication
-  It is a slow paced progress to improve your mechs, do not expect to buy your way to victory.  Even if you put hundreds of dollars into it, you still have to grind the XP for your mechs to improve them
-  The controls are complex but intuitive once you learn them
-  The game is for a mature audiance and by that I do not mean 17+ because of language and nudity but because the players are primarily veterans of the Mechwarrior games from the late 90's/early 2000's.  That doesn't mean you shouldn't play, just be aware that it's not a game for those of little patience
-  Yes, they ask for money.  You can buy mechs outright or grind out money and items.  The game is NOT pay to win and you can play it completely free if you're willing to take the time to work through it.  The stuff you pay for is getting mechs/equipment early or for cosmetics
So, if you're looking for a game that requires true tactical teamwork, has arguably fair pricing, looks amazing and can feel pretty rewarding then this game is something you should check out.

I was tempted to save myself the effort of a semi-long review and just smugly declare this the NEW DEVILS SHARE.  In SPACE, no less!  Then it occurred to me that unless I also incorporated words like "spoopy" and "pants" into my review, I'd get no end of thumbings-down for my lazy efforts.  So...sigh...in the interests of full disclosure and being found "helpful" and blah-blah-blah, let me describe to you my "experience" of Project Pulsation thus far.  (Well, hopefully FOREVER.)

REALLY nifty opening cut-scene.  One of those classic, slow-moving tracking shots along the outside hull of a vast spaceship, a la so many quality, big-budget sci-fi movies which you've no doubt seen.  With a suitably eerie, machinery-in-deep-space style rumble to accompany said visuals.  Things then start to go a TINY bit awry once we get past the credits - I mean, how could they possibly ♥♥♥♥ up writing their OWN NAME? - and into on-screen captions such as "inside the hidden artefact, his and you have to find"...and then, BAM!  We're straight into the game (i.e. abruptly, without the above highly enigmatic statement even reaching its no doubt eye-widening conclusion).
So the first level is "Elevator", apparently.  Hmmm, that's an interesting concept for a first level.  Oh, I see...in almost total darkness, with a not-very-helpful flashlight to help us to see, we're going to travel down an elevator shaft via a mixture of moving elevators, jumps across to other elevators, and...wait for it...free-falling huge distances which don't seem to kill you (or even make the vaguest semblance of a sound) when you strike a hard surface tens of metres below.  Which one would take to mean that you are invincible for the rest of the game.  A "rest of the game" which I, regretfully, am perhaps destined to never see, mostly due to this game being AN UNFORGIVEABLE, STEAMING PILE OF ALIEN DOO-DOO.
Oh, speaking of which, did I mention the strange red "monsters" crawling about on the walls of the elevator shaft?  The first one seemed so preoccupied with crawling in one spot, and subsequently never getting anywhere, that he just allowed me to shoot him to death with my laser-pistol multiple times before he simply, er, disappeared (not even sure the word "dissipated" covers it) in a highly unsatisfying and decidedly un-gruesome manner.  There were many more such monsters, as I travelled further down.  They all died with a similar lack of spectacle, and no attempt, that I could see, to ever "attack" yours truly.  As for myself, well, I think I "died" when I finally took a HUMUNGOUS fall of perhaps a half-mile and maybe - just maybe, I really can't confirm - striking what may (?) have been the very bottom of the elevator shaft?!  Again, I'm not sure, it may have just been the game crashing...'cause after this highly eventful occurrence, I couldn't move, or exit to a menu screen or anything.  So I was forced to restart my whole computer, which is always a benchmark of the highest quality in a video game, I'm sure you'll agree.
Oh, and just in passing, did I mention that you can't remap the controls, and I saw no visible sign that any of my attempts to change the graphics quality actually made a lick of difference?  Do you need any further convincing?!  Sigh...then just waste five of your own bucks and find out for yourselves...

The gameplay is reminiscent of the first Deus Ex with 2 significant changes:
1.Chest hight walls
Yes, I am afraid that trends of modern gaming didn't pass HR completely by, so get ready to shoot people from behind cover. While shooter part is diminished by ever present chest hight cover, the stealth part is actually enhanced- it is extremely convenient to be able to see behind corners, and plan your approach accordingly.
2.Level design
While Deus Ex provided HUGE open ended areas, with a lot of freedom, HR' s levels look more like corridors. We are still able to choose from a verity of approaches, (vents, breakable walls, sewers and so on), but the illusion of freedom of movement has been diminished somewhat. We are still however have an absolute freedom in game play aspect of problem solving: stealth or  direct approach, lethal or non lethal, guns or melee  takedowns.
The story  itself I will break into 3 parts: plot, setting, and  philosophical context.
1.The setting.
Simply amazing. Frighteningly realistic, it menages to build a bridge between our reality and the bleak  dystopian future of the first Deus Ex. Geo-political disputes, ethically bankrupt  corporations, shadow governments and rampant abuse of technology create a world almost as believable as it is repulsive.
2.Philosophical context
HR's main focus is on  transhumanism and the plethora of questions around it: The ethics of human augmentations, self controlled human evolution and the line between the man and the machine.
3.The plot
The weakest link in HR. While the plot itself is serviceable, characters don't  have arks, motivations are lacking, and  by the end the plot runs out of steam, disconnecting you from the story and characters completely.
The missing Link DLC included in the director's cut provides about 2 hours of gameplay and indeed  enriches the story, but itself consists of nothing but straight corridors with even less freedom to explore.
In conclusion: A masterpiece. Highly recommended.

SUMARRY: Definitely the best Naruto game to date! Great for the sale price of $17, a must buy at that price.
PROS:
- The story is amazing, and not just the content but the execution as well. You have two paths for each branch of the story (One Yin and one Yang) which converge on a final point where the actual story (in the anime) converges together. For example in the beginning you have the path of Sasuke and Naruto when Naruto is fighting Obito and Madara, and Sasuke when he finds Kabuto to bring back Orochimaru, etc.
- Smooth combat, stable gameplay, everything just flows together better than all of the previous iterations of the series.
- So many characters! I have a hard time picking who I want to be :/
- All new partner ultimate jutsus, almost every character has a new ultimate jutsu that changes based on who you team him/her up with. For example if you use Naruto/Sasuke/Sakura you do the Three-Way Deadlock summoning with some extra. (My favorite is Pain-Konan, which involves Pain using planetary devastation, and when the opponent is in the big rock Konan covers the entire thing with paper bombs and makes a big boom! :D)
- Online combat has a reliable connection now.
CONS:
- Not too many people play online, and those that do often chakra-dash spam and seek to win more than they want to have fun.
- Some of the ending fights (In the story) can be quite ridiculously challenging.
- I have no friends that have this game... I have no friends at all actually, but still, you get the point.
Overall: 9/10
Note: I'm a fan-boy of both the naruto series and fighting games so my review is a little bias, just a little. If you are a fan of the series however, you'll love the game!

It's rare that a developer goes from make a adult game about crime with very adult themes. To making a game about a high school kid who moves to a school for child delinquents and socially challenged kids, but in a lot of ways Bully is like a GTA. For example Bully is a giant open world with stuff to collect, bike races to do, arcade games to play, and much more to just kind of find.The mission structure is very similar to GTA, you do a bunch of work for one of the factions;like the jocks or the nerds, and the more the more you do work for one faction it can effect your standing with others. Which in turn can effect the way some of the people treat you at school. The combat is very similar but instead of machine guns and rocket launches. Your playing with slingshots and stink bombs. There are also a lot of things that are different about Bully that really makes it feel like your in high school it feel very structured, but that's not a bad thing at all. Like you have classes two times a day everyday until you pass the highest level of that class, and of you don't go the prefects or any adult of authority. All the classes have there own perks like one of the classes shows you where all the collectibles, and unlike the protagonists in GTA jimmy is 15 and needs his sleep so if your out past 2 you just pass out on the spot which can make some night missions feel a little too time restrictive.
The story starts you out in a car ride with you and your mom and what seems to be your new stepdad. They then drop you off in the front of Bullyworth academy where you meet the principle and some of the teacher, but the fun starts to come in when you go to your dorm room and meet your new friend Gary, who is a sociopath, i don't know how else to put it.You soon start to become manipulated by him, and you two soon go your separate ways and you start to see less and less of him. You then start to do work for the other factions of the school. Playing Bully it kind of puts you back and makes you think about your time in high school, I know the archetypes aren't as plain and simple as they are in Bully but it does a great job of boiling a lot of the high school experience down to a 20 hour game.
Then there are a few technical issues with bully I didn't really have too many other then the game crash on me a couple of times, and that just sucks after that happened for the first time a started saving much more frequently. I can't really say definitely how the game will turn out for you, but it didn't seem to bad. From my experience with it. Over all the game is well made but parts of it just seem kind of repetitive and broken;overall though I think it's a great game.

Excellent Roguelike, a perfect example of how depth and replayability can grow from very simple mechanics. Difficulty is not to be underestimated, stats system as of the current version is relatively unique and takes some consideration when leveling up / gearing up / choosing forms.
It is always nice when you have a turn-based game where you can casually rush through the "grind" parts, and then stop and seriously plan out the tricky fights.
The grave-goods system (being able to keep an item from a previous run) is more than an interesting mechanic - the first few levels can be slow, but starting with a higher level item can really expedite the grind and get you back to where you died pretty quickly.
Future patches seem to be planning to add more content based on what I've read. In it's current state, I'd give it a solid 4/5 and say it is more than fairly priced for a game developed by just a couple main developers (?) and other help. If more content is added, easily a 5/5 and the best turn-based roguelike to surface on Steam in YEARS.

Here's a small section of my review for MidBoss as a part of my YouTube series, The Show. You can find the full review in my video linked below.
There are a number of aspects to MidBoss that make it different to its genre-friends, most notably the core mechanic, which sees you possessing your enemies, taking over their corpses to utilise their abilities to your advantage in order to achieve your ultimate goal - showing those jerky jerk jerkface monsters that you’re cool and awesome and can do good things if they’d just give you a chance and you’re gonna be the new boss if you have to kill every last one of them.
Impressively, MidBoss has a some great accessibility features that are considered “advanced” by a lot of standards. A lot of the options allow you to tweak various aspects of the game’s difficulty, which is so much better than just having a vanilla “Easy/Medium/Hard” selection, because different players will struggle with different aspects. The feature that probably impressed - and surprised - me the most, though, is the “Queasy Safe Mode”. This feature toggles the sound effects and animations for things that players might find gross, or perhaps inappropriate for younger players, such as blood and guts and stuff. The “child safe” mode is a nice bonus, but what this has another great use for is people with, for example, emetophobia, because this mode explicitly states that it removes all visual and audio references to barfing within MidBoss.
