I have completed AdCap twice on mobile and once on PC. So, why am I giving it a negative review? Well, let me just say that the mobile version is far better for a number of reasons, even if it too is a bad game. The mobile version is actually less glitchy overall, running better on a crappy phone than it does on a massive PC. It also lets you watch ads for a variety of boosts, which lets you complete the game in a decent amount of time. The PC version once had this, but they were removed as the devs realized people weren't buying Gold, the pay2win currency. As a result, the PC version drags on and on and you come to hate it by the time you beat it. If you have to play a version of AdCap, play the mobile version.
That being said, why is this game a hunk of steaming garbage? Events are a huge part of why. Every other week, a generally holiday-themed event pops up, offering badges that boost your profits, MegaBucks which allow you to boost profits a few times before becoming absolutely useless, and Gold, which is the only currency you can buy with real money, and thus the one that is the most broken. Why is this an issue? Well, the events only pays out anything worthwhile if you reach the end of the event within the allotted time span, which is typically a few days. Unfortunately, as the developers are absolute trash when it comes to balancing, these events take much more time to complete unless you a) spend real money or b) cheat. Alternatively, your total score during the event gets you placed on a leaderboard and depending on which tier yours places you in, you get a small reward for your time. The issue remains the same. The only way to get decent payout from the event is to a) spend real money or b) cheat. Worse, even if you place anywhere, there's a good chance the rewards won't payout at all without having to email the devs and pray that they actually notice you. I've played maybe 7 events and only gotten 1 payout.
The issues with events sum up the issues with the rest of the game. The two other permanent levels, the Moon and Mars, end much faster than the base game, with the Moon having large gaps in progressing quickly and progressing at an infuriatingly slow pace. The developers aren't even trying to get rid of cheaters or balance, as all you need to cheat is an AutoClicker or Cheat Engine (which is ridiculous in itself, as the game only lets you play it Online).
tl;dr: The game is an inferior PC port that is an imbalanced, p2w, hackable mess that you should stay away from.
Seriously, if you want a good, non-p2w idling game, just play the desktop Cookie Clicker game. It's not on Steam, but it's better in effectively every way.

When i first heard of the steam controll i was a huge skeptic, i mean, touch pads for joysticks? My only experiance with touch pads has been those horrible things that come in laptops that i always disable in favor of a mouse.
I finally got around to buying the steam controller, and it has very much impressed me. I first played something i knew would work well, portal 2, and after quickly getting used to the touch pads, it feels great, the aiming is not nearly as difficult as it would be with an xbox controller. Then i tried skyrim, a game that i knew would support it well, but might take configuring, and i was right, but it was easy, i just used someone else configuration that they made and i was playing skyrim just fine. Now i wanted to put it to a real test, i wanted to play something that does not natively support controllers, I played black mesa source, a game i have played and hated playing with an xbox 360 controller in the past. And it worked perfectly, unlike the xbox controller, i did not have to set it up or even configure anything, it just worked, and aiming was not hard at all, in fact i soon found myself immersed in the gameplay and not even thinking about the controller. But like all great things there is a setback, the force feed back in the steam controller fells pretty awefull and makes a horrible buzzing noise that makes me disable it. A good plus is that you can bind any button to any keyboard or mouse button, and there are gestures like double tapping the touch pad, and swiping, The controller is far better then the ps4 and xbox 360 controllers, but not quite as good as a mouse for those twitch shooter games where precision and reaction time is key to winning, such as in counterstrike. Other then that, i would gladly reccomend this controller to anyone.

If you're like me and you like cars, engines and mechanical engineering concepts, you'll probably enjoy this game as much as I have been. I tend to spend hours on one vehicle, tweaking suspension, frame size/weight/length/width, tires until it is just right. This game makes that kind of gameplay available.
Where this game really shines for me is the suspension. I can't believe how amazing it looks and feels while going over bumps and taking sharp turns. The possibilities of suspensions you can make seem endless, and you're not even limited to just the shocks that are a provided part. You can even use frame parts with elasticity tweaks and come up with your own suspension designs, as you may see when checking out the workshop (which has many, awesome designs).
I personally don't like shallow and arcade-style physics games that invovles vehicles. This one is the opposite.

Overall I give this game a thumbs up! For the price, it's definitely a good deal and plenty of enjoyment.

EDIT: 1/30/16. Alright I'll expand on this, having spent a little more time with the game. MWO is a mech game along the lines of previous MW games (of which I've only ever played MW4) but with obviously modernized visuals. Now, I quite liked MW4, but it was much more of a single-player experience for me, whereas MWO is entirely multiplayer as of the time of writing this review. I do believe that they have plans to put a polished campaign in place, further down the line (at some point this year, even?), but as of right now, gameplay in MWO centers entirely on wrecking enemy mechs in your own heavily customized walking steel mountain.
Pros of this game? Extremely high skill cap, heavily reliant on team communication and cooperation. Mechs do not handle as simply as an fps - your legs move separate from your torso, and torsos have different degrees of movement based on the particular mech your piloting, so it does take some time to master. A good mech pilot will always need to be mindful of how his legs are positioned, so he doesn't get caught out in a bad position by the enemy team. Another great thing about this game is just how many freaking mechs there are to choose from - I think there are around 50 - 55 mechs in the game right now, ranging from 20 to 100 tons in weight, all with 3 to 7 variants each. And did I mention that you can customize the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of your mechs? Feel free to change armor values, upgrade internal structures, and swap out different weapons and modules and utility systems to your heart's content. FREAKIN' AMAZING.
There's also faction play to be had, where you can sign up with a unit (or hell, just play a mercenary lone wolf if you want) and earn rewards by playing for one of the game's 2 main factions (Inner Sphere and Clan), which are themselves split into smaller factions. I haven't gotten to play in any faction play quite yet, just because my friends and I are still pretty new to this and we're working on building up our arsenals, but it looks super exciting, not to mention that there are some pretty huge updates to faction play incoming that look absolutely awesome.
Finally, the game is free to play, and on top of that, it isn't even pay to win in any way that I can tell. Yes, there are some mechs that can only be bought with real life cash currency, but those mechs are in no way superior to mechs that can be bought with in-game money (i.e. think sidegrades, not upgrades). This is, in every sense, a skill-based game, and a pretty awesome one at that.
Cons? I'm probably biased but it's hard to think of any. The developers are in constant communication with the community and seem to push out updates frequently and pay super close attention to balance. It'd be nice to have a few more mech bays available to you starting out, since you can't buy them with in-game currency, but honestly they're so cheap even when they're not on sale (I think less than $1.50 each?) and occasionally they do have sales on both MC (cash currency) and mech bays that push the cost to literally cents. Oh, and also you can get a few mech bays as rewards from faction play.
Tl;dr - Awesome game.

I've played this one since the open beta and really enjoy the combination of tinkering with the mech you bring into battle and the slightly slower pace of gameplay as a fairly tactical shooter (the mechanics mean you take quite a few hits to die in game which, in turn, slow things down a bit). There is a good range of different successful gameplay tactics and a huge range of customisable different mechs you can bring to a fight.
After several teething issues (pre-steam, so don't worry) game balance is now pretty good between the two main factions ("inner sphere" and "clan") and the online population are fairly friendly in a wallaby-name-calling sort of fashion (see Gh1d0ra's review later!).
The "storyline" part of the game, "community warfare", is fun with much more structured in-game challenges. However as it is pretty much "end game" content, it works best as part of a pre-organised team (lots of these accessible via the MWO website community links) and needs a top-line mech.
It's main limitations are the initial learning curve and a limited number of maps and game types. Hopefully the developers will continue to respond to this in the next few months. Personally, I'm really hoping for some sort of intermediate gameplay between the random quickplay maps and the involved CW game (some sort of FFA deathmatch tournament would be great...)
All-in-all, it is good fun, especially as a free-to-play game, and I would recommend having a go through the initial cadet bonus stage, customing a bought mech until it is suitably bristling with lasers, ballistic weapons and missiles, blowing up the opposition team/going down in a blaze of glory and seeing if you enjoy it!

If you are a Battletech fan and want to play this because of Battletech, leave now. Do not play MechWarrior Online!!
Here are just a small list of the glaring examples of how MWO has nothing to do with Battletech:
Community Warfare leaves a lot to be desired. Quite simply, it’s pointless and boring.
The game needs more maps – maybe slow down on the ‘Mech releases and create more maps for a while.  (Though I really do love seeing Marauders and WarHammers in the game.)
With the exception of River City the redesigned maps haven’t really impressed me.  Forest Colony is especially horrible; it went from being my favorite map in the game – by far – to my third most hated (after Terra Therma and Viridian Bog.)
If this game was called Giant Stompy Robots Online (GSRO) – which is what I am going to call it from here on out – I would be a pretty big fan of the game.
The improvements made to GSRO in the last year or more have been slow, but plentiful and (generally) well done.  It's true that PGI may never repair the trust they lost with many of us Founders; however, as a generic Giant Stompy Robot shooter goes, it is good and getting better.
The quirk system is mostly working, 'Mech modules are a neat way to add minor (but helpful) features to your 'Mech, and any balance problems seem to be minor.  Remember, an online game like this is always in flux as the players and meta-game change.
If you’re the type of person like likes to play a game for 30 minutes, knock out a couple of drops then return to reality, you can’t go wrong with Giant Stompy Robots Online.  If you’re like me and you binge play for a few hours once a week, you still can’t go wrong with Giant Stompy Robots Online.
---------------------------------------------------------
As much as I do not want to like this game – (
and I want to keep making horribly offensive remarks toward the PGI development team) –
keep hating it. Some day, someone will make a real Battletech/MechWarrior game, until then Giant Stompy Robots Online will keep me entertained.
It’s NOT Battletech no matter how you try to ram that down my throat.
It is a good Giant Stompy Robot Shooter.  The changes they have made in the last few months really have improved the game substantially.
Against my own angst and animosity toward MechWarrior Online and PGI,
I play it, I have fun, and I look forward to playing it more.  Just remember, it is NOT Battletech or anything legitimately belonging to the Battletech/MechWarrior IP.

Since servers can't be user-hosted, that leaves the game in a state of horrible decay. It is next to unplayable unless you select specific servers. Deus Ex: Human Revolution is the prequel to my favorite game ever made: Deus Ex. Since I had already put the precursor to this title on a pedestal and was hyped to all hell, how does this game fare in comparison?
Not bad, actually.
Because this game is a prequel, it is totally fine to jump in and start playing it even without playing the previous games, although I caught many references and call backs to Deus Ex throughout. In fact, I’d probably recommend most players today to start with this game, as Deus Ex hasn’t really aged all that well in terms of graphics/ mechanics.
Deus Ex was a Cyberpunk dystopian FPS/RPG hybrid that was full of deep choices and free-form gameplay. The storyline dealt with world spanning conspiracies and epic world ending narratives, but Deus Ex: Human Revolution takes a smaller, more focused approach, mainly dealing with the basic morality question of human augmentation, corporate espionage, and how technology positively and/or negatively impacts the “natural” human experience. This smaller approach was somewhat disappointing at first as it’s not nearly as “epic” as the first game, but it still told an interesting story, full of little peeks at the larger conspiracies overall. The main character has the  pretty cliché motivation of revenge and delves into a complex web of intrigue that’ll keep you guessing until the very end. The ending is somewhat lackluster, but the upcoming sequel Mankind Divided promises more nuanced endings that depend on factors through the game. All in all, the many different character’s motivations and the many moral choices you make in the game paint a convincing near future cyberpunk world that is easy to get immersed in.
This game isn’t the prettiest, being initially released in 2011, but even back then it didn’t look so great. 2011 was the year Skyrim, Dead Space 2, L.A. Noire, Battlefield 3, and Arkham City were released. Deus Ex: Human Revolution already looked dated back then compare to these titles. However, the game remedies this with clear art direction. Most locations are flush with a calming and surreal old yellowed parchment art style that bathes the world in amber-yellow hues. The effect was designed to give the world a Renaissance style, with people learning so much about the human body and augmentation that extreme advancements were occurring rapidly, without the necessary societal changes to keep up. There is also plenty of Icarus/ Daedalus parallels as well, with humanity flying too close to the sun and getting burned as a result. Animations are mostly decent, but facial animations are pretty wooden and everyone looks somewhat like plastic. However, this game’s strikingly distinct art style more than makes up for the lackluster animations and textures and is one of the more memorable parts of the game.
The great part of this game’s design is it’s free-form approach to quests. You can complete the game without killing a single character (except the boss fights), and in some situations you can talk your way into areas that would normally be considered trespassing. For example, a quest near the beginning of the game requires you to retrieve something from a police station, which is off limits to civilians. However, you can either talk your way in (using CASIE augmentations if necessary), stealth your way in through a back alley, or kick in the front door and start shooting people in the face. Anytime a game allows me multiple approaches makes me feel like I’m actually using my own wits and not just blindly following a waypoint, although there are some quests that boil down to just that, unfortunately. Nevertheless, this level of freedom does a good job of reminding me why Deus Ex 1 was so good, as there were multiple approaches in that game as well. Going in guns blazing is viable, although the shooting mechanics feel a bit clunky compared to other FPSes.
This is also an RPG in addition to being an FPS, and there are different augmentations(skills) to put Praxis Points (Level ups) into. For example, if you’re making a loud, guns blazing character, you may want to invest in recoil management, Dermal Armor, and the Typhoon Explosive System, essentially an AOE attack that blows everything up in a 360 angle around you. However, if you’re a sneaky beaky kind of guy you may want to upgrade your ability to see enemy’s cones of vision on your minimap, as well as cloaking yourself. If you want to explore all the nooks and crannies the game has to offer you may want to upgrade your legs to jump super high and land from great heights without taking fall damage. There are many different things to level up, although I wished there were a bit more. It looks like Mankind Divided will have many more skills to try out, which I’m very excited for. One thing I felt was pretty OP was the cloaking in this game. Enemies can still hear you running around, but as long as you have plenty of cyberboost proenergy candy bars, you can make your way through most levels just by constantly gorging yourself on candy bars with cloak activated and running through the levels, awkwardly sidestepping enemies like Harry Potter with his invisibility cloak. Hopefully in Mankind Divided they nerf this, or at least make special enemies who can see through cloak or something.
Deus Ex: Human Revolution is a great Cyberpunk FPS/RPG that everyone who has an interest in the genre should play. It’s a prequel to one of the best games ever made in my opinion, and while it doesn’t quite live up to the first game, is still a fantastic experience in its own right. This game often goes on sale for $5, and at that price, it’s a no brainer considering you’ll get 20-25 hours of solid entertainment out of the experience. I’m very excited for Mankind Divided.

I have completed AdCap twice on mobile and once on PC. So, why am I giving it a negative review? Well, let me just say that the mobile version is far better for a number of reasons, even if it too is a bad game. The mobile version is actually less glitchy overall, running better on a crappy phone than it does on a massive PC. It also lets you watch ads for a variety of boosts, which lets you complete the game in a decent amount of time. The PC version once had this, but they were removed as the devs realized people weren't buying Gold, the pay2win currency. As a result, the PC version drags on and on and you come to hate it by the time you beat it. If you have to play a version of AdCap, play the mobile version.
That being said, why is this game a hunk of steaming garbage? Events are a huge part of why. Every other week, a generally holiday-themed event pops up, offering badges that boost your profits, MegaBucks which allow you to boost profits a few times before becoming absolutely useless, and Gold, which is the only currency you can buy with real money, and thus the one that is the most broken. Why is this an issue? Well, the events only pays out anything worthwhile if you reach the end of the event within the allotted time span, which is typically a few days. Unfortunately, as the developers are absolute trash when it comes to balancing, these events take much more time to complete unless you a) spend real money or b) cheat. Alternatively, your total score during the event gets you placed on a leaderboard and depending on which tier yours places you in, you get a small reward for your time. The issue remains the same. The only way to get decent payout from the event is to a) spend real money or b) cheat. Worse, even if you place anywhere, there's a good chance the rewards won't payout at all without having to email the devs and pray that they actually notice you. I've played maybe 7 events and only gotten 1 payout.
The issues with events sum up the issues with the rest of the game. The two other permanent levels, the Moon and Mars, end much faster than the base game, with the Moon having large gaps in progressing quickly and progressing at an infuriatingly slow pace. The developers aren't even trying to get rid of cheaters or balance, as all you need to cheat is an AutoClicker or Cheat Engine (which is ridiculous in itself, as the game only lets you play it Online).
tl;dr: The game is an inferior PC port that is an imbalanced, p2w, hackable mess that you should stay away from.
Seriously, if you want a good, non-p2w idling game, just play the desktop Cookie Clicker game. It's not on Steam, but it's better in effectively every way.

Most people might not like it, but I happen to enjoy it. I've been using it for almost a year now and it's still working perfectly, so here's my review.
Pros:
+Comfortable to hold.
+Extensive configuration to make it work perfectly for any game.
+Wired AND wireless.
+Able to be used as a keyboard and mouse outside of steam
(though, not very useful if you actually own a keyboard and mouse, still nice to have).
Cons:
-The touch pads aren't very great for aiming, and make some games tedious. Though, I rarely play fps games with a controller (because mouse and keyboard provides significantly more precision).
-Button placement isn't great, occasionally I'll try to press the Y or B buttons and end up moving my camera, not a big deal really.
-Configuration could be confusing to new users, but I'm sure there's a guide somewhere.
Overall, I really like this controller over any controller I've used in the past, it works amazingly for games like Skyrim, The Witcher 3, GTA V (for driving, can't stand trying to aim with it), and it works perfectly for games that don't require you to move the camera, because I still haven't gotten used to the touchpad. I mean, seriously, the best part about this controller is having the ability to configure every button on it to do whatever you could possibly want.

I love my Steam Controllers: they are awesome, from smell to how they feel, they work out of the box and they are perfect for many games, but there's a category of games they are awful with: twin stick shooters. And no amount of custom control schemes will ever fix that. So unless you are stuck in couch and want to play first person shooters, Civilization etc without mouse and keyboard - I advise buying something else.

My instinct is to wrap one or both of my hands around the whole grip while I play, which would have me accidentally pressing the underside buttons, although it helps to assign one of them to a game's sprint function, which frees the index finger on the same hand from having to switch between the trigger and its adjacent shoulder button (which may or may not be to which the sprint function was orriginally assigned). The touchpad however is a piece of garbage. For accuracy, you may find yourself sacrificing speed. Jittery under default settings, I've had to use the joystick to help center the reticle on what I'm aiming at (or attempting to view) more often, choosing to adjust my position rather than touch the finicky thing more than I have to. Even worse is the low area coupled with the tracking motion one is forced to use to spin about.
The creators of the Steam controller failed at what they set out to do, and it pushes me back toward keyboard&mouse for whatever it is I'm playing for the superior accuracy and panning. This is an example of how one of a product's features can spoil the whole thing, especially if it's the main selling point.
You will get frustrated with this conttroller at first but once you grow comfortable with this thing you'll never want to go back.

absolutely worthwhile and absolutely not pay to win.
There is a learning curve, and the game needs to be learned to be appreciated, but it's more about reading your HUD and making good decisions than actual twitchy shooter skill.
If you look on the website and the ingame store you might think that the game looks pay to win, but play it for a couple days and you see that it's not. Skilling up and mastering a mech is grindy as hell, but not prohibitive. This game actually has a pretty good cushion for noobness as long as you play through the tutorial.
The only way they try to get you is the same way every free to play game does- Limiting the amount of stuff you can own, which is in this case, mechbays- The number of slots in your garage to hold robots. However, this is easily remedied by playing the faction battle game mode and ranking up your rep grinds, because there's a ton of free mechbays handed out at low tier for every faction.
You also get fat checks for your first 25 matches as a noob, to give you a cash cushion to buy your first mech.
There are character mechs that can only be purchased in a cash shop, but except for a handful of really good ones, they're mostly on the level of the normal mechs or just plain mediocre, so even for pay 2 win mechs, there's still no pay 2 win. You can still kick their asses in a vanilla mech.
The devs also regularly run events that are pretty easy to complete, and these event rewards include cash shop items, aesthetic items, and even free mechs and mechbays. If you stick around long enough and keep up with current events, the devs will eventually just hand you something you want for free.

If firearms interest you, then this is a fantastic way to feed your interest in the subject. Even if it isn't, then it still serves as a wonderful memory game. Its very straightforward, take apart the gun, put it back together, shoot it and play around with its features, and do the more difficult modes and quizzes to rack up points to get the next gun. Its very simple, but surprisingly addicting.
Some problems I have with it is the fact the game is somewhat picky in the order you disassemble the gun. After a while, you just kind of accept it, but it is a pain to see that you failed one of your attempts at "super game mode" just because you didn't take a part out of the gun the way you would have in real life. Still, it adds to the challenge of it being a memory game, despite the tradeoff of realism. But honestly unless you are an OCD gunsmith or armorer or someone like Larry Vickers, I don't see this as being much of a problem. Also the amount of information on each given firearm is not always consistent, some guns seem to have an entire essay written about them while the others are just a few paragraphs long. All are ripped off of Wikipedia, which i have no problem with, but I would have liked the developers to write about the weapons in their own words.(thats just me) Graphics leaves some room for improvement, but i honestly can't complain that the graphics don't rival games of a major big budget franchise as it is free. I've read some technical difficulties, but I personally haven't experienced any. Perhaps they patched it all up. More reason for you to get it right?
All in all, I recommend it. If you are a firearms nut, then its an absolute must in your library.

They did this in order to pour all resources on Smite, and despite doing something so "♥♥♥♥♥♥" to a rather unique game that only needed a tiny bit of love they also ignored the cries to let the community mod the game. So this means that the main reason the older Tribes games are still around is totally non-existant here. There are no new maps, no new waepons and definitely no new updates coming.
What this means for new players is that they are pretty much getting a "complete" game, whether the game itself is complete or not. This is not too bad, to be honest. I can't quite say that it is balanced, when it comes to weapons, and you will most certainly get wrecked by players who played this game longer but I think that is the charm. There are no totally overpowered weapons (even though the sniper rifles and some other weapons can get really annoying) and this is mostly down to how the weapons work. It takes time to get good enough with a weapon to even hit players. It takes even longer to get a Blueplate with a spinfusor (hitting a person in the air with a spinfusor weapon) or just hitting people with the automatic rifles. For me that's what the charm of the game is, there's a lot to do with how good you are at it.
Another thing to note is that this game is all about teamwork, you need people to defend your base, some to attack and disrupt the enemy defence, cappers to get the flag and chasers to chase the enemy flag carrier. Ofcourse, this is the optimal setup and doesn't always come into play on pub servers, but sometimes it does. And this is another charm of the game itself, if you are bad at shooting at people, then maybe try your hand at capping the flag. Or if you can't ski that great, can try vehicles or being a juggernaught bombaring the enemy base from far away.
All that is all good and well, but the fact that the game is "dead" for the developer is a huge blow. And while I would recommend this to any player who wants a fast, skill-based shooter, I would also say that you might get pretty bored because there's no chance of anything new added or any of the totally crappy maps being changed for the better.

So I've owned this controller for the better part of 8 months and I figured it'd about time to give a review.
So at first, I was vastly disappointed. As someone with small hands it felt a little uncomfortable and there was a long adjustment period before I adapted. This isn't a controller you fall in love with at first glance. And I used to press the wrong button a lot, notably I'd press Y when I meant to press X.
I think this controller isn't very suited to small hands. How you hold the controller is something that a lot of people fuss over, but as long as you're comfortable it's relatively fine. I personally hold it with 3 fingers on the base, 2 on the paddle and the pinky on the bottom for leverage, one on the triggers/bumpers, and of course the thumb for the face. It works well with my small hands, but sometimes I can have slight issues with the bumpers. Adjusting my position so I have two fingers on top works, but makes me accidentally hit the paddle when I'm using the triggers, and accidentally hit the triggers when I'm using the paddles. If there's any input I can give to valve, it's to look into the ergonomics of the controller.
That being said, I still prefer this controller to a ps3 or xbox 360 controller (and by extention, a ps4/xbone controller). Minor ergonomically issues withstanding, the customization options pretty much cover all your needs. For any game that accepts x360 inputs, it works well. For most games that don't accept controllers, it still works well. If you have any outlying configurable needs, it does that too. For example if your fingers don't have a lot of endurance and you find yourself wanting to mash through dialogue, you can easily configure a button or combination to do that for you. If a game has multi-button inputs, you can configure single buttons to do that for you (usually the paddles). As an example, in Dragon Ball Xenoverse 2 you have to press B+Y to do a knockback kick, I just press the right paddle. It's perfectly consistent and comfortable. Similarly for dark souls, I bind up + r1 to the left paddle to do a kick. Once again, perfectly consistent and I don't have to worry about accidentally attacking into a parry when I meant to kick. I also bind the d-pad to the outer edges of the right trackpad so I can easily swap spells, items, or weapons while still moving. Not to mention all the other configuration options like haptic feedback, mouse region, rapid fire, edge cases, etc. There's seriously so much customization it's phenomenal.
Little things like that really push it ahead for me. Furthermore, you can control your desktop with it in case you want to watch youtube from your couch or bed or whatever. I have my TV hooked up to my computer so it works well. I also set it so big picture automatically changes my default screen to my TV so I can just play games from bed whenever. Nice and convenient. I'm not the biggest fan of how the on screen keyboard for the controller works, but it works well enough for general use.
Alright back to some cons. Big picture mode. Big picture mode is pretty core for steam controller use, and it has some minor problems. Firstly the web browser sucks, but I rarely use it anyway so it's passable. The general control scheme also doesn't work so well, but it's easy enough to navigate to your games and message your friends which is the most important part. However the biggest issue with Big Picture mode is that it takes an inordinate amount of CPU usage in the background when you're launching a game. Something that steam doesn't do when in regular mode. I'm not sure what causes it, but it's a documented issue and I think it has to do with the bubble overlay it keeps running in the background. Either way, if you're playing a game you barely have the specs to play then big picture mode is going to be a noticeable FPS hit. Which sucks because I still rather like big picture mode for playing my computer games with a console like experience.
So overall, it's a good controller. I do recommend it, but I also acknowledge that it has a few problems. Problems that I feel are more than made up by the fact that it's easily the most customizable controller on the market. I would say that if you're the type of person who just takes a controller and launches a game and doesn't want to mess with controls at all, this might not be the controller for you. Sure you can just use a community preset and roll with it, but tweaking it to your needs is one of the biggest advantages of the steam controller. If you're the type of person who doesn't mind fiddling with controls then there's no other device on the market that has the versatility the steam controller does.
I'd say if you really want a new controller, get the steam controller when it's on sale. It's on sale very often for around $35 dollars or so. If it's bundled with a game it goes down to $30 I think, so keep an eye out for bundles with games you want. Otherwise, maybe wait and see if they release a second edition of the controller that addresses some of the ergonomic complaints people have.

A living example of how you can not reinvent the wheel no matter how smart and resourceful you are.
Of course given what a fantastic piece of hardware the Steam controller is, and how many innovative ideas and added functionalities it offers, you could say it does so reinvent the wheel but, the price to pay for all these great new features is steep: it is less comfortable and intuitive than the xbox controller and for many games it requires extensive and sometimes complicated setups and fine-tuning.
Because of this, i would say that this item was not designed to replace the tried and tested xbox or ps controllers for standard games, it was designed to shine in those many situations where the standard controller is not ideal or doesnt work.
A few examples: All FPS games and especially FPS games with no controller support (you can play Stalker superbly with this controller),  games that dont recognize a controller at all, you can map any kb and mouse button to any button on this controller, PC games where you need to use a lot of keys (the steam controller offers two extra buttons compared to xbox and you can double the number of controller butons by use of a shift-button)
It offers very good mouse emulation for a controller, and in some ways it even surpasses a standard mouse, offering trackball functions, dual mouse function, one for each side, and more customisation options.
Fiddling with the insane amount of options is not necessarily easy or intuitive, but it was fun for me, i would say like playing a puzzle game, challenging but very satisfying when you manage to make things work your way.
Jokingly i could say the steam controller was one of the better games i played recently.
To sum it up i would say that for those games where the xbox controller works perfectly, its a bad idea to use the Steam controller, but there are so many games where the Xbox controller is less than ideal or doesnt work at all, and thats where the Steam controller will shine and bring improvements and added functionality that a standard controller cant dream of, making this controller a must have for any player that is willing to deal with the setups required.
There is probably one important thing that i have to add and that is not often mentioned in reviews: this controller will only work on steam, it wont work outside of steam (unless you add the games to the steam library and the steam interface works), so keep that in mind too.

Heres the things I like about it:
Heroes are much more Dynamic in their leveling, with their own skill trees and abilities.
The races are more diverse while still containing the same point buy system from its predessors.
The planetary anomolies, giving bonusses and penalties to planets throughout the galaxy.
Some things I hate about it:
While the card system is an interesting idea, it still dosen't change the fact that combat is either an automatic uninteresting button click, or a painfully long cinimatic experience. Though to be fair it is an improvement to MoO2.
Late game fleet managment is a nightmare of navigating through menus and figuring out who is where and who still has a turn.
The AI (both Player and Improvement) is terrable. The Improvement AI will constantly Build military building that aren't nessasary and eat up your dust (money).
final thoughts: If you like MoO2 or Alpha Centauri and want another game like that than you have to look no further. If you were expecting something else, then it's best to keep moving.

I've followed Midboss for a long, long time. I've been playing traditional roguelikes for over twenty years, and even as the genre is in the midst of a renaissance, Midboss has innovated with some truly excellent design decisions. One of my favourite mechanics in Nethack is intrinsics: abilities you gain from eating the corpses of certain monsters.
Midboss takes that and builds it out into an incredibly deep system where you possess different monsters and level them up to gain new abilities and attacks. You can mix and match these monster forms to counter, kill, and possess the next, tougher monster as you progress.
In addition to getting skills, there's also a robust loot system, and if you're the type of player that hates the punitive aspects of permadeath, you can even carry a powerful item over into your next playthrough. In addition to that, the death card system lets you share a copy of the dungeon and the items you got on your run with your friends.
This year has seem a lot of great, smart roguelikes, but it's a mistake to sleep on Midboss.

I'm not usually one for roguelikes, but there are three things that keep me coming back to MidBoss time and again - a brilliant soundtrack, the unique possession mechanic, and seemingly always new tricks to learn.
Well, OK, four - the fourth being the dialogue with Mid, and just Mid in general.

I'm a big roguelike fan, and have played a lot of them recently. This is the first one in a while that's really grabbed my attention. Effectively, you run around possessing monsters to gain their abilities and use their bodies as combat. If your monster form dies, you revert to a weakened form and will probably die an unceremonious death. However if your hp is low in your monster form, or your weakend original form, you can possess a new monster and go back to full health. This ends up creating a lot of risk-reward situations in the game where you have to choose either taking a new, weaker monster form, or risk delving deeper into the dungeon and risk dying. This is just one of the many mechanics that makes this game enjoyable.

MidBoss is a very very very lovely game and I WISH I HAD MORE TIME TO PLAY IT. So many different aspects appeal to me super hard. The art style is cute, the writing is fun and silly, the music is pretty and fits the general vibe of the game super well, and the gameplay is *tight*. It's good ole dungeon crawling, with a super neat possession mechanic. Your base form, Imp, has its own stats, health, stamina, etc. But if you tag an enemy with your Possession spell and then defeat them, you (SURPRISE) possess them. You became that which you killed, replacing your stats with that monster's stats, as well as picking up skills from that monster as you level up in your new-found body. If you max out the level of that form (the level cap varies from creature to creature) you can then equip that form to your main form, assuming you shed it. Gaining bonuses and a neat color swap depending on the creatures you have equipped, as well as access to all the skills you learned.
This is just a VERY basic explanation to the mechanic, but this mechanic alone is a crazy huge driving point for the gameplay in general and it seemed like the best thing to focus on for this review. You can have some wicked fun with it, and there's a lot of other fun mechanics that mesh well with it. So I HIGHLY recommend making sure you don't miss out on this gem. <3

It's a great modern roguelike! I love, love the rhythm of the possession mechanic in this game - you don't heal by resting or by using fountains, you heal by possessing the enemies you defeat and taking their forms. This is also how you learn skills, get better stats, and become cuter with every iteration of yourself!
But, okay, let me back up. MidBoss is a game about being a lowly dungeon imp who decides to become the biggest, baddest monster in the dungeon while everyone's distracted fighting heroes. Cue possessing your former allies to steal their skills, killing everyone, and selling loot to the thoroughly neutral merchant so you can buy more powerful equipment.
As it's a roguelike, the core gameplay loop is simple: explore, get better at learning when to run vs fight, mastery over your skills, etc etc - and then you make a mistake and die. Which is fine! The gameplay is so tight you'll enjoy playing more of it and getting better with every run - or luckier! My last run I found a flaming sword I could possess, and it was really good at killing things! I swapped over to an acid bat when it got low on health, but misjudged if I could take on a zombie or not. That was my fault, and I'll be more careful next time - and the next, and the next!
Death lets you carry over at least one of your items - and oh, items! You find all kinds of things, equipment, potions, scrolls, earrings - all kinds of stuff you pick up Diablo-style (press alt to make the items show up on the floor with fancy icons) and then throw into your inventory. Here's a flaw: you can't auto-sort your inventory, and it's kind of tight, but it's a minor hassle at most. It's easy to dump stuff and money isn't too tight.
So! MidBoss is good: it's beautiful, has music, plays really well, and has enough depth to justify going back in again and again. I know I'll beat it someday, and until then the attempts are fun. (And why yes, I do see those options in the "custom game" section. Mix up the gameplay? Don't mind if I do~)
Final note: MidBoss has a unique death card system where when you die, it makes a pretty little image of your final moments and a cute summary of how you played. It's a good way to reflect on your mistakes, and share them with your friends. I like it a lot!

Deus Ex: Human Revolution is a fantastic game.  From the story, to the gameplay, to the style, Deus Ex: Human Revolution is a more than worthy predecessor to the original Deus Ex game from 2000.  Whilst tis game is definitely more action-oriented than the former, there is still a ton of depth and character to found here, especially in today's age of releasing half-complete games.
You play as  Adam Jensen, a security manager working for Sarif Industries.  The story is laced with cyberpunk themes and intrigue that will keep you playing for hours at a time.  The basic gunplay is satisfying and all the unique enhancements. or augmentations, add another layer to the combat.  Using Praxis points you can determine the way you want to play the game, whether it be stealthy, gun-ho, or somewhere in between.  This game wants to cater to whatever playing style fits you best, which makes playing the game that much more fun.  These RPG elements keep the game rewarding and fresh, especially if you go for a different play style on a second or third playthrough.  Out of all the augmenations, make sure you purchase the "social enhancement", as it will really help in the later encounters.
This biggest problem I have with the game is the fact that there aren't any other good cyberpunk games quite like it.  When I finished playing through the game the first time (on my Xbox 360), I really searched high and low to find a game that would scratch that sci-fi itch.  Unfortunately, there really isn't anything, other than the original games of course, the hits the spot quite like Deus Ex does.  I suppose any of the Thief games would be adequate alternatives, but I digress.
If you want a game that oozes style, provides dozens of hours of exciting espionage gameplay, a great story, characters, and setting; Deus Ex: Human Revolution has you covered.  I honestly cannot recommend this game enough, and I feel that anyone who considers themselves a fan of great storytelling and gameplay should play this game.

PROS :
- The editor is practical. Using the 3 different views you can easily and precisely place a point wherever you want. A grid allows you to create well aligned stuff. It may look scary at first, but it's far, far, FAR simpler to use than a 3D modeling program. Within a few hours you will have understood all the basics required to make a complete car, chassis and bodywork, without having to read any kind of tutorial.
- The games seems to be very optimized. You can add hundreds or parts to a car without ever noticing a framerate drop. It seems for example to be a lot optimized than other games such as Scrap Mechanic. As of today I have been able to create whatever I wanted to create without even thinking about performance.
- The physics are realistic. Each part can strech, compress, vibrate, etc.
- The (only) developper of the game seems to be very active and seems to care about the feedbacks of player, which is a very encouraging point.
- The price. I paid this game about 11€. I think it's a fair price for this game in its current state.
CONS :
- The game has currently  very little content. You can do races along a track vs little ghost cars. You can drive around, trying to reach a checkpoint after another. You can roam freely to test your creation. And it seems like you can also play online multiplayer, without collisions between players, but I've no tested that yet. This is not surprising considering that this game is only a few monthes old. You wouldn't expect such a recent game to have a lot of content, especially since there is only one developper working on it.
- There is not a lot of information about how to use the game. There is an in-game help which provides informations about the parts and their physical properties. However I think it would have been nice to have a little wiki and a few more tutorial videos for beginners. For instance, I took me a while to search information about what the "angle lock" part was used for. All the tutorial videos I could find were created before the update that introduced this part, so I couldn't find more information about it.
- The developper working on this seems to be almost alone. While he seems to be very active, I'm not sure whether we can expect frequent updates or not, and how much content will come with each update.
- The graphics are really outdated. I know that it's not what people would come for when buying this game, but since it's about being realistic, graphics matter too. Currently there are no asphalt marks, the wheels sometimes seem to sink a bit into the ground because the hitbox of the wheels get deformed based on tire pressure while the 3D model remains solid, there are no beautiful shadows or god rays, and since the maps can be procedurally and randomly generated, there are not many details. I think some official race tracks where players could compete would have been great.
CONLUSION :
I think it's a game worthy of its price which provides you with a freedom that you will never find in any other game that currently exist. There are concurrents like Scrap Mechanic or even Garry's mod, but none of them have the good performances and the freedom of building provided by Dream Car Racing 3D.
Just like with any other early access game, the game has very little content, but it already allows you to create fully functionnal creations without any performance issue and that can be shared on the workshop, which is a very good start. The developpers seems to be planning to add more parts like wings, which suggest that we will be able to create other things than wheeled vehicles in the future.
So in the end, if you like creating and inventing stuff, showing other people what you're capable of and enjoy realistic physics, if you have time and patience, if you care about creating quality stuff, then go for this game. You will probably like it, and even if you don't, well that's not even the price of a meal at McDonalds...

I'll put the TL;DR at the front this time: DOOM is awesome. DOOM is so satisfyingly awesome you'll need to take breaks between levels from awesome overload. That's how great this game is.
Now for the long version:
At its core, DOOM is a game about gameplay above all else. It's a pattern you'll see in almost all aspects of the game. This core gameplay is fantastic. It's everything you'd want from a DOOM reboot. DOOM plays like a fast-paced, old-school shooter put into an modern FPS environment. The game tells you to "rip and tear, until it is done", and that's exactly what you'll be doing. The feedback loop of shooting, tearing, and dodging at breakneck speed keeps the tension and excitement high while still making you feel like a god. Health drops from enemies when you gib or glory kill them, and the arena-like rooms where big fights take place force you to constantly move and kill, reinforcing the gameplay loop. It's fast, keeps the action high, and is undeniably DOOM.
Music: I'm not normally one to pay much attention to music in games, but Mick Gordon's sound design is the best I've heard in any game. What you hear from the OST and trailers don't do the music the justice it deserves. DOOM's music is unique in that it constantly adapts to what you're doing. As big battles start, the music starts to build up, and it winds down as battles are finished, seamlessly. DOOM's fast-paced gameplay allows for an equally fast metal soundtrack as badass as Doomguy himself. The dynamic soundtrack means the best parts of the songs always gets plays during the best parts of the action. In smaller encounters the music will wind up a little bit to match the action without dragging it out of proportion. While you're exploring it'll play with a more atmospheric style. When you go for a glory kill in a big fight, the music even pauses for a second to give you a sort of "wait for it..." moment before carrying on as you rip and tear through more demons. The only complaint is on occasion at the end of big fights you'll have one smaller enemy left and the music will still play as if you're in the heat of the big fight while you try to find and kill it. Beyond that, the sound design for this game is flawless.
Setting: One of the things DOOM does differently than most FPS games is how it completely disregards its story. It's there if you want it. It gives you some context and explanation for the world, but it's never the focus of the game. You're there to kill demons. In the first minute of the campaign, you're given a bunch of exposition from a voice transmission, but instead of sitting there quietly while the NPC spouts off about how everything's quite literally gone to hell, Doomguy shoves the panel away and goes to find his almighty shotgun. When told to carefully remove a fragile lens to preserve it for later use, Doomguy just stomps on it with his boot, satisfyingly smashing it to pieces. Just like the player, Doomguy isn't there to debate philosophy or even save the world. He's there to rip and tear through demon hordes like a ball of rage and fury, and it shows through every first-person animation of the mute protagonist. In an era full of games that try and fail to deliver a cinematic experience, it's refreshing to see DOOM give traditional story elements the middle finger and focus purely on gameplay.
I haven't played the multiplayer, so I can't give much of an opinion on it. All I can say is that I don't think multiplayer belongs in a game so tied to its core single-player gameplay and design. It's not something that would translate well.
As for SnapMap, it's only okay. While making your own levels for a game like this seems great, it's done in a very spotty way. The biggest issue I had is that a lot of the mechanics just seem a bit off. SnapMap launches a completely separate version of the game, with different settings (controls included), UI, and gameplay mechanics. Upgrades earned from the campaign aren't available in any way, nor are they unlocked all at once like in Arcade mode. Map interaction is seems very rough and unpolished, since there are no scripted animations for that. It seems like the people who worked on SnapMap took an earlier version of the game and split off in development and adding things differently than the main campaign developers did, or in some cases, didn't add them at all. It also can get painfully obvious how important good level design is in a game like DOOM; bad level design can often ruin the core gameplay loop when levels are too sparse, too dense, or put enemies, items and objects in places that discourage the aggressive playstyle of the campaign, and this shows in meny user levels.
The alternative mode I enjoyed most was Arcade mode, which is incredible. Arcade mode essentially takes the campaign's fast, high-action gameplay and ramps it up to be even faster and more intense. You get a score multiplier based on how fast and consistently you kill demons. You get bonus points for doing it with style (such as glory kills, direct hits with explosives, headshots, death from above, etc.). You also start fully upgraded in each level so you can focus less on just clearing the level and more on clearing the level in the fastest, most badass way possible. It's immensely satisfying to play, especially in short bursts when you have less time to explore or try for weapon upgrade challenges.
Overall, this game is one of the best single-player FPS games out there, and for me one of the best games I've ever played. It's the perfect game for when you want to jump in for fast action without a care. I'm not going to give it a rating, since that's just not what DOOM is about. It's an awesome game. Go play it.

I've played the first Mechwarrior, Mechassault for Xbox, and Mechwarrior 4. MWO is an enjoyable 12v12 mechwarrior game, but it's grindy.
Very grindy and in different ways. You need to complete basic skills for 3 of the same mech to access elite skills. Then there are pilot skills that seem to take forever to gain experience. Then there's the money needed to buy the mech, and then customize it with the parts you want. After the cadet boost expires after 25 matches, money will be a bit tough to come by, even with the premium boost.
If you don't care too much about customization or progress, there are always 16 trial mechs available for play with 4 for each weight class. Others can use those to figure out what kind of mech they want to purchase and customize with the in-game currency. Some mechs are very expensive, so a trial run is a smart move to not waste money. You start with 4 mech bays and can earn some free ones from Faction play or events.
The sound effects are great. Firing any of the lasers feels and looks good. The same goes for the ballistic weapons. I didn't care too much for the missiles, but if you like firing volleys of them and hearing them blast off into the distance, this game will let you do so.
The damage displayed on the mechs is visually satisfying. I'm a big fan of shooting arms off. Mechs will be covered in bullet holes and damaged metal. They'll walk with limps if one of the legs is destroyed.
Anyhoo, this game can offer a good time. Just make smart purchases and have fun with your builds. I have read that the higher tiers require optimal builds, so keep that in mind, but I'm still in Tier 5 after 30 hours. Go crush some trees already!

Let me start by saying that I have played this game more or less continually since closed beta.
Everyone asks if it is pay to win. No. It is NOT pay to win. Pay for convenience, absolutely. I spent the first year or so that I played without dropping a dime. It will take you time to build up a large reserve of cash and mechs if you don't invest anything but you absolutely can. Sure there are a few things that you can only buy with real world cash, about two dozen mechs, mech bays and paint. The mechs are nothing special, the bays can be won in some challenges/in-game achievements and the paint is purely aesthetics.
The next problem I see people have is that there is a large learning curve. The game has become much more newbie friendly recently with the addition of a training academy tutorial and a tier system that will help to place you with similar skill level pilots. The issue many people have coming into the game is expecting a Hawken or CoD like shooter. This game is about tactics and attrition. You will need to hit your opponent more than once to bring him down at the same time avoiding as much damage as possible. My number one recommendation is to join a unit. Your peers are going to be a HUGE help with teaching tactics, mech building and the like.
There is also a quickly growing competitive side to the game with PGI even hosting a tournament with a 100k cash purse. There are player driven leagues with cash prizes and a shout casts on twitch and with the new spectator tools allow for some really fun to watch battles.
Overall I strongly recommend this game.

This is a very well made game.  If you are looking for an answer to "Should I buy this?" my answer would be yes, for sure.
To add a little more depth, Midboss follows along with the classic rogue formula (permadeath, potion identification, etc.) but adds the twist of learning skills through the possesion of the various monsters you fight while descending through the dungeon.  Throw in some RPG elements such as character progression through level-ups and the result is a very addictive game.  The overall experience is a much more streamlined and focussed game compared to many roguelikes.  This isn't going to replace DCSS or TOME4 for your go-to deep gaming experience, but we all need something a bit lighter from time to time.  This game reminds me a bit of Dungeons of Dredmor rather than Nethack.
The killer feature of this game is really the death card system.  Every time you die, a death card is generated.  You can use this card to carry over one item to a new run through the dungeon.  If you have multiple death cards, you can pick one item from each (up to six I believe), so even upon your inevitable death there is something gained for another try.  Even cooler, these death cards can be shared with other players.  You can examine another player's card to see how they built that character, what forms they used the most and what skills they preferred.  It is a neat way to learn about the game from other players.
There is still room for improvement, and the developer is eager to hear from players and is very receptive to suggestions.  A few areas that will be receiving some attention are inventory management and better explanations of the various statistics.  Melee builds could probably use a bit of a buff while magic builds could probably stand a bit of a nerf.  None of these issues take away from a very well made and fun game right now however.
Also, major kudos for a native Linux build from the start.
The music and sound effects are also top notch.
If you are a fan of roguelikes, Midboss should be on your radar (and in your library).

What a great game and a neat, unusual take on the hardcore Roguelike formula. If you at all like Roguelikes, get this immediately.
First off: even if you have played hundreds of hours of ToME, ADOM, Qud, Cogmind, DCSS, etc., don't expect to not die a lot in your first hour or three of this game. It's a very different beast and quite clever. It hides its great complexity behind a very polished GUI (although more actions need keyboard shortcuts).
I really don't want to say more, because frankly a lot of the fun for me was playing this game with really almost no preconceived notions of what it is and how it works and discovering it for myself. However, I will say a few things to whet your appetite.
The primary game mechanic is possession of other dungeon dwellers. Your powers and skills merely modify the capabilities of the creatures you possess. When you're not in possession of someone else, you can use some of your abilities learned from your possessees, but if your not-in-possession self dies... Game over. (Of course, it's a roguelike.) You also don't have any health regen (nor its attendant food mechanic), which took some getting used to.
The second really unusual (unique to my experience) mechanic is the Death Cards. From a purely mechanical standpoint, they let you carry one item over from another game. However, more than that they are shareable records of your game, allowing you to replay the exact same seed or challenging your friends to that same seed. And, they look cool to boot.
The author contributed to a recent episode of Roguelike Radio. It's worth a listen - but I recommend a few hours of play first so you don't get any spoilers. :)

Loadout is a multiplayer first-person-shooter with some twists. (Don't all fps's have a twist these days?)
You get to design your own gun. It's not as simple as it might sound. There are basic parts like a scope and stock. These function as expected. There are all kinds of crazy parts and modifications available. You can do quite a lot with what is available.
The primary choice is weapon type: Rifle, Launcher, Beam or "Ball". Within each are unique choices, and some general ones. You can go for a rapid-fire, or for single-shot. This choice has a big impact on your damage and playstyle. You can fire grenades from the launcher. You can modifiy the grenades with homming ability, stickiness, bouncing, or even turning into smaller grenades before exploding. You can even combine some aspects!
The general theme of the game is one of an old 1940s (or '50s) cartoon. The characters are all goofy, and live for no other reason than to blow each other up.  Which is fine because you respawn within seconds. If you like crude humor or violent cartoons, you should enjoy it. If not, it might make you a little sick.
Although I recommend the game, it is difficult to play. The once popular game has become very niche. The playerbase is very small. Playing ranked mode is impossible due to the lack of players. You can get a regular game, if you are lucky. Most of the time, the only game I can find is Co-Op vs. Bots. Which is of limited fun.
Of course, if you manage to get a real match... the problems have only begun. Because so few play the game, those that do are very good. As one progresses, your weapons become better and better. As a result, anyone that has been playing for some time, will have very powerful weapons. So not only are these players good, but they have infinitely superior weapons as well. If you are spotted for longer than 2 seconds, you will be dead.
Worst of all, a representative of the company that makes Loadout made some statements. He said that the company had let go of it's PC developers to focus on the PS4 version. He said this was due to budget constraints. (Actually it was worse than that, but anyway...) The future of this game is in question.
If nothing else, you should try this game. The gun-creation-system is really cool. I've never seen anything quite like it.

"Oaf!"
You were screamed at while walking slowly through your Stronghold. There were drunk people everywhere, mothers with their babies and a group of lumberjacks just crossed your path, muttering "Greetings my lord" while walking past you.
You don't really know what happened, but you knew that whatever happened was something very fast. It seemed like all of the sudden, buildings appeared around you, following a certain pattern. A system of managing food was required and you ordered your people to start building farms and harvesting wheat, which then was crushed in mills just to be processed to good bread afterwards.
It somehow worked. Even though you felt like it all happened in a matter of seconds, you of course knew that it was you ordering all of this. A stronghold had to be build, it was necessary to claim the land that god gave you and in order to succeed, you had to purge the infidels that inhabited this land like rats and pigs.
You knew that there would be vengeance for your actions. You basically just stranded here on this island, taking as many men as you could and take as much land as you could before facing resistance.
People looked up on you and envied your power, but uneasy lies the head that wears a crown.
There was so much to do, so much to oversee and so few time to do so. You never had time for the fun aspects of the burden of being king, you never had the joy of talking to friends or not dealing with starving citizens for a moment or wondering if there is more wood needed.
You went back to your castle. It was a small, but safe one. While walking upstairs you met a mother with her baby. She greeted you with respect and it may be the way she looked at you, but you smiled at her.
Obviously stunned by that rare gesture of sympathy, you asked her to come to your room and after giving the baby to one of the other women in the castle, she quickly followed and wondered what your majesty had in mind for her lesser being.
Once in your chamber, you looked at her closely. A young, attractive woman, mother of only five children and in the good age of 15. Your ambition was clear, you wanted her and you clearly didn't want to wait for that.
After touching her breasts she whispered that she couldn't do this, as she was married, but you promised her to not tell god and pushed her on the pile of straw that resembled your bed. You slowly removed her clothes and started to let your tongue explore all of her young and fresh skin, which made her tremble.
You told her that all would be well and you wouldn't hurt her too much, before you grabbed her derière and entered the sacred catacombs with your horse.
The walls of the catacomb were relatively wet and surprisingly soft and your horse was satisfied with what it sensed below its fur. While exploring the deepest corners the horse felt the rising need to neigh intensively and clear the nose of all that is not wanted.
It wouldn't be long until a scream travelled through the entire castle, a mix of a male and female voice combined in the spirit of joy. You quickly got up, took a deep breath and pushed the woman out of your bed.
You told her that all is well now and that her service is no longer needed. Obviously shocked of your mercy and power, she ran out of the room, naked. Outside of your chamber behind the closed door you heard the sounds of crying women and words about too much horror happening way too often to all females in the stronghold, but you suddenly felt the intense need to both ignore the voices outside as well as take a deep and satisfying nap on your comfortable straw bed that by now had entered various holes of yours.
You fell asleep and had that one dream again. Your kingdom, safe and prosper, surrounded by mighty walls and in it, a lot of happy female citizens, all here to please you and all grateful for the very opportunity to live in what you had build for them. No enemies to threaten your position, no problems in your borders that you had to deal with. It was better place, a peaceful place. It was your mission that you had to make reality one day.
After a long and happy night of dreams, you got up to work again. Make those lazy farmers work and expand your kingdom. It's time to crush the rats under your power and create the kingdom that you dreamed of so often already.
But this time you would have enough wood.

Great educational game. Aurora Nights does not teach you the location of the constellations in the night sky, but rather how to spot the constellation if you were to see it among the many stars of the night sky. In other words, for example, it is like learning the name of every country and their borders, but not their location on a globe; although you may not know their place on a globe, you can simply look at any globe and be able to name the countries you see because you have memorized the names respective to the borders you see.
Additionally, Aurora Nights changes the background-stars of the constellation you are learning to spot, and will notify you if you choose the wrong star; the background-stars reset and you start over connecting the dots. This gives you the opportunity to really learn and gain the confidence you need to accurately spot the constellations. I see this method of learning to also be useful in teaching you to ignore the "noise" of other stars as they too can "change" depending on how clear the night sky is where you go - you might go to a VERY remote area of earth and notice there are many more background-stars, but because you are confident in the "changes" of surrounding stars, you can still accurately spot the constellation.
peaceful and educational and for $1 you can't go wrong.

2. More constellation information - The few facts and tidbits of info were nice, but I'd love to sink my teeth into something more since we're already thinking of this as an educational game. Give us some more information/trivia to keep our minds entertained.
3. I understand the Northern Hemisphere is the most recognizable constellation map, but what about the Southern Hemisphere? Possible DLC for later? Or perhaps something to add into the game in a future update. *wink, wink, nudge, nudge*

I always get really nervous posting negative reviews on positive games. Oh well.
I grabbed Aurora Nights under the impression that i would learn something about constallations. It's a pretty cheap game that frequently goes on sale for 66 cents, but honestly i regret buying it at all. There are two main issues i see with this game:
1. The base gameplay is pretty simple, pick a constalation to "spot" and then just click on all the highlighted dots. These dots will reveal the contallation, and admittedly seeing the first couple of constallations reveal themselves is pretty neat. It doesn't change there is very little effort required to press on dots highlighted for you and i found myseld incredibly bored. I imagine this is meant to entertain incredibly small children, but i have a houndred games that babysit for me on my phone and they probably will hold a child's attention for much longer.
2. The educational value is nonexistant in the main gameplay. After you've played follow-the-birght-dots you can go to the main menu to find more information on each constallation in text. While i'm sure the devs put a lot of time and effort into making those entries i just couldn't care less about them. I come to a video game to play not to read, and it really comes as a shock when a game that market's itself as an " entertaining educational game" has all the educational bits stored away in menus rather than the core gameplay. Admittedly i'd rather the books be here than none at all, but i don't see anyone learning about constallations playing this game.
Now to be fair, you get to see the shapes of the constallations and if you want to three star a level in the game you have to memorize the constalation. That's neat, but to beat the game you only need to do it once and you'll probably be too bored of the game to play through every single map 2 more times. The three stars system feels like padding, but they're also where all the games challange is so hey if you want to entertain your kid beat the game once and see how they fare when they have to actually learn.
Also the top part of the map is cutoff so there is a constallation just you just can't see. Tried changing from windowed mode to fullscreen, still couldn't see one of the constalations.
Overall i was just dissapointed in the game. There's just nothing here behind a unique theme and the ability to left click.
Educational and entertaining for me. Not just connecting dots, but you also learn the story behind every constellation.

The idea of the Steam Controller is great. It works great with the community layouts. If you don't like the controls for the current game you're playing, but don't really want to spend time changing the entire layout, someone has most likely made a good layout. The idea of adding the extra 2 buttons on the grips is also excellent. But I simply can't recommend this controller due to the right track pad. It's like the dev team brainstorm about what could be cool to have on a controller, and someone said "Hey, a mouse pad on a controller would be cool" and then they implemented it for the sole reason it was a cool idea without even considering functionality.
The controller is excellent for every game that doesn't require a camera control. But the moment you want to play a shooter or maybe a third person open world game like Mad Max(it's absolutely horrible for Mad Max) you just spend way too much time trying to control your camera. You can't aim accurately(I almost couldn't get past the slow-motion- shooting-Activsion-advertisement-scene in Deadpool due to how impossible it is to aim). You can't play Metro, since you can't hit squat so you have to spray and pray which means you'll run out of ammo.
So while the Steam Controller is a great idea, it's just not very useful for your average couch game, which was the entire reason I bought this thing.
I'd say that if you have a computer that has something like a track pad, or you just prefer controllers to keyboards, than you should definitely get this.

Unfortunately, that's a very subjective thing that you can't really learn from any review (not even this amazing one here hey rate this up please), so I recommend that you move your cute little tooshie to a local electronics store and ask to play with a Steam Controller for a while. TL:DR A really enjoyable semi-open stealth game that gives you lots of options to complete you goals. Let down only slightly by the terrible boss fights.
Full version: Deus Ex HR has you playing as Adam Jensen, an ex-cop turned security officer for the augment company Sarif industries, who's girlfriend Megan is killed in a terrorist attack on the Sarif building. Jensen himself is badly injured but saved by Sarif who also augments him. He returns to work a few months later and begins investigating the attack which draws him into a deeper plot.
The gameplay is semi-open stealth focused with a lot of flexibility in how you want to complete your objectives. You can hack terminals to acquire info or passwords, hack locks to open doors, discover vents and alternative routes through levels and you have a variety of lethal and non-lethal weapons. Though the game tries to steer you towards non-lethal stealth via more exp you can absolutely loud and violent if you want. Conversations and convincing other characters also play a part as well.
The Directors Cut adds the DLC Missing Link into the main story, slightly improved boss fights and a new game plus mode that carries over your unlocked augs.
Good points:
- Great stealth gameplay
- The wide variety of options you have to go about your tasks is refreshing and its just as fun finding your own path to complete a mission.
- Has some great level design to the open hubs of Detroit and Hengsha and the various other compunds and buidlings you have to infiltrate.
-The upgrade system is fantastic as you can unlock new augments are improve or add stuff to the ones you have, which opens up more options for you when tackling a level.
Bad points:
- While they have been improved to make stealth more viable the boss fights still suck. Playing a non-lethal stealth? Well the game throws you into a small room with a powerful gun toting bullet sponge. The DC edition has more options in the boss fights for a stealth build now but they still suck.
- The Missing Link DLC feels a bit shoehorned into the main campaign. As it was initially a seperate chapter you played, you lose all your upgrades and weapons at the start. Given you play it late in the storyline this is kind of annoying. It also has a lot of backtracking though it has its good moments. You do get all your upgrades back at the end as well as keeping the ones you earned in Missing Link so thats a bonus at least.
really good story and gameplay style makes this game a really good game for the price,the graphics also are not that bad after 3 years of its release.
