Loadout is a fun little thirdperson shooter where two teams battle on a few differnt maps... but after playing the game for a few hours it becomes very boring.

THE GOOD:
Loadout is a unconventional shooter game set in arena style maps with a third person perspective.
The game tries to innovate with weaponcrafting, a feature that lets you slam parts together to make your own guns. There are four weapon types and while there are less viable builds then the game praises itself for. However, the amount of viable builds is still large enough to deserve praise. The combat is very fast paced and the controls respond well and feel really nimble as you can jump really high, allowing more diverse combat than usual in this sort of game.
The cartoonesk visuals are not the best graphics but fit the spirit of the game very well while making sure even older machines can still run the game. The level design features funny details such as a sign stating ''0 days since last accident'' or a pair of underpants in a brewery to filter beer.
THE BAD:
The community, really, these people love to accuse you of hacking, call you names and so on. Personally I find this really humorous but I am aware I am a minority in this aspect. The bad matchmaking does not help either, the game states how it has good matchmaking capabilities but then decides to mix up newbies and top-tier players in a match without evenly distributing the different skill levels well, this is a dealbreaker for new players. The lack of maps does not help either. It is too common to get into the same map game after game.
THE AWFUL:
The company behind it, very rarely new weapon parts or maps get added to the game and the promised PVE campaign still isn't released after the beta test for it went down - it been a half year now. New players only got the tedious ''vs bots'' options to gain experience but this is really lackluster as the bots got an Iq lower than your shoe size, so the contrast is enormous and there is no true low level PVP in the game.
HOWEVER, it is a free and innovative game and if you are willing to get in the steep PVP curve, go ahead.

OK, so here's my take on the crashing thing:
THIS GAME CRASHES. A LOT. It crashes roughly on-par with any Bethesda game with mods or memory issues, which is maybe twice every couple of hours. I played a full hour before I even found my first crash.
I've seen A LOT of people giving a variety of stories on their own experiences with the crashes. Some saying extreme things, like the game doesn't even run in the first place, or that they can place only about 10 minutes before it crashes. I haven't experienced this.
My first experience with the crash was by the mission "Save Algie", which is maybe the 4th or 5th mission in the game. I figured, "Oh, there it is-- the mythical crashes!" No problem, I thought, I'll just load a save..
Oh..
Oh... I forgot to save since the beginning of the game.
SO BUY AT YOUR OWN RISK-- Be aware that Steam will refund the game if you decide you don't want it within 2 hours of gameplay; I would DEFINITELY recommend this game, crashes and all, if it were less than 10$, so definitely get it if it's on sale
The game itself is amazing; I've played it on every console I've ever owned, I've played it since I was a small child, I can even associate many of the events of my early life to playing the game. I even went back on the day I graduated high school to play the game with my friends. It's an instant classic and is tons of good fun, so this game would be golden if not for it's technical issues.
All of this said, I *can* recommend the game with a bit of an asterisk next to it: SAVE OFTEN. Do a mission, and return to the dorms to save. I, myself, can have plenty of fun with this game so long as I remember to save after every event, which is not too hard as there's various places to save in the game. That said, if you do buy the game and find you crash too frequently to return and save your game, then feel free to refund it.
TO SUMMARIZE: The game *does* crash, but I think it's a managable issue that makes this game worth it depending on your definition of "worth it"-- i recommend potential buyers buy the game, see what severity they have of the issues, and decide for themselves if they want a refund.
Oh, and of course, this isn't to say that Rockstar or /anyone/ shouldn't patch the game-- Come on. If Steam is gonna pull 15$ in on this game, then they need to make sure it isn't working worse than their FREE games. It's not that dated-- I can play Wolfenstein 3D with minimal issues on Steam but can't make a PS2-era game work. Bull.

I personally have mixed feelings about the steam controller. It has potential to be the best controller on the market, but it currently has a few flaws. The buttons and analog stick are placed to close to center of the controller, making them somewhat uncomfortable to use. The second trackpad on the left, is nice for some games, but for others can be really annoying. It would be nice if there were a version of the controller that has a regular D pad. Aside from that, it is a very good controller. The trackpad on the right is real nice feature that many games benefit from. I also love how customizable it is. Any button can be remapped to any other button or key. The trackpads can be customized to preform one of multiple functions. The customizability is definitely the main selling point of this controller. I would like to see a version of the steam controller that fixes these problems. For now though I will still recommend this controller, but it does need a few improvements.

A very comfortable, ergonomic device. The steam controller has satisfying, tactile feedback to all inputs, from the ABXY buttons to the triggers. This controller has really enhanced most games that I have tried it on straight away - in particular the driving aspects - and that's before I went in and explored the wide range of customisations available for the controller. Valve have definitely made an effort in making the steam controller as user-friendly as possible when playing on Steam.
To add, alongside games designed with controller support in mind, I've found that older games or games designed for use with a keyboard and mouse are resoundingly easy to play with this controller. Customising the keys is easy, but I find you need to use Big Picture Mode in order to get the most out of the controller. I'm not too fond of this, but the pros far outweigh the cons when using the controller.
The two flat pads on the front offer many methods of input: rolling your thumbs along the surface and pushing in different regions on the faces. The one small joystick is in a relatively good position for my hands, although you may strain your thumb after a while if you have particularly small hands (but you'll probably find that with most other controllers anyway). The buttons on the front are solid and comfortable to rest your thumbs on. My favourite part of the design is the six-trigger layout along the top and back of the controller which all have a very nice feel to them, especially the unique back bumpers that you can press with your middle/ring finger(s).
I would recommend this controller at full price. It shipped to the UK in under a week, which astonished me, and was virtually plug and play. To get the full experience, you'll have to customise it for each game, which personally I find quite enjoyable. If you're impatient, then take this as a warning, but I'd still recommend the hardware.

An interesting and engaging cyberpunk game set decades before the classic Deus Ex game, Human Revolution is a stealth-action FPS featuring an alternate history where mechanical and cybernetic augmentations became widely spread among the world's population, with mega-corporations starting to assume control of society as our protagonist, Adam Jensen, plays a pivotal role while the world faces a true revolution.
Deus Ex: Human Revolution is a game set in a cyberpunk world, with this interesting contrast between technology rising to an apex, and society facing a status of decay. The game begins in 2027 with Adam Jensen, an ex-SWAT now working as corporate security advisor for a large bio-tech company, Sarif Industries. During an attack at Sarif HQ by an unknown military unit, Jensen is critically wounded, and is forced into surgical procedures to remain alive. While Adam survives the incident, his body has undergone enormous changes due to the cybernetic augmentations. Now made a true super-soldier, with his new set of skills he must find out who was behind this attack and what were the reasons for it to have happened.
The world the player meets is one with a massive duality. On one side, biotechnology and cybernetics have been taking man to new extremes, with augmented senses, intellect, abilities and giving normal lives to once-disabled citizens, painting a bright picture for some. The less fortunate, however, are faced with poverty and an economic crash with massive worldwide oil shortages, as well as the augmentees who could not pay for maintenances and a necessary drug to avoid implant rejections often end with being driven into insanity and other drug overdoses, causing a tone of tension, apprehension and uncertainty about the future. The population is polarized between those who support the improvement and usage of augmentations, as a hope for a brighter future, and those who oppose this, as it's being exploited as a mean to control the population, and blurs the line between human and machine beyond a reasonable point.
Jensen's actions-- and views on this world, are only for the player to take.
Human Revolution's story progresses from what seems to be a tragic incident of corporate warfare against Sarif Industries, as the bio-tech industry sparks animosity between population to the point violent demonstrations occur from both sides. These attacks, and violent demonstrations prove to be different parts of a grand scheme, as Jensen finds out the truth and the plot unravels.
The story decidedly had some thought and care put into it. Details both small and large are to catch the eye and this unique world-building provides an interesting base for a debate on the matter of what measure would be human as the augmentations in the game both show how far new abilities can take augmentees, and how high the cost is when the barriers are pushed too far and start to blur between a decided human and a machine.
In Human Revolution, players are provided with a variety of skills and tactics to play through and a number of different approaches to try the game. Lethal, actiony combat, nonlethal combat, stealth infiltration and approaches, are among some of the possible gameplay tactics a player can adopt. Having done a Pacifist, a mixed and a guns-blazing run on the maximum difficulty, it's somewhat safe to say the combat and overall gameplay value will depend on how the player chooses to act, and how well they do at it.
A skill tree with cybernetic augment abilities and a variety of weaponry provide the player with a number of choices. Sensing enemies through walls, optical camouflage, physical strength among others are some of the abilities the game offers, along a selection of sniper rifles, crossbows, sub-machineguns, handguns and assault weapons.
The game is rather dated, so admittedly, graphics didn't exactly age the best. In my personal opinion, it's nothing to write home about but they do an acceptable work of conveying a good visual experience along the gameplay.
Environments such as factory and laboratory interiors as well as warehouses provide this variety of industrial machinery and computer sounds, while the streets and alleys of the city hub areas give the player a sense of a busy urban center.
The soundscape is paired with the original soundtrack featuring lead composer Michael McCann (also known for leading soundtracks of
and
) provides a sense of mysterious tension and a suspense among Human Revolution's world of dualities, as it's filled with a fast-paced mixture of heavy percussion and synthesizers along orchestrated pieces for combat tracks, and synth ambient tracks for non-combat situations.
Personal favorite pieces include Sarif Industries' ambient theme, Derelict Row's Combat theme, "Hengsha Daylight" on both the ambient and combat segments, the title song "Icarus" and the finale's theme for the
.

I’ve played many hours of Sandbox early access building games running on the unity physics engine so naturally I was attracted to the game when I came across it on Youtube. I must admit I bought the game on impulse without knowing too much about it but I thought the price was very reasonable so I took a chance although I’ve been disappointed many times in the past.
I can now confidently say that the game has exceeded my expectations and is more than worth the price tag. If you are expecting another Besiege, Scrap Mechanic or Robocraft you are in the wrong place. The game will not hold your hand, this is not a Lego style “stick a bunch of blocks together and attach wheels” type of game. At first you will be frustrated after spending 3 hours building a car only to see it collapse under its own weight. You will go back to the drawing board, re-design the frame, re-tweak, test and repeat until finally you have a solid frame with awesome suspension and steering and you get that sense of satisfaction and accomplishment.
As far as Sandbox games go, this is proper Sandbox as you are not limited by blocks and you don’t have to stick to square angles. With only a handful of building parts you can make complex vehicles in any shape or size.
What other content is in the game? The integration into the Steam workshop gives you endless things to play with as new maps are uploaded. Make your own racing tracks or just fool around with other people’s creations. There is Single player and multiplayer that I haven’t even tried yet (Not sure if Multiplayer is out yet). In a nutshell you won’t get bored as there is plenty to.
I was very impressed when I had questions or needed help in the Steam Community Discussions that the developer actually takes time to respond to you and assist where he can. The community also seems very helpful over all. The game is off to a great start for an early access and I haven’t found any major bugs. I am very excited to see where the developer can take this.

You're the weakest critter in the dungeon, and you're tired of it. Midboss is a tactical turn based RPG roguelike. Along with the expected mechanics of looting, stats, experience, and levels, you must also possess the bodies of your enemies to learn new abilities and gain additional power. Not only does possession restore your health, you also have limited capacity to combine the abilities of previous forms with your current form. The tactical implications of this possession mechanic is compelling, and it is satisfying to hunt, collect, and master powerful forms. The character and environment art is simple and mostly static, although it did give me a pleasant dose of Diablo nostalgia. The game does have a couple of questionable mechanics. You must manually rest to restore mana. Although your rest can be interrupted by patrolling monsters, this isn't particularly common, and clicking the rest button after every fight get tiresome quickly. You're also encouraged to smash everything you see for loot and to free the curious cratefish creatures for further reward. Being a game that is tile based and turn based with static animations, smashing things is time consuming and dull*, pulling you away from the best aspect of the game: possession based combat and progression. The game also includes a mild social aspect; run seeds are saved as 'death' or 'victory' cards that can be shared with others, or cannibalized to boost new runs. Midboss is an intriguing challenge with a great balance of the familiar and the novel. Key provided courtesy of developer.
*The release version reduced the number of crates and other smashables, relieving the problem slightly.

I have to say that sorry but my first impressions are not positive.
The main gimmick of the game is possessing mobs which is fine. The graphics are nice enough. Loot is Diabloesque which appeals to certain people (I'm one of them). There's a touch of rogueLITE-ness about it though in the form of "death cards", one of which is generated every time you die. You can use this card _once_ to start a new game but keep one item from the run the card is from. A cool feature is that you can post the card to social media and then other people can use it once too. I didn't test that feature.
The bad parts though:
1. A bit pricey for what it is
2. Unskippable animations. The standard attack animation is a "bounce over there, hit it and bounce back" affair. You have to wait for it every time. Destroying furniture, opening chests and even collecting gold uses this animation! You can speed things up a bit using the options but even at minimum they are still very annoying.
3.The isometric view may look nice but it makes movement annoying compared to if it was just overhead view. Maybe it's just my brain but 8 way movement in isometric never comes naturally. Since movement is the most basic and common thing in the game it makes playing not a pleasure.
4. Too many items to destroy. Like Diablo games there are objects to destroy which might give you loot. The trouble is there's tons of them and destroying them is a pain. I previously wrote about bookcases which take two hits to destroy and it was pointed out to me that they drop their loot on the first hit if they are going to so you don't need to destroy them but still. Anvils take a ridiculous number of hits. Even though crates only take one hit to kill you might find 15 of them in a room and going round hitting them with the attack animation is not fun at all. It's a chore. I don't want to play a game that feels like a chore.
5. Minorish annoyance but there's some story at the start and when you first meet a merchant. You can skip the dialogues with esc but why do I have to do this EVERY SINGLE GAME. It's boring. Drop it.

Looking to be an imp possessing other monsters and using their stats and abilities to crawl out of a dungeon? Well, that's what this game is about.
STORY - N/A
Not much of a story going on in the game but more of the idea that you just want to get out of the dungeon. The idea of a story can also conveyed through your game where the player could die and get a death card, in which the card talks about your death.
GAMEPLAY - 8/10
The gameplay is pretty simple since you aren't gonna struggle memorizing which key on the keyboard does what. The letters associated to the certain action you want to take are there and key bindings are available to change. You can also just use your mouse throughout the game. The game is kinda complicated since it has lots of stats and numbers. Someone who is not fan of number crunching might have a rough time trying to enjoy this game. Possessing enemies is a unique key feature to the game and it's important to the game since it allows player to get the enemies' powers, buffs, and stats. The game has many items, weapons, and armors where they all have random stats and effects that can boost your chances of survival. Through my playthrough, I don't know if there was an end but there seems to be plenty of floors and I don't know if there is a boss level/floor but would be interesting if it had one.
AESTHETICS - 7/10
The rooms are quite simple looking but doesn't distract the players as much. Items look quite plain as well but it also will not distract players and has enough to convey what they are for. Characters for the most part are the uniques bits for the game since some look interesting. Music for the game is also unique because it makes me feel like I'm in medival times.
OVERALL - 7.5/10
I recommend the game for players who like strategy games or RPGs that has them planning out their next moves. Players will not struggle much at the start but most players will see that struggle as they go through higher floors.

We all know you have to "grind" your way through f2p titles, but there isn't another game that makes you forget instantly that you are "grinding" anything.  Playing Quick Play over and over again to work out your masteries on a chosen 'Mech is just fun.  Your first 20 matches gives you an insane amount of money to buy just about any 'Mech you want, and depending on what class and chassis you pick, you can even get your three variants to achieve mastery.
Here's how not "grindy" the grind is: I played my first 17 hours and bought three heavy 'Mech variants, and achieved mastery of them without getting bored at all.  In fact, every match that I start, every time I click Quick Play, every time the oh-so-familiar 'Mech computer says "weapons online, sensors online, all systems nominal" I get goosebumps like I'm that kid I was back in 1995 when I first played MechWarrior 2, or when I saved my lunch money instead of buying lunch in middle school so that I could buy MechWarrior 4 in 2000.
There is near limitless fun you can have just jumping in with Quick Play without ever giving PGI a dime.  Seriously there is not any reason someone who casually wants to shoot big robots in a walking tank would need to spend money.  But once you start finding yourself reading guides, learning strategies, working through your masteries on your first three 'Mechs, something will change.  You'll probably buy a 'Mech bundle, which somehow feels ok, it feels like an even trade, you won't look at your bank account and cringe at that impulse buy for a f2p title and you'll probably get more hours of enjoyment out of those three+ 'Mechs than you would from most $20 title on Steam.
Play this game and:
-you will become a MechWarrior, when you see the animation of your character booting up the 'Mechs systems and jiggling the controls, you will be transported to that cockpit and your chair is now the pilot's seat
-you will call out contacts as they appear on the map, you will work together with your lancemates to flank and confuse and split up the enemy forces
-you will turn your head and cringe when you hear "warning incoming missles"
-you will cheer and sound crazy to the people around you when you kill an assault 'Mech while you are piloting a medium or light
-you will be late to work and you will lose sleep
-you will see lasers converging on a point when you close your eyes

I find it funny that I decided to make this review, because for a very long time I actually disliked Paladins, classifying it as just an Overwatch clone. Only when I actually did play the game did my opinions change.
Paladins is, in many aspects, very similar to other class-based FPS shooters. There's clearly defined champions as the playable classes, along with class groups of Damage, Flank, Tank, and Support. There are three different modes for King of The Hill, Escort, and Attack/Escort. Gameplay in the matches is very fast-paced and focuses heavily on good teamwork. There are also only five players per team, encouraging a more competitive environment.
The game definitely managed to draw me in, even though it did so for only a few months. It was a nice break from the current multiplayer games I was playing and i did actually enjoy it. The characters themselves were not terribly interesting, but not forgettable either. My main complaint was the card system that was in place. Cards allow for upgrades to specific champions, but I never really quite understood why that needed to be implemented in the first place. I would have enjoyed it more had there not been the card modifier system. Hi-Rez has changed the card system since I last played however, so be wary of the new changes.
I rate this game a 6.5/10

An interesting and engaging cyberpunk game set decades before the classic Deus Ex game, Human Revolution is a stealth-action FPS featuring an alternate history where mechanical and cybernetic augmentations became widely spread among the world's population, with mega-corporations starting to assume control of society as our protagonist, Adam Jensen, plays a pivotal role while the world faces a true revolution.
Deus Ex: Human Revolution is a game set in a cyberpunk world, with this interesting contrast between technology rising to an apex, and society facing a status of decay. The game begins in 2027 with Adam Jensen, an ex-SWAT now working as corporate security advisor for a large bio-tech company, Sarif Industries. During an attack at Sarif HQ by an unknown military unit, Jensen is critically wounded, and is forced into surgical procedures to remain alive. While Adam survives the incident, his body has undergone enormous changes due to the cybernetic augmentations. Now made a true super-soldier, with his new set of skills he must find out who was behind this attack and what were the reasons for it to have happened.
The world the player meets is one with a massive duality. On one side, biotechnology and cybernetics have been taking man to new extremes, with augmented senses, intellect, abilities and giving normal lives to once-disabled citizens, painting a bright picture for some. The less fortunate, however, are faced with poverty and an economic crash with massive worldwide oil shortages, as well as the augmentees who could not pay for maintenances and a necessary drug to avoid implant rejections often end with being driven into insanity and other drug overdoses, causing a tone of tension, apprehension and uncertainty about the future. The population is polarized between those who support the improvement and usage of augmentations, as a hope for a brighter future, and those who oppose this, as it's being exploited as a mean to control the population, and blurs the line between human and machine beyond a reasonable point.
Jensen's actions-- and views on this world, are only for the player to take.
Human Revolution's story progresses from what seems to be a tragic incident of corporate warfare against Sarif Industries, as the bio-tech industry sparks animosity between population to the point violent demonstrations occur from both sides. These attacks, and violent demonstrations prove to be different parts of a grand scheme, as Jensen finds out the truth and the plot unravels.
The story decidedly had some thought and care put into it. Details both small and large are to catch the eye and this unique world-building provides an interesting base for a debate on the matter of what measure would be human as the augmentations in the game both show how far new abilities can take augmentees, and how high the cost is when the barriers are pushed too far and start to blur between a decided human and a machine.
In Human Revolution, players are provided with a variety of skills and tactics to play through and a number of different approaches to try the game. Lethal, actiony combat, nonlethal combat, stealth infiltration and approaches, are among some of the possible gameplay tactics a player can adopt. Having done a Pacifist, a mixed and a guns-blazing run on the maximum difficulty, it's somewhat safe to say the combat and overall gameplay value will depend on how the player chooses to act, and how well they do at it.
A skill tree with cybernetic augment abilities and a variety of weaponry provide the player with a number of choices. Sensing enemies through walls, optical camouflage, physical strength among others are some of the abilities the game offers, along a selection of sniper rifles, crossbows, sub-machineguns, handguns and assault weapons.
The game is rather dated, so admittedly, graphics didn't exactly age the best. In my personal opinion, it's nothing to write home about but they do an acceptable work of conveying a good visual experience along the gameplay.
Environments such as factory and laboratory interiors as well as warehouses provide this variety of industrial machinery and computer sounds, while the streets and alleys of the city hub areas give the player a sense of a busy urban center.
The soundscape is paired with the original soundtrack featuring lead composer Michael McCann (also known for leading soundtracks of
and
) provides a sense of mysterious tension and a suspense among Human Revolution's world of dualities, as it's filled with a fast-paced mixture of heavy percussion and synthesizers along orchestrated pieces for combat tracks, and synth ambient tracks for non-combat situations.
Personal favorite pieces include Sarif Industries' ambient theme, Derelict Row's Combat theme, "Hengsha Daylight" on both the ambient and combat segments, the title song "Icarus" and the finale's theme for the
.

At first I was happy to have a controller, and it seemed to work really well before I knew how I wanted to use it.    Now, at over a month since my purchase, I am seriously disheartened with the quality and design of it's many features.
I've been getting better at rocket league, which is the only game I use the controller to play.  After figuring out that I needed to learn how to roll left and right while flying, I realized that to improve and fully control the car I would need to use the left thumb stick and both paddles, all four triggers and the right thumb pad OR change the controls to double thumb pad/triggers.

Using the left stick/right thumb is NOT ergonomic, and would probably give me carpal tunnel's syndrome.  To not have that happenand ,  I would need to use the left thumbpad and right thumbpad at the same time - something i can do.
Unfortunately, the left thumbpad is primarily a directional button and cannot be set otherwise AND the sensitivity, tracking, and functional reliability of both the right and left haptic thumbpads is absolutely inadequate.   They don't seem to work at all unless you're moving the thumb or pressing down, so constant precision aiming with them is pretty much out.
I would use it for playing Battlefield 1, where the press button on the thumbpad would be useful, but the unclear instructions on BPM's and turning off features which cannot be turned off haven't helped me get that working yet.
4/10.   It's a controller, and I'm not going to try to return it and I will continue to use it.  However, I am disappointed that I cannot use all of the functions and features to the full effect I had imagined.
If your right handed, buy it.    It's  designed for the 90% of all people who happen to be non-ambudextrious and entirely right handed who just want a fancy controller.

I just...  I have no idea what to say about this device.
I bought it solely to play XCOM 2 which basically amounts to extortion because unlike it's predecessor, that had *amazing* controller support and pioneered how a lot of future games would be developed with it in mind on the PC, XCOM 2 had a deal with Valve and that's not cool at all man.  Not cool.
The controller is full of features and feels solid.  Requiring two AA batteries is lame but manageable because I already have dozens of rechargeables.
The controller *works*.  I'll get that out of the way first.  It absolutely does do what you see in the videos.  It plugs in, syncs up, updates it's firmware, and the haptic feedback is refreshing and extremely cutting-edge.  I mean Valve no disrespect with this review- this controller needed to be made years ago.  Unfortunately for those of us who game in multiple environments- myself, living room couch and desk, where both are viable for mouse+keyboard if I have to thanks to owning a Corsair Lapdog and K95 mechanical- there are situations that my Dualshock 4 could never be replaced by anything than the next Dualshock Sony releases.
Every. Single. Game.  Every one, requires you to sift through "official" and "community" presets that don't really seem to have much regulation to them.  Everything in these presets sometimes including the touch sensitivity boils down to how one single person prefers to play a game.  Behaving and working like a standard gamepad?  Never.  It simply *can't* do that, by design.
So XCOM 2 is pretty capable with it but I feel cheated out of 50 bucks because no way in hell would I ever use this controller to play a FPS or anything that requires anything resembling precise mouse emulation.  In games like Fallout 4, Skyrim, Splinter Cell, etc, which I use a controller for 100% of the time, it feels like I'm treading water trying to figure out how to "map" everything out.  This reminds me of the worst flaw in the "preset" library, which is how it nags and nags about going into Steam Big Picture and when you change presets it overwrites *every single keybind* you might have had in a game.  Fallout 4 actually bugs out and loses a menu option for binding essential keys like "run".
For a first person game, no freaking way.  I tried DOOM for 5 minutes with it, and it feels like using a late 90's mouse with Windows forcing it's unique brand of god-awful mouse acceleration and smoothing down your throat.  I'm sure there are tons of people who don't mind playing this way- it is a device that's supposed to bridge the gap between the living room and desk, after all- but holy hell, if this is the future, they might as well add auto-aiming to every new game that supports the Steam Controller.  It's absolutely that bad.
Maybe with future revisions and software updates this thing might get used (by me).  Force-feeding us Big Picture is a massive letdown, because we all know it's part of Valve's strategy to instill the branding in every situation possible.  I don't think that's even a negative or bad thing!  I *want* to see them get better with the market.  They need to remember that part of the audience that they're catering to isn't going to magically adopt a device like this over lugging a keyboard, mouse and a controller with them wherever they go.  It's the same reason we don't see people prefering laptop touchpads or analog sticks for classic games.  I shudder a bit thinking that I'd actually jump in a competitive BF4 game with only this controller.  Hold up, I might puke...
Slap another analog stick and a D-pad on this thing FFS.  Give us the ultimate controller. The biggest and final patch is live for MidBoss and that includes even more quality-of-life updates. There's possibilities for more inventory space, additional modes to get you acquainted with the mechanics (1UP and Story), and etc. Few bits of my original review has been updated.

MidBoss features a procedurally generated dungeon, with every click and movement counting as a turn. Your fellow enemies are your swords to wield and your shields to bare. Their bodies are at your disposal, their spells are a part of your arsenal, and their stats are yours to improve.
, you need it. You're the squishiest asexual fire demon in all the dungeon!
Death Cards are a unique feature in this game that saves your progress, inventory and map. They can be activated once to acquire one single item from your previous inventory to take with you in a new game. You can stack a number of different cards before a run to better your odds.
The consumable potion in the game are always unidentified, requiring the player to test out a vial and place their life on the line or to utilize the rare breed of identification scrolls. Even when discovered for their negative effects, potions cannot be used on enemies and get consumed by the player themselves. While you can sell them, all knowledge you gained about the potions become obsolete immediately after your death. Every new run will randomize the potions and their effects.
Identification scrolls are better kept for items at that point, and every unidentified potion becomes vendor fodder. Unless you're a pack rat, this will feel like a wasted gimmick.
As of the final patch, many of the useless items that took up inventory space are now useful. Not only that, inventory has gotten an overhaul that wasn't needed, and I (to my shame) can no longer do without it.
The cute humor and art can be misleading in how difficult the game can be. While most pixel games built from the ground up feel retrogressed, this feels closer to 16-bit, and tolerable. The main complaint during dungeon exploring is the isometric view, which does not rotate and leaves you wishing for more control.
The final patch added additional modes to get you to acclimate to the play mechanics or to get into the game purely for the story progression. This allows for player-scaled difficulty and less controller-throwing stress.
The soundtrack is worthy of a MidBoss. It doesn't jump at you, or have you whistling cheery theme songs. After a few loops, you will find yourself turning on sportify.
MidBoss is a definite pick-up-and-play for those who found fun in challenging titles like FTL and Darkest Dungeon. The sense of progression is on par with the aforementioned titles, and you will curse that sting of defeat as much as you will relish in your victories. The high replay value alone makes MidBoss a worthy title in any library.

I glanced at my "Played Time" for Endless Space: Disharmony and realized I should probably tell my friends what a good time I've been having.
Endless Space (and it's expansion, Disharmony, which I have not played without; it's basically version 1.5 of the game) manages to be a 4x game that feels like an updated, smoother MOO2, with a massively improved UI and tactical combat that plays like a (heavily) accelerated and simplified nod to Sword of the Stars.  There is very little I do NOT like about this game.
Enjoy micromanagement?  Do it to your heart's content.  Dislike it?  The system-control AI actually makes good choices.  Dislike the combat vignettes?  There's an option to preplan your maneuvers in a fight and just get the after-action report.   Like making your own races?  It's not quite as flexible as MOO2 (you've got to choose a basic techtree/affinity template) but you then throw on the resource, homeworld, research, military, and diplomatic modifiers of your choice, and there's enough variety in those base templates I haven't yet been unable to build a race that I want to play.  Ship design consists of allocating mass on a given hull design to about 20 different subsystems; you can research better versions of these systems, skip mounting them entirely, and in the case of most of the offensive systems change what they're specialized at.
"Turtling" in a system by building defenses cannot break a blockade or damage/drive away invaders.  While you can buy a decent amount of time to mount a response with defenses, and make it very hard, time intensive, and resource intensive to take over a system, Endless Space recognizes that it's awfully hard to fight up and out of a gravity well, or from static platforms in an arena as large as a solar system.  The only way to go on the offensive is to build ships and send them to an area.  By the same token, a well-planned invasion can cripple an enemy's economy by parking blockade ships above a number of his systems, and having a siege fleet move from system to system doing the actual work of besieging if you've got the time.
The ability to damage population/infrastructure makes economic warfare a valid and useful tactic when fighting a larger empire.  Strategically maneuverable ships can slip from system to system in the enemy's backfield, bombing infrastructure and killing population, forcing the opponent to pull ships off the frontline to defend his rear.  This can be a dangerous game for your forces, though, as a defensive fleet of sufficient size can still intercept them coming into a system, and the further you are from your own territory, the more likely a fleet is to be lost when retreating in disarray.  Don't have the time to besiege a system and force a surrender with an enormous fleet overhead?  Build transport ships and send your citizens into battle.  Casualties will be high, but you could take over the system in a single turn.  Like that tactic a lot but don't have the population base to support it?  At least one of the race templates can develop the technology to use clones as troops, removing the population cost.
Conflict between ships is broken up into three phases: long, medium, and melee (close, not ramming) distance.  For each phase, you select a maneuver you want your fleet to execute.  Your opponent does the same, and some maneuvers can negate others, meaning that playing to the obvious strengths of your designs may make you predictable.  Sometimes it's better to rely on those strengths and use them to force your opponent to maneuver in a particular fashion.  Three primary weapon types (missiles, beams, and kinetics) are nominally best at long, medium, and close range, but you can reconfigure them to be specialized at different ranges, which changes their overall tonnage use, damage profile, and interaction with defenses.  Systems such as fighters, bombers, and point defense also come into play should one or both sides bring them to a fight.
TL;DR: Endless Space: Disharmony is a solid 4x game with a lot of variety and a good UI that I've gotten dozens of hours of entertainment out of.  Play it.

At any difficulty level, there alway seems to be an opponent who will immediately start building up a fleet of warships from Turn 1 so that it can lay the smackdown on you within the first 30 turns, which is incredibly irritating when you're playing a non-martial race.
There's not a lot of help available, and the tutorial is totally lacking in substance.  The ability tree overview hasn't been updated since before Disharmony came out, resulting in misinformation that I just find annoying, but would probably frustrate the hell out of your average first time player.  Wording on technologies, abilities, and battle cards is vague and leads to confusion.  I'm still not entirely sure what actual effects some of the battle cards have.  Balancing seems to be an ongoing issue, with 2 races that had to be entirely reengineered because they were bricks from the get-go.
And yes, I'm going to kvetch about the Vaulters, because I shouldn't have to purchase another game from a different genre to make the game I already paid for complete.  That's just silly.  Amplitude said the rest of us would get them eventually, when Dungeon of the Endless was released, but that was 9 months ago and the game is still in Beta.  I've already lost my interest in the game, and I doubt it's going to come back because the upgrade cycle appears to have already finished and there's not going to be any further content updates.
tldr: Can be fun, but suffers from cheap AI and lack of support.  Generally lacks substance.

Endless Space is a turn based Sid Mires Civilization 5 like empire building game except it’s with a space theme, and by it’s like civ5 I’m not joking not that it’s a copy or that I’d even be upset if it was. However it’s much easier and quicker to explain if I compare it to civ5 because of the similarities.
I am going to talk about the problems with this game, and really I can’t really call them actual “problems” because the things I don’t like with the game are very much opinion so please keep that in mind. My most trivial complaint is that I don’t really like the whole space setting because there is not much to look at. It’s just stars suns and black space. Which makes it tired to look at, although, this is a problem I understand is quite difficult to avoid with a game about space which is why I say it’s my most trivial complaint.
This is my biggest complaint, the combat. I do not like the combat at all in this game it is VERY boring, and it’s the old and annoying luck more than strategy troupe. It’s essentially a rock paper scissors but with more options. You simply get several cards to choose from that do a variety of things to your ship, boosting attack but lowering defense etcetera. But the reason I dislike this is that you just choose a card, you don’t actually command your troops you just pick a card and watch your guys fight to the death. Normally this battle would be the games saving grace like in the Total War franchise. That game is saved by battles because it’s almost like there are two different games inside the game that both affect each other. Speaking as a former gaming journalist and gamer who's had MOO2 installed on every PC he's ever owned since it was published, I don't think people have been fair to this game. It's belongs in the 8s, not the 7s, IMO.
As many have said. It's pretty.
Something not many have said is that the UI is uncharacteristically strong for the genre, which is something I especially appreciate now that I write UI rather than game reviews for a living.
Most importantly, it scratches the MOO itch like nothing else has for me to date . I tried but could never really get into Gal Civ. SoTs was heaps of fun while it lasted but not really a similar enough experience to satisfy the same cravings. More than any other 4X sci-fi game I've played to date, Endless comes closest to the MOO2 experience not because it's trying too hard  as a me-too game, but because deep in the roots of Endless's game design, you can see that its designers really understand a lot of the critical aspects of what made that game fun (and even some of the things it could have done better).
There's definitely some stuff that I wish was different of course.
For instance, the best terraforming tech is way too far up the tech tree. By the time you've come close to perfecting all of your worlds, the AI will be threatening to clobber you with one of many non-eXterminating victories if you haven't all but stomped it into near oblivion at that point. Enjoying the role of magitech one-climate-world planetologist as much as I have in many games over the years, it bummed me out a little but I haven't tried fiddling with the settings that slow the game's pace down yet.
To be fair, however, there's plenty of planet-tinkering to be done and the game takes the stances that there really should be no useless planets. Asteroids bring unique system improvement opportunities. A certain hero gives insanely beefy boosts to gas giants which give the strongest resource boosts per colonist but to a high degree of specialty and with a very low max pop. Barren and volcano worlds suck for the reasons they typically do but can actually boost their specialty resource production higher than more ideal equivalents once a given system can afford the unhappy colonist hit.
For the most part, upgrades are system-wide (which makes high world count systems extremely desirable since most resource-boosting improvements are per-colonist) but each planet can also have an "exploitation" built for it which essentially gives an added boost in one of the resource types with additional boosts for specific planet types.
Resource balancing is pretty unobtrusive. If one of the four resource units isn't in enough supply you'll notice in the form of things not happening as fast as you would like them to rather than disaster. No food means zero pop growth, rather than starvation, for instance. I'm a little dizzy at times so I appreciate this. I also like that the game won't let you end a turn without research selected as there are a ton of topics and research can move pretty fast.
Happiness is the thing you have to really think about or risk being punished for it. Colonists dislike excessive expansion. They can actually get grumpy at you for overpopulation and excessive expansion at the same time (uncanny realism for the human-originating factions, IMO). This effectively eliminates colony-spamming as the one-true-colonizing strategy, making it better to focus not just on quality systems at first but on where you're colonizing them due to the game's zone of influence mechanic, which is basically a♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥on/flag-planting mechanic where colonies sprout faction territory zones after (arbitrary perhaps, but it works) 30 turns. Zones grow and push each other and you can't colonize inside another faction's  zone, which forces a lot of interesting strategic decisions and requires thinking about colonization rather than Zerging it.
I actually like the AI for the most part. The only thing I'm still on the fence about is the fact that a faction will sometimes go to war on you because your score is getting too high. I kind of wish I could turn that off because that makes the AI opponents feel more like simulations of not-very-smart human opponents than simulations of other alien factions but that brings me to a point I really love about the AI. I know that the AI declared war on me for that reason because THE GAME TOLD ME. It's possible the AI will go to war on you for stupid reasons, but never for "no reason" as the most helpful review to date reports. The game tells you why the AI did what it did. All you have to do is read the event report and it usually makes sense.
The other thing that's fun about the AI is that it isn't stingey and it knows when to quit.  When an AI faction declares war on you and you immediately start gobbling up its colonies like popcorn it will offer you several systems to get you to stop in the hastily offered surrender agreement. It's a nice change from those cheap ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s trying to hock their antimissile rockets for your Xentronium armor for the 20th time in a game or having to conquer 3/4 of their entire empire before they'll even consider peace.
It's still terribly stupid when it comes to evaluating circumstances like the fact that every ship in your considerably smaller armada has 4 layers of kinetic shielding and beam weapons and every ship in its fleets has kinetic weapons and zero beam shielding but I wouldn't have it any other way. Punishing that kind of stupid is fun.
Combat and ship design were satisfying enough for me, but could use more nuance and there's essentially no tactics. There are three weapon types that each work best at a certain range/phase of battle. Each has a counter defense. Weapons and defenses can be added in quantity at their respective hardpoints. There are a variety of support and special modules but most serve to add fixed modifiers to that essential formula (fighters and bombers being an exception). So design is really around offense vs. the defense and what the AI is likely to be fielding (hint: mostly kinetic in the early game).
Fights consist of setting targeting priorities and special power cards to play for three phases/ranges of battles that can cancel other player's cards out if they're of the right category and then hitting "manual" to watch the fight play it or "auto" if you feel safe not watching a different algorithm sort the battle out, potentially killing ships that would otherwise be nigh impregnable in a watched battle.
As I said, satisfying enough and I like the cards better in practice than I did on paper. Hero levelling and tech unlock fairly interesting ones and they won't overturn a major disadvantage. But I prefer gadgets and a wide variety of weaponry with quirks and unique behavior within a given type. There's no clever gyro-destabilizer/tractor beam combos to be had here and absolutely no thought to be put into whether you want the next level of kinetic, beam, or missile weapon because it's just bettter and there's really only one upgrade path for each. I definitely hope we get something more tactical and varied if there's an ES2 as this is one of the few spots I felt the game overstreamlined things.
One thing that impressed me on the other hand is the way they handled custom factions. ES has MOO's faction detailed individuality cake (granular stuff like research specialties and other races they liked/hated) and eats MOO2's customization too by giving each of the established factions a faction affinity that's a sort of template of specialized abilities, tech tree options and diplomatic dispositions that are decoupled from a fairly detailed point-buy system and whatever appearance you choose.
Any criticism aside, this game is a very solid addition to the genre with a lot of good ideas. It may not have the 1000+ hours longevity like MOO2 has had for me but it might have MOO1's and I fully expect to get a lot of play out of it.

My position as a beta tester:
For one to think that I am merely just another beta tester would simply be uninformed. I have distinctly left my mark on this game. That being said, I am just that, a beta tester. A beta tester lucky enough to get included in a project where he could make a difference. I have beta tested many games, but never have I enjoyed it as much as I have enjoyed beta testing this game. I do not understand why he chose my email over anyone else's, but in the end (Speaking from that it is two days before release) I took the opportunity and ran with it.
My opinion on the development of DCR 3D:
I feel this game has the potential to be the next big thing. Roman (RoKo0) is an absolute genius (Coming from someone with a 140 IQ, I'm no genius, but I can recognize one), I can distinctly see where he made decisions in developing his IP (Intellectual property) that many would have mistakenly overlooked. For example, his decision to make 2D variations of his IP before making a 3D one. Doing this bagged him a following before he even started work on the 3D version. He stuck to his guns through the beta testing period, where I frequently pushed him to make the game more realistic. In the end, I feel he found the perfect balance between realism and the softer cartoon-ish side of the game that makes it so charming (Something that I milked with my recent map and car designs).
How I started playing DCR:
I first saw DCR on Flonga many years ago. I tried everything I knew to crack the game. Even downloading the flash version of the game and running it in an isolated environment and searching for changing variables with cheat engine (I.E, I would search all variables with cheat engine, then earn money search for changed variables, not earn money, search for unchanged variables etc...). The simple fact that I could not crack his game, hooked me and I soon bought the first iteration of his game (Admittedly, if it was more expensive, I would have tried harder and eventually at least hacked credits).
My opinion of DCR 3D:
Right now it is really fun (10/10, I mean it has kept me till the 240th Beta Test post, which is my 88th, and 170 in-game hours so far), but looking at his plans for the future, it is going to be so much better. I look forward to watching this game spread its wings, but I am not convinced that this game is completely ready to leave its chrysalis. That being said, I recognize that the game needs to be released sometime and that there is no better time than when you have everything working perfectly.

Writing the review from the POV of a mainly solo-queue player who has been around since the beta.
Positives:
Giant robot death machines.
It's free-to-play.
The game looks and sounds great, and the designs for the Mechs themselves have never been better.
The core mechanics and "feel" of the game are fairly solid, with the team deathmatch and conquest game-modes being in a pretty good place right now.
Mech customization leads to a particularly compelling meta-game.
The weekend challenges can really spice things up a bit, if you are lucky enough to have the time to grind through them.
Giant robot death machines.
Negatives:
The payment model is still far, far too expensive for what is on offer.
Balance is still an ongoing issue, leading to a rotating roster of overly powerful "Meta-Builds" tending to dominate proceedings. Given the price of outright buying mechs, this can give players willing to pay over the odds a significant headstart in earning a strong gameplay advantage. (In PGI's favour, this aspect of the game has been steadily improving over time.)
"Assault" mode is still a complete waste of time.
The auto match-maker appears to take great joy in setting up hilariously lopsided matches.
The weekend challenges, while spicing things up a bit, can quickly turn into a chore for those who aren't lucky enough to have a lot of free time to grind at weekends.
TLDR:
The game, while still having issues relating to balance and pricing, is fun, and it is possible, with a little research and pre-planning, to play successfully as a free player. Just be prepared for some frustrations along the way.

I find it funny that I decided to make this review, because for a very long time I actually disliked Paladins, classifying it as just an Overwatch clone. Only when I actually did play the game did my opinions change.
Paladins is, in many aspects, very similar to other class-based FPS shooters. There's clearly defined champions as the playable classes, along with class groups of Damage, Flank, Tank, and Support. There are three different modes for King of The Hill, Escort, and Attack/Escort. Gameplay in the matches is very fast-paced and focuses heavily on good teamwork. There are also only five players per team, encouraging a more competitive environment.
The game definitely managed to draw me in, even though it did so for only a few months. It was a nice break from the current multiplayer games I was playing and i did actually enjoy it. The characters themselves were not terribly interesting, but not forgettable either. My main complaint was the card system that was in place. Cards allow for upgrades to specific champions, but I never really quite understood why that needed to be implemented in the first place. I would have enjoyed it more had there not been the card modifier system. Hi-Rez has changed the card system since I last played however, so be wary of the new changes.
Paladins is a game with a lot of potential, but it's really only fun for a few months.

This game... oh wow. Talk about "won over by a game"  or "missing out for too long".
I did play the original Deus Ex wayyy back when, but for some reason I wasn't interested in the sequels, and didn't try them. And this one... I had heard good things about it, but for some reason, either some other game kept me busy, or I simply wasn't interested.
Until now. Boy, did I miss out.
Story
HR is IMO quite in the spirit of the original DE... there is stealth, but you can also try to fight openly. There are different methods of solving a situation, there are secrets, and...there is a great storyline.
Indeed, the story is quite fascinating, and even though The Fall sucked, you might wanna consider reading "The Icarus Effect", a novel that is kinda set in between The Fall and HR (no spoilers though!)
Anyway, so the story is rather deep, and there is a strong Mass Effect vibe to it all. You get sucked into it, and your answers in conversations do make a difference. If you want to, you can enhance yourself to be able to "read" people and manipulate them.
Stealth
Which leads me to one of the coolest parts about the game - the stealth approach. Stealth in this game works great, and it is so satisfying to sneak through a large area, dodging all enemies, not alerting them. If you fail, you can still fight openly or try to get away, so it's not as frustrating unless you really want to avoid being detected or killing anyone... if you wanna do that, it can be quite challening, but o so satisfying once you nail it.
The augmentations can be very helpful, allowing you to fall from great heights, find alternative routes or even becoming invisible for a short time.
The stealth-system, to me, was insanely fun. You can try to play this Rambo-Style, and I think that can be fun too, as the cover-system works well (IMO even better than in the more recent The Division), but to me, it was all about being a ghost.
The Director's Cut makes quite a difference - because the boss battles now have new methods of winning them. In the past, before the DC, if you were fully specced and equipped for stealth, the boss fights felt pretty frustrating and not like fun. I mean, you spend 90% of the game trying to be sneaky, and then have to do an open fire-fight with a strong boss?
Each boss has a method you can use if you are more into stealth or using tools (again, no spoilers). It doesn't make them totally trivial, as using those methods still can be tricky or risky. With the first boss, I didn't find the "stealth method" at first, and felt totally put off by that fight, until I experimented and suddenly found... again, no spoilers.
Exploring and always looking for alternate routes (vents) will allow you to avoid most fights.
Gameplay
Controls work great (used a controller), but I did switch to a mouse for hacking. Hacking is a mini-game which is essential for the game, as it unlocks doors, shuts down security traps, unlocks secrets etc. Fortunately, it isn't that difficult (again, I found doing this with a mouse quicker and easier, compared to the controller), unless you wanna pick up special bonusses you get from nodes in the hacking grid... it's your choice.
I recommend to save often, and use the quicksave (F5) a lot. If things go wrong, reload and retry.
The AI is not incredibly smart, but it's decent, and I had fun taking the guys out with the stun gun.
Graphics:
The graphics ARE showing the age of the game a bit, but they're still decent and add a lot to the atmosphere.
Music:
Just great, nuff said.
Pros:
- Fun stealth system
- Lots of optional methods to solve situations
- Enhancements
- Storyline/writing
- The dialogue game
- Alternate methods for bosses, especially the "stealth solutions" added in the DC
-  Challenging, depending on your difficulty settings and your own goals (Non-lethal, stealth etc)
- Lots of optional secrets and "lore"
- Atmosphere
- Good performance even on older systems
Cons:
- Showing it's age a bit
- A lot of running forth and back on rather small maps
- Clunky management of the small inventory imo
- If you pick up a weapon you already have, you only get the ammo. No way to pick up the wep and sell it for profit. Money isn't all tjhat essential, but allows you to buy more skillpoints, so if you're a packrat, this fact and the small inventory might be a downer
Verdict:
At full prize, 8.5 of 10, at anything between 5-10 EUR (sale) I give it a 9-9.5. Yes, it's showing its age and has some flaws, but the stealth, the story, atmosphere and protagonist make up for all of that IMO. It's really really good, and if you can't get into the much older DE because it feels a bit too old school, please consider giving this one a try. I love it.

When I first purchased this game, I was thinking this was going to be some kind ofmemory game... And well, it is... but it's so much more...
First off, this is a memory game, but not just any memory game. It's a game about disassembling, reassembling, and even remembering how each gun is taken apart and put back together with & without using the guides. This game is really about remembering the order in which you have to assemble the parts. There's also a shooting range for each gun so you get an idea on how to use the gun as well as teaches you how to spare your ammo for each target and on how you can learn to use each gun on aiming, handle and even practice on moving targets.
One thing to note about this game is that, although it is called "World Of Guns", it's not just about guns. There's also sections of the game that lets you disassemble and reassemble skeletons, army vehicles (Tank & humvee), sports cars, and even a harley.
During the course of playing the game, you also get some really neat info about each weapon, vehicle, and skeleton. Details about the make, model, history, concept, and what went into making each weapon.
What I like most about this game is how well detailed the designer put into making each part of every weapon. Someone did some serious homework on this game based on how many parts each gun has. I found this game not only fun, but also informative, and even help me to learn to respect weapons. Learning how the mechanics and insides work was the best part about his game.
I have read some other reviews and they seem to claim that some parts of the game were too hard. Although I can somewhat understand, this is more of a memory game as each gun, vehicle, skeleton as an order in which it's assembled, so you have to remember the order of the parts in order to get a good score. This is a memory game, not so much a shooter game. Some guns have as much as 100+ parts to remember, while a few guns only have say 20-30 parts. Every part has it's place, every part must also be done in a certain order, so you got to use your head more than use your speed. Once you know how the parts go, speed will follow. This is is a trial and error game as well as memory game. If you like memory games, this is a good game to get.

The original Stronghold is still the strongest or second strongest (to Stronghold Crusader) entry in the Stronghold Franchise. It's dual nature as both a city (or in this case, castle) management game and a medieval war game gives it great depth. You can focus on only one side through the various standalone missions, or play through the campaign to experience both, almost always together.
Most of the strategy on the combat side will mostly be unit composition and tactical positioning. There aren't really any special abilities to cast, so picking units is mostly balancing efficacy of units against their cost, and using units is mostly placing them in the best position to take as little damage as possible while dealing the most damage possible.
The castle management, while rather basic, can be challenging given the scarcity often present. Sometimes you won't have enough peasants, other times not enough food, or maybe not enough space, or all of these together. Many things are also dependent on each other, and if one part falls, the rest can collapse like dominoes. Placement efficiency to reduce travel time and increase output is a rather big part of the game.
All in all, Stronghold is a great all-around strategy game that should appeal to some part of strategy fans of all types.

It's been a long ride.
I'm usually a hardcore KB+M gamer; I've played some games on my PS2/3 and it's been fine, but kb+m is superior.
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
I purchased the controller back in December. Barely touched it for several months, as it felt... weird. Everytime I decided to, it felt like it was not worth the trouble.
And then, I finally decided to put some effort into it.
The result was horrible when I started. Truly was. It requires so much to learn in order to make any game remotely convenient. Touchpads are so weird, it's like playing an FPS on your phone... on two screens, not just one. Customization  can take hours when you're new to this - I did not know how to set it up, so I literally had to experiment for hours.
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
THEN something magical happened. After ~30-40 hrs with over all games, I made a positive K/D ratio on Dirty Bomb?
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
Suddenly, it all felt... natural.
I decided to buy an Xbox One controller too. I was now hooked on playing with controllers (KB+M is STILL more convenient, however, it comes with some back pains and worn out wrists :)). I though, well, I have some experience with the standard sticks on the controllers, XBone should feel even better.
Imagine my surprise after spending $100 on XBone controller.... it felt horrible! The sticks felt ancient and outdated. The overall feel was frustratingly limiting.
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
And then I got back to the Steam Controller again. I don't think I can ever go back. This gadget is so much fun! I still have a lot of getting used to to go to actually replase KB+M, but once you get over the weirdness from the start and the tough learning curve, it is most definately one of my best gaming purchases for the past few years.

Like many of the negative reviews, I want to like this controller.
In fact, I do like the controller. It's comfortable as all hell in your hand, has grips on the underside, which add two additional buttons total, and is customizable beyond belief.
However, that's as far as it goes. I like it as something that sits in my hand, not for playing anything.
-For multiplayer FPS's, nothing beats the traditional mouse and keyboard.
-For more laid back FPS's that I personally enjoy using a game pad with (Bethesda games, for example), I still prefer a regular game pad.
-I thought maybe I'd like it with Dark Souls, since I'd be able to bind the grips to jump attack (a move that otherwise requires a specific input of analog and trigger). Even still, controlling the camera with the right touch pad was unbearable.
That's really what it comes down to: the touch pads. Maybe I'm at fault for not putting days and days of effort into fiddling with the sensitivity, and learning the track pad until it felt more natural. But it feel like the complete opposite of natural. And even if I had put that effort in, I wouldn't have more of an edge using the Steam Controller, versus a standard game pad.
If you're on the edge, I'd suggest looking elsewhere.

A nice idea but a horrible execution.
This game should be fun -- use your cue ball to get the other balls into pits, avoiding obstacles etc.
Sadly, this game isn't fun. It looks and plays like an incomplete demo rather than a full game.
Controls are keyboard only. You cannot fine-tune shots at all, you just have to hope you somehow get the right angle by mashing wasd or the arrow cluster. Once you start powering up a shot and overshoot your desired power level, you're out of luck -- the only option is to release, shooting the ball, or to let it fill up the bar completely and fire.
Every proper shot earns you point, every shot you don't pocket a ball gives you a penalty. Go negative, and the level resets. Whenever you hit an obstacle with your cue ball or a shot ball, you get another penalty.
The ball physics aren't realistic at all and, worse, don't seem to be consistent. This makes puzzles incredibly difficult for all the wrong reasons, as you combine bad physics with trial and error.
Did I mention that levels fully reset whenever you make a mistake? There is no rewind, there is no undo -- you have to perfectly complete a full level or just start over.
Any one of these on its own is forgivable. Combined, they make the game bad and simply not fun.
Normally I wouldn't review a game with such a short play time, but this game offers me absolutely no incentive to keep playing. If the first four levels are already incredibly flawed and more frustrating than anything else, I'm not going to sink more time in it.
To the dev: add some fine-tuning to controls, if you can't add mouse aiming. Even Peggle has this! Also add a rewind/undo last shot option. When I have to pocket 8 balls and a simple error on the 7th forces a full level reset, it doesn't make me want to play any longer.

MidBoss is a dungeon crawler where you get to possess the bodies of your defeated enemies. By defeating more enemies and playing those characters, you unlock new skills and are able to use their skillsets even when you repossess some other monster. That opens a room for many different skill and build combinations.
•	The main idea: there are lots of monsters with unlockable abilities (you have to unlock them on every new run) that you combine into your own character builds. Each monster can have up to 3 active abilities chosen at the time. Some of the monsters don’t have 3, others have much more, which makes you choose. Those 3 abilities can be transferred to the next monster upon death, which opens space for LOTS of combinations.
•	The way how new runs are handled: the beginning gets repetitive, but “grave goods” system that allows you to transfer one item from your previous characters really helps the random factor and introduces the missing “roguelike” element: no matter what decisions you take, you will be stronger on the next walkthroughs if you are using the grave goods system properly.
•	Challenging difficulty done just right: the game is easy to get into, but hard to master. You’ll have to experiment a lot in order to find valid builds.
•	The art is not bad and is done in a consistent style. It’s a bit generic for a dungeon crawler, but not low quality.
•	Random generation: the rooms often feel empty and not decorated enough. Additionally, the random generation also strongly affects the loot, so there will be games that you lose simply due to randomly generated items not being strong enough.
•	Not many stats compared to other roguelikes. When you level up, you can choose one of four stats only. Those affect your other attributes like dmg / block chance. So in that regard – levelling up your main character is pretty limited.
•	The UI: Menus are a bit clumsy. You cannot bind items on hotkeys (yes, even activated items). You cannot equip items at once when you pick them (even if you right click on them), you always have to open inventory and choose them.
•	The fonts are blurry and hard to read. The whole game graphics are blurred out (probably by intention), but I’m assuming that the blur shader is applied for the whole scene on rendering. This should not be done this way: the good idea is to render UI / Text after the relevant gameplay scene has been rendered. My eyes were not getting tired, but that overall impacts the UX and decreases the perceived quality of the game.
Compared to other roguelikes, this game is remarkably easy easy to get into, but that does not make it easy to play (in a good way). The main possession mechanic is deep and well thought-out, but other aspects don’t feel very developed compared to other dungeon crawlers. I can recommend the game to those who are looking for a way to get into the genre or just don’t enjoy crawlers where you have to read tons of text. However, MidBoss seems quite overpriced right now and I’d personally wait for 66% discount and grab it close to $5 (or your regional equivalent), simply because there are other alternatives on the market.

the depth of mechanics in the game is quite amazing, with layers and tactical gameplay in every corner. Turn based it might be, but even so Slower zombies take fewer turns, and faster enemies might take an extra one. Where the game loses some of its luster is the procedural generation part of the game... mostly due to the overall feel of Emptiness in the levels. Corridors are good and fine, but i do like a nice statue, or painting, or maybe a vase, carpet or two... hell, at this point i'll take a pile of dismembered kittens to spice up the walls. What art is has and where its available from its generated maze - it looks... fine. But its often very Empty, and that is a damn shame.
This doesn't take away from the mechanics (or ability to customize the game play to your preference in a myriad of options), but it does make you wish it threw in a particle effort or 50 in there.
Overall - if you enjoy the Rogue Like experience, then this is an example that does a good job at being exactly that and well worth the hours invested for enjoyable experience in being a literal zombie.

If you like 4X games such as Civ 4/5 and you like Sci-Fi - pretty much a wet dream come true.

Cons - (it seems alot, but I have just elaborated on 2 points, stick with me here!)

You cannot control the ship movement (as its linear movement) or designate targets (this is AI). Because of the way space combat is designed (Long rage, medium, and Melee phases) this was intentional, keeping action 'turn based'. I would have liked an option in the start menu to have autonomy of space battles, rather than the current system - but thats personal opinion.

You can train different types of troops (rocket, advanced) and you can designate them as 'normal' or 'elite' in ship building, but you cannot designate ground tactics, which is a BIG oversight, in my eyes.
Graphics:
Smooth - runs perfectly on my laptop (Nvidia 740m, certainly not top of the range!)
Planet graphics are great.
Battle graphics are seamless (and loading times are extremely quick!)
Verdict:
Just buy it already! Well worth the cash. And to the devs (keep it up, more updates, maybe even a battles overhaul? pwetty pwease?)

More of an interactive experience and less of a game Aurora Nights features a simple mini game where you connect stars to reveal 35 Northern Hemisphere constellations on the night sky map.
While there isn't much to be said about the gameplay aspect of the game, if you're into amateur stargazing or simply want to know more about constellations, then Aurora Nights is a good place to start.
There's a slight difficulty level which awards you more stars for 100% completion but getting that 100% shouldn't take more than hour or so.
For its price I believe is worth it, there's trading cards involved and the achievements are quite easy.
Truth be told, the game could have been even better if they included more details regarding each constellation, such as more history regarding the name (you get a couple of sentences at most in the game itself), the stars themselves, visibility during seasons and more astronomical information.
Nonetheless this is a recommendation for the game for people who want to learn more about stargazing and constellations. It's short, simple and educational enough to be really good for children as well.

DXHR is worthy of the Deus Ex title and doesn't disappoint compared with the original Deus Ex. It is certainly a better game than 'Invisible War'.
Though styled as a FPS in interface, it's more like an RPG in spirit with stealth strongly encouraged (though you don't HAVE to be stealthy). Like any good RPG you earn XP points, collect items, complete quests, and upgrade your skills ('augmentations') which are either passive abilities or active skills.  Non-lethal approach is just as rewarding (in fact there's an achievement for not killing ANYONE except bosses). In most levels there are many ways to get to your objective - secret passage ways, hack the security, stealthy take-downs of the guards, all guns blazing - you name it.
Graphics still looks great and detailed (down to names of books on bookshelves), and isn't too much of a resource hog (even on medium settings on my mid-range older PC it looks really nice with decent FPS). Sound/music is a little forgettable compared to how good the soundtrack from Deus Ex original was. The story is nicely told through both the excellent main quest mission, side quests, and also background atmospherics like TV news, ebooks, billboards etc. A nice touch that came to mind was the TV newsreader (whom I didn't pay close attention to in the first playthrough in earlier parts of the story) who becomes a part of the storyline. It's a way of helping you immerse in the world without you even realising it, until the background information suddenly becomes highlighted and you go, 'ah HA!' - most satisfying for FPS/shooter genre which is not always known for strong storytelling.
The Director's Cut (which I haven't finished yet) has revamped some of the boss fights to give more options for the stealthy player (though boss fights remain a weakness of the game given how scripted they are) and incorporated the DLC into the main storyline.
Highly recommended. I'd give this 8.5/10.
