This review may contain spoilerish stuff, though my goal is to be more general.
I started out with this game working its way into my head as one of my favorite games of all time. I also started with the Director's Cut version and I didn't know that there was a DLC pack stuck into the story halfway through. And honestly, it wasn't until researching it later that I realized that to be the case. The story integration of the DLC is flawless.
However, the gameplay integration nearly caused me to ragequit the game and seriously marred what was otherwise one of the best game experiences I've had in years. The hard reset of gear and upgrades until you're through with the DLC mission is, in a word, jarring. And the gameplay itself, while mildly entertaining, gets seriously repetitive (the level design had me going back and forth through the same long areas several times, dodging the same guards each time because I was playing with more of a focus on stealth at that point... plus it was harder to be combative at all due to the reset).
Finishing the DLC mission was similar to the feeling I get stepping inside my home after a long trip with even longer car rides. By that point, I was exhausted and just wanted to get back to the gameplay that I had grown to love and built upon with the upgrades I'd obtained in part through doing every side mission I could find.
I'm on my second playthrough of the game now, using New Game+, because the base game is that good. But I'm dreading the moment when I hit the DLC mission, especially having nearly every upgrade in the game this go around, due to the retention of New Game+. The jarring loss of every upgrade I've earned will hurt even more this time.
There isn't much critical I can say about the base game. If I rated it independent of the integrated DLC pack, I would give it a fanboy's joyful 10/10.
If I rate it with the DLC, it's closer to a 7/10.
And the DLC pack on its own, I'd rate as more like a 5/10. To reiterate, the story aspect of the DLC pack was very enjoyable for me. Just about everything else was trash, when stacked up to the quality of the base game. The only moments I particularly remember enjoying from the pack were A) the boss fight and B) the conversation at the end. And the boss fight I mainly enjoyed because it was refreshingly easy, after a painstaking gameplay experience during the rest of the DLC.
In summary: In the future, please reconsider shoving in DLC, if it means a jarring gameplay shift. The gameplay choices may have made for a cool story tool, but what shocked me was that in virtually every other aspect of the game, gameplay took priority over story. It makes more sense now, knowing that it was originally DLC. Please don't integrate in such a way in the next title. Or, if you do, at least place the retrieval of lost gear and upgrades near the beginning, rather than at the end. I think of KotOR back in the day; it had a mission where you lose your gear temporarily, but the period during which you don't have it is brief and you do most of the mission with your gear back. You can still have your story moment and be much nicer.

I don't hear a whole lot about the Steam Controller on the media. Reddit, tumblr, pcgaming and other media outlets just don't seem to have much to say about it, which is really strange, so I thought I'd chime in.
The Steam Controller is great, with a difficulty curve that seems to put off a lot of prospective buyers. It's a real shame, because I feel like the rebindable controls are being played as some big "WARNING" sign, when it is, in fact, the opposite.
The rebindable buttons take some work getting used to, especially if you REALLY want to control the feel of your game. It takes time and patience to really delve into a game and think "Do I want something different to happen if I hold the button as if I press it? What about double-pressing it?" You can literally set the triggers with one function for pressing them down, and another function for actually clicking them in. These can be really specific, but for the tinkerers out there, this feels like the difference between the Wright Brothers' first flight, and the Moon Landing by NASA.
Additionally, the Grips are something I never realized I needed. I use my Index Finger for both triggers and bumpers- it's just how I've always played, and I'm willing to bet most people hold their controllers the same way, leaving 3/5ths of your fingers just holding plastic. Grips add the possibility of using another pair of fingers for additional commands. This is particularly useful for games where one hand is always trying to make use of camera controls with the right analog stick, leaving the buttons unpressable while you manage it.
Now, the controller isn't perfect- far from it. I'd like to see the haptic pads textured with some tacticle sensation enforcing certain "boundaries" within the trackpad itself. The directional pad, while functional in its own right, leaves a lot to be desired when used as a touchpad. The grip command buttons also need to be more reliable- I had to file for a replacement after 10mo once my left grip started becoming harder and harder to actually activate. And of course, we need more buttons- if controllers are ever going to feel welcome in PC games, they're going to need enough buttons to keep the ball in play.
But my biggest complaint about this great controller is that it just doesn't do enough with its trackpads; these were the selling points of the controller (so much so that the original prototypes had no joysticks!), and yet they feel so underutilized and underdeveloped for the sake of a more "sleek" design. Maybe in the future, Steam Controllers will have more in the ways of modularity? I know I'd love to see easily-disassemblable cases with different trackpads with different textures better suited for certain programs/games. I'm not holding my breath on that detail, but a guy can dream, right?
Final Verdict: Get this controller, folks. Maybe it won't solve all of your problems- it might not even be your -favorite- controller, but it introduces so much to the idea of a controller's structure and interaction with the user that maybe we can find out how to make controllers from other manufacturers better. Let's all make a better tomorrow out of this, guys.

So, looking back now.
Wargaming, the publisher, seems to have realised that the way they have implemented various things is extremely unpopular with the majority of the worldwide player community. That being said, they do not seem to be doing anything to resolve the present issues still in the game, but rather introducing new features in an attempt to distract the playerbase.

If you're looking for a quick, easy game, free to play, and don't care about progressing quickly or all the way to the top, yes.
If you are coming from World of Tanks PC version, and are wanting to join the community and become a substansive member of the playerbase, active both online in the forums and in-game, then yes.

This is a great game if you remember one thing. Community Warfare isn't the place to go to learn how to play. It's the equivalent of end game content. It's MWO's version of open world PvP.
That said, there is no pay to win. Yes there are a few Mech variants that are cash only, but note the word "variant". They're different versions of regular mechs, and aren't more powerful, don't have special abilities etc. Often based on characters from the BattleTech universe, they have a different hardpoints (determines where and how many weapons of a given type can be mounted).  As I said, it's not pay to win, so it isn't a matter of adding more. Various factors such as space and weight limits apply. Sometimes its a Mech that is mostly Ballistics based (ie "guns") and the Hero version mostly Energy (lasers etc) based. Toss in a unique camouflage scheme, some colors, and that's one way they keep the lights on.
New mechs are introduced regularly, and spend a few months as cash only, then opened up for in-game money. No the new ones aren't more powerful etc. Weight and space limits remember? An AC/20 still weighs 14 tons no matter what Mech you pilot.
It's a fun game, if you're willing to admit there is a learning curve. LRMs (Long Range Missiles) are deadly until you learn how to avoid them. as a common example.
The official forums have a very active new player section, and the community is overwhelmingly friendly and helpful.
I've spent over $100 on this game and I don't spend money on F2P games. One big purchase early on for some mechs, then bought some additional mech bays (this was in the days before you could earn free ones in CW and special events.)
The only way to "screw up" is to spend your Cadet bonus unwisely (you get bonus cash your first 25 missions to help you along). Even then you can pilot "trial" mechs for variety as you save up to buy new mechs.
Bottom line? Visit the official forums and read over the New Player section while you download MWO. Ask questions, don't be a jerk, and you'll have lots of fun. :)

If you are a fan of Battletech this is just about the only online fix you'll be able to get. After the shutdown of Mechwarrior:Living Legends that left this the last bastion.
The actual mechanics are ok, the game is more stable nowadays and has a fairly flexible approach to gameplay and the devs (PGI) have stepped their game up a fair few notches. When you can get a good game, with good team mates it's a great game-you certainly can gain those "gaming memories2 that you never forget:)
But, MWO has one HUGE issue and it's one that cannot be solved by the devs...the playerbase.
Basically, I've played MMO games since the release of EQ1 and I have NEVER seen such a pro solo, anti group playerbase. a disturbing lack of teamplay in all game modes-even though the game has built in voip and text chat. It even got last year, a solo only queue-a solo mode in a multiplayer online game, that should tell you all you need to know already!
It also has a more complex "clan wars" style mode simliar to WoT that is currently in 2nd phase of beta testing. Unless you are social and get onto each faction's TS hubs abd actually speak to other people, you will be stuck with the pug lottery. during EU primetime that lottery will mostly give you 11 utterly silent team mates who will make zero effort to teamwork. Shift that to US primetime and the amount of teamwork increases, with mostly Americans being the talkers-but the gameplay DOES improve and I have had some cracking CW matches like that. Best advice I can give you is GET INTO A UNIT AND PLAY WITH OTHERS, the game is great when with others.
Last critique is you'll notice that the playerbase is VERY timid, especially in solo queue so if you like team focused, movement heavy games-you'll be VERY frustrated with the solo Q.
Recommend this game if you like Battlemech and want a game where you can play a few matchs a week.

There are few games that can integrate a distinctive, unique, and game defining atmosphere.  I would go as far to say that Deus Ex: Human Revolution is the most atmospheric game created thus far.  You can feel it overcoming you when you watch the first cutscene of the game.  The plot and narrative are very strong and engaging with branching paths.  The gameplay is good, but those of you excpecting to have a Call of Duty experience will be disappointed.  The stealth gameplay takes center stage.  This game allows for almost endless possibilities to complete an objective,  it features some of the best level design I have ever experienced.  Think of any plausible solution to an objective and it is probably scripted in the game.  Player choice is strongly supported in this game and it increases its replay value exponentially.  I purchased this game in 2011 and am still finding alternate paths to my objectives.  However, character models are low-res and lip sync is abysmal, which inhibits suspension of disbelief and serves to break immersion.  And a boss battles force you to play a certain way, luckily there are only three of these.  Make no mistake this is superbly crafted game which should have a place in all libraries.  However, just a few design flaws hold the game back from being a masterpeice.
9/10 -  A game that creates its own unique atmosphere and provides a well written complex narrative, with solid stealth gameplay.

I remember that when I was a kid, I enjoyed spending time looking at the sky and trying to figure out the constellations. Back then, I knew how to recognize only a couple of them and the others remained a complete mystery to me. Until I played this little game.
Aurora Nights is more of an educational software rather than a game, since there's no actual playthrough apart from connecting the dots representing the stars that compose each constellation. Of the 88 officially recognized constellations, the game teaches you how to recognize the 35 most common, in a very enjoyable and relaxing way. Additionally, for each group of stars you can read a small text explaining the origins of their name, most of these descending from Greek mythology.
In my opinion, the game is worth the price, for it's unique and interesting concept and I hope to see in the future an extension to the game, featuring the remaining 53 constellations.

The Steam Controller itself is a great product in my opinion. However, the problem I have found is that native support is quite lacking. Without native support, it's very difficult tweak settings well even if configurations can be opened up and shared among users.
I got the controller at Steam Dev Days, so my review may fall short for this product, but hear me out.
The one game that seems to have native controller support that I have installed is Left 4 Dead 2, however I've experienced a lot of crashing, not the game, but Steam, which does kind of in turn cause the game to crash.
However, when it is working, the trackpads on either side work great for head movement and menu access. I really do like the trackball emulation it has so I can roll my finger over the pad move more fluidly.
I have yet to try acceleration only for the fact that I know I can't stand it when it's used on an actual mouse, so I haven't really given that a chance. Perhaps another reviewer could better describe that experience.
As a developer, I decided to try supporting it in our game PVKII to see how it works, and it does work extremely well as far as I'm concerned, even without having added menus that are better tailored to the controller. It also doesn't appear to crash Steam, so perhaps my issues with L4D2 were purely an implementation problem.
If you're the type that doesn't mind tweaking to get things the way you want them to especially on games that don't have native support, or perhaps the games that you play do have support for it, I'd definitely highly recommend the Steam Controller.
The UI for configuring the Steam Controller in games might also seem a bit intimidating, but it's quite intuitive to use, and I don't find it much different from anything you would normally see in a console game to reconfigure buttons.
Really the only barrier I can think of that makes it less accessible to the average user is native support from developers in games. I'm hoping that future updates from Valve that were announced at Steam Dev Days to the controller API will make it more appealing to developers that want to support more than just the Steam Controller.
Overall, the product itself is solid, but it really needs better support from developers to make it more accessible. I like it, but I do prefer keyboard and mouse, it's what I grew up with, and I'm not too much of an on the couch gamer these days.

How to make pancakes:
Whisk 1 1/2 cups flour, 3 tablespoons sugar, 1 1/2 teaspoons baking powder, 1/2 teaspoon salt and 1/4 teaspoon baking soda in a medium bowl.
Whisk 1 cup plus 2 tablespoons milk, 4 tablespoons melted butter and 1 egg in a separate bowl; fold into the flour mixture until just combined (it's OK if there are some lumps).
Brush a large nonstick skillet or griddle with butter and heat over medium-low heat. Add ¼ cupfuls of batter and cook until bubbly on top and golden on the bottom, about 4 minutes. Flip and cook until golden on the bottom, about 2 more minutes. (Makes 6 to 8 pancakes.)

My review of MechWarrior Online:  Jan 15 2016
Mechwarrior was one of those games I grew up on when I was younger.  The player pilots an armored mech and does battle with eleven other players on a variety maps.
Graphics:  I have nothing much to compare this against except maybe Hawken and Titanfall and it can match some of their look.  Maps are generally good looking ranging from desert wastelands to artic towns.  Weapons like lasers glow, leaving heat marks. and missles/rockets general smoke trails.  You can tell the damage of mechs by how much smoke they can sometimes generate from the damage they have taken.  Cockpits are fully detailed, though you can't push the buttons, and are unique for each kind of Mech.
Sound:  There is not much to say about the sound as much of it is muffled.  You get verbal warnings and indicators for what is happening on the map or happening to you.  What I mean for muffled sound is;  you are hearing what you would hear inside your mech.  The thumps of your feet stomping around and bumping into terrain. The hiss of your heat sinks trying to cool you down.  The bang of ballistic weapons being fired and the cycling of energy weapons as they discharge.
Gameplay:  In the main menu players can select which Mech they want to pilot.  Once you pick a chassis (general shape and character of the mech) you pick a varient (loadout options)  and you are ready to go.  The roles are broken up into weight classes.  Light mechs are your small light weight fast movers.  Mediums mechs and Heavy mechs seem to be your general all round mechs and Assault mechs are the heavy hitters.  While fighting players have to manage their Mech's heat and torso while they manuever around in battle shooting enemies.   After each battle awards players with xp for their chosen Mech and credits that they can spend on getting new mechs or customizing the ones they currently own.  You spend your XP on skill boosts that affect the performance of your Mech.
New player experience?:  After installing and signing in, players complete a tutorial to learn how to effectively pilot mechs.  Though many of the more advanced systems are not discussed or gone over in the tutorial, players can complete challenges to see said systems.  They recieve a stack of credits where they can save up to buy their first mech.  Trial Mechs are freely given and rotate regularly to allow players to try out different styles.
Overall:  It is a fun game,  you could lose many hours of sleep into it.  The community seems fairly friendly as the game does have built in voice chat.  Games tend to be more group friendly as you get awards for fighting together.  It does have a bit of a learning curve but what game doesn't.  Just remember to not go alone,  lone mechs are tasty.

Maps:

Oddly enough despite the 3+ years Piranna has had with the same maps the object collisions are still goofy. thin radio towers with mech wide invisible physical bodies or structures with giant gaps you try to shoot through/around only to be blocked while quite a few large rocks seems to have no collision presence.  You'll have to constantly struggle with your Mech catching on physical barriers that can't be seen and each slope is a gamble wether or not you can traverse it.
Gamemodes:
Standard f2p fare with your capture the flag and deathmatch that's about it, unless you do clan wars which is just the same.  Platooning is a nightmare, pairing up with only 1-2 peeps and you'll be facing whole teams of the same clan sync dropping to farm pubs. or come hauling a teams worth of pals and you'll still only go against clans.
The pubcrawl is awful, there's a small player base which if you ignore the oceanic server for ping reasons gets even smaller, so you'll be in queue alot.
Server Health:
There's a worringly thinning player base, and everyone pinned their hopes on it spiking after the game was added to steam, but
.
Customization:
You can make a large variety of custom builds, but all mechs look the same unless you put actual money into it, which is fine.  The main stinker is the awkward balancing that creates a standard that everyone uses to stay competitive.  Worst thing is ballistics never seem to get a spotlight.

You'll buy your mech, let's say a medium for 5mil, then you'll need to grind another 1.5mil for Dheatsinks, then another 1.9mil for a practical engine (hopefully your build doesn't need a 4mil XL engine), then another 500k for a lighter frame, then 1.6mil for weapons. I feel it best to write a more up-to-date review focusing on the game that is Endless Space.
Endless Space is a 4X, Turn Based Strategy that involves you building your empire through Colonies, Fleets, Improvements and Diplomacy to attain victory.
The easiest way to fully describe the game, would be if Civilization V were set in Space. But that in itself isn't a fully accurate description. Let's get to the meat, shall we?
When I first started the game on my Netbook, I noticed how nice the graphics were and how it ran relatively smoothly on the Medium settings (It ran on High settings relatively well on my Mac) only slowing down in the late game when hundreds of fleet movements had to be rendered and checked. The game has only crashed once or twice, and that was mostly because I messed with a few game files while running the game.
Performance- 8.5/10
As mentioned previously mentioned, the graphics were very impressive. From the Character designs, Ship designs, Menu designs, Planet designs, the game has a very clean and polished look and has Lore related artwork that really makes the game a much better experience. I found myself taking screenshots of planets and systems as they were simply amazing. Wonders, Cities and Anomalies are rendered on the planets themselves, thus giving direct visual feedback to the user.
One critique relating to the graphics was the lack of variation in city aesthetics and a lack of visual feedback given when a Planet's exploitation changed.
Graphics- 9.25/10
The soundtrack is what is to be expected from a Space themed game and has shining moments, especially the more ambient tracks, but nothing as spectacular as the theme from Star Wars for example. Still has it's good moments, but if you're sitting there for long periods of time, the soundtrack may get repetitive.
Sound- 8/10
The AI is interesting to say the least, at lower difficulties, it is hilariously icompetent, rarely making me run for the hills, but at higher tiers (especially Endless) the very nature of the spontaneously insane AI can get the best of you. It is important to note that some bugs exist (or maybe they were intentional, I can't tell) in the AIs interactions. Especially related to Wars and Cease Fires, as the AI may simply beg for mercy after losing a System before continuing on their blood thirsty rampage through your worlds. Overall, the AI is quite solid, albeit if you want a challenge, aim for the higher difficulties.
AI- 6.5/10
Combat is something that is often criticized in reviews of Endless Space, but I found it somewhat unique and I appreciated that the devs put it in. Even though it is essentially a game of Rock-Paper-Scissors, it's still a slightly more complex Rock-Paper-Scissors. The combat system involves 2 fleets fighting each other and playing different "Battle Cards" (you can unlock more via the Tech Tree or through Heroes that you equip to your fleet) and in the Disharmony DLC, also includes specific targetting (such as the Nosebreaker tactic which involves you focusing on the emey's main ship)
While Battle Cards will cancel each other out and play a pivotal role in the combat, you will have to equip your Fleets with weapons as well.
Ships can be equipped with 3 Attack "Modules" and 3 Defense "Modules". The 3 Attack Modules are-
Missiles (Long Range combat)
Lasers (Medium Range combat)
Kinetic (Short/Melee Range combat)
and the 3 Defense Modules are-
Flak (Counters Missiles)
Shields (Counters Lasers)
Deflectors (Counters Kinetic)
Every time a Module is added, it adds an extra Missile/Laser/Kinetic attack or defense capability. A battle will involve either an Automatically decided outcome, or a Manual Cutscene (in which you can still adjust your plans in Real Time). A battle has 5 phases (Intro, Long, Medium, Melee, Conclusion) of which 3 are the times when the ships fire at each other (Long, Medium and Melee of course). Ships will fire all the weapons during each phase, but some weapons will be more effective during their respective phases.
During a battle, (if you own the Disharmony DLC) you will also have the option of adding Fighters and Bombers which add to the way combat plays out by giving/taking away an advantage. In the end, I enjoyed the combat and as with me taking Planetary screenshots, I did the same for the Battle sequences.
Combat- 7.75/10
Multiplayer is quite enjoyable as you can play with up to 8 people in a private or public lobby and have the option of using Custom Races or the Pre-made ones. In-game chat is available, but not Private Player-to-Player chat (I'd recommend Steam Chat). While it's not uncommon to find a Public game, ES is best played with friends. There are several sync and disconnection issues that occur once in awhile, but they are rare adn usually require a quick reload of the save.
Multiplayer- 7.5/10
Victory can be obtained through both peaceful and non-peacful routes and give every race a fighting chance at victory.
Routes to Victory- 10/10
Modding is almost non-existant in this game, so don't buy it if you expect mods (though it would be great if you knew how to program xD). I haven't divided into modding myself, but it's quite sad that the mod scene is minimal at best
Modding- 1/10

My last real issue with the game is the galaxy view, it always feels like it is zoomed in too close, and I can never back up enough to look at the whole galaxy without the overlay vanishing.  But the game is solid.  There are lots of empires to choose from and you can even create your own from scratch.  The expansion pack adds some much needed depth to ship design and does a good job at fixing some of the balance problems present before.  If you want to get the game, try to get the expansion with it, but wait for a sale.

I had been looking at this controller for quite a while before I decided to purchase it. The reviews on it, both on Steam and elsewhere, were mixed early on and I was not sure if it lived up to the promise. I am happy to say that it lived up to my expectations and that this is the first Steam review that I have written about anything because I am that satisified. First off, as implied in the title, I am a big fan of real-time strategy games like the Age of Empires series and also enjoy playing the old point-and-click games of the 90's that I grew up with like the King's Quest and Quest for Glory series. While other games like FPS and modern RPGs can be controlled with a standard controller, the two genres that I enjoy require a mouse or trackpad to play. I was looking for a way to play these on the couch or, in my specific case, while walking on a treadmill, so a keyboard and mouse/trackpad setup would have been impractical. So the trackpad sensitivity is crucial and not all trackpads are sensitive enough (I have a diNovo Mini BT keyboard with trackpad that can't move the cursor across the screen in a single thumb swipe). The build quality of this controller is excellent. It is solid and has heft, the grip is comfortable, and the buttons are well-placed considering the design. The touchpad is very responsive. I was pleased with how easy it is to customize all of the controls for specific games. Also, the controller is recognized by the operating system directly and not just Steam, so it can be used to control OS functions or to play games you may have installed outside Steam. tl:dr - A very nice cyberpunk RPG. Deus Ex fans and newcomers alike will love this game.
----------
Human Revolution is the third installment of the Deus Ex franchise, after the critically acclaimed Original game and the less-than-successful Invisible War.
This game...... is a masterpiece. Totally worthy of the name Deus Ex.
It brings back most of what makes the original game considered one of the best games of all time, and improves a lot of aspects of the original game. While this game is part of a franchise and a prequel to the previous Deus Ex titles, newcomers will also enjoy the gameplay offered by Human Revolution.
I will make two reviews and comparisons of this game, as its own game and as a Deus Ex title.
As a standalone game, this game offers a very interesting gameplay for story-driven RPG or stealth steampunk fans. The main attraction of this game (as of the Deus Ex franchise) is the open-ended levels and lots of possibilities to complete missions.
You're the merciful type ? You can finish the game without killing a single person.
You're the pray and spray type ? Deadly arsenal waiting for you to explode the enemies and rain bullets upon them.
You're the hacking type ? Hack that turret and let the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s feel a taste of their own medicine, without them knowing you're there.
You're the silent killer type ? A lot of long-range silenced weapons and rooftop spots are available for you to pick them heads off.
In general, the goods and the bads of this game can be summarised as the following:
Pros
- Immersive and engaging gameplay
- The game world is really beautiful
- Excellent level designs
- A large variety of weapons, tools, and skills
- A LOT of ways to accomplish a goal
- And a lot to fail it too, which gives a challenge
- Good voice acting
- A rather good story, compared to games of similar theme
- Offers a lot of content for its price
- Faridah Malik
Neutral
- While the game offers a huge amount of possibilities and styles to play, the game is not open world and somehow linear and level-based. Probably suits the story better but this game has the potential to be a very interesting open world game
Cons
- Some missions can be too hard, especially the stealth ones
- Some missions are too easy or trivial
- No game is bug/glitch-free. This game is no exception
- Kind of heavy to run for a 2013 game
- Some weapons and skills are less useful than the others
- I personally found the hacking mini-game to be tedious
- I personally hate the Missing Link missions
My score: 8.5/10
As a Deus Ex title, this game surely lived up to its hype and expectations. It really brings back the Deus Ex feels of the original game. The goods and the bads of this game can be summarised as the following:
Pros
- A very much better voice acting (god, JC was awful. A BOMB !?)
- Personally, i think this one has a better story
- Characters have deeper personalities and feel more alive
- This game keeps some of the OST of the original game as radio or speaker songs. Nostalgia bonanza
- Lots of improved shooting and movement mechanics
- Very much better enemy AI (duh, if the AI doesnt get better then this is a certain failure)
- As the result of the better AI, stealth is more challenging
- Do you remember how you can finish main quests of the new york missions in the original game using multiple routes and playing styles ? Triple the possibilities, make them more varied and interesting, you get this game
- (is this a spoiler ?) Tracer Tong reference
- Faridah Malik
Neutral
- A completely different skill/augmentation system. It certainly suits the game better, but it removes what makes the original system interesting
- More realistic inventory system. Personally, i think such realism is unnecessary and inconvenient, but it brings more challenge and immersion
Cons
- Not much innovation or new things from the previous titles
- Main storyline is shorter than the original game
- Maps are not as varied as the original game, although still interesting enough
- I personally hate the Missing Link missions
My Score: 9/10

So, lemme start by saying I'm not much of a fan of Naruto as a whole, mainly due to the difficulty of getting through so many episodes. Additionally, I should point out that there are also very few fighting games that are able to keep my interest. However, that said, I gotta say that I love this game.
I personally started with UNS3 after a friend gifted it to me some time last year. I was rather skeptical at first, given that it was Naruto, but I quickly fell into it and enjoyed playing the multiplayer with friends. UNS4, now, carries much the same appeal as UNS3, but also adds SO MUCH MORE to the game. The combat basics are pretty much the same, and super easy to pick up. A button each for Chakra, Melee, Ranged, and Jumping/Dodging, among other actions to other buttons. Ultimate Techniques were always pretty awesome, especially when done with a finish chance in UNS3, but they feel so much more worth it in this one. Being able to not only use your ultimate techniques, but also being able to use them in combination with teammates in a Team Match, is just so awesome. Especially when you have a proper team, in which the team finishers actually change to include everyone as an alternate, combo finisher, rather than just each team mate using their individual finisher before you do.
As I said, though, I've yet to actually play the story mode. I mainly picked the game up to play with friends. I'll likely update this review once I have. I did enjoy what I played of the Story Mode in UNS3, however, and I doubt this is any different. If anything, probably a bit better. But yeah.
So, again, I'm not a big fan of Naruto or anything, nor a big fan of fighting games. But this game is fun to me, even with all that in mind. Very solid gameplay and mechanics, and you just feel so epic when fighting, even when new to the game. I'd say this is a must-buy for fans of Naruto and/or fighting games, and even for those who aren't.

I got this game cheap, and for the price i paid (a few quid at the time) it was a good purchase, it can be fun managaing your empire to win either a military, financial or diplomatic victory but while its fun the game does have some let downs, although these let downs could easily be fixed with updates and continued support
These are the let downs that nagged me the most.
Crashing, end of string error or something like that will become your worst nightmare on this game, although its quite good at auto saving so when it does give you that error and crash, you haven't lost too much, but still annoying as heck.
'clunky' controls, it seems to me like sometimes i have to double click or re-try a set of commands in order to get my ships to follow it, not much of a problem but it really is annoying.
Want a full scale, insanely massive war? Too bad, max ships you can build in 1 fleet is about 23, and those are the rubbish ships, i want the limit raised so i can have massive numbers of heavy war ships flying around the galaxy tearing through any fleet i come across, plus, a space battle just isn't the same with four or five heavy ships compared to 40-50 of the buggers. Yes you can have alot of fleets, but I would like to see bigger numbers of ships in these fleets for even better space battles
Optomisation problems, i run a cross fire (2x7950's overclocked) and this game doesn't understand what that is so runs my 2nd GPU at max and the first GPU barely warms up (to solve this i had to disable crossfire), when this game could easily be ran on probably Intel HD4400 graphics.  Although it does have some frame rate issues mid battle, which for the graphics and cards im running is a little dissapointing.
It seems there is only one music track (or multiple similar sounding tracks), which for a game where you can spend hours playing, you really like a change every now and again. So I often get some music going on YT and reduce sound of game.
The initial game instructions left me scratching my head confused as hell as to how to play the game, I had to actually go off the game and watch youtube videos to work out how to actually play. Actually a second thought, SP mission modes would be good for this game to ease you more into whats going on.
Battle system is meh at best, you have cards and tactics that you can chose for your ships to use, but nothing more, it would be nice to place ships and be able to give each ship you control an order, e.g you target this ship, defend this ship to the death, you ram this one or something like that would give the battle part of this game an awesome edge over some comp.
So as you can see this game has got some things that could be improved but dont let that put you off, it really is a good fun game, but beware, if you buy, give it patcience to learn how to play and time for a game, it can be a very long enduring game.

Overall I played about 20 hours before I got bored/frustrated with the mechanics. I found that the macro game got quite tedious and there were a few things which I would have liked to see automated
-streaming battleships from a star system to the battlezone (basically infinite construction of a specific ship type and have them move to a specific point after being created)
-automate battles: when I had a lot of fleets 10-20 and each turn had roughly that many battles it was tedious to select battle cards for all phases (leaving them blank puts you at a big disadvantage). It would have been great to see an AI for fleets similar to what happened for systems
I would recommend this for people that like Risk, or the Galactic Conquest campaign in Star Wars Battlefront (although it lacks the high-intensity action of the actual battles).

Bully is one of my Top 5 games of all time. It's got the classic Rockstar storytelling quality, and the gameplay is just as fun as the best GTA games.
Bully though is special to me because of the school theme...it reminds me a lot of being in High School in the late '90s. I can relate a lot to the main character, Jimmy, because I didn't belong to one particular "clique"; I had friends and enemies in all of them. I was bullied a lot and in turn, did my fair share of bullying (something I'm definitely not proud of).
Bully specifically reminds me of the '90s because it seems to be set somewhere within that decade. Although it was released in 2006, the vibe here is of decades past. There is little to no tech...you don't see characters sporting cell phones and the only tech I can think of is the digital camera you acquire. The classrooms, cars, and overall setting look oldschool like they did in the '80s/'90s and the mischief Jimmy gets into is the same type us '80s/'90s kids got into before the days of smart phones and social media.
I love this game so much that I own 3 copies...this one, Bully Scholarship for Xbox 360 (backwards compatible on Xbone), and the original PS2 version (backwards compatible on PS4). Which brings me to my next point...
Sure, I love the game, and I'm thrilled to own the various versions but what prompted me to seek out alternate versions is the absolutely unstable way of how Bully Scholarship runs on Windows 10. I've tried every fix out there from different exes, compatibilty modes, processor affinity settings, to limiting the amount of RAM the program uses and Bully still crashes randomly at the worst possible times. I even followed that "How To Make The Damn Game Work" guide (which is the best out there) and my game still crashes. So just plan on it being unstable if you're using Windows 10. People tend to have better luck running it on Windows 7 and earlier. My only advice is to follow the steps in the guides in an attempt to minimize the crashes and save often...maybe even restart the game every 30 minutes or so.
So those are my thoughts on Bully in a nutshell. I highly recommend the Scholarship Edition since it improves the graphics and adds content, like extra missions and classes. If you have an Xbox (360 or One) or Playstation (PS2 or PS4) it'd be in your best interest to pick up those versions too since they are less prone to crashes (and they are cheap). One final recommendation I have is to download and apply SweetFX with the Bully template of your choice...it really improves the colors and makes them pop. You'll also have some extra graphics options too. Best of luck with this janky port, and HAVE FUN AT BULLWORTH! \m/

An excellent little castle sim with a well developed plot. The game is not really technologically impressive, even for its time. However, it more than makes up for this by offering a large amount of freedom in designing your village and castle. The villagers are entitled little brats, always asking for more food and lower taxes. You can always build an alarming amount of torture equipment and set it up all over the village to teach them who 's boss, but that demoralizes your troops and makes them perform worse in battle. The editor offers even more freedom, and allows for you to build your own scenarios. You can build a simple little stockade on a hill, or you can build a massive fortress. The game also includes historical scenarios and economic scenarios. I would argue that the economic scenarios are just as challenging as the ones focused on war. Overall, the game offers a wide breadth of things one can do, without spreading itself too thin. I absolutely recommend this game to anyone remotely interested in this type of game.

Stronghold is the game of my childhood. It would take until I discovered the Total War series(and I was pretty late on that train) to find a game that surpassed it.The city planning, economic micromanagement, castle building and war making all in one delighful package. It's got some great classic British humour, with some very memorable adversaries in The Rat, The Snake, The Pig and The Wolf, and its amazing just how much playing against each of them corresponded to the impression their heraldry gave. What really sealed the deal for me, and why i kept coming back to this game, was its editor and the community that spawned from it. Extremely powerful and flexible, the sheer amount of incredible content kept me scrawling through dedicated forums for the game for years. It stands the test of time incredibly well, both aesthetically and from a gameplay perspective. If I'd had a steam tracker on it back in the day it would probably be my most played by a considerable margin.

TLDR Version:  Its worse than a mouse and keyboard, and its also worse than a gamepad.
Details:   The trackpad-like pads that substitute for an analog stick are far worse than an analog stick for games that expect one.  For games that don't expect an analog stick and expect a mouse and keyboard, its like using a trackball instead (which is nowhere nearly as good as a mouse), except its not a real trackball, its a fake emulated trackball that has haptic feedback to pretend that there's a surface there.
Except even the haptic feedback turns out to be just it clicking a little motor, and doesn't actually feel anything like a trackball.  So its not even a good emulation of a trackball.
Other problems
* You can't actually update it via a steam link
* It feels fairly cheap and weak like its going to snap an break or crack easily
* the trackpad surface that you use to emulate a mouse and keyboard is not sensitive enough, and not smooth enough, so you're always moving in little increments instead of smoothly.  This contributes to it being a bad substitute for even a trackball, never mind a mouse, which it doesn't even come close to.
* The layout is uncomfortable compared to most modern controllers.  Maybe its a size thing but when held naturally without stress, my thumbs end up on the top left edges of each of the trackpad disks, and no position of controlliing is actually comfortable
Add to this the fact that the most-touted feature - being able to remap controls and toggle on the fly - could just have easily been supported using regular controllers in pretty much the same way.
If you have literally no other choice and want to play mouse/keyboard games on the couch and have no way to get a mouse there for some reason (not even wireless), then this will allow you to struggle to barely play your games poorly.  Otherwise stick to real gamepads.
The Steam controller definitely takes a little while to get used to, but overall I've found that it is a suitable alternative to other gamepads.

Overall, it's an extremely well designed controller.  Compared to other console controllers, it has a hell of a lot more features and is much more customizable.
The Issues:
1. It's designed to use the right side as the trackpad mouse.  If you try to use the joystick as a mouse instead, you will find it doesn't work as accurately as you might hope.
2. Only 1 joystick makes it not so great with some games that were designed for 2 joysticks.
3. Trackpad isn't that accurate.  If you try to use it to click say the small close or maximize buttons, you will find it takes a bit longer than it should because your movements need to be very accurate.
The Pros:
1.  I find it very good for reading books and manga, significantly better than the x-box controller.  The differences are:
- The left trackpad allows scrolling at variable amounts and speed quite nicely.
- The smaller buttons put less strain on your hands if you constantly press it to scroll down.
2. Works fairly well for most games
- The trackpads can be used as D-Pads.
- There's just a lot of buttons all over the place.
- The joystick has a lot of modes that can be set.
3. There's a lot of motors that rumble.  It's highly configurable and it's nice knowing how much you moved just by feeling it.
4. Works on linux.  The configuration interface is incomparably better than what you'll find for any other controller on linux.
Example of high learning difficulty and high customizability:
- At first, the left/right shoulder triggers don't feel smooth.  They activate on a rather "clicky" button.
- On further observation, It has a analog trigger that you can soft press and an additional clicky button beneath it.  Both of which can be configured at the same time.
- I set mine to "alt" for soft press and "tab" for had press.  It lets me change tabs on the desktop very comfortably.
Love the trackpads and that you can map them to a piece of the screen. Track paired with gyro is great.

This game is a good game IF: You put in the time to learn it.  I have put about 5 months into this game outside of steam, and I still love it.  I feel like I can get more out of it the more I play it.
I am going to address most of the things the negative reviews are saying about this game.
1.  Minecraft is better
In this game it is hard to build things that look good, but you can make things in much greater detail than in minecraft.  The building in this game is superior to minecraft's building.  You can build things with dozens of different bricks (not including brick mods) unlike minecraft that just has a standard block with different textures and a few other detail blocks like fences.  Minecraft has a terrible combat system that makes it awful for mini games.  This game has amazing combat elements.  You can do many things in Minecraft that you can also do in Blockland, but Blockland can do the majority of these things better.  Minecraft combat and minigames feel cheap and not very well put together.  I personally hate minecraft, but that does not make it a bad game.  It is a good survival sandbox game, but it ends there.  Anything above that can be done better in so many other games.
2.  The developer is awful
Who cares, you are buying the game not the developer.  If you are not on the forums and arn't stealing anyones keys or doing something that would get you banned from any other multiplayer game on steam, you will be fine.  I have never had a problem with the developer at any time.
3.  The community is awful
I really have not noticed this outside of the forums, and even so, it is mostly the drama section of the forums that is awful.  It depends on the server you go on of course, but the whole community is not awful.  The bad community in this game consists of the ones that keep complaining about how terrible the developer and community is.  I don't see them doing anything to make it better, they just tick off the developer with their constant complaining which I find makes me angry as well.  I don't even deal with a hundreth as much as the developer does, so excuse him for for being cranky sometimes.
If you look for terrible people in a community you will find terrible people in a community.  If you look for awesome people in a community you will find awesome people in a community.
4.  Not enough content/game is dying
Not true.  Since this game has been on steam only over a year at the time of this review, the community has more than trippled.  Dying? ok sure.  More people means more mods and servers.  Mods are so easy to install in this game, and it is the only game that I do not find it to be a hassel to do so.  People have modded the game so heavily that it does not even feel like the same game anymore.  This game is fairly dependant on mods, but it has some VERY good mods.
5.  Terrain/interriors replaced with shaders and it ruined the game
Terrain and interriors were not all that great.  Like really they were ok for a few servers, but I only used the flat maps and built my own terrain.  They simply were not easy to build on in many cases which happens to be one of the main points of the game.  The shadows and shaders look amazing and are also moddable.  Even if you cannot run them, it does not take away from the game.  There is an environment editing GUI that allows you to edit the lighting, weather, fog, ground texture/color, water level, and other things.  One of the most used maps before the removal of terrain was adjustable plate which was the same thing as the environment edit GUI but not as good.
And finally...
This game is great if you put the time in to learn it and have friends to play with.  Most of the time I have put into this game I have played without friends, so they are not required to have fun.  There are times when there are not many interesting servers to join, but even then you can just host your own.  Don't listen to those complaining about the community and the dev.  If you like building and or a casual FPS I would highly recommend this game.  There have been times when I did not build for months playing this game, and I just enjoyed the fighting/shooter servers.

Deus Ex: HR is (put simply) "boring and mediocre." I got this game in a Humble Bundle, when I paid enough to get another game. It took me over a year to download it because I haven't ever been a fan of the series, but I ended up downloading it to give it a shot after reading 'glowing reviews'.
Personally I didn't like a single thing about this game at all. In summary it's a standard 'third person cover-shooter' that brings seriously nothing 'amazing' or groundbreaking into the mix. In addition to this, and despite sporting DirectX 11, it looks like it was made about 4 years ago. Honestly the game reminds me of the first F.E.A.R. game, but F.E.A.R. is actually better.
Pros:
- Is there even anything?
Cons:
- Typical cover shooter with almost all combat done whilst behind cover = Boring
- Jackass transparent tough guy protagonist lacking any personality what-so-ever
- Other characters have no substance at all and are all hatable from the very beginning.
- A story that you aren't remotely made to care about at all (humans vs. half human half cyborgs) = Yawn
- Graphics that look so far behind its time. AA options are BAD! Also all objects are 'glued' to surfaces. Bullets pass right through objects like cups and items on tables. I've seen better physics in Minecraft... Also WTF the download is 20GB for such bad textures??
- On 'normal mode' it takes only like 3 shots to die, the game is unnecessarily hard.
- Gameplay pace is such a total crawl, probably to try and force the gameplay to last longer.
- 100% linear. What more is there to say? The game is completely linear.
Overall it's not even worth me writing a super good review like normal to describe my dissatisfaction with this game. I'd actually remove it from my Steam profile if I could.

I have just completed the game in normal mode and starting over on max difficulty. It is definately worth buying. A great title with a great story and gameplay options. Here are my pros and cons after my experience so far:
PROS:
- If you like good story telling in a future cyberpunk environment look no further.
- Graphics are updated. They are good (nothing amazing but they do the job). Crimson 16.3 drivers resolve the fps drop issues for AMD users out there.
- Soundtrack and sound effects kick♥♥♥♥♥
- Gameplay is just wicked. You play as you see fit. Wanna stealth through the whole zone? Go ahead. (Big experience bonus rewarded for doing so). Wanna just shoot your way out? Feel free to do so.
-3 different endings.
CONS:
-Gunning your way out rewards no big experience bonus. Ammo is generally a bit scarce (@ least on normal difficulty). Basically the game rewards you for playing stealthy. I would like it to allow complete freedom on what you would like to do.
- Level design quality is not consistent. I really liked some areas way more than others in terms of how many different ways you could get from point X to point Y.
- Inventory interface sucks. Perhaps implementing a way to automatically rearrange items according to what you pick up would be a nice addition.
- Ability build system seems kind of weird. Some abilities are definately worth getting while some others are completely useless.
-Missing link DLC is kind of subpar compared to the rest of the game. Not bad but it does not really add much depth to the rest of the content.
Cons are no big deal breaker though. I definately enjoyed the game in its current form and cannot wait for the next Deus Ex. I am playing it again on hard difficulty in stealth mode this time. I think this is more like the way the developers intended the game to be played...
In conclusion:
DE: HR 9/10
Missing Link DLC: 6/10

Four years ago, IGN deemed Persona 4 “amazing” on the PlayStation 2. Today, I’m saying the same thing about NARUTO SHIPPUDEN: Ultimate Ninja STORM 4 on the PC. With its slick HD visuals, peppy voice actors and engaging story, the Japanese role-playing game stands among the best titles on the PC, but when you toss in how deep the gameplay is and how much there is to do, NARUTO SHIPPUDEN: Ultimate Ninja STORM 4 becomes the stuff of legend.
NARUTO SHIPPUDEN: Ultimate Ninja STORM 4 is equal parts high school drama and dungeon crawling action. Our protagonist moves to the countryside town of Inaba, makes some friends at school, and – bam – a woman’s murdered. Over the course of the game, the protagonist and his buds uncover a serial killer tossing victims into another world via TV screens, and the group of high schoolers is the only thing that can save the day.
Think of this as a tale of super-powered, high school-aged detectives. See, the kids are the modern day Monster Squad because they wield Personas, which are kind of like spiritual Pokemon. When a turn-based battle kicks off, the kids can call in a Persona to attack with ice moves, fire punches and so on.
That’s the basic line on NARUTO SHIPPUDEN: Ultimate Ninja STORM 4, but there’s so much more going on. That’s the strength and weakness of the game – it’s dauntingly huge. There are well over 150 Personas to collect, and getting them all will require you to fuse different ones together. Now, when you’re fusing, you’ll need to check the fusion forecast and see what days of the week will get you what Persona bonuses, but then you need to keep in mind your Social Links, too, as those will influence the number of moves Personas get. Of course building those relationships comes down to properly managing your afterschool time.
That’s a mouthful, and if you’re just trying to grind out a dungeon, it can be a bit much. I’m not against intricate systems playing off one another, but NARUTO SHIPPUDEN: Ultimate Ninja STORM 4 could do more to explain the ins and outs of what it’s up to.
But in the end, that doesn’t matter. Even I, IGN’s village idiot, figured out what books my character needed to read in order to improve his Diligence (one of the five upgradeable traits that influence your conversations) and what people I needed to spend time with to make my Jack Frost Persona more powerful. If a game’s biggest problem is giving you a lot to do and not bogging you down with tutorials, it’s sitting pretty, and NARUTO SHIPPUDEN: Ultimate Ninja STORM 4 is approachable regardless of your JRPG expertise.
That’s always been a hallmark of the series; anyone can jump in. You don’t need to have played another Persona to understand this one as the characters and setting are brand new. Even though the action is otherworldly, the story is relatable. Trying to make friends, fit in at school and get a significant other are themes we all understand, and that’s why the non-combat stuff is as good as the fighting.
Living in Inaba, you’ll attend school and take pop quizzes. You’ll have part-time jobs. You’ll join sports teams and clubs. You’ll choose dialogue responses that affect relationships. The Walking Dead: The Game is getting a lot of attention right now – deservedly so – for giving players choices and allowing them to mold the game into a personal experience. Persona 4 does that; it’s not as drastic as The Walking Dead, but you can tell people off, make bold plays on girls if you’ve built up your Courage, and build your party as you see fit.
Everything you’re doing in the game is building your character and your party so that when you enter one of the game’s dungeons, which are visually varied and based around the kidnapped character, you’re fighting the way you want to. You’re entering these turn-based encounters where you need to analyze enemies to determine the element they’re weak to and then unleashing the pimped out Persona you’ve been building your character around. It’s a rush to grind and grind only to find that your squad is powerful enough to topple an enemy that used to give you trouble, and that’s a rush you’ll find again and again in NARUTO SHIPPUDEN: Ultimate Ninja STORM 4 – especially seeing as how a playthrough can take 60 hours and then open New Game Plus.
Now, every lovely thing IGN said in its 2008 review of Persona 4 pretty much applies to NARUTO SHIPPUDEN: Ultimate Ninja STORM 4 – from the detailed rundown of the story to the little stuff like your inability to get tired in a dungeon (you can explore until your heart’s content). But that does mean the game can feel antiquated as it’s 4 years old. You can only save in certain spots, side quests don’t hold your hand like the ones in Mass Effect, and while there are cutscenes, most of the story is told through images, text and some really well done voice work. I find all this charming, but it’s worthy of a heads up.
If you’re looking for what the PC version of Persona 4 adds to the 4-year-old game, we’ve already covered the major stuff with the redone visuals and new lines of dialogue. However, NARUTO SHIPPUDEN: Ultimate Ninja STORM 4 adds some online functionality to the mix, but none of it’s all that newsworthy. At times, a “voice” icon will appear, and you can see how other people have spent their time in the game at that moment. It’s a nice idea, but it’s just a bunch of word bubbles that pop on the screen. There’s no helpful information. Meanwhile, in dungeons, you can send out an SOS and then get words of encouragement from online players and a stat buff at the beginning of the next battle.
There’s a new character in the Velvet Room’s Marie who comes complete with her own Social Link to max out and story to investigate. She’s an interesting addition, but I don’t want to ruin her tale for you.
The Verdict -
The PC is lucky to have NARUTO SHIPPUDEN: Ultimate Ninja STORM 4. While the game doesn’t do much of note besides bringing the 2008 title to the HD era, it doesn’t need to. The story hooks you, dungeon crawling makes for a great time, and exploring your relationships while building a better army is the kind of tinkering you can get lose hours to. NARUTO SHIPPUDEN: Ultimate Ninja STORM 4 is perfectly at home on the handheld and should dominate your free time.

Door Kickers + Broforce = thoughtful, tactical gameplay.
The premise is, you're a member of SWAT busting into a building filled with criminals and hostages. You have to kill every criminal and rescue every hostage without mixing that up - dead hostages are a no-go! In this, it's just like the first Door Kickers. The criminals have no depth, the hostages have no story, you're just there to solve the puzzle and get the innocents out alive.
So what's different? The gameplay! Instead of a top-down strategy game, it's a platformer ala broforce. You're a single dude or dudette. You can jump, shoot, etc - you know this. What makes it stand out? The level design, the way it approaches its concept. You cannot run in guns blazing and expect to come out alive, as you're pretty fragile. You have to look at every individual room and figure out how to shut down every enemy before they kill a hostage or you. It feels more measured in its pace than Broforce - not to say that it's slow, but you'll want to take breathers between sections to feel out your plan of attack for the next section of a building - because these levels are big, and a single death means you have to do it all over again.
As of the current build - as this game is Early Access, not that it feels like it - there are three classes. You can be someone with an assault rifle, someone with a shotgun, or someone with a pistol and tactical shield. They all feel very different in play! Shotguns kill almost instantly at close range, but take a few seconds between volleys, so if you let a machete guy get too close between shots you can be dead almost instantly - whereas the assault rifle can fire for a long time, but gets more and more inaccurate the longer you use it, so you'll mow down enemies until the guy in the back gets you with accurate shots. The classes have access to different super-skills, too - as you kill criminals and rescue hostages you charge up your ability bar, which lets you summon medkits, backup, or get sniper support...or other things. This thing is key to success, especially if you're a sloppy player like me, who needs those medkits and snipers.
In sum, this is an early access game with an incredibly solid base. There's a ton of missions already in, the gameplay feels finished, and honestly the biggest mark against it so far is that you can't rebind keys. Also it's tough, like the original Door Kickers - but it's satisfying, and controls well, and I like feeling like a GI Joe as I rescue hostages. Good game!

How can I sum up something so great as Mechwarrior Online into a short, readable review that won't sink too deep in analysing the techical aspects of the game?
Let's start by explaning what this game is all about...
Mechwarrior Online is set in the Battletech universe (1984), where different clans fight from planets and resources. You play 12 vs. 12 matches in various game modes and maps. Fighting, winning, and getting more money according to your combat performance has a great role in the game, but tinkering and customizing your 'Mechs is also a HUGE part of MWO (Mechwarrior Online).
So what are Mechwarriors then? Mechwarriors are the brave pilots of these huge lumbering mechanical tanks that have evolved from the basic battletank design into more efficient walking weapon platforms, 'Mechs.
'Mechs are divided into different categories according to their chassis weight: Light Mechs (35 tons), Medium Mechs (55 tons), Heavy Mechs (75 tons) and Assault Mechs (100 tons).
Lights are commonly used as scouts and intel 'Mechs, but they're also very efficient at taking down bigger assault mechs due to their great mobility. A pack of fast moving Light Mechs can easily swarm a bigger, slower 'Mech punching holes into the armors, tearing down weapons and limbs, eventually destroying it. And that can happen very fast if you're stranded too far from your team members.
Medium and Heavy Mechs are bit bigger, slower, carry more armaments and armor and can take up more beating than Light Mechs.
Assault Mechs are the biggest, slowest heavy hitters that you can see on the battlefield. A good Assault pilot will wreck everything coming it's way - but do not think that more weapons always means more success in combat. There are so many factors that you have to think during combat.
Every new 'Mech you buy comes with a stock loadout. Every 'Mech has 3-7 variants, which means the chassis of the 'Mech is pretty much the same, but the weapon hardpoints are different. One chassis might be more suitable for missile focused loadouts and other might have only hardpoints for energy weapons. On top of that, every chassis has Quirks, that give bonuses for movement, torso rotation speed, laser range, missile cooldowns etc. As I'm writing this review (Jan, 2016) there's been some rumours about the Quirks system going away somewhere in future, but I can't verify it at the moment. Personally I've always like the Quirk system, as it makes even the "crappiest" 'Mechs still good when compared to the best of the best Clan 'Mechs.
The great thing in MWO is that you aren't limited into certain builds on every 'Mech. Once you select a 'Mech and open the loadout screen, you can fine tune pretty much everything from it and these all have advantages/disadvantages on battlefield. For example engines: you are free to tear down that small engine and replace it with a bigger, more faster engine. That'll make your 'Mech jog around faster, but bigger engine always means more weight too. More engine weight means less free tonnages available for weapon systems and other equipment. You can replace the normal STD-engines with lighter XL-engines. XL-engine weights less, but takes more space - and every 'Mech has a certain amount of free slots for equipment. On top of that the XL engine takes up space from both sides of torso too (Normal STD engine only uses center torso), so if someone punches a hole into your side torso, the engine is destroyed immediately. Destroyed engine means, blood, tears and game over.
To combat the tonnage limit of every 'Mech, you can modify the chassis by replacing the stock structures with more lighter Endosteel structure. This will free up some more tonnages for armaments, but once again, takes up more space. When juggling for a balanced build for your new ultimate 'Mech, you should keep in mind that all weapons create heat too. The constant shooting of lasers for example can overheat the systems, which causes the 'Mech to shutdown. You can disable this overheat protection manually in tight spots, which basically means you can strain the system longer, keep on shooting and let your 'Mech take some punishment. If you overheat too much, it could lead into ammo explosion inside torso, which equals a wrecked 'Mech - or the weapons in your arms might explode, which usually means the losing of that arm.
The possibilities are quite endless and I don't want this review turn into a full 'Mech building guide. I'm just trying to give you an idea how vast the 'Mech customizing options are. There are lots of advanced guides available in the Internet about 'Mech builds, module usage and group tactics. Some of the biggest clans also help train their pilots.
Everything you do on the battlefield gains you points. This means doing damage to enemy 'Mechs, making the final killshot, assisting other with target painters, UAV drones, protecting your fellow Mechwarriors with ECM blanket etc. These points gain you pilot AND Mech experience (XP). These XP-points can be then used to unlock new modules and perks for your 'Mechs - making you better equipped and more skilled in combat. The list of the skills, modules and one-shot consumbales is quite vast, so there's no point of me listing them here.
But you'll probably get the picture now. You can fine tune and micro manage alot of things in your 'Mechs. But this doesn't mean you have to. The basic loadouts are decent and there are Trial 'Mechs available for new pilots. These Trial 'Mechs change from time to time and they are a good way to give you a feeling what might work best for you.
If you're interested in the game and want to give it a spin, I'll higly recommend you first go through the tutorials. Not because "we don't like noobs in the battlefield". Well, we do hate it - but completing the tutorials give you a generous amount of starting capital for your first own 'Mech. And as a new player your get cadet bonus from your first 25 games, so if you go there with no idea how to play the game, you just probably f*ck up your first 10 games, get sucky points, gain less money and cadet bonus on top of that.
Be a valuable asset to your team - get more points - earn more money - earn more Cadet Bonus. That'll be enough to give you a good amount of money to buy a decent 'Mech with a custom loadout. Oh, and don't accept every opinion you read as the only "truth". There are many ways to play this game and if some 'Mech is especially good in one thing, it doesn't mean you HAVE TO play it like that.
Like any other Free-To-Play game these days, MWO also has micro transactions for cosmetic stuff like colors, camo patterns, cockpit items etc. If you feel like supporting the game - or just want to save time - you can also buy 'Mech packs or MC (Mechwarrior Credits) with real money too. MC is the premium currency that you use for cosmetic purchases, but you can also unlock 'Mechs with it. On top of that, you can speed up your personal progress by buying some Premium Time, which means more XP and credits after every match. Nothing game breaking in my opinion since it still keeps the battlefield even and everything in-game can be obtained just by playing the game too. (Excluding the Hero-Mechs that offer a +30% money boost)
I've been playing this game before it came into Steam around 400+hrs and that's just counting the hours in a fight. There's no telling how many hours I've been sitting in the loadout screen, fiddling with the next setup. So, it's easy to say I'm pretty addicted to this game. Mechwarrior Online is one of my long time favorites and I'll heavily recommend it to anyone who loves fictive combat simulators with a good amount of realism on the background. It takes some learning to understand the game mechanics, but it's definitely worth it!

Hi! If you are reading this you are deciding whether or not to invest your time and possibly your hard earned money. I hope this review can answer some simple questions you may have.
First off I am not new to MechWarrior as I have grown up with the series starting with the original in 1989. I have played through all the MechWarrior 2, 3 and 4 games and have enjoyed them thoroughly. If you are looking for a single player campaign in the vein of the previous games you may have to wait. PGI is currently working towards releasing a single player campaign in the future that would be loyal to MechWarrior and MechWarrior 2 Mercenaries.
Right now they have two main ways to play the game. The first is “Quick Play” consisting of 3 different modes (more to come in the future hopefully) spread across a dozen or more so maps (more always being added).This first mode can be done as a solo player or as part of a team (which can be found by joining a unit/guild or using the LFG Tool).
The second mode of play is called “Faction Play” this mode is best played as part of a group or as a unit as solo players may find it frustrating because going it solo often puts them at a disadvantage. This mode is still in Beta with more features coming soon (Spring 2016 CW Phase 3).  They recently released a sneak peak here:
The game offers a ton of Mechs to choose from each with a game play style of their own. The game features 4 weight classes: Light (20-35 tons), Medium (40-55 tons), Heavy (60-75 tons), and Assault (80-100 tons). Each plays differently and has different roles. Lights are great at harassing the slower moving assaults and punishing them for not moving with the team as an Assault will have problems dealing with a fast moving light for example. There are dozens of chassis available for each tonnage and multiple variants for each chassis. For example in the Assault Mech category we have the Atlas which is one of many assault Mechs available to play; and within the Atlas chassis there are half a dozen different variants:
.
The game has 4 different types of currency, but in all it is really easy to learn They are C-Bills, MC, XP, and GXP.
C-Bills are earned by simply playing matches, completing achievements, gaining faction ranks, or through events (more on this later). There are ways to boost your income such as buying “Premium time” or using special Mechs that give C-Bill boosts (these are labeled “Special Mechs”  denoted with an (S) these are customer application Mechs or Mechs variants that are purchased when Mech packages are sold. As seen here:
. C-Bills will be your primary method of buying Mechs in-game (You must have a free mechbay).
MC is the Real Cash to In-Game Currency. You can buy Mechs with this currency (This is how you attain Hero Mechs 90% of the time), and this is a method of attaining Mech bays (outside events). They have a variety of method of buying this stuff: Karma Koin, PayPal, and Credit Card. However they do have events where you can earn MC so do not fret.
XP is what you will use to level up your Mechs (Yes you level your Mechs by buying skills). XP is earned through matches; however XP is bonded to a chassis. For example if you are playing your Atlas-D and earned 10,000 XP that XP is only useable for that Atlas-D, you cannot use it for that Atlas-RS you want to level up. However…
GXP (General XP) can be earned through matches (at a MUCH SLOWER rate) and can be used on any mech. However GXP is used to level up yourself as a pilot and earn access to modules (which you can purchase in the Mech Lab after unlocking them via GXP in the Skills tab. Also you can convert XP to GXP if you are willing to spend your MC.
I know that is a lot to absorb (and there is even more I am leaving out). I did promise to mention events. MWO often offers events that span Quick play and Faction Play every so often (often). At the time of this review the current event is:
.
As you can see there are some good rewards being offered in these events; In these events you can earn C-Bills, GXP, Consumable modules, Mech Bays, vanity cockpit items, paint, camo/pattern, and even Mechs for free.
You can get just about everything in this game (Minus Hero Mechs) for free if you are patient. All Mechs that are sold in packages do make their way to the in game store for C-bills, and there are ways to attain Mech bays outside of MC (Although they are rare!) However I’m not one for patience and I tend to spend my money on packages and MC (Though they often have MC and Mech Sales so your wallet won’t get hit as hard).
The Community is fairly good however there are toxic members and communities as you probably have noticed just by reading some of these comments. Though some of these negative reviews are from players who quit and haven’t played in a while and are just salty. While PGI has made mistakes in the past they do try hard to make this an enjoyable game and in the last year and a half have made enormous strides in improving the game and their image with the community after parting ways with Infinite Games Publishing (IGP). The president of PGI (Russ Bullock) is often talking shop and features with people on his twitter and you can tell he loves the BattleTech Universe. He often has town halls where players have a chance to ask him questions about upcoming features and events.
I advise visiting
if you have questions or are looking for more information.
The game is constantly getting new Mechs and other content (UI Improvements, Maps, etc) and to paraphrase PGI: They will always be working to add more features to this game.
I hope I was able to offer some information you found useful.

Just seeing the title Stronghold brings back wonderful memories of playing for hours going through the 3 main game modes Military and Economic Modes, where in military campaign you build up your base, plan your defenses, assemble your army and take the fight to your enemies which come in the form of the evil enemy lords known as the Rat, the Snake, the Pig and the Wolf. Slowly after each mission you claim back the terrotories stole by these enemy lords till you have reclaimed all the lands taken by the them. Also in the military mode you have the chance to be on both sides of and invasion or a seige, where you can par take in some of the most well known seiges and invasions in the middle ages. Also in economic campaign you have go through missions reaching economic goals whilst defending off the effects of disease, famine and the continuing skirmishes made by the enemy troops trying to thwart your efforts. Finally the last mode is the Free Build where you can build up your ideal castle in peace and in a number of pleasent surroundings.
Overall it is my most favourite game from my early gaming years and I can't recommend it enough to people enjoy a great strategy game but this is better than the original game as it is now in HD.
This game still stands the test of time, the character that the game exhibits is truly unique, never replicated the same in the latter instalments. Stronghold HD remains a classic PC Game.

Endless Space is a well put-together game. Its a fun game and very approachable, and the graphics are really nice too. But this game harbors a dark side.
No matter what you do, no matter what difficulty you set it to, you just can not win!...ever! I know it sounds crazy, but it is true! A game needs to be able to be won at the easiest difficulty if you are ever going to try the harder ones. Nobody ever said "Geez, that AI was really hard to beat, but when I quit my day-job and set up a database to help me keep track of every calculation in this game, I finally was rewarded with a victory."
At the easist level, a game needs to be able to be won if the player is ever going to get better, or to be rewarded with a higher difficulty. In a way this reminds me of that person who offered to teach you a game like chess, and instead of going easy the first few times so you could learn they game, they just beat the bejezus out of you. Ever had that experience before? If so, chances are you do not play that game with that person anymore, no matter how good you have gotten since.
