A breath of fresh air in a stale gaming world.
The first Deus Ex was genre-defying landmark title along with the system shock series that tackled philosophical questions and gave players a unique freedom to play the game in any way they wanted. After a disappointing sequel, that I personally didn't find remotely as terrible as die-hard fans of the first one, the series became eerily quiet for a long time and it seemed like the times for such unique titles were over. Fortunately we were proven wrong and we finally got Deus Ex: Human Revolution. Fans were anxious if a new developer would be able to follow up on the first game's merits but luckily Eidos Montreal succeeded to create a game that outshines the original in many regards.
Deus Ex is a cyberpunk first person stealth RPG set in the not so distant future where human cybernetic augmentation has become commonplace. The lengthy game spends a lot of effort to acquaint you with all the different factions and takes you on an interesting journey that I want to spoil as little as possible, but the common themes are mortality, the basic nature of our human experience, ethics, transhumanism, religion and the power structures in the economic and political world we all take for granted now. The greatest strength of Human Revolution is that it doesn't force these themes on you, you are free to dive in as deep or as shallow as you wish, since most of the information is woven in organically with the highly detailed game world. The atmosphere is quite incredible. A plausible if slightly exaggerated version of the future created with a lot of thought that you don't see often. It's also one of the few games that actually deserves the cyberpunk label, unlike other titles that copy the genre tropes but don't adopt any of the basic ideas represented and manifested in the works of the pioneering William Gibson. Human Revolution deals a lot with moral grey areas, at the end of the plot full of intrigue and discovery not a single character is left untainted. Not bad for a storyline that basically begins as a remake of robocop.
If you are not that interested in the storyline there's plenty of gameplay to draw you in. You have an incredible freedom to explore the hub areas and play all the missions the way you want. You can stealth your way through missions and never be seen only knocking out select enemies (if at all) or just kill everyone in sight. There's a sizeable amount of augmentations to choose and everyone of them changes the basic nature of your play style (sometimes drastically) and opens different paths and methods. Multiple playtroughs are absolutely encouraged. You constantly make decisions that change how people react to you in the world. A moral choice system that doesn't stumble into the usual embarrassing and clumsy pitfall of having a bar that shows how black and white your affiliation is.
While not state of the art in the graphics department upon release I still consider it one of the best-looking titles around based solely on the strength of its incredible design. The yellow tint of the visuals might not be everyone's favourite but the sound design and music are pretty much flawless, although the score isn't as memorable as in the first game. A wonderful attention to detail creates a believable lived-in world that you would usually only find in movies such as Blade Runner.
Human Revolution is not without its flaws. The storyline while intriguing carries some baggage inherent in the Deus Ex series that was based a lot on TV shows like the X-Files although the sometimes borderline conspiracy theorist ideas are handled far less clumsily than in the original. The boss fights also seem a bit out of place. While the Director's Cut alleviates some of the problems by allowing strategies beyond shooting the bosses repeatedly in the face the encounters aren't as memorable as they could have been and feel strangely videogamy for lack of a better term and arena-esque in a game that usually makes you forget you are playing a game and handles its progression more organically. I have the feeling Eidos Montreal peaked at the Metal Gear Solid series a bit. The problem here is that that series while wonderful and superficially similar, rides a fine line between serious and masterfully cheesy over-the-top never taking itself too seriously and puts a lot of effort into acquainting us with the colourful bosses before we fight them. A totally different beast altogether. This is by no means a dealbreaker though.
The reason why I like this game so much despite a few flaws is that it feels like a game made by adults for adults. A rare occurence in the videogame industry that while increasingly accepted as a unique art-form often struggles to find an adult voice and is moving forward very slowly, especially when it comes to storytelling. Many modern titles while stunningly beautiful and expertly crafted resort to aping films too much, degrading the player to the backseat camera man and thus lose all impact. This is unfortunately to be expected in an era where all forms of creative expression, be it games, films, music, series etc. struggle for relevance and compete with other barely related media in the big blurry slurry of home entertainment instead of competing and evolving internally in their respective medium. Deus Ex 3 while not without its share of cutscenes (which are expertly handled) never forgets it's still a game and uses that medium's strength to tell a story, while simulatenously not using the medium videogame as an excuse to only tell a superficial story.

When it shines, it's a beauty, but when it stinks, it kills everything good about it.
I want to like this game. It has that "one more turn" factor. Visually it's well done, and the UI is pretty clever with most complex orders only a few mouse clicks away. But then you find reordering production queues to be unusually clumsy. Most of the game is like that. A few solid hits then a terrible miss. [Queues have been improved in a recent update]
The races are good, well designed and presented, each with their own strengths and each requiring a slightly different set of priorities to succed. But then the difficulty modifiers kick in and the whole race balance goes out the window. Enemy AIs get bonuses to production NOT intelligence and you fight races that can outperform what you could do with them.
Then the AI itself shows irreconcilable stupidity. If i could tolerate 6-7 dumb things the AI does per turn, it would do 10. All too often the AI fleets that could potentially beat you choose to flee (but waste your time, attack, or leave ships behind that blockade you), while i have had one completely unarmed and undefended fleet of invasion ships try to fight back (with tactics, not weapons ofc) and even somehow managed to flee with a few survivors. [AI stupidity has also been adressed with updates]
The AI can sometimes use tactics wisely and from what i saw has no knowledge of your own tactical choices, but the battles are a lottery decided far far ahead, back when you designed the ships. Some survive, some have no chance, and if your ships are very good, then AI will either allways retreat, or allways die, depending on whose territory you're fighting in. Sometimes the very outcome of a war or even game can hinge on the AI doing something remarkably stupid or you failing to understand some of the BASIC fundamental rules of the game. That... is beyond bad, that is awful.
The diplomacy model is one of the better i have seen. Most of it is really good, except of course the one part that kills it completely. It's all meaningless because ultimately your empire exists and therefore it would be better for a rival to take it all away from you. You're the weakest empire? Then die. Wait, you're strongest? Then die. You're in the middle, and a long term trading partner as well as supplier of strategic resources, benefits that far outweigh the problems caused by close borders (and you can see the exact numbers too)? Guess what? Today is the day none of that means anything. Prepare to set the relationship score to -200. And die.
Colonisation and expansion is arguably the strongest part of the game. Exploring the galaxy, triggering some halfhearted random events, scouting good spots for colonies. First contants. All good. But. The game actively penalises you for each and every system you own. Wheter you colonise it or capture it, just having a system increases the penalty higher and higher. Eventually it becomes high enough that it starts to hurt morale and that in turn drops production, research and cash flow. Yes, by colonising a system at a wrong moment, you can drop overall empire wide production by some 10-20%. Does that make any sense?
Yes, there are technologies that reduce the penalty, and yes, it's there to counterbalanc expansion but i am here to play a game, be emperor of space, not to oversee active game modifiers. They should be invisible and subtle, not hit me in the head. When i deliberatly skip average systems that are still well positioned, all just to avoid getting the expansion penalty down the road, i think i am playing a flawed game.
Combat is neither good nor bad except when it's completely illogical. Designing the ships properly takes some experience and knowledge and if you do a good job your fleet will usually serve you well and survive for a long time or you will produce enough replacements for losses to not matter much. The main problem with all the tactical options, counters, different ranges, weapon optimisations, support ships, repair capacity, fighter/bomber cover, is that you very often feel like you just can't take your ships and tell them to "$#%^&* go and kill the enemy!", the MOST BASIC OF PURPOSES for your fleet, but somehow it gets lost in the myriad different things you have to tweak before you can fight. Long story short, i know what i want, the game wont let me, or i have to obey some rule/design feature/balance mechanic.
So while it starts pretty well, and has enough to be fun for a while, it eventually becomes a chore to try to complete a game. The AI has too many choices to make and inevitably it makes poor decisions (compare to SOTS' very basic but lethal AI) and all the strengths of the game are drowned out by the weaknesses.
The best turn based space 4X games have already been made. Master of Orion 2 and Sword of the Stars 1. Maybe even Birth of the Federation, though i am biased about that one. Other games of the genre try to do things differently which is unfortunate because sometimes imitation is the wisest form of flattery. Case in point: Xenonauts. For ages developers tried to recreate the perfect succesor to XCOM - UFO Defense. UFO: Aftershock is 99% as good, and UFO: Alien Invasion is an extremly good remake (but still unfinished). A slew of other games missed the mark completely or admittedly used the old game as a springboard for a new experience. Then Xenonauts imitated the original and surprise, surprise, it hit the bullseye.
Ultimatly Endless Space isn't solid enough to satisfy demanding 4x players, and it isn't "mainstream" enough to captivate the casual audience. So it ends up in between. Better than most, but not good enough.
EDIT - 20 Dec. 2014
Some of the complaints i've ♥♥♥♥♥ed about have been adressed by several patches released since this review. Production queues and enemy retreat logic have been adressed. Better late than never? Or thumbs up for devs supporting their game well after release? Both pretty much, and the game can't be hurt by extra polish & fixes.
I will not change my verdict, but i will say it's still a game i would like to like. Probably more so than before with the recent updates.
If you're sitting on the fence know that you will probably enjoy exploring the game if you choose to buy it. Exploration and expansion are strong suits of Endless Space. It's just that ultimately i felt dissapointed with what i found, but have to admit it was fun exploring.

To Preface: I've been playing very consistently since the beginning of open beta, eons ago.  My actual experience is more than Steam hours suggest.
MWO, in its current development, is a solid and reasonably fleshed out shooter.  More specifically, it's a Mechwarrior game, meaning it's at least somewhat loyal to the Battletech universe.  It's fun to play, fun to plan out, and quite challenging as you progress through the Tiers (skill level system that tries to match you against similarily skilled players).
The good:
1. Lots of big robots of varying kinds, each with unique qualities, shapes, weapon options, and experience.
2. Quite a decent list of different locations/planets/terrains/environments to carry out a match in.
3. Decent selection of weapon types to suit different playstyles, ranges, loadout mixes, and flavour/interest.
4. The beginnings of an overarcing goal in the form of a galaxy map where you can expand/defend your chosen faction.
The bad:
1. Not a lot of gamemodes to play, and fairly limited variance between them.
2. No real reward/benefit to conquering planets on the Faction/galaxy map other than ego.
3. No missions or similar kinds of matches to make it feel like a real galaxy/war that you're fighting in.
In the end, MWO is a lot of fun to play - so right there I have to recommned it.  Everything is free, if you want, so you really don't have to invest any cash in it at all.
I find myself regularly logging in after a couple of years, and still having a good time.
I think MWO could really expand to the point of having a lot of depth - which would make it a really killer option.  In reality, though, it still feels a little bit incomplete/lacking.  The matches themselves are fun, but there doesn't seem to be a grander purpose - which I think would be valuable in a galactic game with a rich story background.
Worth checking out.  Stompy robots, my friends, with big guns.

The core game is more strategical than most shooters. Because it takes a while to kill someone and you can't easily reposition, the tactics behind your attacks are invaluable. There is strength in groups, because in this game there's no cheap one-shot kills. If someone shoots there will be plenty of time to react for the opponent, because you won't kill anyone with just one shot and going back behind cover takes getting that robot up to speed again. If the guy you shot has 5 friends you'll be shot back way harder. So attacking goes in groups, that way the odds won't be stacked against you. More people is more joy, because if you brought 8 friends along the enemy will have a lot worse of a time. Then of course there's flanking and attack routes to keep in mind, maybe sending 4 guys to flank can be an advantage etc., you get the gist. Shame there's a lot of pubnoobs who don't care for strategy.
The meta-game is building your mech, which is another collection of strategic decisions I won't go too much into depth on. The basic idea is that you can't have it all, you'll have to choose your strengths and weaknesses. The grind is more important. Basically free players can have 1 mech up to full power, if you want to max level another mech you'll have to buy space and get the mech you want 3 times over. Grinding up the money and premium currency for a second fully powered mech takes so incredibly long I'd actually say it's not possible. For all intents and purposes you get 1 max-level mech, you'll have to pay real money for more or settle for not-max-level-mechs. That sounds really bad, but keep in mind that not-max-level-mechs are pretty decent and usable.
Its a game when you run around in big stompy robots and shoot other bit stompy robots with big flashy lasers.

I started playing MWO back in Closed Beta and have played it consistently since that time. It has gone through a LOT of changes and is STILL undergoing changes (which isn't a bad thing). For me, it is still a lot of fun to play.
Is it perfect? Of course not. Few, if any games are perfect.
Is it Pay to Win?
Not at all. There is nothing you can purchase for real money that gives you any advantage over those who use ingame currency. It may give you the opportunity to play new mechs early, but other than that, no advantages at all. All the Weapons available in the game work the same no matter on what Mech they are equipped (now, Clan weapons work differently from Inner Sphere but they work the same across all Clan mechs). There are no "Gold Weapons" or "Gold Ammunition".
Why do mechs cost so much?
That is indeed a good question and one I wish they would explain myself! Personally, I feel they would be better off selling them for less money to sell more but I guess they figure their price point currently maximizes their profits. And they are a company out to make a profit (who isn't)! That said, every mech (other than Hero and Champion Mechs) are available to purchase at some point using ingame currency that you can earn while playing the game.
Hero Mechs? P2W!
While it is true those mechs are only available for real money, they aren't P2W mechs. They are just mechs with a special paint/camo, and offer a Cbill % Bonus to your earnings. Hero mechs will have a weapon loadout that is not available on any other current variant usually but then suffer from some other disadvantage (perhaps it can't carry as many weapons as the others). But, the key point here ... all weapons perform the same, regardless of the Mech on which they are installed. So a Medium Laser is the same across all the Inner Sphere Mechs.
Champion Mechs
Champion Mechs are exactly the same mech as their normal variant, just with a (C) designation and a boost to your Experience earnings.
Trial Mechs
These are what you will start with if you do not purchase any mechs with real money. They are free for you to use. You just cannot modify their loadouts whatsoever. You don't own them but you can play them to earn Cbills to purchase your own mechs.
Learning Curve
MWO is going to be wildly different from most other FPS type games. It is supposed to be a Mech Simulator, whatever they mean by that. Anyway, there will be a pretty steep learning curve for this game! To me, it was worth it and makes it so much more fun and involved. You have to learn how to Torso Twist to spread damage across your mech to increase your survivability. What this means is the upper half of your body can turn independently from your legs. You can be running one way and facing another (the degree of twist is dependent on the mech...some can turn more than others). Mastering the ability to Twist your Torso independent of your legs is a MUST.
Aiming Reticles. You will likely have 2 sets of reticules. Your Arms can also move somewhat independently of your torso (depends on Mech) to some degree. The small Circle reticule is where your Arm mounted weapons will fire while the + reticule is where your torso mounted weapons will fire. Oh, the OTHER thing you have to keep in mind is WHERE on your mech these weapons are mounted as far as height goes. While your Reticule may not appear to be obstructed by terrain, low-mounted weapons may not fire over the hill you are standing behind (for example).
Heat Management
This is going to be one of your MAJOR things to master in MWO. Every weapon you fire (with the exception of the Gauss Rifle) generates some measure of Heat. Your Mech can only handle a certain amount of heat before you risk shutting down and/or doing internal damage to your mech. Each mech has Heat Sinks that add to your heat capacity and also contribute to dissapating the heat you have accumulated. So, the greater the number of weapons you fire at once, the greater the amount of heat you build up. Also, the faster you fire, the more you generate heat. Heat is your biggest concern and the thing you HAVE to learn to manage.
Ghost Heat
This is something the developers added as a "balance tool". It's not very well described in the game. What this means is they have set up a limit to the number of weapons of the same type that can be fired at the same time without incurring a "Ghost Heat Penalty". If you fire more than the allowed number at the same time, then you incur additional heat, hence the term "ghost". This penalty increases quickly based on how many more weapons past the limit you fire (so 3 more than the limit is penalized much more than 1 past the limit). You will get an indicator in the Mech Lab that warns you of the limit if you have more weapons of that type installed on the mech. For example, you can fire 4 SRM 4 missile packs without a penalty but if you fire 5 at the same time, you start incurring the Ghost Heat penalty. This is only if you fire them all at the same time. If you fire them one after the other (Chain Fire) you are fine or if you fire in smaller groups and pause at least .5 seconds between you are fine as well.
So, it is a rather complicated game to learn but once you begin to understand and master the skills, it becomes second nature. The game still has some improving to do...matchmaking isn't the best in the land and the game really needs a Lobby available full time in my opinion, but they are slowly getting those things added. I find the core game a lot of fun to play.

This is a very interesting piece of software to play around in. Designed to create space station designs for RPG games, it can also be used for anywhere you need inspiration for a space environment. I've personally used an earlier build to write a short story set on / around a space station.
There are a lot of options, with the basic layout great for generating a lot of stations for inspiration, standard for if you already know roughly what you want, and advanced for people who want to put in the time to get precisely the kind of station they're after. You can even tell the app what the purpose of the station will be (Engineering, Farm, Navy, and about a dozen others) so it knows what kind of rooms it should be generating for you.
The additional tilesets (Dark Alien is my personal favourite, but the "lettered" rooms are incredibly handy) are a nice touch, and there's also options for what kind of grid you want and even an interactive fog of war that would be amazing for DMs running a campaign.
So I guess it does basically everything you could want from something that generates space stations for you.

Before I review this I believe a bit of my background as a gamer is needed. Among the first games I started playing were the Command & Conquer games (they were SO good, until Zero Hour.. Then it went downhill), so I have experience with fast paced RTS's. I also have sunk many hours into Alpha Centauri, which is more of a 4X/Civ building game. I have played games such as Rise of Nations, Empire Earth, Age of Empires, and many other Strategy games. Now I feel like I know a good Strategy game when I see one, and let me tell you this one of those good ones. Endless Space is a great game for those of you that are 4X/CIv Building fans (not so much for the faster paced RTS fans though you may still enjoy it with the game speed cranked up). If you liked Alpha Centauri, and games like it, you will likely love this game (it is not as in-depth compared to Alpha Centauri too). So far I have sunk 40+ hours into the game (playing on normal speed, so that's only been 1 completed game and 2 that I have yet to complete). I have only played as 3 races thus far. The Sowers have been my favorite of the ones I have played as, they seem the most balanced and have a great late game ship class. The other races I played as, the Siphons and Sherydn (not sure on the spelling of those two), didn't seem as well balanced but are still very playable. Graphically and soundtrack wise the game is great too. I have had a few minor bugs (ship health being displayed incorrectly and one of my fleets derping out) but they were not too bad. As I said, just minor bugs.
Overall, it seems like a well put together game. If you're a fan of Alpha Centauri or games like it, get this for sure. I got the game on a Steam Sale, but I would have payed full price for it. It is well worth 30 dollars. Sorry, about the long review. Again, my main point is if you are a strategy fan and want a good space/sci-fi game then get this!

I see a lot of comparisons to Broforce, which does this game a disservice. The only real similarities are the art style and the sidescrolling perspective.
Door Kickers: Action Squad is an action game, for sure, and will test your reflexes, but you will not succeed if you rush into rooms blindly. As a spinoff of the original Door Kickers, which was a top-down strategy game, Action Squad translates parts of what you need to succeed into a game of an entirely different genre. You will need to make on the fly threat assessments as you clear levels room by room. The enemy with a machete charging you is more dangerous than the one with a pistol, but less so than the one wearing a bomb vest. Oh and be sure not to hit the hostage he's standing next to! Using your gear (breaching charges, flashbangs, etc) and your special abilities is imperative to success as well.
I've mainly spent the time in solo but it's a very good game already just on your own, though it is clearly designed for 2 player co-op. Two things to keep in mind. You can only shoot in the left or right directions so when you need to hit anything above or below you things get tricky. I don't know if they plan to add more directional shooting later on but it's not a huge deal. 2nd thing is, I would highly recommend having a controller to play this.

This game has a lot going for it, but also a lot of major issues.
Pros: Very detailed and accurate gun models. Gameplay is surprisingly engaging. I found myself trying to optimize ways to strip and reassemble the guns to get the fastest time. It's pretty cool they managed to make gun maintenance fun in a video game.
Cons: A few...
1. Poor performance. Even on a 4670k and R9 295x2 the game will still occasionally crawl to a halt and stutter. This is probably the fault of the Unity engine.
2. Ridiculously long tutorial that still somehow manages to not explain things very well.
3. Incosistent on what parts are grouped into assemblies and which are counted individually. Sometimes you have to remove individual pins/screws, other times you don't.
Now the big problems:
4. Free2Play mechanics. The game is set up so that completing every game mode and getting most/all of the achievements for a gun will give you just barely enough XP to unlock the next gun. You essentially have to grind each gun until you can do it fast enough to get enough XP to progress. They then offer expensive "boosters" and DLC to help you progress faster. No thanks.
5. (Final straw) The shooting range mode is apparently totally broken. I unlocked the 1911 shooting range and after a couple tries managed to complete all of the challenges. However the game did not recognize this at all, and when I returned to the map my >4000 XP had disappeared and I was at 0 XP. This is a ridiculous game-breaking bug and is unacceptable in a final release.
This game is good in concept, but terrible in execution.

There's two sides to Mechwarrior Online.
The good side is that it's actually a really good game.  The core 'drive a giant robot and shoot other giant robots' simulation is well-implemented and quite fun. And the Mechlab, where you customize your giant robot from a huge list of components and weapons, is also very realized.  These two core components are what will keep you coming back to MWO.
The bad side is that I just listed all the good parts. There's no single-player campaign, so forget your fond memories of Mechwarrior 2/3/4's single player. The multiplayer game modes are essentially limited to team deathmatch, so if you get tired of that, there's not much else to do. The persistent element are thin and the social tooling is weak. If you need more than giant robots with a variety of weapons shooting each other, then MWO won't make you come back.
Those two points said; I keep coming back to MWO to shoot more giant robots, and I think anybody that finds the idea of shooting giant robots appealing should at least try MWO.

I got the Steam Controller a few weeks ago while it was on sale, and I'm glad I did. This has got to be the best controller I have ever used! It may take a bit of getting used to at first, but once you do, it's a great controller.
The Steam Controller fits quite comfortably into my big hands, and it feels very well-built and solid! The button placement may feel a bit off if you're coming from an Xbox or PlayStation controller, but it doesn't take long to get used to it. The face buttons are the same YXBA buttons on an Xbox controller, the joystick feels nice and grippy, and the two paddles on the inside of the controller handles can be very useful for any quick moves, like stunning an enemy in Arkham Knight.
The main highlight of this controller are the two sensor pads. They may feel extremely weird and clunky at first, but once you get used to them, they'll feel more accurate and smooth than your typical analog thumbstick. The haptic feedback they give during use are a nice feature, too.
Other cool features are the ability to use custom, user-made configurations for your games, the ability to map the individual controller buttons to various keyboard keys or Xbox gamepad buttons, and being able to use this even with games that have partial or no controller support at all. The cool little 8-bit arcade noises the controller makes when you turn it on and off are also a nice touch.
I have tried this controller with many games, such as Portal 2, Borderlands 2, Super Meat Boy, Mandagon, and Batman: Arkham Knight. I have not been disappointed with any of the results. I highly recommend this controller! It definitely won't replace a mouse and keyboard, but it's great for platformers, and it's certainly better than an Xbox controller once you get used to it!

Like broforce, but with an adult's attention span. This game trades out the cascading explosions and supermeatboy meat grinder for an action-puzzle, much like Mark of the Ninja or the dev's own Door Kickers. Quick thinking and smart threat assessment is as valuable as your twitchy trigger finger.  The art style is subdued but highly detailed and readable, making the most of the industrial settings with wide level design variety and garish splashes of blood where violence has occurred.
New tactical situations are presented at regular intervals, requiring flexibility and a willingness to try new equipment or higher risk maneuvers.
This is good tactical fun on solo play, but the game really shines with couch co-op. Character classes are symbiotic, and you'll quickly develop your own preferred breach-and-clear playbook. As the challenge increases, good communication is key to getting perfect scores (and the upgrade points that come with them).  Fast reload times and high player mobility keeps 2-player deaths from being frustrating, instead keeping the 'let's try it a new way' impulse alive. It's also damned funny to experience those botched attempts together.
There's a lot to like and an impressive amount of detail and polish for an alpha.  I played at a friend's house and immediately on getting home, bought myself a copy. Whether you're in it for the 80s contra vibe or the learn-as-you-go tactical challenge, there's far more to discover and enjoy than what you'd expect. Catch some co-op on YouTube if you're on the fence, but don't stream too many levels - discovery and improvisation is part of the fun!

Samudai is fighting game. It's a pretty impressive looking game but not for PC. I probably made for console then ported to PC. It's a very well made for Co-op with your friends. There ain't story but since when and we needed one to nearly kill each other. You play as a ninja cat cool right? The game could have been better.
The graphics are pretty awesome. The animations is stunning. The textures are detailed. The background and surrounding are also good. The art works are great.
The soundtrack is great. The sound FX are also good.
The gameplay is a pain if you are using a keyboard. You can't control it right no matter how much you try. It's made for a gamepad users. The default key bindings are so bad. The tutorial is not for the keyboard users which makes it so hard.
There are six different modes to choose from.
1. The Main mode which is basically a Co-op mode where you play against your friends.
2. Lone Samudai mode which you play solo in a different levels facing waves of enemies.
3. Yarn Ball mode which is playing with a ball and trying to score goals while defending at the same time. More like FIFA or PES.
4. Hold you Ground mode is like a challenge where you must defend the highlighted area from the other players. Every second in the area reduce the counter. The one hits zero first wins.
5. Emperor of the Hill mode which you got to take control of the hat and defending it from the other players till the time runs out.
6. Last Cat Standing mode which is an elimination mode. You fight against you friends and the last one alive wins.
The options sucks. You can only change the music and sound FX volume. You can only change the resolution, video options or key binding outside the game.
There are twenty three achievements and you get three card drops of six cards badge.
Cannot recommend this game. Nothing fun here for me.

This seems to have been written for consoles and hastily ported to PC, which is a bit weird.
Implementation of this game is generally good but it's let down by content - the format doesn't allow for much, 2D platformer/brawlers are really a console thing.  Quality is fairly high for an indy game.   Support for 4K is also a plus, gameplay is very smooth, although as a 2D game it's not really touching the capabilities of PC as a platform.
Also, the controls are obviously console orientated - keyboard/game controller only, no mouse (although again, kudos to the developers for including control customisability, many people have experienced some issues with that, unfortunately).
Gameplay is fairly high brow for a consoler, you have about to worry about movement as well as parrying/attacking etc etc.
Unfortunately at the end of the day this is what very much appears to be a console game on a platform it doesn't belong on.    While the price is suitably low, so is the general interest.  I would thoroughly encourage the developers to move into more serious game development, the quality ethos is there, and along with that can come success, if it's aimed in the right direction.

I'm gonna write this negative review, and then not reply to ANYONE that whishes to whiteknight this turd for no reason other than the fact that, in their hearts, they wish that they were space nazis with no parents.
Look, I was there.  I played this game on a table top, where company-level games between two players took an hour for one turn, and I loved it.  I played many incarnations of Mechwarrior on the PC, from Cresent Hawks Inception the Mechwarrrior 4, and I loved it.  I was there in the early days of closed beta, when we still had all the goodies that Cryengine 3 could deliver, like inverse kinematics and all that, and I loved it.
Now, like three years later, after launching a beta product as a general release, after not having more than two game modes between pick up death match and community warfare (and don't come back and say that there are three game modes in public death match, they all boil down to skirmish in the end), I have absolutely no reason to believe that this product is anything more than a shameless cash grab aimed at the absolute bottom of the gamer community, one that thought that the previous games were too "hard" or too "niche", as made by a developer that has a track record of making bare-bones minimum viable products, or as we like to call it for short, SHOVELWARE.
This guy Russ, whom I hope I can run into in real life on the streets of Seattle one day just so I can cry in his face about how he♥♥♥♥♥♥♥one of my favorite IPs and got away with it, is so desperate for good reviews he has to beg players to start Steam accounts just so they can thumbs up this crap even if they have no intention of playing it on Steam, is nothing more than a craven raider of popular titles, and he figured he hit some real pay dirt with the Battle Tech license, didn't you Russ?
TLDR; This is a beloved robot combat simulator dumbed down into a mediocre arcade shooter, play if you want, but try not to spend any money on it.  That is the one good point, you don't have to spend money on it if you are patient and have very little life outside videogames.

Its quite clunky, especially the graphics/physics, but overall i enjoy this game,
and even decided that its worth spending money on it.
The damage/weapon-system is interesting and the battletech universe in which MWO plays is rich in lore and there are over 100 novels since the 80s. The balancing was not good the last years since its release as far as i uncovered (there are 2 sides Clan and Inner Sphere which battle each other with different levels of technology), but there was a recent patch in December which seemed to turn everything to the better. I started late December so i cant tell the difference. :)
The game is not overcrowded in CW and its not adviseable to join those as a random because you will get stomped 9 out of 10 matches by highly organised and trained units, but its easy to get into solo battles and pew pew away.
If you want to do more team oriented stuff like CW or the soon to be introduced 4vs4, join a unit.
There is a skill-matchmaking in place, which has 5 levels.
You start with 5, and you can be matched with ppl that are 2 levels up or down.
This just grants you to make the first steps in peace, after like 70 hours you come to level 3 and can be matched against the best.
If you want to play in the long run, you need at least premium time if you want to get new mechs regularly,
but unlike WoT you can buy any mech you want immediately and level it.
Its not so easy to get to know the game, since the factions mechs have differences with Omnipod and Quirksystems and the weapons are very different, but if you just use google and read the MWO guide for beginners and the comics, you should be fine to start.
If you like vehicle combat, just give it a try.

All 'quick play' matches have the same strategy. The team clumps together and sits at cover while shooting the enemy clump. All design elements in the game just force this play style further. Assault mechs generally start furthest away so the rest of the team just waits for them to reach the front line. Because of the clumping, trying to do anything besides standing all in a group results in you getting picked off by half the enemy team at once.
Matches are decided within the first few minutes of a game. As soon one team gets a 2-3 kills ahead they will win 90% of the time.
Long Range Missiles are basically the anti-fun weapon. You can get your armor torn away and limbs blown off before you even see an enemy. (This is the reason I quit playing before.)
Even after saving up to buy a mech, the equipment it comes with is usually so♥♥♥♥♥♥you could need to spend multiple times the purchase cost to make it usable. (I bought a medium mech for just under 4mil, but a new engine alone would be over 4mil.)
Buying anything besides the mech packages listed on the website is a waste of money. You could get a single assault mech in game for around $30, or buy one of the premium packages on the website for $15-$20 and get 3 different versions of a mech, slots to store them, a month of premium time, and some cosmetics.
Also, these premium packages give you access to mechs long before they are listed in game. You can't preview them or look at more detailed info without buying them. And in an attempt to get you to spend money, they offer extra perks for buying packages months before the mechs are actually available.
On the last note for 'premium' things, you can get consumables in game with normal credits that can help out in battle. Dealing damage from an airstrike / artillery barrage, deploying a UAV that spots enemies for the team, or making your mech cool down faster so you can shoot more. If a normal player buys these their profits will drop significantly, but a player with premium time will earn a big credit boost that allows them to make more than a normal player even if they use consumables.

Full disclosure - I've been a fan of the franchise since I discovered BattleTech in grade school, right around the time Mechwarrior 2 came out.
I have a ton of fun playing Mechwarrior Online. There is a huge variety of 'Mechs and wide scope for customizing each 'Mech. I'm mid-tier 3 right now, and matchmaking is fairly quick even in the early hours of the morning. Balance between the Clan and Inner Sphere tech bases is getting better as they tweak it. The Community Warfare/Faction Play part of the game is very much in development, but has additional features en route and I have high hopes.
Whether you're in Faction Play or Quick Play/Solo Queue, teamwork is essential. Stick with your buddies, focus fire, and reap the rewards. Get separated from your team and focused by the red team and you'll have a bad day.
That said, it is an imperfect game, partly due to the difficulties of translating a turn-based tactics game (BattleTech) into a real-time first person stompy shooter. It's coming along, and it seems that PGI has been a lot more responsive to/involved with the community lately when it comes to making changes.

This game is a fairly typical turn-based strategy. The 4-branch tech tree and custom factions and units make it a little different from many I've played. Endless Space is a game of management, strategy & patience.
If you find creating & updating templates for your ships, forming fleets, updating planetary build orders,  selecting what to research, upgrading hero abilities etc. boring and tedious... then this game is
for you. Otherwise, if you like strategy, you should enjoy it, and (on the higher difficulty levels) find it challenging.
As far as space strategy 4X games are concerned, this is one of the better ones. It's graphics and (once you learn it) relatively simple rules, lift it in my opinion above most of it's competition. For this reason I give it my recommendation.
The tech-tree is a perfect example:
It's four branches would seem to indicate that you can concentrate research on the branch that interests you the most. This is an illusion. If you want to build a strong empire you'll need to concentrate on
branches uniformly. Once your have played for a while (and are more familiar with the research techs), you will discover the ways that certain techs (in different branches) relate with each other.
Pirates are another example:
Since victory in the game is all about expanding your empire (as quickly as possible), and colonising systems (before they are colonised by other factions), the appearance of pirates can inhibit this (at the most critical time). Prevention is better than cure. Random events aside, pirate fleets will only spawn in systems not under any factions influence (or surveillance). Station scout ships (if possible) in systems to prevent their spawning and / or station strong fleets at strategic systems to prevent their entry into your space.
The use of heroes is another example:
Heroes can have a very significant effect on your success in the game, especially in fleet combat. Although all heroes will gain experience over time, speed this up as much as you can. A good way to do this is by assigning them to fleets based at systems on the borders of your space. Use them to fight pirates, enemy faction ships etc. In this respect (if your fleet is strong enough) pirates and cold war can be a good thing.
Keep a close eye on what the other factions are doing (if you can). It is easy to lose a game because another faction has reached a victory condition before your faction has.
Although, far from perfect, there is much that can be enjoyed from this game.
Enjoy!!

This game is a ton of fun and I hope they keep expanding on it for quite some time.
It is strategic like Door Kickers is; you can't just barrel your way through enemies, guns blazing.  You need to think about your choices before commiting to them, and the devs require you to utilize your resources and abilities to clear levels.  It's a very different experience from Door Kickers, though.  Combat is always in real time and the game overall is much more action oriented.
The pacing and ramping of difficulty is nice; it eases you in while you get familiar with the mechanics, but gets quite tough in later maps.  Progression is similar to the original Door Kickers in that upon completing objectives, you earn stars that can be used to unlock new weapons and gear.
The map variety is good.  Most maps have many vertical levels to traverse, which really adds to the variety of choices you have for progressing through them.
The game is also a blast to play with friends via local coop; that alone is a feature that's not too common today, and the fact that they are also looking into expanding online MP features is awesome.
This game is a steal whether you're coming for the silly 80's-style humor, the strategic depth of SWAT-based objectives, or want an intense action shooter.

Mechwarrior: Online is one of the deepest shooters I have ever played.  Has a deeper metagame before a match then almost any other shooter I have played, and requires dedicated teamwork to succeed at high tier gameplay.
I have been playing MWO since 2013 and I have put in more then 6000+ matches in MWO and have played at the top tier of competitive play in the game in multiple leagues, and cannot recommend the game enough if you care about an in depth shooter.

Hello fellow gamers. Firstly I want to point out that I am a Legendary Founder of this game and so I have been through the entire roller coaster ride of the good and the bad of MWO.
I must say that overall MWO is quite a fun game to play. Since I have been playing for so long there have been times were I get a little bored and I'll head off to occupy my time elsewhere. I find myself always coming back to play for a little bit here and there and eventually coming back in full force. It comes down to the fact that the core gameplay is simply fun. I love tweaking my Mechs to fit my playstyle and/or to try and get that edge to ebst my opponents.
I typically play as a solo pugger because I like the no strings attached, play a few games and then get some work done. Obviously this means that you're in for some fun with the grab bag of players out there but I generally have a good mix of good and bad games. I must say that if you have the chance to drop with a group it will exponentially increase the amount of fun you experience. The tactical gameplay that emerges from group combat is like no other.
Even though the game is great now, it is continuously expanding. As of this review there are already teasers for the next rounds of improvements. There are even hints to a single player or possibly co-op campaign! On top of this, the president of the company is very active on Twitter and is very helpful in answering questions or providing juicy tid bits of imformation to keep us excited about the future of the game. I find that developers/owners of a company being involved with their community is such a rare treat. I find really helps improve the flow of feedback and generally creates a positive atmosphere.
There is a lot more I could write about this game but instead I will try to summarize some additional points that I feel stand out.
Gameplay
-Core gameplay is very addicting.
-Mechlab can provide hours of entertainment by itself as you tweak your Mechs to suit your needs.
-Faction gameplay is a little lack luster currently.
-Big improvements to Faction play in the very near future will help breathe new life into this mode.
Mechs
-New Mech releases are fairly frequent Helps keep excitement up.
-The current selection is quite plentiful and helps keep the battlefields varied.
-Free-to-play grind can be a little extensive but at least the new player experience gives quite a substantial amount of in game currency to get you started.
Maps + Modes
-A decent variety and styles of maps to keep things interesting.
-More maps on the way but at a fairly slow pace currently.
-Game modes help to change the dynamic of the battle which helps with the map variety.
Overall I find this game quite enjoyable. The beauty of it all is that the game will continue to expand and improve as time goes on. I definately recommend this game. Even if you don't play hardcore, it can be nice to break up the monotony of continuous gaming with a few matches of MWO to keep things fresh.
Hope to see you on the battlefield (on the blue team of course :)

"The Thinking Man's FPS"
TL;DR Big mechs shoot each other in a rich setting and beautiful maps with a focus on tactics and customization and teamwork.
I've heard this game called that from the community as I've played and I must say it is very accurate. There is a LOT going on in a typical match for MWO. Constantly knowing where my allies are moving, keeping an eye on the Assaults (the slow behemoths) to make sure we don't leave them behind, scanning the targets that the lights (the small speedy ones) are scouting, and always monitoring heat while being under fire by the enemy team. It is exhilarating!
Mechwarrior Online is set in the Battletech universe that has a ton of history and lore to back up the mechs in the game. While this game is less canon and more action, it is a still a great place for lovers of the setting to get their fix. The lore is unimportant to gameplay, so there is nothing stopping a complete newcomer to the game to feel left out.
This is a game about tactics. You choose your mech from a starting roster of trial mechs after a tutorial that just BARELY gets you ready to dive into the deep ocean that is MWO. There are four "weight" classes: Light, Medium, Heavy, and Assault. Upon first look, it appears to be a rock, paper, scissors type of scenario, but that is entirely not the case. This game offers a ton of customization to certain mechs (which are available in two separate "makes" that are similar to factions) so that your assault can run with the heavies, or allow your light to carry more firepower than some Heavy mechs. It can be tough to pick a mech in the start and there is no right or wrong mech, but after a good game and some quick deaths, one quickly learns the pros and cons of each class.
As I mentioned before, there are two "factions" that really only shine in the Community Warfare gamemode, which puts the player in a mercenary position accepting contracts from one of the separate factions in the game. Otherwise, a mech's faction has no real difference besides the level of customization. Mechs can be outfitted with weapons based on the "hardpoints" found on the frame. For instance, an arm could allow three energy weapons while the right torso could allow a ballistic and a missile. Mechs must be build around what is allowed by the hardpoints and weight limit while keeping survivability in the amount of armor and heat management that the build will allow.
The Inner Spere mechs (IS) are special in that they allow one to customize engines, jump jets, and a host of weapon customizations. However, the IS mechs have special "quirks" that allow them to really shine with a certain weapon type that should be taken into consideration. This allows the IS mechs to be specialized to a certain blend of combat and makes for each mech to be slightly different from another mech of the same build but on a different frame. The Clan mechs are a different beast entirely. While the IS mechs can change engines and loadouts, the Clan mechs cannot change the default engines or jumpjets in their mechs. They do allow one to swap out pieces called omnipods that change the hardpoints on a certain piece of the mech to allow for greater variety in weapon loadouts.
This game has a great community with a nice dry humor while at the same time being very competitive. From my time with this game, salt and toxicity has always been rare, something that I contribute to the personality that is drawn to the lore and gameplay. Being a free game, there is an incentive to buy mechs with cash to gain early access, but every mech in the game has a variant that can be purchased with in game currencies. There are also "hero" and "champion" variants to most mechs that give a boost to mech xp or in game currency rates, but they don't feel necessary. If you enjoy the game, the grind will be something you enjoy and not a burden. The only cash item that is "mandatory" or addition mech bays that allow you to own additional mechs. These are occasionally given away during events, but mostly will need to be purchased.
In the end, I recommend this game to anyone who considers the RTS style games enjoyable and to anyone familiar with Battletech in general. It is a fun game and a great way to spend an evening.

I received my first controller as a birthday gift, and decided to buy a second one on my own. So, I now own two Steam controllers, one wireless Xbox 360 controller, and one wired Xbox 360 controller.
I've tried using the Steam controller on Fallout 4; it does the job okay. I quickly fell back to using mouse and keyboard because I became frustrated with sliding my thumb furiously over the touchpad like a failed Pokemon Go capture, so I think for FPS and precise aiming I'm sticking with the mouse. I've yet to use it in 3rd person games, like Shadows of Mordor or the Batman series, but I think it will do an equivalent job to the xbox ones (since it's not for aiming). It's just pretty hard to get used to touchpad on the right thumb when most other controllers use a second thumbstick in its place.
Where I think this controller shines is working with casual, couch co-op games and on games that didn't normally have controller functions included. I heard Valve is going to make the Big Picture mode take care of all that infrastructure, so I expect to see a lot more games I can use the Steam controller with in the future.
Pros
- Efficient use of battery; change AA batteries less than I do for my Xbox 360 controllers
- Two touchpads work great for the dual thumb keyboard typing
- Seemingly infinite ways to configure all the buttons (and I think from the recent update, I really mean ALL the buttons)
- Macros, in case you want to UP UP DOWN DOWN LEFT RIGHT LEFT RIGHT B A SELECT START your way to winning
- Profiles, also seemingly infinite
- Two more back/trigger buttons than the Xbox 360 controller. I love buttons.
- Came with cable to use controller in wired mode
- Sturdy manufacturing, not a cheap plastic feel. Has a bit of heft to it. If you're a electronics geek you'll get a kick out of the screenprint that says Valve Corporation on the PCB and flat cables (google "Steam controller tear-down")
Cons
- No second/right thumbstick and instead has a touchpad, which takes a lot of getting used to
- Touchpad needs adjusting, default low sensitivity - end up thumbing across several times to get cursor/character to move (probably in the settings somewhere)
- Left thumbstick and the 4-color buttons placed far into the center of controller. It's noticeably in the center compared to the Xbox controller. If you have small hands like I do, you have to stretch past the knobby palm rest things to reach them.
- Still some issues with some games, ie) needing to restart the game and big picture mode to get out of a freeze when controller used
- Spring loaded battery cover. This could both be a pro and con. Easy to change batteries, but the spring mechanism may break down.
- Left side of left touchpad arrived scuffed or blemished, like some angry Aperture sentry turret kiss-lasered it on its way through the automated factory (yes, it's still there and I'm still a little sore about it)
Overall I recommend borrowing this controller from a friend first, see if you like the touchpad for the right hand and if it fits well in your hands. If it does, by all means go for it. While I need to have much more time to see if I'll get used to the touchpad instead of thumbstick, I'll definitely be busting out my two Steam controllers when my friends come over for video game nights.

I've played with a Keyboard and Mouse my whole life, having used controllers for nothing more than the rare visits around friends' houses. I love this thing to bits.
Yes, it takes a while to get used to, the settling in period will probably be about a week. But that's far less time than it would take a complete newbie to play with a Mouse or an Analog Stick for their first time, so why this is an issue I have no idea.
The customisation on this thing is *ridiculous*. Nothing you've ever seen. Your left trackpad could be an override for your mouse to point at a small area of the screen. Or, it could be a scroll wheel that rotates either by circling your finger, or swiping up or sideways. Or, it could be a touch menu with functions you assign to it that pop up on the screen, or not if you don't want it to. It's insane.
This is the single biggest myth surrounding the Steam Controller. Anyone who tells you otherwise is incredibly impatient or hasn't tried. Ever since I picked this thing up last Christmas my performance on the Controller is exactly on par with my Keyboard and Mouse performance. In fact in some ways it's better because....
...It's way more comfortable than another controller or keyboard. Those little grip buttons on the back are a Godsend. Rocket jumping is a doddle.
People complain that the trackpads are hard to use. If they are, that's because the user is not making use of the
. This allows the user to simulate a mouse input along with the trackpads. Set up the Gyro with a low sensitivity for precision movements, and set the trackpad to a high sensitivity for reaction movements. Spend a little bit of time learning it and it's a match made in Heaven.
Don't like having that configuration? You can create another one with an entirely new
, and assign an input to allow you to switch between them. This means you can remap the entire controller. That is incredibly powerful. For more individual changes you also have
Hold down a button, and another set of buttons can have an entirely new function.
The one caveat of the Steam Controller is the biggest one:
. Effective use of the Controller requires that you take the time to figure out what the settings do as you go along and what works for you. Be patient with it. Take care of your Controller, and it will take care of you.

For a 15 year old game it's aged OK. Playing fine in full HD with graphics which could kinda be considered retro now. At it's standard price of £3.50 it would have been a totally worth while £11p/hour for me, so even better from a Steam sale; a no-brainer for base builder fans scouring the back-catalogue. This original Stronghold version seemed to review far better than it's more expensive successors, and I can certainly believe that being justified.
There's a collection of historical siege scenarios, set up for you to survive with only what's given, and multi-player too, in theory (I never tried). But the single player is all that's really needed: an ample 'military' campaign with a bite sized 'economic' chaser (of 5 missions with minimal/no combat but random problems thrown at you without warning). There's no need to play a tutorial, as the main campaign is nice and gentle with introducing it's mechanics, buildings and units. It's strung together with spoken dialogue interludes, with almost passable voice acting, that step through a caricatured Britain of 1000 years hence.
The vast majority of missions are build up and/or defend against a few waves of different attacks. This was definitely the modest pace I was after. I only felt the need to YouTube help with one of these types of mission, just to expedite a solution after a couple of quick failures, and that still felt rewarding. A more major frustration was that controlling military units can be clumsy with the isometric attack ranges being tricky and unintuitive, for example. This was one aspect that made the three (or so) assault missions seem unreasonable brutal. Even after watching a couple of tutorials right through, I just couldn't pull it of, so had to switch down to the lowest 'easy' setting and save my progress at stages throughout. Still, was a good feeling to finally complete these, making you really work to finish the game, which I did, like brutal end boss sections. I can imagine some gamers actually enjoying these puzzles and wanting more, like a large scale, medieval Rainbow 6, or something.
One important tip: some of the keyboard shortcuts seemed literally indispensable, so look those up (e.g. game speed adjustment, terrain flattening and view angle).

Short Version:
Everything is orange. Everything can kill you quickly with well-placed headshots, so get in cover. The cover system is clunky. The lethal guns are fun. Not enough explosions or destruction for me. The story is meh and hte game feels a little short... But still nice.
7/10 would reccomend to buy on sale, but is still great either way.
Long version:
Everything is clunky, but ok in it's own odd way, and every gun in the game is useful (at least the lethal ones, I didn't bother with silly concepts like "restraint" or "stealth and subtlty" or "mercy" or "doing the right thing." :P) I blasted my way through the game and had fun getting yelled at by every character who had a problem with it (I only wish you could flip them off more often.)
I found myself dying and reloading saves often, and my advice is to use the weapons you have now, and not bother with sparing ammunition. You'll almost always have the resources to spare, especially near the end of the game where you're an expert at placing one-hit-kill headshots on your enemies like no tomorrow. So seriously! Hurl that grenade, don't stash it! You'll miss out on all the fun if you're just using the pistol all the time or saving your superpower energy!
I kind of wish the game's story was a little clearer. I still don't know what Adam's initial mission was- something about figuring out who's behind a terrorist attack at the Sans Serif Font Building or something. The relationship between Adam and the girlfriend was shoehorned into the plot, and Adam Jensen's voice actor doesn't emote half the time, and needs a throat lozenge (seriously, it's really bad. I reflexively cringe half the time that he talks.)
All three endings to the game (without spoiling anything) are just essentially slideshows, like Fallout.
Unsorted thoughts on the game:
-Alcohol blurrs the screen really badly, and it's unreasonable. It's also hard to use items in your inventory. You would think that sorting your inventory by clicking and dragging would be easy, but somehow it's not. Using items that aren't on your hotbar requres the use of a dropdown menu, like you're in windows Explorer. Even dropping items.
-Your inventory gets pretty small, even when you can upgrade it. It would be kind of fun to not have to worry about inventory space, like in Half Life, but meh.
-Everything is orange. I suggest downloading a mod to remove the silly orange filter, because it gets kind of annoying, especially when you get to the China area.
The city hubs are a little... Dull. Not a lot of things going on, just lots of people standing around in the street. There are two city hubs: Detroit, and Generic China Future City with bad stereotypical accents. I hate "China City Who's Name I've Already Forgotten." It's layout is like a maze, and you get lost easily, even with a map and a compass. A simple task of getting from objective to objective turns into a game of wandering until you find the right path.
Mine templates are useless. It's hard to gauge how far a thrown weapon will go, and sometimes you'll have to throw a second grenade because you missed. Stores don't sell enough ammo. There's not enough superpowers, but the ones you have are awesome.
The cover system is really poorly implemented, and sometimes it doesn't even work right in firefights- jerking your gun around suddenly or in directions that you didn't expect.
Even with full armor upgrades, a pointblank shotgun blast will still almost always kill you in a single hit. This makes the game unforgivingly hard.
One last note: I -HATE- the sprint function. You run for literally three seconds at maybe 10% faster speed, then have to wait three seconds to recharge it. Sure, you can spend valuable exp on expanding that sprint by two increments of 2.5 seconds each, but it doesn't do much of anything.
All in all, a flawed gem.

This is a great 4x game with amazing visuals. It has a unique and simple battle system so anybody new to 4x games will know what to do.
Every game you start feels different from the last one, even if you keep to the same setup. Also there is no solid learning curve as there are many possibilities and out comes. Even if you do come across a situation that feels familiar the out come and your position with in the game may lead you down a completely different path than the one you were expecting. This makes every game you play highly unpredictable.
The game can be quite difficult and frustrating for beginners, even on easy. The level of weapons tech of your enemies very quickly matches yours if you do not invest in your own weapons technologies during a conflict. This makes the game challenging on every level.
After long play the game can get repetitive. Dealing with all your planets on each turn can get complicated and frustrating. You can save on any turn.
The game graphics are stunning. The level of detail they have put in, on the planets, the galaxy and the battle scenes are amazing. You can tell they have taken there time to get this game looking good.
The sound effects are not quite in the same power of the graphic. However they are simple and effective for this type of game. The sound track is very good and sets the tone of the game well.
The controls work very well. You can operate most of the game with just a click of a mouse. You do have the option to name planets and ships which obviously requires a keyboard.
I do recommend this game for the amount of detail they have put in to the graphics, storyline and descriptions of technologies. However some players may find it difficult and also after long play you may find it repetitive and frustrating.

I can really only recommend this game if you enjoy playing 4x strategy games. Overall this game is very visually appealing with interesting character designs and stunning ship designs. Initially I thought that the introductory lore behind each of the races was compelling but the story doesn't develop any further than that and there isn't any real interaction between races outside of diplomatic actions. After trying out the game with all of the different races there is not a whole lot of really distinguishable differences in gameplay between the different races and even the tech trees for all of the races are exactly the same, so it becomes less of a tech tree and more of an arms race. The space battles are fun to watch, especially once the largest ship types are available. However the battle strategy is determined before the battle starts which may turn some people off. Endless Space is a worthy entry in 4x strategy games, however I'm hoping if a sequel is developed that Amplitude Studios improves on what is good with this game and adds more story, more interaction between races, and maybe just maybe include some gameplay that goes more indepth into invading a system and laying siege on individual planets. Maybe even include some mechanic where each colonized planet in a system has to be conquered before a player can take control of a system? Come for the art design, stay for the space battles.

You can tell that it's not the most high-res game in this mode, but it's still fun and has a great set of things to do. Not a fan of playing online since I'm a baddie, but everything else seems great from my perspective. The only set-back is the huge lack of settings... but I guess that's a port for ya.
If you're into Naruto, grab a controller (or your keyboard), and pick this game up!

One of the best 2D co-op old school games I've ever played.  I've played many games on the NES, SNES and a few other old school systems, but this is by far the most addictive and fun game I've ever played.  Heck, Mega Man Powered Up isn't nearly as addictive as this, even with its level editor.  I honestly can not wait to see what this game has coming.  We are, in theory, going to get a level editor sometime soon.  If that is true, this game will never run out of ideas.
You can play this game co-op in a non linear campaign.  There is no real story, you are just a SWAT officer who has to stop thugs and terrorists, rescue hostages and defuse bombs.  There are three classes you can play as, but I only play as the assault class, just because I'm really good as him.  Co-op can be played online and offline.  Kicking down doors is really fun, and blowing them up is even more fun.  The AI for a 2D game is actually decent.  They will shoot you on sight and if they are a suicide bomber, they will charge you as fast as they can.  Like I said above, the game is non linear so you can play any of the missions as long as they are unlocked.  You use stars to unlock gear, weapons and other stuff to play the game and save the day and it's got a really good soundtrack.  Like, it's really good.  Check it out if you want a lot of fun.  I will update more as I play more.

Stronghold HD is a RST "simulation" game considered a classic. However the game aged a lot, and only nostalgics can truly enjoy it (this is what reviews show actually), it suffers from to many flaws unacceptable by nowadays standarts.
Let's do a list :
- Graphics : the "HD" part is nonexistent. This is just some kind of zoom to adapt to the screen size. However the game is perfectly playable, this is not smth which should stop you play the game.
- The UI is also not efficient, but again, we can forgive the game since it's old.
Ok here come the real issues.
- The tutorial is nonexistant. It gives you the basics of the basics, and forgets (easily) 90% of the important informations. Fortunaly today we have Internet. Still it's a bother.
- You must place a stock pile next to another one. Why ? Because ♥♥♥♥ you that's why. This is a mere square of stones, so obviously it can't be placed freely. Results, sometimes you can't because you put your castle on a hill (the stockpile being put at the same time next to it) and the ground must be perfectly flat. This is also completely inefficient since workers must travel long distance to dispose of their ressources. There is a trick to build a long line of stockpiles then destroy the ones in the middle. It's long, tedious and not always possible, but whatever...
- Once a stockpile is full, you can't empty it, you must build to spend ressources.
- The granary works the same that the stockpile.
- The land is cursed. In one minute I managed to get fire which destroyed all my plantations, wolves and bandits (at least wolves and bandifs fought each other).
- The objective of every mission is gathering said amount of ressources (stone, bread, maces...) and sometimes smth like complete the castle. But the difficulty remains the same whatever the level of difficulty you choose. The only thing changing is how much ressources you must gather.
- This game feels like a try and die. You must repeat the same mission again and again to understand every mechanics and do a perfect game. The issue ? A mission can last several hours each time. Of course you can save, but it's hard to know beforehand if your game is already ♥♥♥♥ed or not.
- When you manage to play well enough to reach the goal before the end of the time (because of course it's time limited), the game adds difficulty to prevent you to (such as bandits onslaught).
- Building must run on coal or oil (including farms and plantations) because they're subject of spontaneous combustion. Actually to prevent fire you must build a well by building. Of course when the guy from the well (yes because there's one guy by well, other people don't try to stop the fire, it's not their job after all) come back drawning water, he goes to HIS well, even if it's at the other side of the map, not the one just next to him.
- The game is supposed to be a "simulation", still bandits can destroy (stone) building by hitting it with maces in a AoE way. And they do a lot of dammages.
- Bandits have better gear than your own troops (except the most powerful ones).
- Workers are the most courageous people you could meet. They fear nothing. That's why they take the shortest route to their destination. So if there is a fire or bandits on the way, YOLO, what could happen ? Results you lose tons of workers because they're too stupid to understand that fire burns and bandits kill (they don't run away either if bandits come to their workplace, children in the game are programed to do it, workers should do the same).
- Ranged troops (archers, crossbowmen) don't move if they're too far of a target, they just say they can't reach it. You must move them to a point then ask them to fight. Incredibly tedious, especially when the target is moving itself. Also, if they start fire to the target and this one becomes out of reach, they simply stop shooting.
- Sometimes troops stop doing a taks you gave them, because, well, because. Killing the wolves eating all my friends ? Nah I didn't like them anyway. Killing the army of rabbits eating every crops ? Nah I'm strictly carnivorous. Must be smth like that.
Reminder : the game was released two years after Age of Empire II, so several issues with the game (such as range units not going to the target themselves) are unacceptable, even for a game that old.
I'm stating facts, so only a fanboy blinded by nolstagia could accept such flaws.

Ddespite all of that, the game manages to stay enjoyable. But with too many flaws to justify spending time on it. There are far better games on the market.

This game has given me so many hours of fun, originally bought as a none HD version and on a DVD (remember them?) So I had to buy it to have in my collection as the DVD is gathering dust somewhere in my house. Such a beautiful game with a classic style of graphics and a great atmosphere. Just one of those games that will never be replicated by any amount of 3D visuals and modern effects that Firefly continue to create. It holds a certain charm all of its own and undoubtadly one of fireflys best crowning titles to date. They have tried to revise the formula but always end up falling short by a country mile. Which is a shame as this is such a unique game.
Basically you build castles in order to protect your Lord from dying at the hands of other Lords. Depending which game mode you play but ultimately you will play the Campaign, the main core of the game. In order to do this you are required to support a community by sourcing building materials and food stocks. Different types of food are more quickly accessible but others have longevity but are more difficult to produce and require more input to get the supply lines off the ground. You also need to build weapons and weapons systems to aid you in Defence as well as attack. As once you establish a stable economy and food supply you will be required to move onto Vanquishing your Foe. Who vary from 'The Rat' 'The Pig' through to 'the Wolf', all who hold different tactics and means to plague you or even destroy you.
You can also choose which way to rule, a caring ruler or a cruel ruler. Enforce taxes to increase your coffers..the heavier the tax obviously the more unhappy the people become. To the point they will just leave your settlement. You can sweetnen the deal though by laying gardens or placing entertainment to take the peoples mind off being fleeced of all their hard earned. A nice trick to really squeezing all you can from them is to get them hammered on booze, then crank up the taxes and watch the gold flow in to aid your war machine. Alteratively you can dot the odd gallows around the place or cages to remind the people what will happen if they do not comply. This has a negative effect though.
The scribe feeds back on your orders and it is funny to lisen to him, 'Bit much these taxes' The voice acting is awesome, the best in the series...the artwork is superb too, all the little illustrations in the books etc. Really well done, it seems furture incarnations of the game have become diluted in this retrospect.
Anyway it is a brilliant game, looking it's age now but like a fine wine holds it's own against the younger newer kids on the block. A true classic in every sense of the word.

I've put in over 250 hours so far with this controller in various games (mostly Dark Souls 1/2/3) and it's honestly difficult to go back to using a normal X360 controller. The back buttons and the ability to remap and adjust button combinations, both really nice.
It's perfect for basically any game that isn't a first person perspective game, it's not horrible for FP games, but a KB+M would obviously be the better option. And personally, if I were to choose between a standard controller or a steam controller, I probably would go with the steam controller.
And one suggestion for something thinking about buying: REMEMBER TO CREATE TEMPLATES. If you play lot games that have a similar perspective (top down, first person, third person, etc.), it's crucial that after you spend a while perfecting a control scheme for a game, to save it as a template so you can use it for other games without having to re-map everything.
Overall a really great device, though buyer beware, this takes a LOT of time to understand what each option does in the configuration menu.

My initial review
It is hard for me to say much in comparison to other controllers since I am a mouse and keyboard gamer. I recently received this as a gift and enjoy using it in certain situations. It feels of high quality craftsmanship and design. It fits comfortably in my hand and isn't overly heavy or too light weight for that matter.
I really like the way I can customize the controls for every game so easily. That is my favorite feature thus far. I haven't tried using it on Street Fighter yet but that will be the ultimate test of whether it is solid for that type of gameplay or not for me.
Oddly, I find it doesn't seem to fit the bill for the games I thought it would be best for at all. Those which are console ports that were made with controllers in mind. They seem to require a level of solid detailed control that the rather large dual thumb pads on this aren't capable of pulling off comfortably, at least not in my hands.
I will be continuing to practice using it for the console ports and other 1st person shooters and hoping to find a setup that does provide me with that level of precision and control that the mouse and keyboard have always given me. If I find that, I will certainly update this review.
This controller is actually much higher quality than I expected it would be. I am glad I got it as a gift since I wouldn't likely have picked one up for myself anytime soon. What it does do, it does well and the ability to customize so much with such ease is fun and empowering in itself. I see so much potential in this product and I have barely scratched the surface yet. I certainly do recommend it.
