I've been playing on-and-off since Closed Beta, with most of my time played after the original publisher (IGP) departed.
I'm not going to touch on the history of the game, nor its previous states. If anyone out there hates PGI or this game for its history, I think their opinions are valid but I'd like to focus my review on what the game is here and now.
Mechwarrior Online is a game about piloting giant walking tanks.
As far as these things go, this is the best on the market. The initial learning curve can be pretty steep, but once you get your bearings this game provides an experience like no other. Half of the game is customization; swapping out weaponry and equipment on your massive death machine. The other half is tearing other players' mechs apart; shearing off limbs and blasting holes in their torsos.
This is a game where your hitboxes, health, and loadout all go hand-in-hand. You might be missing your entire left half, about to die from one more shot to the chest, but still have armor on your right arm. Many times victory will hinge on your ability to shield your critical components just long enough to get one more shot at the enemy. This game truly shines when both sides are locked in this desperate struggle, trying to mitigate incoming damage while simultaneously finding moments to strike.
There's nothing quite so satisfying as firing the massive, deafening AC20 and watching an enemy mech rock with the impact. No other game makes me laugh with such maniacal glee, as my 100-ton Atlas obliterates an enemy with a cluster of short-range missiles. Nothing gets my heart racing quite like speeding around the map in a light mech, scouting the enemy team's location and harassing mechs several times my size.
I couldn't possibly hope to cover all the tactical elements or loadout considerations in this review. What I can tell you is that all the research pays off. The more time you invest in looking up strategies, loadouts and mech roles, the better you will perform and the more fun you will have. You'll learn which mechs to fear, and the range of their most likely loadouts. You'll learn where to shoot each mech to most efficiently disable or destroy them. You'll learn the best way to play to your mechs' strengths, and the result will be a game that keeps your mind racing as you work to counter each new enemy.
This is a game I can't recommend enough. Nothing feels quite as cool as becoming a Mechwarrior.
If you enjoy throwing things together and seeing what works this is a good place to start.

This is the first (and so far only) competative FPS that I have loved to play.  It is fast paced and fun, assuming you can find a good server (which I have had some minor difficulties doing).
One of my favorite things about the game is that there are few "hitscan" weapons, allmost every weapon fires a projectile, so you have to lead your target.  This adds to the learning curve slightly, but once you get the hang of aiming with these, every hit feels so much more rewarding.
Tribes: Ascend is also well optimized technically, and can achieve 60 fps or higher on most systems, including on some laptops.  It has all the options you would expect from a competative pc fps (fov, rebinding, mouse acceleration off, etc.), and it even has a third person mode (which I have never used during a game, but works just fine in the training levels).
On the other hand, it is worth mentioning that the developers essentially abandoned this game in favor of Smite, which was a good business decision, but still makes me a little sad.  The game has not grown a very large playerbase, and some people have claimed that there are cheaters, but frankly it is still fun and reasonably fair.

Long version:
Everything is clunky, but ok in it's own odd way, and every gun in the game is useful (at least the lethal ones, I didn't bother with silly concepts like "restraint" or "stealth and subtlty" or "mercy" or "doing the right thing." :P) I blasted my way through the game and had fun getting yelled at by every character who had a problem with it (I only wish you could flip them off more often.)
I found myself dying and reloading saves often, and my advice is to use the weapons you have now, and not bother with sparing ammunition. You'll almost always have the resources to spare, especially near the end of the game where you're an expert at placing one-hit-kill headshots on your enemies like no tomorrow. So seriously! Hurl that grenade, don't stash it! You'll miss out on all the fun if you're just using the pistol all the time or saving your superpower energy!
I kind of wish the game's story was a little clearer. I still don't know what Adam's initial mission was- something about figuring out who's behind a terrorist attack at the Sans Serif Font Building or something. The relationship between Adam and the girlfriend was shoehorned into the plot, and Adam Jensen's voice actor doesn't emote half the time, and needs a throat lozenge (seriously, it's really bad. I reflexively cringe half the time that he talks.)
All three endings to the game (without spoiling anything) are just essentially slideshows, like Fallout.
Unsorted thoughts on the game:
-Alcohol blurrs the screen really badly, and it's unreasonable. It's also hard to use items in your inventory. You would think that sorting your inventory by clicking and dragging would be easy, but somehow it's not. Using items that aren't on your hotbar requres the use of a dropdown menu, like you're in windows Explorer. Even dropping items.
-Your inventory gets pretty small, even when you can upgrade it. It would be kind of fun to not have to worry about inventory space, like in Half Life, but meh.
-Everything is orange. I suggest downloading a mod to remove the silly orange filter, because it gets kind of annoying, especially when you get to the China area.
The city hubs are a little... Dull. Not a lot of things going on, just lots of people standing around in the street. There are two city hubs: Detroit, and Generic China Future City with bad stereotypical accents. I hate "China City Who's Name I've Already Forgotten." It's layout is like a maze, and you get lost easily, even with a map and a compass. A simple task of getting from objective to objective turns into a game of wandering until you find the right path.
Mine templates are useless. It's hard to gauge how far a thrown weapon will go, and sometimes you'll have to throw a second grenade because you missed. Stores don't sell enough ammo. There's not enough superpowers, but the ones you have are awesome.
The cover system is really poorly implemented, and sometimes it doesn't even work right in firefights- jerking your gun around suddenly or in directions that you didn't expect.
Even with full armor upgrades, a pointblank shotgun blast will still almost always kill you in a single hit. This makes the game unforgivingly hard.
One last note: I -HATE- the sprint function. You run for literally three seconds at maybe 10% faster speed, then have to wait three seconds to recharge it. Sure, you can spend valuable exp on expanding that sprint by two increments of 2.5 seconds each, but it doesn't do much of anything.
All in all, a flawed gem.

After owning it on the 360, and now on the PC, I have to say that this is a really good game. It's not only a decent game, but it is a great Deus Ex game. Especially considering the failure that was The Fall, and the controversial Invisible War, DEHR is a fantastic installment to the series.
The graphics, the gameplay mechanics, the inventory, item construction and customization, the character upgrades, all of these are solid. Then we get into the story and dialogue. They are like nothing I have experienced before. Once you get the dialogue Praxis upgrade, it opens up a whole new gameplay feature, one that allows you to not only witness the effects of your choices during the dialogue sequence (not just after), but gives you a whole new way to play the game. It allows you to actually strategize during a conversation based on the individual person you're talking to and their personality, along with their emotional state at any given time, not just click one phrase and hope that the NPC has a favorable response to that particular selection.
I am one of the few who actually like DE: Invisible War, but I have to admit that the inventory and (oh god) the dialogue and voice acting were bland and boring at best. Human Revolution doesn't fall victim to any of the failures of its older brother (and some would say a VERY distant relative). The voice acting is superb, the inventory is akin to The Conspiracy, item upgrades are more like the original, and the story and missions give you that sense of urgency that the original had.
It's not just a good shooter, but it is a fantastic RPG. I've got to say that this is one (pre)sequel that I am proud to own and experience. Definitely recommended. A solid 9/10

Before reading this review, keep in mind that this is my first experience within the Deus Ex franchise, and will not be comparing to earlier titles. I will simply give my opinions on it as a standalone piece of entertainment.
I won't say anything very plot specific, but I'll give a short summary. The game takes takes place in a not so distant, but very dark future. The current scientific focus of Human Revolution involves augmentations, so called enhacements to the human body. This has caused a split between the people who think agmentations are wrong and unnatural, and those who profit from it, and think it's the way of the future. However, neither side is clean. Corruption, backstabbing and inhumane and unethical actions are a common occurance on both ends.You play as Adam Jensen, a security specialist working at the megacorporation Sarif industries (who specializes in augmentation technology). Throughout a lengthy campaign you strive to uncover a conspiracy plot, where no person or corporation can be trusted.
This may seem like a paper thin plot with the way I've described it above, but the story quickly picks up the pace, and turns into some really deep, complex and disturbing stuff. It also ties in some other themes, like what it truly means to be human (even though that question has been asked a number of times before). My only real gripe with the story is that quickly goes from being basic to complex rather quickly. If you're not paying very close attention the entire time you're playing, you might end up not knowing half of what the hell is going on. The game expects you to remember a large number of names, corporations, events and so on, and this stuff stacks up. I might be the only complaining about this (or I might just be ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, who knows), but definitely something to keep in mind.

The graphics do their job well, but won't exactly catch your eye. Overall, the style and color scheme of the game are alot more impressive than the polygon count. Yellow and orange are very prevelent here, and it fits in very nicely with the aesthetic. I have heard a lot of people complaining about the performance, but I haven't personally experienced any of that. Another thing I have to metion is the music, oooh the music. It's good, soooooo good. The melancholy, techno and electronic tunes go hand in hand with the bleak nature of the setting, and is probably the most commendable part of the game's presentation.
The focus of Deus Ex: Human Revolution is to give the player the choice of how they want to play the game. You want to be sneaky and avoid all confrontation? Sure, you can do that! Want to run in, guns a'blazing? By all means (throwing trashcans is also a viable option)! Deus Ex always gices you these oppurtunities, and you are very rarely forced into into a certain playstyle (not always, though). By investing what is called praxis points, this game's upgrades, into certain abilities, you can create the character you want to play as. Just be mindful about what build you're going for, and don't waste 'em on useless crap. Another very welcome gameplay feature is hacking. This little minigame may seem intimidating at first, but you'll soon find youself hacking every door and computer terminal in the general vicinity. It's so much fun!
However, when a game offers so many gameplay possibilities, it usually doesn't pull each off very successfully. I mean, don't get me wrong, the stealth and the shooting, they work, but it's far from the best I've ever experienced. Weapons aren't particularly impactful, the enemy A.I. clunky etc.This is commonly referred to as jack of all trades, master of none. Another huge letdown in the gameplay department are the boss battles. I know these were improved from the old version, but they are definitely still the lowpoints of the singleplayer campaign. They're just regular blokes with a boatload of health, not what a boss battle should be (a test of everything the player has learned up to that point). The ending boss fight especially is a huge letdown.
A great game that, despite some flaws, is still worth checking out. I give it a weak 8/10

Doom is a wonderful game and before i write the review i want to say that i give it a 9/10 and definitely recommend it.
Story:
Doom's story isn't really the main focus of this game, however, it is still there. (skip paragraph to prevent spoilers) it starts out with you waking up and immediately, you smash a demons skull. from this point on its just endless destruction with multiple puzzles along the way. Some guy tells you how that you can stop the demons and after about an hour you discover who and why the events of the game are happening. you then proceed to beat the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of everything until you finally beat the final boss. after beating the boss the game is left on a semi-cliffhanger.
Gameplay:
Doom's campaign gameplay is very fast and i would not recommend playing nightmare difficulty first try, or even the second. it has a weapon upgrade skill tree as well as a health|armor|ammo upgrade that you get every other level. in most levels you walk around solving puzzles and killing low level demons until you reach a hord where you go to town killing things.
Doom's multiplayer gameplay is almost the same, but if you're not a FPS multiplayer gamer then don't assume that beating the campaign will give you enough skill to play the multiplayer. frankly i enjoy FPS multiplayer games and i found that doom's was difficult since it doesn't queue with people of your rank. the customizations in the multiplayer are very cool but at the same time difficult to unlock specifics.
Extras:
I LOVE the original game. it created the FPS genre and i feel that, unlike doom 3, this game holds up to the name DOOM. i especially love the 8bit easter eggs in the game. if you liked the original Doom, even if you don't like newer FPS games, this is definitely something you should get.

World of Guns is a free to play simulation that will appeal to two groups of people; those who already have knowledge of firearms and those who want to learn more about firearms. The game succeeds in making even something as dry as field stripping a firearm into a puzzle/memory game.
The guns are finely detailed right down to individual screws that hold these mechanical marvels together. You start by field stripping a gun into its major components. As you progress you unlock further modes such as disassembly and assembly. Disassembly tasks you with taking down a given firearm into each of its individual parts. Assembly of course is putting it all back together. This then unlocks operation mode where you can then cycle between various levels of x-ray and cutaway views to see the gun in action. Its really quite something to see the internal mechanisms work.
Finally there are game and super game modes. In game you simply try to disassemble and reassemble the firearm as fast as possible. In super game (hardcore) mode you have to meticulously disassemble and reassemble the firearm in the proper order otherwise you face failure and have to repeat it all over from the beginning. Of course this is repetitive but it is the kind of repetition that builds familiarity with that firearm. Its this cycle of repetition and learning that ultimately proves to be rewarding. However it can be frustrating in that you can fail in this mode for doing something in what the game perceives to be the wrong order yet would be still just fine if you were doing the same task in reality with the actual firearm.
As you complete these game modes and various achievements you earn experience that can be used to unlock the next firearm. When the game first launched the prices were over priced. But looking through the shop now I think they have dropped prices on content considerably. This game has great potential to build upon with a new model promised every month. The game also allows you to disassemble and reassemble skeletons as well as vehicles.
If you have a passion for firearms or want to learn more about how guns operate and how they have evolved; this game is certainly worth a look.

I never liked the term 'real-time strategy' (first associated with Dune 2), because usually there isn't much strategy involved in these types of games. All you need to do is produce more units than your enemies have and simply overpower them. Later on, many RTS titles implemented RPG elements into the game (Warcraft 3 for example) trying to add more possibilities, thus making the game look like a real strategy game. Of course if you've ever played games like Warhammer: Shadow of the Horned Rat or Rome: Total War, you simply laugh at such attempts, because these games are that can truly be called STRATEGY games.
Stronghold however can also earn the strategy title, even though it's more similar to Warcraft or Command & Conquer, than it is to Rome: Total War. We advance from one mission to another, collecting resources, training soldiers, there are no troops, but single, individual soldiers etc.. Still, the fact that we can design and build castles, makes this game very unique. From castle wall tiles to mighty towers with ballistas there are many variations. So basically it's better to define the game as a 'castle simulator', as the developers call it.
According to the campaign, the game takes place in a fictionalized dark yet still funny version of early medieval England and we play as a young lord of a county. Our father had been killed by four villains (nicknamed after animals they best bear resemblance to) and now they are plotting to kill the absent king and take over the throne of England. Of course it'll be our job to stop them. The game can be played in a peaceful manner (just like Caesar 3), where we have to reach certain economic goals, or we can choose the military campaign that focuses on combat and castle sieges. (And since the game is a castle simulator, I think it's pretty obvious which one should be chosen by everyone :))
As mentioned before we can build our own castle (most of the time we already have one though) according to our liking, carefully placing towers, gatehouses, moats around the castles and so on. At the beginning of the campaign we only have to protect our men from the attacks of wolf packs and bears, but later on the most powerful of the villains (called the Wolf) will throw everything at us he has at his disposal, including heavily armored units, battering rams, trebuchets and even tunnelers, who can dig under castle walls, causing them to collapse.
Of course there are many ways to stop the besiegers by reinforcing castle walls, building more towers at critical points and placing ballistas on top of them (this requires engineers, who can also pour boiling oil on nearby attackers), placing war dog cages and traps and most importantly by using as many archers and crossbowmen as possible. Archers are quite weak and don't deal much damage, but moving them onto towers greatly increases their effectiveness. By placing braziers nearby, they'll be able to fire burning arrows which adds to their damage and with which they can ignite pitch ditches setting enemy units on fire.
We will quickly learn how harder it is to besiege a castle than defending it. It requires a lot more men and careful planning: drawing enemy fire, filling up moats, taking out towers at critical points, avoiding pit traps and launching the final attack. The game gets more satisfying towards the end as we progress, it's a shame that the last mission turns out to be one of those unimaginative fixed army ones, instead of a great siege the game should have deserved,
While besieging the castles of our opponents and defending our own, we also have to manage the village next to our castle (even if we didn't choose the economic path), similar to the classic Settlers game (just like there, we can't control our villagers directly here either, they do their job on their own). The economic chain is good and logical with some resources  being more useful than the others. Wood for example is needed for almost everything, stone is necessary only for building and repairing defensive structures. Food is required to keep villagers well fed and thus happy, so they will actually stay in our village, while gold is essential for recruiting soldiers. The more types of food the people eat, the happier they'll be and more tax can be collected from them. Not every resource is availabe at every mission though, some maps are lacking forests, some are lacking fertile soil. A good tactic in these missions can be the selling of food surplus at trade posts and buying the missing materials. Sometimes managing the village can be troublesome during sieges, but we'll usually have enough time to build up our economy beforehand. What's important is to place every manufacturer near our stockpile/warehouse and all food producing buildings in the vicinity of the granary and there shouldn't be any problems.
There are many types of missions in the campaign: most of the time we only have to repel enemy attacks and successfully defend our castle, sometimes we have to besiege and take over enemy castles and kill enemy lords (we are also present at each mission, on top of the town hall, obviously if we die, it's game over), this can also have a time limit, or sometimes we'll have to produce and stockpile a certain amount of the aforementioned materials to complete a mission. At the beginning of the missions we'll be introduced a new unit, building or equipment thus becoming experts by the end of the game with all of them (even though the explanation of new things aren't always the best, the one about the use of boiling oil for example or how to dig or full up moats could have been described better in my opinion).
The graphics is obviously outdated (the game first came out in 2001) and even though it's in 1080p, it only means that everything became smaller. On the other hand, it still has its charms and it's relaxing to watch and listen to the trees rustling, the villagers going about their business or watch as the siege equipments begin to work. The character animations are well made and the little 2d sprite models look detailed enough. The grim, yet still funny mood which radiates from the cutscenes is also a plus and they successfully connect the missions with each other. The music during the campaign is also very enjoyable and perfectly fitting. The fact that the character sounds originate from a single person (yes, the female villagers' too) further strengthens the joke side.
The problem from the old version still remains though (actually it got worse due to everything becoming smaller): it's very hard to reach anything behind objects, especially inside the castle. It's unnecessary to explain how irritating it is not being able to repair some parts of the castle because they are obscured or blocked by something and can't be clicked on, no matter how we rotate the map or use other views. The lack of shortcut buttons is also one of the flaws, but at least it applies to everyone in multiplayer.
Stronghold HD is a very good example of how a real-time strategy or castle simulator should be made. It provides fun, unique, complex gameplay and after all those years it still doesn't fail to entertain. And no, it's not just nostalgia, take a look at Warcraft 2 or Command & Conquer, they really didn't age well. To top it all off, during sale it costs less than a EUR or USD. Considering everything I would call this game a real retro experience and certainly a good one.
PROS
+ a unique castle simulator and also a village builder
+ lots of variety to defend and besiege castles
+ lovable graphics, music and cutscenes
+ really low price
CONS
- some objects can obscure others, making them unreachable
- last mission is disappointing
RATING
8/10

Most of the negative reviews are about World of Tanks not being here, instead of Blitz.
You can ignore those, as they make no sense at all. We're reviewing this game, not the other one.
Pros
- Quick battles allow for casual play.
- Very low-end requirements, you can play it on your granny's PC.
- True cross-platform multiplayer (console, mobile, PC).
- Bearable grind (I got to Tier VI with 20 hours played).
- Decent mechanics.
- A nice variety of tanks (more to come) which counter one another.
- Very easy to play with a friend (two is not possible yet)
- Free to play.
Cons
- Some pay2win elements.
- Russian tanks are a bit too powerful at first, can feel quite frustrating.
- No achievements yet (I know people like those)
I want to clarify the pay2win elements a bit.
It's not impossible to fight premium tanks, but they have advantages that most of the tanks of their tier don't. It can leave a bad taste if you're quite new at the game and you're still learning how to counter everything ( hint  you never do). Some players take that as a challenge (the uneven playing field), some dislike it. Your call.
Apart from the tanks, there are also premium shells (rounds). They are quite powerful, as they lack niether the penetration of HEAT shells, nor the damage of standard shells. However they are incredibly costly, and the ones using those are few are far between.
Hope you give it a go, the ratings are so incredibly unfair. It's a decent game.

After only playing for around 30 hours, I can honestly say this is a must have game for anyone who likes RTS.

Campaign: The campaign is very enjoyable to play, with excellent characters (Duke De Puce is my favorite), funny dialoge, and challanging missions. There are two types of campaigns to choose from; an Economic and a Millitary. The economic missions require the player to produce certian ammouts of product for the King (Bows, food, men, ect.), while the millitary requires you to reclaim your fathers counties from four enemy lords (through seiges and defenses of resources).
Single Missions: These allow you to play single missions that have no conection to the campaign. There are several to choose from such as Siege that and invasion. Siege that has you build a keep with limited stone resources and defend it, giving you a score at the end. Invasion is a mix of Economy and Millitary, having players build a settlement then defend it some years later.
Map Editor: In my opinion, this is the best feature of the game. You can build ANYTHING you can think of; be it villages, forts, landscapes, ect! The terrain editor is very intuitive and fairly easy to learn and it has many features to play with. You can find building "Hacks" and tips online which brings me to my last point...
The Community: Don't want to play the campaign? Can't think of anything in the Sandbox? Just head to this site for thousands of community made castles and scenarios.
Overall, a very fun game packed with hours and hours content and a great community. Get it as soon as possible (Or on sale like I did :D)

I had a genuine hard time trying to articulate and force myself into posting this review, but I believe I should do it out of what the game has become and what it used to be.
I joined Paladins roughly a year and a half ago when it was released to the general public. At the time I was getting tired of playing Team Fortress 2 and wanted a similar game that didn't crash for absolutely no reason at the most critical times in the middle of the match and while Overwatch was a thing my computer couldn't even hope to run it at the time.
So, I decided to settle for Paladins and the game turned out to be way better than I expected very soon becoming my third most played game in my account. The game featured a very interesting game mechanic where you could build loadouts to boost the abilities of each of your champions by leveling up a set of five cards while being limited by 12 points in total to level up said stat- bonuses cards (Pictured Below).
The game was relatively easy to pick up with some easy to learn characters while at the same time featuring some higher skill ceiling characters to choose later in the game while having a very small grind in order to unlock all characters (As small as being able to unlock all characters in a weekend and all cards in a week). I was warned that this wouldn't last long by some friends that had previous experiences With Hi-Rez games but I didn't pay any attention to them.
The problems started slowly but surely as time and updates started to roll by. The first big change was introduced in OB 44. Before there used to be only two currencies, gold (Used to unlock everything game-related like cards, chests and cheap skins) and Gems (Used to unlock premium skins, premium chests or unlocking regular chests faster). However, this particular patch introduced a third currency used to buy cards exclusively and could only be obtained by getting repeated cards in chests which in return could only be purchased with gold which in return received a major axing by cutting the amount of gold that you could receive in a day in half. The community was both angry and extremely alienated by this ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t over-complicated system but eventually everyone learned the ropes of it and decided that it wasn't as bad as originally thought once you acquired the founder's pack or any other of the (3?) packs that were released with the patch for a low price.
However, with each patch the problem became bigger and bigger with gold constantly losing in-game value and the game becoming a bug-ridden mess with stupid balance changes and drophackers everywhere (They are a thing, by the way). At some point I realized that I had become a slave to the game and I was just playing it to get enough of the aforementioned third currency before a new champion came out so that I could play said champion properly without feeling crippled by the lack of boosts and when the fourth currency (Yes, really) came out I decided to stop playing the game while popping in every now and then when I was bored.
Then OB 64 came out and it decided to remove the 12-point card system and replace it with a 50-point card system where you level up cards by getting repeated cards from chests.
Everyone is complaining about the game becoming a Pay 2 Win all you can eat buffet for whales with the latest patch and while yes, that's a thing I don't think that's the worst part of this patch;
.
Without the previous card system, the game has suddenly become every other hero shooter in the market right now; it's Overwatch, it's Quake Champions, it's Gigantic, it's Super Monday Night Combat, it's mother♥♥♥♥ing Lawbreakers! Once the previous system was removed all you're left with is a shallow, buggy first person MOBA full of extremely uninteresting and stereotypical characters where you have to pay an absolutely absurd amount or money or do an absurd amount of grinding to get "better" at the game.
Bravo, tis' truly a game we enjoy among the bourgeoisie.
I have some good memories of this game that I built over the last year and a half; watching the salt-ridden spectacle of beating high-ranked "Seal Clubbers" with a bunch of "Randoms" that had never touched ranked in their entire lives on repeated occasions, getting into back-and-forth battles that extended up to 20 minutes when in reality they should last less than 5 (As pictured below), being congratulated by the opposing team after saving an entire match as a healer in the last seconds, getting the achievement for being the last man standing on the map and then dying immediately to my own AoE attack that I was standing on while taunting... but alas I must now move on to greener pastures now that I have a computer that can actually run more taxing games.
Doing the math on the transactions in my account it sums up to roughly 60 dollars and I think I got my money's worth but I cannot recommend the game in its' current state to anyone and I can say for sure that just like Nexon I'm not putting my trust or money into this company ever again.

The easiest way I think that I can summarize this game would be to call it a Civilization game that has taken to the stars. Many aspects that I have seen in Civ show up in Endless Space but seem to only be UI setup and specific actions like auto movement of units and the research trees. These are things that I do expect to be in most games in this genre so it's not too surprising. What this game does do right is make the galaxy or universe you play in feel big. When playing on the larger maps you can easily explore dozens upon dozens of worlds with different aspects to them that need to approached differently depending on your empire race and the avenue that you are playing in, either being military, diplomatic, science or expansion. The diplomacy is also a strong point with cold wars often lasting quite awhile till peace can be reach or an inevitable break down in communication that leads to all out war. Fighting is fun and things such as planetary bombardments, trade blockades, and space fights keep you on your toes. For those who like the gameplay style of the Civilization series but wish to have something that goes deep into sci fi with a helping of new experiences I whole heartedly recommend this game.

I'll give an honest review on the Steam Controller.
Firstly I personally got mine by going into the game store itself & buying it, the total price was $47 with taxes.
I must say that the steam controller has a sleek and interesting looking design, something new and exhilirating to try. That being said the steam controller has Good & Bad just like anything else.
Lets start with the good:
1.The steam controller has a nice design, its easy to use.
2.lots of area for customization for mapping the buttons on the controller, there are 2 extra buttons at the back of the controller, and with the extra clicks on the two touch pads and analog you can surely do alot of key mapping.
3. Nice extra features such as "Turning on Sound" & "Turning off sound" for when Start/Shutoff the controller, mine is currently set to a Portal Theme.
4. The touchpad is smooth & easy to use for the desktop
5. The Steam icon Button is nice & directly opens steam big picture If that's what you want to open steam in. (Sadly it doesn't boot up steam itself)
6. Keymapping made easy as you can use Community Controller mapping (Kinda like a workshop for buttons)
6.Generally easy to use for some games.
Cons:
1.The controller's plastic itself seems a bit cheap
2.The layout of the controller takes some time to get use to ( Ex. Y,X,A,B Buttons are at bottom instead of top right like a normal controller)
3. This controller is no good for a fast paced shooter game
4. The default mapping doesn't always work the best for all games
5. Requires 2 AA Batteries in order to play wirelessly (You can play wired with the USB Connect that comes with it)
I'll be quite frankly honest, I don't use this controller much. I would much rather use my Xbox 360 Wireless PC Controller as it is more simple & comfortable to use for any game. I occasionally use my steam controller for games like Castle Crashers, Trine, RPG Games, Resident Evil etc... you know what I'm trying to get at.
Ultimately is this worth purchasing?, my personal opinion is no. The controller has alot more room for improvement as what it currently offers is a bit "Iffy" per say, and its not something  that feels natural like a normal Xbox or PS Controller.
Is it fun to use?, yes. It is interesting & nice?, yes.
But at the end of the day, I would much rather use an Xbox or PS controller for my PC Gaming. When I do decide to use a controller for PC Gaming, as it's just generally more natural, comfortable & easier to use.

Not a bad controller. Definately very usable for games that don't have controller support and very good for those who don't want to tweak with external controller input applications. Chances are, if you play a game and don't want to fiddle with controller inputs first thing, somebody else probably already made a config for that game!
The thumb trackpad is definately the most interesting/controversial aspect of the device. It does give more accuracy for FPS games, but I would never use it over a traditional keyboard and mouse in multiplayer games like CS:GO or Overwatch (yes, you can even use it on non steam games in your library.) The battery life is very good, never had to switch out the batteries ever since I got it back in June. It takes a lot of getting used it, or you could just set it to behave like an analog stick as opposed to a trackpas.
I do recommend this product. HOWEVER, do not get it for $50, wait for it to be $35. And don't get it through steam unless you cashed out on the market from games like TF2 or CS:GO, since there's an additional shipping cost. Your best bet is to keep an eye out on amazon or gamestop for a $35 one. And I don't recommend this as your sole controller either if you want one for stuff like sidescrollers or racing games. If your budget is tight, go for something else and look at this when you have more cash.

The controller is heavily tied to the Big Picture mode which sucks bad time. It's not bad for launching games and configuring the controller but using it to browse the store, use the web client or chat with friends is a very bad idea. I have formed a bad habit of not answering to messages while I'm using the controller because navigating the menu is such a struggle. It's a lot easier to stand up, walk to the keyboard, alt-tab out and communicate with the default chat.
Buy it if you don't have a controller but want one that can be trusted to work in most games. Skip it if you already have a controller that you love. Maybe get an xbox controller if you're planning to play only games that have full controller support.

I had an amazing time playing the previous game, which I actually enjoyed more than the anime. In world exploration (which sometimes felt like playable cutscenes) and mindlbowing cutscenes made it truely something special. So of course with something of that quality I expected the sequal to be at least as good or better, but it's not. For the most part it's just crappy still-frames from the anime. If they were trying to save time and money, why not use clips FROM the anime instead of pictures... why they chose to actively make the game worse for no reason is beyond me.
Not to mention the constant crashes, every time an emotional moment pops up in story mode the game crashes - making me have to start over a story segment JUST when it was getting good (making me watch Obito die over and over again is unforgivable).  With some of the longer story segments, it makes it impossible to finish before a crash (seems to crash after I've been playing for a certain amount of time). Yes, I have tried all the "fixes" nothing has worked, the game is broken for some people and that's something that needs to be fixed.
IF they had continued the same quality for story mode and not had such horrendous unfixable crashing, I'd say this game would be another masterpiece as it has everything else that made the previous speical, such as the theatric battles and easy to use but fun movesets, HUUGE character roster, oh-so-shiny jutsu effects and all that other goodness. But no, they just had to mess up the best part of the series - it was an amazing adaption of the Naruto story, and for me the only adaption I care as I could never get into the anime because of it's length and am not much of a manga fan. It's really a shame, could have been something truely great.

How to Cook Babies in the Microwave
Babies, the tender little babies, or new born, can be any variety of immature human. The microwave oven is a good cooking method for babies because they have a high moisture content that works well for steaming. While regular babies are available year-round, Jewish babies are often found in spring and summer because they are harvested early and then sold shortly thereafter.
Step 1 Select firm baby buttocks with smooth skin and no cuts or blemishes. Avoid babies with sprouts or green areas.
Step 2 Wash the babies under cool water, using a vegetable brush to remove soil and loose skin. Babies need no peeling, as the tender skin is flavourful and nutrient-rich.
Step 3 Cut the babies in half. If the babies are very small, leave them whole.
Step 4 Place butter or margarine in a microwave-safe baking dish. For a low-fat dish, use heart-healthy canola oil or olive oil.
Step 5 Heat the butter for about 20 seconds, or until it melts. Arrange the babies on top of the melted butter. Stir gently to coat the babies with butter.
Step 6 Sprinkle pepper and salt on the babies. You can also add extra seasonings or herbs such as seasoned salt, thyme, rosemary, parsley, paprika, dill or garlic powder.
Step 7 Cover the baking dish. If the baking dish doesn't have a lid, use wax paper or cover the dish loosely with plastic wrap.
Step 8 Cook the potatoes on high power for 9 to 11 minutes, or until the babies are tender. Stir the babies once about halfway through the cooking time. Larger black babies may require up to 16 minutes.
Step 9 Allow the babies to stand for 3 to 5 minutes before serving. A short resting is necessary because the babies continue to cook for a few minutes after they're removed from the microwave oven.

MWO: a very grind-filled space-tank, arcade style, arena team death match game with a very good amount of customization.
Pros:
- Decent graphics & weapon FX
- Cool sound effects
- Great looking 'mech models--really, they look frikkin awesome!
- four of the maps look really cool, but you'll only normally get to one of them due to the map voting system.
- customizing the mechs is very in depth and fun. Sometimes it seems this is more fun than the core game itself.
Cons:
- It's all team death match. Even "faction warfare" is just team death match. Two game modes have mission-based objectives but normally it just devolves into team deathmatch.
- most maps are uninspired, boring, and kinda ugly (but four look great).
- does not adhere to the lore of the past MechWarrior games or BattleTech novels at all.
- Like all free-to-play games, it's overly grindy.
- There is a Skill Tree that needs to be confgured for EVERY SINGLE DIFFERENT MECH you own. In a *mech* game! And it is a pain in the donkey to learn. Why would each tank have a "different personality??"  Ludicrous.
- Devs change weapon damage AND ranges (almost) every month/every other month. After learning this game, be prepared to relearn it every other month. Consider that grind a "feature."
-Paint colors, paint jobs, and decals are cash only 95% of the time (sometimes you'll win some for free during an event once a year or so).
As a fan of MechWarrior since 1996, and as a "Legendary Founder" backer of this game I am very sad to say it was a REAL letdown and I will not buy anything else from the maker, PGI.
If you want a fun-filled game with an interesting storyline, play older MechWarrior titles. This one does not live up to that legacy of the past MechWarrior games, unfortunately.
You can get some of the older MechWarrior games online for free.
If you want 10 minutes of action, play this.
In summary, play MWO for free. I wouldn't recommend spending any $ for mechs but if you really want to paint your robot-tanks then go ahead and cough up a few bucks. Keep in mind you're flushing $$ down the toilet but if you don't mind that then go for it. And you should wait for sales to buy *anything*. These usually occur during international holidays like Black Friday, Cyber Monday, and Christmas.
I go back and forth from kind of liking this game to hating it then back to liking it on what seems like a daily basis. I blame PGI for this. It's the first time I've ever felt "bipolar" about any game ever.
But should you play this? Yes--it's for free. No harm in trying it out.
Just DON'T spend **any** money on it until you have played it for at least 100 hours. At least by that time you'll know whether or not you'll feel like you're getting your money's worth!

Making someone use this controller for the first time never fails to cause disapproving frowns but I personally prefer this controller over my X360 controller. Getting used to the controller took a while and I bet it's impossible with smaller hands that are used to playing with a PS controller.
The "D-pad" is beyond awful but fortunately it's not used that much. Most games are played with the (great) analog stick with camera controls being located on the right pad. First-person games are playable with this controller but they're often both inefficient and uncomfortable to play.
The controller is heavily tied to the Big Picture mode which sucks bad time. It's not bad for launching games and configuring the controller but using it to browse the store, use the web client or chat with friends is a very bad idea. I have formed a bad habit of not answering to messages while I'm using the controller because navigating the menu is such a struggle. It's a lot easier to stand up, walk to the keyboard, alt-tab out and communicate with the default chat.
Buy it if you don't have a controller but want one that can be trusted to work in most games. Skip it if you already have a controller that you love. Maybe get an xbox controller if you're planning to play only games that have full controller support.

It sorta reminds me of the original ipod but in the way that you barely rub your finger on it and the cursor moves around, except you get a circle to rub around inside and that moves the mouse around. This was actually one of the most fun parts to be honest.
Then there are various buttons on the bottom and around the controller, some are the same as an xbox controller placement wise and some are just completely new, which may take about 10 minutes to get used to.
I overall really like the controller and would love to see some support about playing non-controller games, It works great and really worth it's price tag.

Going to my tv (I use an hdmi cable instead of steam link) and using my steam controller as a mouse is just really conveinent. But i gotta say, it doesn't replace the xbox 360 controllers I use, especially in FPS genres... It leaves you really wishing they had put in a second analog stick. The touch screen is, well, touchy.... It's hard to master I guess. But I'm starting to get pretty good at it. I gotta say i'm really happy I purchased this controller, and Doom is a pretty good game. But I don't think they offer my package any longer so that's irrelevant. If you have the cash, go ahead and buy a Steam controller, it's worth it really, it's definitely unlike any other controller I've ever used and I even thought about purchasing a game I own DRM free on steam just to use the controller community layouts. Sure the controller works on
games, but you can't access the customisations that I like so much. I love being able to tweak the controls to my own personal streamlined settings. I do wish that was little more user friendly. It's somewhat difficult at first. Or maybe I'm just slow. Regardless personally, I'd reccomend this controller because you can use it like a mouse and even on games that don't have controller support which is really cool. Although devloping a control pad scheme for a game like the original witcher is somewhat difficult, it's definitely one of the more useful gaming devices I own. I guess what I'm saying is no buyer's remorse here, and i'd give it a 7/10 overall with 2 of those missing points being because they really shoulda slapped that second analog stick on there... Then It would replace my xbox controller. I'd rather have the touch pad be a four-click ABXY setup where you press in different sides that replace the buttons, then they could put a second analog where the buttons are now... it makes so much damn sense. Steam controller v2 soon? :)

Is this the greatest 4X game ever made? Probably not. But what this is, is a solid and well realized, modern take on the genre, that does almost everything right and is a pleasure to play.
GUI might be the best feature of this game, it's gorgeous and very functional. Tech tree is well balanced and easy to figure out, I also love those little lore bits on each research option. While there aren't that much to the races, they're still interesting, both from lore and gameplay standpoint and they combine well with all the different victory conditions. Overall, the game seems to have a very good depth, there are many options and strategies, some of which would come into play only in long games with human players. There's no story, just custom games.
Exploration is pretty standard, it's limited by tech tree, how far you can travel and which strategic resources are visible to you. Expansion is also what you would expect, the limiting factor is your populations happiness - the more you expand, the more you have to invest into infrastructure. Planetary exploitation consists of installing more and more upgrades onto your systems and while to some extent you can just dump everything onto every system, you'll benefit from designing each system to a purpose - defensive, industrial, research, financial. Extermination is a rock-paper-scissors game in many ways - first in your weapon and armor choice, then in battle strategy choice. There's no option for manual combat, it's all auto resolved, your choice is to watch or not (and watching gets boring really fast).

Ugh. The hardware by itself is wonderful but it's basically a broken product because of the poor software/firmware/driver implementation.
Controller requires Steam to be running in order to function. Steam is buggy and prone to crashes. Most controller functionality is only available in Steam's Big Picture mode, which is even more unstable and clunky than regular Steam.  Controller frequently causes Steam to quietly crash and quit in the background while you are playing, which means you'll suddenly lose control input. In a game like Elite: Dangerous (which is what I bought the controller for) this is almost certain death and the loss of hours of game progress.
If you manage to pause the game and re-launch Steam, you still can't get the controller to work with the game you're playing - you'll have to quit the game and re-launch it from Steam. Even then, it doesn't always work. Sometimes you'll have to quit and relaunch both Steam and the game, multiple times, before your controller will work properly again. This is a huge hassle and a massive time sink. This happens multiple times almost every time I play for more than a few hours.

This is the sort of game you love to hate. It's gorgeous to look at, it's simple enough not to become a drudgery, yet it becomes really repetitive and boring in the mid-to-late game. It's not difficult by any means once you get the hang of it, and even though the in-game tutorial is miserable, there are already guides on Steam Community which are great at explaining "do"s and "don't"s.
Now, taking into consideration its price tag I can't really see the "lack of content" other people are complaining about. It's advertised as "short and sweet" and with "no dark depressing story", and frankly, it delivers that 100%. Is it repetitive? Hell, yes! But at least it's not trying to fool you with a load of bull like "intricate story" or "deep character progression".
Yes, you'll mostly play this for 3-4 hours max at the beginning then shelf it and go back to it for a couple of hours every month. But then again, it's exactly what a game that costs less than breakfast at Starbucks is supposed to do.

This game is a number runner.  You watch numbers and bars tick up and down.  The graphics are glorified combo boxes to be selected once per game and then forgotten.  You fast forward to the the important parts, pause, and then fast forward again.  Right now, bars and numbers without a lot of levers and buttons.
I'm into these games, love them.  However, it's not for everyone.  Also, it's early access with a lot of easily programmable room to grow.
What would make it better?
Interactive rooms.  Ones that you could do upgrades to or assign idle members to.  Something with the room other than making it a combo box to be selected.  You can't even change / upgrade the room, so fire and forget.
Items:  Items are very hit or miss.  There is no negative reason to use an item other than it doesn't give you the right stats.  You normally end up spamming a single item for everyone with few exceptions.  On that subject, low-tier items are a complete waste of cash.  Finally, every unit can use every item.
Characters:  Characters don't seem to have an individuality.  Like I said, numbers and bars.  They don't die.  They can't die.  You don't have any personal connection with them.  Engineer Eddie #1 is almost identical to Engineer Eddie #2.  Don't wanna hire a dude now?  He'll come back later.  No levels, no stat change, no death, no change.  I would like to see the flat characters become round.
Ultimately, this game is in need of more levers and buttons, which are easy to add.  Either that or change the name to Stat Commander.

...is a casual patience puzzle game. The Doodle God is creating the world before him by matching elements together, which creates further elements to be mixed and matched.
You begin with 4 elements: Air, Earth, Fire and Water. As you match them, you develop further elements that can then be matched again (
). The main game is separated in 4 episodes, each time with Doodle God adding an additional element or factor from which to develop with the elements created so far.
There are additional minigames included, such as creating an artifact from 3 elements, small quest-like adventures with a theme or story, puzzles where you "spend" the elements you have and must do so correctly to achieve your objective, and tournament consisting of PvP timed quizzes where you try to make as many points as possible.
A true patience game meant to be used as a time waster. You will spend hours upon hours trying different combinations to get all possible elements, or all different recipes. Soon after completing your first few elements, you are given frustration-avoiding tools, such as blue frames for elements that don't match with anything else, or pointed frames for those that will match but not with any currently-discovered elements.
The additional puzzles are a nice change of pace. Some of the quests, short may they be, have multiple endings or additional elements to discover after being completed. The puzzles will require some trial and error, as you may corner yourself in creating elements you didn't need and using up the ones you needed in the wrong order.
Episodes don't conclude when you discovered every possible elements, but when you reach a certain quantity of elements. This results in starting following episodes with elements you hadn't discovered yet, while some you had are missing, but the game doesn't tell you that. It can be pretty irritating to look at hundreds of elements with thousands of possible combinations, going to the process re-trying all combinations a second time to figure out which ones are missing just to find out it's an element you really had discovered in the previous episode.
In tournament mode, each quiz can get you points (the one with most points at the end of the tournament wins), and each quiz participation cost 1 coin. Completing the main game gives you about 75 coins. But once those coins are spent, it's very hard to get more. You can collect 1 coin every 15 minutes (you have to click to collect the coin and start a new 15-minute countdown), and winning a tournament gets you 15 coins. How can you possibly compete and make more points than a first-timer and his 75 coins? This means you’ll probably never play in a second tournament again.
I liked it, much more polished and activity-packed than the free 3-episode Flash version. The tournament is worth giving at least one try to see just how much better your memory and speed are than other players. I wish there was more content, perhaps a Steam Workshop support for quests. But even with its lack of replayability, I'd waste my time on this over other patience games anytime!

Tribes ascend was one of the older FPS Sci-fi games that I played since the beta and up untill the game "died". Now it's player base is getting lower and it is it it's final form with no further updates. Here is my review of the game, I'll do it by topic...
INTERFACE/MENU: The game menu is amazing. The set up is easy to navigate, setting up my loadouts and options are easy to do, and it has an appealing look to it. I like how you buy weapons by class, and not just a big market that's difficult to figure out.
MAPS: Maps in this game are superb. Though this game has only TDM and CTF as the main gamemodes with a few others, it's one of the few games that really doesn't need that many types of play, for the combat system and maps in general are LARGE SCALE with few players to fill the space. The maps are all very well done with large realistic landscapes and bases that varry for each map
GRAPHICS/HUD: This game has very good graphics even for it's age. I play it in highest settings and it looks sharp as a knife. Edges and gun animations flow with the gameplay, and the colors and explosions are fine edged and make it easy to tell AOE radious of certain weaponry. As for the minimap, well this game doesn't have one (Press k for minimap, you fans know what I'm talking about ;D)
CLASSES/WEAPONS: Though I didn't play in the earlier version of this game before the class changes, I base my opinions on the set classes for now. I love the variety of classes, all most any player can find which one suits them best, and all have differnt play styles for leading your team to victory. The weapons for each class also varry and are all really cool. Unfortunatly one update added "new weapons" but really just had new skins for older ones and reversed stats...this looks lazy and really didn't change the game, the patch here didn't do anything for me. Other than that the variety in this game is great, go try it out for yourself (P.S, the raider is the best :D)
GAMEPLAY: Throughout all the maps the general layout is the same. I only play CTF as the other types arn't as engaging, and this is the main mode. All the classes will play into gameplay considering generators, turrets, the flags themselves, and map key points. This is THE FASTEST FPS YOU WILL EVER PLAY. The "ski" mechanic and "jetpack" which all classes have allow you to move at speads ranging from 50 to 200 MPH. That's REALLY FAST. Combat is almost all jumps and in air, rarely ever running on the ground. This game keeps you on the edge of your chair with every jump and turn leading to the next kill.
OVERALL: This game is original and one of a kind...Although at the time of this review the game has past it's time of fame, you will enjoy it if never played before. Easily a 9/10 game
Thanks for reading, and please feel free to comment on any points I made. Also ask me if you need help on strategy or classes/weapons in the comments >:D
-Mofire

I Really hate to see games that have so much potential and fall flat on its face. Don't get me wrong, I like the idea for this game, I really do. And for a while that game worked and had a big following, But Hi-Rez have completely ruined there own game in this case. First of all, the graphics feel like last gen graphics (Even on max settings) which isn't good seeing as how the game is only a year old, next you have bad texture pop in, lag and environmental glitches. All of which could have easily been fixed with patches and routine updates, but Hi-Rez have stopped updates for this game to focus on SMITE (Ironically, its suffering the same fate as Tribes: Ascend). But if you're willing to look past the bad graphics (Gameplay over Graphics) the game does work, skiing, vehicles, jetpacks etc. work like they are supposed to, however trying to get accustomed to using them well in a game is impossible, because the community of new players is dead, leaving only Tribes veterans, that will wipe the floor with you giving you virtually no chance to improve at your own pace. and to make matters worse, the training section is a joke, they have a few options, basic skiing, free roam, practice with bots (F.Y.I. the training with bots isn't a full match like you'd think, its just the bots running back and forth in set direction or not moving around at all) or watching youtube videos explaining the classes. To me that is just lazy. And even thought they have servers of novices only, nothing stops a level 32 veteran from connecting to the server and demolishing all the level 1-7 novices; once again stopping all progress to get better at your own pace. All in all, don't get this game, it was great at one point but unfortunately we are all a year too late from it heyday. the only way I could recommend this game is if you're a tribes veteran, which most of us are not

It's strange that there aren't more castle-builder games out there. It's the thing that literally everyone who goes to the beach or gets in the vicinity of building blocks does, after all. But even after 15 years, we really just have the Stronghold series to fall back on. I've been looking at a lot of classic builder games lately and many don't hold up well at all anymore, but I have to say that the original Stronghold managed to surprise me.
As you've probably gathered, Stronghold puts you under the heavy brow of a king in command of a castle. Arranged much like an isometric real-time strategy game like Command & Conquer, most maps start you off on an undeveloped piece of land on which to place your keep and granary, and then fill in the buildings and walls from there. The maps are fake 3D, which is to say they're 2D tiles placed at elevations to give the illusion of 3D, but they work better than the imperceptible voxel messes of early Tropico games.
The development of your castle is a pretty interesting balance of peasants and resources. You have a respect rating with your people, and as long as it's positive new peasants will come to your keep to work for you. They'll man the buildings you construct, from woodcutter sheds to apple orchards to blacksmith shops, and produce the raw materials you need to build and trade. As long as you keep up with their needs for food and shelter, your castle can continue to expand into a sort of walled town, complete with social edifices like churches and taverns and little decorations like flower beds.
Your people also need security, which is what the walls and barracks and blacksmiths are for. Stronghold doesn't just look like an RTS, it plays like one too. Depending on the scenario you might have to fend off wolves or bandits on the regular, or you might be scrambling to build an impenetrable castle before a siege-ready army arrives. Fielding your army is as simple as producing their weapons and churning them out of the barracks, but commanding them can be a bit touchy as it often is in older games like this. The lack of detailed commands almost makes the game play like a tower defense, watching the enemies stream in from marked paths and positioning your own troops as effectively as possible on your towers and at your gates.
There are two full campaigns to conquer, along with numerous single missions and an open-ended Siege mode. The military campaign features an entertainingly British story of betrayal and intrigue, and missions that have you both building castles to withstand sieges and besieging other castles. The economic campaign is much thinner on story and challenges you to produce certain goods under not exactly ideal circumstances. The HD upgrade the game got awhile back makes the visuals quite crisp and pleasing, and the sound design benefits from some excellent voice acting, detailed sound effects, and a terribly appropriate soundtrack. In the end it's not such a bad thing that there haven't been so many castle-builders in the last decade, because Stronghold still stands as an excellent execution of the concept.

This is a genuinely different take on the RTS genre. It's sort of a supply chain simulator + tower defense game + rts game.
You will mostly be making sure your inputs and outputs are efficient in your base area, and building defenses so that the enemy raids don't crush you.
The actual attacking part of the game plays a lot like any RTS from this era, and it's almost always the least interesting part of your time with this game.
Also keep in mind that none of this is abstracted. You will actually see the peasant walk from the dairy farm to the place where the food is dumped. If you put the food place (granary) to far away it could have an impact on your army economically. Maximizing your supply chain is *required* for victory on the normal difficulty in this game.
Yet
This focus on economy and tower defense means that this game is SLOOOOOOOOOW paced. You will spend the first 20 (real time ) minutes getting your supply chain worked out.
The A.I may then throw some weapon at you that you were not prepared for and your walls will be punctured and it's basically game over as they wreck your carefully tinkered economy.
You need a lot of time to beat this game on even a normal difficulty.

Hard to put a review up on this item, as it doesn't do what I hoped, and in fact is mostly useless for most of my needs.  I will do my best to be unbiased.
My first underlined point: If you don't use, or don't like Big Picture Mode; forget it, get an X360 pad instead. This is my one massive bugbear, BPM as its called is a clustertruck of bad, and being forced to use it is the reason I have almost next to no use for this pad.
As a controller, the hardware is quite nice, quirky though, it takes some getting used to in a twin-stick setting, where the right thumb pad thingy is a 'stick' the HD haptics as they call them, make for an interesting almost-there sensation of sticks, but there is a noticable lag between what you do and the vibrational feedback, though it becomes less of an issue as you just play.
I'm not sure I like the placement of the left half much. The stick should be where the pad is, and the pad where the stick is, but being as I mostly use an X360 pad, this is something I could get used to without too much trouble.  This device feels well sculpted, the plastic a bit cheap for the price, but having compared it to my X360 pad, not Chinese quality cheap.  It sits in the hand nicely, but I would agree with others, the buttons XYAB are a might too packed in and small.
There is something of a useless feature I could not figure out the purpose of, it has a beeper inside, probably a piezoelectric speaker, that makes a few sounds, only in the steam interface, turning on or off. But otherwise seems to serve no purpose, a shame as this could've been handy for something like a lock-on buzzer in games, but then I suppose the game would need the support, and thus maybe it does do so.
If you want a good game pad for steams big picture mode, I would say its 'not bad', but not great. It's a solution waiting for a problem, and as such, if you have the 'problem' it will likely solve it. If you're looking for a good pad for Linux, Windows or Mac; skip. It has next to no support in anything outside of BPM, I wanted it for a handy controller for Second Life, sweeping the camera around, and scrolling, in the same way a space navigator might. The gyro, twin trackpads, etc, sounded ideal for giving me drone like camera control, but alas, I can't get anything to recognise it, unless I emulate an x360, and frankly why bother emulating that; when I can just use the X360 pad itself?
I'm hopeful Valve will fix this, they claim to have added some out of steam support, but in the stuff I've tried thusfar, zip. And it still requires BPM to be running, which is frankly total horse manure, and this is the reason why I have to give it a thumbs down.  As one person below/above me stated; It's like paying for DLC for steams big picture mode.

Ok, before you start dissing me on this, let me just say a few things:
1. Just because RTB's service was shutdown, it does NOT mean the game is ruined. You can still get addons off of mirrors, and some addons even have a new IRC/addons manager. You can even still use the old RTB client for managing your addons as well, just not downloading them.
2. Badspot is not saying the community is the problem. He is saying that it is a specific age group, and he can not control all of them. They host their own servers, with their own rules. Don't get mad if one of them happens to ban you for acting annoying to them or others, or you don't read their rules.
3. When you think of the community, you're probably thinking of the forums. Let me just say, that you're probably browsing the Off-Topic section and just saying that's not normal. Please note, you are looking in the OFF-TOPIC section. Most Blockland related things are in the Blockland, Files, and Modification Help sections.
Alright, now to the review.
This game is a load of fun, mainly because you can honestly do whatever you want. You can build a house, make a sprite from a game in blocks, have a deathmatch with some friends, it's almost ALL customizable.
There's also addons you can download to add new blocks, events, weapons, tools, and other things to the game. A example of a new way to play is Unlimited Mining, which is exactly what it says on the tin: Mining that can stretch forever. It may seem boring, but it's not just the same ores. The deeper you dig, the closer you get to the Core, which has more valuable and radiated ores. and then, there's the secret area above grounds, that's very difficult to find...
The multiplayer's fun as well, you just need to be careful on what servers you go on, and read their rules carefully. Some people don't seem to get this, and end up joining random servers, get banned, and get all flustered wondering what they did wrong. People have their own rules, and others might not want you on your server.
And finally, there's the downtime. Normally, this isn't our fault. It's a problem with a few other people, like BDX, or Man of Reason, DDoSing the server when they feel like it, causing the master server and forums to go down. The master server is how you are able to see the server list. If that's down, you probably won't be able to join any servers.
Even though this game may seem off due to bad reviews, this game is what helped me finally play with others and have some fun. It was fun in 2008, and it's fun now. Try buying it while it's on sale, when it ever does, so you can spend less to try it. Even better, you can download the demo here:
You'll have to buy the game in order to play past the block limit, but trust me, it's much better when you're not limited.

Guild Commander is a Sim game of controlling a guild and sending out heroes
that feels more like a time management game, a happy dream of an accountant.
The game provides a large variety of tutorials that can help you as you go through
the game.
The game has a time system, and you earn income by sending your heroes
out on quests. Gold is spent rapidly on rooms you can add to your guild, and
your gold is depleted daily in order to maintain those rooms you have added.
The longer the heroes are gone stay in the guild, the less gold is earned daily, and the longer they are in the guild, the more money and resources they drain from you. The game
fails in its base management, and can get boring as you watch your heroes come
and go, but have no control over the individual money spent.  It becomes more
about getting your heroes out of the guild hall ASAP, so they don't bankrupt
you.
There is no management over what actions your heroes take; there is no
way to cancel their quest and call them back, and despite putting them in
precarious positions, I have yet to experience a hero dying.  There is no
personalization of the characters, which takes away from immersion into the
game.  You don't feel like your character is growing and improving;  they
become more of an impersonal number.
The continual repetition of  tasks makes this game boring.  It is more
of a money management game than anything else.  It feels like it doesn't have
any depth;  more like how to manage money dumps.  There is no challenge; except
to stay awake while you play it.

Pros:
-Everything about the controller is tweakable to an insane degree
-direct keyboard and mouse bindings make it work with litterally any game
-the 2 button triggers and back paddles can be really useful depending on the game
-Battery life is awesome, i can go 2-3 months of heavy usage before it dies on me.
-It can be used as a mouse outside of games in a pinch
-both wireless and wired options
-Multiple profiles can be saved to it so it can be programmed differently for every game you play with it. Profiles can also be loaded to any game so you dont have to reprogram for other games that use similar control schemes (eg. Fallout 4 and Skyrim)
Cons:
-The track pad takes a while to get used to. I had to spend several hours tweaking it to get it to an acceptable point for Fallout.
-I can't use it in competitive online games. Despite being marketed as a competitive alternative to mouse and keyboard gaming, the controller doesn't live up to it.
-No real option to make it rechargable. The controller uses 2 AA batteries and recommends that you don't put rechargable AA batteries in it. it can be ran wired in a pinch if need be at least
Other notes:
- A lot of people are complaining about the ABXY button placement, i personally had no issues with it
-I used an Xbox 360 controller before this and definitely prefer the Steam Controller over all.
Over all i like the controller and use it regularly.

I wasn't expecting much when I purchased this controller. I was curious and I wanted to try it out. I am not disappointed with the controller, but at the same time it isn't anything spectacular. The ability to rebind the controller's inputs for different games is pretty cool. The touchpads are nifty, but using them to click is obnoxious. With the exception of the joy stick and the ABXY buttons, the buttons are way too stiff; this is especially the case with LB and RB, which has forced me to rebind the two extra buttons on the back to LB and RB. Haptic feedback is an interesting, but it ends up being annoying. Turning off haptic feedback or rebinding any of the inputs requires going into big picture mode, which is also pretty annoying, especially if you don't use big picture mode, but at least you can exit it when you're done editting the settings. Overall the controller is pretty "meh" and I would only recommoned purchasing it if it is on sale.

Awful story - but that's not the game's fault. All the deus-ex machina and the whining about "friendship" (the most common cliche in the shonen book) destroyed the story - but nevertheless made for some epic action sequences! Mechanically probably the best in the Storm series, to the game's credit.
Things you may want to know before buying:
- Combat's much more versatile now, with character switching in-battle and in-combo, so chaining them feels really good. And smooth.
- Visually, the whole thing is spectacular.
- Story mode is pretty short and follows a linear cutscene-fight-cutscene sequence (unlike its predecessors), but there's an Adventure mode (non-canon) to extend that - with the free roaming style of the previous games.
- Has a HUGE character roster.
- AI feels smarter than the previous games, at least in the later stages. I have a few Bs in later matches.
Basically, it's a more refined version of the fun Storm experience we all love so much!

I'm very torn as to whether to give this a positive or negative review. The level of immersion is wonderful. Everything is extremely customizeable. The whole tactic of having to balance your resources within the system--managing happiness and food--makes it a very unique experience (especially when these systems are highly randomized). There are a number of factors that make replayability extremely high, including the wildly diverse tech trees, unique factions, race-specific technologies, advantages, and disadvantages...
...but my god. The tutorial system.
As someone whose job description includes writing how-tos, I can say, with tenured authority, that their tutorial system is absolutely horrible.
The 'tutorials' are screens that pop up the first time you play, and give you a screen cap (of a sampel screen) with numbers, and a wall of text on the right. No context, nothing leading you through--it's like getting an instruction manual, whose pages are only accessible while you're playing the game. To put it into context, it's as though you were taught to play Monopoly using a tutorial that didn't tell you that you could buy houses until you've acquired your first set by pure accident.
There's no campaign, no tutorial mission, no walk-through, no 'live example'--hell, the damn thing doesn't even tell you how the various win conditions work.
Which, with a game as rich and deep as Endless Space, is absolutely appauling.
What's worse, the complete lack of interactivity makes the tutorials extremely boring, and the fact that it only pops up to let you read once you've encountered an immediate need for it means that these boring walls of text will pop up as you're finally getting into the action, bringing the whole experience to a grinding halt.
If you've got a lot of time and patience to learn all the subtle nuances (mostly on your own, since the tutorials, boring as they might be, are also woefully inadequate in offering context), then you'll likely (eventually) get a hell of a kick out of Endless Space.
For everyone who doesn't have that kind of time, and just wants to be able to jump on, colonize some planets, sign a treaty, kill a bug, and shuffle along your merry way, then I cannot warn you vehemently enough about how throughly the tutorial will ruin your gaming experience.
