HISTORY:
Tribes is an old franchise that goes all the way to 1999 with Starsiege: Tribes. It differentiated itself from other futuristic shooters by having wide open maps, vehicles, class system (similar to what Battlefield 1942 did 3 years later) and jetpacks. Then later on, Tribes 2 came and further expanded on the idea, adding skiing (which is one of the few cases of a bug becoming a core feature of a franchise). It was well received and a couple of years later, Tribes: Vengeance came out and it was the first attempt to try streamlining the formula, however it wasn't well received by fans. And so, Tribes IP languished year after year, at one time developer called GarageGames (who made Fallen Empire: Legions, heavily (by heavily I mean almost completely copied) inspired by Tribes) bought the IP with the intent of remaking Tribes 1 for their InstantAction platform (which might be defunct now), til Hi-Rez bought the rights and set on to develop Tribes: Ascend.
BASICS:
Tribes: Ascend can be best described as "Battlefield meets Halo, fast-paced". It is a first-person shooter which pits teams Blood Eagle between treacherous Diamond Sword, each team can have max. 14 players with 3 armor classes in disposal. It is very team-oriented (as you might've noticed) and each player needs to accomodate and communicate between teammates to win. It's not as easy to learn as other games in the genre, you need to have at least some knowledge of the game, but it is gratifying as you soar into the sky with your jetpack and then ski 200 km/h (or is it mph), get into duels and so on.
GAME MODES:
There are many game types you can play, however the main type of Tribes: Ascend is Capture-the-flag. Each team fights for other team's flag and 5 captured flags end the game or if the time runs out with the score difference of two or one without other team holding the flag. Team Deathmatch is also widely played and recommended for newbies to try out. There are other game types like CTF Blitz (changing flag positions), Arena (akin to Quake's Clan Arena)... The maps are gorgeous and vast and the action feels really good, with plenty of weapons to wield (which need to be unlocked though).
PROGRESS:
UPDATE: Completely overhauled experience system. Now it's far easier for newer players to learn the games because pay-to-win elements have been unlocked. Grinding has been removed, everything not cosmetic is unlocked from the start. The whole loadout system has been rebalanced. So kudos to Hi-Rez.
CIRCUMSTANCES:
The community playing this game is rather small. Hi-Rez cut support for the game a few years back because it was "complete" (even though there are still bugs that need some work, Hi-Rez mismanaged the game and consequently many players have left the game, but with the rebalancing I highly recommend that you come back.
CONCLUSION:
+ Fast-paced action
+ Beautiful maps
+ A rather successful attempt to modernize the Tribes formula
+ Not pay-to-win (anymore)
- Small number of players for now
- Not as easy to pick up as other FPS's

Management sim that oversees sending off strong heroes to fortify provinces, in order to bulk up for the final encounter, quite like in FTL: Faster Than Light. Mostly covers running a profitable guild with slider-focused gameplay like Democracy 3, but also throws in random elements, requires constant vigilance over regions and has sufficient RPG side content to try different play styles; all for a small price.

Guild Commander is a game with an interesting concept, that sadly falls flat in the execution. While I will insist that the concept is pretty good and can work to become a very good game, full of interesting interactions, intrigue, and many enjoyable hours, this is not the game that will do justice to the concept of managing an adventurer's guild.
While the graphics are pretty good looking, and I am a sucker for isometric stuff that also manages to look pretty decent, there are a few too many problems with this game to make it worth spending time, money, and effort on. To continue on with graphics, your entire gameplay area is your guild hall. No, you can not build the building itself, you only have the rooms there which you can fill up in different, but still pre-determined ways.  Characters do not move around in your guild either, they merely teleport to their destination. You can not zoom out to see your entire guild hall at once, and to find anyone in it is a pain due to how close the camera is. This is less about being a guild commander, and more about being the guy who rents a pre-made guild house and then just waits for something to happen.
In short, there is no interaction.
You can send out your adventurers to other regions, but at no point are you shown any of this. You do not even have a map of the place, and the explanation on how to do things has basically shown you the entire game. There is only so long that you can look at a building in which nothing changes before you become bored, and while the vaguely humourous adventurer names and tooltips help you dull the monotony of not doing anything, they do not solve the problem.
I was reminded of Progressquest, the game about waiting. Except in this game your adventurers do not even level up. Aside from their equipment, nothing about them changes.
The list of things that could have gone so much better just goes on and on. Equipment is useless, especially if you consider making some yourself. You have no control over your adventurers aside from sending them out once or twice a month, and even that takes 3 or more clicks if you want to send them to some place that can actually use them. Adventurer's stats recover both too fast and too slow, depending on the situation, and it overall just lacks gameplay.
This is more of a waiting game, or perhaps an interactive screensaver, which requires that you keep clicking it or it will give you a gameover.
Interesting concept, but sadly it is all just squandered potential. Guild Commander is not something I would recommend to anyone. Not to people who are fans of strategy, nor to simulation fans, and most certainly not to anyone who wants to build or be creative. This game does not offer that - though I am still not sure what it *does* offer.

I 'beat' the game, but after getting over the hurdle of your first trade guild it's just going through the motions.

After beating the game, I feel I can chip in my two cents about it.
Story, setting and general content has been covered by the product description and other reviewers, so I'll refrain from going through all that again and instead focus on the good and the bad.
PROs
+ Quite a unique setting - only other game that comes anywhere near it seems to be Kairosoft's Dungeon Village
+ Decent graphics for such a small game - no great animations, but the texture quality is really okay
+ Light-hearted humor - I love me some smiles and chuckles while playing
+ Actually really nice music - normally, I'll turn of music within minutes. Here I didn't. Says something, at least for me.
CONs
- Lack of variety - it feels kind of repetitive to organize your heroes and thus makes the game very shallow
- Becomes a drag after the early game - after you research everything and equip your heroes, you spend most of your time waiting for the next thing to happen. Which often felt to be too long.
- The end - while I didn't expect much of a story (and didn't get one), the end was very... unsatisfying, especially after the long and forced wait until it actually triggered.
Conclusion:
It actually feels difficult to give a simple "yes or no" answer to the question whether I recommend this game.
It has its weaknesses. Annoying and very time-consuming weeknesses. It lacks depth in terms of content and possibilities. If you're into complex simulations, steer clear of this, you'd be disappointed.
However, if you're looking for a quite entertaining simple little pastime in a unique setting, you'll probably get your money's worth. I feel like I did. That's why it gets a thumbs-up from me.

When you open up the read more section on the Steam page the Gameplay section starts with “This is a small simple game”. That sums up the game in a nutshell, a resource management game which has been reduced to small simple task causing gameplay to become tedious in large portions and while you could say to take it in small steps, with playthroughs lasting for 2-3 hours it’s a hard game to come back to.
It suffers from limited options when it comes to what you can do for your heroes and the control you have over your guild. There are no internal guild strifes, no camaraderie between guild members and what you end up with is a blank slate of stats in which you push the square peg through the square hole to get the optimal result.
It also has a huge amount of RNG similar to something you’d see in a roguelike. The difference here being that you have so little control over your actions and because the RNG is non-reactable it causes more pain than it does pleasure, entire playthroughs can be ruined depending on where and when the calamities hit and the type of heroes your Guild can recruit.
The high points would include such things such as a good though generic graphical style and tooltips for everything so you’re never lost, though they get overshadowed by a repetitive experience which while unique isn’t as stimulating as I would have hoped for.
In a way it’s like a cake without flavour, it has the right stuff in it to make a suitable cake but lacks all the extra flavour that makes the cake stand out from the rest and making me come back for more. I just hope this style of game is expanded upon through this developer or another, management of people in a guild/fantasy setting is a game grouping we barely see and really has unlimited potential.
Some bugs and problems with design (character stats can be increased, but the increase can't be viewed; inventory management is cumbersome) but for the price, a nice little game.

Guild Commander essentially tasks you with seeing to your guild members' needs and sending them out on quests to keep the many provinces from falling to the enemy.  You can construct rooms which, in turn, produce an imaginary resource (strength, energy, etc.) which is then distributed amongst all your guild members.  There are some other hidden mechanics not explained all that well and you'll probably fail horribly your first time out like I did.  Assuming the game takes two-three hours as advertised, I do believe $5 is a fair price to ask considering that some $60 FPS's feature 4-5 hour linear campaigns. Your guild hall will have the same layout from game to game, so there's not a lot of replayability (though I would probably still enjoy coming back anyway from time to time).  Had this game been any more than $5, I wouldn't have been able to recommend it.  Hopefully some future patches will introduce more variety and customization, though I'm not sure if that'll ever happen.

I wanted to give a quick review for once, but I could not, so the first paragraph is for those who want it fast.
To be quick & frank: I wanted to play this as a teenager when it came out, and I never got to. As the franchise developed over the years I quickly lost interest as reviews basically warded me off. Recently Stronghold HD came up as a flash sale on steam for some thing like $1.67, and remembering that I never had the chance in my youth I said "why the ♥♥♥♥ not! It's only the cost of a coffee!". I have not been dissapointed at all. As far as being an HD release, it's optimized, bugless (at least so far and I'm 8+ hours in), and seems to have all it's assets there (nothing seems to be cut from what I gather), it's about as good of an HD-Re-release as AoE 2 has been and I've had countless hours of nostalgic fun with that title.
The rest of this review is simply trying to sell it to those who've never played it, or have experiances with similer games like AoE 2.
Stronghold puts you in the position of a lord, you build your castle, and you essentially play 'wave defence' threwout the campaign protecting said lord unit, while that isn't the only mode the game offers an 'economic campaign', instant siege, freebuild, etc. It isn't quite the same RTS layout as much of the genre has created, but almost half of a city / supply management game combined with specific aspects of medieval combat and primitive RTS atributes, it isn't actually as simple as I'm making it out to sound, for example to build bow units, one must have a supply of wood, then have a fletcher, he will deposite units of bow into your armory, in which then you can subtract from your unemployed towns people and spend the gold to create the unit, in which the bow in your arsenel becomes used up, and same goes for some foods, ale is a two stage process and wheat is a three stage process, luckily the game diversifies with food types, as well as material types. You have many more resources then a general RTS, but they aren't very complicated and any one who gets a few concepts of the mideval ages shouldn't have any problem grasping the concepts.
Combat & units: There is unit control, but there isn't worker control (You just have to build the woodcutters hut, not specifically tell a guy to go cut wood such as in AoE), you will have to shift your men around to defend your castle walls, and there is a plethora of objects to build, all with different functions. There is several different classes of units ranging from basic archers to knights. Siege units are also avialable from ballista to catapult. Unit control is primitive for its time but you can still patrol and move; to be honest and true to my word- the AI is generally very good especially for 2001, for example when you station spearmen on the wall and even tell them to patrol, as ladders raise and the enemy climbs, they automatically find the closest targets all along said wall and deal with and dispatch them however they best should at the time- FOR ONCE YOU REALLY DON'T NEED TO MICRO MANAGE YOUR MEN!!!!, in short: tell your units which towers and walls to cover, thats it. Ctrl Groups can be set (Ctrl + Num). Honestly theres still more defences in this game that I'm learning as I go, but the basics are all there, spike traps, hot oil. Missile units gain height advantage; especially in your towers! Walls actually deflect arrows and give your men HUGE survability bonuses. It's definetly not as quick feeling as a lot of other RTS games are, you generally have a lot of time to rethink things or shift men around if need be, the game speed can be adjusted in the options of course but the units don't quite feel as responsive/quick to move as other RTS's, but they aren't bad in any regards either especially after a few movements with a group has adjusted your perception of how quickly the games actually moving.
Campaign: The game offers 2 as I'm aware of, one leaning heavy on combat and defence while the other economic based- though I haven't played it. It's a crude campaign, heavy in story and sequences, the voice acting really screams '2001 game from left field!' as some of the characters are more annoying then interesting, and most of it is how the characters overall present themselves, it could have been much better written, there really isn't anything poetic about the campaign or most of the cast. The first few missions as I mention somewhere else in the review, will 'hold your hand' and present little challange but to build a handful of resource or a dozen men to dispatch wolves. Very very quickly does the difficulty ramp up, it can be adjusted before every mission but you won't know what 'difficult' is until you're nearly completed a mission and suddenly lose it very quickly due to your arrangement of defences or how and what resources you managed first. Dated but still enjoyable campaign.
Resource & worker mangmnt: is overall primitive but quick to grasp every concept as you discover which buildings work with what, the game also offers an in depth help psuedo-wiki with essential concepts of the game and general things to keep in mind while building defences and expanding yourself. There is also a trade building, it doesn't seem to have a persistant economy but really you won't want it with the ammount of gold you'll pull in, while you can make a lot, generally your living conditions will deter you less you have the food to fill the bellies or the aesthetics / fear factor built into your castle. Your peasents will have a general opinion of you, and there are buildings you can construct as well as decorations that will remind them of how nice or horrid of a ruler you are. Both concepts add two distinct and different aspects though, fear or 'bad things' will boost your workers effeciancy but lower your opionion while 'nice things' and being pleasent will only add to your overall opinion- but also cost gold and take up very limited space!
The building some times does get quite constrictive, especially in the campaign for the first few missions (they almost seem like half a tutorial that presents 3 'gimmie' missions where you essentially don't really have to do anything but figure out how economy works), and there are certain areas of the map you cannot build in (reinforcement points / town limits). While I do say there is a bit of managment, it's almost minimal and it's quite simplified, the learning curve is very small.
The last part I wanted to mention was the overall castle building. It is vast and while primitive and dated, allows for some very customized defences. Every crenulation you add to your walls as well as how thick you decide to build or extend them will add to your survival averages, as well as initial building placement and workflow. 2001 did not have very complex games overall, but this was definetly way ahead of it's time, especially in the defensive building style of RTS's. Another strong aspect of this game is the ability to 'hide' or 'lower' your walls for viewing / fine building purposes, you can either force the 3D terrain to become 'flat' or simply show everything as 2D tiles, this allows you to really fine tune / delete specific segments of wall and generally beautify the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of your castle without too much frustration and fretting.
Overall;, I would definetly recommend this title to any one who is even slightly a fan of castle / city builders, at full price of $7 CDN dollars, If you were a fan of the core concepts of AoE 2 you will definetly get your monies worth if not ending up loving it!
Con: Biggest con worth mentioning is that since it's a game from a much older time, and I know it is because of coding of the original engine that it could not be enhanced/fixed is the map size is overall small for RTS's, 400x400 I believe is the largest you can have, which actually is fairly big in this game, it isn't quite the massive 10 player battle sized maps of AoE 2 or Empire Earth.

The idea of the game sounds good in theory but it has not been executed good

-- GRAPHICS --
90% of the in-game textures do not display and, instead, show a blank pink. All of the cards in the game display as pink rectangles. I tried to fix it - I really did. I tried verifying the game cache, and that didn't fix it, though it did find a file in error and redownloaded all 0 bytes of it. I tried changing the graphics quality, which did nothing except alter how laggy the opening video was. I tried uninstalling and reinstalling, and that did squat.
Due to this, I can definitely say it's an issue with the game files players are given, and not something caused by the player's computer or a Steam glitch. There's no way for anyone but the developers to fix it, and they have yet to acknowledge it as an issue.
I did see a couple of the menu screens, though, and they were...uh...decent, I guess.
-- SOUND --
It sounds like a generic party game. Was not able to hear any of the sounds past the menu due to not being able to play.
-- GAMEPLAY --
Due to the graphical issues, I wasn't able to play in the slightest. Was sort of laggy, even on the lowest graphical setting, though.
But I can say that for a party game, I am noticing a distinct lack of multiplayer features. Hmm.
-- SUMMARY --
Don't spend your money on this game if you want something to play. If you REALLY want to play a Top Trumps game, you have other options. Better options.

I was not sure of getting this game since I had some credit left and just needed a few dollars to cover the rest of the cost. But after playing it a while, it seemed like a neat idea. But then it gotten pretty boring. You are extremely limited to what you can actually make in the game with a very limited about of combinations to make new elements. Plus it is hard as heck to even figure out how to make sure elements without using hints. I was tempted to use Gamefaqs or youtube videos to find the combinations, but that would have take the "fun" out of the game. It is almost required to find the combos on the internet to make any progress.
Sadly I only got far enough to get to the artifacts parts and it seems you need the right elements to make them. Not sure if the game would have gotten better if I found more elements, but I have a slight feeling it would have barely gotten any better.
Plus once you start gathering the elements, you can't really do much with them other then solve future puzzles. I wish you would have been able to help build your own civilation, help the people futher themselves, maybe do quests or help a person or group on a epic quest adventure. Sadly you can't do that. I think that would of made the game more fun. Plus it would have helped if you can make your own fairly custom things like some different technology, creatures, etc, that would have been pretty fun.
So sadly I would not recommend the game. But what I suggest could be a great game that could be started on Kickstarter or something. If anyone ever gets interested in the idea, let me know and make sure I get credit or something out of it.

Doodle God is an engaging way to while away the time while listening to a podcast or music. Beginning with four elements, you must discover combinations to build your way from Earth, Air, Water, and Fire to Magic and Technology. The later elements are somewhat difficult to devine, as you are not instructed what you're trying to create. It can lead to repeated mindless clicking as you try to combine any and all elements available to you. Nevertheless, it kept my interest long enough to work at completing the game, and some of the unexpected results of element combination were quite amusing.

Steam needs a mixed review option.. Doodle God is a casual puzzle game with a creative mechanics that you will combine 2 elements together to create something new. The game is fun at first but after having so many elements, it becomes rather tedious with trial and error approach to combine things. Besides, some elements should combine but they don't, and some combining elements don't really make sense. The hint system also needs rework to make the game more enjoyable. Still a pretty good experience nonetheless.

I've had a Steam Controller since last Christmas, so I feel like I've seen most of what I will get from it for the kinds of games I like to play.
First off, it's a pretty big controller. Whenever I play my PS3, the dualshock 3 just feels like a child's toy. While it is big, it feels very natural to hold, with no awkward buttons. The face buttons are in a different position than usual, occupying the center right position where a 2nd stick normally is, with a stick in the center left, circular D pad on the top left, and another circular pad on the top right. The face is rounded out with a steam/home button in the upper center, with back and start buttons flanking it. Lastly, there are the usual shoulder and trigger buttons on both the left and right, with the final inclusion being a pair of buttons attached to the battery cover on the underside.
What it's good for: Rocket League, 2D side scrollers, XCOM, the FF library and similar games
What it's not good for: Anything that requires rapid camera movement --> 3D adventure stuff, Shooters (KBM is superior to controllers anyway so this is a non issue)
Rocket League, Ori and the Blind Forest, XCOM, and several FF games all were fantastic experiences, but playing SOMA was frustrating when trying to focus on specific objects. I personally don't get why there aren't 2 thumbsticks, and have yet to encounter a game in which the programmable D pads are really useful. The best explanation I can think of is that any FPS is better designed for KBM play, and this fills in for the rest of the games that don't require the use of 20 different hotkeys (hello Dota and Starcraft).
Overall, I highly recommend this controller for the niche of 2D, Rocket League, and most games that don't require quick and precise target acquisition. If you play these games, go for it. It would be perfect for me if it had a second thumbstick instead of the right configuration pad so that first person adventure games were more playable, but for the niche that it fits, it is a fantastic controller.

Manage weapons production (iron for good armor/swords, leather (dairy farms) for mid-level crossbowman and macemen, wood for bows/crossbows, etc.).

Setup your castles defences (walls, gates, traps, towers (and types), engineers, and siege weapons).
Assault rival castles (ladders, moat-filling, fire, siege weapons, how to best storm which positions first). This will happen fast, so plan beforehand, as you likely won't get backup (at least for awhile).
Overall, a fun, complex, easy-to-learn castle sim. A must for any RTS/Castle-Sim player.

Doodle God is a simplistic puzzle game where you, as God, must create the universe.  You start with the four basic elements of nature (fire, earth, wind and water) and by combining them you must create items ranging from oceans, volcanoes, rocks, plants and animals to humans, tools and weapons and eventually machines such as automobiles and rockets.

The developer markets this game as requiring logic and ingenuity in order to succeed , but it's really little more than a guessing game where you'll frequently find yourself using trial-and-error to find the right combination of items needed to progress.

I do believe that Doodle God was a great idea when it was first released as a free online game many years ago, but I don't believe this version offers enough additional content to justify the price.

My all-time favorite turn-based space strategy is Masters of Orion 2. I have a copy that I dive into at least three times a year. So when I look at new space games, I always compare it to MoO2 and they don't always hold up. Endless Space is very much like my favorite parts of MoO2. The parts I have encountered are very well done. First of all, the user interface is VERY friendly and easy to master. Second, the tutorial is very thorough and explains the windows and the mechanics very well. Third, there are an amazing number of customizable options, including the ability to make new custom races and change the randomness of the galaxy you want to play in. Fourth, the research, hero, system- and planet-development, ship customization and diplomacy sections of the game all feel like they were given 110% focus. While each section has plenty of things to work on to further your empire, none of them are so complex that you have an aneurism trying to keep everything organized and in order. Combat was an interesting system, incorporating a card-like system to give general orders to your fleet as a whole much like an admiral would. Leveling heroes is alot like playing an RPG, with many options for improving them.
While I may wish for an espionage system like MoO2, and that I could have more control in combat like MoO2, I have enough fun with the shinier planet development and research tree. Overall, this is a very good game.

After giving this game more of a chance and completely ignoring the combat system which is still stupid entirely... view a new, more fair review.
Endless Space is a Master of Orion 3-style 4X game which has it's own lore and story.
First off, the first thing I must address, is the good.
I like the systems in the game. The Approval is like happiness, only it is a percent instead of a raw number, which makes it alot more manageable.
The other yields are the typical ones to be expected.
The Financial Yield is Dust, which is basically a currency left over all over the place by the game's Elder Race called The Endless. Hence the name.
There are 12 races, 8 of which are humanoids. I will describe each race in a small, possibly vague nutshell, then with how they play best , and then i will say their focus (basically which victories can they easily get compared to others, according to the game)
- First there's the "obligatory" human race, which is evil. I could say Ofcourse there, but only if they were neutrally aligned would ofcourse not be applicable. The United Empire. They're mainly colonists with a defensive/military focus.
- Then there's the Sophons, the game's nerds, basically. Ofcourse they're good, since... you know... smart people are good in most games since common sense. They're scientists with a... well... Science focus.
- The Hissho are... well to put it simply (If you're offended, don't be, this is just a literal 1 second guess) They are basically evil bird asians. They play like an actual mean person would, via conquest and whatever glory is, with a focus on military and population.
- The Amoeba are the "obligatory" aquatic race, only this time, they're literally evolved forms of amoebas. Like all aquatic races in most 4Xs, they are peaceful and good, playing like a nice explorer person with a focus on military and diplomacy.
- The Automatons are automatons and "obligatory" for Sci-fi 4Xs, but this time, they're not a walking cliche. They are actually peaceful loners and have a focus on diplomacy and economy
- The Sheredyn are possibly humans who are also evil, playing like colonists with an economic/military focus.
- The Cravers are insectoids who, unlike the Automatons, are walking, talking cliches more so than orcs usually are in Fantasy, or just as much. They don't give two craps about you, even if you also are a Craver, they kill everything or die trying, consuming everything on their path, with just a military focus.
- The Horatio, are basically what you get if you clone a super "pretty" model about a billion times and make them an empire. They're humans, being literally related to the United Empire, since Horatio all come from one guy and he was a United Empire Citizen. They see the universe as less pretty than them and seek to basically fix that. They Expand like mad and have a focus on wonders and population.
- The Sowers are basically construction robots left over by the Endless. They are neutral builders with a focus on wonders and military.
- The Pilgrims can also be called the Rebel Alliance as they are good, while canonically being rebels of the United Empire. They play as explorers/diplomats with a focus on diplomacy and military. Oh, almost forgot to mention that they're the religious group who whorship the Endless like a god.
- The Harmony is the rockpeople faction. They've lived since the dawn of time (whenever that is) and they're neutral. They're isolationists, but also explorers (even if that's contradictory in a sense.) who have a focus on Wonders and Population.
- The Vaulters are basically "ancient" nomadic humans with female leaders instead of male ones. They are Defensive scientists with a focus on Science.
and now for the moment I've been waiting for... the combat system.
The Combat System has about as much depth to it as Rock Paper, Scissors, if 4 others were added, plus a godmode one which forces a draw. With the AI, it's a guessing game that feels as rigged as the difficulty makes it. It's literally not worth using. At all. There is no strategy to it, this would work better as a Risk game mechanic.
There Are Wonders. Yes, this is a negative point on the game because when you put wonders into a game, they become instrumental in some victories and people rush to them. Like in Civ, each wonder gives special bonuses.
Unlike Civ, these wonders are restricted to specific planets, you will find them if you explore and colonize enough. This kinda makes it alot better in my opinion.
There are about 6 victory types. Military, Science, Expansion, Diplomacy, Wonder and Score. 3 types too many in my opinion.
Each victory type is literally what you expect them to be.
- Military is also called Supremacy, is just means kill everyone else.
- Science is basically get the last tech.
- Expansion basically means own 3/4 of the galaxy.
- Diplomacy is literally make friends with everyone.
- Wonder victory is based on wonders, and is one of the reasons why I never turn this one on. Ever. You build Invulnerable Empire improvements 5 times, gained from the last Exploration and Empire tech branch. So this could actually be a Science victory, but isn't because reasons.
Restoring wodners you find would be a better alternative, seriously.
- Then there's Score. You just amass enough points and you win once the turn limit reaches it's end. Nothing really complicated here. So basically, this victory type is the one where you literally win just by living and doing the best long enough.
- There is actually also Supremacy, but that's owning all original homeworlds. not as much fun as the normal Military victory.
Just my opinion, but Military, Diplomacy and Science victories are all you really need. All other systems aside from those are just extras to help you win in those 3 ways.
Now for much shorter parts of this review, but also the other parts of the Game.
AI is rather basic. Its Easy mode is stupid completely. Until a certain turn number, the AI will rarely attack, but once you do, the AI will send hordes of ships at you, regardless of what victory types are available and even if you're on beginner.
You cannot win if you hardly do anything, despite the tooltip for beginner saying so.
Despite this game being made by Indie devs, the game has been out for atleast a couple years and Endless Legend is out... This is a fairly large negative.
You will win if you pump out sheer numbers, as they always will due to the combat system.
The game as a whole feels like it's trying to emulate Master of Orion with a spin on it... but it fails rather horribly, borrowing parts of Civ and all of Rock, Paper, Scissors, while mostly sticking with the cliche races of other 4X Sci-Fi games.
The soundtrack is nice but doesn't really change much.
I may have talked about Approval, but i jsut want to also say that, that itself is kind of a negative that it even exists. If it was happiness as a raw number, this part of the review would be identical.
Pros:
- Wide selection of Races.
- Tons of Ways to Win.
- Has an original story.
- Has a non-existent Elder Race in the Story.
- Most of the races aren't cliches.
- Good Visuals and Audials.
Cons:
- Some races are total cliches.
- 4, maybe 5 races are humans. Literally.
- 8 out of 12 of the available races are humanoid.
- Basic AI with absurd difficulty spikes coming out of nowhere.
- The Combat System is ridiculous and might aswell be up to RNG.
- AI makes the combat system horrible as it feels fixed 80% of the time.
- Combat system makes quality over quantity irrelevant if you fail at getting used to it like me.
- Too many ways to win, there should (in my opinion) only be 3. Science, Diplomacy and Military.
- There is a Turn Limit, based on game speed, essentially making for the same experience everytime. as game speeds scale everything else to match.
5/10 - If you want another 4X, Endless Space is okay.

This game has a compelling atmosphere. From the very beginning, the music played when we launch the game makes us feel flung into its world. As a result however, it does make any disappointment a very frustrating experience.
It is an excellent game nonetheless. For the reason I just mentioned: the atmosphere is so compelling it reminds me of the first time I played Half-Life 1. We really feel like we are Adam Jensen and we have responsabilities. When I failed to save someone in some parts of the game, I really felt it was my fault. Talking about the music, the intro music is even so good I suffer pain quitting the game or loading a save. Characters are endearing. Jensen's personality isn't extremely original, but still is extremely convicing, as for all the other characters in the game : Sarif, Malik…
But this game as awesome also because it has a broad gameplay well made in every aspect. Hacking, stealth, combat, debate, exploration, side quests, deciding your ameliorations and weapons : it's impressive a game can have so many different gameplay aspect yet excels at each one. It is fun and really simple to handle.
Now, as I said, this game isn't perfect. I encountered a few bugs : sometimes, a 2 second part of a music was looping, the game has frequently lags, it has also minor bugs with shadows and water effects, it also happened rarely though that the game simply stopped working. The radgoll is also rarely very buggy. Once, I tried to hide a body, but for unknown reasons he got stuck in the floor, so I couldn't move it, and the other guards noticed it. Or another time, a body I was hiding as well just roused itself from me and landed just before a guard. That was annoyng :p
But bugs did not alter the overall game's experience. The same can't really be said for the other big problems of this game. Because it feels so real, any disapointment is extremely frustrating.
Let's talk about side quests : There is one character, not linked with the game's plot at all, who has a very endealling personality. You can help her getting out of an extremely bad situation. However, as soon as you do, you won't see her anymore. She disappears without explanation. Side quest is done. As if you only saved her because you're completionist and have to do all side quests. There's that other character who has a very big problem as well. When you finished helping, and if you come back to speak to her, she just talks like a decoration NPC, saying "thanks" while looking at her Iphone or whatever. Such aspects of the game should have been more worked. I do as many side quests as I can and I feel really flung into them, for that reason it really makes me feel those aspects of the game are botched.
Now the ending : I found it weak. I'm not talking about the story, but how they made the ending. Adam Jensen has a choice to make. I only tested two choices, and they're dispaointing. For two reasons. The first it that it only gets us to see a video made of real videos (which doesn't fit at all with the game and seems to be botched) where Adam Jensen is reading a pupil's dissertation, quoting Albert Einstein like any dumbass do (I'm sorry if you do, but let's admit it, it's as stupid as mentioning the nazis in a debate, as I just did in some ways :/ ).
The second reason is going to spoil :

The controls are a bit stiff; robotic in a way. But nevertheless, its a pretty fun game and pretty good graphics. It is the type of game where you're basically directed thru every mission. Simple answer is the DLC systems. Every model is unlocked by either xp or credits. xp is easy to get seeing as you can get a pretty nice login bonus for logging in daily for 7 days in a row. Also, there is a model quiz that helps too. Credits on the other hand are the premium currency. All the models can award usually one credit for getting a top score on one of the modes. This is on a daily rotation so it  is not hard to earn credits.

The game is really fun and definitly unique to other shooters. The card system lets you tweek your champion's abilities in different ways to find a playstyle you like. want your frontline to be better at flanking? you can do that. There are a alot of champions to play as, each with their own uniqe qualities to bring to the fight. Right now i only wish there were more gamemodes to choose from, right now there are 3 different kinds.

Most of the negative reviews on this game right now are about the new card system, which took away alot of freedom in making card decks. Overall i think the change is good, even tho at first i hated it, because the system they had before was a pain. You had to grind tirelessly to get a card you wanted, some taking a week+ to get 1 card, unless you played all day, everyday. With balancing changes, the game will be alot better then it once was, as before you could lose simply because you couldnt afford the better cards simply because you didnt have 1000+ hours into the game like some others.

The new system they added, you now have all the cards, you dont control how good they are, but rather upgrade them overtime. which is not as bad as people tend to make it. Cards level up relatively fast, and you get free chests to upgrade a specific champions cards just by winning matches with them each day, or by buying their chest with ingame currency. Almost all cards are usable in their 1st lvl, and gain very little boosts with each level.

Often i hear people complain that its become a pay to win game. What they fail to mention is that even the (pay to win) method is STILL RANDOM, you only control what champion class you will get cards for. And with champion chests, the ones you get by winning games or by BUYING THEM WITH INGAME currency, makes it much more practical to just play the champion you like.

There is also a game mode called Bound mode, where all cards are set at equal levels for a balanced fight.

Ummmm Yeah... This is Bill Lumbar reporting in for my first review of MWO.
I started playing MWO around 2 years ago.  I have always been a fan of the BT table top, grew up playing it as a child and young adult.  38 now, and through the years I have played many of the BT games on sega, super Nes, playstation, xbox and pc to name a few.  I used to head up to chicago to the BT center as a kid with my dad to get my fix.
Life took over and I found myself not playing BT games anymore, and for years.  I got that hunger again around two years ago and googled new BT games.  First hit I got was MWLL and I happened to have the old Cyris game so I was all set.  Jumped right in and I loved it... then bam!  MWLL got shut down/they stopped developing it.  I then read the rumors surrounding the "why" and came across MWO and downloaded it and started playing it more then I would like to admit.  For a solid 6 months, I dropped over 6000+ matches.  Within the last two plus years I have spent around $90 dollars on this game between two accounts, one IS, and the other straight Clan.
This game has faults..... that is for sure.  One of the two biggest issues for me has always been the painful "grind" and snails pace one progresses at in this game, even when spending hundreds or even thousands of dollars on it.  Thankfully, right before the Steam release... PGI decided after 2 plus years of very low ingame earnings to increase the C-bill and XP earnings.  I don't believe its where it needs to be, but it is up around 15-25% of what we all used to make per match.  I wanted and felt a 50% increase was long over due, but hey its a start.
Secondly, Prices for everything in this game besides Mechbays are pretty much crack priced.  How they unlock camo, patterns, and colors is just insane for the price.  All the bling for the cockpits, prices are pretty much insane IMO.
Third game lacks serious content and depth.  It needs so much more, and it has been screaming for more for a very long time!
Now to the good things,  Core game play is fun.  I am looking for more of a sim type game when it comes to BT... because I like to build sim pits... I love BT... and I hope they keep it moving more towards that style of play in this game.  for what ever faults this game does have, PGI has come a long way with this game.
I took a several month vaction from this game... going from playing around 100-200 matches a week, to only 5 matches a week.  The  last 3 months I have just got back into playing this game and am back up to maybe 30-50 matches a week.  This was mostly to do with PGI ignoring the pleas of many on the forums/forum warriors that earnings needed to be brought up so this game didn't feel like a snails pace.  Even with PT it still felt very slow, making not buying PT a no brainer.
All in all I would recommend this game to others, core game play is fun.... and I have met some really cool people in game.  The forums are a trip some times... much hate...but there is also a lot of love out there and some really cool people that love to help and also even share/give aways.  One piece of advice...spend wisely, and don't go on a crack spending spree....seriously, its not worth it IMO.  If you have the dollars to do that and want a place to blow them, by all means, knock yourself out.  Plenty to blow money on in this game...golden mechs.... you name it, PGI will sell it!

MWO is a free to play game based on the Mech Warrior series which is based on BattleTech. The mech combat is good, possibly some of the best in the series' history. I've played the TT and franchise for over 20 years and can safely say that at its core, MWO is true to the premise of piloting a big battlemech.
There is an extremely steep learning curve for new players that is not helped by lack of good documentation explaining some of the more important mechanics. The community is really good at filling in the blanks though and most are more than willing to help new players get acclimated.
The artwork is gorgeous and if you are able to play on higher settings the game really shines. Although a bit dated now, you can see that the artwork is top notch.
It's a very fun game, especially being free and I would reccomend it to anyone looking for a new game. This isn't your typical shooter though, it tends to move at a much slower pace when it comes to combat and it is heavily team oriented. Those that try to take down the enemy team solo ala CoD will find nothing but frustrating losses.
That's not to say it is without issues. The gameplay itself is repetitive and most modes equate to stomp forward and kill them all. There are additions in the pipeline to include new modes that should break up the monotony but if you're the type of gamer than enjoys a lot of diversity in modes such as CtF, KoH, etc. this may not be your cup of tea.
The pathfinding is frustrating, especially when you're stomping along in a 100 ton assault mech and are brought to a complete stop due to a "rock" no higher than your mech's ankle.
The mech customization is amazing with literally thousands of mech and weapon combinations. It's one of the few F2P games out there that does a very good job of walking that line without getting into P2W territory.    The developers are very responsive and interactive with their community via Twitter which is exceptionally rare in this industry.
Overall I would give it 3 out of 5 stars (which could easily jump depending on what the company does with the recently released Phase 3 of Community Warfare). Ah, good times. True to its word this is a castle sim and not really a RTS or at least not a traditional one.
For one thing you see everything on the map right when you start so you don't explore it at all. The size of the map is fairly small too usually.
The focus is on just you actually. If you're defending you want to muster up as many troops as you can to repel enemy invasions or if you're attacking it's about using your army well so you don't take needless losses.
And making an army from scratch isn't easy either. You not only need a free peasant but also any weapons or armor that the particular unit needs. For more basic units this is just the weapon but you'll also need to make the armor for more powerful units.
Getting resources isn't a quick process. A hunter has to shoot a deer, bring it back to his area, cut it up and bring that to your castle's granary. If you want to make your peasants eat bread, you need to make the wheat, turn that into flour and turn that into bread, so that's 3 different peasants you'll need right there.
Your peasants need to be fed of course, Otherwise they become very unhappy and will likely leave your castle before long so making them happy is a good idea. It's pretty easy to manipulate it though with how much food you give them and how much tax you want out of them. But as your population rises so too does the rate at which your food depletes.
What's interesting is that you can make buildings instantly, including the walls so you don't have to spend time worrying too much about that aside from some buildings that need to be placed on certain places.
The military campaign is where the main story is. There's a economic campagin but it's not nearly as long or interesting. The voice acting in it is cheesy in a good way. It can be pretty difficult though.
The game looks about the same as I remember it but being able to play in 1920x1080 is nice.
At the price it's asking for I'd say it's worth it. I play it on a Windows 7 machine and I don't have any issue running the game.
One of my favourite games of all time. Worth a go. Whilst it's 2D, the graphics are much more detailed than in Stronghold 2. It's a shame there's no kingmaker style mode.

StrongholdHD was the first game in the series taking place in medieval Europe. I highly reccomend you play this game before getting any other stronghold game. Its a strategy based castle building game released about 15 years ago back at 2001. Its really old, but that doesnt make it a bad game. AMAZING music and voice acting. You will also learn a thing or to from StrongholdHD This game was like smoking weed when I first got it. If your tolerant of old games, and like what I said above, I highly reccomend it for you. Its price is a bit too high for a old game at 7-8(UDS) on steam, but you can also wait for a sale, or go to a trustful website that sells games really cheap. They have really good prices, and it actaully works.(I got all my total war games with  for a cheap price, but you cant refund them)
You basicly have 3 modes. Combat, Economic, and Map Editor. The other tab is basicly saves. Combat is basicly for people who want to get right on into battles, sieges, and campaign. Economic is more peacful as you fufill orders in a certain amount of time like making weapons, troops, food, ect. Map Editor you can create or own maps. Saves is self explanatory.
In the military campaign, you take on a lord whose kingdom was beaten back by 3 forces, the rat, the snake, the pig, and the wolf.(Please correct me if im wrong, I haven't played this in a long time) You start to retake counties from the 3 enemies. All of this is taking place in the UK looking map I belive. So the game starts of from starting off small with pity archers and spear men with wood palisade walls to mace man, crossbowmen, with stone walls. As the game progresses, it teaches you slowly, rewards you with new buildings and troops. Really this is the reason why I reccomend to play this game first. Games like Stronghold Crusader dont tutor you like a newb. They think you know how to play the game. The only bad thing I find about this is that theres barely any siege for you, and if there is, its freaken huge for a beginner sieger.
Then we have siege battles, premade castles for you to siege, or defend. Theres a ton of maps to choose from. I think almost all of them are historical and gives information about each siege. I actaully learned that the London tower was actaully a castle at first. Interesting.
Invasion basicly invades more than a castle. So if you have villages or forts around your castle, its an invasion. Again, alot of maps and historically accurate for some.
Economic is really simple and more peaceful, expect for wolves. You get orders to build troops, weapons, food in a limited amount of time. You will get obstacles like plague, theives, but its really not a big deal. I reccomend playing this after military.
Map editor is a sandbox. You can free build your castle without any mace men tearing up your walls, OR, Build your map, make your levels. You can adjust the terrain, add trees, troops, oceans, rivers, rocks, resources, really in depth and nice. I belive you cant make your own 1000v1000 battles but I think you can do it in Stronghold Crusader.
Saves. Well this is what pisses me off. You have to manually save your games. It's 100 percent my fault, but make sure you SAVE your game.
AS far as multiplayer goes, you will need to have GameRanger and even if you have it, theres barely any games, but Stronghold CrusaderHD as a ton of multiplayer games.
StrongholdHD is a game that requires tolerence in order to enjoy. If you like old classic medieval castle building games, this is for you. If your looking to get into other stronghold games, play this. I will make a review on Stronghold Crusader soon because thats considered the best game in the series.

Contrary to all the negative reviews this game has engendered due microtransactions for hints, now removed, I find this game ridiculously addictive.   You can still purchase hints through lightning bolt money, which now is gained primarily by completing missions.  All that said, I have played the game entirely without once purchasing a hint once.  If you want to use hints, they do recharge, which can admittedly take a while.  But that makes perfect sense since if you had unlimited hints, then this would be less of a challenge.
The basis of this game is to incrementally combine "elements", which initially are air, fire, water, and earth into other elements, and so on, until you have built up to more complex elements like human and tools.  The game consists of four chapters, where in each you need to form up to a certain number of elements.  What separates chapters is adding an extra special element, as well as being able to combine some elements to form new ones not previously available.
These combinations are not random.  They are a combination of logic, intuition and humor.  Sometimes you can form the same element multiple times in different ways.  Some elements like philospher's stone, have a property to "undo" other elements.  For instance, it combined with vampire, gives human, since vampire was the combination of blood and human.
However, I will say the longer you play and the more elements you have at your disposal, the more difficult it can be to make any progress without getting a hint.  There are primarily three types of hints for the main game.  The first, which is rare, simply gives you a new element by combining two existing ones.  I don't like this one since it is just telling you the answer basically.   The second, which is the best, gives you two  groups from which then you know that you get a new element by combining an element from each.  At worst, you can just go through all pairing possibilities until you stumble onto a new element.  This hint recharges each 10 minutes, so it pretty much guarantees it will advance you in the game.  The last hint, which is the main one to use, is that it simply shows a new element that can be formed.  Just by knowing what one can be, gives you the chance to try and figure out what you can combine that could give that particular element.
FInally, this game also has various mini games, such as puzzles, where you need to build up to a final element, like Christmas tree, not available in the normal main game, through a sequence of combinations from limited initiali materials.  In these puzzles, some of the combinations you have seen, and others you haven't.
All in all, I find this to be a fairly polished game.  Compared to the mobile version, I prefer the Steam version since it is more clear how many more elements are left to discover for a group, plus additional features such as an encyclopedia of discovered elements and the quotes that can go along with each as they are discovered.
Is this game worth $6?  By no means, but if you can get it part of a bundle as I did, or on sale for $1 or $2, then it is worth a little bit of time and money.

It is a good port of the classic mobile hit Doodle God, A logic puzzle to create elements by combining two elements together.

Doodle God is weird in bad ways. I suppose it's technically a game. Put icons together to make other icons, with some flavor tech thrown in to add humor. JoyBits is at least honest in saying "Mobile. Social. Casual."
I can't really talk too much about the game, as it is not inspiring to any degree. New icons are added as the game progresses, but it's still simple combos. Puzzles and artifacts are also available, but they play out the same. It's not thoughtful enough to be a puzzle, but the amount of icons prevent brute-forcing strategies. It's almost an easy 100% with guides, but the Patience achievement can be finicky.
Doodle God is just not fun, and shows the flash/mobile game roots even after purchases have been removed. I feel like the game is aimed at younger kids, but the content doesn't seem appropriate. There are multiple icons related to sex and alcohol, and some flavor text with vulgar words, so I can't imagine many parents would be happy. If the game is for matured gamers, I can't imagine that they will be intellectually or mechanically stimulated. New content (more of the same) may be added, but bigger changes are reserved for mobile sequels (Doodle Kingdom, Devil, 8-bit, etc) available for purchase. I expect those games will be boring bundle fodder, which is where I got my copy. Don't bother at any price.

If you are a new player, Blitz offers few advantages over the non-mobile/non-steam version. If you are an old player, you'll be kissing all your progress goodbye and re-grinding tanks for a more limited selection.
+ Tutorial system is more inviting
+ 7v7 matches means theres more agency and control over a game
+ Different crew system were all perks are shared means less of a grind, and less variation between player progress.
+/- 'Rebalanced' Tiers, feels like you are more likely to be playing in the Top Tier of a game but Scout Tanks have not been rebalanced.
+ New sfx and new maps make for some welcomed novelty.
+ No premium consumables
+ Reduced modules at least at low tier, less of a grind, don't have to worry about tracks and radios for a while. But can mean less options for weight and builds.
+/- Cross platform play makes for additional seal clubbing action
+/- Said seal clubbing usually means mobile and some new players will drop out before they reach higher tiers. At which point its seasoned players re-grinding a simplified version of the desktop game.
+/- Just as a grindfest as normal World of Tanks
+/- Multiuse consumables in match
-No consumable/module management. AKA SUPER CREDIT TAX. You sell all ammo every time you mount a turret or change a gun. Consumables are either On or Sold.
-No Artillery Class Vehicles, means less options in dealing with certain heavies and tank destroyers
-No French or Chinese Trees (yet)
-Missing many non-SPG vehicles available in World of Tanks such as high Tier American Autoloaders like the T69
-Ping Spikes on PC
-Account is locked to server, progress is locked to server, so all the money and time you put in does not carry over from servers or World of Tanks.

I consider myself a pretty heavy Space 4X afficionado.  I have played a very wide range of titles in the genre, including MOO2, Sins of a Solar Empire, Space Empires IV and V, Galactic Civilizations II, StarDrive, and Endless Space.  I have even played some of the much older titles, such as Stars! and Spaceward Ho!
Unfortunately, I have to agree with TotalBiscuit's assessment of this game: it is well put together, and it is executed adequately, but it lacks soul.
THE GOOD:
*The user interface in this game is one of the most easy-to-use and informative Space 4X UI's I have ever seen.  I can usually get all of the information I need with a couple of clicks.  Queueing up production, changing tax percentages, or checking which systems needed my immediate attention was very accessible and intuitive.  Gone are the days when I had to make 5+ clicks just to find the information I was looking for, and then 3+ more clicks in order to implement a decision based on that information.
*The music in this game is fantastic.  If I could, I would rip the music from this game and use it in the other Space 4X games that I enjoy.  I was also impressed by the fact that the music was somewhat dynamic; when I was in the main space view, the music played with its full instrumentation, but when I went into system view or ship design, the instrumentation scaled back dynamically and played a more sparse version of the same music.  I suspect they have two simultaneous tracks going on at the same time and the game dynaimcally fades from one to the other based on user actions.
*The game is challenging early on.  If you don't expand quickly into different systems and establish the borders of your empire, other races will come in and take neighboring systems much earlier than you would expect.  Moreover, if other civilizations don't see you building up a strong enough military early in the game, many of them will simply declare war on you because you look like an easy target.
*The tech tree is extensive and varied.  With four main branches to work through, there is plenty of new tech that can be researched through early, mid, and late stages of the game.
*Victory conditions are varied and well developed.  The traditional military victory is available, of course, but you can also win the game by expansion (own a certain percentage of the galaxy), science (research enough tech to 'ascend' to a new form of existance), diplomacy (ally yourself with most/all other races, and prevent war for a certain amount of time), economic (earn/control a certain amount of resources/cash), and others.
THE BAD:
*Combat is by far the most disappointing aspect of this game.  Don't get me wrong--the combat is rendered beautifully, with cinematic camera movements and fabulous explosions.  Sadly, however, combat is NOT user-controllable.  Granted, you can pick rock-paper-scissors style cards that have effects on the stages of combat, but that is as far as user control goes.  I wanted to be able to direct my big battleships and dreadnoughts to strategic positions on the battlefield, while keeping close tabs on the ships that were damaged so that I could steer them away from danger.  No such luck.  As beautiful as the space battles are in this game, I found myself simply picking auto-combat again and again.
*Though the races in the game have interesting back stories and differences of starting attributes, in actual gameplay, the races don't really feel much different from each other.  Sure, there are a small number race-specific techs that can be found in the tech tree, but even these don't feel much different than what can be researched by other races.
*Planetary colonization and development is boring and forgettable.  There are a few key structures that you can build on each specific planet, but for the most part, the entire star system feels like a single 'colony', for which you build system-wide improvements.  The 'value' of each of these 'colonies' is vastly determined by the number of planets in the system and the amount of population that you can grow system-wide.  Gone are the challenges of a single, resource-rich, but barely colonizable planet that you have to carefully grow to become a viable production center; as long as there are other more hospitable planets in the system, then a low-value planet is virtually pain-free.
*Diplomacy in this game is absolutely ridiculous.  While I like the fact that you have to research more advanced diplomacy actions (i.e. trade treaties, tech swapping, alliances, etc.), I felt like the AI was grossly weighted against you in most diplomatic situations.  Even when I was fully allied with a race, with full friendly relationships, they would still ask me for my arms, legs, first-born child, and the soul of my fleet admiral in exchange for a single new technology.  After many attempts, I simply gave up trying to trade technology with my neighbors.  Furthermore, even good races would break treaties with you seemlingly on a whim--I found myself unable to reliably predict how long my good relations with other races would last.
*Ship design doesn't allow much as far as meaningful decision-making.  Most of the time, you'll be designing ships with the absolute best weaponry and armor that you have researched; there is very little reason (aside from production cost) to ever use a lesser tech.  Every once in a while, I created a specialized ship (such an invasion ship with high planetary attack capacity but very little ship-to-ship offense, or a carrier that had very little weaponry but loads of fighters and bombers on board).  In many other Space 4X games, I have the ability to design support ships (i.e. refuel, re-supply, repair, or even mobile ship construction yards), transports, miners/resource collectors, star bases, etc.  Not in Endless Space.
I wanted to love this game.  I really did.  I put more than 80 hours into it, playing as various different factions (good, neutral, and evil).  But in the end, the lack of controllable combat, the clumsy and unforgiving diplomacy system, and the uninspiring planet/system management process eventually made me decide to go back to other Space 4X games.

"Who is Piranha Games?"
8 out of 10 Tell your friends Mechwarrior Online is live!
-----Skip the first two paragraphs if you just want to learn about the game play.
When I first tried it in 2013 I felt a nostalgic tug for the game Mechwarrior 2: Mercenaries that I used to play. I lost interest for reasons. But I do recall the game felt like it was missing a lot of mechs.A year later I turned the game back on and found the developers, Piranha Games, has been busy adding content and even a whole new series of game play modes related to the Inner Sphere and Clan factions and taking place on a star map of the inner sphere. If you're a fan of the Mechwarrior games you'll like MWO. It turns out Piranha Games has been busy on MWO since 2011!
If you're not a seasoned Mechwarrior expect a steep learning curve, the game is very strategic. Then expect long periods of learning. One fast huge tip -- Don't sell anything ... keep all the stuff you get because you'll want it later. Just keep increasing your C-bill worth. Every piece of equipment is c-bills you dont need to spend later for a laser and can go to a new mech chassis. If you save up and buy a mech, don't sell it, or the parts that came with it. It will really pay off after you own your first few mechs and want to change them up a bit.
The game itself is a multiplayer Omnimech, Battlemech, Mechwarrior 12v12 (first person or third) with 2 modes, Quickplay and Clan Warfare. There are three game types for Quickplay mode. Skirmish, a team battle - last mech standing. Conquest, there are multiple points on the map which teams must capture to earn victory points. Assault, when the teams can capture a single base to win the game. In any Mechwarrior Online match the game is won when all enemies have been killed.
The second gameplay mode is Clan Warfare. This mode puts the mechwarrior in the front seat of a battle on a galactic scale. Incorporating a star map of the inner sphere, players can battle to gain territory or defend what they have. Players must choose allegiance to a faction (Innersphere houses or Clan). The mechs you can select and play in Clan Warfare mode depend on your faction. For Clan factions, only clan mechs will be available, same for IS factions. Players can then select the star planet they wish to attack (or defend). Depending on the status of the contested planet different game scenarios can play out.
Players might find themselves "Holding ground" on a recently conquered enemy territory, in this case an attack mission has become a defense mission. Eventually, if your faction persists and succeeds, the planet will be converted to your faction's territory. The starmap changes over time as different factions gain/lose territory.
Add up to twelve of your friends to a unit and smash the opposition. This game features automatic matchmaking and in-game voice communication on par with other popular games. The game has a great "Play for Free" model. You can become a powerful and rich mechwarrior with out spending money and eventually will unlock items that cost money for free in special events held frequently.
EDIT---------September 15, 2016
After having this game on my computer for years and now steam for almost a year, I have to say, it is on the list of my favorite games. Coming back to it and comparing it to when I started playing in 2013 isn't even fair. This has become a whole new game, better, faster, more versatile -- more fun! This is the Mechwarrior game you've been dreaming of since the late 90's.

The first time I gave it a try, I was quite dissapointed, because I couldn't get to terms with it. A friend was trying it, and he liked it a lot, so I gave it another try. I must say, I was not dissapointed anymore.
It may sound weird but the big mistake I did the first time was, that I expected a controller. Well of course it is a controller, but you should rather think as a mouse/keyboard extension about it.
After realising this I tried some of my favourite shooter games, which are typically hard to play with a controller and lo and behold! I can now play Painkiller just as well, as with my favourite keyboard/mouse combo. Something that no other controller can do for me. I purchased pinnacle andl also tried inputmapper and others, but it never felt comfortoable, and sure it was impossible to play games like Painkiller or Quake 3 in a way that feels not mediocre. The steam controller is the first one, that can do this for me, so I can definitely recommend it!
Be prepared to take some time get used to this way of playing, but once mastered, it doesn't feel different than playing with mouse/keyboard, as any PC gamer should. ;)
UPDATE: After using it for some time now, I notized that the USB port is flaky. I bought a new cable because I thought the cable has a loose connection but it wasn't. When the controller is moved and the cable is connected, it frequently shuts down and restarts loosing the power connection. The steam client software also crashes frequently (probably because of this it seems). Had to order a replacement.
I will order another and see if this has the same problem. As I don't like to play remote, I always use the controller via cable.
If this is a general problem I will update this review.
Update: After getting a brand new controller (haven't gotten the replacement back yet) I can see that this is indeed a general problem. Attaching the cable the USB port already shows small signs of being loose, so I expect that the problem gets worse after some playing. Therefore I change my vote to Not Recommended until this is fixed properly. As long as you play wireless it shouldn't be a problem for you. Yoou decide...

Since this game is on Summer Sale 2014, I feel like it's my duty to give my 2 cents regarding the gameplay. I have mixed feelings regarding this game, although I've spent a well 92 hours in-game. It's fun on certain levels and lacking in depth in other levels.
While I will recommend this game, I have to add that it's more or less for those "I want to build a customized fleet and do constant battle" type of people, rather than going the diplomatic or scientific victories. Other parts of the 4X elements are rather a little shallow.
This is a fun 4X game that captures the space battle and galactic expansion feel extensively, especially with the Disharmony expansion with the addition of bombers and fighters. Basically, it's all about creating your fleets, customizing your ships depending on their hulls, weaponry and similar, and send them off into battle.
Unlike Civilization or other similar 4X games, the combat in this game opens up a battle scene. Sadly, the only direct control the player can have in battles is the "battle cards" that is selected in each phase (long range, medium range, melee range). The rest is how your fleet and ship is set up. It's more or less like the combat in Paradox games (you have very, very limited control) unlike the tactical battles as in the HoMM or AoW series, but much less shallow than the Civ series (where it's basically two units with fixed stats with minimal variety battling each other).
The galactic expansion portion is fun, too. The planet colonization is satisfying. However, buildings, technology advancement, racial variety, diplomacy etc. lacks in depth somewhat.
Hence, I recommend this game VERY MUCH for those who wish to buy it for the "space battle simulator" feel where you pre-set your fleets, pre-set your ships, classes, leaders, ship stats, focus (long-range, mid-range, maybe melee, maybe beam weapons, missiles or kinetic weapons, or maybe fighter/bomber-heavy fleet), but not for its 4X depth to be honest.
So, here's my 2 cents. Now buy me something from my wishlist :P

Endless Space is a lot like the older "Sword of the Stars" game, with turn-based strategic elements of 4x and some tactical decisions during battles.  Unlike SotS, you can't actually control every detail of combat, but you do decide things like formations and targeting preferences, which can be setup prior to the battle or updated during each of three "combat phases" while you watch the fireworks.  Ship customization is much more detailed, letting you choose which hulls and gun-by-gun loadouts to use (no hardpoint assignments, though).  You also manage the planetary systems more, and have many more diplomacy options.  Ambient music and polished graphics throughout.  I've always had some problem with the camera during the battle sequences but since I usually skip that part it doesn't bother me much.  I've run across a couple of minor graphic glitches but nothing game breaking. The different races do play differently from each other based on their racial bonuses and special abilities, and the somewhat race dependent tech tree is all laid out so you can see what you're getting into with a line of research.    All in all a worthy 4x.

A great game for people with a fascination with mechanical workings, and with a want to take stuff apart. Also, a great way to find stuff to nitpick games about mechanics, like when an AK has the charging handle on the wrong side.

At first, things are hard to buy, the quiz is failed at almost every attempt, and you rip your hair out when you forget the slide lock of a pistol. But the game is a great way to hone your memory. For example,  I have managed to memorize the 500 someodd part ZIS gun,a seemingly impossible task, but then again, some people have memorized Pi to the 100,000th place. Credits are awarded for those who are willing to try, and try again, to reach that #1 spot, and be crowned champion. The feeling is extraordinary. The first gun I did that on was the StG. 44, about 10 places from the beginning.
So, for those of us willing to put time and effort into our gameplay, this is a completely F2P game (aside from texture packs), and well worth the effort.

Its a pretty fun game. I really enjoy the concept of people able to modify your armor and weapons loadout. You have limitations, including a total ton limit and certain parts of the mech can only hold certain types of weapons, and you have "slots." But within these, you can do just about anything you want. You can stick a really big engine and a bunch of machine guns all over your mech to make him fun to play with but annoying to other people, but to do this you will probably have to sacrifice armor. Or you can load your mech down with lots and lots of missiles but you probably won't have much room for other upgrades. You can choose to protect your ammo, or risk it exploding. You can switch standard heat sinks with more efficient doubles, or ferro fibrous steel instead of the standard in order to make your mech a lot lighter.
The main problem I have with this game is money. In the beginning, the game does give you a ton of money for your first 25 games, but you better use this very wisely. I am a mediocre gamer, not bad, not great, and I average 75,000 per battle. So I would expect a really good gamer to earn 150,000-200,000 at best. The cheapest that you can buy a new mech is around 1.5 MILLION but the good ones are going to cost you at least 6-8 million, and the best reach 15 million. Even just buying a new engine will cost you at least a half a million. And very simple, small weapons like machine guns and small lasers will cost you 10-25,000 and it only gets more expensive from there, with some getting close to a million. The point being...it takes FOREVER to make any real progress in the game.
If it weren't for everything being expensive and it taking a long time to earn the money, this would definitely be one of my favorite games, but unfortunately things are expensive and the game has simply become tedious as I have only had 2 mechs since getting the game a couple months ago.
Perhaps the game designers intended for you to have this problem though. They do give you trial mechs that you can play with for free and automatically change every so often so you can still have fun using those. All in all, not a bad game.

This is a great addition to the MechWarrior franchise. I've been playing it for years and PGI (the developers) keep making improvements. I wish the real-world prices for some of their mechs was a bit lower, but otherwise they've done a very good job of keeping things balanced and not letting only those with real cash get an advantage.
The key to success is patience. Stay with the group, concentrate on the same target(s) as everyone else and don't wander off alone or stand in the open. Don't play this like you're in a Gundam. I personally find this game a lot more enjoyable when I play with friends.
Oh, and in case you were wondering, this game is PVP only (for now). No solo campaign yet.
