Tribes: Ascend.....what can I say about thee?
To just say really fast, on its own, Tribes: Ascend is a decent first-person shooter game. Compared to the heritage of the previous games, it falls miserably short of the legacy of Tribes 1 and 2. Gonna add, I have 150 hours on Steam, but total in-game for TA is ~800 hours. Tribes 2 ~300 hours, Tribes 1 ~100 hours. TV, couple thousand, but this one was the gateway drug for the much more addicting stuff.
Movement, map design, weapon balance, band-aid fixes, devs who really didn't listen.....the problems with the development of this game do go on. They did try, but did they try their hardest? No, not even close. It has a passing resemblance, but that is it. I really, really, REALLY enjoy the old Tribes games, and so when I heard they were coming out with a new game, I was very excited. Then, it came out. I enjoyed it, although looking back, I think I was avoiding its flaws because it was a new game I was looking forward to so much, and I did not want it to be a disappointment. The more I played, though, the more prominent the problems became.
Problems listed above, and I will not go in-depth with them, because I am not sure this review has enough space. If you would like to know more, message me and we will have a LOOONG chat about them.
My recommendation for this game has 2 scores: from a classic Tribes veteran point of view, then of a shooter fan.
As a shooter fan, I say give the game a try. See if you like the type of gameplay. If you do, try out Tribes 2. Tons of fun, refined maps and gameplay. Not too many people play anymore, but still give it a try.
If you are a Tribes vet: Only if you want to miss the good ol' days of Tribes 1 + 2, and go reinstall them immediately. You can see the old gameplay, but it does not even come CLOSE to matching it.
Overall, it gets a 6.5/10 from me.

this is not a Noob friendly game in the slightest, and it is also very much Pay to win, now let me explain why.
the combat is nothing to hard to understand(weapon placement can be a bit tough to get used to at first), if you have played the Mechwarrior games before then its not to different from what i can tell(i only speak from watching a friend play it a bit and playing a round in a Mech Warrior Multiplayer Arcade thing once). building your own mech is quite complex, you have to first buy a mech, and there are lots to chose from. there are also several varrents of the many mechs of the same name because they each have different weapons they can equip(they are referd to as Hard Points). it can be quite a challenge to figure out how to best gear your mechs.
now, what makes this game P2W is; all the mechs have varrying prices, and getting enough of the Ingame currency to buy one after you buy one is quite a lot of work. once you have a mech, you might want to get some different weapons on it. that can end up costing more then the mech alone. you also will need to use the mech in combat to gain Mech EXP so you can unlock skills to make it perform better, and to unlock higher tiers of skills, you need multible varrents of that mech, AND unlock all the skills of them as well. Mech EXP can be used on other mechs... but it costs the Premium currency.
i played in several Faction war missions, and every time, my team lost. every time, my team faced off against several players in the same unit. the logic some might say is well, get into a unit and maybe you might start winning, to that i say if i dont have any mechs that would be of much use, then im dead weight, and it wouldnt be much fun.

Overall, I really like this piece of hardware. Switching from a XBox 360 controller to this took a little while, but once I made that transition, I completely prefer the Steam Controller. So now that we know I recommend the controller, let's see what I consider "Pros" and "Cons". Please note that the cons are all relatively minor and are not things that would keep me from purchasing another controller in the future.
Pros:
-It feels good when you're holding it
-It is wireless
-I have big hands and don't experience any fatigue from using this
-The community profiles for games that don't natively support gamepads are excellent
-Support for profiles that are for "non-steam" games
-The haptics feel nice and the touchpads are responsive
-Firmware updates keep improving the experience
Cons:
-Sometimes the batteries get "knocked" when setting down the controller, leading to me having to open the back and push the batteries back into place.
-No built in charging method, but that's alright. Grab a pair of rechargeable batteries and a charger and call it done.
-Single analog stick, not really a con, but using the right touch pad takes a bit of getting used to.
Well there it is, nothing too fancy but hopefully useful to some people considering making the purchase.

I can tell you right now with 100% confidence, you are either going to be in the I love this or I hate this camp, there is no middle ground. I personally fall into the first group and will tell you straight up this controller is not for everyone and has a steep learning curve and you need to commit some time to truely learn and get the most of this thing, if this fact right here scares you, quit reading now, and go buy a 360 contoller.
Frist off I am going to start off with what I don't like about this thing.
1. Since I just mentioned the 360 controller, yep same plastic, it feels cheap even though it is fairly sturdy, no foam or rubber grips.
2. This doesn't replace my 360 controller, frankly the controller just doesn't feel right for certain games, especially fighting games, some folks can get it going ok, I can't, and believe me I have tried. Any game that requires percision Dpad controling like Mortal Kombat or Street Fighter, is just hard to replicate, some platformers do seem to be ok using the trackpad, but I will always go with the analog stick if I can or go back to my 360.
3. Speaking of the analog, it isn't bad, but I personally wish it was concave, this is a preference thing.
4. The Gyro still has some issues, and I have had one of these since day one, its probobly a firmware thing, but on a rare occasion you need to turn the thing always on to let it calibrate, and then revert it to normal mode.
5. Lastly the absurd requiring to run in Big Picture mode, you can get some funtionallity without pig picture mode, but it is required, and if steam crashes or closes for some odd reason while your playing your game, your controler freaks out.
Now if Ihavn't ran you off by this point, you may be like me and find this controller to be one of the best things ever made.
1. After getting use to the odd feel, you have limitless customization options, this freature alone outweighs all the negative feelings I have for the controller. This is where that steep learning curve comes into play. How many times have you played a game where you are locked into certain control scheme you don't like? How many times have you played a game where it says it has controler support but it is total crap or there is no contoler support at all on games that should have it? With this you can map any keyboard and mouse funtion on the controller in a way only limited by your imagination, (and a few minor options limits). If you like FPS games but non't like being tied to a keyboard and mouse, this can get you very close to the percision of a keyboar and mouse, I don't recommend if if you are big into competitve play, but if you are even an enthusist, if you put the time and effort into getting the feel down and callibrating this just right, you play in games like Paladins and Team Fortress 2 and still perform well.
2. I have to say I like the shape, the handle bend the opposite direction other controllers do, at first I thought this strange, but with the way the trackpads work, it actually feels natural.
3. I am going to emphasize the cutomization again, becaus that is the selling point of this thing, I will ofter have multiple funtions mapped to a single track pad, where I can have it funtion like a mousle slider on the leftpad, and with the alternate mode option have pressed command funtion like a standard Dpad. I can have my right pad funtion like a track ball which is great for 1st person shooters, make it so if my thumb is just touching the pad it cicks in the gyro and I can treat it like a mouse controlling the sensitivity on  each separatly and even dampening the movment when I have a soft pull on one of the triggers (this is how you get the high percision aiming, it takes practice but you can). You can set outer ring bindings for things like mouse spins and a button activation (great for your typical left Shift + WASD on the analog for running) You can contol where the soft pull starts and ends.You have large hands you can adjust the orintation of your track padsto up and down are off center to better suit you.
In closing, I personally cannot sing enough praises for the Steam Controller, there are a few things I would like to see fixed, better support outside of big picture mode, the skins may make it feel less cheap (I need to look into that), but you are going to get back what you put into this guy, and with a few exceptions, this is usually the contoller I go to 1st, it's not for everyone, but I love the thing.

Not a fan. Just wish I could send it back in for an update if they ever get around to redesigning it as something comfortable for my hands. While originally excited for the product and what it seemed capable of, it is blown away by the console companies offering in build quality and user comfort.
In general I dislike the product across the board, from it's proprietary wireless dongle to the lack of a built in battery pack. Obviously this product works wonders for many players however I will continue to stick to my DS4 as I did the year before purchasing this (Winter '14) since while the SC features a robust amount of settings for games launched in Steam, another caveat, it is a pain to for me to hold and sit with comfortably for over 10 minutes.
This coming from someone who has used almost every mainstream controller under the sun over the last 25 years. That said, I'd place this controller next to the Xbox Duke controller (which some preferred) in comfort, somewhere near a general Mad Catz controller in build quality, and as a positive, a unique step forward when it comes to the amount of customization one can do, when again using Valve's software while running applications within Steam.
On a side note, the trackpads are neat, however, with most games currently designed around the DS4/XBOne controllers the joystick and buttons are pretty questionable in design and comfort as well. It is almost as if Valve wanted the player to see them as useless additions, forcing the user to play titles using one or the other rather than allowing the entire controller be usable in syncrasy.
So in the end, I can't recommend it in its current form, and in fact forget it exists except when advertisements pop up prompting new players to give it a shot. It doesn't replace the M+K, doesn't compete with the DS4, and its unique offerings are easily overshadowed by design and quality. However, for a first outing, things could have gone a lot worse, yet the Steam Controller falls behind today's competition vastly in its effort to be idiosyncratic within a niche need of Valve's own market.
That said, I'm looking forward to the next version (if it exists) in hopes that it will be a product I will fully enjoy.

I've given this game a positive review, despite some very clear issues.
When I first bought the game, it's controller support was non-existent. About a month later, they updated. Since I could finally play with my gamepad, I decided to try it. About four missions in, the game suffers from an obnoxious turret scene which was not balanced or fun and terrible out of place in a dog-fighting game. BUT....
-As many people pointed out, the music isn't terrible. I actually enjoyed it and didn't really notice a lack of variety. I was busy blasting fools with laser guns.
-Many people complain about the voice-acting. Why? It is terrible, but it is also kind of funny (as in, so bad it is almost good). I am disappointed because it seems like a little more effort on the parts of the voice-actors could have improved everything, but really, the cheesy one-liners the characters deliver are sort of better when they aren't delivered seriously.
-Bad/Linear Plot- The missions and overall story line are not very strong. Each mission is fairly short and I'm not really seeing much continuity seven missions in. But I got to shoot things in space in almost every mission and they were kind enough to add either amusing moments or serious ones to make me feel like there was a reason for shooting things in space.
-My only real complaint is slow turning. The controls on the gamepad are fine (except for the right joystick controlling throttle in some unexplained way?) but the turning speed for some of these ships is monstrous. Every time I do a 180 manuever or just try a regular turn with the left joystick it seems like my ship and the screen is stuck in mud. It isn't lag, just slow turning. Weird. Not game-breaking though.
-Super stupid turret mission. Hated it. I quit playing for 6 months after failing that so many times.
Overall, this is an amusing game with good visuals. It should probably be bought on sale. But keep in mind (I think most of the negative views failed to remember this) its regular price is $4. This isn't a game that gets featured in Gaming Weekly. It's a bargain bin game made by a small group of artists and developers. They took the time to TRY and build something epic. They failed (it's good, but not epic). Instead of trying to scam us out of 20 bucks like some other steam 'developers', they put down a fair price and occasionally have sales. That's decent and you can't ask for a better bargain.

Endless Space does not seem particularly interesting or unique, being yet another space-theme 4X game we find relatively common these days. And it's really not, frankly, it's a fairly by-the-book 4X game. It's not particularly polished, and there are some relatively severe balance issues between victory types, battle research, and resources. Yet, Endless Space still creates enjoyable experience through its plethora of balanced races each with unique goals and playstyles, along with a really nice, polished UI, and the game's great ability to make macro managing fun. Endless Space gets a very, very imporant aspect very, very right, it is definitely a grand strategy game. It's somewhat simple, and there are certainly gripes, but the game, although not very original, is incredibly solid. But, you should probably know about the gripes.
First off is the AI. It's irrationally agressive and frustrating to deal with. It can be enraged by the slightest offense, and will pester and deny cooperation repeatedly until you make a considerable effort to win their favor. It's incredibly annoying early game, but balances out mid-game after you research more and more tech allowing for stronger bonds between races. Although, the AI is never quite fully satisfied with you, and it is near impossible to get the entire crew of alien races to like you while still mantaining significant power on the board. It makes the diplomatic approach infuriating and way more difficult than any path in the game.
That brings me to my second problem. The victory balances. The victories are just clearly unbalanced. Supremacy (World Domination), Scientific, and Diplomatic victories are all much, much more difficult than the Economic and Cultural/Wonder victories, and the Expansion victory in middling difficulty. In fact, it'd be just stupid to get a Supremacy victory, which means you own all the other races' homeworld, before getting the Expansion victory, which is owning 75% of the map, except in very particular cases. Similarly, it's just way easier to build of Dust (money) or Industry to build wonders than enough Research points to win a Scientific victory. None of them are impossible, but Supremacy and Diplomatic particularly are extremely difficult. It's kinda nice to play each for the novelty, but not competitively, competitively you'd just go straight towards Wonder or Economic every time. In fact, the only times I've seen the AI come remotely close to a victory has been from one of those two methods.
The last major issue is the combat. The battles are neat, but the combat is incredibly boring. The only military research that matters is Kinetics and armor, everything else can be ignored. The macro combat aspect of the game is just one giant min-max challenge with one dominate strategy, and it's boring. The micro combat itself is a bit more interesting, it involves this weird cross between a card game and rock-paper-scissors. You have cards that are each specific tactics with different advantages and disadvantages. You uncover more tactics through leveling your captain (a Hero), and through research. Although, the AI is fairly predictable, and you'll soon form a dominate strategy that you'll just spam every encounter. It's just a big min-maxing number-measuring contest. Boring.
Now, the best aspects. The first are the races. Each are fairly different and offer various attributes tailored for different victory types. Each race has their own cluster of buffs and debuffs, and each has an unique perk. One race is at a constant state of war, as their entire goal is to consume planets, another race make great diplomats and start with the entire map unlocked, allowing quick grabbing for the best local planets for colonization, and another race has an absolutely huge scientific boost at low taxes. The DLC race is also really neat, as they do not use the Dust resource at all, and as a result has to use ways to cope with the rest of the galaxy's Dust-lust.
Another great aspect is the macro planning. No matter what victory you're heading for, you have to make long-term investments, plan for the unexpected, and participate in military and sometimes diplomatic shenanigans in order to acquire particular resources or planet sites that pertain to your victory plan. The tech tree is large and in depth, and it's a lot fun planning out your plan based on your overall victory and what opportunities are immediately available to you. That coupled with clean and deep micro-management of planets and development makes you really feel like a galatic ruler. Simply said, the game does its job, it's a very competent 4X game, even with it's issues.
Ultimately, I would say you should wait for a discount, as it seems to go on sale often, perhaps about 50% off. I would also suggest you get the DLC if you enjoy the game, likewise on sale, as it adds a good little bit to the game and melds with it well. If you like more casual 4X games, and you can afford it, I recommend you pick it up. Just don't plan to play too competitively.

Let's list every good thing about this game:
1: Some item combinations are mildly amusing.
2: The art is decent.
Okay, done. Here's all the bad things:
1: It's a bad mobile port and the entire UI is clearly designed for touchscreen, and plays awfully on a computer
2: At least half the game is essentially advertisement for GameFAQs, because the item combinations are so arbitrary as to be impossible without a walkthrough or brute forcing. The only reason that the combinations are as nonsensical as they are was to sell more Hint IAPs, and it makes the game completely unenjoyable.
3: There's a few combinations I found which actually had a different result depending on when in the game I combined them - meaning that I actually had to enter the exact same input twice expecting different results to complete the game.
4: The game costs $6 despite merely being a port of an IAP-laden port of a sequel of a clone of a flash game from 2004. You could just play the first Doodle God on Kongregate for free and get an identical experience, if not a better one thanks to a UI that was actually designed for the platform they released the game on.
5: A significant amount of these are near-identical to other combinations of items so you can't even complete the game without repeating yourself constantly (e.g., there's ~8 types of alcohol, all of which count as different combinations with nearly any material that combines with any alcohol)
6: The game has 4 or 5 different gameplay modes, but I honestly can't tell the difference between any of them. The gameplay loop is exactly the same - pick a random thing, rub it against another random thing, hope the developers concocted some story as to how they fit together, and then rinse and repeat.
7: Every time you do luck out and find an arbitrary combination of elements that makes something new, you get thrown out of the combination screen and into a tedious animation of that new object appearing on a globe. This is mildly interesting the first 2 or 3 times. Less so after the 200th. In a game that's already frustratingly slow thanks to an awful UI and necessity of brute force, it just exacerbates the irritance.
Just save your money and play the thousands of free flash games that do this much better.

Slow and Boring
-----------------
The player character feels like an inconsequential little mote in a map that is inevitably going to destroy him, and that's not a very fun experience.  I can think of a few things that contribute to this feeling:
- Many pitiful weapons.  Some of the weapons and buffs do add some player agency, but it takes a while to get them.  Some are so buggy that I feel robbed when I finally do invest in them (EX: claymore).
- The player character is very slow moving, so it takes forever to traverse a relatively small map.
- His pickaxe is painfully slow, so it just feels like a dumb slog during the initial phase, especially considering the player's movement speed.
Few Players
------------
Every game mode felt insanely empty or just plain impossible with only a two or three players.  It would be nice if there were other game modes (or variations of the existing ones) that were better designed for few players.  There just aren't enough people that know about this game to make public online play any fun when the game modes all ache for a ton of players.

This Meant that MP servers were now boring, as most modded gamemodes can't be played. I won't say that the community was ever perfect, it used to be good, but now RTB is abandoned and Blockland servers are basically empty shells of what they used to be. There's also the fact that the blocks that can be used to build are practically LEGO Blocks, which means that even building simple square houses is a tedious process. Overall, Blockland is a true gem lost in time, what used to be a thriving gaming community has become a desolate wasteland and has fallen prey to Money-Hog Developers that can't be bothered to fix their already ruined game.

I enjoy playing MWO and will recommend it but will also point out the positives and negatives of the game from my eyes as well.
The positives.
It is a very good mech "shoot em up" game. Perhaps one of the best i have played.
There is a vast selection of mechs, most of which can be purchased through the in game currency.
It is truly a Team Game, meaning that usually the team that communicates better most likely wins.
The developers explain their plans with the community as well as answer questions from the community from time to time.
The developers constantly run events during weekends and holidays that can net you extra mechs, ingame currency, and sometimes even Real money currency.
The negatives.
As a new player, the learning curve is very harsh. It will take some significant time to learn most of the nuances of the game.
Additional Mech Bays cost Real currency (MC) which means after your first 4 free mech bays you will have to spend  MC to gain additional Mechs.
The Community Warfare is a hollow shell of what it should be.  It is nothing more than Team Deathmatch to take over colored pixels which mean absolutley nothing. Hopefully this will be adressed in the future, but to this point it has not.
These are my honest opinions of the game, if you like a " shoot em up "  mech game and are willing to spend time learning the game , like to work as part of a team, then this is probably the game for you.

I did not know Stronghold until I bought it. It is a really good game if you like strategy games. Sure, the game is old, but it is fun and interesting. You can find yourself overwhelmed at first by so many things to do, and all the available resources, but once you get used to this (the game gives you a lot of tips), you will enjoy it.
The game itself consists on a Military Campaign, which contains a storyline and 21 missions. You can also replay historical or fan made castles, like Camelot. You can also play Economic Missions, were you have to get "x" resource/s, or do other stuff in a limited amount of time. Apart from this, you can edit your own scenarios and play them. You can also play Sieges (attack or defend the castle), Invasions (hold against the enemy) Free Build or Multiplayer games.
There are four difficulties: Easy, Normal, Hard and Very Hard. The game is, I believe, fairly balanced. Your troops vary from crossbowmen and archers to pikermen, macemen, knights, catapults, laddermen, rams and other units. There are random events that benefit or harm you, like a fair or wolves attacking your villagers.
So, I'd recommend this game to any fan of Strategy games. The only critic I would make is that the HD could be better (in my opinion). Other than that, it's a solid game.
Stronghold HD is a worthy upgrade of the original game, which is, as of today, still the best of its series.

Every now and then a mobile developer tries to take their successful, beloved mobile game and bring it to a more traditional gaming platform. These efforts always result in dumpster fires of failure. It isn't that mobile games are necessarily worse than their more traditional counterparts, just that different audiences expect differetn things from their gaming experience. People that want to waste a couple of minutes on the ride to work aren't going to want the same exact thing when they actually sit down and play something in their own free time, and Doodle God is just the latest example of that.
Doodle God, however, is just a mess from top to bottom. I don't understand how even mobile gamers enjoyed this. If you took a point-and-click adventure game item combination puzzle, and removed the context, goals, story, fun, and coded it entirely in goat's blood, you'd get Doodle God. You start with four elements, and start combining these elements to make more elements. These elements can then be combined with other elements to make more elements, and these elements can then be used to finally get you to the end goal: making more elements. That's all there is to the game. Rubbing two items together, hoping they work, and then seriously reevaluating where your life went wrong.
You may think that combining elements to make more elements (made so you can make more elements) might sound pointless and boring, but you're wrong. It's also frustrating too. Unlike most games where you're combining things, the game doesn't really give you any hints as to what you should be making. The game has you making stuff like octopi and ghouls, but other common items aren't in the game's dictionary. However, the game doesn't actually tell you it wants octopi and ghouls, and you just sort of have to guess. This is fine in the early game when you don't have many objects, but at some point you have over 100 at one time and without the game hinting what the hell it actually wants you to make you just sort of have to guess. Doodle God is that annoying partner you had back in college that always wanted to go out to dinner but wouldn't tell you what he or she wanted until you actually guessed it.
And to top it all off, a lot of the combinations don't make sense. Alright, so a warrior and a firearm makes a soldier. I suppose I can see that train of logic. But a fish and knowledge makes an octopus? What the hell does that even mean, Doodle God? "Just gotta keep on reading to the fish...gotta make them an octopus through education... hmm," one of the developers overheard an insane man mumbling to himself on the subway one day and that idea made it into the game somehow. Since some of these combinations were seemingly just pulled out at random from a hat, inevitably you will reach a point where you just need to randomly start combining things and hoping for the best. Or you could just wait until the hints refill and do it that way. Or you can close Doodle God, delete it from your computer, then burn your computer on the off chance some of the awfulness from this title somehow seeped its way onto your harddrive.
I'd recommend the third option. Or, the vastly superior option, never buying or downloading this in the first place and doing something better with your time like playing any other game available on Steam, going outside, or sitting perfectly still and allowing your mind to slowly deteriorate. Any of those option are better than ten minutes with Doodle God.

I became interested in Doodle God because of my job.  I figured any game that could keep a special needs child entertained and quiet (and not poking his neighboring van mates) during an hour long ride home AFTER being cooped up in school all day had to be worth looking into.  The game is certainly mind absorbing, with all the combinations of "elements" that can be combined in the main game alone (249 total).  Now add to that all the other "mini" games that can be played.  Hours of entertainment, or at least mind absorbing nullness.
For those who do not know about Doodle God.  It is a game of combining "elements" such fire, human or zombie with other "elements" like water, apple, or internet to make new elements.  In the main game there are 4 stages, ultimately working up to a total of 249 elements.  Some of the combinations are very logical while others are not.  The main game is basically a game of elimination where the player takes a single element and combines it with every other element to see what happens.  Then repeat with a new element.  (Special thanks to MakoSipper and their achievement guide God of Patience.  I am quite certain without this guide I would have never gotten that achievement.)
Beyond the main game there 7 Quests, 14 Artifacts, 11 Puzzles, an on-line Tournament, and an Encyclopedia (a compliation of every element and element combination from all the games (main, quests, artifacts and puzzles).
The Quests are specific scenerios such helping Santa build a sleigh or surviving on a desert island.  Artifacts is simply a puzzle where the player takes three elements and combines them to make a particular object like Stonehenge or a Light Saber.  (The best guide for this is Quests & Artifacts by ReivaX.)
The Puzzles are more active thinking then simply random combinations.  The player must use the correct combinations to achieve the desired outcome such making a firecracker or a Jack O Lantern. It is easy to make the wrong combinations and get stuck.  If stuck, undo combinations or start again. (I made a visual guide for the Puzzles since there was not one already.)
This game is not for everyone, and requires patience, tenacity and perseverance to get through (and/or earn all the achievements which is a different sort of patience, tenacity and perseverance.)

While not a religious person myself if there is a god and they are even a little like the god showed in this game it's pure proof against intelligence design .
Starting with just the four basic elements start smashing them together to discover new elements.  Then take those new elements and smash them together, repeat this process finding newer and weirder combinations.
If there was a consistent logic to how the combinations were unlocked this could be a reasonable puzzle game, however after the initial basic ones it all goes off the rails and becomes the the worst part of adventure games: combining stuff inside the inventory.

Mixing elements to form new ones is fun. Seeing a barren world gradually become populated with some of those newly created elements makes one feel like they're really creating something.
Most of them show funny quotes and proverbs when created to add more flavour, and the intro scenes for each chapter are usually funny.
Once you run out of the initial logical and fun way to combine elements (and patience), you're mostly stuck using brute force combinations or a guide. Once that happened, it became quite tedious.
Puzzles and side games are a nice addition, especially the puzzles. Elements have to combined in a specific manner to form the required final element.
Overall, can be quite tedious and frustrating, but it's still a good game. So I'm giving it a 'thumbs-up'.

I grew up playing games like this on SEGA, and they've always been a hell of a lot of fun with friends. Anything that brings that loungeroom fun back, and does it with online multiplayer gets my vote instantly. Ultimately, my best comparison from my childhood would have to be Liero, that real-time worms game that ran on DOS. Easily played at school because it would fit on a single floppy disk. I can't believe I just typed that, I haven't mentioned floppies in so, so long.
Gun Bombers is actually faster paced than I realised; my first game, I ran into the other player with a pistol and clicked my mouse to fire; shoot..... shoot... .. shoot, shoot shoot. The realisation that it plays more like Soldat or Crimsonland than .. Something much slower, was surprising to me, I don't know why. I guess I looked at it and expected bomberman, a game of timing and strategy, when in fact it's an action game. I only mention this in case some of you haven't realised this, as I hadn't.
In a nutshell, you have multiple rounds where you have to divide your time between trying to kill the other players and mining for minerals to gain currency to be spent buying weapons before the next round. Surprisingly similar to Counter-Strike if it also had random piles of cash around the map which you could go for prior to planting the bomb.
Honestly, there's not too much I can say about the game. It plays great and feels very solid. I guess there are a few things about it that I'd like to see improved:
• The UI is based on its spiritual precursor, a SNES(?) game, so there's of room for improvement there. Weapon selection included.
• The digging mechanic; having to aim in the direction you want to dig was annoying at first, but became second nature after a few matches. I still find myself accidently digging while running toward or away from someone, would be nice to have to confirm an intent to dig, a key or something.
• Mines and claymores are not visible to enemies and can be placed without any real warning to other players. They slow the pace of the game due to their lethality. My friends and I always have these disabled.
• Zoom. I love the zoom feature, but feel I am disadvantaged when using it, so it is rather redundant. If larger maps were ever going to be a thing, I'd like to see everyone forced to the same zoom level, not necessarily being able to view the entire map at once.

To cut it short for those who don't want to read; the game is mainly ruined by its community. I waited all these hours before making this review just to make sure I didn't make a mistake.
I originally started playing this game due to wanting a game other than Counter-strike to play with my colleagues at work. This turned out to be a very good choice due to how well it runs on my work computer. It is an i3 with Intel HD4000, quite low specs compared to the majority of PCs today.
I'll start with praising how well optimized this game appears to be; I get about 45 fps solid on lowest settings, and it looks great. I have experienced it on my home computer, and the graphics are of course, even more impressive; but that's not where I choose to play this game.
The game has a cool concept; build your own gun and fight in teams in various game modes. When you first play it, you'll get a very TF2-style vibe from it. It's fast paced and cartoony.
The first problem arises in the perspective of third person. This isn't a heavy criticism, because the developers are trying something a bit different here; setting third person in a fast paced environment. In games like this, I like to be able to look around a lot, checking my back, and it gets a bit annoying with the camera behind you. This is just my personal criticism, so I'm sure some people like it this way.
There is something incredibly off-feeling about the aiming in the game, someone I know also noted this. I'm experienced in playing shooters, and I cannot at all get the hang of this, after 70 hours. There is some weird depth-perception issue for me, where I will often shoot the ground in front of myself, instead of an enemy further back. I can't put my finger on this, but I'm going to note it in the review (and yes, I have increased the FOV).
Next, the servers and client issues. There is a lot of client-side control in this game, it seems. You will often die, but still manage to kill someone after it's stated you are dead; simply due to lag. You might not see yourself die for a few seconds, giving you chance to shoot at people before it updates. With the gamemode 'Jackhammer', the hammer carriers will very often kill each other at the same time. Some might say it adds more fun into the game, but I find it mildly fustrating and in general it just looks buggy.
Now, the main gripe. The community. To put it simply, the community is not what you expect. It's not friendly like TF2, nor is it as awful as counter-strike. It's worse. I hesitated for a long time for atleast 30 hours of gameplay, deciding on whether to recommend this game or not. It's a cool game, but in the end, the community just makes it not worth it. Third, the price point is very reasonable - especially when you consider it has way more features than a standard xbox controller.

This is the best controller I've ever used.  The touchpad is a major improvement over a second joystick for 'look' in 3d games.  The accuracy and control is truly impressive. Takes a while to get used to, especially the right track pad replacing a right joystick. You really need to customize that trackpad to get it to work and feel appropriately for most games as well. It took me a few hours to figure out a decent configuration for dark souls 2 sotfs camera.
Other than that, the shoulder buttons seem to be specifically designed with the idea that you use both your middle and index fingers to click despite the popular method is index only. The video for some reason shows the player using only his index finger and doesn't show how awkward it is to reach the bumper shoulder buttons that way. I personally have to either stretch my fingers or shift my palms slightly.
Besides that, you will end up constantly clicking the grip buttons by accident. I love the idea and I still use them but putting a button in the place where you hold the controller doesn't make a whole lot of sense. You'll probably end up removing them from your settings or just putting unimportant actions on them like talking to npc's or something.
Despite what I've said up to this point I only really have 3 gripes with this controller.
1. The design of the controller puts the shoulder buttons in an awkward position. People with large hands or even flexible fingers may not have this issue but neither I nor most of my friends fit that description.
2. The grip buttons are too easily pressed by accident. This is something you tend to be able to avoid more as you get used to the controller but it was just a poor design choice altogether and you'll never entirely avoid it.
3. The battery compartment. I love the idea of using the batteries to balance the weight of the controller but tons of people are having issues getting their batteries back out when they need to swap them. You either need a tool to push those little sliders or risk bending your nail back because it is not an easy task. And if you have luck like mine and so many others, the battery itself will get jammed, the metal conductor will bend from you trying to get it out and then every battery after that will also get jammed.
Overall I still love this controller a lot. It's wireless, super customizable and works with ALMOST any game. The number of buttons is fantastic and basically means you can use it in place of any kind of controller so it works pretty well for emulators too I would imagine. The battery life is pretty fantastic but it seems to have issues turning off sometimes if you exit big picture mode so take that into account. I wouldn't choose this over a 360 or playstation controller for any one game but if I were to only use one controller for all my games, it'd be this. I really only use my 360 controller for high precision platformers or games that require a lot of shoulder button pressing like enter the gungeon.
Be warned, despite the whole thing about the steam controller being that it will work well for all games, there are still some that it doesn't like pirate warriors 3. It's not the controllers fault so much that it is the games inability to recognize it as a controller type that it will use.

Beyond Space is a third-person space shooter that has some very good visuals, but not quite enough content, as half the missions doesn't involve the visuals. The trailer promised some huge space battles where you're one fighter among many other fighters among the huge starships pounding at each other. Yet it's seriously underdelivered. The missions seem to be completely disjointed with no progression. One mission you're playing scout for your space navy, then next mission you're a mercenary flying for some unknown benefactor, then next mission you're flying an obstacle course time trial! And yes, it's the same guy "Max Walker".  They even threw in a turret defense mission!
The writing is almost... high school bad. "Hal" was so idiotic it's basically the straight man for any sort of bad joke, taking things too literally. That Irish / Scottish accent is just ARGH! And why is he like in command of the fleet or something? He's basically the primary guy Walker talk to... not only fleet control, but scout report, jump gate control, and more.
The game is also notorious for "giving" you new weapons, but made it impossible to mount them. The scroll menus for the weapons and components (primary, secondary, shield, and booster) are IMPOSSIBLE to scroll. They require dragging with the mouse, and even then it's nearly impossible. Furthermore, once you did select it, you have to click an additional button to SELECT this weapon or component or else your scrolling were in vain.
Once in the cockpit, the visuals are good, but the controls are just... ARGH. None of the ships seem to turn fast enough, and enemy ships seem to be able to turn within its own length. And what's the point of rolling the ship port or starboard? Yet there are two buttons dedicated to that. They don't seem to actually evade anything.
Back to the enemy's ridiculous turn rate. You chase down this enemy and you're right behind him, and a few seconds later, the enemy ship had managed to turn 120 degrees and flew past you WITHOUT slowing down. And what's worse, this happens from the smallest light fighters to even corvettes / gunboats that are much larger than fighters. And in this universe, corvettes have afterburners (WTF?!) and can pull away from you, even on full afterburners.
The weapons don't feel much different. Primary weapons are infinite ammo, being energy based. Any improvements are minor (like slightly higher firing rate, or trade firing rate for damage, and so on). The "secondary" weapons are either heavy guns or missiles, but with limited ammo that has no replenishment within mission... once you're out, you're out, period, and had to rely on guns only.
The weapons controls are also weird. With only two buttons, you'd think they'd just do one button for primary and one button for secondary, but no. It's one button to shoot, and one button to switch weapons. That's right, you can't shoot both guns together. ARGH! No "all guns" alpha strike!
Which brings me to my main complaint: the bosses. There are a couple boss fights in this game, where you need to take down a supership, that's heads and tails better than yours, but may also be escorted. The bosses are usually corvettes of some sort... but they are hardly slow moving. No, they are as fast, if not occasionally faster than you, and they have 360 tracking turrets so deadspots where you can't get hit are almost impossible to find (hint: try the "bottom")  They also launch missiles (sometimes) and may be escorted by fighters (sometimes). And you need to kill them by wearing them down... and yes, they can be shielded too.  So what usually happens is they keep lobbing missiles and turret shots at you, while you try to shoot them to wear down their shields so you can bust them with heavy weapons, but due to the bad turning radius of your own ship (and their cheating ships) you end up using all your heavy weapons to no appreciable effect, or got it half dead, then you got chewed to pieces when you try regular strafing runs. The bosses are just TOO HARD, too maneuverable.
Sound is not too bad, dialog is professionally recorded, and I'm sure the voice actors did what they could. But it's not a good script. Have to say though, visuals are gorgeous on 1680x1050, and didn't have to much with the resolution much. Just make sure your gamepad is connected and ready BEFORE you start the game, or else the game won't see it. period.
All in all, bad bosses, bad humor, missions that really make no sense, and so on, made this game ibarely tolerable, and you should instead pay for the classic Freespace 2 or even Descent: Freespace for about the same price and enjoy that instead.

Played this years ago online for free (you can still find it on Kongregate and such). This paying version has a lot of added content: a world map and tons of minor minigames with the same basic game mechanic.
+ It can be fun for a short while to try to combine random stuff, and sometimes succeed to make new random stuff out of them.
+ The world map is pretty, and populating it adds a sense of progress.
+ Each combination comes with a quote and a link to the Wikipedia article of the item :D Almost feels educational.
+ In this version you can look up items by initial. Yay, no longer have to memorise which semi-arbitrary category each item happens to be in!

All of that aside the concept of the game is pretty solid, mainly because it's not a pay to win game, that many PvP games fall victim to. To the best of my knowledge you cannot pay real money to get better (upgraded) equipment. The best you can do is pay real money to get accelerators that help you upgrade equipment faster. That said, upgrade equipment is a small bonus at best, and normally not even noticeable. I believe the only one I really noticed was upgrading a clip to having 52 round clip instead of a 50 round clip (there were a few other aspects upgraded but the percentages are very small), in the grand scheme those 2 bullets aren't going to give me much of an edge.
Now you do have to unlock most of the parts in the game, the different barrels, sights, triggers, clips, etc. You can try them out before you buy (as long you have the prerequisite part) so you can quickly get the set of parts you like with minimal grinding against bots, if you feel for some reason the stock parts give you such a huge disadvantage (they don't) against a team based PvP match that will get you there faster, regardless of your K/D ratio, or if you win.
While they have added parts in the past, I can understand them not adding many more simply for balance reasons.
But because of the lack of updates and new content the player base has drastically dwindled, which is very fatal to a game focused on PvP (though they are adding PvE now... on the PS4 first of course).

I have had the Steam Controller since launch. I also have the Xbox 360 Controller.
The Steam Controller is my First Choice of the 2 controllers.
The fact that i can play my keyboard and mouse games on it is a huge plus.
And i like that you can designate what buttons do what in each game.
There are a few drawbacks and i will list them here-
1. There are some games where the xbox controller is better, Like GTA5... ( i am able to aim better and quicker with the xbox controller)
2. It seems that DirectX12 doesnt support Steam Controller (Rise of the Tomb Raider works fine with the Steam Controller when using DirectX11, but for 12 there are issues)
3. Some games will get updates that will make you change the Steam Controller Configs. (this mainly happens when the game was only Keyboard and mouse, but then the devs introduce controller support and the SC settings gets nerfed. This happened to me on 2 games - Dead by Daylight and Terarria).
Now for the Positive aspects,
1. Battery Life is awesome,,, 4 times longer than my xbox
2. The controller works on the desktop as a mouse and keyboard as well, so i am able to surf the web from the couch or navigate thru twitch without having to get other hardware.
3. The community and forums are really good... whenever there is a bug, the forums normally has some type of work around.
4. There are ALOT of customizations for the controller.
5. Works well with emulators and other games that are not Steam.
I reccomend this controller,,, but you should still have an xbox controller as well.

I've had the controller since the launch and have had many hundreds of hours use so far within steam, navigating Kodi and just general desktop use. I use the controller from my sofa in my lounge onto my main tv - the way the guys at steam envisaged it being used and I have to say I personnally think the controller is great, but it can make some games a nightmare to play unless you put the time in to change the controls to what suits you or if your lucky someone else has already done it.
Theres lots of reviews covering the software & customisations, if your willing to put the time in to setup the controller you will benefit - although this seems frustrating at first, i came to realise how many of us have poured over specs of graphics cards and spent hours trying to tweak a few extra Mhz out of a chip?! this is really just more of the same, setting up your pc to achieve your desired result so if you prefer to pick up a controller and play, you may be better off with a PS/Xbox pad.
I personally don't like the shiny/gloss finish but I can live with that, after all, how long do you actually spend looking at it?! some options for colour/finish would've been nice though.
I'm also not keen on the noise the buttons make when pressed, it makes the controller seem cheap and I think it ruins the experience sometimes, during quiter moments you think "wait, what was that noise.... oh it was the button.." - it may sound daft but that pulls you out of the experience and you can loose you concentration.
However, regarding a different type of noise, the haptic feedback, this is fantastic for feeding you info or even confirming what mode your in; an example is changing the sensitivity of the trackpad for aiming when the left trigger is fully pressed, you can change the haptic feedback to a higher setting to match the higher sensitivity of the pad - it doesn't sound like much but in game its useful and informative.
The controller doesn't tick all boxes but its a good middle ground between the two main forms of control, I still use my keyboard/mouse setup but I have to say I use my xbox pad less and less....

EDIT:
Updating this review after 1.5 years with the Steam Controller:
The Steam Controller is limited only by the time and attention you invest into it. It may not have the sleek product design and craftsmanship of a dualshock, but the extent to which you can customize and tweak the controls for this controller is unparralled in any other gamepad.
We have a dedicated media-server / couch-gaming machine connected directly to our living room TV. I have a 150 or so games in Steam, and I also very actively use Plex and other streaming services from the machine. At first I was switching between a wireless keyboard and mousepad combo and the controller, but over the last year I simply stopped using anything other than the SC. I invested hours into programming useful 'Steam Chords'  and a robust desktop configuration for when I'm not using games. Short of writing a text based document or programming, there's very few tasks I can't just do on the controller now.
I've added a number of emulated games from other systems, and the Steam Controller is amazing... I have multiple action sets to fulfil so many different needs for these games now... I have gyro usage in Wii and GC games. I can launch anything from Steam and alt-tab (steam chord) to change music quickly, etc.
The controller feels fine in my hands. The touch pads took getting used to, but now it feels natural.
There are certain M&K games that may never work properly, but they are few. The community has many well crafted layouts for you to use or get started with.
I've since bought a second one, and have actively sought out couch-friendly local co-ops games.
For $30-35, this controller is pretty amazing.
------
The steam controller is my main interface device for my HTPC. I've made dozens of meticulously crafted configs, not just for games, but applications (plex, etc.,) that I launch via steam big picture. It's perfect. I can't imagine this being possible with any other game pad or controller, not like this. For $50 it's damn worth it.

Stronghold is one of those games I keep coming back to again and again over the years.  It's easy to pick up and start, and it's amazingly deep and entertaining.  They storyline is super cheesy, but fun.  It doesn't take itself too seriously, which is a good thing.  The villains, while two dimensional and easy to hate, are also rewarding to fight.  Each one has their own personality and fighting style, and when you finally defeat them, it makes it all the sweeter.  The focus of this game isn't on the plot or the storyline, but the castle-building aspect.  As such, they give the villains just enough depth to make you want to kill them, and they give you just enough plot to make the ending desireable.  There's no plot twist or big surprise.  Just a long trek through the campaign with the reward of killing the big bad at the end.  And it's a sweet ending when you get there.
The game has several modes.  The military campaign is the "story" mode, but there is also a much less linear but still entertaining economic campaign.  There are also a slew of one-off siege and castle defense scenarios, where you are given a set number of troops and a castle to either defend or conquer.  Finally, there is a free-build mode with highly customizable settings.  There is even a tutorial mode which is essentially free-build with easy objectives to help introduce the basics, but the military campaign does a good job of introducing new game mechanics at an easy-to-learn pace without making the campaign missions themselves boring.  The wide variety of modes focusing on all the different aspects of the game really help give it some replayability.
The one downside to this game is the pacing.  There are frequently times where you could probably get up, leave your computer, and let the game run without you needing to supervise.  Waiting to hit 500 of a resource while your castle wall is literally filled to the brim with archers and crossbowmen basically means that you can endure any attack, you just have to wait until the economy finishes gathering the resource.  Essentially, once you hit a certain point, the game turns into a waiting game, as you know you've won the mission but the tedium of actually finishing the objective for the map hasn't been done yet.  This is a minor issue at best, and only relevant in the missions focusing heavily on economy, but it's common enough to bear mentioning.
Later games change the system.  Crusader is probably the crown jewel of the Stronghold series, and Stronghold 2 is still fun.  But this is the game that started it all, and frankly, it's inspired.  Everything is original, and very little is done wrong.  It's rare for the first game in a series to do nearly everything correctly.  Don't expect a compelling plot or deep three dimensional characters.  This game comes with one purpose - to be fun to play, and to give you a thin reason to throw hordes of macemen at the enemy's castle just to see how far you get.

Pay to Win Changes.  Microtransaction Greedy Company.  Ruined a Good Game.
The game has changed a lot.  When I started playing it I would have highly recommended it.  Not anymore.  The company is completely obsessed with getting money through microtransactions.  The entire game changed to maximize the microtransactions.  Unless you want to pay oodles of money, stay away.  I'll discuss it further if you'd like to understand better before getting involved.
Game play:
The actual game is fun as an idle clicker.  There are three different investment paths you could play as well as live events with badge rewards for completing them.  There are slow periods and it can take a while to finish if you aren't that active with the game.
Here's where it went wrong:
They changed the live events to be competitive with leader boards and offer "rewards" to the top players.  This has changed everything.  Even if you try to ignore the live events your main game now suffers dramatically.  The only way to make you play better in a live event is to buy different types of boosts with gold.  Gold is/was given through regular game play.  Most importantly, you can buy gold with cash (the microtransactions).  If you can't see how this is going... keep reading.
Changes:
You once got daily rewards for logging in that gave you a very small amount of the in game currency (gold or mega bucks).  This was to make up for the Kongragate users getting these free for watching ads.  They've removed the feature in steam (without warning anyone) because they no longer want to give you gold as they want you to buy it instead.  Remember, gold is used in buying boosts in the game and most notably the live events for competition.
When you complete your main game path (Earth) which can take from 4 months of constant playing to years of casual playing, you are given a gold reward once if you reset Earth and started all over from scratch.  The reward was 5,000 gold.  I, along with so many others, got this reward.  Suddenly, without warning, this was change to 500 gold.  They claim that the 5k was just too much gold and people could compete unfairly in the live events.  This is actually inaccurate, as I'll explain later.
Live events have changed as well.  When I started playing they lasted a week and you could complete the event without using gold as long as you did tend to the management in a somewhat timely basis.  Some of them were fun and required strategy.  They were held about once a month around holidays or the like.  When they started adding the leader board stuff they began playing the events almost constantly and replaying recent events.  They also started making them shorter so you absolutely had to spend gold to finish them.  They were ramming then down our throats trying to get those microtransactions.
Leader boards are a joke.  I had the 5k gold, finished all aspects of the game several times over again, so I could spend the gold on the events.  Spending 100 gold and sitting there constantly playing for the entire time would mean I would rank around the 2k mark.  You actually had to be active for about 24 hours a day to keep up with the game to hold on to the 1k position.  I forgot about the game for half a day and dropped to 6k rank.  One of the reduced time events I decided to dump a couple hundred gold to see how it would go, 1k with playing constantly.  In order to place in the top 100 you would have to spend all 5k free gold and monitor the game straight without take sleep breaks and then you still might not be able to do it.  500 gold reward from completing Earth is a slap in the face if 5k won't cut it.
There's rampant cheating in the leader boards.  There is no way anyone can legitimately compete.  From using autoclickers to apparently (it's been written about but I don't know) tweaking the time on your computer you can fool with the system there is unfairness in the leader boards.  There's other things that cause you to wonder about the legitimacy of it like the names on the leader boards are highly suspicious, when you should get a big boost on the leader board but stay in the exact same rank, or when the game just starts and the top ranked has so much that it would be impossible to get.
Why it matters to the casual player:
You cannot actually compete in the events and will struggle more to complete the regular games.  They made it even harder for those who just want to relax with the game with their gold changes.  You are forced to spend gold on live events now to finish them.  However, they have cut the gold you can get through playing the game.  It makes it so much harder for the new casual player to get anywhere.  Live events give badges with the last badge for finishing the event being a multiplier for the regular game.  You need to collect the badges to help your normal game progression.  If you can't complete the live event your game suffers.
Gold is used in the regular games for boosts that dramatically help your game progression.  Having the daily rewards removed means you can no longer help your game along.  You will get a bit of gold through playing, but you now have to save that for the events that have the badges that you need.   Even if you finish Earth you no longer have enough gold to buy the different object to help your games on resets.
Basically, Hyper Hippo has said screw you casual users we only want super competitive wealthy microtransaction buying players.  I used to praise this company and play all their games.  I have stopped playing every single one of them for various reasons, but this particular game and what they did was egregious.

"Doodle God" from the developer JoyBits. This game strangely similar to a mobile game called "Alchemy." And so the concept should be more or less the same thing.

Tournament: Online mulitplayer. Compete against other players in creating elements within given time-frame.
Encyclopedia: Collection of facts on the elements from the game.

Final thoughts, I felt that this game is good, but it can get tedious somewhat; discovering what is the best combination to create new elements. As for the game's replay value it's low. I would recommend this game but not at the full price.

A quite good 4X game which seems to take its inspiration from the legendary classic Master of Orion 2.
True to its forefathers there are custom races which compete for the mastery of the galaxy with multiple possible victory options. This means planet management, technology trees, ship design and to an extent diplomacy with heroes added to the mix. The space combat is nicely animated (if you want to have a look at how it goes) and is resolved neatly in phases with rock-scissors-paper style tactics which can make or break the battle.
Even though at it seems to have all the elements and these are decently implemented, there is still something missing, which eventually drops the game to only quite good. The problem is that it is streamlined and polished to an extent that nothing really sticks out. The technologies go forward and help you in your campaign, but there are no death rays or anything else to look forward for. The events in the galaxy are only text boxes to click through and diplomatic relations feel the same regardless of the races involved. So in a long run it just dries up to turns executed in a routine fashion and statistics. Still, while this game does not really compare to the legends, it is still an entertaining exercise to play though and can be recommended to fans of the genre.

I see the reviews for this game show mixed opinions and I might as well give my own plus some information about it.
This version of World of Tanks was originally a mobile phone exclusive. Since the average mobile phone has way less powerful hardware than an average PC, the requirements to play this game are significantly lower. In comparison to its PC equivilant, this version of course has less graphics, smaller match sizes (14 players vs 30 on regular WoT), and a more visualized interface (big buttons and other stuff).
As Wargaming makes an attempt to create a cross-platform version of WoT, Blitz was introduced on the Windows 10 App store and now Steam. I am happy that this game is now on Steam since you no longer need a phone or a PC with Windows 10 to play this game. Not that I don't have Windows 10.
Besides toned down features from WoT, the map sizes are smaller and there are no indirect fire SPGs. There are less tech trees and they are smaller but the damage models are revised and you can see where your shells can and can't penetrate. Other than that, in summary, this is a more simplified version of WoT.
Now for my opinion of this game, considering I've been playing this game for months with over 1000 battles of experience, I actually like this game better than the original WoT. Now don't get me wrong, World of Tanks is a great game, but I don't think it appeals to my taste. I've played the original WoT for about dozens to a hundred or so hours just to give you how much experience and to be honest, the matches I've spent in that game are pretty sporadic. There's just so much going on that you have little control over the entire match and you can struggle as a result. Yet, maybe if I decide to play that game again and try my best, I may get a different experience.
But for now, World of Tanks Blitz appeals to my taste. It isn't the only tank game I play as I also play War Thunder which I have over 1000 hours of playtime in planes and tanks. If your wanting to try something new, whether you've played regular World of Tanks before or not, give this one a try. This game is free to play so you don't have to pay for anything whether you happen to like it or not. Also if you ever want to find me, my WoTB tag is "ArmoredMustelid" (this is my third wargaming account that I started with WoTB)

Loadout is an amazingly fun casual TPS that is all about guns. The gunplay is smooth and fun, gameplay is fast paced, and. Holy♥♥♥♥♥♥the guns. There are HUNDREDS of gun customization options from the wacky and crazy, to the average and practical. And it all surrounds on a currency known as blutes.
As you play you get blutes, which you use to buy 7 gun options, there is the payload, the type, the trigger, sight, stock, magazine, and the barrel. And you can purchase different types as you progress and get blutes.
The payload is what bullet type the gun shoots, there are 5 different payloads, slug, an average bullet, tesla, electicity which passes to nearby enemies, pyro, which burns things, healing, which can heal teammates, and you get healed by it as well. And then "The Juice" which increases your allies speed and damage.
Then the type, what kind of gun is it? there is beam, launcher, which explodes, rifle, and finally pulse, which is like rifle on it's own, but can be batshit crazy with some customizations.
Now the trigger, this decides what fire type it is, there  are several different options for this, that I won't go into full detail on.
Then the sight, this decides how you see when you aim down, by default there is the iron sights, but there is also a health sight, which shows enemy and ally health, laser guided system, which is great for launchers, and sniper, self explanetory.
The stock... I actually never bothered with the stock. NEXT
Magazine decides how much ammo you have and how much damage you can do. you can get one with low ammo capacity, but a lot of damage, or another one which is the oposite, plus a ton more I won't bother to explain further.
Barrel can increase spread, or accuracy.
Now, is this a good game? YES, it's a fun team based TPS with amazing cusomization. and getting any gun is completly free. there is no way to pay money for ingame customizations. there are ingame hats which cost money, but those don't effect gameplay.

Before actually reviewing the game itself, I need to ask if the description of the product is sarcasm or honesty. I have to go with the benefit of the doubt and say it's sarcasm, since I'm sure no developer would call this a "breathtaking space adventure" or "epic space odyssey worthy of the greatest hollywood blockbusters".
- - - - - - - -
Conclusion
- - - - - - - -
Figured I'd put this up in front of the rest of the review: if you can look past some uninspired story, bad voice acting, messy mouse aiming, generic sounds/music, and sometimes lousy menu navigation, then I'm sure you'll enjoy it. I, however, could not. If you see it in the 99 cent aisle, sure, it can give you an hour or two of fun. But for $4, I wouldn't.
- - - - -
Review
- - - - -
In short, the game isn't bad. In fact, the gameplay is quite nice. It's a simple, 3D shooter with multiple ships and weapons to choose from. And the graphics are fine for the kind of game it is. But everything else is pretty terrible.
Controls aren't impressive, particularly mouse control. I prefer using a mouse for high precision aiming, but this game doesn't have precise aiming. You merely influence the direction the ship goes, almost like there's some sort of mouse acceleration. If you don't want to use this odd aiming, you can try your luck with a joypad or using the arrow keys for aiming. Unfortunately my joypad has a deadzone issue, and while it would have been nice to have an option within the controls to fix that issue, I don't expect it as it's a hardware problem on my end and not theirs.
Story (there's a story?) isn't all that immersive. Then again, this game doesn't aim for story, assuming the description of the game is sarcasm and that it really doesn't aim to grab the audience through its "space opera".
Voice acting is abysmal and at times, cringeworthy. I'm sure with better scripts, the actors themselves could have done something more impressive. But there's just something about the dialogue that has me shuttering when I hear it.
Music isn't bad, but it's nothing special, either. Take any generic space-orientated game and pull the music from it, that's what you have in Beyond Space.
Sound effects are fitting enough, but once again, nothing special.
Menu navigation. I noticed I had new weapons to choose from but couldn't figure out how. I then figured out that you had to swipe through the weapons in order to view the new ones added to your inventory. As far as I can tell, there are no arrows to click for viewing other weapons. You have to swipe the mouse.
I experienced some performance issues in the tutorial and really can't pinpoint the reason. One of my CPU's cores were at full usage for some reason and it gave me some stuttering in the game, but all other levels didn't really have that issue. At least the ones I played, as I wasn't interested in playing for much longer than I already had.

Ugh, I know a bunch of people are going to dislike this, but I got bored. That's why i only played 2.5 hours. Ok, now the reasons.
8BitMMO is a fully player built world, that's a bad idea because there will be a bunch of players leaving blocks everywhere that serve no purpose. I have to go into my inventory, select the item, click the box to drop it, and that's it. Why can't I just select the block I currently have, and place it, like in games like Minecraft. Also, the game is shallow, there are only 3 npcs that give you quests. I would like more npc quests to be added, like in other mmos, so I don't have to run around doing horrible player quests, (more on that later). Also there's this place that looks fun that I need to be level 4 though. You know why i'm not level 4? Because of the bad player quests.
The players make horribly lazy quests, a lot of the time, they don't put me where the quest is, they give me directions that don't seem to work, and I get lost. Also once, I got a quest where I had to collect keys, and the only keys I found belonged to someone else. Thanks whoever made that quest. I even got a quest to visit a gold/xp farm. Does the developer even monitor this game? What doesn't help is that I progress slowly, and I keep getting the quests I don't want over and over again.  I never get anything new. Okay, so OB64 has released. And now after actually playing it for a while we, the community, can finally give a non-'OMG EVERYBODY FREAK OUT!!!' review. (Fyi this is also a note to people who are just bashing on OB64 in this reviews section. Those people should read this too)
After playing both on my old account and a new account i created specifically for testing the OB64 new player grind I have come to the conclusion that the game is still Paladins. It is still the game we know and love. (At least for an Androxus, Evie, Maeve player like me)
Among good things to come with the patch are the reworked ammo generating cards for some flank characters. my androxus deck now gives me a 14 ammo clip instead of 12, which can make all the difference in a fight.
None of the characters have had their playstyles majorly changed either (from what I can tell). Quite a few of the new legendaries are really good too, such as evie's. You give up major self sustain and mobility for the occasional huge boost in damage.
The introduction of bound casual before the patch release was a close save. If it wasn't included I might have quit right then and there.
Not all of the legendaries are totally balanced. Lian's new death and taxes cutting off 70% of healing from the start of a game? Adding level 1 cauterize gives an instant cauterize 3. Not fun.
Unbound mode sucks. I cannot wait for bound onslaught. Level 10 cards are totally unbalanced. Don't play unbound unless you have all of your loadout cards at level 9 or higher.
Finally, to address the grind. It isn't too bad. The quest system keeps the grind from being totally unbearable, and the first win of the day awards also give a nice cushion. The game rewards good play.
Having all of the cards unlocked immidiately feels great. I literally want to melt into a puddle and simmer a bit, that is how wonderful it feels.
Of couse the grind still takes a long time. It wouldn't be a grind otherwise right? So don't complain about it.
We are still waiting on the patch that only fixes major bugs and glitches, but otherwise it is still a wonderful game. The new card system is a change, but not an entirely bad one. The community isn't all bad either. If you are on the fence about whether to download the game or not, just get it. OB64 has not ruined the game, only changed it a bit.
Was a really great game, now, not. Shame they don't listen.

Only just in favour of this game.  The original was, at the time, playable and engrossing.  The only change here is that the screen resolution now goes up to HD spec.  The graphics themselves have not been updated or redrawn, which is a little misleading, and could have been developed for the re-release.  In an attempt to turn a retro game into a modern game the designers have missed the boat, and could easily have done an entire makeover, as is happening with many other "revived" titles.  This boils down to an attempt to make you buy the same game all over again.  Compared to modern games, even those small-budget indie releases that have pretty basic graphics, this is some way down the line, losing out to titles like Banished.
If you've acquired this as part of the Stronghold bumper pack, then I'd suggest Stronghold 2 worth avoiding.  While it appears to have improved graphics, theres a sense of insolence aimed at users by the programmers, and it quickly becomes a pointless bit of nonsense with little connection to the "castle age" of our history.  It's a case of them putting the sim into simper.

I see the reviews for this game show mixed opinions and I might as well give my own plus some information about it.
This version of World of Tanks was originally a mobile phone exclusive. Since the average mobile phone has way less powerful hardware than an average PC, the requirements to play this game are significantly lower. In comparison to its PC equivilant, this version of course has less graphics, smaller match sizes (14 players vs 30 on regular WoT), and a more visualized interface (big buttons and other stuff).
As Wargaming makes an attempt to create a cross-platform version of WoT, Blitz was introduced on the Windows 10 App store and now Steam. I am happy that this game is now on Steam since you no longer need a phone or a PC with Windows 10 to play this game. Not that I don't have Windows 10.
Besides toned down features from WoT, the map sizes are smaller and there are no indirect fire SPGs. There are less tech trees and they are smaller but the damage models are revised and you can see where your shells can and can't penetrate. Other than that, in summary, this is a more simplified version of WoT.
Now for my opinion of this game, considering I've been playing this game for months with over 1000 battles of experience, I actually like this game better than the original WoT. Now don't get me wrong, World of Tanks is a great game, but I don't think it appeals to my taste. I've played the original WoT for about dozens to a hundred or so hours just to give you how much experience and to be honest, the matches I've spent in that game are pretty sporadic. There's just so much going on that you have little control over the entire match and you can struggle as a result. Yet, maybe if I decide to play that game again and try my best, I may get a different experience.
But for now, World of Tanks Blitz appeals to my taste. It isn't the only tank game I play as I also play War Thunder which I have over 1000 hours of playtime in planes and tanks. If your wanting to try something new, whether you've played regular World of Tanks before or not, give this one a try. This game is free to play so you don't have to pay for anything whether you happen to like it or not. Also if you ever want to find me, my WoTB tag is "ArmoredMustelid" (this is my third wargaming account that I started with WoTB)

Upon entering MWO, despite how modernized this title is by comparison, I felt an instant rush of nostalgia -- a throwback to the days of other treasured mid-90s games like Descent. Obviously, the mechanics in MWO greatly differ from its old-school predecessor(s) but the tutorial was relatively quick and simple.
I will say that the system requirements listed on the store page seem to be underqualified for this title, giving my GPU (Radeon R7 240 2GB DDR3) fits even on mid-low settings but gameplay is still surprisingly smooth. Unlike most of the MMOs available via Steam, the MWO community is seemingly overwhelmingly friendly. To be fair, I haven't even logged a full hour yet but in my three matches, interaction with friend and foe alike was peaceful and informative even.
I'm looking forward to investing more time into this title going forward and give it a resounding 10/10 already.
