A tentative thumb up.
It's a fun game with a few caveats depending on what type of gamer you are. The 'stomping death machine' part is done well but the lack of alternative game modes (essentially just team death match atm) will wear thin quickly. The Community Warfare mode currently in beta is a step in the right direction but considering it's been dangling since 2013, it may or may not turn out for the better.
The hook of the game is living the dream of piloting the dozens of mechs from the Battletech universe. Unfortunately, the F2P grinding required is one of the worst I've seen and even in real money terms, mechs and various cosmetics etc are very expensive.
In the end, if you are a fan of Battletech like me and willing to plunk down at least $30, you'll have a good time. If you are looking for COD+Titan Fall then please step away.

I really wanted to like this game, seriously. The thought of playing a castle builder / siege laying / medieval RTS game made me excited, but probably a bit too much excited.
While the game itself is fine, I felt like it kinda aged. Not too badly, but still not too well.
The main campaign is divided into 2 parts, one "combat" part and another "economical" part. I only played through a quarter of the combat based campaign, took me around 1 hour to get there but... it felt quite dulling. You're only granted archers for quite a long time while the enemy got pikemen, archers, ladder carriers and catapults. It doesn't means it's difficult to beat them, in fact it's quite easy since you're in a defensive position. And that's where it's dulling.
I only managed to almost lose one time during this playthrough. The game isn't difficult and after a bit of tweaking you get a winning strategy quite quickly. While the game is kinda quick paced, you just have to pick up the pace and that's it. The lack of diversity in the units given out makes it even more boring for those first parts of the campaign since... well you only have one single strategy to apply.
Out of boredom, I switched to a free play to discover in one go everything the game had to offer. While it's a good thing to keep stuff simple, the game oversimplifies things a lot. Building construction mainly requires wood and stone (for fortification mainly), you only have 4 type of food (and you can just focus on one since having diversity is cool but really unnecessary) and special other resources are mainly for army building (iron, leather and horses). Buildings are constructed instantly (and so are military units) which is great for impatient people but at the same time making it unrewarding. I basically built every single building and military units under 30 minutes in freeplay.
There’s a lot of other stuff that the game oversimplify that made me go meh but I’m gonna keep it “short” and stop there.
This lack of diversity (and ultimately of strategy) got me bored in less than 3 hours of gameplay. This game might have been great at its time, but, as of now, other games that were released in them mean time might’ve made me too demanding for this one.

Overall I've enjoyed this game and recommend it without reservation (ie not a "don't wait for it to go on sale" recommendation).
The combat is solid. The two core aspects are your officers and your ships. Each ship gets an officer to command it, each officer has a pool of skills they might have, and each ship has a pre-defined set of skills. So it's important to re-roll your officers (5 chances are given when recruiting an officer) until you get useful skills. Really you only need 1-2 useful skills on each officer for space combat.
An important aspect of combat is that some skills inflict status effects, while other skills exploit them. Exploiting a status effect lets you do more damage, but also removes that status effect (some effects do damage over time, so it can be beneficial to keep those on as long as possible).
After a while, and especially if you want a fully powered team of Tier 5 ships, space combat gets repetitive and tedious. However, this can be minimized if you take care when choosing which ships you have and the officer's skills. Combat is much quicker when your team is constantly inflcting/expoiting status effects.
Another downside to space combat: it's always in your best interest to simply pick the strongest ships/officers with the strongest attacks. While damage over time can be useful, it's simply too slow. I attempted to make a proper Damage Over Time fleet, and it just takes *forever* to finish a fight. Single target healing skills remove all status effects, so you can spend an entire round loading up DoT skills only to have them wiped clean before they do any actual damage.
DoT problems notwithstanding, you can build a strong fleet out of a variety of ships. The obvious choice is to have one of each type (Tactical, Engineer, Science) but there are other valid builds.
The good to space combat: the right strategy will let you keep your fleets going forever without stopping for repairs, officers level up, and so do ships. This allows you to train ships with strong officers and hand them off to weak officers (as hand-me-downs) as you build new and better ships. So, your level 10 officer gets a brand new ship, and the old one gets handed off to a lvl 4 officer who now has a badass ship that already does tons of damage. There are tech-tree skills you can research to level up all officers in bulk (to lvl 4, 7, and 10) so it's easy to end up with 3+ really powerful fleets at end-game.
Ground combat seems to be lacking, and it's more of a matter of finding your AoE skills and pumping those up early. While you can inflict/exploit status effects, it's not really necessary, and AoE skills will do more damage than single target over long periods of time. You don't really need to spend any time preparing for ground combat, except for the fact you'll need a team of lvl 13+ officers near the end of the game, and that goal is easily achieved. So ground combat just wasn't very satisfying, but it's such a small portion of the game it doesn't really matter.
Base building is OK. Not great, but OK. In order to speed up how long it takes to do things in the base, you need to assign officers to tasks. Which means those officers can't be out in a fleet fighting. This can be annoying, but if you have two fleets and two teams of officers (which happens early in the game) you can rotate between those two in order to level up everyone evenly, so you'll always have a team at the base and one out and about, with the option to have 2 out fighting in times where there are a lot of threats.
There's some valuable choices to make in regards to who your allies are. The easier route is to befriend everyone, while the more challenging route is to fight them all.
The dialogue is funny and quirky. and each race has a unique feel to it. I enjoyed the music but it's not the kind of soundtrack that I'll go out of my way to hunt down. And, of course, the graphics are the 2-D voxel style.
Overall: there's some problems, but I still recommend this game. It's a lot of fun and has replayability. There's value in the strategic decisions you make in regards to combat, how you build your base, and how you prioritize threats.

I really, really, really loved the original Doodle God and Doodle Devil. So much so that I played them through several times. So much so that I wanted to at least like this "2".
I did not.
Yes, the first part ('episode') was fun enough. Makes sense, since it's basically the original Doodle God game. But the fun ended a long time before I finished it.
When playing the original, I remember people wanting to see the world being built. Yeah, that was a fun idea. The execution... nope. It's plain annoying to get redirected to see a mindless little twinkle of an animation on the globe after making certain combinations.
The episode structure disrupted the game experience. I know this plus this makes that, but I flippin' well can't make it because I'm missing that one thing to unlock episode II. Unneeded. Unlocking the higher episodes your elements get reshuffled under different groups. That's mighty convenient, nothing better than searching Fire for 20 minutes 5 hours into the game. Also, now that you mention it, I really did want to make that disappearing Ice three times.
The quests and puzzles and artifacts? Yeah, not really feelin' 'em. The Island one had promise, Inventions was surprisingly fun too. But they all felt like the results of a brainstorming session titled 'so what are we gonna do to make this feel new and exciting? we need their cash. anyone?'.
Most people seem to be mad about the microtransactions. I have no idea what they are, I did not come across them. Sounds nasty tho.
The pros? I did not pay a cent for this. The person I got this from did not pay a cent for this. I got 30 cents in tradeable cards. For some moments this was a fun walk on memory lane. I still can go back and play the originals for free on Kongregate.
See the amount of time I played and the number of my achievements. I feel... dirty. Not recommended.

As the last game of the series, I have this to say. Is this a good game? Of course. It's a Naruto fighting game that is the last in the series. Is it the best game? Debatable. The features introduced in the game make it so but it still feels lacking for me. For a game that has been delayed for months, I felt underwhelmed at some points.
Good points:
- The leader change system was the best feature introduced in the game. It makes combat way smoother but it may be a bit overpowered (spamming leader changes and chakra dashes against an opponent who likes to substitute way too much).
- The story ending grants a feeling of closure to fans of the game and/or the anime.
Meh points:
- The wall running system was something I felt wasn't impelemented properly, considering it was only used in, what, 3 or 4 fight scenes, all of which could been just as good without. It might have been better to implement it on free battle as well as on story mode.
- The costumes were somewhat of a bit of a disappointment for me, but not necessarily a world-breaking one. I expected, at least, one DLC to have new costumes, not all three DLCs to have costumes from previou Storm games. You know something is wrong when the way to acquire alternate costumes is split between the in-game store and DLC. I could give plenty of ideas for alternate costumes (a swimsuit for the rest of the female characters or a flak jacket outfit for Naruto, Sasuke, and Obito, perhaps) that would have been a better choice than using costumes from previous Storm games.
- The characters were also a bit of a dissapointment, also not anything devastating. Aside from the new versions of existing characters (Naruto, Sasuke, Kakashi, Obito, Gai, and Madara - what else is new?), there were only 8 new characters to the roster (Kaguya, Rin, Boruto, Sarada, and the Sound Four). For a game that is to be the last of the series, there was an entire list of names that could have been added but they glossed over: the Seven Swordsmen, the Gold-Silver Brothers, and the entire support characters from the previous games. In my opinion, movie characters (protagonists and antagonists alike) might have made the game more interesting; after all, the devs already started the rumor mill with Naruto, Sasuke, Sakura, and Hinata in their Last costumes and Road to Ninja costumes (in Storm 4 and 3, respectively).
- The cutscenes felt rushed, compared to the previous games. It reminded me more of Generations than Full Burst or Revolution. It may be voiced, which is a nice touch, but most of the cut-and-paste pictures from the anime detract from the immersive experience.
Bad points:
- The PC version of the game was poor upon release with the lack of graphics options that were in the previous games, FPS problems, crashes, and freezes. It was fixed eventually but it reflected poorly on the game.
Overall, this game is still fun to play, considering the ups and downs that the game presented. I myself find it a good game to play from time to time, but it won't be considered one of my favorite games on PC (it is on PS4, though).

Mechwarrior Online is an awesome game of (simulated) BattleMech combat. It takes some practice just to get your machine going in the direction you want it to, but fortunately they do offer a training academy that is slowly getting better as time moves on. I recommend running through the academy several times in order to get a feel for the machines.
Another word of advice: Considder changing some of the option in the game. Turn on Torso Twist, for example. It's better to learn now, before you develop a bad habit. Secondly, set it to first-person mode. It just makes the experience that much better. I would couple this with nudging the "FOV" slider up, to you can see out all of your windows.
If you're a battletech fan, this is a good Battletech game. Forget what the naysayers yammer about. I've been playing since 2012, loggin on averag over 40 hours a week. Yes, there is a bit of a grind, but nowhere near as bad as World of Tanks. Yes, there is premium content to purchase, but none of that will guarentee victory. Mostly, premium items and 'Mechs have a cosmetic value to them. Most of the actual builds can by built on standard, non-premium machines.
If you like a multiplayer game with a bit more thought to it that the endless deaths of Call of Duty, consider this title. Not only do you get to lumber across the landscape of alien worlds in a machine massing between 20 and 100 tons, you will also be rewarded for utilizing proper team tactics. The only truly "overpowered" component to this game is teamwork. Everything else can be countered.
There is also a very large number of 'Mechs to try out. Find the weight class that suits you best, and you will be left with plenty of options for play, further expanded by the ability to completely customize your Battlemech.
I would avoid Faction Play until you've gotten comfortable both with your 'Mechs, and the fact that you tend to die a lot. Faction play is pretty brutal right now, and dropping in without a team can be very frustrating.
The takeaway? This is Mechwarrior. If you've ever been a fan, whether it's from the tabletop game or MechAssualt, then this is the latest chance to imagine yourself in the cockpit, controlling 75 tons of heavy armor and even heavier weapons.
An excellent game that is constantly improving. Highly recommended!

The game does have some positives.  The story isn't bad, and they do a good job of interjecting humor through most of the game.  Ultimately though the game felt more like a chore than a fun game to play.  The two primary reasons for that?
-  The combat is very repetitive.  Outside of a couple of boss battles, they really are all the same fight.  For the most part you'll use the exact same attacks/tactics every single battle.
-  Easily the worst resource gathering game I've ever played.  Why?  It takes a fair amount of resources and building time to automate the gathering of a single resource point.  It's extremely cheap however to create a pilot and shuttle to go around and gather the stuff.  They do not however give you the option of automating the pilot doing the resource gathering.  It feels like you'll spend 90% of the game just instructing your shuttle pilot where to pickup resources next.  It sounds like they tried to address this a bit in the lightspeed addition, but I don't intend on doing another playthrough.

Decent story, good art, trailers make it look great... but the actual experience is rather lacking.
I bought it on sale and under no circumstances should someone pay full price for this game.
I love the story and look of the game, but I would never encourage one of my friends to buy this.
List of issues:
1 - Combat is rock/paper/scisors based on the Status Effects. Combat is all about applying a status effect with one unit, and the next unit using an attack that expliots(and removes) that status effect from the target for a +150% damage boost. SInce not all units can apply & exploit all ststus effects you MUST have one of each class in a fleet for maximum effect.
Once you find a rotation of attacks you like, you stick with that and never change it.
Because of this combat options feel extremely limited and always feels like a grind/chore.
2 - Researching and building higher tier ships never really feels to give you an advantage. Specifically, random enemy fleets will ALWAYS have ships relatively equivalent to yours in tier. You just built a new fleet of all new Tier 3 ships? All random enemy fleets will now have all Tier 3 ships.
This mechanic of enemies always advancing to be your equal always feels crappy to me.
Specific story encounters are exempt from this rule. Enemy fleets in main story missions seem to be locked, so it is possible to be slightly over/underpowered for these encounters.
3 - Base building is rather lacking. I'm close to the end of the game and I'm pretty sure I'll never use 1/3 of the rooms on the station. There's just nothing useful to build.
-addition - Just finished the game and there are some unique useful items you get to build.  Still didn't use 20% of the rooms at the end.
4 - Numerous attack animations are VERY bright. Some people may not even notice this, but I find it rather annoying. Many attack animations are extremely bright white for portions of them and take up a decent portion of the screen (15-20% or more). This difference between the game's base brightness level and when these animations happen is so drastic that you can easily tell even with your eyes closed.

Deus Ex: Human Revolution is the prequel to Deus Ex 1, a game considered by many to be one of the greatest PC games of all time. You take the role of Adam Jensen, chief of security at Sarif Industries, the leading firm in biotechnology and cybernetics. It seems like an exciting day at work, the next step in human evolution is on the horizon. And all of sudden some three augmented ♥♥♥♥♥ attack your workplace and give you a wedgy so hard you needed to replace your♥♥♥♥♥♥ From that point on you're involved in a global conspiracy, with suprises at every turn.
HR is a First Person RPG in which you are given various paths to  your objective, Something DX 1 was famous for was just how many ways there were to solve given problems. Want to go stealthy and hack through every door you can find? you can! Want to leave behind a trail of corpses, neatly arranged to lead to the bathroom, confusing any bystanders? you can! Thats something that HR more or less sticks to.Though, unlike DX1, where each combo of skills will always lead you  on a different path, in HR you'll generally end up taking similar paths each time due to the skill tree not having enough radically different skills or proper alternatives , or having little impact whatsoever aside from quality-of-life improvements.
The writing is excellent, unlike DX1,where it adresses things like politics and existential philosophy, HR is focused more on the theme of transhumanism, something that might become soon relevant to us. An era where humanity is rapidly changing,  the lines of what can be still considered "human" are starting to blur, and when only some are able to afford to make themselves better in every way, what happens to the rest? It deals with the subjects elegantly and leaves you to make your own judgements.
This is the Director's Cut, it differs from the original in that it has all the preorder content added in, the DLC added as part of the main game, and most noticeably, the boss fights are a lot less awful now. Though, its very buggy, mainly because its not an update of the PC game, its rather a console port,And depending on your tastes, you might miss the yellow tint as well.
All in all, you probably won't feel like your time or money was wasted.

Pros
Interesting approach
Let me play games with a controller that would normally be a mouse and keyboard game

There are a lot more just tiny cons, that I'll leave off.

Made me wish that my Xbox One Controller had the underside triggers. But otherwise, after almost 3 weeks of playing with the steam controller I switched back to the Xbox controller for one day and my appreciation for the Xbox controller went way up. In my opinion it is just leagues better for every game. Wish Steam would allow the customization and inter-play for other controllers. That would be phenomenal. As a new player, I think MWO is great. And as a new player I notice that this game gets a lot of hate for the product it used to be, rather than what it is.
As it stands, the game is generally very stable. I've been disconnected twice at the time of writing this and once was because of an earthquake at their server locations. It's a deep, tactical shooter with a lot of customization available. If you value positioning, constant map reassessment, tactics, and precision over snap accuracy then you should try MWO.
The F2P model is reasonable enough, and the game is not P2W. Within the first couple dozen games, anyone can afford a top tier mech layout. I don't know if MWO is going to continue with the frequent events they've been doing, but with them the grind is much less noticable with things like mech credits (paid currency), c-bills (in game currency), and premium time all being given out for free. I'd actually say the rate at which you get new stuff is about right with these events, so it may be too slow without them.
There is a little bit of an extra grind to get to the top which is with modules. Modules require global XP to learn the skills to use them and the modules cost a lot of c-bills (like as much as a new mech without being outfitted). Because of the ELO system in the game, Pilot Skill Rating (PSR), you won't really being playing against people with this gear in quick play. You will, however, be playing against these people in Community Warfare (CW).
CW is a fun mode that's a nice alternative to quickplay as the objectives are no longer symmetrical. It's meant to act as the global scale war that fits in with the lore of MechWarrior. It's not fully fleshed out yet though, and the main benefit for participating is ranking up with the various factions which do have some unique rewards. But the feeling of making a true impact isn't there yet. It's also not completely balanced between the factions.
Customer service has been good so far. I had an account issue that they resolved quickly, even with the holiday hours.
Bottom line: MWO is fun to play, offers a good freemium model, and the company seems to have changed their mentality in running this game for the better.

I cheated. Yes. I cheated.

I happily agree with whomever said this is a strange mix of FTL and XCom. But it works. The controls are a bit odd but they're solid. The graphics are fun and very reminiscent of FTL or the (awful) Star Command mobile game.
This has the same kind of die-a-lot-but-don't-care feel as FTL, XCom or Dwarf Fortress.
Game's premise: If FTL is Next Generation, Halcyon 6 is Deep Space Nine. In FTL, you fly a ship through a long mission to destroy the enemy at the end. In Halcyon 6, you have a home base from whence you send out ships and fleet to do missions and you even get to beam out away teams. Combat is all turn-based (not real-time like FTL) and that works just fine.
I highly recommend this game. If you like FTL, XCom or Final Frontier (a Civ 4 expansion that turns it into Civ in space), I'm sure you'll LOVE Halcyon 6.

HALCYON 6: STARBASE COMMANDER
PUBLISHER/DEVELOPER – Massive Damage
GENRE – RPG/STRAT/ROGUELITE
THE BASICS:
You are in charge of Starbase Halcyon 6 and a small complement of officers – you are some of the last few survivors of the human race, after Earth was devastated by an alien race known as the Chruul. Your mission is to explore your little sector of space, looking for other enclaves of humanity in nearby star systems, nebulae, and asteroid clusters, while protecting them from the predations of the merciless Chruul invaders. In the meantime, you also need to explore neglected areas of your own starbase, excavating the areas and clearing out any lingering alien presence within them. Research new facilities and ships, level up your officers, and clean house. If you're lucky, you'll even make some new friends along the way from among the nearby alien cultures.
THE FLOW AND THE STORY:
You begin with yourself – the standard unseen overmind/leader –  plus one “Legendary” officer of your choice (meaning, one who can unlock a special, unique skill later on), who comes with their own ship; and one other officer, each chosen from among the three types: Science (support, debuffs, and healing/repairs), Tactical (high offense and buffs), and Engineering (high defense and mix & match powers). You will need to recruit more officers as you go, and each of them has their own complement of both ship-to-ship combat and ground combat abilities; each set of three recruits (one of each class) can be re-rolled up to two times if you don't like what you see (save for the Legendary starter and any unique officers you find as part of the story). Officers will come with some passive abilities (whether boon or bane), and will learn more over time as they encounter specific enemy types. In addition, they will each earn skill points as they level up, which are used to improve their active combat abilities. The crews of individual ships will also distinguish themselves after enough fights, adding minor bonuses to their vessels. Unlike the officers, they stay with their ships, and cannot be reassigned. Each officer has their own unique grouping of abilities, drawn from a specific pool based on their class. The ships, however, all have pre-set abilities based on their type, and each Tier has two ship types to choose from; you will have both of them to draw upon in combat.
Combat is turn-based, with a clear row of icons at the bottom of the screen displaying the current turn order. Space combat abilities will range from DoT (damage over time, such as Bleeding) and AoE (area of effect/multiple-target) attacks (better yet, some do both!), messing with enemy sensors, raising your team's shields, supercharging your weapons, setting up repair drones, and the like. Many attacks serve a dual purpose, setting up a debuff or a DoT on the enemy; Certain other attacks will “exploit” an existing DoT, thus doing significant extra damage in exchange for canceling the DoT early. It's up to you whether to let the DoTs run their course, or to use an Exploit attack and hope it does enough damage to kill the enemy right then. If it doesn't, you'll have ticked it off when it's ready to counterattack. The game keeps track of aggro/which character or ship each enemy hates the most, and the enemies will tend to focus on that character when the time comes.
You need to seek out and gather resources from the local star systems; if survivors are present, they'll continually produce Materials, Dark Matter, Fuel, and Crew members (via cloning, perhaps?), all of which are needed to keep your fleet going as it gets bigger and badder. Naturally, the enemies are getting bigger and badder, as well, while opening portals to allow more of their their buddies access to your star system. You'll need to destroy the fleets guarding the portals in order to shut them down. Later on, you'll get more advanced “bases,” such as Spires, which have tougher defenders and more of them, and also require that you send in a team of ground troops to neutralize the enemies running the base. Meanwhile, any enemies left unchecked will seek out your active resource-gathering locations and attempt to destroy them. Once you get into the meat of the game and complete the first major section, diplomacy with nearby alien factions will come into play. Play your cards right, and you could end up with some really good new officers and ships to help you out. Screw it up, and you could find yourself fighting a multi-front war with only one or two squads of experienced officers to handle them all.
CONTROLS:
Primarily mouse-driven. Click on an unexplored area to send an officer there to check it out; click on an established facility to use it; click a celestial body to send ships out there to collect resources and/or fight whatever baddies may have taken up residence there. You get up to three ships for each fight in space combat, and you will always have three members for ground combat – redshirts will fill up any open spots when the time comes. Just as you might expect, they're basically cannon fodder, and they die spectacularly; but, better them then you.
GRAPHICS:
16-bit style graphics done right! Incredible amounts of detail for the medium. Attacks and other Ability effects range from your basic “pew pew” lasers to massive explosions to drone swarms and laser barrages. All of them do their job, and many feel “meaty”, giving a sense of impact. Widely-varied backgrounds for the space battles and many different ships, on all sides. Your ships will tend to get bigger and “chunkier” as you progress through the research tiers and create new models.
SOUND:
Modern chiptune music and sound FX which fit well with the milieu.
OVERALL:
Fun times, plenty of sci-fi book/TV/movie puns (especially in the cheevos). Excellent sense of atmosphere. Fun combat, different officers are distinct, even from others of their same basic class.
SYSTEM REQUIREMENTS: Nominal

tl;dr: The game was abandoned. You may still play it but don't spend any cash on it.
I bought Steam Launch Starter Pack in June 2014. I played the game a bit and I loved it but I removed it shortly after that. So a few days ago I decided to give it a try again. I bought Blutes and XP boosts and I tried to play the game again. I thought people still play Loadout. Boy, was I wrong.
Turns out the game was almost completely abandoned. It used to have about 30 000 people playing it at the same time, now this number is closer to 500. I have a feeling most of them randomly found Loadout on Steam Store, saw it's free and decided to play it a bit. Casual matchmaking is still possible — just select European or American servers depending on time of a day.
Moreover the game was abandoned by its developers. It used to get updates almost every week. Now they won't even add PvE mode (PS4 received it almost right after launch in January 2015). After PS4 launch Loadout's creative director left the development team. Shortly after that 12 people working on Loadout were fired and the game does not receive any more content.
So don't do the same mistake as I did: do not invest money in this game, it's dead. Feel free to try it. It's sad actually, the game itself is pretty decent. I have a feeling Edge of Reality is going to keep servers running until they can cover expenses. They already shut down Australian servers.

With all the initial negative reviews on this game, I almost didn't buy it.  The truth is that I love space shooters -- ever since I was a kid.  With the price down to $4.00 and a recent update that fixed the controls (the biggest complaint among many early reviewers), I decided to go for it.
Well, it turns out that I was happily surprised by this game.  Foremost, I love the graphics and the space shots of this game.  The initial cutscene was just awesome.  I also enjoyed blowing up the bad ships since it has such cool explosions.  There really is a lot of eye candy in this game.
The controls have definitely been fixed and you can mostly use a gamepad (I'm using a wireless Xbox 360 controller).  It still needs some polishing (i.e. the tutorial still requires you have a keyboard even though you're using a gamepad) but I had no crashes and almost everything played well.  One time the maneuverability of my space ship slowed down and I couldn't tell whether it was intentional or a glitch.
I found the level of difficulty not too hard or too easy.  I would say it plays more like an arcade game and less of a simulation (I hate complicated space simulations).  Nonetheless, it was definitely enjoyable so far and I didn't find it repetitive.
I look forward in playing this game some more and I'm definitely hooked.  Therefore, if you were initially disappointed by the early reviews, I say give this game a shot since you might be pleasantly surprised as I was.
Again, it needs some tweaking and polishing, but overall I'm really enjoying the game.  It is definitely worth the price and then some!

Doodle God is an interesting and fun puzzle game. The puzzles and combinations are generally good. Some combinations don't really make sense sometimes, but you'll have that.
When compared to the version I played on Android a while back, some of the additions for this version can be a little annoying. The world view frequently pops up, taking you away from play in the main game. There are a lot more combinations and groups here, which makes it endlessly more difficult to find something specific if you haven't been using it since nearly the beginning of the game. It also doesn't help that things get moved around in the last section of the game. The only thing that saves this is the search, but the search goes away as soon as you click. It would be nice if I could keep the search open on both sides and drag directly from them.
The quests, when done right, will tell a neat little story, such as saving a princess or getting stranded on an island and getting rescued (if you play that one right). They're a nice addition. The added content in general sometimes feels like it's purely to extend gameplay though. It does mean that there's a lot more stuff to play around with and discover in the game.
Yes, it offers microtransactions, that you would have to turn on to be able to get. It's only for people that don't want to solve the puzzles. You can get the same stuff by just playing, or if you don't feel like discovering stuff on your own, you can use a walkthrough, which there are many out there for Doodle God.
There are several things I don't like about the game, but at the core, it's still a fun and interesting game. The good of the game really does outshine the mild annoyances I find in it, so it gets a thumbs up from me.

I remember when the first Deus Ex came out for PC, I bought a video card so I could play it. The idea of a first/third person shooter with RPG elements and a heavy sci-fi story line sounded amazing to me, still does today. That first installment was a hallmark for gaming innovation. I would venture as far to say that Human Revolution sets yet another hallmark for an immersive gaming experience.
There are a lot of things to like about Deus Ex: Human Revolution. From the hacking mini-games, to the fast paced, tactical fire fights, these experiences feel seamless and complete. Gameplay goes deeper as you gain experience and distribute points to different attributes with their own individual skill trees. There are different aspects to your attributes as well, you have attributes based on verbal character interaction, physical character interaction, hacking, and stealth; it all depends on your play style. Human Revolution affords one the ability to choose their play style throughout the entire game, there are multiple ways to approach every scenario and one does not have to stick to one particular play style to navigate their environment. You can shoot and kill everything or sneak and tranquilize your way through the entire game. The game sets you in the right direction from the get go with an option for what kind of character loadout you'd like to start out with.
One of the sweeter parts of the game are the instances where choosing what to say next affects the outcome of the scene and the game as a whole somewhat as well. There are multiple endings to Human Revolution depending on your decisions and play style. Replayability is High with this one folks, especially with the Director's Cut featuring all DLC for Human Revolution and some extra little goodies as well.
Full Controller Support for those of you who are scared of mice.

This is a great game (if you want something different than any other FPS right now)
(1000 hours on this game pre-steam release)
MWO is a strange thing for sure. Will you like it? Well it really depends on what you expect from a FPS.
In here, you will not run like a headless chicken (except if you drive Locusts), you will not instantly kill your opponent with a lucky (or skilled) headshot, you will not respawn, you will not magically heal the damages you took during the fight.
You will take care of your team mates, you will run for cover under heavy missiles fire, you will sacrifice part of your Mech just to shield your engine while charging, and you will unleash the power of 20 tons of weapons (or more) against giant walking tanks.
Pros:
- Mech building: before you fight, you have to build your Mech. You choose its weapons, its engine, how much armor it has for each part, how much ammunitions, electronics... The Mechlab is a place where you are gonna spend a lot of time, as it determines a  lot of what you will be able to do in a game, but you'll spend Good time on it.
- Simulation feelings: you are in a huge machine of death, but not a fast Japanese Meka. You're heavy, slow, and the controls feel that way. You have to plan your movements because you can't turn back in the blink of an eye if enemies show up. Then again, you are just driving some kind of a giant tank with arms and legs, so it's not that hard to master.
- Unique combat style: in MWO, you can shoot with lots of weapons, on the same Mech, all at once... The only thing restraining you from non stop fire is the heat your weapons generate when fired. You have to manage this heat so you don't shutdown from overheating (which means standing still while your Mech cools off - a bad thing). You also have one life per drop, and no healing. Your Mech will lose some parts during a game, and learning how to spread damages as the fight goes on is a key component of being good at MWO.
- Beautifull visuals: the Mechs are amazing, all of them. Of course, you will love some and hate some, but the redesign are all incredible. Why "re"design? Because next point:
- A 30 years old universe: yup it's an old license, with lots of famous heros, feared mercenary organisations, long stories for every factions and clans.
- Continuous development: there is a full team of developers on this game and you can see it. 2 updates per month since  3 years is pretty awesome, as the game is still evolving and switching towards a great balance (which has its Cons).
- Giant robots!: we all love them, you know it, and there's currently undreds of mechs to choose from.
- Trully Free-to-Play: All the game is available for free. You can't buy with real money better gear or Mechs. There are Hero Mechs you can't buy with the in-game curency, but they are far from being even "top" (some even far from being good - but that's another story).
Cons:
- Very steep learning curve: This game is hard. It really is. Movement, damage, heat, weapon firing, Mech building, all need a lot of time to be mastered, and you have to re-learn some of those each time you buy a new chassis.
- It's not CoD: as said before, this is a slow paced game where you need to think. You need patience, teamwork and strategy to avoid getting wrecked.
- Balance??: MWO comes from a 30y old franchise, ok, but that license has its flaws. Rules from the TableTop games were broken because they were not meant for a real-time FPS, and the MWO team does his best to rebalance everything while not going to much away from the original material, but there is still room for improvements (still, there aren't real "cheezy" Mechs or weapons, just some that are a bit better and some that are useless).
In the end, the game is really enjoyable if you want a tough game that has nothing to do with any other game on the market so far. The feelings from moving from a cover to another under enemy fire while twisting your torso to spread damage all over your Mech, running and harassing while in a Light Mech- knowing you will die if you get hit-, or being a tower of destruction in an Assault Mech... In MWO, you feel like fighting, and the fight is a 12vs12 brawl. With missiles. And giant lasers.
You don't need money so give it a try. Maybe you'll stay (I know i did, since 2012).

The usual reason to play WoT Blitz is to speed up waiting - be it on the Porcelain Throne, on a bus or in a queue. Now I can add 'just for the heck of it (without using BlueStacks)' to my list.
After 826 battles, I've unlocked:
Chi-Nu, Japanese Tier 5 medium tank,
AT-2, British Tier 5 tank destroyer,
SU-85, Soviet Tier 5 tank destroyer,
KV-1S, Soviet Tier 6 heavy tank,
Leopard, German Tier 5 light tank.
I was initially very impressed by others bouncing dozens of shots off the armor of the KV-1 and decided I must also have it. The Soviet heavy tree has been a boring grind for the most part though with the only exception of the T-46 (tier 3). The KVs are very slow and virtually blind. It's a lottery if you'll manage to position yourself for a few hard-hitting shots and absorbing a good amount of damage or you'll get♥♥♥♥♥♥♥from behind by a Leopard within the first 2 minutes. The KV-1S was incredibly weak until I got the best gun for it (costing 20k experience), but even now it reloads so slow that a single miss can mean I'm more of a burden than a boon to my team.
The British AT-2 is the closest you get to cheating in this game. In a battle where you're the highest tier and you manage to keep enemies off your♥♥♥♥♥and shooting at your front you'll quickly ruin the other team's game. It has 203 mm of frontal armor, which would be good at tier 7 (you're tier 5). You're going to sacrifice speed (it's really-really slow) and view range, so you kind of still depend on your team to scout baddies out for you, but this is probably the easiest tank to steal the show with by shrugging off thousands of points of damage and destroying most of the enemy team.
The Soviet TD line has been pretty much okay all-around. SU-85 has a nice low profile for hiding behind rocks and hopefully making the enemy aim a bit too high and miss.
German light tanks require skill. A masterful Leopard can punch much higher than it's weight, but it's also really easy to speed into a group of enemies and get killed within 30 seconds of the start of the battle. It's an okay tree to unlock, but nothing that exhilirating. German TDs are quite enjoyable, especially the Hetzer with it's small frame and very well angled armor plates for bouncing off shots even if you do get spotted.
Surprisingly the Japanese tech line has been by far the most fun for me. I chose the light branch (Ha-Go, Ke-Ni, Ke-Ho) winning 62, 61 and 50 % of the battles respectively, being 'productive' in each battle. The tier 5 Chi-Nu is on the useless side starting out but also quite good when fully upgraded. What made the light Japanese tanks so fun was that I could reach any mountaintop, their small size (all stats being equal, a smaller tank is better) made almost any bush viable for total camoflague and guns with high maximum depression angles and fast reload times enabled me to keep shooting almost every second of the battle. Shooting opponents is the fun part of WoT Blitz and the Jap tanks offered lots and lots of this.
I think it generally holds true that the higher level you play at, the more boring it gets. At Tier 6+ everyone's pretty much a veteran, knows all the sweet spots on the map and punishes any mistake you make harshly. Battles where you can kill 3-6 tanks on the enemy team via sniping cleverly are pretty much behind you by then. So I think it's fair to recommend playing multiple low level tanks instead of focusing hard on one.
Why I generally like WoT Blitz:
1) Best time killer app I know - kills lots of it without getting boring, difficult or whatever, effectively a time machine when waiting at the dentist's for example
2) Very short match queues - I don't want to queue while I queue
3) Progressing through tiers of tanks feels good
4) At least for now, no-one cheats, almost no-one pays to win
5) I get to learn tank names
6) A lot less of a cl*sterf*ck than the original WoT for desktop

"It's up to you now, Commander."
That line really got me in the end of the game. Sending in the final fleet, my favorite officers, with amazing personalities and whom I have grown to love.. sent to sacrifice themselves to defeat a god and save humanity and bring.. universe peace?
Taking down enemies is a core piece of the gameplay. Portals spawn up in random locations on the map, and you have to send a fleet two dispatch of it. If you don't, more Chruul ships will leave the portal and attack stars. Enemy and ally ships will also be sent to your station to challenge you, request something, or even bring you a gift. You are also faced with quests from crew, such as building a certain type of room in the station. You are also faced with distress signals from other systems, and can either help or abandon an ally or enemy. This game revolves on your decisions, and that makes the gameplay even better. Knowing that you are making a difference is a real great feeling.
Wether it be pirates, aliens, or the dreaded Chruul, or even bosses, the battle system affects gameplay. There are 3 types of officers; Tactical, for dealing damage, Science, for providing your ships with HP or status effects, and Engineer, which I think is a balance of damage and providing. The battle system is turn-based; depending on how fast one of your ships or enemy ships are, they will get to go before a slower one. Slower ships tend to be tanks and deal more damage, but are unable to attack as often as fast ships, which are able to attack more often in exchange for HP and possibly defense. Bosses are one of my favorite aspects of the game. In total, there are 6; 5 different Chruul ships, one that comes directly to your base, and the other 4 that attack other alien civilizations. Then the final boss, which is amazing, by the way, comes directly for you. Finally, there are skill trees that you are able to activate by using points and leveling up officers. They can range from status effects, healing, and many various different tactical uses. Ground combat is less complicated, as it's basically just like 3v3 Pokemon.
Progressing through the game can determine wether you make or break your entire playthrough. Sending ships out to repair factories, mines and old colonizations is one of the key aspects of the game. Colonizations provide crew, which can be used for various things, and quite possibly the most valuable resource. Mines are used to gather minerals, which can also be used like crew; they can build rooms, but they can also research tech, and much more. Factories, I am pretty sure, are for dark matter, which is in almost everything minerals are used for. Progressing also involves building your station's rooms, such as an Officer Academy, for recruiting new officers for duty. Tech is also a vital part of your game, an example would be that you need better ships to take on more powerful enemies. Never fear, tech is here, with it's ever-so-helpful way of providing us with Tier 2 - Tier 5 ships.

If you make it to the end, this was a pretty long, but ultimately rewarding game.
I say "if you make it" because the other reviews about a long and tedious grind are accurate.
At the close of the first "half" I was ready to throw in the towel, but, instead I loaded a trainer to supply me with infinite resources, and settled in for another try. Things became much better. The relentless background struggle for resources was finally over. I could focus on building ships, fighting battles, exploring, side missions, base expansion... Basically everything else in the game.
At its core, the game is pretty simple, but the sheer number of things going on at once means there is always something to do to keep you occupied.
I thought the graphics were perfect; they reminded me of the sets used in plays with multiple layers, and each layer able to move independently. Sound was good it reminded me at times of my old Atari 2600. The music I finally turned way down, but I tend to do so in most games.
Combat can get repetitive if you try to complete every task with a single fleet. I found that maintaining 2-3 fleets and associated officers kept combat a bit “fresher” since I had to adapt my fighting style to match the strengths of the fleet I was controlling. You'll need/want these extra full strength fleets as well.
Overall the game was enjoyable, give it a try. Then give it another try after “fixing” yourself up with 999,999,999 of each resource type.
If anyone is making mods, or updates for the game, my only suggestions for improvement are:
* Allow the main map to zoom in/out
* Maybe add a "search" or "find" tool to locate a specific solar system?
* Modify the "tech tree". I'd say make it zoom in/out as well, but that is just a Band-Aid fix. By end game it devolves into a tech bush, and it can be tough to spot research options in it.

Doodle God is a popular mobile game. You match elements and items to create new ones. Although that seems simple the game is actually quite witty and advanced. It really helps to pass the time while waiting in line, taking transit or countless other times you are in your phone.

Microtransaction is CLEARLY OPTIONAL if you want to burn money for hints and automatic actions then do so, if not then DON'T no one is asking you to pay for it, not buying hints will NOT result in failing the game.

Having read other reviews, it seems that the main criticisms levelled against Doodle god are that a) it contains microtransactions even though you've already paid for it, and b) it's pretty much a port of the mobile version, which is cheaper (albeit containing even more microtransactions)
I must say however, that even though you can pay for hints to help you solve the game's puzzles, it's by no means necessary to do so. The hints recharge at a fairly decent rate and so you basically get them for free anyway, paying for them is just a way of hurrying things along and so there's no need to shell out any more cash than you've already spent.
True, there is a cheaper version for mobile devices, although I can't verify that it's exactly the same... From what I can surmise the Steam version contains a bit more content and doesn't require you to pay any where near as much for what you basically should already get in a bought game.
The above issues aside, Doodle god is actually a pretty decent example of this type of setup. It looks great, presentation is superb and playing it is a pleasure. I love the way that as you progress, your creations start to appear on a nicely illustrated planet and the game consistently rewards you when you get things right. The music is relaxing and never grates on the ears. The only thing I would say though is that there is no volume control, no excuses for that really!!
There's quite a bit of gameplay to keep you going, the main quest will probably take you 8 hours and then there are extra quests to do which will probably take you a few more. The puzzles for the most part are fairly logical but some can be a bit off the wall.. For instance Corpse + Electricity = Death metal?? I mean, I get it but.. I wouldn't automagically think to make that one.. It is a game that is suited to playing in bursts of about an hour at a time, but it's pretty addictive and you'll probably find yourself going back to it to catch 'em all.
Overall it's quite a decent game for the price and I'll give it 6.8/10, I've had a lot of fun with it, but it's marred by annoyingly unnecessary microtransactions and a lack of volume control. If the developers change these aspects then the figure will rise.

#2: It's a direct mobile port. From the text saying "tap" to even the app pop ups saying "RATE OUR GAME". While it doesn't run bad on PC and the buttons still feel ok for the most part, it's still annoying that they just ported the game over.
In my personal opinion I like this game. I don't mind the micro transations because they don't effect the game, they just make it a bit easier if you want to buy them. I also don't mind the direct port from mobile since the buttons are still ok.

I really wanted to like the game and I actually did. It plays very fast-paced for a 4v4 arena shooter and is extremely easy to get into. Using a variety of weapon mods to make your own novel (and questionably effective) gun is a great concept. Its F2P model is also extremely fair, using common sense as its compass for avoiding the proverbial "pay-to-win" stigma.
However, support for the pc version has been indecisive at best since they released a balance/bugfix patch last March (2015), but before that it was nearly a year.
The Playstation version of the game is doing much better off but it's a bit disheartening to see the pc version in stark neglect, and in turn its playerbase whiddling down to merely a stagnant collective of familiar veterans who are not newbie-friendly in a fight with their much deeper pool of weapon modifications. But if you do kill them you can take their weapon and use it for the match. So there's that equalizer.
It's just impossible for me to recommend a multiplayer abandonware.

Simply put, XBOX controller is for XBOX, PS controller is for PS, Steam controller is for PC.
If you want to play as many PC games as possible with a controller, you don't really have a choice. Nothing can compete with it. It's the ultimate answer to the diversity of PC games.
While some controllers are specialized on and are perfectly suited for some genres or specs (I use XBOX gamepad for platform arcade games, wheel for race games, keyboard and mouse for real-time strategy games), Steam Controller can do everything. It may not be perfect for every single case, but it can be configured to do anything.
There're so many options I feel like I'll spend days exploring them all. If you like configuring everything, you'll love it. Want to swap butons? Want to make a button a toggle switch? Want to enable auto-clicking on some button? Want to switch button layouts on the fly? All these features turned out to be very useful even in games which support controllers, don't require keyaboard and mouse or any special magic features of the Steam Controller like joystick-mouse-pads.
I feel like I'm in control of the input devices again. This is what PC is about.
My view on the controller's ergnomics so far:
1. I love touch pads. They're way better than stupid tiny sticks.
2. I hate tiny ABXY buttons and their placement. This is somewhat offset by configuring the controller.
It takes some time to get used to it, but it's nothing new. It took me weeks to adapt to a wheel controller, even though it's supposed to be much better suited for race games than a keyboard.
P. S. If you consider buying Steam Link (and you really should, unless you've already solved the problem with HDMI cable or something else), then Steam Controller is pretty much mandatory. Mere XBOX controller is just not enough.

The build quality is fine.
Relatively cheap.
Cons:
The track-pads have a button press, which takes more force than I like, although I have never needed to use these as buttons.
Steam only lets you update the firmware and adjust the settings in "big picture mode". This isn't really a problem.
The range of the dongle isn't amazing. Perhaps 6-10 feet.
I give it an overall 9/10 It's a great product.

IMO one of the biggest benefits is how great it is with fighting games when using just the trackpads for the stick and bottons.  It does not replace mouse and keyboard for shooters BUT it's really close when you use the trackpad with the gyro controls.  Since buying this I haven't reconnected my xbox one controllers to the pc, the steam controller is just superior.  Overall great hardware.

As an avid shooter (been shooting since I was 8) I thought I knew everything about guns, until I found this game/simulator/thingamajingy! It's the perfect thing to have if you want to learn exactly how guns work, or how to possibly make them. You can also show it to someone else when you're introducing them to shooting. A beginner would feel much more comfortable and confident when they know exactly what's going on in their hands during that split-second when they squeeze the trigger.
Anyway, it's a really good game, it's free, so what have you got to lose?? Check it out! It's really great if you're interested in actually learning how guns function (or you could just go back to listening to those stupid politicians that keep calling magazines clips). I won't force you anyhow, learning is fun when no one makes you do it. ;)
However I have only two cons, like the sound. For instance, on some guns they make the superficial "quiet" sound when you put on a suppressor. The other con is how you don't exactly have complete total freedom when playing in operation mode (and this game is supposed to be all about freedom amirite?), like how you can't put an extra round in the chamber, or you can't reload a shotgun when it still has some rounds in it (hey man, details matter).
Those two tiny insignificant cons are all I have to complain about, besides those, this game is really cool and I highly recommend you check it out.
Note to Devs: It would be REALLY cool if we could see detailed x-rays of the cartridges as well! There's a few things going on inside those little firecrackers that would be neat to see, like the primer being punched and the gunpowder bursting into flames! (ok it doesn't have to be THAT detailed, you know what I mean)
In conclusion, I rate this game 9.9 freedoms out of 10. Have a good day and God bless America. :)

tldr - don't buy this game, you're better off playing either the free flash version (Doodle Blitz) or the app, which this game is a port of. The developers disgustingly put in microtransactions, asking players to pay for important functions which should be free from the getgo, and in turn stopped Doodle God from being the good game that it should be.
Full Review:
To be honest, I am pretty disappointed with Doodle God. It is actually just a Steam port of their mobile app. Seeing as how this has a higher asking price, I assumed that the game would already contain the additional useful functions which you had to pay extra for in the app and free flash versions. Appallingly enough, they still aren't made available to you despite the fact that we have paid a higher amount for almost the same game!!
The functions that I mentioned are the ability to have repeated reactions disabled and to show which elements still had combinations available. Now, if you have never played any of the games in this series, let me sum up the gameplay briefly: You start off with a particular set of elements, and you combine them in the hopes of creating new ones. As you create new elements, more and more potential combinations are made possible. At first, its easy to keep track of which combos you have already made, but when you have, say, 75 elements, available, it becomes difficult to continue keeping track. After a while, Doodle God becomes less of a game and more like mere tedium. Doodle God is tagged as being casual, but instead of being that it ends up simply brainless. This is largely due to the fact that those aforementioned functions aren't available to us. Had we been given them, the experience would be MUCH more enjoyable.
As if asking us to pay for those functions weren't offensive enough, the developers had the audacity to PUT A PRICE ON ADDITIONAL HINTS. Do you really think anyone would pay money for hints when they can just search up solutions/walkthroughs online for FREE?
The only difference between this game and the mobile version is the Tournament mode which is not that fun to begin with due to it being buggy. There is no incentive for players to participate because it gives the top ranked players a useless prize, additional hints. I assumed that seeing as how they are selling it for an increased, they would give players access to disabled repeated reactions and the border guides, functions which you would have to pay for on the mobile and free flash versions.
I won't deny, there are plenty of clever, funny moments in this game. However, the microtransactions and the withholding of functions that should be free, left a terrible taste in my mouth, despite being a fan of the series. It had the potential to be a nice, light, casual game. Hopefully the developers see our dissatisfaction with this and changes this, because right now, I cannot recommend people to pay full price for this. Just play the app or free flash version if you are REALLY interested. I wouldn't recommend buying this :/

First of I really don't get it why so many people give this game a negative rating. What do you expect for €3,99? The next block buster Space Combat Shooter? Anyway, here's my, positive, review:
Beyond Space is one of those few games that actually suprised me in a very pleasant way. After seeing it on Steam and buying it during a promotion, I booted it up and expected, well, just one of those casual space games.
But, oh boy, Beyond Space had me there.
First, the art style (Graphics and the way things are presented on the screen) is just warm and nice to the eye. You instantly get the feeling that this game has been designed by people who have their own idea of a Space Combat Game. Which is kind of refreshing.
The ship models and basically all the other 3D thingies.., they're very rich and beautiful. This is also one of the few games with ships in the hangar that make me wonder: "Hmm, which one do I like more? They all look so cool!"
The sound and speech in this game are well done and really add to the story. For instance; the music in this game and the intro itself. Oh my, wow, just wonderful to listen to and to watch.
The controls are not that many, but respond just the way you would expect. fast and precise. I play this game with a game pad (Not the so much proclaimed X-Box Controller, But a genuine Windows PC Gamepad of a leading brand. X-Box Controllers where never meant to be used with Windows PC's. Do some historical research if you want to learn more about this topic), because I didn't like to play it with the keyboard/mouse and the X-52 Pro is a bit overkill for this game. (That's what I'm thinking anyway)
So far the only thing I didn't really understand, or kind of dislike, is the way missions are presented. At this moment, I've flown about 20 missions, all are just presented as a single, stand alone, map/level/mission. There's for some reason not really a feeling of "connection" between the seperate missions. As is with the games of "Eterium"/"Free Space" for instance. Maybe that's because you never really return to a flight deck or something similar. The mission just ends/fades out.
But, beside of that, Beyond Space is a very well made and welcome addition to any would be space fighter jockey.
You like Space Combat? You like setting up your ship and load out? Buy "Beyond Space"; you can't go wrong.

Firstly i want to say that its not terrible for what is currently a $4 game, but it is a mixed bag
the good, then the bad
As this is a simulator, the defining combat is okay, the enemy ai is above par and are very good at swarm tactics, and enemies have different weapons weaknesses and strengths, making it challenging and somewhat more realistic. however the current control layout heavily favors controller support, where the vanilla computer control is counter intuitive and needs to be redone.
the weapon and ship variation is decent, however progression is a mixed bag. the ship and weapon combinations are really a trial and error test to find which suits your flying/fighting style. there is an clear effort to make the ship designs more than a reskin and a stat modification with certain weapons not being available on certain craft.
finally the graphics are really well done given that this is a relatively cheap game, however that ends the list of good stuff, brace yourself.
The voice acting ranges from passable to very awful
they attempted to do a story here but it draws on very tired cliches and uninspired pratfall tech jokes that are guaranteed to make you cringe at the terribleness
as previously mentioned the controls need to be reworked for the computer. the actions with which they are associated are good and have a SNES Starfox feel to them, but unless you the buyer want to figure out a better layout like i did, it's better to wait for a tweak,
the ship modding screen needs to be fixed to allow scrolling for the computer. in its current state it is unbearable and i'm usually very resistant to relatively minor things like this. it's that bad.
there is a massive difficulty spike early-ish on in the game that unless you knew about it in advance you will not be prepared to deal with it, and you have to know what mods and ship to use otherwise you simply will die again and again.
to end this list the graphic again while really good for this game, personally i could do with fewer solar flares, but that's a personal preference derived from my membership of the "lens flares make Space annoying" camp. In this game sometimes they work and make sense and makes things challanging, othertimes they just give me a headache
while i really cant say that i like or hate it i cant recommend it; at least not until some of these things are fixed

Graphically, things are fine. It's no next-gen title, but what do you expect from a game that costs less the £3?
It reminds me of Freelancer (a game I loved), but until they incorporate the mouse, or the triggers on the controller (they do nothing - the right bumper is 'pause') this game will just be too irritating to play.

Fun alternative to Xbox controllers for couch gaming. I'm currently using this with a Steam Link to stream games from the couch. Games like DOOM, Batman, Skyrim, ARK, etc. all work -- provided that you find the best community controller profile. However, the most important part of the controller, what is essentially its main selling point, is a rage-inducing nightmare. I'm talking, of course, about the trackpad. This thing is supposed to make playing FPS games with a controller a breeze, and you can configure it a whole lot to achieve that purpose, but at the end of the day, some issues simply persist:
-The thing is too small to turn around without high sensitivity
-High sensitivity makes every little twitch of your thumb screw with your aim
-Accidentally rolling your thumb even just a little will have the same effect as sliding it
Sure, you can play platformers and other 2D games just fine, but the controller is sold as a substitute for a mouse and keyboard in FPS games, so there's really no reason to buy it if it doesn't even do that right.
Sorry, Valve. I still love your games, though.

As a console gamer first, I've been accustomed to controllers. As I've slowly moved on to the PC sometimes I will prefer to use a controller because it's more convenient to play with all my buttons close-by than a keyboard. After my second X1 controller issue, I finally decided to try the Steam Controller back in February.
This is my second time evaluating the controller. After my first three months, I thought I had a grasp on what games worked best with the controller. However, after an extended look at configuring my own set-ups I feel I have a more detailed understanding of what games work than simply the genre. Recoil, changing aiming speeds (ex. iron sights and hip fire vs. cover-based shooting), and more are all details that make knowing how to configure each game more to your liking.
None of this is to suggest that you will never adjust to the new controller; it takes some time, but not too long if you know what you're doing. The issue is knowing what key factors will improve your experience per game, and what games work best with the controller. The real question to decide if this controller is for you is if the added complexities of experimentation are worth buying a non-standard controller over a controller with limited configurations (X1 or PS4).
Over the seven months of various hundreds of games, I have boiled down what works best with the controller, what is tolerable, and what is not ideal (but may be doable):
The common issue that can be said for the Steam Controller is knowing from the  textile feedback of the trackpad where to stop. Games with less or zero recoil work best because you don't have to account for adjusting your aiming whereas games that require you to aim precisely and work with recoil are not as flawless. It's also a problem for games that require fast precision with your mouse cursor which is difficult to do given a trackpad, or they require two aiming schemes (iron-sights). Lastly, the issue that is somewhat hard to gauge is when you set-up multiple control schemes (controller & mouse) for some games it may create new problems for quick-time events (Metal Gear Rising w/ controller & mouse aim).
If you take into consideration this general guideline of information, then there is virtually few games (aside from typing games) that cannot be configured for a controller. You can play PC titles thought impossible for controllers such as Baldur's Gate, Deus Ex: GOTY, XCOM: UFO Defense and Diablo 2 with a controller comfortably.

Even if you don't play old-school on PC, the freedom to make any control scheme to your liking is something that adds up in the smallest of ways. (Don't like to sprint with analog sticks or a trigger, then configure it with the grip buttons.) This is because the Steam Controller can have up to 50+ configurable buttons in your hands.
Each trackpad can have four buttons (or a touch menu of 12 buttons each, so that is twenty four); then you have the six buttons on the back, triggers, shoulder buttons and grips; the four directions of the analog stick can be buttons; the four XYBA buttons; and there is the Start & Select buttons. Simply put, you have more than enough buttons to make any game viable if you know what are the essentials.
In most cases you will not utilize every button as you will either use the trackpads or analog stick for movement or for moving the camera, but you can also have multi-layered buttons in combination to free up space. You can also download templates given in general for games or community-made control schemes made by Steam users or, in the rare cases, by the developers themselves.
However, it's best to adjust the control schemes to your liking because you might find a better method in your own way. If you have played the game already, it is easier to configure a controller method for it than playing something new (20 - 30 mins for fine-tuning the first few times.) But I have a few suggestions of the most important aspects for fine-tuning:
That last section is important as it will keep your camera from constantly being nudged. Once you have found your preferred situation, you can then make a template of that for yourself and copy it over to other similar games--and then fine tune it to the next game.
That last comment highlights what may be the greatest benefit or sin about the controller is that each game set-up becomes a process; it never ends after one game as there is no common standard appropriate for all.
As someone with some patience, I don't mind adding an extra half-hour--worst case scenario--to get the game working but I can understand if others find that too demanding. In most cases, if I know what I'm doing, it will take five minutes for me to map a control scheme with all the buttons I need and my friends can hardly spot the difference.
If you can get this controller at a discount, like I did for $35, or buy it in conjunction with a game you know you want to experience with a controller (DOOM, XCOM 2, etc.) at the same price,  then I think it's absolutely worth the fuss. Like a cat, if you put up with its antics long enough you may eventually find it being cozy with you on the couch.
As someone who always was skeptical of this controller, I am impressed how much I have grown attached to it. It's probably for the fact that once you've tasted the freedom it can offer you will find it difficult to go back to limited control schemes.

This controller might not be what you're expecting. It's definitely amazing for games that require a mouse and keyboard to play. The button placements are great and the back "Left" and "Right" mouse buttons make a lot of sense. The feel in your hand is fine.
However, for games that are built for controllers this is not a controller you want to use. I tried it in the new Tomb Raider and it seemed to work fine, but when I went to Portal, simply holding your right thumb on the right pad without moving it caused the screen to wobble. Tomb raider if you didn't move your thumb the screen did not move. With portal it was all shaky cam like. As if the input couldn't tell you weren't moving. It made the game unplayable.
I don't know why there is a discrepency in how certain games handle holding your thumb steady. Maybe there is a setting to fix this? I certainly couldn't figure it out.
Next I tried magicka. Again, this game is setup for a regular controller and the steam controller did not work with it properly. Girlfriend had a regular xbox controller and you could push the right stick in any direction and hold it, then swipe left/right up/down to select the correct spell (there are 8 spells bound to the controller stick). With the steam controller if you push the pad in any direction it stops inputting that you're holding the "pad" in a direction after 0.25 seconds or so. So with the regular xbox controller you could push and then swipe making spell selection very easy, but with the steam controller you had to do a push and swipe at the same time otherwise the spell selector disappears from the screen. It made selecting a spell very difficult. Often you would select a spell from the direction you swipe to and not the initial direction you pushed in. So sliding my thumb up and then swiping right would select a spell as if I slid my thumb right then swiped up. Super confusing.
One thing I found surprising and very cool was the right pad has sound, and it's a very interesting sound. It's like a geiger meter sound. So if you swipe your finger fast you get these quick little ticks vs slow ticks when you are basically massaging the pad slowly.
The mapping options for this are insane. I can't see any room for improvement with what the mapping can do. It has everything. Maybe the only thing to improve is better explanations of what all the settings do.
I should note, that the initial setup was dicey. When I was playing tomb raider, I could play in game no problem, but as soon as I went to the menu I couldn't exit it as none of the buttons seemed to work. I had to stop steam and restart it before it worked correctly. I did notice you can map the buttons to different things while a menu is open vs in game, so maybe something was wonky there before I restarted it.
All in all, I recommend this, but I think you still want a regular controller in your life as this will cause some frustation. It really is a mouse/keyboard replacement and not a regular controller replacement.

It's an okay game, but a WONDERFUL guide to gun mechanics. The whole reason this game is worth it is there is nothing out there as interactive when it comes to the inner workings of a firearm. Sure, there are detailed blowouts and schematics you can cruise around the
for, as well as a few animation clips of them in motion. To actually be able to interact, slow down and watch how all the parts work together to show you how pulling a piece a metal leads to the firing of a bullet is just MARVELOUS. I love telling all my gun buddies about this game/guide, and they all react the same way: Mouth agape. The game modes are fun; good way to test the old brain memory function like playing sodoku with gun parts. You can unlock all the guns for $50 (or $35 when it's on sale) and it's totally worth that price for all the information and knowledge imparted onto thee about firearms. Or you can be cheap like me, and grind your way  to every gun in about 100 hours. That sounds like a lot, but honestly, it didn't even feel like 20 with all the fun I had learning with it. So, as a game, it's probably a 'meh...' to those who aren't interested in firearms; to those who are, it's a 'Oh, YEH!' on my scale.

- collecting resources is exhausting
- the characters in the ships are just meaningless text descriptions with abilities that you are not motivated to even read at selection. I mean they don't even look that different. I couldn't even say who is who if not for their level.
- But the worst part of it all are the battles. You need to afflict weaknesses and then exploit them. The thing is: if you have your characters and a good set of abilities you will do the same every battle. The game even encourages this, because you have a set of high level characters. You always just click the same stuff over and over again until there is the next small piece of story that you can enjoy.
