For me this game could have been great seeing as it's in space, and is turned based stratergy but soewhere between initial concept and develpment they made some interesting choices. I found the number of races a little disapointing having come out of Civ 5. Admitidally in Civ 5 there is much less to differentiate between each empire except colour and indiidual units but some races seemed a little lazy for example The Terran Empire and A Machine Race share the same ship designs which was annoying for me. I also found the interface anoying and unhelpful. An example of this was when I had amassed several very large fleets of top end ships and decided to declare war. The interface told me my strength was 2nd. Nothing else and no indication of who was the strongest and weakest. Regardless I plowed on and declared war. After some rather poor Rock Paper Scissor combat in some systems (more on that later) I started my invasion, only to find that in my next turn I was being opposed by (in one system) 17 fleets.  This is just an example of how the game refuses to give you important and in depth information like a game such as Civ 5 does. Where you are able to find out your milatary strength against others and are advised on whether you at least stand a chance of winning in a war against an opposing empire. Another problem I have with the interface and general magement is the management of your systems. Again if we use Civ 5 as a comparison, in Civ 5 you are prompted on production in your cities and are once again advised on what to build depending on the direction you are going. Endless Space however desides to do none of this and will gladly let you waste valuable turns not doing anyting in systems making management a chore as I ended up constantly checking my economy screen to see if anthing was bone idle. The game was also rather unhelpful when it came to deciding what to build. Yes a game that holds your hand each step of the way in games like this isn't fun but at least an indication or a sugestion that if your citizen satisfaction is 0% try building these would be nice instead of forcing me to wonder for hours why everyone is striking. Now to the combat, Endless Space bosts a big cinematic battle where from artsy camera shots you can watch your fleets go toe to toe with enemies in epic space battles. Sadly this is not the case, yes you do get to watch as fleets fight each other but your only involvement is through picking 'cards' to use in a rock paper scissors type match. This completely mechanic ruins the combat for me and ruins the game as I watch helplessely while my vastly superior fleet gets destroyed becus their card trumped mine. The other annoying part of the combat is that I was unable to choose which enemy fleet to attack( even when there are 17 of them) which caused more frustration as I find I can't attack the same fleet twice (if I have several fleets and they have several fleets in the same system). This frustration and the combats complete shallowness adds up to make rather boring battles overall. Especially when you compare it to something like Civ 5 which lets you choose who you want to attack AND if your unit is superior to your enemies one you win. Revolutionary! Overall then this game looks good on the surface but on the inside (for me at least) the core is thoroughly rotten. Give this one a miss a miss and if you want a turn based trategy game get Civ 5 its much much better

MWO a.k.a. Stompy Robots is of course nothing like the videos shown here.  They have actual game play in them, but like most games really do not reflect actual game play.  If you want to see that, hit up Youtube and look for MWO matches.
As for the game itself, I've played Stompy Robots here and there from beta release on and steadily over the last year and a half.  I have really enjoyed Battletech, Mech Commander and the Mechwarrior lines over the last 20ish years and consider myself a lore purest.  The big draw for Stompy Robots was the release of Clan mechs and the promise of the Community Warfare (CW).  Unfortunately, regular matches and CW have not had the mechanics changed to account for the technology disparity.  Instead PGI has decided to move away from Lore and is attempting to balance out the two technologies against one another using negative and positive Mech Quirks and changes to the Clan and IS weapons.
From my perspective, the overall balance has not brought balance to anything.  At one time the Clan Mech greatly ruled the battlefield, like it should, but now it has shifted to the IS side.  Attempting to balance Stompy Robots can only be achieved by actually leveling the two technologies and making them the same.
What PGI should have done was used match mechanics to help with balance, but have not.  CW had much promise, but again with their narrow focus on balancing the two technologies and insisting on 48vs48 matches, CW will fail.  At one point there were indications that Resource Management was to play a big part in CW, but that seems to be gone now.  Again, that would have helped bring balance to the game.
Overall, if you are looking for a shooter game that has it's basis in Mechwarrior, this is it.  If you are looking for a true Battletech-Mechwarrior game, this is not.

Pros:
-Looks pretty good for an mmo that's a couple years old.
-Overall gameplay is fun and doesn't get boring.
-Not pay to win. Mechs that can only be purchased for real cash like hero mechs are just unique variants, they don't provide an actual advantage (they do still provide a bonus in how much cash you earn). Similarily, champion mechs are just the most popular variant of a non hero mech with a better stock loadout and an xp bonus. There are plenty of trial mechs to use for free that are switched every once in a while, and you earn a very large casy bonus in your first 25 games. Grinding also doesn't get boring because, well, your job consists of blasting apart other mechs.
-Though development was previously hellish (and there are many, many stories that attest to this), that is no longer the case. They have been doing a much better job since they split from the publisher.
-You can customize mechs in many, many ways. You can add or remove armor, equipment and weapons of your choice. Inner sphere mechs can also swap engines, and clan mechs can swap arms and side torsos.
Cons:
-Gameplay can sometimes be rough. The learning curve is a big one here, and even though I previously played mechwarrior 3 quite a bit I still mostly suck :). Mechs are piloted like walking tanks in mechwarrior (seperately moving arms, torsos and legs), so if you played WOT you may have an advantage.
-Some balance issues, especially between clan and inner sphere mechs, but the devs are always working to improve on this.
Though this game isn't perfect, it is still very fun overall. As a previous player of Mechwarrior 3, I was inially somewhat skeptical about how fun mechwarrior could be without a campaign, but I think it's pretty fine as it is.

Try as I might, I have not been able to get to grips with the Steam Controller... and it is all due to the right-hand trackpad.
I was using it for "Gods Of War III" on the new PS Now service. I was offered a quick-time event where on a normal DualShock 4 controller (or an Xbox One controller, as the PS Now service supports that also), I would press BOTH analogue thumbsticks down. Of course, when you are using both thumbsticks, this isn't a bad move to do. But with the Steam Controller, this involves clicking the left (AND ONLY) analogue thumbstick, and clicking the right pad. While the QTE is supported by the Steam Controller, it is a cumbersome move to perform on the Steam Controller.
Maybe my issues in this regard are because the placement of each "section" on both sides of the Steam Controller are swapped vertically, as compared to the Xbox One controller. This means on the left side, the analogue thumbstick is BELOW the D-pad (on Xbox One, it is ABOVE the D-pad). Similarly, on the right side, the "A B X Y" buttons are BELOW the trackpad (on Xbox One, the buttons are ABOVE the right analogue thumbstick).
Another issue I have is that the right trackpad seems to "stick" when moving. I know about the dead zones, and I have tried configuring these based on many websites that I have found on the subject. Nothing seems to stop it from sticking. It also sticks when I am using it in "Desktop Mode". Trying to navigate around the Steam interface in Desktop Mode is a real pain when it sticks, because the links are small. I know I can use Steam Big Picture Mode, but I have issues with that also (discussed momentarily).
Another issue is with the Steam Big Picture mode (where the Steam Controller is used). Best controller I have ever had. Can be used to play any game well. I have played minecraft with a touch pad and keyboard, smash with a keyboard, wiimote, xbox controller, ps4 controller, n64 controller, and gamecube controller. I would pick the Steam controller every time based on three qualities:
-Best analog stick I have ever used. Precise, no drift, no phantom input.
-$50 for a controller that holds up in everyway, you can get a custom controller for a lot more, but the virtual customization of this controller makes it a better buy.
-The buttons and touch pads. The four basics (X, Y, A, and B) are nice, though they are more comfortably accessed on an xbox controller. The grip buttons are fantastic, the triggers are nice. The touch pads allow for emulation of any input you'd like. They do work, my example is Dark Souls 1 and 3, I used a joystick-mouse on the right touch pad for the camera. It works better than any joystick I have ever used, sliding your thumb across or around a pad is easier than a joystick.
The only thing to remember with this controller that it is innovation. It feels better to hold for a longer period of time than any controller I have used  in the past. But, it does take some practice to learn the input well. Once you have, it works for any games from Dark Souls, to Rivals of Aether, to any console game like Banjo Kazooie on an emulator. It works well for $50.
I still haven't bothered to buy rechargeable tripple A's yet, playing Rivals of Aether as much as I do, I'd expect the batteries to give out faster. Two AAA's lasted about 2-4 months.

so ive been using this thing for a few days now and i'm still not quite sure if i'd recomend it to anyone, which is sad because i love almost everyting about it. i know that sounds confusing but bear with me for a moment.

first, for use navagating my computer both in and out of steam, i f'ing love it. the right pad was automatically picked up by my compy as a mouse with the triggers as r/l click and the left pad as a scroll wheel. it's awesome. as someone who uses my tv as a monitor i've found it completely replacing my wireless mouse. it feels better, and i dont have to find a flat surface to lay it on whenever i put it down. all controllers should behave like this.
second, for actually playing games.... i have mixed feelings. the addition of the grip buttons is good, like very good. the activators and motion controls are pretty sweet though i havent really had a need for them i can see them being quite handy. i like the stick and the buttons feel nice and responsive. its a little strange that the handles curve the opposite direction of literally every controller ever made, but i got used to it surprisingly fast. the left pad is great for everything but precision fighting games, but that's true of every controller made after the PS2.
then there's the right pad... it doesnt feel right at all. i spent 45 minutes in skyrim trying to get it to behave like a look stick before i gave up and decided to try a different game. same problem in everything ive used it in. either it barely moves at all, or it goes flying around like crazy. the diagonals have a different sensitivity than the pure directions, and every option i've tweaked (all of them) still leave me feeling like my camera is completely drunk. i'm not sure if you've ever tried to play an FPS with a laptop touchpad, but thats about how well it worked. to make matters worse, every time you change the behavior template all the configuration options change. and the options i need to change to make any given template work, are only available on the other templates. now i know that's a software issue and it could be fixed in the future, but that doesnt help me now. i cant figure out why adaptive centering, deadzone shape, and edge spin aren't changeable in every behavior.
either way i shouldnt need 6 hours and a degree in controller dynamics to make this thing spin a camera like it isnt an alcoholic with parkinsons. long story short, if it had 2 sticks and one pad it'd be the best gaming peripheral ive ever held. but it doesnt, and being that close to perfect makes me hate it so much more for missing the mark.
even after all the trouble it gave me i still held out hope that maybe mine was just defective, and others would work better. so i brought it back to the store and exchanged it for a fresh one. no difference whatsoever.
but despite it's inability to operate a camera it does everything else perfectly and even works well in games that arent built for controllers, so long as they arent first person. so i'm gonna say grab one, just not from steam. buy it in a store, so if you dont like it you can return it.

Halloween Forever isn't going to blow your mind.
But does it have to? Is there a rule out there that says all games must contain XYZ amount of... I dunno, new ideas?
Actually, that feels unfair to Halloween Forever, because as far as games go, this character, this type of shooter, in this setting, IS actually pretty unique. It may lack the depth and verve of a retro-esque game like Shovel Knight, but it still manages to be enjoyable. Halloween Forever is a short, simple, and charming little game about Halloween with 8-bit graphics and chiptune music.
On the surface, it may be easy to write this off as another "cheap" pixel art game, but there are signs that the developers gave it their love and attention. Simple as it may be, this is a tough little game to finish, particularly because it doesn't save your progress -- a move that seems to be done intentionally. It'll save which secret characters you've unlocked, but as far as actually playing this game goes, it gives you no quarter. 1ups are scarce, death comes quickly, and there are no continues. Game Over means starting back at level 1.
Shockingly, the game doesn't feel cheap for doing this. Halloween Forever isn't a game that feels mean, or like it's punishing you for being less than perfect. It just asks that you value every move you take, and play smart. There's no masochism here, just focus.
Secrets are well hidden without being too obscure OR too obvious, and a lot of achievements involve doing things you might not normally think to do (including a couple of weirdly challenging ones). All around, it's pretty solid and just varied enough to hold your attention.
For five bucks? Less, if it's on sale? You won't see many articles celebrating this as a masterclass in anything, but I say go for it. It's a good little game and I am satisfied with it.

I owned the Augmented Edition of Deus Ex: Human Revolution on the Xbox 360 when it first came out. Long story short, it was such a good game that I had to buy the Director's Cut on PC. The storyline is engrossing, and intricately carved with subtle references to Deus Ex and Invisible War, with gameplay that lets you choose how you want to go about things, and a semi-linear level design. This game isn't perfection, but it's as close as gaming's been to it since the first Deus Ex.
The movement feels pretty great with a keyboard and mouse, and the cover system just works. Firefights feel sleek, giving off that cyberpunk feel, but heavy at the same time, making it feel more intense. The game prides itself having more choices than just dialogue, as players can be stealthy but lethal, stealthy and non-lethal, loud and lethal, et cetera. Hacking and inventory management are like fun little minigames, and augmentations bring new gameplay experiences to the table, and makes it easier for players to adapt to challenges that they face throughout the game.
Not much to say here. The game looks pretty good, graphics aren't outdated, but they aren't perfection. Cutscenes are great though, and the takedown animations are satisfying and fresh. There are some minor problems here and there, but they can be easily overlooked.
From Sarif Industries to Panchea, I was on the edge of my seat the whole way. (Not literally, that would have made playing the game rather hard.) Adam Jensen felt like a relatable character, even though he differed from the "silent protagonist". There wasn't a point in the game where I said "I wouldn't pick any of these dialogue choices", and the conversations have something to offer everyone. The characters are fit to the storyline, and you begin to see their darker secrets as the storyline and
unravel.
Deus Ex: Human Revolution is the reminder of what game developers can do when they're unafraid. Ambitious and sleek, this is the perfect RPG. While the protagonist's character development is a bit lax, gunplay and other gameplay mechanics compliment the intriguing storyline which ultimately leaves you wanting a sequel. It's not the next-gen, but we can see it from here. This is the best RPG I have ever played, I would give it a doubtless 10/10.

Deus Ex, the original game from 2000, is often regarded today as one of the biggest landmarks within Cyberpunk RPGs and  I am still today convinced that the game is one of the biggest staples of PC gaming. However, Eidos Montreal managed to go above and beyond all expectations. While I will say that the scale of Deus Ex: Human Reovlution is not on par with the orginal Deus Ex in terms of story, it holds up very well in terms of immersive gameplay and atmosphere that pays heavy tributes to the franchise and is a incredible reboot of the series.
However, like many, the boss fights from the orginal release were completely unexpected and porrly implemented segments that felt out of place in this game. However, the Director's Cut does alot more than just fix the boss fights (although there are still the issues of that you need to fight them regardless). But it givres Hd textures, a massive overall of the graphical options and manages to implement the DLC the Missing Link (which is fantastic all on its own) into the main storyline along with the expansion packs. With this game, I can safely say was one of the best games to come out of th 7th console generation and Deus Ex: ManKind Divided will hopefully be able to live up to what this game provided for us.

Before we even get started, some people might say "Oh, this looks like a Minecraft copy." but that is incorrect, as it was around way before Minecraft was even thought up of. It's not like Roblox either (Ah the famous Blockland vs Roblox wars...) because of the more solid platform and no subscription. So what is this then? Good question. I think Badspot, the creator of the game, can sum it up quite nicely:
"Blockland is an online multiplayer game where you build things with bricks.
It's like playing with legos on the internet."
In my mind, Blockland is one of the best construction/building sandbox games ever made. It is one of my personal favorites that I've played since 2007. I probably have over 600 hours ingame. (Not including Steam) You can do just about anything in this game, from FPS Team Deathmatches to racing to <variable>. Blockland is quite fun by itself, but the real reason you get it is for the high modability. Thousands of community creations keep the game interesting, and populated. Vehicles, weapons, gamemodes, scripts, events, this game has it all for customization. While singleplayer lets you experiment and test, multiplayer is where most people will choose to spend their time. There is always a server up for a specific type of play. (And they usually have good admins)
There is one part where Blockland has an issue...
The community is not amazing. (Most of the modders are amazing though) If you go on the official forums you will most likely see tons of hate/spam/garbage/negativity. The moderators do a good job of clearing out the useless and hurtful stuff, but I feel as if its always been like this. If you are like me, you really don't let it get to you; but I can see how it might be unacceptable to others.
Other than this (really) small issue, I completely and fully recommend Blockland to anybody that is even slightly interested in sandbox games or being creative.
10/10
November 2017 Update
Blockland is still in my mind one of the best games I have ever played. However, time is showing. There hasn't been an update for 2 years. With the death of RTB (Return to Blockland, a great mod that really gave the game life) I don't see this continuing. However, substitutes such as Blockland Glass/whatever they call it these days may keep it alive longer. The server population is growing more sparse too.
If you're interested in a fun building game, definitely pick this up. Even with no community left, you can still browse the forums for timeless add-ons and massive save files from skilled builders. And of course, there's a small, but dedicated playerbase still lingering.

Don't let the past MWO, it's earlier problems,upset users and IGP dissuade you, PGI has turned this into a very fine game & one of the last holdouts for lifelong Battletech/Mechwarrior fanatics while making it accessible to all.  It's current state has a good variety of machines, a good, mature community, and large scale persistent factional warfare.  There are genre and some playstyle/mechanic/cash store similarities to games like World of Tanks, and the purchasable machines do not (despite claims otherwise) possess godlike pay2win powers.  It's a slow, deliberate game, meta game, and progression.  If you miss Mechwarrior 1-4, Battletech: Solaris, Mechassault, or the legendary Battletech tabletop miniatures wargame & it's accompanying pen & paper rpg Mechwarrior, this is for you.

If you've played and enjoyed Mechwarrior titles in the past, definitely try this out.
Don't let the negative reviews out there stop you. There are a lot of them out there, but if you look closely you'll find many were written a few years ago (when the concerns, now fixed, may have actually been valid) or are written by those obviously so attached to the idea of what the game "could be" if it were designed by themselves. Think of them like the crazy neighbours crying about government conspiracy because the garbage pickup wasn't on time, and "something should be done because by God, I've lived on this block for 20 years!"
I'm writing this a few weeks after picking up the game and can say PGI has done a great job. The devs have captured the original feeling of Mechwarrior that made me fall in love with the series decades ago.
PGI has also been unfairly accused of being greedy. But remember, this is a free game. Any money you choose to spend on this game is a choice. And having played against some wallet warriors, I can say the mechs/upgrades that can be bought with cash do not generally provide players with an unfair advantage.They generally only speed things up, marginally. And really, please don't shame private companies for trying to make a buck, especially when you don't have to pay anything at all -- these guys gotta eat!
Please be ready for a complex game: this ain't no Call of Duty. Mechs are slow, they're big targets, have long cool downs between shots (for some weapons), and generally depend on having support mechs around to survive. You'll have to do things like watch out for overheating, tagging targets for team mates, taking cover from sniper fire, turning your mech so damage is evenly distributed around your armour, etc, etc.
For me, the complexity is what makes the game exciting -- things such as the dread of having my mech shut down in a fight because I forgot to override the engine overheat safety shut off (yes, you can do that), or remembering to turn on infrared vision in a foggy map to see the heat signatures of enemy mechs through the mist.
Because of the complexity, skill at playing this game will come more with time rather than with reflex. You will rightfully feel like other players are better at first, simply because they've learned to use the control buttons not taught in the tutorial. Press F1 for the button layout.
Other than that, enjoy and hopefully I'll see you in game!

The precision is insane. I'm so happy to finally not have a deadzone... They're gone, the deadzones are really, finally gone. They're just gone!

I'll write this review to give some feedback for the future version of the Steam Controller.
The controller is really capable. It does what it promises and very well. The options provided by the customization software in tandem with the grip buttons, the dual action triggers and the touchpads are limitless, and some games shine of new light with this controller.
There's some complaints to do though:
Touchpads: they're precise and snappy, and the aptic feedback is so, so welcome. But I really would have liked some reference point on the right one. Like a center mark or some cutouts. In some games when I want to have my thumb exactly in the center for my resting position this becomes somewhat of a problem.
Batteries: bigger and rechargeable batteries would be really welcome.
Last complaint: no more glossy plastics!
Correct these few points and I'll definitely buy a second version of this Controller. For now I'm fully satisfied with this one.

Endless Space is a turn based strategy game with a few good ideas but poor execution.
The number one gripe i have with endless space is the randomness of the combat.Combat involves picking cards to play during the  phases of combat,before the battle begins.You never know if the cards you picked will be countered or not by the Computer opponent. this means that even with a stronger fleet you can still lose a battle due to bad card choices.
Also laying seige to a planet takes far to long.Even with multiple seige vessels it can take upwards of 20 turns to conquer a single System!!!!
There is also little variation in the weaponry used by all factions.Though the ships from each faction look different,you will find yourself facing the same exact weaponry that your faction has researched.This causes stress beyong measure as you must constantly design new ships to counter the enemy factions vessel's,only to deploy those ships and find them countered by a new design from the enemy,forcing you back to the drawing board.
Overall there are simply to many great games similar to Endless Space that are less random,more in depth and simply more fun to play. Namely:Sins of a solar empire and Space empires gold edition.

World of Tanks Blitz is quite the same as its big brother but more nervous and fast paced due to smaller arenas and smaller teams.
Drive a tank and work (or rather try to) with your teammates to defeat the enemy team by anihilating it or capturing zones.
Individual skill has a meaningful impact as every teammate or enemy killed weighs quite a lot in the balance, and the lack of SPG in the game removes the biggest threat there was to the Heavy Tanks, making the assaults more brutal and relentless than ever.
Contrary to WoT PC, the feel you get at low tier is quite similar to the feel you get at higher tiers since you no longer have to cover a lot of ground to see the action and the lack of "capture the enemy base goal" means that your team no longer camps (at least not too much).

As a fan of the old
, it had been a long wait since the early 2000's for a worthy addition to the franchise. Set 25 years before the original,
is a very convincing take on the FPS/infiltration/adventure genre with yet another compelling story whose ramifications deepen as you progress through the game. The numerous characters are supported by a very solid voice acting cast, and the quality of the writing helps create a strong feeling of immersion.
The game gives you a degree of freedom in how you handle situations, but in spite of providing you with a vast array of weapons, it greatly rewards stealth and non-lethal takedowns. You are also given multiple choices in how you approach interactions with other characters, and can sometimes persuade them to help you a little more than they were prepared to. As the plot thickens, so does the level design: between the first mission and the later stages of the game, the areas you have to work your way through become more and more complex, and stealth becomes more and more of a challenge.
Luckily, progress through the game allows you to upgrade your character's abilities with a simple-yet-rewarding XP system. Will you invest points into your hacking abilities? Enhance your social skills with a body language analyzer? Upgrade your dermal armor in anticipation of unavoidable combat situations? The choice is yours! This system succeeds in giving you more options without ever turning you into an overpowered killing machine. On the highest difficulty setting, combat will always be hazardous as you can die very quickly: all the more reason to go for a stealth-based approach.
The
version is supposed to offer revamped boss fights (the original ones were an abomination). A commendable effort that is supposed to give you more options, but shooting them in the face remains the most viable one. A more convincing selling point is the integration of the game's only DLC campaign (
) into the adventure. Good DLC,
- intriguing story elements, good characters and some well-designed new areas to infiltrate will provide for a very welcome extra few hours of gameplay.

Two of my old time favourite shooters were Unreal Tournament 2004 and Halo.
That was, until I played DOOM.
This game brings the intergalactic story, weird alien tech and mysterious relics from Halo.
And mixes it with the fast-paced, multi weapon gameplay of Unreal Tournament.
-You can find a great range of weapons almost all upgradeable with different mods to suit your playstyle.
-The game forces you to be agressive to get your health by having more health dropped when executing enemies up-close.
-Creative environments, with the exception of hell, all looking fairly different from each other.
-New enemies being introduced on the regular by first showing one of them and then bombarding you with three more the next room.
_________
Negative things include:
-multiplayer, don't buy for multiplayer. It feels slow, has a two weapon limit and couldn't be futher from the classic arena shooter gameplay if you tried.
-Snapmap is ok, but has some odd limitations. Meaning some nice maps with creative mechanics, but a lot more straightforward maps that bore quickly.
-difficulty options needs more choice.
In each difficulty, the enemies do 2x more damage than the previous difficulty, meaning that you can find one option too forgiving while the next one too brutal.
-Two perticular enemies that break to flow completely.
Shield guys, with a shield to strong to attack long-distance and a shotgun and turning speed to quick to attack him up-close.
(Becomes a whole lot better when you get some strong, easy to aim explosives)
Lost souls, they aren't a problem on their own, but the enemy spawning mechanics makes them homing missiles that spawn out of nowhere.

I first played this game on an ipod touch, and much has changed since it came out. But the basics are the same.
You combine various elements to create new elements. In the beginning you have fire, earth, air and water at your disposal. And then it's up to you to create just about every element there is in the game. And there are many. And almost every time you discover a new element, you will also read a quote that's related to the element at hand.
The main game spans over four episodes. The Beginning, Technology, Modern Age, and The World of Magic.
As you combine elements and creatures, tools and buildings, the once barren landscape beneath you comes to life. Snow and grass begin to cover the landscape, and animals and mythological creatures roam the world. This game looks good, and much attention has been put into the art that's basicly everywhere.
Without saying too much more, I'd like to point out that there are also six quests, which work as individual mini-episodes, with a focus on a specific area. Save a princess from a dragon, counter the sins of doodle devil or 20'th century inventions.
There are also Puzzles, which are even smaller, and possible to fail. (and start over)
There will probably be more content for this game, and since they've released it for free for so many, why is it wrong to allow them to actually sell their game to the people who are willing to pay?
But yeah, you can probably find this game for free if you look for it.

I really love this game. The visual and sound design is just oozing polish and the character designs are very charming. The gameplay is straightforward, a simple jump and shooter, but that simplicity is perhaps the game's greaest strength, and the variety of enemy and level designs make for an enjoyable experience. This developer clearly knows what they are doing when it comes to game design. Some may complain about the game overs, but I like how the game forced me to actually improve my play. You can't possibly make it to the end playing recklessly. In this way, the game truly captures the NES spirit (Get it? Spirit? Halloween? I'll see myself out.). The game would be way too easy and over too soon without game overs. Even then, the game is somewhat short; I managed to complete the game with all 6 runes and unlock all 4 playable characters in about 100 minutes. But, at this price range and with how much I enjoyed my time with it, I'd recommend Halloween Forever to anyone looking to scratch that NES itch.

If you are wondering about the challenge level: I beat the final boss with only 1 hp left and no extra lives remaining, so I'd call it finely tuned.
The unlockable characters are quirky, which keeps replays fresh (they and are also OP in some levels, so try a new character if you are having trouble).
The graphics are both scary and cute at the same time; it's a real Halloween treat.
CONS(?): the music will be stuck in your head for days
